Mind is the forerunner of all things, mind is their chief, and they are mind-made. If one speaks or acts with an impure mind, suffering follows him even as the wheel follows the hoof of the ox.

## 1. Yamakavagga
## 1. The Story of Elder Cakkhupāla

The Blessed One taught this Dhamma discourse while residing in Sāvatthī, concerning the Elder Cakkhupāla.

## Praying for Children

In the city of Sāvatthī, there was a wealthy householder named Mahāsuvaṇṇa. He possessed great wealth and vast resources, but he had no children. One day, after going to the bathing ghat and bathing, while returning, he saw a great forest tree (vanappati) with lush leaves and branches. Thinking, "This tree must be inhabited by a powerful deity," he had the area beneath the tree cleared, a wall built around it, sand scattered, and banners and flags raised. Having thus adorned the forest tree and performed a circumambulation, he made a prayer: "If I should obtain a son or a daughter, I will perform a great offering to you, O deity." Then he departed.

## Birth of a Son

Not long after he had departed, a child was conceived in his wife's womb. Knowing she was pregnant, she informed the householder. The householder provided her with prenatal care. After ten months, she gave birth to a son.
3:
## Mahāpāla and Cūḷapāla

On the naming day, because the son was obtained by relying on the forest tree he had protected, the householder named the boy "Pāla". Later, when the wife gave birth to a second son, they named the second son "Cūḷapāla" and renamed the first son "Mahāpāla".

## Establishing a Household

When the two brothers reached the proper age, they were bound by the bonds of household life. Later, when their parents passed away, the two brothers alone managed and governed all the family wealth and property.

## The Buddha and the Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika

At that time, the Blessed One, having set in motion the Noble Wheel of Dhamma, arrived in due course and resided at the great Jetavana Monastery, which the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika had built by spending fifty-four crores of wealth. There, the Buddha established the multitudes on the path to heaven and the path to liberation (Nibbāna).

The Tathāgata spent only one rainy season (vassa) at the Nigrodhārāma Monastery, built by his relatives—eighty thousand from his mother's side and eighty thousand from his father's side, totaling one hundred and sixty thousand families. He spent nineteen rainy seasons at the great Jetavana Monastery built by Anāthapiṇḍika, and six rainy seasons at the Pubbārāma Monastery built by the female lay devotee Visākhā, who spent twenty-seven crores of wealth. Thus, out of consideration for the great virtues of these two families, he spent twenty-five rainy seasons depending on the city of Sāvatthī. Both the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika and the great female lay devotee Visākhā went to attend upon the Tathāgata twice every day. When going, they never went empty-handed, thinking, "The young novices will look at our hands." When going before the meal, they took various kinds of food. When going in the evening, they took the five kinds of medicine and the eight kinds of drinks. In the houses of Anāthapiṇḍika and Visākhā, seats were always prepared for two thousand monks. Among the food, drinks, and medicines, whatever a monk desired, he was provided with it to his heart's content. Among them, Anāthapiṇḍika had never once asked the Blessed One a question. Why did he not ask? He thought, "The Blessed One is a Buddha and is delicate; he is a King and is delicate. If he thinks, 'This householder is of great service to me,' and preaches the Dhamma to me, he might become weary." Thus, out of excessive love and devotion for the Blessed One, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika did not ask any questions. However, as soon as the merchant arrived and sat in his presence, the Blessed One thought, "This merchant protects me where I need no protection. For four incalculables (asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons (kappa), I fulfilled the perfections—cutting off my own adorned head, gouging out my eyes, extracting my heart's flesh, and giving away my children and wife who were as dear as life—all for the sake of preaching the Dhamma to others. This merchant protects me where I need no protection." And so, the Buddha would preach a discourse to him.
4:
At that time, seven crores of people lived in the city of Sāvatthī. Among them, five crores of people, having heard the Dhamma from the Teacher, became Noble Disciples (ariya-sāvakas), such as Stream-enterers, while two crores of people remained worldlings (puthujjanas). Among those people, the Noble Disciples had only two duties: in the morning, they would give alms; in the evening, holding perfumes, flowers, and the like, and taking robe-cloth, medicine, drinks, and so on, they would go to listen to the Dhamma.

## Mahāpāla’s Ordination

Then one day, Mahāpāla saw the Noble Disciples going to the monastery with flowers and perfumes in their hands. He asked, "Where is this great crowd of people going?" Upon hearing that they were going to listen to the Dhamma, he thought, "I shall go too." He went, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat at the edge of the assembly.

When Buddhas teach the Dhamma, they look for the spiritual potential (upanissaya) for such things as taking refuge, observing the precepts, or ordaining, and they teach according to the disposition of the listener. Therefore, on that day, the Teacher, seeing Mahāpāla’s potential, gave a graduated discourse (anupubbikathā). That is to say, he explained the discourse on generosity (dāna), the discourse on virtue (sīla), the discourse on heaven (sagga), the danger, vanity, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefits of renunciation (nekkhamma).

Having heard that discourse, the householder Mahāpāla thought: "When one goes to the next world, neither sons and daughters, nor brothers, nor wealth follow him; even one's own body does not go along with oneself. What is the use of living the household life? I shall ordain." At the conclusion of the teaching, he approached the Teacher and requested ordination. Then the Teacher asked him, "Do you have any relatives who should be consulted?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, I have a younger brother." "Then go and ask his permission," the Teacher said.

Mahāpāla accepted, saying, "Very well, Venerable Sir." He paid homage to the Teacher, went home, called his younger brother, and said, "Dear brother, whatever animate or inanimate wealth I have in this house, all of it is now your responsibility. Please take possession of it."

"But what will you do, brother?" he asked. "I shall ordain in the presence of the Teacher," Mahāpāla replied. "What are you saying, brother? You are like a mother to me since our mother died, and like a father since our father died. There is great wealth in this house; it is possible to do meritorious deeds while living at home. Do not do this."

"Dear brother, having heard the Teacher's Dhamma, I am unable to live in the household life. The Teacher has taught the Dhamma, which is beautiful in the beginning, middle, and end, based on the three marks of existence (tilakkhaṇa), which are extremely subtle and profound. It is not possible for one living in the midst of a house to fulfill this Dhamma."
5:
"The limbs become worn out by old age and do not obey;
For one whose strength is thus destroyed, how shall he practice the Dhamma?"

"Dear Cūḷapāla, my younger brother. For whomsoever the hands and feet are worn out and decayed due to old age, they no longer follow one's will. For such a person whose strength is gone, how can he practice the Dhamma?"

When asked, "What will you do, brother?", he replied, "I shall ordain in the presence of the Teacher." The brother said, "Brother, what are you saying? You are like a mother to me after our mother passed away, and like a father after our father passed away. You have acquired much wealth in this house. It is possible to perform meritorious deeds while staying at home. Please do not ordain in this way."

Then the householder Mahāpāla said, "Dear brother, because I have heard the Teacher's Dhamma, I am unable to live in the household life. The Teacher has taught the Dhamma, which is beautiful in the beginning, middle, and end, by establishing it upon the three extremely subtle and delicate marks of existence. It is not possible to fulfill this Dhamma while living in the household life. Dear brother, I shall ordain." Then the younger brother said, "Brother, you are still young and tender. Wait a while; you can ordain when you are old." Mahāpāla replied, "Dear brother, for an old person, even one's own hands and feet do not obey one's will. What then can be said of relatives? Therefore, I will not follow your words; I will only fulfill the practice of a monk," and he recited this verse.

Saying, "My brother Cūḷapāla, I shall certainly ordain," and while his brother Cūḷapāla was still weeping and lamenting, he went to the Teacher, requested ordination, and became a monk.

## Elder Mahāpāla Requesting Meditation Instructions

After becoming a monk, the Venerable Mahāpāla stayed with his teachers and preceptors for five years. When the rains retreat was over and he had performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, he approached the Teacher, paid homage, and asked, "Venerable Sir, how many duties (dhura) are there in this Sasana?" The Teacher replied, "Monk, there are only two duties: the duty of study (ganthadhura) and the duty of insight (vipassanādhura)."

Then the Elder Mahāpāla asked, "Venerable Sir, what is the duty of study, and what is the duty of insight?" The Teacher replied, "Learning one or two Nikāyas or the entire Tipiṭaka, the word of the Buddha, according to one's wisdom, and then bearing, reciting, and teaching it—this is called the duty of study. But for one of light livelihood, who delights in secluded dwellings, establishing the meditation on rise and fall (khaya-vaya) in one's own body, and developing insight through constant and continuous effort until attaining Arahatship—this is called the duty of insight."

Then the Elder Mahāpāla said, "Venerable Sir, since I ordained only in my old age, I shall not be able to fulfill the duty of study. I shall, however, fulfill the duty of insight. Please teach me a subject of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna)."

## Journeying to a Border Village with Sixty Monks

Then the Teacher taught him the meditation subject leading up to Arahatship. The Elder Mahāpāla, after paying homage to the Teacher, sought out companion monks and, having found sixty monks, set out with them. After traveling a distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas, they reached a large border village and entered it with his followers for alms.

When the people saw the monks who were endowed with proper conduct, their hearts were filled with faith. They prepared seats, invited them to sit, and served them with excellent food. They asked, "Venerable sirs, where are the noble ones going?" When the monks replied, "Lay disciples, we are going to a place that is suitable and conducive (sappāya)," the wise people understood that the noble ones were seeking a dwelling for the rains retreat. They said, "Venerable sirs, if the noble ones would stay here for these three months of the rains retreat, we would take refuge and observe the precepts."
6:
"We shall establish ourselves in the Refuges and undertake the precepts," they said. Those sixty monks also consented, thinking, "Depending on these lay supporters, we shall strive for liberation from the cycle of birth." The people, having received the monks' promise, cleaned the monastery and prepared suitable places for night and day, then offered them. Those sixty monks regularly entered that village for alms. Then, a physician approached the monks and invited them, saying, "Venerable sirs, in a place where many people live, illness often occurs. Should any discomfort arise, please inform me; I will provide medical treatment."

## Relinquishing the Posture of Lying Down
Elder Mahāpāla called those monks on the day of entering the Vassa and asked, "Friends, in how many postures will you spend these three months of the Vassa?" "Venerable sir, we will spend it in four postures," they replied. "Friends, is it appropriate to spend it in four postures? Should we not be diligent? We have come after taking meditation subjects from the presence of the living Buddha. Buddhas cannot be pleased through negligence; they must be pleased with noble intention. For a negligent person, the four woeful states are like their own home. Friends, be diligent." They then asked, "Venerable sir, in how many postures will you spend it?" "Friends, I will spend it in three postures; I will not stretch my back nor sleep," he said. "Venerable sir, it is well. May you be diligent," they replied.

## Suffering from Eye Disease
Then, for Elder Mahāpāla who did not sleep, after the first month had passed and the middle month arrived, an eye disease arose. Streams of tears flowed continuously from his eyes like water leaking from a broken pot. The Elder practiced the Dhamma of a recluse throughout the three watches of the night and entered his chamber at dawn to stay there. When it was time for alms-round, the monks went to the Elder and said, "Venerable sir, it is time for alms." "In that case, friends, take my bowl and robes," he said, and went out after letting them take his bowl and robes. Seeing the tears flowing from the Elder's eyes, the monks asked, "Venerable sir, why is this?" "Friends, the wind is piercing my eyes," he said. "Venerable sir, has not the physician invited us? Let us inform him." "Friends, very well," he replied.

## Rejecting the Physician's Advice
When the monks informed the physician, he prepared oil and sent it. When the Elder applied the oil to his nose, he did so while sitting and then entered the village for alms.

Pālita, my friend Pālita. Let the eyes, which are cherished and loved, break. Let the ears break, and likewise this body. Let all these parts, great and small, which depend on this body, break. For what reason, Pālita, should you be negligent?

When the physician saw Elder Mahāpāla, he asked, "Venerable sir, is it true that the wind is piercing your eyes?" "Layman, it is true," he replied. "Venerable sir, I have prepared and sent oil. Did you apply it to your nose?" "Layman, I applied it." "How is it now?" "Layman, it is as painful as ever." The physician thought, "I sent oil capable of curing with just one application. Why is the disease not cured?" Then he asked, "Venerable sir, did you apply the oil while sitting or while lying down?" The Elder remained silent. Even though he was asked repeatedly, he did not speak. The physician thought, "I will go to the monastery and see the Elder's dwelling." He said, "Venerable sir, if that is the case, please go," and after dismissing the Elder, he went to the monastery. Upon inspecting the Elder's dwelling, he saw only places for walking and sitting, but no place for sleeping. He then asked, "Venerable sir, did you apply the oil while sitting or while lying down?" The Elder remained silent. Then the physician pleaded repeatedly, "Venerable sir, do not do this. The Dhamma of a recluse can only be practiced by maintaining the body. Please apply the oil while lying down." The Elder dismissed the physician, saying, "Layman, you may go for now. I will consult and decide."

## Consulting Only with the Body
In that village, the Elder had no relatives, nor were there any siblings. With whom should he consult? Desiring to consult with his own physical body (karajakāya), he said, "Friend Pālita, you speak. Will you look after your eyes, or will you look after the Dispensation of the Buddha? In the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra) whose beginning is unknown, there is no counting the number of times you have been blind. Hundreds and thousands of Buddhas have passed. Among those Buddhas, not even one could prevent your blindness. Now, I have resolved not to sleep for these three months of the Vassa and will strive continuously throughout the three months. Therefore, Pālita, let your eyes be destroyed or let them break. Uphold only the teaching of the Buddha; do not uphold the eyes." Having consulted thus, Elder Mahāpāla, wishing to admonish his body which depends on the four great elements, recited these verses:
8:
## The Physician Gives Up

Having exhorted himself with these three verses, he administered the nasal drops while remaining seated and then entered the village for alms. Seeing the Elder Mahāpāla, the physician asked, "Venerable sir, have you administered the nasal drops?" "Yes, lay follower," he replied. "Venerable sir, how is it?" "Lay follower, it still hurts as much as before." "Venerable sir, did you administer the nasal drops while sitting or while lying down?" The Elder remained silent. Even though he was asked repeatedly, the Elder said nothing and remained silent. Then the physician said to the Elder Mahāpāla, "Venerable sir, you do not do what is suitable. From this day forward, do not say, 'Such-and-such a physician prepared the medicinal oil for me.' I, too, will not say, 'I prepared the medicinal oil for your benefit.'"

## Not Discouraged Even When Renounced by the Physician

Since he had been renounced by the physician, the Elder Mahāpāla went to the monastery and, wishing to exhort himself, said, "Monk, you have been renounced even by the physician. Do not abandon your posture." He then recited this verse:

Paṭikkhitto tikicchāya, vejjenāpi vivajjito.
Niyato maccurājassa, kiṃ pālita pamajjasi.

Pālita, my dear Palita. Tayā, by you. Tikicchāya, for medical treatment. Paṭikkhitto, you have been rejected. Vejjenāpi, even by the physician. Vivajjito, you have been abandoned. Maccurājassa, by the King of Death. Niyato, you have been marked or listed. Pālita, my dear Palita. Tvaṃ, you. Kiṃ pamajjasi, why are you negligent?

## Becoming a Sukkhavipassaka Arahant

Having exhorted himself with this verse, he practiced the ascetic Dhamma. Then, as the middle watch of the night passed, the Elder Mahāpāla's eyes and his defilements were destroyed simultaneously, neither before nor after the other. The Elder Mahāpāla became a Sukkhavipassaka Arahant and remained in his room. (From this point on, he was known as the Elder Cakkhupāla.)

## All Become Arahants

When it was time for the alms-round, the monks came and said, "Venerable sir, it is time for alms-round." When he asked, "Friends, is it time?" they replied, "Yes, venerable sir." "If so, you go," he said. When they asked, "But what about you, venerable sir?" he said, "Friends, my eyes are gone." Seeing the Elder Cakkhupāla's eyes, those monks, with eyes full of tears, said, "Venerable sir, do not worry. We will look after you." After comforting the Elder and performing the major and minor duties that should be done, they entered the village for alms. Because the people did not see the Elder Cakkhupāla, they asked, "Venerable sirs, where is our noble one?" and were told of the situation. Upon hearing this, the lay followers sent rice gruel, went themselves taking alms-food, paid homage to the Elder, and wept while rolling at his feet. They comforted him, saying, "Venerable sir, we will look after you. Do not worry," and then departed. From that day on, they constantly sent rice gruel and food to the monastery. The Elder also continuously exhorted the other sixty monks. Abiding by the Elder Cakkhupāla's instruction, as the Pavāraṇā day at the end of the rainy season approached, all those monks attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights.
9:
## Going to Pay Homage to the Buddha

After the rains retreat, those monks, wishing to see the Blessed One, approached the Elder and said, "Venerable Sir, we wish to see the Blessed One."

Having heard their words, Elder Cakkhupāla thought: "I am weak, and on the way, there is a forest haunted by non-human beings. If I go with these monks, everyone will be exhausted and they will not be able to obtain alms. I will send these monks ahead first." Then he said to them, "Friends, you go ahead first."

When they asked, "But when will you come, Venerable Sir?", he replied, "I am weak, and on the way, there is a forest haunted by non-human beings. If I go with you, everyone will be exhausted. You go ahead first."

"Venerable Sir, do not do this; we will go together with you," they pleaded. "Friends, do not let it be your wish to go with me. If it is so, it will be inconvenient for me," he said, and then added: "When my younger brother sees you, he will ask about me. At that time, tell him about the loss of my eyesight. He will send someone to me, and I will come with that person. Pay homage to the Blessed One and the eighty great elders on my behalf." With these instructions, he sent them away.

## Sending Pālita

Those monks, having asked for the Elder's forgiveness, entered the village. When the people saw the monks, they invited them to sit, offered alms, and asked, "Venerable Sirs, it appears you are preparing to depart."

"Yes, lay devotees, we wish to see the Blessed One," they replied. Although the devotees pleaded repeatedly, knowing the monks' firm desire to go, they followed them for a distance, weeping, and then returned.

Those monks eventually reached Jetavana and paid homage to the Blessed One and the eighty great elders on behalf of Elder Cakkhupāla. On the following morning, they entered the street where the Elder's younger brother, the householder, lived for alms. The younger brother, Cūḷapāla, recognized them, invited them to sit, and after exchanging pleasantries, asked, "Venerable Sirs, where is my elder brother, the Elder?"

Then the monks told him the news. Upon hearing this, the householder rolled at the monks' feet, weeping, and asked, "Venerable Sirs, what should be done now?"

"Elder Cakkhupāla expects someone to come from you. When that person arrives, he will come together with him," they said. "Venerable Sirs, this youth is my nephew named Pālita; please send him," he requested. "It is not possible to send him in this appearance; there are dangers on the way. It is proper to ordain Pālita as a novice and then send him," they replied. "Venerable Sirs, please ordain him and send him," he said.

Then they ordained Pālita, trained him for about half a month in how to hold the bowl and robes and so on, showed him the way, and sent him off. The novice Pālita eventually reached that village, saw an old man at the village gate, and asked, "Is there a forest monastery depending on this village?"

"Yes, Venerable Sir," he replied. "How many venerable ones live in this monastery?" he asked. "An elder named Pālita lives there," he said. "Show me the way to go," he requested. "Venerable Sir, who are you?" he asked. "I am the nephew of Elder Pālita," he replied. Then the man invited the novice and led him to the monastery.

## Elder Cakkhupāla's Return to Sāvatthī

The novice, after paying homage to the Elder, performed the major and minor duties for half a month, serving the Elder well. Then he said, "Venerable Sir, my uncle, the householder, expects your arrival."
10:
"Please come, let us go," he said. "If so, take hold of the end of my staff," the Elder said. The novice took the end of the staff and entered the village with the Elder. The people invited the Elder to stay and asked, "Venerable sir, does it not appear that you are about to depart?" "Yes, lay devotees, I will go and pay homage to the Teacher." Those devotees pleaded in various ways but, failing to persuade him, escorted the Elder halfway, then let him go, returning as they wept.

## The Sound of the Wood-gathering Woman's Song
As the novice led the Elder by the end of the staff, they reached a village called Kaṭṭhanagara in the forest, where the Elder had previously resided. Leaving the village, the novice heard the song of a woman gathering wood in the forest and became infatuated with the sound.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Monks, I do not see any other single sound that so takes hold of a man's heart as the sound of a woman."

The meaning is:
Monks, I do not see any other single sound that can so captivate and take possession of a man's heart as the sound of a woman.

The novice, infatuated with that sound, let go of the end of the staff and asked, "Venerable sir, I have some business to attend to; please wait a moment," and went to the woman. Seeing the novice, she remained silent. The novice committed a breach of virtue with that woman.

## Let Death Come, I Will Not Travel with a Vile Person
The Elder reflected: "Just now a song was heard. That woman's voice has stopped. The novice has also been gone a long time. He must have fallen into a breach of virtue with that woman." The novice finished his business, returned, and said, "Venerable sir, let us go." Then the Elder asked him, "Novice, have you become an evildoer?" The novice remained silent, and even when the Elder asked him repeatedly, he said nothing. Then the Elder said to him, "There is no need for one of such evil conduct as you to hold the end of my staff." Struck with remorse, the novice removed his robes, dressed as a layman, and said, "Venerable sir, I was a novice before, but now I have become a layman. Even when I ordained, I did not do so out of faith; I ordained out of fear of the dangers on the road. Come, let us go." The Elder replied, "Friend, an evil layman or an evil monk is just evil. While you were in the state of a monk, you could not even fulfill your virtue..."

(Nissaya translation: Sakka, the thousand-eyed Lord of Devas, who bears the glory of the state of the King of Devas, came in that instant and approached the venerable Elder Cakkhupāla.)

"How will you practice well as a layman? There is no need for one of such evil conduct as you to hold the end of my staff," the Elder said. "Venerable sir, this forest road is infested with non-human dangers, and you are blind and have no guide. How will you stay here?" When he asked this, the Elder said to him, "Friend, do not think so. Even if I lie here and die, or roll back and forth, I will not go with you," and he spoke these verses.

Hearing this, the novice was struck with remorse, thinking, "I have committed a grave, rash, and unsuitable deed." He wailed with arms raised, ran into the forest, and disappeared.

## Sakka Approaches Elder Cakkhupāla
Due to the power of Elder Cakkhupāla's virtue, the Pandukambala stone throne of Sakka, King of Devas—which is sixty leagues long, fifty leagues wide, and fifteen leagues thick, red like a hibiscus flower, and naturally sinks when sat upon and rises when stood up—showed signs of heat. Sakka looked with his divine eye, wondering who wanted to displace him from his seat, and saw the Elder. Therefore, the ancient teachers said:

Seeing the Elder, Sakka thought, "If I do not go to this venerable one who censures evil and honors the Dhamma, my head will split into seven pieces. I will go to him."
12:
## Sakka, Disguised as a Traveler, Holding the Staff

Having approached, he made the sound of footsteps not far from the Elder. Then the Elder asked Sakka, "Who is this?" "Venerable Sir, I am a traveler," he replied. "Layman, where are you going?" he asked. "Venerable Sir, I am going to Sāvatthī," he replied. When the Elder said, "Layman, go then," he asked, "But where will the Venerable Sir go?" Then the Elder said, "I too am going to Sāvatthī." "If that is so, Venerable Sir, let us go together," he requested. "Layman, I am weak because I am blind; if you go with me, there will be delay for you," the Elder said. "Venerable Sir, I have no urgent business. By going with the Venerable Sir, I shall gain one of the ten bases of meritorious action (puññakiriyavatthu). Therefore, I will go together with the Venerable Sir," he replied. The Elder thought, "This must be a virtuous man," and said, "If so, layman, take hold of the end of my staff." Sakka did as the Elder said, and by shortening the earth, he reached the Jetavana Monastery in the evening. Hearing the sounds of conch shells and drums, the Elder asked, "From where does this sound come?" "Venerable Sir, it is the sound from Sāvatthī," he replied. When the Elder said, "In the past, when we traveled, it took a long time," he replied, "Venerable Sir, I know a straight path (shortcut)." At that moment, the Elder noted in his mind, "This is not a human; it must be a deity."

The thousand-eyed lord of gods, the bearer of the glory of the celestial kingdom,
Having shortened that path, quickly arrived at Sāvatthī.

Devirajjassirindharo: the bearer of the glory of being the king of gods. Sahassanetto: the one who possesses a thousand eyes. Devindo: Sakka, the lord of gods. Taṃ maggaṃ: that path. Saṅkhipitvāna: having shortened. Sāvatthiṃ: to the city of Sāvatthī. Khippaṃ: quickly. Āgami: arrived.
13:
That Sakka led the Elder to the leaf-hut built by his younger brother, the householder Cūḷapāla, for the Elder's residence. Having seated him on a couch, he went to the younger brother in the guise of a dear friend and called out, "Friend Cūḷapāla!" When asked, "Friend, what is it?", he said, "Do you know that the Elder has arrived?" "I do not know. Has the Venerable Mahāpāla arrived?" he asked. "Friend, he has arrived. Just now, I went to the Jetavana Monastery and saw the Elder sitting in the leaf-hut built by you, the householder, and have come here," he said and then departed. The householder also went to the Jetavana Monastery and, upon seeing the Venerable Cakkhupāla, rolled at his feet and wept, saying, "Venerable Sir, because I foresaw such suffering, I did not give permission for you to ordain (when you asked)." Having said such words, he made two young servants bhujissa (meaning they were made freemen, not slaves) and had them ordained in the presence of the Elder, instructing them, "Bring gruel, rice, and so on from the village and attend to the Elder." The two novices performed their duties and attended to the Elder.

One day, monks living in various regions came to the Jetavana Monastery to see the Buddha. After paying homage to the Blessed One and the eighty Great Disciples, while wandering from dwelling to dwelling through the monastery, they reached the dwelling place of the Venerable Cakkhupāla. Thinking, "We shall see this place as well," they turned towards the dwelling of the Venerable Cakkhupāla in the evening. At that moment, a great rain cloud arose, and those monks thought, "Now..."

## Mind is the Forerunner

(1) Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā, manoseṭṭhā manomayā.
Manasā ce paduṭṭhena, bhāsati vā karoti vā.
Tato naṃ dukkha manveti, cakkaṃva vahato padaṃ.

Dhammā: The three mental aggregates (nāmakkhadha) are preceded by the consciousness aggregate (viññāṇakkhandha). Or, they have the consciousness aggregate as their forerunner. Manoseṭṭhā: They have the consciousness aggregate as their chief. Manomayā: They are accomplished by the consciousness aggregate. Yo puggalo: If a person. Paduṭṭhena manasā: With a wicked or corrupt mind. Ce bhāsati vā: Should speak. Ce karoti vā: Or should act. Tato: Because of such speaking or acting with a corrupt mind. Naṃ puggalaṃ: That person. Dukkhaṃ: Suffering. Anveti: Follows. Kimi-iva: In what manner? Cakkaṃ: Even as the wheel. Vahato padaṃ: Follows the hoof of the ox that draws the burden. Anveti iva: Just as it follows.

It was very late at night and the rain was falling; they decided to go and see in the early morning and thus returned. The rain fell throughout the first watch and cleared at midnight. The Venerable Elder was full of diligent effort and was accustomed to constant walking meditation. Therefore, at dawn, he went down to the cloister.

## Criticism of Cakkhupāla Thera for the Death of Insects

At that time, many insects were moving about on the ground that had just been moistened by the first rain. For the most part, those insects perished and died while the Venerable Cakkhupāla was walking in the cloister. The novice disciples living within had not swept the walking path early in the morning. When monks coming from various directions arrived to visit the place of the Venerable Cakkhupāla, they saw the dead insects in the cloister and asked, "Who walked in this place?" When told, "Venerable sirs, our preceptor, the Venerable Cakkhupāla, walked here," the monks from those directions criticized him, saying, "Friends, look at the deed of the monk Cakkhupāla. When his eyes were good, he lay down and did nothing at all, but now that his eyes are ruined, he says he will practice walking meditation and kills this many insects. While intending to do good, he does what is not beneficial."
15:
## Relating the Past

Thereafter, the monks went and reported to the Buddha, "Lord, the Venerable Cakkhupāla, while walking in the cloister, has killed many insects." When asked, "Did you see Cakkhupāla killing them?", they replied, "Lord, we did not see it." The Buddha then said, "Just as you did not see Cakkhupāla killing them, so too Cakkhupāla did not see those insects. Dear monks, for Arahants, there is no such thing as the intention to kill." Then the monks asked, "Lord, why did his eyes perish despite his having the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for the fruit of Arahantship?" The Buddha replied, "Dear monks, his eyes perished by the power of the karma he himself had committed." When they asked, "Lord, what was the evil deed committed by that Elder?", the Buddha said, "Dear monks, if that is so, then listen," and related the past.

## The Past Story of Cakkhupāla Thera

In the past, when King Kāsika reigned in the city of Bārāṇasī, a certain physician went to villages, market towns, and the countryside to practice medicine. Seeing a woman with weak eyes, he asked, "What is your ailment?" When she said, "I cannot see with my eyes," he said, "I will treat you." She said, "Sir, please treat me." He then asked, "What will you give me?" She replied, "If you can treat my eyes so that I can see normally, I and my children will become your slaves." The physician accepted, saying "Very well," and prepared the medicine. With just one application of the medicine, her eyes became normal. The woman thought, "I have promised to become the slave of this physician along with my children. Even if I have promised so, he will not speak to me or employ me with gentle words. I will deceive this physician." When the physician came and asked, "Lady, how are your eyes?", she replied, "Formerly my eyes pained only a little; now they pain excessively." The physician thought, "This woman has the intention to deceive me and give me nothing. What use is the medical fee given by this woman to me? Now I will make her blind." Planning thus, he went home and told his wife the matter, and the wife remained silent. Then the physician prepared a certain medicine, went to the woman, and said, "Lady, apply this eye-ointment," and she applied it. Both her eyes were burnt and destroyed like the flame of a lamp. That physician became the Elder Cakkhupāla. "Dear monks, the evil karma committed by my son Cakkhupāla at that time followed him again and again."
16:
"This evil kamma follows just as the wheel follows the hoof of the ox that draws the load." Having preached this story of Elder Cakkhupāla, the King of Dhamma, connecting the sequence and establishing the conclusion like a royal seal, spoke this verse.

At the end of the verse, thirty thousand monks attained Arahantship along with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial and fruitful for the assembled audience.

The Story of Elder Cakkhupāla ends.

## 2 - The Story of the Youth Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī

(Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī Vatthu)

The Teacher spoke this second verse, beginning with "Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā," while staying in Sāvatthī, concerning the youth Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī.

## The Father and Son Brahmins

In Sāvatthī, there was a Brahmin named Adinnapubbaka. He had never given anything to anyone; therefore, people knew him only by the name "Adinnapubbaka" (One who has never given). He had an only son, who was dear and pleasing to his heart. Desiring to have an ornament made for his son, he thought, "If I have it made by goldsmiths, I will have to pay them wages." So, he himself hammered the gold and made a pair of burnished earrings for him. Because of this, his son became known as "Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī" (One with burnished earrings).

## Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī Falls Ill

When Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī reached the age of sixteen, he was afflicted with jaundice (paṇḍu-roga). His mother, looking at her son, said, "Brahmin, your son is ill; have him treated." He replied, "My dear, if I bring a doctor, I will have to pay him a fee. Do you not consider the loss of my wealth?"

When he said this, the Brahmin woman asked, "Then what will you do, Brahmin, if you do not have him treated by doctors?" He replied, "I will do it in such a way that there is no loss of my wealth."
17:
## The Brahmin Goes Out to Find Medicine

Having said that, the Brahmin Adinnapubbaka went to the doctors and asked, "What medicine do you use for such and such a disease?" Then the doctors told him about various barks and leaves. Adinnapubbaka took those barks and leaves mentioned by the doctors and treated the youth Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī. Even as he was treating him, the youth's disease grew more severe and reached an incurable state.

## The Doctors Abandon Him

The Brahmin, realizing the youth's weakness, called a doctor. The doctor, just by looking at the youth, said, "I have some business to attend to; call another doctor and have him treated," and he left, abandoning the patient. The Brahmin, knowing that the youth was about to die, thought, "People who come to see this boy will see the wealth inside my house; I will move him outside." He then carried his son out and laid him on the front veranda.

## Spreading the Net of Knowledge

On that day, at the very early hour of dawn, the Blessed One arose from the attainment of Great Compassion (mahā-karuṇā-samāpatti). Wishing to survey the world with the Buddha-eye for the sake of seeing those who are ready for liberation (veneyya), who have performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and have abundant roots of merit, he spread the net of omniscience over the ten thousand world systems. At that time, the youth Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī appeared within the net of omniscience, lying on the front veranda. The Teacher saw Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī and, knowing that he had been brought out from inside the house and laid on the veranda, reflected, "Will there be any benefit if I go to the place where Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī is?" and he saw the following:

## Many Beings Will Attain Liberation

"This youth, having developed a clear mind towards me, will pass away and be reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in a golden mansion thirty leagues in size, surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs. The Brahmin, after cremating Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, will wander about the cemetery weeping. The celestial son, looking at his own form which is three gāvutas in size, adorned with ornaments weighing sixty cartloads and surrounded by a thousand nymphs, will wonder, 'By what merit did I obtain this glory and prosperity?' Realizing it was obtained through a clear mind towards me, he will think, 'This Brahmin, out of fear of losing his wealth, did not treat me, and now he goes to the cemetery every day and weeps. I will make him realize his error.' While the father is weeping, he will come in the form of Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī and lie down not far from the cemetery and weep. Then the Brahmin will ask him, 'Who are you?' He will reply, 'I am your son, Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī.' When asked, 'Where were you reborn?' he will reply, 'In the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.' When asked, 'By performing what merit?' he will explain that it was by developing a clear mind towards me. The Brahmin will then ask me, 'Is there anyone who, having developed a clear mind towards you, is reborn in heaven?' When he asks this, I will tell the Brahmin, 'Not just hundreds, or thousands, or hundreds of thousands; they cannot be counted,' and I will speak a verse from the Dhammapada. At the end of the verse, eighty-four thousand beings will attain the Dhamma, and Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī will become a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna). So too will the Brahmin Adinnapubbaka."

When he asks this, I will tell the Brahmin, "This many hundreds, this many thousands..."
18:
Adorned with polished earrings,
Wearing garlands, smeared with yellow sandalwood.
With arms upraised, you wail.
What suffering afflicts you in the midst of the forest?

Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī: one who habitually wears smooth (polished) earrings. Alaṅkato: one who is habitually adorned. Māladhārī: one who habitually wears various flowers. Haricandanuṣṣado: one who is smeared with golden sandalwood. Tuvaṃ: you. Bāhā: arms. Paggayha: raising up. Vanamajjhe: in the midst of the great forest. Kandasi: you weep. Kiṃ dukkhito: by what suffering are you oppressed?

"It is impossible to calculate and distinguish such a vast number in the hundreds of thousands," He said, and would preach the verse in the Dhammapada. At the end of the verse, eighty-four thousand beings would attain the Dhamma; the deva Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī and the Brahmin Adinnapubbaka would be established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti). "Depending on this one young man, many people will realize the Dhamma," He saw.

## Saving by Emitting a Ray of Light

Having seen this, when dawn arrived, after attending to His physical needs, surrounded by a large assembly of monks, He entered Sāvatthī for alms and gradually reached the door of the Brahmin's house. At that moment, Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī was lying down facing the interior of the house.

Then the Blessed One, knowing that the youth could not see Him, emitted a ray of light. The youth, wondering "What is this light?", turned over while still lying down and looked; seeing the Blessed One, he thought, "Because of my extremely foolish father, I did not get the opportunity to approach such a Buddha to perform physical service (veyyāvacca), to give alms, or to listen to the Dhamma. Now, I do not even have control over my hands; there is no other task to be done," and he directed his mind towards faith alone. The Blessed One thought, "This much devotion of mind is enough for this youth Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī," and departed. As the Tathāgata passed out of his sight, the youth Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, with a devoted mind, passed away and was reborn in the celestial realm in a golden mansion thirty yojanas in size, like a man waking from sleep.

## Discussion between the Brahmin and the Deva

The Brahmin, after cremating the body of the youth Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, remained at the cemetery, devoted to weeping. Every day he went to the cemetery and wailed, "Where are you, my only dear son? Where are you, my only dear son?" The deva Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, looking at his own prosperity and reflecting, "By what merit did I obtain this prosperity?", realized it was obtained through devotion of mind toward the Blessed One. He thought, "This Brahmin did not provide me with medicine when I was unwell, but now he goes to the cemetery and weeps. It is proper to make him realize his error." He came in the form of the youth Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī and stood not far from the cemetery, wailing with his arms upraised. The Brahmin, seeing him, thought, "I am weeping out of grief for my son. Why is this person weeping? I will ask him," and he spoke this verse:

Golden and radiant,
A chariot frame has arisen for me.
I cannot find a pair of wheels for it;

Cakkayugaṃ: a pair of wheels. Na vindāmi: I do not find. Tena dukkhena: because of that suffering. Jīvitaṃ: life. Jahissāmi: I shall give up.

Then the deva Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī answered with this verse.
After that, the Brahmin spoke to the deva Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī with this verse:

Whether made of gold, made of gems,
Made of copper, or made of silver.
Tell me, dear youth,

Hearing these words, the youth thought, "This Brahmin did not treat his son with medicine, but seeing me who resembles his son, he weeps and says he will make chariot wheels of gold and so on. Even if he says so, I will rebuke him further." He asked, "How large a pair of wheels will you make for me?" When the Brahmin said, "I will make a pair of wheels as large as you desire," the youth requested, "I have need of the Moon and the Sun. Give those Moon and Sun to me."

That youth said to him:
The Moon and the Sun, both are brothers here.
My chariot is made of gold;
It will be beautiful with that pair of wheels.

Tena cakkayugena: with that pair of wheels consisting of the Moon and the Sun. Mama: my. Sovaṇṇamayo: made of gold. Ratho: chariot. Sobhati: is beautiful. Iti: thus. So māṇavo: that youth. Tassa: to that Brahmin Adinnapubbaka. Pāvadi: said.

When he made this request, the Brahmin spoke again to the deva Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī with this verse:

You are indeed a fool, young man,
You who desire the undesirable.
I think you will die,
For you will not get the Moon and the Sun.

Tuvaṃ: you. Marissati: will die, even if you must die. Tvaṃ: you. Candimasūriye: the Moon and the Sun. Na lacchasi maññāmi: I think you will not get.

Then the youth said to the Brahmin, "Is the one who weeps because he wants a manifest object more foolish, or..."

Are you a deva, a Gandhabba, or Sakka Purindada?
Who are you, or whose son are you? How may we know you?

Young man, are you a deva named Gandhabba? Or are you Sakka, who gave gifts in the past? Who are you? Whose son are you? By what means may we know you?

"Or else, is the one who weeps because he desires an unmanifest object a fool?" Saying this, wishing to ask, he spoke this verse:

Coming and going is seen,
The appearance of the moon and sun is seen in both paths.
But the son who has passed away is not seen;
Who here, among the two weeping, is the greater fool?

In both the inner and outer paths, coming and going (entering and exiting) is seen. The appearance of the moon and sun is also seen. But the son who has passed away is not seen. Here in this cemetery, between the two who are weeping, who is the greater fool?

Hearing those words, the Brahmin noted, "This youth speaks only what is fitting," and spoke this verse:

You speak the truth indeed, young man,
I alone am the greater fool among those weeping.
Like a child crying for the moon,
I longed for my son who has passed away.

Young man, you speak only the truth. Just as a child, while weeping, longs for the moon, I longed for my son who has passed away. Between the two who are weeping, I alone am the greater fool.

"Young man, you speak the truth. You weep longing for the moon and sun. I weep longing for my deceased son. Between the two who are weeping, I alone am the greater fool." Having said this, he became free from sorrow because of the youth's words, and wishing to praise the youth, he spoke these three verses:

Truly, I was burning, like a fire sprinkled with ghee.
Like pouring water, you have extinguished all my distress.

Truly, you have pulled out the arrow, the sorrow based in my heart.
You have removed the sorrow for my son from me, who was overwhelmed by sorrow.

I, with the arrow pulled out, have become cool and extinguished.
I do not grieve, I do not weep, having heard you, young man.

Just as one extinguishes a fire sprinkled with ghee by pouring water over it, so have you, indeed, extinguished me who was burning with the fire of sorrow. You have extinguished all the sorrow that causes distress to the mind.

You who have removed the sorrow for my son from me, who was overwhelmed by sorrow. By that, you have indeed pulled out the arrow of sorrow that was based in my heart.

Young man, because of hearing your words, I am one whose arrow has been pulled out. I have become cool. I am extinguished. I shall no longer grieve. I shall no longer weep.

Then, wishing to ask the youth, "Who are you by name?", he spoke this verse.

Then, the youth, wishing to answer the Brahmin, spoke this verse:

I, having performed a wholesome deed,
Have reached the company of the Tidasa gods.

The son whom you yourself cremated at the cemetery, and for whom you weep and wail, and for whom you grieve and lament—I, that son of yours, having performed a wholesome deed, have reached the company of the Tidasa gods.

I was afflicted, suffering, and ill,

I was afflicted by disease, suffering, and in a painful state, being ill in my own house. (At that time,) I saw the Buddha, who is free from the dust of defilements, who has especially crossed over doubt, who speaks good words (Sugata), and who possesses incomparable and noble wisdom.

I, with a joyful and clear mind, made an añjali (salutation) to the Tathāgata. I, having performed such a wholesome deed, reached the company of the Tidasa gods.

When the youth answered thus, the Brahmin's whole body was filled with joy (pīti), and wishing to express that joy, he spoke this verse.

Then the youth spoke thus to the Brahmin.
