“Today, with a devoted heart, go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. Likewise, undertake the five precepts, unbroken and unblemished.”

Then the Brahmin, having accepted saying “Very well,” spoke these verses.

Then the deity said to the Brahmin, “Brahmin, there is much wealth in your house. Approach the Teacher and give alms, listen to the Dhamma, and ask Him questions.” Having said this, he disappeared right there at the cemetery.

## Asking the Buddha a Question

The Brahmin also went home, called his wife, and said, “Lady, I shall invite the ascetic Gotama and ask Him questions, and I shall perform a grand offering.” He then went to the monastery and respectfully paid homage to the Buddha. After exchanging pleasantries, he stood in a suitable place and said, “O Venerable Gotama, please accept my meal for today together with the community of monks.” The Teacher accepted. Knowing the Teacher’s acceptance, the Brahmin went quickly and had excellent hard and soft food prepared in his own house. The Teacher, surrounded by the community of monks, went to the Brahmin’s house and sat upon the prepared seat. The Brahmin respectfully served the meal. At that time, a great crowd gathered. It is said that when the Tathāgata is invited by one of wrong view, two groups of people gather: those of wrong view gather thinking, “Today we shall see the ascetic Gotama being harassed by the asking of questions,” and those of right view gather thinking, “Today we shall behold the Buddha’s domain and the Buddha’s majesty.” Then the Brahmin, after the Tathāgata had finished His meal, approached Him, sat on a low seat, and desiring to ask a question, said, “O Venerable Gotama, are there indeed those who are reborn in heaven merely by having a devoted mind, without having given alms to You, without having made offerings, without having heard the Dhamma, and without having observed the Uposatha?”

Then the Buddha said, “Brahmin, why do you ask me? Did not your son Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī tell you about his rebirth in heaven by having a devoted mind towards me?”
23:
When the Buddha said, “Did not your son Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī tell you about his rebirth in heaven by having a devoted mind towards me?”, the Brahmin asked, “O Venerable Gotama, when did he tell me?” The Buddha then recounted the entire story of Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, revealing the conversation between the Brahmin and the deity when the Brahmin went to the cemetery today and saw a youth weeping with uplifted arms not far away, starting with the words: “Adorned is Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, wearing garlands and smeared with yellow sandalwood.” (For this reason, this Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī story is known as the Buddha’s word.)

Having told this story, He said, “O Brahmin, it is not just a hundred or two hundred; indeed, there is no counting the number of those who have been reborn in heaven by having a devoted mind towards me.” At that time, the great crowd remained skeptical. 

## The Deity Arrives to Clear Doubts

Then the Buddha, knowing the skepticism of the crowd, made a resolution: “Let the deity Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī come together with his celestial mansion.” That deity Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, with a form three gāvutas in height and adorned with celestial ornaments, arrived, descended from his mansion, paid homage to the Buddha, and stood in a suitable place. Then the Buddha, wishing to ask the deity Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, “O deity, by performing what good deed did you obtain this celestial splendor?”, spoke this verse:

“With surpassing beauty, you who stand here, O deity, illuminating all directions like the morning star. I ask you, O deity of great power, what merit did you perform when you were a human being?”

[Word-by-word meaning:] O deity, you who stand here with a most pleasing complexion, illuminating all directions like the Osadhī star. O deity of great power, I, the Buddha, ask you: what merit did you perform while you were a human being?

Then the deity replied, “Venerable Sir, I obtained this splendor by having a devoted mind towards the Buddha.” When asked, “Did you truly obtain it by having a devoted mind towards me?”, he replied, “Yes, Venerable Sir.” The great crowd looked at the deity Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī and spoke words of joy: “Friends, how wonderful are the virtues of the Buddha! Though he was the son of the Brahmin Adinnapubbaka and performed no other merit, he obtained such splendor simply by having a devoted mind towards the Teacher.” Then, the King of Dhamma, to show the people that mind is the forerunner in the performance of wholesome and unwholesome deeds, that mind is chief, and that a wholesome deed performed with a devoted mind does not leave the person who goes to the celestial or human worlds, just as a shadow never leaves, He concluded the story and, as if sealing a royal decree with the king’s seal, spoke this verse:

2. “Mind is the forerunner of all states, mind is chief, they are mind-made. If one speaks or acts with a pure mind, because of that, happiness follows him, even as one's shadow that never leaves.”
24:
## The Teaching

(2) Mind precedes all mental states; mind is their chief; they are mind-made.
If one speaks or acts with a pure mind,
happiness follows him like a shadow that never leaves.

*Dhamma*: the three mental aggregates. *Manopubbaṅgamā*: having consciousness as their precursor. *Manoseṭṭhā*: having consciousness as their chief. *Manomayā*: made of consciousness. *Pasannena*: pure. *Manasā*: with the mind. *Ce bhāsati vā*: if one speaks. *Ce karoti vā*: if one acts. *Tato*: because of that speaking or acting with a pure mind. *Naṃ puggalaṃ*: to that person. *Su-khaṃ*: happiness. *Anveti*: follows. *Kā viya*: like what? *Chāyā*: a shadow. *Anupāyinī iva*: like a shadow that follows a person wherever they go, closely behind.
25:
## Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the verse, eighty-four thousand beings attained the Dhamma. Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī the deva established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The Brahmin Adinnapubbaka likewise became a Stream-enterer and donated and distributed great wealth in the Buddha's Dispensation.

The Story of the Youth Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī ends.

## 3. The Story of Elder Tissa

(Tissatthera-vatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Akkocchi maṃ," concerning Elder Tissa.

## One Proud of Lineage and Difficult to Speak to

That Elder Tissa was the son of the Buddha's paternal aunt (the son of Queen Amitādevī, the sister of King Suddhodana). Having ordained in his old age, he enjoyed the gains and offerings that arose for the Buddhas. He had a stout body and, wearing well-pressed robes, he usually sat in the assembly hall in the middle of the monastery. Visiting monks who came to see the Tathāgata, seeing him and thinking, "He must be a great elder," would approach him and ask to perform duties such as massaging his feet. Tissa remained silent. 

Then a young monk asked him, "How many years (vassa) have you been ordained?" When he replied, "I have no vassa; I ordained in my old age," the monk snapped his fingers and said, "You ill-disciplined old man, you do not know your own measure. Seeing so many great elders, you do not even show proper respect. When asked about duties, you remain silent. You have not even a bit of remorse."

Tissa, giving rise to his warrior-caste pride (khattiya-māna), asked, "Whom have you come to see?" When they replied, "To see the Teacher," he said, "Who do you think I am? I will cut you off at the root!" and crying, distressed and unhappy, he went to the Teacher.

Then the Teacher asked him, "Tissa, why have you come distressed, unhappy, and crying with tears on your face?" Those visiting monks, thinking, "He might go and cause some trouble," followed along with the monk Tissa, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat in a suitable place. When questioned by the Teacher, the monk Tissa reported, "Venerable Sir, these monks are insulting me." When asked, "Where were you sitting?" he replied, "Venerable Sir, I was sitting in the assembly hall in the middle of the monastery."
26:
Then the Blessed One asked, “Did you see these monks coming?” He replied, “Yes, Lord, I saw them.” “Did you get up to welcome them?” He replied, “No, Lord.” “Did you ask to take their requisites?” He replied, “No, Lord.” “Did you ask about their duties or offer drinking water?” He replied, “No, Lord.” “Did you bring a seat, pay homage, and massage their feet?” He replied, “No, Lord.” 

Then the Blessed One said, “Tissa, all these duties must be performed for senior monks. A monk who does not perform these duties is not fit to stay in the middle of the monastery.” He continued, “It is only your fault; apologize to these monks.” Then the monk Tissa replied, “Lord, these monks insulted me; I cannot apologize to them.” When the Blessed One said, “Tissa, do not do this; it is only your fault; apologize to them,” he replied, “Lord, I cannot apologize.” 

Then, when the monks said, “Lord, this monk Tissa is difficult to speak to,” the Blessed One said, “Monks, not only now is he difficult to speak to; in the past also, he was just as difficult to speak to.” When they requested, “Lord, we have now seen his present stubbornness; what did he do in the past?” the Blessed One said, “In that case, monks, listen,” and he brought forth the story of the past.

## The Past Story of Elder Tissa
In the past, when the King of Bārāṇasī was reigning in Bārāṇasī, an ascetic named Devela lived in the Himalayas for eight months. Desiring to stay near the city for four months to consume salt and vinegar, he came from the Himalayas and, seeing some children at the city gate, asked, “Where do monks who arrive at this city stay?” They replied, “Lord, they stay in the potter’s workshop shed.” The ascetic Devela went to the potter’s shed, stood at the door, and said, “Potter, if it is no burden to you, I would like to stay in the shed for one night.” The potter handed over the shed, saying, “Lord, I have no business in the shed at night; the shed is large; stay as you please, Lord.”
27:
While the ascetic Devela was staying in the shed, another ascetic named Nārada also came from the Himalayas and asked the potter for a night’s lodging. The potter thought, “I do not know if the ascetic who arrived first will want to stay with this one or not; I shall free myself from responsibility,” and said, “Lord, if the ascetic who arrived first agrees, stay according to his wish.” 

Then the ascetic Nārada approached Devela and requested, “Teacher, if it is no burden to you, may we also stay in this shed for one night?” When Devela said, “The shed is large; enter and stay in a suitable place,” Nārada entered and stayed behind the ascetic Devela who had entered first. Both ascetics engaged in friendly conversation and then lay down to sleep.

At the time of sleeping, Nārada noted the place where Devela was lying and the position of the door before lying down. However, when Devela lay down, he did not sleep in his original place but lay down crosswise across the middle of the doorway.

## Stepping on the Ascetic Devela’s Matted Hair and Neck
When Nārada went out during the night, he stepped on the tips of Devela’s matted hair. When asked, “Who is stepping on me?” he replied, “Teacher, it is I, Nārada.” Devela said, “Wicked ascetic, you come from the forest and step on the tips of my matted hair!” Nārada said, “Teacher, I did not know you were sleeping in this spot; please forgive me,” and he went outside even while Devela was grumbling. 

Devela thought, “This ascetic Nārada might step on me again when he returns,” so he turned around, placing his head where his feet had been. When Nārada returned, he thought, “Previously, I offended the teacher. Now, I shall enter by the side of his feet.” As he came in, he stepped on Devela’s neck. When Devela asked, “Who is this?” and he replied, “Teacher, it is I, Nārada,” Devela said, “Wicked ascetic, first you stepped on the tips of my matted hair, and now you step on my neck. I shall curse you!” Nārada said, “Teacher, I am not at fault. Because I did not know you were sleeping like this, I offended you the first time. Now, I entered thinking I would enter by the feet; please forgive me.”

## The Ascetics Cursing Each Other
Then, when Devela said to Nārada, “Wicked ascetic, I shall curse you,” Nārada pleaded, “Teacher, please do not do this.” Devela, disregarding Nārada’s words, cursed him with this verse:

“The sun has a thousand rays and infinite heat, it is the dispeller of darkness.
When the sun rises in the morning, may your head split into seven pieces.”

Thus he cursed Nārada. Nārada said, “Teacher, even while I am saying I am not at fault, you curse me. May the head of the one who is at fault split; may the head of the one who is blameless not split,” and he spoke this verse:

“The sun has a thousand rays and infinite heat, it is the dispeller of darkness.
When the sun rises in the morning, may your head split into seven pieces.”

Having said this, he countered the curse.

## The Power of the Ascetic Nārada
That ascetic Nārada possessed great psychic power. He could remember forty aeons in the past and forty aeons in the future, thus eighty aeons in total. Therefore, when he investigated, “Upon whom will the curse fall?”
28:
Work does not proceed, O Nārada of Jambudīpa.
By what has the world become dark? Being asked, please tell me that.

Nārada, O Nārada the ascetic. Jambudīpassa, of all the people of the island of Jambudīpa. Kammantā, the carrying out of work. Nappavattanti, cannot proceed. Kena, why? Loko, the world. Tamobhūto, has become utter darkness. Pucchito, the ascetic who is being asked. Me, to me. Taṃ, that reason. Akkhāhi, please explain.

Upon reflection, he realized, “It will fall upon the head of the teacher, the ascetic Devila,” and out of compassion for that ascetic Devila, he prevented the dawn from rising by the power of his psychic potency. When the dawn did not rise, the citizens went to the palace gate and lamented, “O Great King—the dawn does not rise during your reign; please make the dawn rise for us.” When the King examined his own bodily actions and so forth, he saw no wrongdoing. Thinking, “What could be the cause?” he suspected, “It must be due to a dispute between ascetics.” He then asked, “Are there any ascetics in this city?” When told, “O Great King, there are ascetics who arrived at the potter’s shed yesterday evening,” the King immediately went to that potter’s shed with torches lit and held. He paid homage to the ascetic Nārada and, sitting in a suitable place, addressed him with this verse.

The ascetic Nārada explained the whole situation, saying, “For this reason, this ascetic Devila cursed me. At that time, I said, ‘I am not at fault; let the curse fall only upon the head of the one who is at fault,’ and thus I cursed him back. After cursing, I reflected on whose head the curse would fall, and I saw that at the time of sunrise, the head of the teacher Devila would split into seven pieces. Therefore, out of compassion for that ascetic Devila, I do not allow the dawn to rise (I have made a resolution so that the dawn does not rise).”

When asked, “Venerable Sir, what can be done so that no harm will come to the ascetic Devila?” he replied, “If he asks for my forgiveness, no harm will come to him.” When the ascetic Devila was told, “If so, please ask for forgiveness,” he said, “O Great King, this Nārada stepped on my matted hair and my neck; I will not ask for forgiveness from this rogue ascetic.” Even when the King pleaded, “Venerable Sir, do not do this; please ask for forgiveness,” he still refused. Even when told, “Your head will split into seven pieces,” he remained without asking for forgiveness. Then the King said, “You will not ask for forgiveness of your own will,” and had him seized by his hands, feet, belly, and neck, forcing him to bow at the feet of the ascetic Nārada. The ascetic Nārada then said, “Teacher Devila, please rise; I forgive you.” Then he said, “Great King, this ascetic Devila does not ask for forgiveness of his own will. There is a pond not far from the city. Place the ascetic Devila in that pond in water up to his neck, with a lump of clay placed on his head.” The King did exactly as the ascetic Nārada said.

Then the ascetic Nārada called the ascetic Devila and said, “Teacher Devila, when I release my psychic power and the sunlight rises, dive into the water and emerge from another place to go away.” As soon as the lump of clay was touched by the sun’s rays, it split into seven pieces. That ascetic Devila also dived and fled to another place.

The Teacher (the Buddha) brought forth this Dhamma teaching and identified the birth (Jātaka) saying, “At that time, monks, the King was Ānanda, Devila was the Elder Tissa, and Nārada was I myself.” After concluding the Jātaka, He said, “At that time also, this monk was difficult to admonish.” Then, calling the Elder Tissa, He said, “Tissa, a monk should not think, ‘Such a person abused me, such a person struck me, such a person defeated me, such a person took my belongings.’
29:
He is indeed difficult to admonish.” After saying this, He addressed the Elder Tissa, “Tissa, in one who thinks, ‘I was abused by such a person, I was struck by such a person, I was defeated by such a person, such a person took my belongings,’ hatred is not appeased. But in one who does not harbor such grudges, it is appeased.” He then spoke these verses:

## Do Not Harbor Enmity
(3) “He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me.”
In those who harbor such thoughts, hatred is never appeased.
(4) “He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me.”
In those who do not harbor such thoughts, hatred is appeased.

Eso, this person. Maṃ, me. Akkocchi, has abused. Eso, this person. Maṃ, me. Avadhi, has oppressed. Eso, this person. Maṃ, me. Ajini, has defeated. Eso, this person. Me, my. Dhanaṃ, wealth. Ahāsi, has taken. Iti, thus. Ye ca, those who. Taṃ, that anger and so forth. Upanayhanti, harbor as a grudge. Tesaṃ, for those people. Veraṃ, hatred. Na sammati, is not appeased.

Eso, this person. Maṃ, me. Akkocchi, has abused. Eso, this person. Maṃ, me. Avadhi, has oppressed. Eso, this person. Maṃ, me. Ajini, has defeated. Eso, this person. Me, my. Dhanaṃ, wealth. Ahāsi, has taken. Iti, thus. Ye ca, those who. Taṃ, that anger and so forth. Nupanayhanti, do not harbor as a grudge. Tesaṃ, for those people. Veraṃ, hatred. Upasammati, is appeased.

“Hatred cannot be appeased in a monk who thinks in this way; it is appeased only in one who does not harbor such grudges,” He said, and preached these verses.

## Benefits of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, one hundred thousand monks attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth. The Dhamma teaching was beneficial to the great multitude. The difficult-to-admonish monk Tissa also became one who is easy to admonish.

The story of the Elder Tissa ends.

## 4. The Story of the Ogress Kāḷī
(Kāḷayakkhiṇī-vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana monastery, the Teacher (the Buddha) spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with “Na hi verena,” concerning a certain barren woman.
30:
## The Beginning of the Cycle of Hostility

Once, a certain son of a householder, after his father had passed away, performed all the tasks in the fields and at home by himself and looked after his mother. Then his mother said to him, "Dear son, I shall bring a young woman for you." He replied, "Mother, do not say such a thing; I will look after you as long as I live." When he said this, the mother said, "Dear son, you alone perform the duties in the fields and at home. Because of that, I have no peace of mind. I shall bring one." After refusing repeatedly, the son remained silent. The mother, wishing to go to a certain family to bring a bride, left the house. Then the son asked her, "To which family are you going?" When she said, "To such and such a family," he stopped her from going there and pointed out a family of his own preference.

The mother went to the family he indicated, requested the young woman, fixed the date, and having brought her, settled her in the son's house. That young woman was barren. Then the mother said to the householder's son, "Dear son, you had me bring this young woman according to your own wish. Now she has become barren. A family without children surely perishes; the lineage cannot be continued. I shall bring another young woman for you." Although the householder's son refused, saying, "Mother, it is not proper," she spoke of it repeatedly.

The barren woman, hearing the mother's words, thought, "Sons cannot go against the words of their parents. Now, she will bring another woman who can bear children and will treat me like a servant. It would be better if I myself were to bring a young woman." Having thought thus, she went to a certain family and requested a young woman for her husband. When the parents of that young woman refused, saying, "Dear daughter, what are you saying?", she pleaded, "I am barren. A family without children perishes. If your daughter gets a son or a daughter, she will become the mistress of the householder's home. Please give that young woman for my husband." Having gained their consent, she brought her and settled her in her husband's house.

Then this thought occurred to that barren woman: "If this young woman gets a son or a daughter, she alone will become the mistress of the wealth. It is proper to act in such a way that she does not get a child." Then she said to the young woman, "Dear sister, when a pregnancy is established in your womb, you should inform me." The young woman agreed, saying, "Very well," and when she became pregnant, she informed the barren woman. The barren woman herself constantly gave her gruel and rice. Then, she gave her medicine to cause a miscarriage along with the food. The pregnancy was aborted. When she became pregnant for the second time...
31:
...she informed her, and the other woman caused a miscarriage for the second time in the same way. Then the neighboring women asked her, "Does your co-wife cause you harm?" When she told them the matter, they said, "O foolish woman, why did you do this? This barren woman, out of fear of your supremacy, prepares and gives you medicine to cause a miscarriage. That is why your pregnancy is aborted. Do not do such a thing again." Thus advised, when she became pregnant for the third time, she remained silent and did not speak. Then the barren woman, seeing the young woman's belly, asked, "Why did you not tell me that a pregnancy was established?" When the young woman replied, "You brought me here, deceived me, and caused my pregnancy to fail twice; for what purpose should I tell you?", the barren woman thought, "Now I am ruined," and while watching for the young woman's negligence, she found an opportunity when the pregnancy was advanced, prepared the medicine, and gave it to her. Because the fetus was advanced, it could not be aborted and fell into a transverse position. Intense pain arose, and she reached the point of death.

## The Lives of the Cat and the Hen

As she was about to die, the young woman made a wish: "I am now to be destroyed by you. You yourself brought me here, and you yourself have destroyed my children all three times. Now I too shall perish. When I pass away from this life, may I be reborn as an ogress and be able to eat your children." Having made this prayer, she died and was reborn as a female cat in that very house. The husband seized the barren woman and beat her severely with his elbows, knees, and so on, saying, "You have caused the destruction of my lineage." The barren woman died from those severe injuries and was reborn as a hen in that very house. Before long, the hen laid eggs, and the cat came and ate those eggs. She ate them for the second and third time as well.
32:
## The Leopardess and the Doe
At that time, the hen, thinking, "She has eaten my eggs three times and now wishes to eat me as well," made a vow: "When I pass away from this existence, may I be able to eat her and her offspring." After passing away, she was reborn as a leopardess in the forest. (A 'thit' is a fierce type of tiger.) The cat, however, was reborn as a doe. When that doe gave birth, the leopardess came and ate the young ones three times.

## The Ogress and the Human Woman in the Final Life
As the doe was nearing death, she made a vow: "This leopardess has eaten my young ones three times, and now she is about to eat me. When I pass away from this existence, may I be able to eat this leopardess and her offspring." After passing away from that existence, she was reborn as an ogress (yakkhiṇī). The leopardess also passed away from that existence in that very forest and was reborn as a woman in the city of Sāvatthī. When that woman reached the age of maturity, she went to live at her husband's house in a village near the gate of Sāvatthī. Later, she gave birth to a son.

The ogress came in the guise of a dear friend of that woman and asked, "Where is my friend?" When she was told, "She is inside the room giving birth," she asked, "Did she give birth to a son or a daughter?" and saying, "I will go and see the child," she entered the room. Pretending to look at the child, she seized him, devoured him, and left. When the woman gave birth a second time, the ogress did the same thing again.

When the third time came, the woman, being heavily pregnant, called her husband and consulted him, saying, "Lord, in this place and in this house, an ogress has already eaten my two sons. Now, I will go to my parents' house to give birth to the child." She then went to her parents' house and gave birth to a son.

## The Occasion for Release from the Cycle of Enmity
At that time, it was the ogress's turn to fetch water. Among the followers of King Vessavaṇa, the ogresses must carry water from Lake Anotatta in a relay of head-carrying. These ogresses are released from this duty only after four or five months. (This is the nature of their water-carrying turn.) Other ogresses, having exhausted bodies, even reach the end of their lives.

As soon as that ogress was released from her turn to fetch water, she went quickly to that house and asked, "Where is my friend?" When she was told, "How could you see that young woman? In this house, whenever she gave birth, an ogress came and ate the child. Therefore, she has gone to her parents' house," the ogress, with a mind driven by the force of vengeance, thought, "Let her go wherever she wishes, she shall not escape from my hands," and rushed toward the city with great speed.

On the day of the naming ceremony, the woman had the child bathed and named. Then, saying, "Lord, let us now return to our own home," she carried the son in her arms and traveled with her husband along the path through the middle of the Jetavana Monastery. While traveling, she gave the son to her husband and bathed in the monastery pond. After she finished and while her husband was bathing, she stood nursing the child. Seeing the ogress coming from afar, she recognized her and cried out loudly, "Lord, come quickly! This is that ogress! Come quickly! This is that ogress!" Unable to wait until her husband arrived, she turned back and rushed toward the interior of the monastery.
33:
## Administering the Cool Water of Dhamma
(5) Na hi verena verāni, sammantīdha kudācanaṃ.
Averena ca sammanti, esa dhammo sanantano.

In this world, hatreds are never appeased by returning hatred. Only by non-hatred are hatreds appeased. This—the appeasement of hatred through non-hatred—is an ancient law. Alternatively, this—the appeasement of hatred through non-hatred—is the ancient Dhamma, the path traveled by all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants.

## Both Arriving Before the Buddha
At that time, the Blessed One was preaching the Dhamma in the midst of the assembly. That woman placed her son upon the feet of the Tathāgata and said, "I give this child to you, Venerable Sir. Please grant life to my little son."

The deity named Sumana, who resided at the gatehouse of the monastery, did not allow the ogress to enter. The Blessed One called the Venerable Ānanda and said, "Go, Ānanda, and summon that ogress." The Elder summoned her. When the woman said, "Venerable Sir, here she comes," the Buddha said, "Let her come; do not make a sound." When she arrived and stood there, He said to her, "Why do you act in this way? If you two had not come before a Buddha like me, your enmity would have lasted for an entire aeon, like the enmity between snakes and mongooses, between bears and the spirits of the kakudha trees, or between crows and owls. Why do you return hatred with hatred? Hatred is appeased by non-hatred; it is not appeased by hatred." Having said this, He spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the verse, the ogress was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the assembled crowd.

## The Spirit Who Points Out Benefits
The Blessed One said to the woman, "Give your son to this ogress." She replied, "I am afraid, Venerable Sir." The Buddha said, "Do not be afraid; there is no danger for you from her." The woman then gave the son to the ogress. The ogress kissed and embraced the child, then gave him back to the mother and began to weep. Then the Blessed One asked her, "What is the reason for this weeping?" She replied, "Venerable Sir, in the past, even when I lived by any means possible, I never obtained enough food to fill my stomach. How shall I live now?"

Then the Blessed One comforted her, saying, "Do not worry," and said to the woman, "Take this ogress, let her stay in your house, and look after her with the first-fruits of gruel and rice." The woman took her and settled her in the eaves of the house, looking after her with the first-fruits of gruel and rice. At that time, it seemed to the ogress as if her head was being struck by the tip of a pestle whenever rice was being pounded. She called her friend, the woman, and said, "I cannot stay in this place; put me in another place." Thus, she was placed in the rice-pounding shed, or by the water jar, or at the stove, or in a room, or on a rubbish heap, or at the village gate...
34:
Even when she was placed in those locations, she rejected them all, saying: "In this water-pot stand, it feels as if my head is being split with a pestle. In this water-pot stand, children spit out rinsing water. In this stove room, dogs lie down. In this eaves area, children discard filth. In this sweeping area, they throw away rubbish. In this village gate, the village children play games involving signs and marks." Then, placing the ogress in a secluded spot outside the village, they brought the first portion of gruel, the first portion of rice, and so on to that place and looked after her.

That ogress told her friend, the woman: "This year there will be good rain; plant your crops on high ground. This year there will be a drought; plant your crops only in the low-lying areas." At that time, the crops planted by the rest of the people were destroyed either by too much water or by lack of water. For that woman, however, the crops were extremely abundant. Then the people living in Sāvatthī asked that woman: "Dear lady, the crops you plant are not destroyed by too much water nor by lack of water. Do you work knowing whether there will be good rain or drought? What is the reason for this?" Then the woman said: "Our friend, the ogress, tells us whether there will be good rain or drought. By her word, we plant crops in high or low places. Because of that, our grain is abundant. Do you not see the gruel, rice, and so on being constantly carried from our house? They are being carried for her. You too should carry and offer the first portion of gruel, the first portion of rice, and so on to this ogress; she will also look after your affairs." Then all the city dwellers made offerings and honors to her. From then on, the ogress, looking after the affairs of all the people, became very wealthy and influential, having a large following. Later, she established eight "food-by-tickets" (salāka-bhatta). (Meaning: she constantly offered eight bowls of alms-food; she established a food endowment.) Those ticket-foods are still being offered and honored to this very day.

The Story of Kāḷī the Ogress ends.

## 5. The Story of the Monks of Kosambī (Kosambaka-vatthu)

"Others do not realize..." (Pare ca na vijānanti)—the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching while staying at Jetavana, concerning the monks of Kosambī.

## From a Disagreement Between Teachers to a Split Up to the Brahma Realm

In Kosambī, at the Ghositārāma monastery, there lived two monks, each with a following of five hundred: one was an expert in the Vinaya (Vinayadhara) and the other was a Dhamma teacher (Dhammakathika).
35:
Among those two monks, one day the Dhamma teacher, after attending to his physical needs, left some leftover rinsing water in a vessel in the washroom and came out. Later, the Vinaya expert entered the washroom, saw the leftover water, came out, and asked the Dhamma teacher, "Friend, did you leave that water?" "Yes, friend," he replied. "But do you not know that this is an offense (āpatti)?" he asked. "Indeed, I did not know," he replied. "Friend, even so, leaving leftover rinsing water here is an offense," said the Vinaya expert. "If so, I shall make amends for it," he said. "Friend, if you did it unintentionally or through lack of mindfulness, there is no offense," said the Vinaya expert. The Dhamma teacher then held the view that there was no offense. The Vinaya expert, however, told his own pupils, "This Dhamma teacher, though committing an offense, does not even know it." When those pupils saw the Dhamma teacher's pupils, they said, "Your preceptor, though committing an offense, does not even know it." They went and told their preceptor. The Dhamma teacher said, "This Vinaya expert previously said there was no offense, and now he says there is an offense. He is a liar (musāvādī)."

Then the Dhamma teacher's pupils went and said, "Your preceptor is a liar." In this way, they increased the quarrel and strife among one another. Later, the Vinaya expert, finding an opportunity, performed the act of suspension (ukkhepaniya-kamma) against the Dhamma teacher for not seeing the offense. From that day on, the lay supporters who provided the four requisites to the Vinaya expert and the Dhamma teacher also split into two groups. The nuns who received their instructions, the guardian deities, and the sky-dwelling deities who were friends and associates of those deities—all worldlings (puthujjana) up to the Brahma realm—split into two factions. Starting from the realm of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṭṭha realm, this uproar and commotion spread.

## Advice to be Harmonious

Then a certain monk approached the Blessed One and reported the view of the Vinaya expert and his pupils who performed the suspension—that he was suspended by a legal Vinaya act—and the view of the Dhamma teacher's pupils who followed the suspended monk—that he was suspended by an illegal act. He also reported how the Dhamma teacher's pupils continued to follow him around despite being forbidden by the Vinaya experts. The Blessed One sent word twice, saying, "Let them be harmonious," but hearing only the words, "Venerable Sir, they do not wish to be harmonious," when he sent word for the third time, he heard that the Sangha of monks had split.
36:
At that time, the Blessed One went in person to those monks. He preached on the faults of performing the act of suspension (ukkhepaniyakamma) to those monks who performed it, and the faults of not seeing an offense to the suspended Dhamma-preacher monks. Furthermore, he allowed those monks to perform the Uposatha and other acts within a single boundary (sīmā) in Kosambī itself. He prescribed a rule for the refectory (bhattagga) that monks who were prone to quarreling should sit with a space between their seats. Hearing that they were still living in a state of conflict, he went to that place and said, "Enough, monks! Do not quarrel," and other such words. He said, "Monks, these quarrels, strifes, disputes, and contentions are harmful. Because of a quarrel, even a small quail once caused the death of a great elephant," and he told the Laṭukika Jātaka (this Jātaka is found in the Maṇikuṇḍala Vagga of the Pañcaka Nipāta). He then said, "Monks, be united; do not dispute. Because of disputes, many hundreds of thousands of quails once met their end," and he told the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka (this Jātaka is found in the Hañci Vagga of the Ekaka Nipāta).

Even though he spoke thus, they did not heed the Blessed One's words. Then, a certain Dhamma-following monk, not wishing the Tathāgata to be troubled, said: "Wait, Blessed One, Lord of Dhamma. Let the Blessed One be untroubled and dwell devoted to the happiness of the fruit of Arahantship realized in this very life. We ourselves will be known through this quarreling, strife, dispute, and contention." Upon this being said, the Blessed One brought forth the past:

## The Story of Dīghīti of Kosala

"Monks, in the past, there was a king of Kāsi named Brahmadatta in Vārāṇasī. He told of how King Brahmadatta seized the kingdom and wealth of the King of Kosala, the father of Prince Dīghāvu; how he killed the father who was living in disguise; and how, after Prince Dīghāvu spared his life, the two became united from then on." (This story of Dīghīti Kosala is found in the Dīghīti Kosala Jātaka of the Pañcaka Nipāta and the Kosambī Jātaka of the Navaka Nipāta. It is found in detail in the Kosambaka Khandhaka of the Vinaya Mahāvagga. For the benefit of those seeking knowledge, I shall include that story here.)

## The Detailed Story of Dīghīti Kosala

Long ago, in Vārāṇasī, a king named Brahmadatta ruled over Kāsi. That king was wealthy, with great riches, resources, an army, and a vast kingdom. The King of Kosala, named Dīghīti, was not very wealthy, having few riches, resources, a small army, and a small kingdom.

Once, King Brahmadatta set out with his army to wage war against King Dīghīti of Kosala. When King Dīghīti heard of this, he thought, "I am weak. I cannot withstand even a single battle against the powerful King Brahmadatta. It would be better if I depart and avoid him in advance." Having thought thus, he took his queen and fled the capital. Then, King Brahmadatta seized and ruled over all of King Dīghīti’s army, elephants, horses, and kingdom. King Dīghīti, along with his queen, lived in a certain border region of Vārāṇasī, disguised as a wanderer (paribbājaka) at a potter's dwelling. Soon after, the queen became pregnant, and through the power of the child, she experienced the following longings (dohaḷa): "At sunrise, I wish to see the fourfold army standing on a good piece of ground, clad in dark armor," and "I wish to drink the water used for washing swords."

When she told the king about her pregnancy longings, he said, "Queen, we have abandoned our throne and are living in poverty and disguise. Where can we get a fourfold army or the water from washing swords?" She replied, "Great King, if I do not get them, I shall die."
37:
At that time, King Dīghīti of Kosala went to the Brahmin Chaplain, who had been an old friend, and said: "Brahmin Chaplain, your friend, my queen, is pregnant. She has a craving to see a fourfold army in full array at sunrise and to drink the water used for washing a sword."

The Brahmin Chaplain replied: "Great King, if that is so, we also wish to see the Queen." When King Dīghīti brought the Queen to the Chaplain's house, the Chaplain, upon seeing her from afar, rose from his seat, adjusted his robe over his left shoulder, and paid homage to the Queen, exclaiming three times: "Kosalā rājā vata bho kucchi-gato!" (O friends, truly a King of Kosala is in this womb!). After exclaiming thus, he took responsibility, saying, "I shall see that her craving is fulfilled."

Having taken responsibility, the Brahmin Chaplain approached King Brahmadatta and said: "Great King, the omens are clear. Tomorrow at sunrise, let the fourfold army, clad in dark armor, be stationed on the auspicious ground, and let the swords be washed." King Brahmadatta did as the Chaplain suggested. Thus, the Queen of King Dīghīti saw the fourfold army and drank the sword-washing water, and her craving was fulfilled. When the pregnancy reached full term, she gave birth to a son. They named the child Dīghāvu. Prince Dīghāvu soon reached the age of wisdom and intelligence.

Then King Dīghīti had this thought: "King Brahmadatta has seized our army, our kingdom, and our treasury. If he discovers us, he will kill all three of us. It would be better if Prince Dīghāvu lived outside the city." With this thought, he kept Prince Dīghāvu outside the city. While living outside the city, Prince Dīghāvu soon mastered all the arts and sciences.

On another occasion, a man who had formerly been the barber of King Dīghīti and was now in the service of King Brahmadatta, saw King Dīghīti and the Queen living in the border region in the disguise of wandering ascetics at a potter's dwelling. He reported this to King Brahmadatta. King Brahmadatta summoned his men and ordered: "Capture King Dīghīti and his Queen and execute them."

The men replied, "Very well, Great King," and having captured King Dīghīti and the Queen, they led them from street to street. Prince Dīghāvu, who was living outside the city and had not seen his parents for a long time, happened to enter the city of Bārāṇasī at that moment. He saw them being led along from street to street, their hands bound behind their backs, their heads shaven, and a harsh-sounding drum being beaten. He approached them.

King Dīghīti, seeing Prince Dīghāvu, said: "Mā kho tvaṃ tāta Dīghāvu dīghaṃ passa mā rassaṃ, na hi tāta Dīghāvu verena verā sammanti, averena hi tāta Dīghāvu verā sammanti."

(Dear Dīghāvu, do not look far; do not look short. For, dear Dīghāvu, hatred is not stilled by hatred; by non-hatred alone is hatred stilled.)

When he said this, the King's men asked: "Who is this Dīghāvu? To whom is he speaking? This king has gone mad from the fear of death and is babbling nonsense." The King replied: "Friends, I am not mad. Those who are wise will understand." He repeated this three times. Then the men took him out through the south gate, cut him into four pieces, and left after setting a guard.

Prince Dīghāvu entered the city of Bārāṇasī, brought liquor in the evening, and gave it to the guards. When they were drunk and asleep, he gathered wood, cremated his parents, and circumambulated the funeral pyre three times with joined palms. King Brahmadatta, who was in his noble palace, saw the cremation and thought: "This person must be a relative of King Dīghīti. Alas, I have suffered a loss, and not a single man has come to report it to me."

After the cremation, Prince Dīghāvu went into the forest, wept as much as he desired, and then returned to Bārāṇasī. He stayed with an elephant trainer near the palace to learn the craft. Early in the morning, Prince Dīghāvu would rise and sing beautifully while playing the lute. King Brahmadatta heard the music and was pleased. After inquiring, he took him into his service. Dīghāvu served diligently—rising early, sleeping late, being attentive, behaving pleasantly, and speaking kindly. The King grew very fond of him and kept him as a trusted attendant in the inner palace.

One day, King Brahmadatta went hunting in the forest. Prince Dīghāvu drove the chariot so that they became separated from the rest of the army. When they reached a very remote place, the King, being exhausted and wishing to sleep, asked Dīghāvu to unyoke the chariot. He then slept with his head on the lap of Prince Dīghāvu, who was sitting on the ground. While the King slept, Dīghāvu thought: "This King Brahmadatta has done me great harm. He seized our army, kingdom, and treasury. He killed my innocent parents. Now is the time to take revenge for that hatred." With this thought, he immediately drew his sword from its scabbard.

But then he thought: "My father told me before he died, 'Mā kho tvaṃ tāta Dīghāvu...' and so on, advising me not to take revenge. It is not right to disobey the words of parents spoken at the time of death." With this thought, he put the sword back into its scabbard. In this manner, he thought of killing the King three times, but after the final time, he returned the sword to its scabbard. Then King Brahmadatta woke up from his sleep in terror and agitation. He rose quickly and said: "Friend, I dreamed that Prince Dīghāvu, the son of King Dīghīti, was chasing me with a sword!"
38:
## 
At that time, Prince Dīghāvu seized King Brahmadatta by his topknot with his left hand, drew his sword with his right hand, and shouted: "Great King, I am the prince named Dīghāvu, the son of King Dīghīti of Kosala. You have caused us much harm and killed my innocent mother and father. Now is the time for me to take revenge for that enmity!"

Then King Brahmadatta prostrated himself at the feet of Prince Dīghāvu and pleaded, "Grant me my life, Prince Dīghāvu!"

Then Prince Dīghāvu, who was accustomed to obeying his parents and possessed a gentle heart, granted him his life and requested, "May the Great King also grant me my life." Thus, they spared each other's lives, took each other's hands, and made an oath not to break their friendship.

Later, upon returning to the palace from the forest, King Brahmadatta assembled his ministers and asked, "O ministers, if you were to see Prince Dīghāvu, the son of King Dīghīti of Kosala, what would you do?" Some ministers replied, "Great King, if we saw Prince Dīghāvu, we would cut off his hands," "We would cut off his feet," "We would cut off his ears," "We would cut off his nose," or "We would cut off his head," they said respectively.

"O ministers," the king said, "this youth is indeed the prince named Dīghāvu, the son of King Dīghīti of Kosala. It is not proper to do anything to him now, for he and I have spared each other's lives."

Having said this, King Brahmadatta asked Prince Dīghāvu, "Dear Dīghāvu, when your father was about to die, he spoke the words beginning with 'Mā kho tvaṃ tāta Dīghāvu.' With what meaning did he say those words?"

"Great King," Dīghāvu replied, "the meaning of the words my father spoke at the time of his death is: 'Do not let enmity last long,' and 'Do not be quick to break with friends.' If I were to kill the Great King because you killed my mother and father, those who wish for the Great King's welfare would kill me in return. Then, those who wish for my welfare would kill them. In this way, through such retaliatory killing, enmity would never cease. But now, the Great King has spared my life, and I have spared the Great King's life. Thus, through this non-retaliation of sparing each other's lives, that enmity has been appeased. It was with these three meanings in mind that my father, at the time of his death, gave me this advice with the words beginning with 'Mā kho tvaṃ tāta Dīghāvu.'"

Then King Brahmadatta of Kāsī said to Prince Dīghāvu, "You are able to understand in detail the words your father spoke in brief. You are truly wise; it is wonderful!" Being greatly pleased, he restored his father's wealth, army, kingdom, and treasuries to him, gave him his daughter in marriage, and they lived together in harmony and joy, ruling the country. Thus, the Blessed One brought forth this past story and identified the birth: "At that time, the mother and father became King Suddhodana and Queen Māyā. Prince Dīghāvu became I, the Buddha."

Having preached this Dīghītikosala Jātaka, the Buddha said, "Bhikkhus, those who have taken up sticks and clubs, those who have grasped weapons..."
39:
Even among those kings, such patience, gentleness of heart, and purity existed. "O monks, having gone forth in this well-expounded Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya, you should be those who are patient. You should be those who are easy to speak to and obedient. Such a state would be most beautiful in this Dispensation of mine," thus he exhorted them. Even after being exhorted in this way, he was unable to make those monks harmonious. At that time, the Blessed One, being weary of living in the midst of the quarreling monks, thought: "I am now living in great discomfort, crowded [by these monks]. These monks do not follow my words. It would be better if I were to live alone, secluded from the crowd."

## Departure to the Pārileyyaka Forest to Observe the Vassa
Having thought thus, he entered Kosambī for alms. Then, without informing the Saṅgha of monks, taking his own bowl and robes, he departed alone for the village named Pārileyyaka. In that village, the Blessed One taught the practice of living alone (ekacārika-vatta) to the elder named Bhagu. After that, at the Eastern Bamboo Park (Pācīnavaṃsadāya), he spoke to the three noble sons about their desire for harmony. Then he went to where the Pārileyyaka forest was. In that Pārileyyaka forest, depending on the village of Pārileyyaka, the Blessed One observed the Vassa comfortably at the foot of a Sal tree, receiving the ministrations of the elephant king named Pārileyyaka.

## Lay Devotees Arrange for the Harmony of the Saṅgha
When the lay devotees living in Kosambī went to the monastery and did not see the Blessed One, they asked, "Venerable sirs, where is the Blessed One?" and were told that he had gone to the Pārileyyaka forest. When they asked, "Why did he go?" the monks replied, "Even though he strove to make us harmonious and reconciled, we did not become reconciled. For this reason, he departed." Then the lay devotees asked, "Venerable sirs, having gone forth in the presence of the Blessed One, are you unable to be harmonious even when the Blessed One himself tries to reconcile you?" The monks replied, "Lay devotees, it is true that we are not harmonious." The lay devotees then said, "These monks, having gone forth in the presence of the Buddha, do not become harmonious even when the Buddha himself tries to reconcile them. Because of these monks, we do not have the opportunity to pay our respects to the Blessed One. Therefore, we shall not give these monks a place to stay, nor shall we pay them homage or perform other duties."

From then on, those lay devotees did not show even a sign of respect to those monks. Because they received little food and nourishment, the monks became emaciated. Within just two or three days, they became upright and settled in mind. They confessed their faults to one another and asked for forgiveness, saying, "Lay devotees, we have become harmonious. May you also be well-disposed toward us as before." Then the lay devotees asked, "Venerable sirs, have you asked for forgiveness from the Blessed One?" When they said, "Lay devotees, not yet," the laypeople replied, "If that is so, go and ask for forgiveness from the Blessed One. When you have asked for forgiveness from the Blessed One, we too shall be well-disposed toward you as before." Because it was during the Vassa, those monks did not dare to go to the presence of the Blessed One and had to spend those three months of the Vassa in hardship. As for the Blessed One, he lived comfortably throughout the three months of the Vassa, being attended to by the elephant king Pārileyyaka. That elephant king Pārileyyaka had also entered the forest for the sake of living comfortably, having abandoned the herd of elephants.

## The Elephant Pārileyyaka Attending the Blessed One
That elephant king Pārileyyaka thought: "I live crowded by young elephants, large female elephants, and elephants of various sizes. I have to eat grass with the tips already bitten off. I have to eat broken branches with disheveled leaves. I have to drink muddy water. When I go down to or come up from the watering place, the female elephants bump and push against my body. It would be better if I were to live alone, secluded from the herd." Having thought thus, that noble elephant left the herd and went to the place where the Pārileyyaka forest was, near a pleasant Sal tree full of branches and leaves, where the Blessed One was staying. He approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he looked here and there and, seeing no one else but the Buddha, he cleared the ground at the foot of the Sal tree by kicking and striking it with his feet. Taking a branch with his trunk, he swept the area. From then on, he brought a water pot with his trunk and provided water for drinking and for use. When hot water was needed, he prepared hot water. How did he prepare it? He rubbed pieces of wood together [with his trunk] to start a fire. Having put wood on the fire, when the fire blazed, he put stones in the fire to heat them. Then, using a wooden stick, he rolled them and dropped them into a small pool of water. Then, testing the water with his trunk, which served as his hand, to know it was hot, he went and prostrated himself before the Blessed One. The Blessed One asked, "Pārileyyaka, have you heated the water?" and then went to the place where the hot water was and bathed.

After the Buddha had bathed, the elephant brought and offered various kinds of large and small fruits to Him. Whenever the Blessed One entered the village for alms, the elephant would take the Buddha's bowl and robes, place them on his frontal globes (kumbha), and follow right along with the Buddha. When the Blessed One reached the outskirts of the village, He would say, "Pālileyyaka elephant, from here you cannot follow; bring Me My bowl and robes," and having made him hand them over, He would enter the village for alms. The elephant king would wait right there at the village outskirts until the Blessed One returned from the alms round. When the Blessed One returned, the elephant would go to meet Him, take the bowl and robes as before, place them at the foot of the sal tree where the Buddha resided, perform various duties, and fan Him with a tree branch. At night, to ward off dangers from wild beasts, he would carry a large staff with his trunk and wander about the forest thickets until dawn, thinking, "I shall protect the Blessed One." From that time on, that forest became known as the Pālileyyaka forest, guarded by the elephant king Pālileyyaka. When dawn broke, he would perform all the various duties, starting with offering water for washing the face, in the manner already described.

## One who performs good deeds by following a good example gains benefits

Thereafter, at one time, a certain monkey saw the elephant Pālileyyaka performing the noble duties known as abhisamācārika with great effort for the Blessed One. He thought, "I too shall perform some meritorious deed." While wandering about, one day he found a honeycomb on a branch without any bees. He broke off the branch and brought the honeycomb along with the branch to the Buddha. He cut a leaf from a wild plantain tree, placed the honeycomb on it, and offered it. The Blessed One accepted it. The monkey watched, thinking, "Will He eat it or not?" When he saw the Blessed One just holding it while sitting, he wondered why. He took the honeycomb by the edge of the branch, turned it over, and upon inspecting it, saw some bee larvae. He gently removed those larvae and offered it again. The Blessed One then ate it. The monkey, with a joyful and delighted mind, caught hold of various branches and began to dance. While he was swinging, the branch he was holding and the branch he was stepping on both broke, and he fell onto a tree stump. His body was impaled, and he died with a mind full of faith in the Blessed One. He was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in a golden mansion thirty leagues in size, surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs. Because he had been a monkey in his previous life, he became known as the god Makkata-devaputta.

## The Monks go to the Buddha

The fact that the Blessed One was residing in the Pālileyyaka forest, being attended to by a noble elephant, became famous throughout the entire Island of Jambudīpa. The merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, the lay devotee Visākhā, and other prominent donors sent word to the Venerable Ānanda, saying, "Please show us the Blessed One." About five hundred monks who had completed their rains retreat also approached the Venerable Ānanda and pleaded, "Friend Ānanda, it has been a long time since we have heard a Dhamma discourse from the presence of the Blessed One. Friend Ānanda, it would be good if we could get the opportunity to hear a Dhamma discourse in the presence of the Blessed One."

Venerable Ānanda took those monks and went to the Pālileyyaka forest. He thought, "It is not appropriate to approach the Blessed One, who has been living alone for the three months of the rains retreat, with such a large number of monks." So, he left the monks outside and approached the Blessed One alone. When the elephant king Pālileyyaka saw the Venerable Ānanda, he took up his staff and ran toward him. The Blessed One looked and said, "Pālileyyaka, step back, step back! Move aside and do not stop him. This person who has come to visit is My attendant." The elephant king dropped the staff right there and asked to take the bowl and robes. Venerable Ānanda did not give them. The noble elephant thought, "If this monk is well-trained in conduct, he will not place his bowl and requisites on the stone slab which is the seat of his teacher, the Blessed One." Venerable Ānanda then placed the bowl and robes on the ground.

[Commentary Note: Those who are accomplished in conduct and wise do not place their own requisites on the regular seats or beds of their respected parents and teachers.]

## The Value of a Good Friend

The Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down in a suitable place. The Buddha asked, "Ānanda, have you come alone?" When he replied, "Venerable Sir, I have come together with five hundred monks," the Buddha, upon hearing this, asked, "Where are those five hundred monks?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, not knowing the Blessed One's mind, I left them outside and came alone."

Then the Blessed One said, "Ānanda, go and call those five hundred monks." When Venerable Ānanda called them as instructed, the Buddha exchanged friendly greetings with the five hundred monks. The monks said, "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One possesses the delicacy of a Buddha and the delicacy of a king. For the three months of the rains retreat, the Blessed One must have endured hardship by standing and sitting alone. There was likely no one to perform duties or offer water for washing the face and so on."

Then the Blessed One said, "Monks, the elephant king Pārileyyaka has performed all my needs. If one finds such a good friend, it is proper to live together. If one does not find a good friend, it is better to live alone." Having said this, he preached the three verses from the Nāgavagga.

At the end of the verses, the five hundred monks were established in Arahantship.

## The Elephant King's Obstruction to the Return to Sāvatthī

Venerable Ānanda then conveyed the message sent by lay devotees such as Anāthapiṇḍika, saying, "Venerable Sir, five crores of noble disciples, led by Anāthapiṇḍika, greatly long for the Blessed One's return." The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, if that is so, take the bowl and robes." Having had the bowl and robes taken, as he was departing, the elephant king Pārileyyaka went and stood across the path.

Then the monks asked, "Venerable Sir, what does the elephant king desire by standing across the path?" The Buddha replied, "Monks, he desires to offer alms-food to you. This elephant king has been of great service to me for a long time. It is not proper to upset the mind of this devoted elephant. Therefore, monks, turn back for a while." Having said this, the Buddha called the monks and returned.

The elephant king entered the forest, gathered various fruits such as jackfruits and bananas, and offered them to the monks the next morning. The five hundred monks were unable to finish all the fruits. After the meal of fruits, the Blessed One took his bowl and robes and departed. The elephant king walked between the monks and again stood across the path in front of the Buddha to block him.

When the monks asked, "Venerable Sir, for what reason does he stand across the path and not move?" the Buddha replied, "Monks, this elephant king wants to send you away and have me return; that is why he stands across the path."
42:
## If One Knows and Follows, Danger is Averted

(6) Others do not realize that here we must perish.
But those who do realize this, their quarrels are stilled.

"Ettha": In the midst of this Saṅgha. "Pare": Those other than the wise who engage in quarrels. "Mayam": We. "Yamāmase": Shall go to the presence of the King of Death. "Iti na ca vijānanti": Thus they do not know. "Tattha": In the midst of that Saṅgha. "Ye ca paṇḍitā": Only those who are wise. "Mayam yamāmase": Know that we shall go to the realm of Death. "Tato": Because of such knowledge. "Medhagā": Quarrels. "Sammanti": Are stilled.

At that time, the Blessed One said to the elephant king, "Elephant Pālileyyaka—this departure of mine is one from which I shall not return. For you, in this elephant existence, there is no possibility of attaining Jhana, Insight (Vipassanā), the Path (Magga), or the Fruition (Phala). You remain here." Hearing these words, the elephant king put his trunk in his mouth and followed the Buddha, weeping and wailing. If the elephant king had been given the chance to make the Blessed One return, he would have served him for the rest of his life in the manner previously described. However, when they reached the outskirts of the village, the Blessed One said, "Elephant Pālileyyaka—from this place onwards is no longer your territory. It is a human habitation and is dangerous. You stay here." When he said this, the elephant king stood still, watching with streaming tears.

### The Death of the Elephant King and Becoming Pālileyyaka Devaputta

Afterwards, when the Blessed One had gone out of sight, the elephant king died of a broken heart. Because of his devotion to the Blessed One, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in a golden mansion thirty leagues in size, surrounded by a thousand nymphs, and became known as Pālileyyaka devaputta.

## Proceeding to Jetavana Monastery

The Blessed One gradually proceeded to Jetavana Monastery. When the monks living in Kosambī heard that the Blessed One had gone to Sāvatthī, they went to Sāvatthī to pay their respects to him. King Kosala, hearing that the quarrelsome monks from Kosambī were arriving, approached the Buddha and said, "Venerable Sir, I shall not allow those monks to enter my kingdom."

Then the Blessed One said, "Great King, those monks are virtuous. It was only because of their mutual quarreling that they did not follow my words. Now they come to pay respects to me. Great King, let them come." Anāthapiṇḍika the householder also said, "Venerable Sir, I shall not allow those monks to enter the monastery grounds." Because of this, the Blessed One rejected the request, just as he had with King Kosala, and remained silent. To those monks who arrived in Sāvatthī in due course, the Blessed One provided secluded lodgings in a suitable place. Other monks did not sit with them, stand with them, or pay respects to them. Whenever monks or brahmins arrived, they would ask the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, which are those quarrelsome monks from Kosambī?"

Then the Blessed One pointed them out, saying, "These are the monks." When they were pointed out by finger to every newcomer as "These are the quarrelsome monks, these are the ones," they became very ashamed. Not daring to lift their heads, they prostrated themselves at the feet of the Blessed One, paid their respects, and asked for forgiveness. Then the Blessed One said, "Dear monks, you have committed a heavy deed. Having ordained under a Buddha like me, you did not follow my words when I sought to bring harmony. Ancient wise ones, even when their parents were being killed, followed their parents' advice; though their parents were deprived of life and killed, they did not disobey their words and later came to rule two kingdoms."

Having said this, he retold the Kosambika Jātaka and said, "Dear monks, in this way, Prince Dīghāvu did not disobey the advice of his parents even though they were killed, and later, by winning the hand of King Brahmadatta's daughter, he came to rule the two kingdoms of Kāsi and Kosala. You, however, by not following my words, have committed a heavy deed." He then spoke this verse.

## Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the verse, the monks who had arrived were established in the Fruition of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The story of the Kosambī monks ends.

## 6. The Story of Cūḷakāla and Mahākāla

(The Story of Elder Mahākāla)

The Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Subhānupassiṃ" while residing in the Siṃsapā forest near the city of Setavya, concerning the three brothers who were householders: Cūḷakāla, Majjhimakāla, and Mahākāla.

## Two Brothers Arrive at Sāvatthī

The three brothers Cūḷakāla, Majjhimakāla, and Mahākāla, who lived in the city of Setavya, were all householders. Among the three brothers, the eldest and the youngest traveled to the four quarters selling various goods with five hundred wagons. On one occasion, the two brothers Cūḷakāla and Mahākāla took various goods with five hundred wagons to Sāvatthī and unyoked their wagons between Sāvatthī and Jetavana Monastery. Among the two brothers, Mahākāla, seeing the noble disciples (ariya-sāvakas) of Sāvatthī going to hear the Dhamma in the evening with flowers and perfumes in their hands, asked, "Where are these people going?" Upon learning the reason, he thought, "I shall go as well."

## Mahākāla’s Intention to Ordain

Then, calling his younger brother Cūḷakāla, he said, "Dear brother, look after these five hundred wagons diligently; I shall go to hear the Dhamma." Having given these instructions, he followed them, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat at the edge of the assembly. On that day, the Blessed One preached a discourse according to the disposition of the householder Mahākāla. By way of the Dukkhakkhandha Sutta and others, he explained in many ways the faults, the meanness, and the defilement of the five cords of sensual pleasure, as well as the benefits of renouncing them. Hearing that Dhamma, the householder Mahākāla thought: "All wealth must be abandoned and left behind. Wealth and kin do not follow one who goes to the next life. What is the use of living in the household life? I shall ordain."
43:
## Both Brothers Ordain

Then, after the crowd had paid homage to the Buddha and departed, Mahākāla requested ordination from the Buddha. The Buddha asked, "Is there anyone you should ask for permission?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, I have a younger brother." "If so, go and ask your younger brother's permission," the Buddha said. Saying "Very well, Venerable Sir," he returned and called his younger brother, saying, "Dear brother, take and enjoy all this wealth." The younger brother asked, "But brother, what will you do?" He replied, "I will ordain in the presence of the Buddha." The younger brother pleaded with Mahākāla in various ways but could not prevent his desire to ordain, so he said, "Elder brother, very well, do as you wish." Mahākāla went and ordained in the presence of the Buddha. Soon after, the younger brother Cūḷakāla also ordained, thinking, "I will ordain only to take my brother back [to lay life]."

## Practicing Dhamma in the Cemetery

Later, Mahākāla received higher ordination and approached the Buddha, asking, "Venerable Sir, how many duties are there in the Sasana?" When the Buddha explained the two duties, he said, "Venerable Sir, because I ordained in my old age, I am unable to fulfill the Gantha-dhura, the duty of studying the scriptures. However, I will fulfill the Vipassanā-dhura, the duty of insight meditation." He requested the Buddha to teach him the cemetery-dweller's practice (sosanika-dhutaṅga) leading up to Arahantship. After listening, when the first watch of the night had passed and all the monks had fallen asleep, he went to the cemetery and stayed there. In the early morning, before anyone else had risen, he returned to the monastery.
44:
## Meeting the Cemetery Keeper

Then, a woman named Kālī, who was a cemetery keeper and cremator of corpses, saw the places where the Elder stood, sat, and walked. She thought, "Who is coming here? I will investigate him." Unable to find out, one day she lit a lamp in the cemetery hut, took her children, and hid in a suitable place. Seeing the Elder arrive at the cemetery during the middle watch of the night, she approached, paid homage, and asked, "Venerable Sir, is our noble lord staying in this place?" He replied, "Yes, lay devotee." She said, "Venerable Sir, those who stay in a cemetery should learn the proper duties." The Elder did not say, "Why should we practice the duties you mention?" but instead asked, "Lay devotee, what duties should be performed?"

## Duties to be Observed by Cemetery Dwellers

The lay devotee then said, "Venerable Sir, monks who stay in a cemetery should inform the cemetery keepers, the senior Elder in the monastery, and the village headman of their stay." When the Elder asked, "For what reason should they be informed?" she replied, "When thieves who have stolen others' property are pursued by the owners, they might drop the goods in the cemetery and flee. Then the owners might cause trouble for those staying in the cemetery. If the cemetery keeper, the senior Elder, and the village headman have been informed, they can say, 'We know this monk has been staying in this cemetery for this long. He is not a thief,' and thus prevent trouble. Therefore, it is proper to inform them."

The Elder asked again, "What else should be done?" She replied, "Venerable Sir, a noble one staying in a cemetery should avoid eating fish, meat, sesame, flour, oil, molasses, and so on. One should not sleep during the day, should not be lazy, and should be possessed of exerted effort. One should be without deceit or hypocrisy and have noble intentions. In the evening, when everyone has fallen asleep, one should come from the monastery. In the early morning, before everyone has risen, one should return to the monastery."

"Venerable Sir, if the noble one, staying in this cemetery and following these instructions, is able to bring the monk's task to completion, [when you pass away] and they bring and discard your body, I will place it on a grand bier with a canopy, honor it with flowers and perfumes, and perform the funeral rites. If you cannot complete the monk's task, I will place it on a pyre, light the fire, pull it out with a hook, throw it outside, strike it with an axe, cut it into pieces, and throw it back into the fire to be cremated."

Then the Elder said to the cemetery keeper named Kālī, "Good woman, when you see a certain visual object (a corpse), please tell me." She agreed, saying, "Very well." The Elder continued to strive in his monk's duties in the cemetery according to his intention. As for the Elder Cūḷakāla, his mind was constantly restless, thinking only of the household life and repeatedly longing for his wife and children, thinking, "My elder brother is indeed performing a very burdensome task."

## Meditating on the Visual Object of a Young Woman

At that time, a certain young woman died in the evening from a sudden, severe illness, without having been withered or exhausted. Her relatives brought the corpse of the young woman to the cemetery in the evening along with wood, oil, and other supplies. They handed it over to the cemetery keeper, saying, "Please cremate this young woman's body," paid her, and left. That cemetery keeper named Kālī removed the cloth covering the young woman's corpse. Seeing the body, which had just died and was full of flesh and had a beautiful golden complexion, she thought, "This corpse is a suitable object to show the noble one." She went and paid homage to the Elder and said, "There is such an object. Please come and look, Venerable Sir." The Elder said, "Very well," and had the covering cloth removed. Looking from the soles of the feet up to the tips of the hair, he said, "This visual object is very beautiful..."
45:
Impermanent indeed are formations,
Subject to arising and passing away.
Having arisen, they cease;
Their subsiding is bliss.

Formations (saṅkhāras) are truly impermanent. They have the nature of arising and passing away. Having arisen, they cease. Nibbāna, which is the cessation of those formations, is supreme bliss.

Looking at the body, he saw it had a golden complexion and instructed, "When you put this corpse into the fire and it is being consumed by the great flames, please inform me." Having said this, he went back to his place and sat down. The cemetery keeper named Kālī did as the Elder had instructed and informed him. When the Elder went and looked at the corpse, the parts touched and burnt by the flames looked like the skin of a brindled cow. The feet had slipped from the pyre and were hanging down. The hands were contorted and curled. The skin was gone from the thighs and the forehead. Then the Elder Mahākāḷa reflected, "Oh, this corpse, which just now could cause boundless delight to those looking at it, has now reached destruction and decay." He went to his night quarters, sat down, and clearly contemplating destruction and decay, he recited this verse:

After reciting this verse, as he developed insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahatship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). After the Elder Mahākāḷa attained Arahatship, the Teacher, surrounded by the community of monks, was wandering on a journey and arrived at the city of Setavya, where he entered and stayed in the Siṃsapā forest.

## Cūḷakāla's Return to Lay Life

The wives of Cūḷakāla heard that the Teacher had arrived at the Siṃsapā forest. Thinking, "We will seize our husband," they sent a messenger to invite the Teacher for a meal. In a place not habitually frequented by the Buddhas, a monk who is skilled in directing the arrangement of seats should go first before the Buddha arrives. This is true: the Buddha's seat is prepared in the center, and to the right of the Buddha's seat, the seat of the Elder Sāriputta is prepared. To the left, the seat of the Elder Moggallāna is prepared. Starting from those seats on the left and right, the seats for the community of monks are prepared on both sides.
46:
To the left, the seat of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna is prepared. From there, the seats for the community of monks are to be prepared on both sides. Therefore, the Elder Mahākāḷa, standing at the place where robes are adjusted, sent his younger brother, the Elder Cūḷakāla, saying, "Brother Cūḷakāla, you go ahead and direct the arrangement of the seats." From the moment they saw the Elder Cūḷakāla, the household members and wives began to mock and joke with him. They spread low seats at the end for the senior monks and high seats at the end for the junior monks. Cūḷakāla said, "Do not do this. Do not place low seats at the top; place high seats at the top and low seats at the bottom." The women, as if not hearing his words, said, "What are you doing wandering around? Is it not proper for you to arrange the seats? Whom did you ask for permission to become a monk? Why did you become a monk? Why did you come to this house?" Saying this, they pulled off his inner and outer robes, made him wear white clothes, placed a flower wreath on his head, and sent him off, saying, "Go, fetch the Teacher; we will finish arranging the seats." Since he had not been a monk for long and had not even completed a single rainy season retreat (vassa) before disrobing, he did not know how to feel ashamed. Thus, in that appearance, without any hesitation, he went, paid homage to the Teacher, and returned leading the community of monks headed by the Buddha.

## The Former Wives' Plot

At the conclusion of the meal for the community of monks, the wives of the Elder Mahākāḷa thought, "The wives of Cūḷakāla have seized their husband. We, too, shall seize our husband Mahākāḷa and make him return to lay life." Thinking thus, they invited the Teacher again for the following morning. At that time, a monk other than Mahākāḷa went to arrange the seats. Those wives of Mahākāḷa, not getting an opportunity at that moment, offered the meal while the community of monks headed by the Buddha were seated. Cūḷakāla had two wives, Majjhimakāla had four, and Mahākāḷa had eight. Among the community of monks, those who wished to eat sat and had their meal. Those who wished to go outside stood up and left. The Teacher, however, sat and finished his meal. At the conclusion of the Teacher's meal, those former wives of Mahākāḷa requested, "Venerable Sir, the Elder Mahākāḷa will follow after performing the anumodanā (blessing) for us. May the Exalted Ones please go ahead." The Teacher said, "Very well," and departed ahead of him.
47:
When they reached the village gate, the monks criticized, saying: "Why has the Blessed One performed the act of leaving Elder Mahākāla behind? Did he do so knowingly or unknowingly? Yesterday, because Cūḷakāla went ahead, an obstacle to his monkhood occurred. Today, because another monk went ahead, no obstacle occurred. Now, he has left Mahākāla behind. Indeed, they might create an obstacle to the monkhood of Elder Mahākāla, who is a monk endowed with the practice of virtue."

The Blessed One, hearing the monks' criticism, turned back, stood still, and asked: "Monks, what are you discussing?" They reported the matter to him. Then the Buddha asked: "Do you consider Mahākāla to be like Cūḷakāla?" "Yes, Blessed One, we do. That Cūḷakāla had only two wives, but this Mahākāla has eight. If he is surrounded and seized by eight wives, what can he do?" they replied to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One said: "Monks, do not say so. Cūḷakāla lives frequently dwelling on beautiful objects with a mind that is constantly wavering; he is like a weak tree standing on a cliff. But my son Mahākāla lives constantly contemplating the foul..."
48:
...unshakable like a solid rock mountain." Having said this, he spoke these verses:
