*Asubhānupassiṃ*: one who frequently contemplates things as foul. *Viharantaṃ*: living. *Indriyesu*: in the six sense faculties such as the eye. *Susaṃvutaṃ*: well-guarded. *Bhojanamhi ca mattaññū*: also knowing the three measures in seeking, receiving, and consuming food. *Saddhaṃ*: endowed with mundane faith characterized by belief in kamma and its results, and supramundane faith known as unwavering confidence in the Three Jewels such as the Buddha. *Āraddhavīriyaṃ*: having effort that is aroused. *Taṃ puggalaṃ*: that person. *Māro*: the Māra of defilements. *Ve*: certainly. *Nappasahati*: cannot oppress or overcome. *Yathā kiṃ*: for example, how? *Vāto*: a weak wind. *Selaṃ*: made of solid rock. *Pabbataṃ*: a mountain. *Nappasahati iva*: just as it cannot oppress or overcome.

The former wives of that Mahākāla also surrounded the Elder and said, "By whose permission did you ordain? Will you become a layman now or not?" and so on, desiring to remove his robes. Then Elder Mahākāla, noting the behavior of those women, rose from his seat and, by psychic power, ascended into the sky. Breaking through the peak of the gabled house into two, he traveled through the air and, just as the Blessed One was finishing the verse, descended from the sky while greatly praising the Blessed One’s golden-hued body, and bowed his head at the feet of the Tathāgata with faith and devotion.

## Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the verse, the monks who had arrived were established in the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The story of Cūḷakāla and Mahākāla ends.

119. O Monks! The hunter Sonuttara, a doer of evil deeds, having dug a pit, placed his bow and arrow inside and covered it with planks. Having lowered himself into it, he shot the elephant king who approached the pit with a large poisoned arrow.

120. O Monks! The elephant king, pierced by the hunter Sonuttara, trumpeted a terrible cry three times. All eight thousand elephants also made a fearful echoing sound. Those eight thousand elephants, crushing grass and branches to dust, fled in all eight directions.

121. O Monks! When that Chaddanta elephant king reached out to kill the hunter Sonuttara, he saw the yellow robe (kāsāva), which is the banner of the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arhats who seek the collection of virtues such as the aggregate of morality. Then, to the Bodhisatta who was oppressed by pain, this thought arose: "The banner of Arahatship is inviolable to the virtuous and wise; on the contrary, it is only to be honored." This perception became clear to him.

The following is the sequential account of how the hunter Sonuttara prepared the pit. That hunter Sonuttara reached the dwelling place of the Bodhisatta Chaddanta elephant king in seven years, seven months, and seven days. Following the aforementioned method, he marked the elephant king's dwelling and thought, "I will dig a pit here, stay inside, and kill the elephant king with a poisoned arrow." Having decided this, he entered the forest, cut trees for pillars and other needs, and prepared the materials. When the elephants went to bathe, he dug a square pit at the elephant king's dwelling with a large hoe. He scattered the excavated soil into the water as if sowing seeds. He set pillars upon stone mortars, placed beams and rafters, and laid down planks. He made a hole just large enough for an arrow to pass through and covered the top with dust and refuse. He made an entrance for himself on one side. When the pit was finished, at dawn, he put on a head-cover, donned saffron-dyed robes, took his bow and poisoned arrow, descended into the pit, and waited.

To clarify this matter, the Blessed One said:

The arrow of the hunter Sonuttara pierced through the navel of the Bodhisatta Chaddanta elephant king, crushing the spleen and other internal organs, cutting the intestines, and exited through the back as if struck by an axe, flying into the sky. Blood flowed from the wound like dye from a broken jar. Intense and painful sensations arose.

The Bodhisatta elephant king, unable to endure the painful sensations, being overcome by suffering, let out a cry like a crane three times, making the entire mountain echo at once.
50:
All eight thousand attendant elephants, upon hearing the voice of the Bodhisatta elephant, were terrified of death and let out a fearful roar in response to the Bodhisatta's cry. Hearing that sound and seeing the Bodhisatta elephant in great pain, they ran about, crushing grass and branches to dust, thinking, "We shall catch the enemy."

When the eight thousand attendant elephants had fled in different directions, Queen Subhaddā stood by his side, supporting and comforting him. The Bodhisatta elephant king, enduring the painful sensations, noted the direction from which the arrow came and thought: "If this arrow had come from the east or other directions, it would have entered through the frontal globes and exited through the hindquarters. However, this arrow entered through the navel and exited toward the sky. Therefore, the enemy must be stationed inside the earth." Wishing to investigate the enemy's position, he thought, "Who can know this? What will happen? It is best for Subhaddā to flee." Thus, he said:

"Subhaddā, the eight thousand attendant elephants have fled to various directions to search for my enemy. But you, what are you doing here near me?" he asked.
51:
## The Past Life of Devadatta

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Vārāṇasī, a certain elephant hunter living in Vārāṇasī made a living by repeatedly killing elephants and selling their tusks, claws, nails, small intestines, large intestines, and solid flesh. At that time, in a certain forest, many thousands of elephants, seeking food, would frequent a grazing ground. Whenever they saw the Paccekabuddhas, from the moment they saw them, both when going and returning, they would bow down on their knees in homage before departing.

One day, the elephant hunter, seeing the manner in which those elephants paid homage, reflected: "I have to kill these elephants with great difficulty and hardship. Yet these elephants, whenever they go or come, pay homage to the Paccekabuddhas. What is it that they see and pay homage to?" Having noted that "they pay homage because they see the yellow robe," he thought, "It is proper for me to obtain a yellow robe now."

While a Paccekabuddha was descending into Lake Jātassara to bathe, the hunter stole one of the robes left on the bank. He then went to the path where the elephants traveled, and holding a spear, he sat down covering his entire body, including his head, with the robe. When the elephants saw the hunter sitting there covered in the robe, they departed after paying homage, thinking he was a Paccekabuddha. That elephant hunter would then pierce and kill the elephant that was walking at the very end of the herd with his spear. He would take the tusks and other parts, bury the remains in the ground, and depart.

Later, the Bodhisatta took conception in the elephant womb and, when born, became the leader of the herd, the elephant king. At that time, the elephant hunter continued to act in the same way as before. The Great Being, the elephant king, noticing the depletion of his followers, asked, "Where have these elephants gone? Why have they become few?" When they replied, "Lord, we do not know," he thought, "When going to any place, they would not go without informing me. There must be some danger." Suspecting that "there must be danger from the one sitting covered in a yellow robe in a certain place," he thought, "It is proper to investigate him." He sent all the elephants ahead and followed behind himself, lagging intentionally.
52:
## The Teaching

(9) He who is not free from stain (of defilements), yet would wear the saffron-dyed robe, who is devoid of self-control and truth, he is not worthy of the saffron-dyed robe.

(10) But he who has discarded the stains (of defilements), who is well-established in the virtues, and is endowed with self-control and truth, he indeed is worthy of the saffron-dyed robe.

'Anikkasāvo' means one who still possesses the stains of defilements such as lust (rāga). 'Paridahissati' means one will use it by way of wearing, dressing, or spreading it out. There is also a reading 'paridhassati'. 'Apeto damasaccena' means devoid of or separated from the restraint of the senses (indriya-dama) and from verbal truth which belongs to the side of ultimate truth. 'Na so' means such a person is not worthy to wear the saffron-dyed robe. 'Vantakasāvassa' means one who has vomited, discarded, or abandoned the stains of defilements through the four Paths (magga). 'Sīlesu' refers to the fourfold purity of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla). 'Susamāhito' means well-established or well-composed. 'Upeto' means endowed with the aforementioned restraint of the senses and truth. 'Sa ve' means such a person is indeed worthy of that fragrant saffron-dyed robe.

As the other elephants departed after paying homage, the Great Being, seeing the hunter as he approached, the hunter gathered his robe and threw the spear. The Great Being, approaching with mindfulness established, stepped back and caused the spear to miss. Then, thinking "This man has destroyed these elephants," he rushed forward to seize him. The hunter hid behind a tree.

Then, as the elephant king was about to encircle the hunter along with the tree with his trunk, seize him, and strike him against the ground, he saw the yellow robe that the hunter had pulled out and shown. He reflected, "If I were to harm or kill this hunter, my sense of shame before the many thousands of Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahats would be broken." Thus enduring it, he asked, "Did you not destroy this many of my kinsmen?" When the hunter confessed, "Yes, Lord," the elephant king said, "Why did you commit such a grave deed? By wearing the robe that is unsuitable and unworthy for yourself, but suitable and worthy only for the passionless ones (Arahats), and committing such an act, you have done a very grave thing."

Having said this, and wishing to further rebuke and admonish him, he spoke the verses: "Anikkasāvo kāsāvaṃ... sa ve kāsāvam-arahati," and after saying, "You have done what is improper and grave," he released him.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the elephant hunter was Devadatta, and the elephant king who rebuked him was I myself." Having thus concluded the Jātaka, he said, "Monks, not only now, but in the past also, Devadatta wore a robe that was unsuitable and unworthy for him," and he spoke these verses.

(This meaning should also be illustrated by the Chaddanta Jātaka.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the verses, the visiting monk who resided in that region became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). Many other monks also attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth. The teaching became beneficial to the great multitude.

The Story of Devadatta, the seventh.

## 8. The Story of Venerable Sāriputta
(Sāriputtattheravatthu)

"Asāre sāramatino..." While residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching concerning the refusal of Sañjaya to come, as reported by the Chief Disciples. In this story, the following is the sequential account:

## The Bodhisatta Sumedha Laying Himself as a Bridge

Counting back from this world-cycle, four incalculable periods (asankheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons ago, our Teacher was born as a young Brahmin named Sumedha in the city of Amaravatī. Having reached perfection in all arts and sciences, and after his parents had passed away, he gave away wealth amounting to many millions in charity. He then renounced the world as an ascetic and lived in the Himalayas, where he developed the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and supernormal powers (abhiññā). While traveling through the air, he saw the Sudassana city of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara...
53:
“It is the time, O Deva, O Great Hero! Arise in your mother’s womb. Rescuing the world together with the devas, awaken to the Deathless State.”

O Great Hero, you who possess great exertion. O Deva, the Bodhisatta King of Devas. For you, the time has come to become a Buddha. Please be born in your mother’s womb. While rescuing and assisting the multitude of humans together with the devas, please realize Nibbāna, the Deathless State.

“The time, the region, the island, the clan, and the mother as well—having observed these five, the Great Renowned One is born.”

The time of becoming a Buddha; the Middle Country (Majjhima-desa) where Buddhas are born; the island of Jambudīpa where Buddhas are born; the clan, namely the Brahmin or Khattiya clans, in which Buddhas are born; and the mother who is worthy of a Buddha—having observed these five, the Bodhisatta of great renown is born.

Seeing people clearing and preparing the path for the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara to enter the city of Rammavatī from the monastery, he [Sumedha] also took a portion of the ground to clear. Before that section was finished, the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara arrived. He made himself a bridge, spreading his antelope skin (ajina-camma) over the mud. (Note: *Ajina-camma*—a certain type of black leopard is called *thit-net*. As they are creatures with very little sensual lust, their skins are highly valued and used as robes or seats by noble hermits who practice to diminish lust.) He lay prostrate, thinking, “Let the Buddha, together with the assembly of disciples, proceed by treading upon me instead of treading in the mud.” Upon seeing the hermit Sumedha, the Buddha immediately prophesied: “This is a sprout of a Buddha. In the future, at the end of four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons, he will become a Buddha named Gotama.”

## Receiving Predictions from the Twenty-Four Buddhas

After the time of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, he also received predictions in the presence of these twenty-three Buddhas who had appeared and illuminated the three worlds with their radiance: Koṇḍañña, Maṅgala, Sumana, Revata, Sobhita, Anomadassī, Paduma, Nārada, Padumuttara, Sumedha, Sujāta, Piyadassī, Atthadassī, Dhammadassī, Siddhattha, Tissa, Phussa, Vipassī, Sikhī, Vessabhū, Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa.

## The Deities and Brahmās Request the Bodhisatta

He fulfilled the thirty perfections in their lower, middle, and highest degrees: the ten Perfections (Pāramīs), which consist of sacrificing external possessions, kingdoms, and so on; the ten Higher Perfections (Upapāramīs), which consist of sacrificing limbs such as hands and feet; and the ten Ultimate Perfections (Paramattha-pāramīs), which consist of sacrificing one’s life. Having fulfilled these, and while existing in the state of King Vessantara, he performed great acts of giving that caused the earth to tremble and renounced his wife and children. At the end of that life, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven. While residing there for the full lifespan of the Tusita devas, the deities and Brahmās from ten thousand world systems gathered in unison and requested him with this verse:

## The Five Great Observations

When they had thus requested him, he made the Five Great Observations. Having passed away from that Tusita heaven, he took conception in the Sakyan royal clan and was born from his mother’s womb after the lapse of ten months. When he reached the age of sixteen, being provided for with great glory and prosperity within the Great Sakyan royal clan, he gradually reached the prime of youth. In three palaces suitable for the three seasons...
54:
Cool indeed is that mother; cool indeed is that father.
Cool indeed is that woman who has such a husband.
For which mother there is such a noble son, that mother is indeed cool (at peace). For which father there is such a noble son, that father is indeed cool. For which woman there is such a noble husband, that woman is indeed cool.

## The Appearance of the Four Great Omens
At that time, while enjoying royal splendor like that of the celestial realm in three palaces suited to the three seasons, and while proceeding to the garden for recreation, he saw in succession the three divine messengers—the aged, the sick, and the dead. Being struck with great agitation (saṃvega), he returned. On his fourth trip, seeing the appearance of a renunciant, he thought, “Excellent is renunciation,” and developed a desire for the monkhood. He proceeded to the garden and spent the day there. While sitting on the bank of the Mangala lotus pond, the deva Vissakamma, disguised as a barber, adorned and decorated him magnificently. After that, upon hearing the news of the birth of Prince Rāhula and realizing the great strength of a father’s love for his son, he thought, “Before this bond of affection grows, I shall cut it immediately.”

## Rewarding Kisāgotamī
After the Bodhisatta had made this resolution, as he was entering the royal city in the evening—
Hearing this verse spoken by his cousin named Kisāgotamī, he thought, “This Kisāgotamī has made me hear the word ‘Nibbuta’ (the state of being cool/peaceful).” He then removed his pearl necklace from his neck and sent it to her as a reward.

## Approaching the Hermits Āḷāra and Udaka
Thereafter, entering his royal apartments and resting on his magnificent couch, he saw the repulsive and distorted postures of the sleeping female performers and dancers. Feeling weary and disenchanted in his heart, he woke Channa, had him bring the horse Kanthaka, and mounting Kanthaka with Channa as his companion, he made the Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana) surrounded by the devas and brahmas of the ten thousand world systems. Having renounced the world on the banks of the Anomā River, he proceeded in due course to the city of Rājagaha. While he was staying in the Paṇḍava mountain cave after wandering for alms in Rājagaha, King Bimbisāra, the ruler of Magadha, offered him his kingdom. He rejected the offer but gave his promise to the King that he would return to his kingdom after attaining Omniscience. He then approached the hermits Āḷāra and Udaka.

## Becoming the Omniscient Buddha
Approaching those hermits, he was not satisfied with the special attainments he gained there, nor did he find them sufficient. For six years, he practiced the Great Striving (Dukkharacariyā). On the morning of the full moon day of Vesākha, he partook of the milk-rice offered by Sujātā. He floated the golden bowl in the Nerañjarā River and spent the day in various meditative attainments in the great forest grove on the riverbank. In the evening, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by the youth named Sotthiya. Being praised for his virtues by Kāla, the Naga King, he ascended the Bodhimaṇḍa (the Terrace of Enlightenment) and spread the grass. He made a solemn vow: “As long as my mind is not liberated from the taints (āsavas) through non-clinging, I shall not break this cross-legged sitting posture.” Facing the East, he dispelled the army of Māra before sunset. In the first watch of the night, he attained the knowledge of past lives (Pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa); in the middle watch, he attained the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings (Cutūpapātañāṇa); and at the end of the last watch, he gained insight into Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) and realized Omniscience (Sabbaññutañāṇa), adorned with all the Buddha’s qualities such as the Ten Powers (Dasabala) and the Fourfold Intrepidity (Catuvesārajja).
55:
Cutūpapātañāṇa = Cuti + Upapāta + Ñāṇa: The knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.

The Ten Powers (Dasabalañāṇa) are the ten kinds of knowledge of things as they really are: 1. The possible and the impossible, 2. The results of kamma, 3. The way leading to all destinations, 4. The world with its many and various elements, 5. The diverse inclinations of beings, 6. The faculties of other beings, 7. The defilement, cleansing, and emergence regarding jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments, 8. The recollection of past lives, 9. The passing away and rebirth of beings, and 10. The destruction of taints.

The Four Kinds of Intrepidity (Catuvesārajjañāṇa) are the four kinds of self-confidence: 1. In teaching the things that are obstacles, 2. In teaching the things that lead to liberation from the suffering of saṃsāra, 3. In teaching the penetration of the Four Noble Truths, and 4. In teaching the destruction of taints.

## The Request of Brahma Sahampati
After attaining Omniscient Buddhahood, the Blessed One spent seven weeks (forty-nine days) at the Bodhi tree. In the eighth week, while staying at the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree, a resting place for goatherds, he reflected on the profundity and subtlety of the Dhamma and inclined towards remaining inactive. Then, Brahma Sahampati, accompanied by a host of Great Brahmas from ten thousand world systems, requested him to teach the Dhamma. The Buddha looked at the world with the Buddha-eye (the Buddha-eye consists of the knowledge of the faculties of beings and their underlying tendencies). Accepting the respectful request of Brahma Sahampati, he considered, "To whom should I teach the Dhamma first?" Realizing that the ascetics Āḷāra and Uddaka had passed away, he remembered the great help of the five ascetics. Rising from his seat, he set out for the city of Vārāṇasī in the Kāsī country. On the way, he met and conversed with a naked ascetic named Upaka. On the full moon day of Āsāḷha, he reached the dwelling place of the five ascetics in the Deer Park at Isipatana. He convinced the five ascetics, who had initially addressed him with improper terms, of his Buddhahood. Then, he set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, causing eighteen crores of devas and Brahmas, headed by Aññāsi Koṇḍañña, to drink the nectar of the Deathless. Having set the noble Wheel of Dhamma in motion, on the fifth day of the waning moon, he established all those five ascetics in the fruit of Arahantship.

## The Ordination of Yasa and Fifty-five Others, and the Thirty Bhaddavaggiya Brothers
On that very day, seeing that the youth named Yasa possessed the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya), the Buddha saw him leaving home in the night out of weariness. The Buddha called to him, "Come, Yasa." That same night, he led him to the fruit of Stream-entry, and the following morning, he led him to the fruit of Arahantship. On another occasion, he ordained fifty-four of Yasa's friends as "Ehi Bhikkhu" and led them to Arahantship. Thus, when sixty-one Arahants had appeared in the world, and after the rainy season retreat and the Pavāraṇā ceremony, he said, "Go forth, monks, on a journey," sending the sixty monks to various directions. He himself went to the Uruvelā forest. On the way, in the Kappāsika grove, he disciplined the thirty Bhaddavaggiya princes.
56:
Among those thirty princes, the one who was the youngest in terms of virtue became a Stream-enterer, and the one who was the most excellent in virtue became a Non-returner. He ordained all those Bhaddavaggiya princes as "Ehi Bhikkhu" and sent them to various directions.

## Converting the Thousand and Entering Rājagaha
The Blessed One himself went to the Uruvelā forest and, after performing three thousand five hundred miracles, disciplined the three ascetic brothers, including Uruvelā Kassapa, who had a retinue of one thousand matted-hair ascetics. He ordained them as "Ehi Bhikkhu." Then, having them stay on the Gayāsīsa rock, he established them in the fruit of Arahantship through the Ādittapariyāya Sutta. Surrounded by those thousand Arahants, he went to the Laṭṭhivana palm grove near the city of Rājagaha, thinking, "I shall fulfill the promise given to King Bimbisāra." Hearing the news that "The Teacher has arrived," King Bimbisāra came with one hundred and twenty thousand brahmins and householders. When the Buddha preached the sweet Dhamma, King Bimbisāra, along with one hundred and ten thousand brahmins and householders, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry, while ten thousand brahmins and householders were established in the Three Refuges. The next morning, Sakka, the king of devas, took the form of a young man and preceded the Buddha into Rājagaha, joyfully singing praises of his virtues. After the Buddha had finished his meal at King Bimbisāra's palace, he accepted the donation of the Veḷuvana monastery and resided there. At that time, Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Moggallāna came to visit the Blessed One.

## Upatissa and Kolita
Even before the Buddha appeared, there were two brahmin villages near Rājagaha called Upatissa and Kolita. In those two villages, on the very day that a child was conceived in the womb of the brahmin woman named Rūpasārī in Upatissa village, a child was also conceived in the womb of the brahmin woman named Moggallī in Kolita village. Those two families had been close friends for seven generations. Both women were given pregnancy care on the same day. After ten months, both gave birth to sons. On the naming day, the son of the brahmin woman Rūpasārī was named Upatissa because he was the son of the leading family in Upatissa village. The son of the brahmin woman Moggallī was named Kolita because he was the son of the leading family in Kolita village. As those two youths grew up, they mastered all the arts. When the youth Upatissa went to the river or the park for recreation, he was accompanied by five hundred golden palanquins. The youth Kolita was accompanied by five hundred chariots drawn by thoroughbred horses. Both youths had a retinue of five hundred young men each.
57:
## The Desire to Seek the Dhamma Arises While Watching a Festival

At that time, in the city of Rājagaha, there was an annual event known as the mountain-top festival. For those two youths, seats were prepared and arranged in a single place. While the two youths sat together watching the festival, they would laugh at things that were laughable, feel terror at things that were terrifying, and give rewards where rewards were due. In this manner, one day, because their wisdom had reached maturity, they did not laugh at laughable things, feel terror at terrifying things, or give rewards where rewards were due, as they had on previous days. While watching the festival, the two of them thought: "What is there to look at in this festival? All these beings will reach a state of being nameless before a hundred years have passed. It is proper for us to seek a Dhamma that leads to liberation from the cycle of rebirth."

Taking this as their object of thought, they remained there. Then Kolita asked Upatissa, "Friend Upatissa, you are not joyful and happy as on other days; you seem to be in a state of discontent. What object are you contemplating?" Upatissa replied, "Friend Kolita, there is no essence in watching these festivals; it is useless. I am sitting here reflecting that it is proper to seek the Dhamma of liberation for oneself. Why are you also in a state of discontent?" When Kolita spoke in the same manner as Upatissa, Upatissa realized that Kolita shared the same aspiration as himself and said, "A good thought has occurred to both of us. For us who wish to seek the Dhamma of liberation, it is proper to obtain the state of a monk. Therefore, under which teacher shall we ordain?"

## Becoming Disciples of the Great Teacher Sañjaya

At that time, a wanderer named Sañjaya resided in the city of Rājagaha together with a large following of wanderers. Upatissa and Kolita, deciding to ordain under Sañjaya, sent away five hundred youths, saying, "Take the palanquins and chariots and go." The two youths then went with one palanquin and one chariot and ordained under the wanderer Sañjaya.

From the time Upatissa and Kolita ordained, Sañjaya came to possess exceedingly great gains, offerings, and fame. Within just two or three days, Upatissa and Kolita thoroughly mastered Sañjaya's entire doctrine and asked, "Teacher, is the doctrine you know only this much, or is there more beyond this?" When he replied, "It is only this much; you have known everything," they thought:

## They Seek Only the Deathless Dhamma

"If this is the case, the practice of the holy life under this teacher is useless. We have come forth to seek the Dhamma of liberation. It is not possible to realize that Dhamma under this teacher. The island of Jambudīpa is indeed vast..."
58:
They thought, "While wandering through villages, towns, and royal capitals, we will surely find a teacher who can preach the Dhamma that leads out of Saṃsāra." From then on, wherever it was said that there were wise monks or Brahmins, they went to those places to discuss and inquire. Other wise men could not answer the questions asked by Upatissa and Kolita. However, Upatissa and Kolita were able to answer the questions of those wise men. Thus, after wandering and investigating throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, they returned to their original place and made a pact: "Friend Kolita, between the two of us, let the one who first attains the Deathless (Amata) inform the other."

## Meeting with Venerable Assaji Thera

While Upatissa and Kolita lived having made this pact, according to the sequence of events mentioned, the Buddha arrived at Rājagaha, accepted the donation of the Veḷuvana Monastery, and resided there. At that time, among the sixty-one Arahants sent by the Buddha to manifest the virtues of the Triple Gem, saying, "Monks, wander for the welfare and benefit of many," Venerable Assaji Thera, who was among the group of five monks (Pañcavaggiya), returned and arrived at Rājagaha. Early in the morning, Venerable Assaji took his bowl and robes and entered Rājagaha for alms. At that time, Upatissa the wandering ascetic (paribbājaka) had also finished his morning meal and, while going to the park where the ascetics stayed, saw Venerable Assaji and thought: "I have never seen such a monk before. Among those in the world who are Arahants or have entered the path to Arahatship, this monk must be one of them. It would be good if I approached this monk and asked: 'Friend, on whose account have you gone forth? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you approve of?'"

Then, this thought occurred to Upatissa the paribbājaka: "It is not the right time to ask this monk questions. He has entered the village and is wandering for alms. It would be good if I followed this monk step by step, just as those who wish to know a path they do not know clearly follow behind." Thinking thus, he followed him step by step. When Upatissa saw that Venerable Assaji had finished his alms round and wished to sit in a certain place, he recognized this and spread out his own ascetic's stool for him. After the Elder had finished his meal, Upatissa also offered water from his own water-pot. Having performed these duties of a pupil, and when the meal was finished, he exchanged pleasant and polite conversation with the Elder and asked: "Friend, your faculties (indriya) are indeed serene. Your complexion is pure and bright. Friend, on whose account have you gone forth? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you approve of?"

Venerable Assaji thought: "These wandering ascetics are opponents of the Dispensation (Sāsana). I will show him the profundity of this Dispensation." Wishing to show his status as a junior monk (navaka), he said: "Friend, I am a junior, not long ordained. I have only recently come to this Dhamma and Vinaya. I am not yet able to preach the Dhamma in detail." Then the paribbājaka said: "I am Upatissa. Venerable sir, please speak according to your ability, whether little or much. It is my responsibility to penetrate and understand that teaching through a hundred or a thousand ways." Thinking thus, he spoke this verse:

Appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā bhāsassu, atthaññeva me brūhi.
Attheneva me attho, kiṃ kāhasi byañjanaṃ bahuṃ.

Appaṃ vā: whether a little Dhamma.
Bahuṃ vā: or much Dhamma.
Bhāsassu: please speak.
Me: to me.
Atthaññeva: only the meaning.
Brūhi: please tell.
Me: for me.
Attheneva: only with the meaning.
Attho: there is a need.
Bahuṃ: many.
Byañjanaṃ: words/phrasing.
Kiṃ kāhasi: what will you do?
59:
## The Dhamma Taught by Venerable Assaji

When the wanderer spoke thus, the Elder recited the verse beginning with "Ye dhammā hetuppabhavā." Upon hearing just the first two lines, the wanderer was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry, adorned with a thousand methods. He completed the understanding of the remaining two lines at the moment of attaining the Fruit of Stream-entry. Having become a Stream-enterer, when Upatissa the wanderer was unable to progress to the higher paths and fruits, he noted, "There must be a reason why I cannot attain the higher paths and fruits at this moment," and said to Venerable Assaji, "Venerable Sir, please do not expand the Dhamma teaching further for the sake of the higher paths; let this much teaching suffice. Where does our Teacher, the Buddha, reside?"

Then Venerable Assaji said, "Friend, he resides at Veluvana Monastery." When he said this, Upatissa replied, "Venerable Sir, if that is so, please go ahead. I have a friend. We have made a pact between us: 'Whoever among us first attains the Deathless, let him inform the other.' I shall release myself from that promise, take my friend, and follow the path you have taken to the presence of the Blessed One."

He then prostrated at the Elder's feet with the five-point prostration (prostrating by placing the five limbs—the two knees, the two palms, and the forehead—on the ground or floor). Having performed the triple circumambulation, he saw the Elder off and headed towards the wanderers' park. At that time, the wanderer Kolita saw the wanderer Upatissa coming from afar and, thinking, "Today my friend's complexion is not as on other days; surely he must have attained the Deathless," he asked about the attainment of the Deathless. Upatissa admitted to Kolita, "Yes, friend, I have attained the Deathless," and recited that very same verse. At the conclusion of the verse, Kolita also was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry and asked, "Friend Upatissa, where does our Teacher, the Buddha, reside?" When Upatissa replied, "Friend Kolita, our teacher Venerable Assaji told me that he resides at Veluvana Monastery," Kolita said, "Friend Upatissa, if so, come, let us go; we shall see the Blessed One."

## Inviting the Great Teacher Sañjaya to Follow to the Buddha

This Venerable Sāriputta was one who always honored his teachers. Therefore, he said to his friend Kolita, "Friend Kolita, let us also tell the Deathless we have attained to our teacher, the great Sañjaya. If he is capable of liberation, he will penetrate the truth. If he does not penetrate it, he will believe us and go to the presence of the Buddha. Upon hearing the Buddha's teaching, he will achieve the penetration of the paths and fruits." Having said this, the two, Upatissa and Kolita, went to the presence of the wanderer Sañjaya. As soon as Sañjaya saw Upatissa and Kolita, he asked, "Dear ones, how is it? Have you found someone who can teach the path to the Deathless?" Then they said, "Teacher, we have found him. The Buddha has appeared in the world; the Dhamma has appeared in the world; the Sangha has appeared in the world. You, teacher, are wandering in what is empty and without essence. Therefore, please come; let us go to the presence of the Buddha."
60:
Then the teacher said, “You yourselves go; as for me, I am unable to go.” When asked, “For what reason are you unable?” Sañjaya replied, “I have lived as a great teacher of a multitude of people. For me to live as a student would be like a large water jar becoming a small water pot. I cannot live as a student.” Although they pleaded, “Teacher, do not do this,” he said, “Dear sons, let it be. You yourselves go; I am unable to go.”

## The Fools Will Come to the Foolish
Then they asked, “Teacher, from the time the Buddha has appeared in the world, the multitude of people, holding flowers, perfumes, and so on, will go and worship only that Buddha. We too will go only to where that Buddha is. What will you do, teacher?” When asked thus, he said, “Dear sons, in this world, are the dull-witted many, or are the wise many?” When they replied, “Teacher, the dull-witted are many; the wise are only a few and appear only occasionally,” he said, “Dear sons, if that is so, the wise will go to the presence of the ascetic Gotama, and the dull-witted will come to my presence. You go; I will not go.” They replied, “If that is the case, you will become well-known, teacher,” and they departed.

## Upatissa and Kolita Becoming Ehi Bhikkhu Monks
When Upatissa and Kolita departed, the followers of the wandering ascetic Sañjaya were split and scattered. At that moment, the monastery of the wandering ascetic became empty. Seeing the empty monastery, Sañjaya became distressed and vomited hot blood. Among the five hundred wandering ascetics who went together with Upatissa and Kolita, two hundred and fifty turned back to Sañjaya. When those two hundred and fifty had gone, Upatissa and Kolita, along with their own two hundred and fifty wandering ascetic disciples, went to the Veḷuvana Monastery. While the Blessed One was sitting in the midst of the fourfold assembly preaching the Dhamma, he saw Upatissa and Kolita coming from afar. He addressed the monks, saying, “Monks, these two friends, Kolita and Upatissa, are coming. They will be my pair of chief disciples, an excellent pair.” Upatissa and Kolita paid homage to the Blessed One and sat in a suitable place. After sitting down, the two friends said to the Blessed One, “Exalted One, may we receive the going forth (pabbajjā) in the presence of the Blessed One; may we receive the full ordination (upasampadā).” The Blessed One said, “Etha bhikkhavo (Come, monks),” and added, “The Dhamma is well-proclaimed; lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.” Immediately after these words were spoken, they all appeared as senior elders of sixty years’ standing, bearing miraculously created bowls and robes.

## Reaching the Pinnacle of the Knowledge of the Perfection of a Disciple
Thereafter, the Buddha preached the Dhamma further to the disciples of Upatissa and Kolita according to their temperaments and habits. With the exception of the two chief disciples, the remaining wandering ascetics attained Arahantship. As for the chief disciples, the work of the three higher paths was not yet completed. Why? Because of the vastness of the Knowledge of the Perfection of a Disciple (Sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa). (Upatissa came to be known as Sāriputta because he was the son of the brahmin woman Sārī, and Kolita came to be known as Moggallāna because he was the son of the brahmin woman Moggallī.) Then, on the seventh day from the day he became a monk, while the Venerable Moggallāna was staying near the village named Kallavāḷa in the Magadha country, he was overcome by drowsiness (thina-middha). The Blessed One, having stirred him and dispelled the drowsiness...
61:
While listening to the discourse on the elements (dhātu-kammaṭṭhāna), he completed the tasks of the three higher paths and reached the pinnacle of the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa). The Elder Sāriputta, too, half a month after his ordination, was staying with the Teacher at the same city of Rājagaha in the cave called Sūkarakhata. While the Teacher was preaching the Vedanāpariggaha Sutta to his nephew, the wandering ascetic Dīghanakha, Sāriputta followed the discourse with his wisdom and, like one eating food prepared for another, reached the pinnacle of the knowledge of a disciple's perfection.

Is it not that the Venerable Sāriputta possessed great wisdom? If so, why did he reach the pinnacle of the knowledge of a disciple's perfection later than the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna? It was because of the magnitude of the preparation (parikamma). To explain: when poor people wish to go somewhere, they can set out quickly. However, for kings, it is proper to obtain a grand preparation such as caparisoning elephants and horses, and gathering an army; thus, they set out only after a long time of preparation. This analogy should be understood in this context.

## Criticism Regarding the Appointment of the Chief Disciples

On that very day, while staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Teacher held an assembly of disciples, appointed the two Elders to the positions of Chief Disciples, and recited the Pātimokkha (gave the exhortation). The monks grumbled, saying, "The Teacher gives gifts by looking at faces (showing favoritism). If he wanted to give the positions of Chief Disciples, he should have given them to the group of five (Pañcavaggiya) who were ordained first. If not them, he should have given them to the fifty-five monks led by the Elder Yasa. If not them, he should have given them to the thirty Bhaddavaggiya. If not them, he should have given them to the three brothers led by Uruvela Kassapa. Ignoring so many great elders and giving the positions of Chief Disciples to Sāriputta and Moggallāna, who were ordained last of all, is indeed giving by looking at faces."

Then the Teacher asked, "Monks, what are you talking about?" When they replied, "This is what we were saying," he said, "Monks, I do not give gifts by looking at faces. I give to these individuals only according to their respective aspirations. Indeed, the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña, while giving the first-fruit offerings nine times during a single harvest, did not give while aspiring for the position of Chief Disciple. Instead, he gave while aspiring to be the very first to penetrate the supreme Dhamma, the fruit of Arahantship."

When he said this, the monks asked, "Venerable Sir, when did he make those offerings?" The Teacher asked, "Monks, do you wish to hear?" When they replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir," the Blessed One brought forth the past:

## The Past of the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña

Monks, ninety-one aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, a Buddha named Vipassī appeared in the world. At that time, there were two brothers who were householders, Mahākāla and Cūḷakāla, who cultivated a large field of śāli rice. One day, Cūḷakāla...
62:
...went to the rice field, peeled a grain of rice in its milky stage, and ate it. It was extremely sweet. Desiring to give an offering of this young rice to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, he approached his elder brother and said, "Brother, let us peel the young rice, prepare it in a way suitable for Buddhas, and give it as an offering." The elder brother said, "What are you saying, dear brother? Peeling young rice to give as an offering has never happened in the past, nor will it happen in the future. Do not destroy the crop." Although told this, Cūḷakāla pleaded again and again. Then the elder brother Mahākāla said, "In that case, divide the rice field into two portions. Do not touch my portion, and do in your own portion as you wish."

Cūḷakāla said, "Very well," divided the field, and requested many people to help with the manual labor. He peeled the young rice, had it cooked with undiluted milk, and mixed it with ghee, honey, molasses, and sugar. After giving the offering to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, at the conclusion of the meal, he made an aspiration: "Venerable Sir, may this first-fruit offering of young rice lead to the first penetration of the supreme Dhamma before all others." The Teacher gave the blessing, saying, "May it be as you have aspired."

When Cūḷakāla went to the field and looked, he saw the entire field covered with ears of rice as if they had been woven together. He experienced the five kinds of joy (pīti) and thought, "What a gain for me!" At the time of the young rice, he gave the offering of the first young rice. Together with the villagers, he gave the offering of the first-fruits of the crop. Likewise, at the time of reaping, he gave the first-reaping offering; at the time of binding, the first-binding offering; at the time of sheafing, the first-sheaf offering; at the time of threshing, the first-threshing offering; at the time of winnowing, the first-winnowing offering; at the time of measuring, the first-measuring offering; and at the time of storing in the granary, the first-granary offering. In this way, he gave the first-fruit offerings nine times during a single harvest. For Cūḷakāla, every place from which he took the rice was replenished; it did not decrease. The crop was endowed with more fruit than ever before. This is true: the Dhamma protects the one who protects it. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke this verse:

## The Dhamma Protects the One Who Practices It

*Dhammo have rakkhati dhammacāriṃ,*
*Dhammo suciṇṇo sukhamāvahati.*
*Esānisaṃso dhamme suciṇṇe,*
*Na duggatiṃ gacchati dhammacārī.*

*Have*: indeed. *Dhammo*: the Dhamma. *Dhammacārī*: the one who practices the Dhamma. *Rakkhati*: protects. *Suciṇṇo*: well-practiced. *Dhammo*: the Dhamma. *Sukhaṃ*: the three kinds of happiness. *Āvahati*: brings. *Esa-eso*: this nature. *Dhamme suciṇṇe*: in practicing the Dhamma well. *Ānisaṃso*: is the benefit. *Dhammacārī*: the one who practices the Dhamma. *Duggatiṃ*: to the four woeful states. *Na gacchati*: does not go.
63:
In this way, Aññāsi Koṇḍañña, during the time of the Buddha Vipassī, gave the first-fruits of the harvest nine times, aspiring to be the first to penetrate the supreme Dhamma. One hundred thousand aeons ago, during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara in the city of Haṃsavatī, he also gave a great alms-offering for seven days. Prostrating at the feet of that Blessed One, he made the aspiration to be the first to penetrate the supreme Dhamma. "Thus, I give to the monk Aññāsi Koṇḍañña only what he himself aspired for; I do not give, O monks, out of favoritism."

## The Past Lives of the Fifty-Five Monks Led by Yasa

When asked, "Venerable Blessed One, what meritorious deeds did the fifty-five men, led by the noble youth Yasa, perform?" the Buddha related the following account of the past:

These fifty-five men, led by Yasa, also aspired for Arahantship in the presence of a Buddha. Having performed many meritorious deeds, they were later reborn during an interval when no Buddha had appeared. They became close friends and, performing meritorious deeds together as a group, they went about taking care of and cremating the bodies of those who died without relatives.

One day, seeing the corpse of a pregnant woman, they took it to the cemetery to cremate it. Among the fifty-five, five were left at the cemetery with the instruction, "You cremate the body," while the remaining fifty entered the village. The youth Yasa, while cremating the body by piercing and turning it with stakes, gained the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā). Having gained the perception of foulness himself, he showed it to the other four, saying, "Friends, look at this body; the skin is peeling here and there, like a brindled cow; it is impure, foul-smelling, and loathsome." They too gained the perception of foulness regarding that pregnant woman's corpse. All five went to the village and told the other friends. The youth Yasa went home and told his parents and his wife. They all meditated on foulness. This was the past deed of these fifty-five monks led by Yasa. Because of this past deed, the perception of a cemetery arose in the youth Yasa while in his harem. Through the perfection of such a powerful supporting condition (upanissaya), the attainment of the paths and fruits was accomplished for all of them. "I do not give out of favoritism," the Buddha declared.

## The Past Lives of the Thirty Bhaddavaggiya Princes

When asked, "Venerable Blessed One, what meritorious deeds did the thirty Bhaddavaggiya friends perform?" the Buddha replied: "These Bhaddavaggiya also aspired for Arahantship in the presence of former Buddhas and performed meritorious deeds. Later, in an interval when no Buddha had appeared, they were thirty rogues. Having heard the advice of the pig Tuṇḍila (the Bodhisatta), they observed the five precepts for sixty thousand years. Thus, these men also received only what they themselves had aspired for. I do not give out of favoritism."

## The Past Lives of the Three Kassapa Brothers

When asked, "Venerable Blessed One, what meritorious deeds did Uruvela Kassapa and the others perform?" the Buddha replied that they too performed meritorious deeds, aspiring only for Arahantship. Counting back from this aeon, ninety-two aeons ago, two Buddhas named Tissa and Phussa appeared. The father of the Buddha Phussa was a king named Mahinda. When that Buddha Phussa attained omniscience and became a Buddha, the King's younger son became the first Chief Disciple on the right, and the son of the royal chaplain became the second Chief Disciple on the left.
64:
King Mahinda went to the Buddha and said, "My eldest son is the Buddha; my youngest son is the first chief disciple; the son of the chaplain is the second chief disciple." Looking at his eldest son, youngest son, and the chaplain’s son, he proclaimed, "The Buddha is indeed my Buddha; the Dhamma is indeed my Dhamma; the Saṅgha is indeed my Saṅgha." He then uttered the solemn utterance (udāna) three times: "Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa." Prostrating at the feet of the Buddha, he requested, "Venerable Sir, at this time, my life span of ninety thousand years has reached its end, like the moment of nodding off to sleep. Therefore, without going to the doors of others for alms, please accept only my four requisites for as long as I live." Having received the Buddha's consent, he continually attended to and served the Buddha.

The King also had three other sons. Among those three, the eldest had an entourage of five hundred soldiers, the middle one had three hundred, and the youngest had two hundred. These three brothers consulted one another, saying, "We too shall offer alms to our elder brother, the Buddha." When they asked their father for permission, they did not receive it. Even though they pleaded repeatedly, they were still refused. At another time, when the borderlands were in revolt, they were sent to quell the rebellion. After pacifying the borderlands and returning to their father, the King embraced them, kissed their heads, and said, "My sons, I shall grant you a boon of your choice."

The sons replied, "Very well, your majesty," and merely accepted the offer. After two or three days had passed, when the father said again, "My sons, take your boon," they petitioned, "Your majesty, from this day forward, let us offer alms to our elder brother, the Buddha. We have no desire for any other boon; please grant us only this." When the King replied, "My sons, I cannot grant this boon," they requested, "Your majesty, if you cannot grant it permanently, then grant us permission for seven years." When he refused again, saying, "My sons, I cannot grant it," they gradually reduced their request to six years, five, four, three, two, and one year. When he still refused, they requested, "Your majesty, if you cannot grant even one year, then grant us seven months." When he refused that, they asked for six months, five, four, and three months. When he refused again, they pleaded, "Your majesty, even if you cannot grant three months to us together, grant us three months by allowing each of us one month." The King finally said, "Very well, my sons, then provide service for three months." Delighted, the three princes paid homage to their father and returned to their own places.

Those three princes had only one treasurer (koṭṭhāgārika) and one manager (āyuttaka), and that manager had an entourage of one hundred and twenty thousand men.
65:
The princes summoned those officials and instructed them, "For these three months of the rainy season, we shall observe the ten precepts, wear two saffron-dyed robes, and dwell together with our elder brother, the Buddha. You must take up this duty of almsgiving and daily provide all kinds of hard and soft food to the ninety thousand monks and the one thousand soldiers. From this day forward, we shall not say a single word."

Those three brothers, taking their entourage of one thousand men, undertook the ten precepts, donned saffron-dyed robes, and lived only within the monastery. The treasurer and the manager joined together and, taking turns from the granaries of the three brothers, provided the alms.

## How they became hungry ghosts by eating the alms first

As for the cooks and workers who performed the duties, their young children cried for gruel, rice, and other food. Those workers gave gruel and rice to the children even before the Saṅgha of monks had arrived. After the Saṅgha had finished their meal, there was never anything left over. Those workers, thinking they would give to the children later, also took and ate the food themselves. Seeing the delicious food, they were unable to restrain themselves. There were eighty-four thousand such workers. Because they ate the alms-food intended for the Saṅgha, when they passed away, they were reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts (peta-loka).

The three princes, along with their one thousand men, passed away and were reborn in the deva world. Wandering from the deva world to the human world and from the human world to the deva world, they spent ninety-two aeons (kappas). "In this way, those three who were once princes—Uruvela Kassapa, Gayā Kassapa, and Nadī Kassapa—performed wholesome deeds while aspiring for Arahatship. Those Kassapa brothers received exactly what they had aspired for. I, the Buddha, do not grant attainments out of partiality," the Buddha declared.

At that time, the manager of the three princes became King Bimbisāra. The treasurer became the lay devotee named Visākha. The workers who served those three princes were reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts; wandering by the power of their good and bad deeds, they remained in the realm of hungry ghosts throughout the three intervals between four Buddhas in this Bhadda Kappa.

Those hungry ghosts (petas) approached the Blessed One Kakusandha, the first to arise in this Bhadda Kappa, who had a life span of forty thousand years, and asked, "O Blessed Buddha, please tell us when we shall obtain food." The Blessed One Kakusandha said, "You will not obtain it during my time. After I have passed away, when the earth has risen by one league (yojana), a Buddha named Koṇāgamana will arise. You should ask him." Having spent that much time, when Koṇāgamana Buddha arose, they asked him. He also said, "You will not obtain food during my time. After I have passed away, when the earth has risen by one league, Kassapa Buddha will arise. You should ask him."
66:
Those petas passed that much time, and when the Buddha Kassapa arose, they asked him. The Buddha Kassapa said, “You will not receive food during my time. However, after my parinibbāna, when the earth has risen by one league (yojana), the Buddha Gotama will arise. In the time of that Buddha Gotama, your relative, who is an official, will become King Bimbisāra. That King Bimbisāra will give offerings to the Buddha Gotama and share the merit with you, bringing you to the attainment of merit. At that time, you will receive divine food and drink.” To those petas, the interval between the two Buddhas seemed like only a single day. When the Buddha Gotama arose and King Bimbisāra gave an offering on the first day, he did not share the merit, so they did not receive the portion of merit. Consequently, during the night, they made terrifying sounds and showed themselves to King Bimbisāra. The next morning, the King went to the Veḷuvana Monastery and reported the matter to the Blessed One.

The Buddha said, “Great King, ninety-two aeons ago, during the time of the Buddha Phussa, these relatives of yours ate the first portions of the offerings intended for the community of monks (bhikkhu-saṅgha). Having been reborn in the realm of petas and wandering through saṃsāra, they asked Buddhas such as Kakusandha, and those Buddhas, including Kakusandha, told them such and such. Having yearned for your offering for this long, when you gave the offering yesterday and they did not receive the merit, they made these terrifying sounds.” When the King asked, “Venerable Sir, if I give now, will they still receive it?” the Buddha replied, “Yes, Great King.” Therefore, the King invited the community of monks headed by the Buddha, gave a great offering the next day, and shared the merit, saying, “Venerable Sir, from this time of offering onwards, may divine food and drink be fulfilled for those petas.”

Just as King Bimbisāra intended and yearned, divine food and divine drink appeared for those petas. The next day, they appeared again, naked and without clothing. King Bimbisāra reported, “Venerable Sir, today they appeared to me again, naked and without clothes.” When the Buddha said, “Great King, you have not yet given robes,” the King, on the following day, gave an offering of robes to the community of monks headed by the Buddha and shared the merit, aspiring, “From this time of offering robes onwards, may divine clothes be for those petas.” At that very moment, divine clothes appeared for those petas, and they abandoned their peta-state and were established in celestial bodies. While the Buddha was performing the blessing (anumodanā), he preached the Tirokuṭṭa Anumodanā, beginning with “Tirokuṭṭesu tiṭṭhanti.” At the end of the blessing, eighty-four thousand beings attained the Dhamma. Thus, the Buddha told the story of the three matted-hair ascetic brothers and brought forth this Dhamma teaching.

## The Past of Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Moggallāna

When asked, “Venerable Sir, what merit did the Chief Disciples perform?” the Buddha replied, “They made the aspiration to become the pair of Chief Disciples, the right-hand and left-hand disciples. One incalculable (asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons ago, Sāriputta was born in a wealthy brahmin family (brāhmaṇa mahāsāla), named...”
67: His name was Sarada the youth (Sarada Māṇava). Moggallāna was born into a wealthy Gahapati Mahāsāla family. His name was Siriwaḍḍhana the householder. These two were childhood friends who played together in the dust. Among them, Sarada the youth, after his father passed away, inherited a vast ancestral fortune. One day, while in seclusion, he thought: "I only know the welfare of this present world. I do not know the welfare of the world beyond. For beings who are born, death is certain. It is proper for me to go forth as an ascetic and seek the Dhamma of liberation from the cycle of suffering." Having thought thus, he approached his friend Siriwaḍḍhana and asked, "Friend and comrade Siriwaḍḍhana, I will go forth and seek the Dhamma of liberation. Will you be able to go forth with me or not?" "Friend, I am not able. You alone should go forth," he replied. Then Sarada the youth thought: "Those who pass on to the next life do not take along beloved friends, relatives, or close companions. Only the kamma one has performed belongs to oneself." Having thought this, he opened his treasury of jewels and gave a great gift to the orphans, travelers, and wandering beggars. Then he went to the foot of a mountain and went forth as an ascetic. Following his example, one, two, three, and so on followed him until there were 74,000 matted-hair ascetics (jaṭilas). Sarada the ascetic attained the five supernormal powers (abhiññā) and the eight attainments (samāpatti), and he taught the preliminary work of kasina meditation to his disciples. All those ascetics also attained the five supernormal powers and the eight attainments. At that time, the Blessed One Anomadassī, the Perfectly Enlightened One, appeared in the world. His birthplace was the city of Candavatī. His father was King Yasavā, and his mother was Queen Yasodharā. The Bodhi tree under which he attained enlightenment was the Ajjuna tree. His pair of chief disciples were Nisabha and Anoma. His attendant was the monk Varuṇa. His pair of chief female disciples were Sundarā and Sumanā. His lifespan was one hundred thousand years. His body was fifty-eight cubits high. The radiance of his body spread for twelve leagues. He had a retinue of one hundred thousand monks. One day, in the early morning, the Buddha Anomadassī emerged from the attainment of great compassion (mahā-karuṇā-samāpatti) and surveyed the world. Seeing Sarada the ascetic, he thought: "Today, because of my going to Sarada the ascetic, there will be a great festival of Dhamma. Sarada the ascetic will aspire for the position of a chief disciple. His friend, Siriwaḍḍhana the householder, will aspire for the position of the second chief disciple on the left. At the end of the discourse, his retinue of 74,000 ascetics will attain Arahantship. It is proper for me to go to the foot of the mountain where those ascetics reside." Taking his bowl and robes himself, without calling any other monk, he traveled alone like a lion king. While Sarada's disciples had gone to collect various fruits, the Buddha, wishing to make his Buddhahood known, made a determination and descended from the sky to stand on the ground just as Sarada the ascetic saw him.
68: Sarada the ascetic, seeing the Buddha's majesty and his physical perfection adorned with the radiance of his body, reflected on the Vedic texts concerning the marks of a Great Man. He thought: "One endowed with these marks, if he lives the household life, becomes a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti). If he goes forth, he becomes an Omniscient Buddha who removes the veil from the world. This man is undoubtedly a Buddha." Knowing this, he went out to meet him, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, prepared a noble seat, and offered it. The Blessed One sat on the prepared noble seat. Sarada the ascetic also took a suitable seat for himself and sat down in a proper place. At that time, the 74,000 matted-hair ascetics returned to their teacher Sarada, bringing various excellent and nutritious fruits. Seeing the seats where the Buddha and their teacher were sitting, they said: "Teacher, we have wandered thinking that there is no one greater than you in this world. But this man seems even more excellent than you." When they said this, Sarada replied: "My disciples, what are you saying? Do not wish to compare Mount Sineru, which is eighty-four thousand leagues high, with a mustard seed. My sons, do not make a comparison between me, your teacher, and the Omniscient Buddha." Then the disciple ascetics thought: "If this man were an ordinary or lowly being, our teacher would not have used such a comparison. This man must be truly noble." Thus, all the ascetics bowed down at his feet and paid homage with their heads. Then their teacher, Sarada the ascetic, said to them: "My sons, we do not have offerings suitable for the Buddhas. The Buddha has arrived here at the time of seeking alms. Let us offer whatever gifts we have according to our strength and ability. Bring the best and sweetest fruits from those you have searched for." Having had them brought, he washed his hands and personally placed them in the Blessed One's bowl. As soon as the Buddha accepted the fruits, the devas infused them with divine essence (ojā). Sarada the ascetic also filtered the drinking water himself and offered it. After the Buddha had finished his meal, Sarada the ascetic called all his disciples and sat near the Buddha, speaking words that should be remembered for a lifetime. Then the Buddha thought: "Let the two chief disciples come together with the community of monks." Those two chief disciples...
69:
Having gathered various flowers and scents together,
Having prepared a flower-seat, he spoke these words:
"This seat, O Hero, has been prepared by me, worthy of You.
Pleasing my heart, please sit upon this flower-seat."
For seven days and nights, the Buddha sat upon the flower-seat,
Pleasing my heart and gladdening the world including the devas.

"Nānāpupphañca" means various flowers; "nānāgandhañca" means various scents. "Ekato" means together. "Sampādetvāna" means having prepared or fulfilled. "Pupphāsanaṃ" means the flower-seat. "Paññāpetvā" means having spread or prepared. "Idaṃ vacanaṃ" means these words. "Abravi" means he spoke or addressed.

"Vīra" means the Buddha who possesses great effort. "Tava" means for the Buddha. "Anucchaviṃ" means worthy or suitable. "Idaṃ āsanaṃ" means this flower-seat. "Me" means by me. "Paññattaṃ" means has been prepared. "Mama" means my. "Cittaṃ" means heart or mind. "Pasādento" means while making it clear and bright. "Pupphamāsane" means upon the flower-seat. "Nisīda" means please sit.

"Mama" means of me, Sarada the ascetic. "Cittaṃ" means heart. "Pasādetvā" means having made it clear and bright. "Sadevake" means humans together with devas. "Hāsayitvā" means having gladdened them with joy. "Buddho" means the Buddha Anomadassī. "Sattarattindivaṃ" means for seven nights and seven days. "Pupphamāsane" means upon the flower-seat. "Nisīdi" means He sat.

Knowing his thought, the Buddha arrived surrounded by one hundred thousand Arahants and, after paying homage to the Buddha, they stood in a suitable place. Then, Sarada the ascetic called his disciple ascetics and said, "My sons, the Buddha's seating-dais is low. There are no seats for the one hundred thousand monks. Today, it is proper for you to make a grand and special offering to the Buddha. Therefore, bring flowers endowed with color and fragrance from the foot of the mountain."

The time of speaking seemed long, but the power of one with psychic potency is inconceivable. Thus, in just a moment, those ascetics brought flowers endowed with color and fragrance and prepared a flower-seat for the Buddhas measuring one yojana. The seats for the two Chief Disciples were three gāvutas, and for the remaining monks, they were half a yojana and so on. The seat for the youngest monk (saṅghanavaka) was about one usabha.

One should not wonder, "How were such large flower-seats prepared in a single hermitage?" Indeed, such a grand preparation was an act accomplished through psychic power.

When the flower-seats had been thus prepared, Sarada the ascetic stood before the Buddha with palms joined and said, "Venerable Sir, for my long-term welfare and happiness, please ascend and stay upon this flower-seat." Therefore, these verses were spoken.

While the Buddha was thus staying, the two Chief Disciples and the remaining monks sat in the seats prepared for each of them. Sarada the ascetic held a large flower-umbrella and stood shading the Buddha's head. The Buddha, reflecting, "May this special offering of these ascetics be of great fruit and benefit," entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). Knowing that the Buddha had entered the attainment of cessation, the two Chief Disciples and the remaining monks also entered the attainment of cessation.

While the Buddha remained in the attainment of cessation for seven days, the resident disciples of Sarada the ascetic, when it was time for alms, searched for and consumed forest roots, tubers, and various fruits, and for the rest of the time, they stood with palms joined in homage to the Buddhas. As for Sarada the ascetic, he did not even go for alms, but remained holding the flower-umbrella for seven days, passing the time with the bliss of rapture (pītisukha). After the Buddha emerged from the attainment of cessation, He addressed the Elder Nisabha, the first Chief Disciple sitting on His right side: "Dear Nisabha, preach the Dhamma of appreciation (anumodanā) regarding the offering of the flower-seats to the ascetics who have made this offering."
70:
Then, the Elder Nisabha, with a joyful heart like a great general who has received a grand reward from a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), established in the Knowledge of a Disciple's Perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa), began to preach the Dhamma of appreciation for the gift of the flower-seats.

At the conclusion of the Elder Nisabha's sermon, the Buddha called the Elder Anoma, the second Chief Disciple on the left, and said, "Dear Anoma, you too preach the Dhamma to the ascetics." The Elder Anoma also contemplated the Buddha's words known as the Tipitaka and preached the Dhamma. Through the preaching of the two Chief Disciples, not even a single ascetic attained realization. Then, the Buddha Anomadassī, established in the infinite range of a Buddha, began to preach the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the sermon, except for Sarada the ascetic, all the remaining seventy-four thousand ascetics attained the Fruit of Arahantship and became Arahants. The Buddha, uttering the words "Etha Bhikkhavo" and stretching out His right hand, called them; at that very moment, their hair and beards disappeared, and they became "Ehi Bhikkhus" with the eight requisites already attached to their bodies.

As for Sarada the ascetic, why did he not reach the Fruit of Arahantship? He did not reach it because his mind was distracted. It is said that while Sarada the ascetic was sitting in the second seat from the Buddhas and listening to the Dhamma preached by the Chief Disciple Nisabha who was established in the Knowledge of a Disciple's Perfection, from the time he began to listen, the thought occurred to him: "Oh, would that I too might obtain the post of Chief Disciple on the right, just as this Elder Nisabha has obtained, in the Dispensation of a Buddha to be born in the future!" Because of that thought, he was unable to penetrate the Paths and Fruits. After paying homage to the Buddha and standing in His presence, he asked, "Venerable Sir, what is the status in Your Dispensation of the monk sitting in the seat immediately next to You?"

"This monk, who follows the Wheel of Dhamma set in motion by Me, who has reached the pinnacle of the Knowledge of a Disciple's Perfection, and who stands having penetrated the sixteen forms of knowledge—he is the one named Nisabha, the Chief Disciple in My Dispensation."

Then, Sarada the ascetic made this aspiration: "Magnificent Buddha, for seven days I have performed this special offering by holding a flower-umbrella. By the merit of this offering, I do not desire any other status such as that of Sakka or Brahma. In the future, may I become the Chief Disciple on the right of a Buddha, just like this Elder Nisabha."

The Buddha Anomadassī, sending forth His Knowledge of the Future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa) to see whether the aspiration of Sarada the ascetic would be fulfilled or not, saw that it would be fulfilled after the passing of one asankheyya and one hundred thousand aeons.
71:
Upon seeing this, the Buddha said to the ascetic Sarada, "Your aspiration shall not be in vain. In the future, after one incalculable period (asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons (kappa) have passed, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. The mother of that Buddha Gotama will be a queen named Mahāmāyā. The father will be a great king named Suddhodana. The son will be named Rāhula. The attendant will be named Ānanda. The second chief disciple on the left will be named Moggallāna. And you shall be the first chief disciple on the right, the General of the Dhamma named Sāriputta." Having thus given the prophecy to the ascetic Sarada and delivered a discourse on the Dhamma, the Buddha, surrounded by the community of monks, rose into the air and departed.

The ascetic Sarada then went to the presence of the elders who were his former disciples and sent a message to his friend, the householder Sirivaḍḍhana: "Venerable sirs, please tell my friend the householder: 'Your friend, the ascetic Sarada, at the feet of Buddha Anomadassī, has aspired for the position of the first chief disciple on the right in the dispensation of Buddha Gotama, who will arise in the future. You, householder, should aspire for the position of the second chief disciple on the left.'" Having sent this message, he traveled by a different route and arrived at the door of Sirivaḍḍhana's house before the elders. The householder Sirivaḍḍhana, thinking, "It has been a long time since my noble one has come," invited him to sit on a seat while he himself sat on a lower seat and asked, "Venerable sir, your retinue of disciples is not seen."

"Friend Sirivaḍḍhana, yes, it is so. The Blessed One Anomadassī came to our hermitage. We performed offerings and honors to that Buddha according to our ability. The Buddha preached the Dhamma to everyone. At the end of the discourse, except for me, the remaining disciple ascetics attained Arahantship and went forth as monks. I, however, having seen the Elder Nisabha, the chief disciple of Buddha Anomadassī, made an aspiration for the position of the first chief disciple on the right in the dispensation of Buddha Gotama, who will arise in the future. You, my friend, should also aspire for the position of the second chief disciple on the left in the dispensation of that Buddha."

When thus urged, Sirivaḍḍhana said, "Venerable sir, I have no familiarity with Buddhas." Sarada replied, "Let the task of speaking with the Buddha be my responsibility. You just prepare and arrange a great offering." Hearing the ascetic's words, the householder Sirivaḍḍhana had an area of about eight min-pe (an area where eleven tin of seeds can be sown is called one min-pe) near his house leveled. He had sand scattered, a pavilion covered with blue lotuses constructed, a seat for the Buddha prepared, and seats for the remaining monks arranged. Having prepared great offerings and honors, he gave a signal to the ascetic Sarada to invite the Buddha. The ascetic Sarada, leading the community of monks headed by the Buddha, went to the house of the householder Sirivaḍḍhana.
72:
The householder Sirivaḍḍhana went out to welcome them, took the bowl from the Buddha's hand, and invited Him to enter the pavilion. To the community of monks headed by the Buddha, who were seated on the prepared seats, he poured the water of dedication and served them with exquisite food. At the conclusion of the meal, he offered the community of monks headed by the Buddha robes suitable for noble ones and said, "Venerable Sir, this effort and preparation is not for a small position. In this same manner, please show compassion for seven days." The Buddha consented.

In that same manner, the householder Sirivaḍḍhana continued the great offering for seven days. Then, having paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood with palms joined and said, "Most Glorious Buddha, my friend the ascetic Sarada has aspired to be the first chief disciple on the right of whichever Buddha he serves. I, too, wish to be the second chief disciple on the left of that same Buddha."

The Buddha, looking into the future and seeing the fulfillment of Sirivaḍḍhana's aspiration, gave the prophecy: "After one incalculable period and a hundred thousand aeons have passed from now, you shall be the second chief disciple on the left of the Buddha named Gotama." Hearing the prophecy of the Buddha, Sirivaḍḍhana was exceedingly joyful and happy. The Buddha, having given the discourse of appreciation (anumodanā), returned to the monastery with His retinue of monks.

"Monks, these sons of mine, Sāriputta and Moggallāna, aspired for the pair of chief disciples in this way, and thus they obtained the positions of right-hand and left-hand disciples exactly as they had aspired. I, the Buddha, do not give positions by looking at faces (favoritism)."

After He had said this, the two chief disciples paid homage to the Buddha and spoke thus: "Venerable Sir, while we were living as householders, we went to see the mountain-top festival (Giragga-samajja)..." They related the entire present story up to the point of penetrating the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) in the presence of Elder Assaji. Then they said, "Venerable Sir, we went to the presence of our teacher, the wandering ascetic Sañjaya, wishing to bring him to Your feet. We spoke of the essence-less nature of his doctrine and explained the benefits of attending upon You."
73:
## Preaching and Guidance
(11) Those who perceive the essence in the non-essential, and the non-essential in the essential, do not attain the essence, as they dwell in the sphere of wrong thoughts.
(12) Having known the essential as essential, and the non-essential as non-essential, they attain the essence, as they dwell in the sphere of right thoughts.

Those who have the view that there is essence in the non-essential—the teachings of sectarians which are like chaff without substance. And those who see the non-essential in the essential—the Dhamma of the virtuous which is full of essence. Those who dwell in the sphere of wrong thoughts, such as sensual thoughts, etc., do not attain the essence of virtue (sīla-sāra), the essence of concentration (samādhi-sāra), the essence of wisdom (paññā-sāra), the essence of liberation (vimutti-sāra), the essence of the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimutti-ñāṇadassana-sāra), and the ultimate essence, Nibbāna.

Having known the aforementioned essence of virtue, etc., as 'this is indeed the essence,' and the aforementioned non-essential as 'this is indeed non-essential.' Those wise ones, established in right vision and dwelling in the sphere of right thoughts such as thoughts of renunciation (nekkhamma-saṅkappa), etc., attain the aforementioned essence.

That teacher Sañjaya said, "At this time, for me to live as a disciple would be like a large water jar becoming a small water-carrying pot; I am unable to live as a disciple."

Then, when the disciples asked, "Teacher, now all the people, carrying flowers, perfumes, and so on, will go only to the Buddha to make offerings; what will become of you?" he asked the disciples, "In this world, are the wise many, or are the foolish many?" When they replied that the foolish are many, he said, "If that is so, the wise will go to the monk Gotama, and the foolish will come to me. You yourselves go to the monk Gotama; I do not wish to follow."

Upon hearing these words, the Buddha said, "Monks, because Sañjaya the wandering ascetic holds onto his own error, he tends to take what is without essence as having essence, and what has essence as being without essence. You, however, because of your wisdom, know the view that has essence as having essence, and the wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi) that is without essence as being without essence. Having abandoned the wrong view that is without essence, you should take up only the noble Dhamma of the virtuous which has essence," and he spoke these verses.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the verses, many in the assembled audience attained the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) and so on. The Dhamma teaching became beneficial to those who had gathered.

The story of the Elder Sāriputta ends.

## 9. The Story of Venerable Nanda Thera
(Nandattheravatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Yathā agāraṃ" in reference to the Venerable Nanda Thera.

## Preaching to His Father and Mother
The Teacher, who is skilled in taming gods and humans, having the noble Wheel of Dhamma set in motion—or rather, having preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta—went to the city of Rājagaha and resided at the Veḷuvana monastery. King Suddhodana sent ten messengers, each with a retinue of a thousand, saying, "Bring my son, the Buddha, and show him to me." Among them, the noble Elder Kāḷudāyī, who was born on the same day as the Buddha and had attained Arahantship, went after all the other messengers. Knowing the proper time for the journey, he praised the beauty of the path with sixty verses.
74:
Accompanied by twenty thousand Arahants, the Buddha was conducted to the city of Kapilavatthu. In the assembly of his kinsmen, he caused a shower of rain (pokkhara-vassa) to fall as the occasion for preaching the Vessantara Jātaka.
