On the following day, while entering for alms, he established his father the King in the fruit of Stream-entry with the verse beginning with "Uttiṭṭhe nappamajjeyya." With the verse beginning with "Dhammañcare," he established the Great Pajāpatī Gotamī in the fruit of Stream-entry, and the King in the fruit of Once-returner (sakadāgāmi-phala).

## The Ordination of Prince Nanda
After the conclusion of the meal, the Buddha preached the Candakinnara Jātaka in reference to the virtues of Princess Yasodharā, the mother of Rāhula. On the third day from then, while the ceremonies for Prince Nanda's consecration, house-warming, and marriage were taking place, the Buddha entered for alms. After preaching the blessing and rising from his seat to depart, he did not take the bowl from Prince Nanda's hand but simply departed. Out of reverence for the Buddha, Prince Nanda did not dare to say, "Venerable Brother, please take your bowl," but thought, "The Brother will take the bowl at the head of the stairs." The Blessed One did not take it even there. The Prince then thought, "He will take it at the foot of the stairs." The Blessed One did not take it there either. The Prince thought, "He will take it when he reaches the palace courtyard." The Blessed One did not take it there either. Although the Prince wished to return and followed unwillingly, out of deep reverence for the Buddha, he did not dare to say, "Venerable Brother, please take your bowl." He followed, thinking, "He will take it when he reaches this spot, he will take it when he reaches that spot."

At that moment, the other ladies-in-waiting saw him and told Princess Janapadakalyāṇī, "My Lady, the Blessed One has taken Prince Nanda and departed; what will you do without him?" Upon hearing their words, Princess Janapadakalyāṇī, with her hair half-combed and tears flowing, ran quickly and said, "Noble Lord, please return quickly!" Those words of Princess Janapadakalyāṇī remained fixed in Prince Nanda's heart as if they had pierced it crosswise. The Teacher, without taking the bowl from his younger brother Nanda's hand, led him to the monastery and asked, "Nanda, will you ordain?" Out of reverence for the Buddha, Prince Nanda did not dare to say, "I cannot ordain," and replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir, I will ordain." The Teacher said, "If so, monks, ordain Prince Nanda." Thus, on the third day after his arrival at Kapilavatthu, the Teacher had Prince Nanda ordained.

## Prince Rāhula Asking for Inheritance
On the seventh day after the Buddha's arrival at Kapilavatthu, the mother of Rāhula adorned Prince Rāhula and sent him to the Blessed One, saying, "Look, my son, at this monk who is surrounded by twenty thousand monks, who has a golden complexion and a form as majestic as a Great Brahmā. This monk is your father. Your father possessed great jars of gold. Since the day of your father's renunciation, we have not seen them. Go to him and ask for your inheritance—"
75:
"Dear son, go and ask your father for your inheritance. 'Father, when I have been consecrated, I shall become a Universal Monarch. I have need of wealth; please give me my inheritance. A son should be the owner of his father's property.'" With these words, [his mother] sent him to the Buddha to ask for his inheritance. Prince Rāhula went to the Buddha, and feeling the love for a father, he became very joyful and said, "Pleasant is your shadow, O ascetic," and continued to speak many other words appropriate for him. After the Blessed One had finished his meal and given the blessing (anumodanā), he rose from his seat and departed. Prince Rāhula followed the Blessed One, saying, "Give me my inheritance, O ascetic; give me my inheritance, O ascetic." The Blessed One did not turn the prince back, and the attendants were unable to stop him as he followed the Buddha. Thus, he followed the Blessed One all the way to the monastery.

## Giving the Supramundane Inheritance to Rāhula
Upon reaching the monastery, the Blessed One thought: "This son Rāhula desires the inheritance of his father's property. That property is subject to the cycle of rebirth and is a cause of suffering. Now, I shall give this son Rāhula the sevenfold Noble Wealth (ariya-dhana) that I attained at the foot of the Bodhi tree. I will make him the owner of the supramundane inheritance." Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Sāriputta: "In that case, Sāriputta, ordain Prince Rāhula." The Elder then ordained the prince. When it was heard that the prince had been ordained, King Suddhodana felt extreme sorrow. Unable to bear that sorrow, he informed the Blessed One of the matter and requested a boon: "It would be good, Bhante, if the noble ones would not ordain a son without the permission of his parents."

The Blessed One granted that boon to the King. Later, one day, while the Blessed One was having his morning meal at the royal palace, King Suddhodana, sitting in a suitable place, said: "Venerable sir, during the time you were practicing difficult austerities (dukkara-cariyā), a deity approached me and said, 'Your son Prince Siddhattha has passed away.' I did not believe that deity's words and rejected them, saying, 'My son will not die without attaining Buddhahood.'" The Buddha replied, "Great King, why would you believe it now? Even in the past, when shown bones and told 'Your son is dead,' you did not believe it." Based on this incident, he preached the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka. At the end of the discourse, King Suddhodana was established in the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala). Thus, the Blessed One established his father in the three fruits. Surrounded by the community of monks, he returned to Rājagaha. Having previously promised Anāthapiṇḍika to come to Sāvatthī, once the construction of the great Jetavana monastery...
76:
...was finished, the Blessed One went to Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthī and resided there.

## Venerable Nanda's Dissatisfaction in the Dispensation
While the Blessed One was residing at Jetavana monastery, Venerable Nanda informed many monks of his dissatisfaction, saying: "Friends, I am dissatisfied; I am leading the holy life (brahmacariya) with difficulty. I am unable to sustain the holy life in the Dispensation. I wish to renounce the training and return to the lower life." The Blessed One, hearing of this, summoned Venerable Nanda and spoke these words: "Brother Nanda, is it true, as I have heard, that you told many monks: 'Friends, I am dissatisfied... I wish to return to the lower life'?" Nanda replied, "It is true, Bhante." "But why, Nanda, are you dissatisfied... and wish to return to the lower life?" Nanda replied, "Bhante, as I was leaving the palace, the Sakyan girl Janapadakalyāṇī, with her hair half-combed, looked at me and said: 'Noble son, please return quickly.' Bhante, as I constantly remember her words, I am dissatisfied in the holy life and wish to return to the lay life."

## Showing the Old Monkey and the Celestial Nymphs to Encourage Practice
Then the Blessed One, taking Venerable Nanda by the arm, used his psychic power to bring him to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. On the way, in a burnt field, he showed him an old female monkey sitting on a burnt stump, whose ears, nose, and tail were cut off and who was unsightly to behold. Then, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, he showed him five hundred pink-footed celestial nymphs who had come to attend upon Sakka, the king of gods. Having shown them, the Buddha asked: "What do you think, Nanda? Who is more beautiful, more fair to behold, and more pleasing—the Sakyan girl Janapadakalyāṇī or these five hundred pink-footed nymphs?" Nanda replied: "Bhante, just like that old female monkey with the cut ears, nose, and tail that we saw on the way, so is the Sakyan girl Janapadakalyāṇī. Compared to these five hundred nymphs, she does not count; she cannot even be compared to a fraction of them. Indeed, these five hundred nymphs are far more beautiful, more fair to behold, and more pleasing."
77:
"Brother Nanda, if that is so, delight in the supreme holy life, which is the teaching of the Buddha. I guarantee that you will obtain five hundred dove-footed nymphs." When this was said, the Venerable Nanda replied, "Venerable Elder Brother, if you guarantee that I will obtain five hundred dove-footed nymphs, I shall delight in the Sasana and practice with great diligence." Then the Blessed One took the Venerable Nanda, vanished from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, and reappeared at the Jetavana monastery. The monks heard, "It is said that the Venerable Nanda, the Blessed One's brother and son of his maternal aunt, is living the holy life for the sake of nymphs. It is said the Blessed One has guaranteed him the attainment of five hundred dove-footed nymphs."

## Venerable Nanda Attains Arahantship
Then the monks who were companions of the Venerable Nanda constantly addressed him with the terms "hireling" and "bought one," saying, "The Venerable Nanda is a hireling; the Venerable Nanda is a bought one. He lives the holy life for the sake of nymphs. It is said the Blessed One has guaranteed him the attainment of five hundred dove-footed nymphs." Then the Venerable Nanda, being troubled, ashamed, and disgusted by the monks' talk of him being a "hireling" and "bought one," dwelt alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute. Before long, he realized for himself through direct knowledge, attained, and dwelt in that supreme goal of the holy life for which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He knew: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being." And the Venerable Nanda became one of the Arahants.
78:
## The Teaching
(13) Just as rain penetrates a poorly roofed house,
So lust penetrates an undeveloped mind.
(14) Just as rain does not penetrate a well-roofed house,
So lust does not penetrate a well-developed mind.

*Ducchannaṃ*: poorly roofed. *Agāraṃ*: a house. *Vuṭṭhi*: rain or raindrops. *Samativijjhati yathā*: just as it can penetrate. *Evaṃ-tathā*: in the same way. *Abhāvitaṃ*: devoid of meditation (bhāvanā). *Cittaṃ*: the mind. *Rāgo*: lust. *Samativijjhati*: can penetrate.

*Succhannaṃ*: well-roofed. *Agāraṃ*: a house. *Vuṭṭhi*: rain or raindrops. *Na samativijjhati yathā*: just as it cannot penetrate. *Evaṃ-tathā*: in the same way. *Subhāvitaṃ*: having well-developed meditation. *Cittaṃ*: the mind. *Rāgo*: lust. *Na samativijjhati*: cannot penetrate.

When the Venerable Nanda thus realized the fruit of Arahantship, a certain deity, having illuminated the entire Jetavana monastery during the night, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and said: "Venerable Sir, the Venerable Nanda, the Blessed One's brother and son of his maternal aunt, through the destruction of the taints, has realized for himself through direct knowledge, attained, and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life." The Blessed One also clearly knew through his golden knowledge that the Venerable Nanda had realized the fruit of Arahantship. When that night had passed, the Venerable Nanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and said: "Venerable Elder Brother, regarding the guarantee that I would obtain five hundred dove-footed nymphs, I now release the Blessed One from that promise." "Nanda, I also knew your mind with my own mind. A deity also came and informed me of this matter. Nanda, from the moment your mind was liberated from the taints without clinging through craving or views, I was also released from that guarantee." Then the Blessed One, having understood the matter clearly, uttered this inspired utterance (Udāna) with great joy:

He who has crossed the mire of sensuality,
Who has crushed the thorn of sensuality,
Who has reached the end of delusion (Nirvana),
Is not shaken by pleasure or pain.

*Yassa*: for whom. *Kāmapaṅko*: the mire of sensual pleasures. *Tiṇṇo*: has been crossed. *Kāmakaṇṭako*: the thorn of sensual pleasures. *Maddito*: has been crushed and destroyed. *Mohakkhayaṃ*: to Nirvana, the end of delusion. *Anuppatto*: has reached. *So*: that person. *Sukhadukkhe*: by pleasure and pain. *Na vedhati*: is not shaken.

Then one day, the monks asked the Venerable Nanda: "Friend Nanda, formerly you said you were dissatisfied. How is it with you now?" He replied: "Friends, I have no more attachment to the state of a layman." Hearing this, the monks went to the Blessed One and reported: "The Venerable Nanda speaks what is not true. He claims the fruit of Arahantship. Having said in past days that he wished to leave the monkhood, he now says he has no attachment to the lay life."

The Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, in past days, Nanda's physical being was like a poorly roofed house. Now it has become like a well-roofed house. This is true. From the time Nanda saw the celestial nymphs, he strove to reach the summit of a monk's duty, and thus his task is completed." Having said this, he spoke these verses.

## Benefits of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the verses, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti) and so forth. The teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.

## The Past of Venerable Nanda
At that time, the monks started a conversation in the Dhamma hall: "Friends, the Buddhas are truly wonderful..."
79:
“You will make a goad for me, with sixteen-finger-breadth thorns. Standing firm in front, and lifting from behind, I will knock out your teeth; know this, Kappaṭa.”

Kappa, O Merchant Kappaṭa! If you make a goad for me with sixteen-finger-breadth thorns, I will stand firm in front and, lifting my hind legs, I will knock out your teeth. Know this fact.

Regarding the Venerable Nanda, who was dissatisfied with the holy life because of Janapadakalyāṇī, the monks remarked, “The Teacher disciplined Nanda by enticing him with celestial nymphs.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit here?” When they replied, “It is this, Bhante,” He said, “Monks, it is not only now; in the past also, I disciplined Nanda by enticing him with a woman.” Then He related the past story:

**The Beginning of the Affection between the Male and Female Donkeys**

Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, there was a merchant named Kappaṭa who lived in Bārāṇasī. He had a donkey that could carry a load of one *kumbha* (A *kumbha* is about one-third of a cartload. The dictionary states that 11 *sita* make one *ambaṇa*, and 10 *ambaṇa* make one *kumbha*; or four *sita* make one *taung*, four *taung* make one *to*, and 20 *to* make one cartload. One *vāha* or cartload is 80 *taung*, thus one *kumbha* is 27.5 *taung*). It could travel seven leagues in a single day. Once, that merchant Kappaṭa went to Takkasilā with other donkey-merchants. While he was selling his goods, he let the donkey loose to graze. While grazing near the edge of a moat, the donkey saw a female donkey and approached her. The female donkey, engaging in polite conversation, asked, “Where have you come from?” “From Bārāṇasī,” he replied. “On what business?” “On the business of trade.” “How much of a load do you carry?” “A load of one *kumbha*.” “Carrying such a load, how many leagues do you travel?” “Seven leagues.” “In the places you reach, is there anyone to tend to you, such as massaging your feet or back?” “There is no one.” “If that is so, you are indeed suffering greatly,” said the female donkey.

## The Donkey's Defiance against the Master

Because of the female donkey's words, the donkey became dissatisfied with his usual work and grew stubborn. When the merchant Kappaṭa, having finished selling his goods, went to the donkey and said, “Come, dear, let us go,” the donkey replied, “You go; I will not go.” After repeatedly pleading with him, the merchant thought, “I will drive this unwilling donkey by beating and scolding him,” and spoke this verse:

“I will make a goad for you, with sixteen-finger-breadth thorns. I will cut your body to pieces; know this, donkey.”

O donkey! I will make a goad for you with sixteen-finger-breadth thorns. I will cut your body to pieces. Know this fact.

When the donkey heard this, he said, “If you do so, I too shall know what must be done to you,” and spoke this verse:
80:
“I will bring you a wife, a four-footed one with a face like a conch shell, beautiful in every limb; know this, donkey.”

O donkey, my dear donkey! I will bring and give to you a wife, a female donkey who has four legs, a face as white as a conch shell, and is beautiful in all her limbs. Know this fact.

“I will bring you a wife, a four-footed one with a face like a conch shell, beautiful in every limb; know this, donkey.”

## How the Master Enticed the Donkey

Hearing the donkey's words, the merchant Kappaṭa wondered, “For what reason does he resist like this?” Looking here and there, he saw the female donkey and thought, “This female donkey must have coached him. I will entice him with a female and lead him away by promising such a female donkey as his wife.” He then spoke this verse:

Hearing the merchant Kappaṭa's words, the donkey was delighted and spoke this verse:

“Kappaṭa, I will travel even further, for fourteen leagues.”

O Merchant Kappaṭa! If you will bring and give to you a wife, a female donkey who has four legs, a face as white as a conch shell, and is beautiful in all her limbs, I will travel even further, up to fourteen leagues. O Kappaṭa, know this.

Then the merchant Kappaṭa said, “If so, come, dear,” and took him back to his own place. After a few days had passed, the donkey said to the merchant, “O Master, did you not tell me that you would bring a wife for me?” Kappaṭa replied, “Yes, I said so. I will not break my word. I will find and give you a female donkey as a wife. However, I will provide a portion of food for you alone. Whether that portion is enough for you and your companion, you alone shall know. Furthermore, when children are born from your union, whether that same portion of food is enough for you and your many children, you alone shall know.” While Kappaṭa was speaking thus, the donkey lost all desire for the female donkey.

The Teacher, having related this Dhamma teaching, concluded the Jātaka: “Monks, at that time, the female donkey was Janapadakalyāṇī, the male donkey was Nanda, and the merchant was I myself. Thus, in the past also, I disciplined Nanda by enticing him with a female.”

The Story of the Elder Nanda ends.

## 10. The Story of Cunda the Pig-slayer

(Cundasūkarikavatthu)

“Here he grieves...” The Teacher, while residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, told this Dhamma teaching concerning a man named Cunda the Pig-slayer.
81:
## Cunda’s Cruel Livelihood
That Cunda the pork-butcher made his living for fifty-five years by killing, eating, and selling pigs. During times of famine, he would take grain by cart and travel through various large and small districts. He would buy piglets raised by villagers for the price of a small measure or two, fill his cart, and return. Behind his house, he fenced off a place like a pigsty and kept the piglets there. When those piglets grew large by eating various small plants and their own excrement, he would choose which pig he wished to kill. He would tie that pig firmly at the slaughtering place so it could not move. To make the flesh swell, he would beat it with a four-sided wooden mallet until it was bloated. When he knew it had become thick-fleshed, he would pry open its mouth, place a stake inside the jaws, and pour boiling water from a metal pot into its mouth. That boiling water entered the belly, loosened the old excrement, and carried it out through the lower part. As long as there was even a small amount of excrement, the water came out turbid. When the belly was clean, the water came out clear and pure, without turbidity. After that, he poured the remaining hot water over the pig's back. That hot water caused the black skin to peel away. Then, he singed the hair with a grass torch and cut off the head with a very sharp sword. He caught the flowing blood in a vessel, kneaded the meat with the blood, cooked it, and ate it in the midst of his wife and children, selling the remainder. In this manner, fifty-five years passed for Cunda the pork-butcher as he made his living. Although the Buddha was residing in a nearby monastery, not even for a single day did Cunda perform an act of merit, such as offering a handful of flowers, a spoonful of alms-food, or any other wholesome deed.

## Suffering before Death and Falling into Hell
On one occasion, a disease arose in the body of Cunda the pork-butcher. Even while he was still alive, the heat of the Great Avīci Hell appeared (burning his whole body).
82:
## The Nature of Evil
(15) Idha socati pecca socati,
Pāpakārī ubhayattha socati.
So socati so vihaññati,
Disvā kammakiliṭṭhamattano.

*Pāpakārī*, the one who habitually does evil. *Idha*, in this present world, in this life. *Socati*, he grieves. *Pecca*, in the world beyond, in the next life. *Socati*, he grieves. *Ubhayattha*, in both lives, the present and the future. *Socati*, he grieves. *So*, that person. *Attano*, his own. *Kammakiliṭṭhaṃ*, defiled unwholesome karma. *Disvā*, having seen. *Socati*, he grieves. *So*, that person. *Vihaññati*, he is tormented.

The heat of the Avīci Hell is such that it can burst the eyes of one looking at it from a hundred leagues away. This is true. The Buddha taught: "Its floor is made of iron, ablaze with heat; it stands always spreading a hundred leagues all around." Elder Nāgasena gave this analogy because the heat of hell is far more intense than natural fire: "Great King, even a rock as large as a gabled house would vanish in an instant if thrown into the fires of hell. However, beings reborn there do not perish, like beings in a mother's womb, due to the power of their karma," so he taught King Milinda.

When the heat of hell appeared to Cunda the pork-butcher, a state resembling his karma arose. This is how it happened: In the middle of his house, he began to squeal and howl like a pig, crawling about on his two knees, going back and forth between the front and back walls. Then the people of his household seized Cunda firmly and closed his mouth. Even though they closed it, they could not stop him; the fruit of karma cannot be prevented even by Buddhas. Squealing and wandering here and there, the people in the surrounding seven houses could not sleep. All the members of the household, unable to prevent Cunda—who was terrified and trembling with the fear of death—from going outside, closed the doors of the house so that he remained inside and could not wander outside. They stayed guarding the house from the outside. Cunda the pork-butcher, tormented by the intense heat of hell inside the house, squealed and howled, wandering here and there. After running about in this way for seven days, he died on the eighth day and was reborn in the Great Avīci Hell. The Great Avīci Hell should be described according to the Devadūta Sutta.

## The Monks' Report to the Buddha
As the monks passed by the door of Cunda the pork-butcher's house, they heard that sound and, thinking it was the sound of pigs, went to the monastery, sat respectfully before the Teacher, and said: "Venerable Sir, it has been seven days since the door of Cunda the pork-butcher's house was closed and pigs were being killed. We suppose some festive ceremony is being held in his house. Venerable Sir, for one who kills so many pigs, there is not even a single moment of loving-kindness or compassion. We have never before seen such a cruel and harsh being."
83:
At that time, the Blessed One said: "Monks, that Cunda the pork-butcher did not kill pigs during these seven days. The result corresponding to the kamma he committed has clearly appeared. Even while alive, the heat of the Avīci hell has manifested. That Cunda the pork-butcher, burning with the intense heat of hell, spent seven days crying out and squealing like a pig, running around his house, and today he has died and been reborn in the Avīci hell." When the monks remarked, "Venerable Sir, having suffered in this life, he has now gone to a place of suffering in the next world," the Buddha replied, "Monks, it is so. Whether a monk or a layperson, one who is heedless suffers in both this world and the next." Having said this, he spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the verse, many attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth. The teaching was beneficial to the multitude.

The story of Cunda the pork-butcher ends.

## 11. The Story of Dhammika Upāsaka
(Dhammika Upāsaka Vatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher told this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Idha modati," concerning the lay follower Dhammika.

## How the Household of Dhammika Upāsaka Performed Merit
In Sāvatthī, it is said there were five hundred lay followers named Dhammika. Each of these five hundred lay followers had five hundred followers of their own. Among them, the eldest and leader was the one named Mahā-Dhammika. This great lay follower had seven sons and seven daughters. Each of these children (that is, every child) offered ticket-gruel, ticket-food, fortnightly food, invitation food, observance day food, food for the Order, and rainy season robes. All these children were known as 'anujāta' children, as they followed the example of their parents.

1. An 'avajāta' son is one who is inferior and does not follow the good practice of his parents.
2. An 'anujāta' son is one who is similar and follows the good practice of his parents.
3. An 'atijāta' son is one who is superior and exceeds the good practice of his parents. Among these three, the 'avajāta' son is undesirable; he is a base son.

Thus, there were sixteen offerings of ticket-food, gruel, and so on, from the fourteen children, the wife, and the great lay follower Dhammika himself. In this way, together with his wife and children, the great lay follower Dhammika was one of virtuous conduct, established in good Dhamma, and delighted in sharing and giving alms.

## The Great Lay Follower Listens to Dhamma While Ill
Later, Dhammika Upāsaka fell ill and his strength declined. Desiring to hear the Dhamma, he sent a message to the Teacher, saying, "Please send eight or sixteen monks to me." The Teacher sent the monks. They went and sat in the prepared seats surrounding Dhammika Upāsaka’s bed. Then he said, "Venerable Sirs, it will be difficult for me to see you again. I am weak. Please recite a discourse for my benefit." When asked, "Lay follower, which discourse do you wish to hear?" he replied, "I wish to hear the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta, which is never forsaken by any of the Buddhas." Then they began to recite the discourse: "Ekāyano ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā..."
84:
## Speaking with the Devas
At that moment, six chariots arrived from the six deva worlds, adorned with all kinds of ornaments, each drawn by a thousand Sindh horses and measuring five hundred yojanas in width. The deities standing in those six chariots said, "We will take you to our deva world! We will take you to our deva world!" and they pleaded, "O great lay follower Dhammika, just as one might break a clay pot to take a golden one, please be reborn on this chariot to enjoy our deva world! Please be reborn on this chariot to enjoy our deva world!" Dhammika Upāsaka, not wanting any disturbance to his listening of the Dhamma, said, "Wait a moment! Wait a moment!" The monks who were reciting the sutta thought he was stopping them and became silent.

## The Monks Depart and the Garland is Placed on the Tusita Chariot
Then the children of Dhammika Upāsaka cried and lamented, saying, "Previously, our father was never satisfied with hearing the Dhamma. But now, having invited the monks to recite, he stops them himself. There is no being who does not fear death." The monks, thinking it was no longer the proper time to recite, rose from their seats and departed. After a short while, the lay follower regained his awareness and asked his children, "Why are you crying?" They replied, "Father, while you were listening to the Dhamma after inviting the monks, you stopped them yourself. Because of that, we cried, thinking there is no one who does not fear death." When he asked, "Where are the venerable ones?" they said, "Father, the venerable ones thought it was no longer the proper time to recite, so they rose from their seats and left." He said, "I was not speaking with the venerable ones."

"If not, then with whom were you speaking, father?" they asked. He replied, "Deities from the six deva worlds brought six adorned chariots and, standing in the sky, they called out, 'Enjoy yourself in our deva world! Enjoy yourself in our deva world!' I was speaking only with those deities."

"Father, where are the chariots? We do not see them," they said. He then asked, "Are there any flower garlands that have been strung for me?" "Yes, father, there are," they replied. He asked again, "Which deva world is delightful?" They said, "Father, the Tusita heaven, the dwelling place of all Bodhisattas and the parents of the Buddhas, is delightful." He then said, "If so, make a resolution: 'Let it hang on the chariot that has come from the Tusita heaven,' and throw the flower garland." The children threw it as their father instructed. The garland caught on the pole of the chariot and remained suspended in the sky. The multitude of people saw only the garland; they did not see the chariot.

Dhammika Upāsaka asked, "Do you see this garland?" and when they replied, "Yes, we see it," he said, "This garland is hanging from the chariot that arrived from the Tusita heaven. I am going to the Tusita heaven. Do not worry about me. If you wish to be reborn near me, perform meritorious deeds just as I have done." Having said this, he passed away and was established in the chariot.
85:
## The Nature of Meritorious Deeds

(16) Idha modati pecca modati,
katapuñño ubhayattha modati.
So modati so pamodati,
disvā kammavisuddhimattano.

*Katapuñño*: the person who has performed various kinds of wholesome deeds. *Idha*: in this present life too. *Modati*: he rejoices. *Pecca*: in the life hereafter too. *Modati*: he rejoices. *Ubhayattha*: in both lives, the present and the hereafter. *Modati*: he rejoices. *Attano kammavisuddhiṃ disvā*: seeing the purity of his own meritorious deeds. *So modati*: he rejoices. *So pamodati*: he is exceedingly glad.

## Final Words Before Death

After saying this, he gave his final instructions: "I am going to the Tusita heaven. Do not be worried or distressed. If you wish to be in my presence, perform meritorious deeds just as I have done." Having said this, when he passed away, he was reborn and remained exactly upon the celestial chariot from Tusita. For that great deity, who was formerly the lay follower Dhammika,

at that very moment, a physical body (attabhāva) three gāvutas in height, adorned with ornaments weighing as much as sixty cartloads, came into being. A thousand celestial nymphs surrounded him. A golden mansion twenty-five yojanas in size appeared clearly.

When those monks arrived back at the monastery, the Teacher asked, "Monks, did you preach the Dhamma to the lay follower?" "Venerable Sir, we preached, but while we were preaching, he interrupted us saying, 'Wait a moment,' and stopped us. At that time, the lay follower's sons and daughters wept. We thought, 'Now is not the time for chanting,' so we rose from our seats and returned, Venerable Sir." "Monks, that lay follower Dhammika was not speaking with you. Deities from the six celestial realms had adorned six chariots and brought them, inviting that lay follower. Because he did not wish for an interruption to the Dhamma teaching, he spoke with those deities." "Is that so, O Blessed One?" When they asked, He replied, "It is so, monks." "Where has he been reborn now?" "In the Tusita realm, monks." "Venerable Sir, having lived rejoicing in the midst of his relatives here in the human world, has he now gone and been reborn in a place of rejoicing once again?" "Yes, monks. Whether they be householders or those who have gone forth, those who are heedful in meritorious deeds rejoice in all places." Having said this, He uttered this verse:

## The Benefits of the Teaching

At the conclusion of the verse, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti) and so forth. The Dhamma teaching became beneficial to the great multitude.

The story of the lay follower Dhammika ends.
86:
## 12. The Story of Devadatta

(Devadattavatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Idha tappati," concerning Devadatta.

The sequence of the story of Devadatta, from the time of his ordination until he was swallowed by the earth, including all the Jātakas spoken concerning Devadatta, would be extensive if told in detail; however, in this Dhammapada text, it is summarized.

## The Sakyan Princes' Discussion on Ordination

While the All-Knowing Buddha was dwelling in the Anupiya Mango Grove, depending on the market town named Anupiya of the Malla kings, on the very day the major and minor marks of the Bodhisatta were read, eighty thousand families of relatives pledged eighty thousand sons, saying, "Whether he becomes a King or a Buddha, he shall wander surrounded only by a retinue of the warrior caste (Khattiya)." When most of those princes had ordained, seeing that these six Sakyan princes—King Bhaddiya, Prince Anuruddha, Prince Ānanda, Prince Bhagu, Prince Kimbila, and Prince Devadatta—had not followed to ordain, people began to talk, saying, "We have made our own sons ordain. These six Sakyan princes must not be relatives of the Buddha. Why do they not ordain?" Then, the Sakyan prince named Mahānāma approached Prince Anuruddha and said, "Dear brother Anuruddha, in our family, there is no one who has ordained yet. Either you should ordain, or I, your elder brother, shall ordain."

## Prince Anuruddha Who Had Never Heard the Word \"No\"

That Prince Anuruddha was of a delicate nature. He possessed abundant wealth and luxury. He had never even heard the word \"natthi\" (there is none/no). This is true. One day, while those six princes were playing a game of marbles (guḷakīḷaṃ), Prince Anuruddha lost and had to provide cakes. He sent a messenger to his mother for cakes. Then, the prince's mother prepared cakes and sent them. The princes ate the cakes and played again. Prince Anuruddha alone...
87:
Repeated losses occurred. Every time the mother sent cakes, she sent them three times, but on the fourth time, she sent word saying, "There are no cakes (natthi pūva)." Since Prince Anuruddha had never heard the word "none" (natthi), he thought, "This 'none' must be a special kind of cake," and sent back word, "Bring me that very 'none-cake'." The Prince's mother thought, "My son has never heard the word 'none'; I will make him understand through this means," and she sent an empty golden bowl, covered with another golden bowl.

At that moment, the guardian deities of the city reflected: "When Prince Anuruddha was the laborer Annabhāra, he offered his own portion of food to the Paccekabuddha Uparittha and made a wish: 'May I never hear the word "none" (natthi), and may I never know the place where food originates.' If this Prince Anuruddha were to see an empty bowl with no cakes, we would not be able to enter the assembly of devas, and our heads would split into seven pieces." Having reflected thus, they filled that golden bowl with divine cakes. As soon as the bowl was placed in the playing field and opened, the fragrance of the cakes pervaded the entire city. As soon as a piece of the cake was placed in his mouth, the flavor spread through his seven thousand taste-nerves.

Prince Anuruddha thought, "My mother does not love me; for all this time, she never cooked this 'none-cake' for me. From now on, I shall eat no other cake." Thinking this, he went home and asked his mother, "Mother, do you love me or not?" When he asked, she replied, "Dear son, I love you more than my own heart, like a person with only one eye loves that eye." The Prince then asked, "Mother, if you love me so, why did you not cook and give me 'none-cake' for all this time?"

Then the mother called the young attendant and asked, "Dear, was there anything in the golden bowl?" He replied, "My Lady, the golden bowl was full of cakes. I have never seen such cakes before." The mother reflected, "My son must be one of great merit who has made aspirations in the past; the devas must have filled the bowl and sent the cakes." Then her son, Prince Anuruddha, said, "Mother, from this day forth, I shall eat no other kind of cake; please cook and give me only 'none-cake'." From that day on, whenever Prince Anuruddha said he wanted to eat cake, his mother would simply cover an empty golden bowl with another and send it. For as long as he lived in the household life, the devas themselves continued to provide him with cakes.

Since Prince Anuruddha did not even know this much, how could he know what monkhood was? Therefore, when he asked his elder brother, "What is this thing called monkhood?", the brother replied, "It means shaving off one's hair and beard, donning saffron-dyed robes, sleeping on a wooden bed or a mat of slats, and living by going for alms. This is what monkhood is." The Prince said, "Brother, I am very delicate; I am not able to become a monk." The brother said, "In that case, dear brother, learn all the household duties and live the life of a householder. It is not right for one of us to remain without becoming a monk." Then he asked his brother again, "What are these household duties?" How could a son of a noble family, who did not even know where rice comes from, know what work needs to be done in the world?
88:
## The Three Princes Who Did Not Know the Origin of Rice

This is true. One day, a conversation arose among the three princes Kimbila, Bhaddiya, and Anuruddha: "Where does rice come from?" At that time, Prince Kimbila said, "It is produced in the granary." Then Prince Bhaddiya said to Prince Kimbila, "You do not know the origin of rice; rice is produced in the cooking pot." Prince Anuruddha said, "Neither of you knows; rice is produced in a large golden bowl adorned with jewels."

Among those three princes, one day Prince Kimbila saw rice being taken out from the granary and thought, "This rice is produced only in the granary." Prince Bhaddiya one day saw rice being cooked and served from a pot and had the perception that "Rice is produced only in the cooking pot." As for Prince Anuruddha, he had never seen the pounding of paddy, the cooking of rice, or the serving of rice. He had only seen it when it was served and placed before him. Therefore, when Prince Anuruddha wished to eat, he had the perception that rice was produced only in the bowl. In this way, those three princes did not know the origin of rice.

## Prince Anuruddha’s Effort to Ordain

Therefore, Prince Anuruddha asked, "What is this thing called work that people must do?" When he heard the description of the tasks to be performed year after year, such as "First, the field must be plowed," he said, "When will the end of these human tasks be known? When shall we enjoy our wealth and pleasures without worry?" Because the tasks were described as having no limit and no end, he said, "Brother, you alone should live the life of a householder; I have no need for this household life." He then went to his mother and requested, "Mother, please give me permission; let me ordain as a monk." Although his mother refused him three times using various reasons, she finally said, "Dear son, if your friend King Bhaddiya ordains, then you may ordain together with him."

When she said this, he approached King Bhaddiya and said, "Friend Bhaddiya, my ordination depends on you." After persuading King Bhaddiya through various means, he obtained a promise from him to ordain together on the seventh day.

## The Ordination of the Six Princes and Upāli the Barber

Then the six princes—Bhaddiya the Sakyan king, Anuruddha, Ānanda, Bhagu, Kimbila, and Devadatta—with Upāli the barber as the seventh, enjoyed pleasures for seven days like deities enjoying divine bliss. They then departed with a fourfold army as if going to a park. Upon reaching another territory, they sent the army back by royal command and entered the foreign land. When they had entered the foreign land, the six princes took off their ornaments, made a bundle of them, and gave them to Upāli, saying, "Here, friend Upāli, take these possessions and go back. This much wealth is enough for your livelihood."

Upāli rolled on the ground at the feet of the princes and wept, but being unable to disobey their command, he stood up, took the bundle, and turned back.

At the moment their paths diverged, it was as if the forest reached a state of weeping and the earth reached a state of trembling. After going back a short distance, Upāli the barber thought: "The Sakyans are fierce. They might even kill me, thinking, 'This man has made away with the princes.' Even these Sakyan princes have renounced such wealth and discarded these priceless ornaments like a glob of spit to ordain. Why should I not be able to ordain?" Having thought this, he untied the bundle of wealth, hung the ornaments on a tree, and said, "Let those who desire them take them." He then followed after the princes. When the princes asked, "Why have you come back?", he explained the reason to them.
89:
Then the princes took Upāli the barber and went to the presence of the Blessed One. Having paid homage to the Buddha, they said: "Venerable Sir, we Sākiyans are proud and arrogant. This Upāli has been our servant for a long time. Please ordain this Upāli first. We will then perform acts of respect such as saluting him with joined palms. In this way, our Sakyan pride will be humbled." Having requested thus, they had Upāli ordained first, and they themselves were ordained afterwards.

## Attainment of Special Distinctions and Devadatta’s Scheme
Among those six princes, the Venerable Bhaddiya became an Arahant endowed with the Three Knowledges (te-vijja) within that very rainy season. The Venerable Anuruddha attained the Divine Eye (dibba-cakkhu), and later, after hearing the Mahāpurisavitakka Sutta, he reached the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). The Venerable Ānanda was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). The Venerable Bhagu and the Venerable Kimbila later developed insight and reached the fruit of Arahantship. Devadatta, however, attained only mundane psychic powers (pothujjanika-iddhi) as a worldling. 

Later, while the Blessed One was staying in Kosambī, great gain and honor arose for the Tathāgata along with the community of disciples. People carrying robes, medicines, and other offerings entered the monastery and wandered around looking for the places where the eighty great disciples sat, asking: "Where is the Teacher? Where is the Venerable Sāriputta? Where is the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna? Where is the Venerable Mahākassapa? Where is the Venerable Bhaddiya? Where is the Venerable Anuruddha? Where is the Venerable Ānanda? Where is the Venerable Bhagu? Where is the Venerable Kimbila?" There was no one who asked, "Where is the Venerable Devadatta sitting or standing?"

Then Devadatta thought: "I was ordained together with these others. They were ordained from the warrior caste (khattiya), and I too was ordained from the warrior caste. Yet people carrying gain and honor seek only them; there is no one who even mentions my name. With whom should I associate and whom should I inspire so that gain and honor may arise for me?"

## Devadatta’s Association with King Ajātasattu
Then this thought occurred to Devadatta: "This King Bimbisāra, upon his first meeting with the Buddha, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry along with one hundred and ten thousand people. It is not possible to form an association with King Bimbisāra. Nor is it possible with the King of Kosala. However, this Prince Ajātasattu, the son of the King, does not yet know the virtues or faults of anyone. I will associate with this Prince Ajātasattu." 

Devadatta went from Kosambī to Rājagaha and, transforming himself into the form of a young boy, he wrapped four venomous snakes around his four limbs, one snake around his neck like a necklace, one snake on his head like a turban, and one snake on one shoulder. Adorned with these snakes, he descended from the sky and sat on Prince Ajātasattu’s lap. The Prince was terrified and asked, "Who are you?" Devadatta replied, "I am Devadatta." To dispel the Prince's fear, he discarded that form and stood before Prince Ajātasattu wearing his robes and carrying his bowl. Thus, he inspired the Prince and caused gain and honor to arise for himself.

## Devadatta Bearing a Grudge against the Buddha and Leaving
Devadatta, being severely overwhelmed by gain and honor, conceived the evil thought: "I will lead the community of monks." Because he conceived this thought...
90:
...at the very moment of conceiving that thought, he fell away from his mundane psychic powers. He approached the Blessed One while the Teacher was preaching the Dhamma to an assembly including the King at the Veḷuvana Monastery. Having paid homage to the Buddha, he rose from his seat, raised his joined palms, and said: "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is now old, aged, and advanced in years. May the Blessed One now live unconcerned, devoted to the blissful abiding of the fruit of attainment (phala-samāpatti) in this very life. I will lead the community of monks. Please hand over the community of monks to me."

When he said this, the Blessed One rebuked and rejected him with the words "lick-spittle" (kheḷāsaka—one who swallows the spittle of others). Being displeased and filled with intense anger, Devadatta bore his first grudge against the Tathāgata and departed.

## Various Efforts to Kill the Buddha
After he had departed, the Blessed One had a Proclamation Act (pakāsanīya-kamma) performed against Devadatta in Rājagaha. Devadatta thought: "Now I have been abandoned by the ascetic Gotama. I will now work for his harm." He approached Ajātasattu and said: "Prince, in the past, humans were long-lived, but now they have short lives. It is possible that you might die while still a prince. Therefore, Prince, kill your father and become king. I will kill the Blessed One and become the Buddha."

When Ajātasattu was established in the kingship, Devadatta dispatched archers to kill the Blessed One. However, those men reached the fruit of Stream-entry and returned. Then, he himself climbed the Gijjhakūṭa mountain, thinking, "I myself will deprive the ascetic Gotama of life." He rolled down a rock, committing the act of wounding the Buddha (lohituppādaka-kamma) so that blood clotted. When he was unable to kill the Buddha by that means either, he again ordered the release of the elephant Nāဠāgiri.
91:
When that elephant Nālāgiri was approaching, the Venerable Ānanda stood in front of the Blessed One, sacrificing his own life for the sake of the Teacher. After the Buddha had tamed Nālāgiri and departed from the city, upon reaching the monastery, he accepted and partook of a great alms-offering brought by thousands of lay devotees. On that day, he preached the Dhamma in progressive order to the eighteen crores of citizens of Rājagaha who had assembled. When eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma, the people remarked: "Oh, how wonderful! The Venerable Ānanda possesses great virtue. When such a fierce and wild elephant approached, he stood before the Blessed One, sacrificing his own life." Hearing this talk concerning the virtues of the Venerable Ānanda, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that he has sacrificed his life for my sake; he did so in the past as well." Being requested by the monks, he related the Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka, the Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka, and the Kakkaṭaka Jātaka.

Devadatta’s deeds were not yet widely known. His actions—causing the death of King Bimbisāra, sending assassins, and rolling down a rock—were not as public as the release of the elephant Nālāgiri. At that time, the multitude raised a clamor, saying: "It was Devadatta who had the King killed; he sent the assassins; he rolled down the rock. And now, he has had Nālāgiri released. The King goes about associating with such an evil person!"

## Schism of the Saṅgha due to the Refusal of the Five Requests

King Ajātasattu, hearing the words of the multitude, withdrew the five hundred pots of food that were regularly provided and ceased going to attend upon Devadatta. The citizens also did not give even a spoonful of alms-food to Devadatta when he approached their houses. Having lost his gains and honor, and wishing to live by pretension, he approached the Blessed One and requested five items. When the Blessed One rejected them, saying, "Enough, Devadatta. Whoever wishes, let him be a forest-dweller," Devadatta said, "Friends, whose words are better, more fitting, and more excellent? The words of the Tathāgata or mine?" He then said, "I speak thus by way of the scrupulous life: 'Venerable Sir, I pray—
1. Let the monks be forest-dwellers for as long as they live.
2. Let them be alms-food eaters (refusing invitations).
3. Let them be wearers of rag-robes.
4. Let them be dwellers at the foot of a tree.
5. Let them not eat fish or meat.'
I speak by the power of the scrupulous life. Whoever wishes to be free from suffering, let him come with me." Having said this, he departed. Hearing his words, some newly ordained monks of dull intellect thought, "Devadatta speaks well; we will go about with him," and they sided with him. Thus, Devadatta, together with five hundred monks, convinced the people who were impressed by austerity through these five items, and by soliciting from house to house, he strove for a schism in the Saṅgha.

Two-thirds of people are impressed by physical appearance. Four-fifths are impressed by reputation or voice. Nine-tenths are impressed by austerity. Those impressed by the Dhamma are perhaps only one in a hundred thousand.

When asked by the Blessed One, "Is it true, Devadatta, that you are striving for a schism in the Saṅgha, for a division in the Order?" Devadatta replied, "It is true, Blessed One." Although he was exhorted with words such as "A schism in the Saṅgha is a grave matter, Devadatta," he did not heed the Teacher's words. After departing, he saw the Venerable Ānanda wandering for alms in Rājagaha and said, "Friend Ānanda, from this day forth, I shall perform the Uposatha and the acts of the Saṅgha apart from the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks." The Elder reported this matter to the Blessed One. Knowing this, the Teacher, moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega), [said] "Devadatta, who relies on what is not for the welfare of the world including the devas, [is bound] for the Avīci Hell..."
92:
Things that are not good and harmful to oneself are easy to do. But that which is beneficial and good is truly very difficult to do.

Attano—of oneself, or to oneself. Ahitāni ca—deeds that are not beneficial. Asādhūni ca—and deeds that are not good. Sukarāṇi—are easy to do. Ve—indeed. Yaṃ kammaṃ—whatever deed. Hitañca—is both beneficial. Sādhuñca—and is good and praiseworthy. Taṃ kammaṃ—that deed. Ve—indeed. Parama-dukkaram—is extremely difficult to do.

Hoti sīlavataṃ attho, paṭisanthāravuttinaṃ.
Lakkhaṇaṃ passa āyantaṃ, ñātisaṅghapurakkhataṃ.
Atha passasimaṃ kāḷaṃ, suvihīnaṃva ñātibhi.

Sīlavataṃ—to those who are virtuous. Paṭisanthāravuttinaṃ—to those whose conduct is characterized by hospitality through both the Dhamma and material things. Attho—the increase of benefits. Hoti—occurs. Passa—Look closely at. Lakkhaṇaṃ—the deer named Lakkhaṇa. Āyantaṃ—who is coming forward. Ñātisaṅghapurakkhataṃ—surrounded by a host of kinsmen. Atha—Furthermore. Passasi—look closely at. Imaṃ kāḷaṃ—this deer named Kāḷa. Āyantaṃ—who is coming forward. Ekakaṃ—all alone. Suvihīnaṃva—being utterly bereft and ruined. Ñātibhi—by his host of kinsmen.

Thinking, “He has performed a great and evil kamma that will cause him to suffer,” the Buddha reflected and preached this verse, and then once again uttered this solemn utterance (Udāna):

Sukaraṃ sādhunā sādhu, sādhu pāpena dukkaraṃ.
Pāpaṃ pāpena sukaraṃ, pāpamariyhehi dukkaraṃ.

Sādhunā—by a good person. Sādhu—a good deed. Sukaraṃ—is easy to do. Pāpena—by an evil person. Sādhu—a good deed. Dukkaraṃ—is difficult to do. Pāpena—by an evil person. Pāpaṃ—an evil deed. Sukaraṃ—is easy to do. Ariyehi—by the Noble Ones. Pāpaṃ—an evil deed. Dukkaraṃ—is difficult to do.

At that time, on the Uposatha day, Devadatta sat with his followers in a suitable place and said, “Let whoever approves of these five points take a voting ticket.” When five hundred young Vajjiputtaka monks, who had not yet reached maturity in knowledge, took the tickets, he split the Sangha and, taking those monks with him, went to Gayāsīsa.

## The Venerable Sāriputta and Others Following to Preach and Devadatta Vomiting Blood

Hearing that Devadatta had reached Gayāsīsa, the Blessed One sent the two Chief Disciples to bring those young monks back. The two Chief Disciples went to Gayāsīsa and, teaching them in succession through the marvel of mind-reading and the marvel of instruction, as well as the marvel of psychic power and the marvel of instruction, they made those monks drink the ambrosia of the Dhamma. Then, taking them along, they returned through the air. Kokālika then said, “Friend Devadatta, get up! Your assembly of monks has been taken away by Sāriputta and Moggallāna. Did I not tell you, ‘Friend Devadatta, do not trust Sāriputta and Moggallāna; Sāriputta and Moggallāna have evil desires and are under the sway of evil desires’?” Having said this, he struck Devadatta in the middle of the chest with his knee. Right there, hot, fresh blood vomited out from Devadatta’s mouth.

Seeing the Venerable Sāriputta returning through the air, surrounded by the assembly of the Sangha, the monks said, “O Blessed One of great glory—when the Elder Sāriputta departed, he went with only one companion; now, upon his return, he is splendid with a large retinue.” When they said this, the Blessed One remarked, “Monks, it is not only now that my son Sāriputta is splendid. In the past, when he was born in the animal kingdom, my son Sāriputta was also splendid when he came into my presence.” He then preached this verse from the Lakkhaṇa Migajātaka of the Ekakanipāta.
93:
Indeed, you have wandered through the forests, pecking at the soft-wooded trees.
But then you came to the heart-wood Khadira tree, where you, the noble bird, broke your head.
Your brains have spilled out, and your skull is split.
All your ribs are broken; now, friend, you truly shine.

O Kalandaka, the woodpecker. Garuḷo, the noble bird. You, being such as you are, have indeed wandered through the forests of sapless silk-cotton and flame-of-the-forest trees, pecking and boring into them with your beak. In those useless forest trees such as the silk-cotton and flame-of-the-forest, you have indeed spent your time. Then, you reached the Khadira forest, which possesses natural heartwood. At that tree, you struck and split your head. That tree is called the Khadira.

Jambuka, the jackal. Your brains flow out. Your head is split. All your ribs are broken. Now, friend jackal, you truly shine.

## Preaching Many Jātakas Concerning Devadatta

Then again, when the monks reported, “Venerable Sir, it is said that Devadatta, having seated the two chief disciples on his left and right sides, is imitating Your Majesty, saying, ‘I will preach the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha,’” the Buddha said, “Monks, not only now, but in the past as well, this Devadatta has striven to imitate me, but he was unable to do so.” He then told this Vīraka Jātaka of the Dukanipāta.

O Vīraka, have you seen my husband Saviṭṭhaka,
The bird who speaks so sweetly,
With a neck as blue and beautiful as a peacock’s?

He who tried to imitate the bird that moves on water and land,
Who always eats raw fish,
Saviṭṭhaka, entangled in the weeds, has died.

Vīraka, noble Vīraka. Have you indeed seen the crow, my husband named Saviṭṭhaka, who has a sweet and pleasant voice, and a neck as dark and elegant as a peacock’s?

O female crow. Saviṭṭhaka, your husband, who tried to imitate that bird who lives on both water and land and always eats raw fish, died entangled in the weeds.

After preaching the Vīraka Jātaka of the Dukanipāta, on other days as well, based on similar circumstances, He preached the Kalandaka Jātaka of the Dukanipāta and the Virocana Jātaka of the Ekakanipāta.

He preached such Jātakas. Then again, concerning the words “Devadatta is ungrateful,” He preached the Sakuṇa Jātaka of the Catukkanipāta.

We have done a service for you according to our strength.
O King of Beasts, salutations to you! May we receive something in return?

For me, who always performs cruel deeds and feeds on blood,
That you are still alive after entering between my teeth—that itself is a great favor.

Migarāja, the lion, king of beasts. Whatever strength we had, with that strength, we performed a service for you. Salutations to you, King of Beasts. I wonder if we might receive some meat to eat.

Always performing cruel and harsh deeds, feeding on blood and flesh—that you are still alive after having entered between my teeth is a great and abundant favor.

He preached such Jātakas. Then again, concerning Devadatta’s attempt to kill Him—

This is known to the Kurunga deer, that you, O Sepaṇṇi tree, are scattering your fruits.
I am going to another tree, Sepaṇṇi; I do not like your fruit.

Sepaṇṇi tree. Because you scatter your fruits in front of me, this is clear to the Kurunga deer. I do not like your fruit, O Sepaṇṇi tree. I shall go to another tree.
94:
“Eyes are broken, the cloth is lost, and there is a quarrel in the friend's house. Both works are ruined, in water and on land.”

Thus, the Buddha preached the Kurunga Jātaka and others from the Ekakanipāta. Then, on the following morning, when the talk arose that “Devadatta has fallen away from both gain and honor, and from the monkhood,” the Buddha said, “Monks, not only now has Devadatta fallen away; in the past too, he fell away,” and he preached the Ubhatobhaṭṭha Jātaka and others from the Ekakanipāta as follows:

“Puriṣa, O man. Te, your. Akkhī, eyes. Bhinnā, are broken. Paṭo, the cloth. Naṭṭho, is lost. Gehe ca, and in the house. Sakhī, the wife. Bhaṇḍanaṃ, a quarrel with the neighbors. Akā, has made. Udakamhi ca, both in the water. Thalamhi ca, and on the land. Ubhato, in both places. Paduṭṭhakammanto, the work was ruined.”

Following this sequence of words, the Blessed One, while residing in the city of Rājagaha, preached many Jātakas concerning Devadatta. Then, traveling from Rājagaha to the city of Sāvatthī, He resided at the Jetavana Monastery.

## Devadatta, Repenting, Arrives Near Jetavana Monastery to Pay Homage to the Buddha

Devadatta was ill for nine months. In his final moments, wishing to see the Blessed One, he called his disciples and said, “I wish to see the Blessed One; show Him to me.” When they said, “When you were capable, you lived as an enemy to the Blessed One. We do not dare take you to Him,” he pleaded, “Do not destroy me. I have harbored malice and offended the Blessed One. But the Blessed One does not have even a hair's breadth of malice toward me. That is true; the Blessed One—

‘Toward the murderer Devadatta, the thief Angulimāla,
Dhanapāla, and Rāhula, He is of equal mind toward all.’

Vadhake, toward the murderer. Devadatte ca, Devadatta. Angulimālake, named Angulimāla. Core ca, the great thief. Dhanapāle ca, the elephant named Dhanapāla (Nālāgiri). Rāhule ca, and His son Rāhula. Sabbattha, toward all of them. Samamānaso, He has an equal mind of loving-kindness.

Show me that Blessed One,” he begged repeatedly. Then they took Devadatta on a litter and set out. Hearing of Devadatta’s coming, the monks informed the Blessed One, “Venerable Sir, it is said that Devadatta is coming to pay homage to You.” The Blessed One said, “Monks, Devadatta will not be able to see me with this body.” It is a natural law (dhammatā) that from the time Devadatta asked for the five points, he would not see the Buddha again. When the monks reported, “Venerable Sir, he has reached such and such a place,” the Buddha said, “Monks, let him do as he wishes, but he will not be able to see me.” They reported, “Venerable Sir, he is one yojana away... half a yojana... one gāvuta... he has arrived near the pond of Jetavana Monastery.” The Buddha said, “Monks, even if he enters inside Jetavana, he will not be able to see me.”

## Devadatta Being Swallowed by the Earth at the Pond Near the Monastery

Those carrying Devadatta set the litter down on the bank of the Jetavana pond and went down into the pond to bathe. Devadatta also rose from the litter and sat with both feet placed on the ground.
95:
Then both feet sank into the earth. Gradually, Devadatta sank up to his ankles, knees, waist, breasts, and neck. When his jawbone was about to enter the earth, he uttered this verse:

“With these bones, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Supreme Person,
The God of gods, the Charioteer of men to be tamed,
The All-Seeing One, endowed with a hundred marks of merit.”

Aggapuggalaṃ, the person who is especially noble among many various groups of persons. Devātidevaṃ, the supreme deity of purity who is nobler than all gods. Naradammasārathiṃ, like a charioteer in taming and leading humans and gods to heaven. Samantacakkhuṃ, possessing omniscience capable of seeing everything without remainder. Satapuññalakkhaṇaṃ, endowed with countless marks of merit. Taṃ Buddhaṃ, to that Blessed One. Ahaṃ, I. Imehi aṭṭhīhi, with these bones. Imehi pāṇehi, and with this life. Saraṇaṃ, as a refuge. Gato asmi, have gone.

He recited this verse. Seeing this outcome, the Blessed One had ordained Devadatta. “If Devadatta does not ordain, as a layman he will commit heavy karma and will not be able to create the cause for escape from saṃsāra in the future. But by ordaining, even if he commits heavy karma, he will be able to create the cause for escape from saṃsāra in the future.” Seeing this, the Teacher ordained Devadatta. That is true; one hundred thousand aeons from this world-cycle, Devadatta will become a Paccekabuddha named Aṭṭhissara.

## How Devadatta Suffers in Avīci Hell

Thus, Devadatta entered the earth and was reborn in Avīci Hell. As if decreed, “Because he offended the unshakable Buddha, let him be cooked while remaining motionless,” his body was born in the hundred-yojana-wide Avīci Hell, being exactly one hundred yojanas in height. His head entered the upper iron roof up to the edges of his ears; his feet entered the lower iron ground up to his ankles. An iron stake the size of a great palm trunk came out from the back wall, pierced through the middle of his back, came out through his chest, and entered the front wall. Another iron stake came from the south wall, pierced the right side, came out the left side, and entered the north wall. Another iron stake came from the upper roof, pierced the top of his head, came out through the lower part, and entered the iron ground. Thus, Devadatta is cooked in that Avīci Hell, remaining motionless.

## Past Stories of Being Swallowed by the Earth

The monks started a conversation: “Even after coming this far, Devadatta did not get to see the Blessed One and had to enter the earth.”

Then the Blessed One said, “Monks, not only now has Devadatta offended me and entered the earth. In the past too, he entered it,” and He preached this verse from the Sīlavanāga Jātaka of the Ekakanipāta, showing how that wicked man entered the earth after he had cut the tusks of the Bodhisatta elephant—who had comforted him when he was lost, carried him on his back, and brought him to safety—returning three times to ask for the tips, the middle, and finally the roots of the tusks, and once he had passed out of the elephant's sight.
96:
To an ungrateful man, who is always looking for a flaw,
Even if one were to give the entire earth, one could never satisfy him.

Posassa: to the man. Sabbaṃ pathaviṃ: even the entire earth. Ce dajja: if one were to give. Naṃ: that base person. Neva abhirādhaye: one would certainly not be able to satisfy his desires.

Akaṇhanetto: the King Piṅgala, who had yellow eyes and acted and spoke harshly so as to cause discomfort to the ears and eyes. Te: to you, the gatekeeper. Piyo: a dear, pleasing, and beloved king. Āsi nu: was he? Kasmā: why. Tuvaṃ: do you, the gatekeeper. Rodasi: worry, grieve, and weep?

Having preached this Sīlavanāgarāja Jātaka of the Ekaka Nipāta, and when a similar conversation arose again, the Teacher preached the Khantivādi Jātaka of the Catukka Nipāta to show how Devadatta, who had been King Kalābu, entered the earth because of his offenses against the Teacher, who had been the ascetic Khantivādī. He also preached the Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka of the Pañcaka Nipāta to show how Devadatta, who had been King Mahāpatāpa, entered the earth because of his offenses against the Teacher, who had been the young prince Cūḷadhammapāla.

## Rejoicing at Devadatta's Death: Present and Past

When Devadatta had entered into the earth, the great multitude of people were delighted and joyful. They raised banners, flags, and banana trees, and set out full pots decorated with lotuses, saying, "O friends, how fortunate we are to have gained this human life!" and celebrated with a great festival. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "Bhikkhus, it is not only now that the great multitude rejoices at Devadatta's death; they rejoiced in the past as well." Having said this, he preached the verses from the Mahāpiṅgala Jātaka of the Duka Nipāta to show how the great multitude rejoiced when the harsh and cruel King Piṅgala of Bārāṇasī, who was disliked by all, had died.

Thus he preached the Piṅgala Jātaka. The monks asked the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, where has Devadatta been reborn now?"

## The Nature of Evil Deeds

(17) Here he suffers, hereafter he suffers; the evil-doer suffers in both worlds.
He suffers thinking, "Evil have I done." Having gone to a state of woe, he suffers even more.

Pāpakārī: one who habitually performs evil and unwholesome deeds. Idha: in this present life. Tappati: suffers and is tormented. Pecca: in the life hereafter. Tappati: suffers and is tormented. Ubhayattha: in both the present and the hereafter. Tappati: suffers and is tormented. Me: by me. Pāpaṃ: base and unwholesome kamma. Kataṃ: has been done. Iti: thus. Tappati: he suffers with remorse. Duggatiṃ gato: if he goes to a state of woe. Bhiyyo: even more than that. Tappati: he suffers and is tormented.

At that time, when the Blessed One said, "Bhikkhus, he has been reborn in the Avīci Great Hell," and the monks remarked, "Venerable Sir, having wandered about suffering in this present life, he has again been reborn in a place of suffering upon going to another life," the Buddha said, "Bhikkhus, it is so. Whether they be laypeople or monastics, those who live heedlessly suffer in both the present and the hereafter," and he spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the conclusion of the verse, many people attained Stream-entry (Sotāpatti) and so forth. The teaching became beneficial to the great multitude.

The story of Devadatta ends.

## 13. The Story of Sumanādevī, the Banker's Daughter

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this legal teaching beginning with "Idha nandati" regarding Sumanādevī.

## Visākhā and Anāthapiṇḍika Appointing Their Beloved Children and Grandchildren for Meritorious Deeds

In the city of Sāvatthī, two thousand monks took their meals daily at the house of the great banker Anāthapiṇḍika. Likewise, two thousand monks took their meals at the house of the great female lay devotee Visākhā. Whoever in Sāvatthī wished to give alms could only do so after obtaining permission from these two, Anāthapiṇḍika and Visākhā. Why? Because when people asked, "Has the great banker Anāthapiṇḍika or the great lay devotee Visākhā come to your alms-giving hall?" and were told, "They have not come," they would disparage the gift, saying, "Even if a hundred thousand coins were spent, what kind of alms-giving is this?"

Both Anāthapiṇḍika and Visākhā knew very well the preferences of the Saṅgha of monks and the appropriate services to be rendered. When they looked after and managed the arrangements, the monks could eat as they pleased. Therefore, whenever anyone wished to give alms, they would only go after inviting Anāthapiṇḍika and Visākhā. Thus, Anāthapiṇḍika and Visākhā did not get the opportunity to personally serve the monks in their own homes.

Because of this lack of opportunity, the great lay devotee Visākhā, considering, "Who can stand in my place and serve the Saṅgha of monks?" saw her son's daughter, her granddaughter, and appointed her in her place. That granddaughter served the Saṅgha of monks at the house of her grandmother, Visākhā. The great banker Anāthapiṇḍika also appointed his eldest daughter, named Mahāsubhaddā. She performed all the duties for the monks, and by listening to the Dhamma, she became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) and then went to live at her husband's house. After that, he appointed the daughter named Cūḷasubhaddā. She also served in the same way as her elder sister, became a Stream-enterer, and went to live at her husband's house. Then, he had to appoint the youngest daughter, named Sumanādevī.
98:
## Reporting to the Buddha with Sadness that the Daughter Died Deliriously

That Sumana Devī, having attained the fruit of Once-returning (Sakadāgāmiphala), while still a young maiden, was afflicted by such a severe and painful illness that she stopped taking food. Wishing to see her father, she sent for him. The great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, hearing the news of his daughter's message while at a certain donation hall, returned immediately and asked, "Dear Sumana, what is it?"

Sumana Devī replied to the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, "What is it, younger brother?"

When he asked again, "Dear daughter, are you delirious and rambling?" she replied, "Younger brother, your elder sister is not delirious or rambling."

When he asked again, "Dear daughter, are you afraid?" she replied, "Younger brother, your elder sister is not afraid." Having said only this much, the maiden Sumana Devī passed away.

Although the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika was a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), he was unable to bear the grief that arose for his daughter. After performing the funeral rites for the body, he went to the Buddha weeping. When the Blessed One asked, "Great merchant, why have you come with a sorrowful mind, with a face covered in tears, and weeping?" he replied, "Venerable Sir, my youngest daughter, Sumana Devī, has passed away."

Then the Blessed One said, "Why do you grieve? Is it not true that death is a certainty for all beings?" The merchant replied, "Venerable Sir, I know that death is certain for all. However, my daughter, who was so full of shame and fear (hiri-ottappa), was unable to firmly establish mindfulness at the time of death and died deliriously. Because of that, I feel great and immeasurable distress, Venerable Sir."
99:
## The Nature of Meritorious Deeds

(18) Here he rejoices, hereafter he rejoices;
The doer of merit rejoices in both places.
He rejoices, thinking "I have done merit";
He rejoices even more, having gone to a happy state.

*Katapuñño*: One who has performed various kinds of merit. *Idha*: In this present world. *Nandati*: He rejoices and is glad. *Pecca*: In the world hereafter. *Nandati*: He rejoices and is glad. *Ubhayattha*: In both worlds, the present and the hereafter. *Nandati*: He rejoices and is glad. *Me*: By me. *Puññaṃ*: Merit. *Katanti*: Has been done. *Nandati*: He rejoices and is glad. *Sugatiṃ*: To a happy state of existence. *Gato*: Having reached. *Bhiyyo*: Greatly. *Nandati*: He rejoices and is glad.

## Teaching that the Daughter is More Distinguished than the Father and Reborn in Tusita Heaven

When the Blessed One asked, "Great merchant, what words did your daughter say before she passed?" he replied, "Venerable Sir, I first called that daughter 'Dear Sumana.' Then she replied to me, 'What is it, younger brother?' Then when I asked again, 'Dear daughter, are you delirious?' she replied, 'Younger brother, your elder sister is not delirious.' When I asked again, 'Dear daughter, are you afraid?' she replied, 'Younger brother, your elder sister is not afraid.' Having said only this much, she passed away, Venerable Sir."

Then the Blessed One said to the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, "Great merchant, your daughter was not delirious."

When he asked, "Venerable Sir, if she was not delirious, why did she address me as 'younger brother'?" the Buddha replied, "Great merchant, she addressed you as 'younger brother' only because of your junior status. This is true. Great merchant, your daughter was senior to you in terms of the paths and fruits (magga-phala). You are only a Stream-enterer, but your daughter was a Once-returner. Because she was senior to you in the paths and fruits, she addressed you as 'younger brother'."

When he asked, "Venerable Sir, is it really so?" the Buddha replied, "It is so, householder."

When he asked, "Venerable Sir, where is she reborn now?" the Buddha replied, "In the Tusita heaven, householder."

Then the merchant said, "Venerable Sir, my daughter lived happily among her relatives here in this world, and even after departing from this life, she is reborn in a place of happiness."

Then the Teacher said, "Yes, householder, those who are heedful (appamatta), whether they be monastics or laypeople, rejoice in this life and in the life hereafter," and he spoke this verse.

## Benefits of the Teaching

At the end of the verse, many people attained Stream-entry and other fruits. The Dhamma teaching became beneficial to the great multitude.

The Story of the Merchant's Daughter Sumana Devī ends.

## 14. The Story of Two Monk Friends
(Dvesahāyakabhikkhu Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Bahumpi ce," concerning two monks who were friends.

## Attaining Different Benefits in Fulfilling the Two Duties

Two young men of good family living in Sāvatthī went to the monastery and, after hearing the Dhamma teaching of the Teacher, renounced sense pleasures, dedicated themselves to the Sasana, and ordained. Having ordained and lived for five years in the presence of their teachers and preceptors, they approached the Teacher and asked about the duties (dhura) in the Sasana. After hearing in detail about the duty of insight (vipassanā-dhura) and the duty of study (gantha-dhura), one monk said, "Venerable Sir, I have ordained in my old age. I will not be able to fulfill the duty of study. I will fulfill the duty of insight."

Having requested to be taught the duty of insight until the attainment of Arahatship, and through repeated effort and striving, he attained Arahatship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). The other monk, however, thinking "I am capable of fulfilling the duty of study," gradually learned the word of the Buddha known as the Tipitaka. He preached the Dhamma wherever he went, recited in the intoned style (sarabhañña), and traveled about teaching the Dhamma to five hundred monks. He became a great teacher of eighteen groups.

*Sarabhañña* means preaching by reciting clearly with a melodic voice. There are thirty-two such styles, such as the *Taraṅga* (wave-like), *Dhota* (washing-like), and *Khalita* (stumbling-like) styles.
100:
## The Defilement of Pride in a Learned Monk who Neglects Practice

The monks, having taken meditation subjects from the Blessed One and fulfilling the duty of insight (vipassanā-dhura), went to the dwelling place of an Arahant elder. Remaining under his instruction, they attained Arahantship. They then paid homage to the elder and requested permission, saying, "Venerable sir, we wish to see the Blessed One."

The elder sent them off, saying, "Go, friends. Pay homage to the Blessed One in my name, and also to the eighty Great Elders. Also, tell the elder who is my companion: 'Our teacher pays homage to you.'"

Those monks went to the monastery, paid homage to the Blessed One and the eighty Great Elders, and then went to the elder who fulfills the duty of study (gantha-dhura), saying, "Venerable sir, our teacher pays homage to you." When the other asked, "Who is your teacher?", the monks replied, "Venerable sir, he is your companion monk."

Thus, as the elder who practiced insight repeatedly sent messages, the monk who fulfilled the duty of study endured it for a short time. Later, unable to endure it any longer, when they said, "Our teacher pays homage to you," and he asked, "Who is your teacher?" and they replied, "He is your companion monk," he asked, "What have you learned from him? Have you learned one of the Nikāyas, such as the Dīgha Nikāya? Have you learned one of the three Piṭakas?"

He then thought to himself, "He does not even know a four-line verse. He entered the forest immediately after ordaining and taking his rag-robes (paṃsukūla), yet he has obtained many resident disciples. When he comes, I ought to ask him a question."

Later, when the elder who practiced insight came to see the Blessed One, he left his bowl and robes with his companion elder, went to pay homage to the Blessed One and the eighty Great Elders, and then returned to his companion's dwelling. Then, the resident monk made the visiting monk perform minor duties, took a seat of equal height, and sat down, thinking, "I will ask him a question."

At that moment, the Blessed One realized, "This monk who fulfills the duty of study might harass my son of such nature and be reborn in hell." Out of compassion for him, as if wandering through the monastery (vihāra-cārika), He went to where they were sitting and sat upon the prepared noble Buddha-seat.

## The Criticism of the Blessed One for Praising the Monk who Practiced Insight

Having sat there, He asked the learned monk a question regarding the first jhāna. When the monk answered, He asked questions starting from the second jhāna up to the eight attainments, and regarding mind and matter (rūpa-nāma). The learned monk was able to answer everything. Then He asked him a question regarding the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). The monk was unable to answer. Then He asked the Arahant elder. The Arahant elder answered. The Blessed One, greatly pleased, expressed approval, saying, "Sādhu! Sādhu! Well done, well done, dear monk!" and proceeded to ask questions regarding the remaining Paths in order. The learned monk was unable to answer even a single thing. The Arahant elder, however, answered every question as it was asked. The Blessed One gave words of approval to the Arahant elder regarding the four Paths. Upon hearing the sound of this approval, all the devas and brahmās, starting from the earth-dwelling devas up to the Brahma-world, as well as the nāgas and garuḍas, gave successive shouts of approval.
101:
Hearing this approval, the resident and co-resident disciples of the learned elder criticized the Blessed One. They disparaged Him, saying, "What is this that the Blessed One has done? He gave words of approval regarding the four Paths to an old elder who knows nothing.
