But to our teacher, who is the bearer of the entire scriptures (pariyatti) and the leader of five hundred monks, He did not even offer a word of praise."

Then the Blessed One asked those monks, "Monks, what are you talking about?" When the matter was explained, He said, "Monks, your teacher is like one who tends cows for wages in my Dispensation. But my son is like a cattle owner who enjoys the five products of the cow (pañca-gorasa) as he pleases." He then spoke these verses:

## Like a Cowherd and a Cattle Owner

(19) Though he recites much of the Sacred Texts,
If he is heedless and does not act accordingly,
He is like a cowherd counting others' cows;
He does not share in the fruits of the recluse's life.

(20) Though he recites but little of the Sacred Texts,
If he lives in accordance with the Dhamma,
Abandoning lust, hatred, and delusion,
With right knowledge and a well-liberated mind,
Clinging to nothing here or hereafter,
He shares in the fruits of the recluse's life.

[Nissaya Translation:]
*Yo naro*, whatever person; *saṃhitaṃ*, the words of the Buddha, namely the three Piṭakas which are beneficial; *bahum*, many times; *bhāsamānopi*, though he learns, teaches, explains, and recites; *pamatto*, being heedless and negligent; *takkaro*, performing that task by contemplating the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) that should be practiced; *ce na hoti*, if he does not so act; *evaṃ sati*, this being so; *so naro*, that person; *gopo*, is like a cowherd who takes cows out in the morning and brings them back in the evening, serving for a living; *gāvo*, the cows entrusted to him; *gaṇayaṃ - gaṇayanto*, counting them thoroughly; *paresam*, to the owners of the cows; *niyyādeti iva*, just as he hands them over without being able to consume the milk as he wishes; *paresam*, to the virtuous who wish to practice; *niyyādeti*, he is said to hand them over. *So naro*, that person who is sparse in practice but speaks much; *သာမညဿ (sāmaññassa)*, of the fruits of recluseship called the Paths and Fruits; *bhāgavā*, a sharer; *na hoti*, is not.

*Yo naro*, whatever person; *saṃhitaṃ*, the words of the Buddha, namely the three Piṭakas which are beneficial; *appaṃ*, even a little; *bhāsamānopi*, though he learns, teaches, explains, and recites; *dhammassa*, for the Supramundane Dhamma; *anudhammacārī*, practices the appropriate Dhamma such as the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhi-sīla), the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), and the meditation on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna); *ce hoti*, if he so acts; *evaṃ sati*, this being so; *so naro*, that person; *rāgañca*, lust; *dosañca*, hatred; *mohañca*, and delusion; *pahāya*, having abandoned; *summappajāno*, being one who knows well and distinctly; *suvimuttacitto*, having a mind well-freed through the liberations of 'temporary' (tadaṅga), 'suppression' (vikkhambhana), 'eradication' (samuccheda), 'tranquillization' (paṭippassaddhi), and 'escape' (nissaraṇa); *idha vā*, in this present world and life; *huraṃ vā*, or in the world beyond and future life; *anupādiyāno*, being an Arahant who has no clinging through the four types of grasping (upādāna); *hutvā*, having become; *သာမညဿ (sāmaññassa)*, of the fruits of recluseship called the Paths and Fruits; *bhāgavā*, a sharer; *hoti*, he is.
102:
## The Benefits of the Teaching
At the end of the verse, many people became Stream-enterers and so forth. The Dhamma teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.

The story of the two companion monks is finished.

The Yamaka Vagga is finished here.
103:
## 2. Appamādavagga
## 1. The Story of Queen Sāmāvatī
(Sāmāvatī Vatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at Ghositārāma near Kosambī, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Appamādo amataṃ padaṃ,' concerning the death and destruction of the five hundred women led by Sāmāvatī, the five hundred women led by Māgaṇḍiyā, and the five hundred relatives of that Māgaṇḍiyā.

## The Renunciation of King Allakappa and King Veṭhadīpaka
In the past, in the kingdom of Allakappa, there was a king named Allakappa, and in the kingdom of Veṭhadīpaka, there was a king named Veṭhadīpaka. These two had been friends since their youth. Having studied the arts in the house of the same teacher, they were crowned as kings in their respective kingdoms, each ten yojanas in extent, upon the passing of their fathers. From time to time, they would meet and stay together, standing, sitting, and lying down. Seeing the multitude of people being born and dying, they consulted each other: 'There is no one who can follow a person who has passed to the next world; at the very least, even one's own body does not follow. One must go leaving everything behind. What is the use of living in a household? Let us renounce.' Having consulted thus, they handed over their kingdoms to their wives and children, and having renounced as ascetics, they lived in the Himalayan region. They discussed: 'We have renounced our royal splendor. It is not because we were unable to make a living that we renounced. If we two, having renounced as ascetics, live together in one place, we are just like those who have not renounced. Therefore, let us live separately. You live on that mountain, and I shall live on this mountain. Every half-month, on the Uposatha day, let us meet together.'

Then, this thought occurred to them again: 'Even meeting once every half-month will lead to delighting in company. You, however, should light a fire on your mountain, and I shall light a fire on my mountain. By that signal, let us know of each other's existence.' Having consulted thus, those ascetics lived according to their agreement.

## The Hermit Veṭhadīpaka Passing Away, Becoming a Deity, Visiting His Companion, and Giving the Hatthikanta Lute and Mantra
Later, the hermit Veṭhadīpaka passed away and was reborn as a powerful king of deities. Then, when the half-month arrived, not seeing the fire, the other companion, the hermit Allakappa, knew: 'My companion, the hermit Veṭhadīpaka, has passed away.' The hermit Veṭhadīpaka, at the very moment of his rebirth, looked at his own celestial splendor and, investigating his past deeds, saw the austere practice he had performed since his renunciation. Thinking, 'I will go and see my companion now,' he set aside that celestial form and, appearing like a traveling man, went to the hermit Allakappa, paid respectful homage, and stood in a suitable place.

Then, the hermit Allakappa asked the traveler, 'Where have you come from?' The traveler also asked, 'Venerable sir, how is it? Do you live alone in this place? Is there any other companion?' When he said, 'I have one companion,' he asked, 'Where is that companion?' When told, 'He lives on a certain mountain. On this Uposatha day, he did not light a fire; he must have passed away,' the traveler said, 'Venerable sir, it must be so.' When the hermit said, 'Yes, friend, it is so,' the traveler replied, 'I am that very hermit who was your companion.'
104:
When asked, "Where were you reborn?", he replied, "Venerable sir, I have been reborn in the celestial realm as a powerful deity. I have come back now to see you, venerable sir. Is there any danger or trouble for you while residing in this place?"

"Indeed there is, lay devotee. I am troubled and exhausted because of the elephants," the ascetic replied. When asked, "Venerable sir, what do those elephants do to you?", he explained, "They drop their dung in the place I have swept. They kick the ground with their feet and throw up the dust. I am exhausted from having to clear away the dung and level the ground."

When asked, "Do you wish for them not to come, venerable sir?", and receiving the answer, "Yes, lay devotee, I wish for them not to come," the deity said, "In that case, I shall make them stop coming." He then gave the ascetic a lute named Hatthikanta and a mantra named Hatthikanta, so called because they cause elephants to be pleased and delighted.

While giving the lute and the mantra, he demonstrated the three strings of the lute and taught the three mantras, instructing: "When this string is struck and this mantra is recited, the elephants will flee, not even daring to look back. When this string is struck and this mantra is recited, they will flee while repeatedly looking back. When this string is struck and this mantra is recited, the leader of the elephant herd will approach, bowing his back." After giving these instructions and saying, "Do whatever you desire, venerable sir," he paid homage to the ascetic and departed. The ascetic Allakappa then lived there, driving the elephants away by reciting the mantra for fleeing and striking the corresponding lute string.

## The Hatthilinga Bird Carrying Away King Parantapa's Queen

At that time, a king named Parantapa reigned in the city of Kosambī. One day, he sat in an open courtyard with his pregnant queen, basking in the morning sun. The queen sat wrapped in a red woolen blanket worth a hundred thousand, which belonged to the king. While conversing with the king, she took the royal signet ring, also worth a hundred thousand, from the king's finger and placed it on her own.

At that moment, a Hatthilinga bird was flying through the sky. Seeing the queen from afar wrapped in the red blanket, it mistook her for a piece of meat, spread its wings, and swooped down. Hearing the sound of the bird descending, the king rose from his seat and entered the palace interior. The queen, due to the heaviness of her pregnancy and her naturally fearful nature, was unable to move quickly. The Hatthilinga bird then snatched the queen, holding her in the hollow of its talons, and flew up into the sky.
105:
As she was being carried away by the Hatthilinga bird, the queen, terrified of death, reflected: "If I scream, the sound of a human voice will cause great terror and agitation to animals. Upon hearing my voice, it might drop me. If that happens, I will perish along with my unborn child. I will wait until it lands in a place to start eating me, and only then will I make a human sound to scare it away." Thus, through her wisdom, she remained patient.

At that time, in the region of the Himavant, there was a great banyan tree that had grown somewhat large and stood like a pavilion. That bird was accustomed to bringing animals such as deer there to eat. Therefore, it brought her to that very place, set her down in the fork of the banyan tree, and looked back at the path it had come. (It is said to be the nature of those birds to look back at the path they have traveled.)

## The Birth of Prince Udena in the Fork of the Tree

At that moment, the queen thought, "Now is the time to scare this bird away." She raised both her hands, clapped them, and shouted loudly, causing the great bird to fly away. Then, at the time of sunset, the birth-pangs caused by karma moved within the queen. A great storm arose, thundering in all directions. The queen, who had been raised in the comfort of the palace, did not receive even a word of encouragement such as "Do not fear, lady," and being oppressed by suffering, she did not sleep at all throughout the three watches of the night. At dawn, the clearing of the clouds, the rising of the sun, and her delivery from the womb occurred at the same moment. Because the child was born taking the season of the storm (utu), the season of the forest, and the season of the dawn, she named the son Udena.

## The Ascetic Allakappa Finding and Caring for the Queen

The hermitage of the ascetic Allakappa was not far from that great banyan tree. By habit, on rainy days, fearing the cold, the ascetic would not enter the forest for fruits. Instead, he would go to the foot of that banyan tree, collect the bones of the meat eaten by the birds, pound them, and boil them to make a broth to drink. Therefore, on that day, thinking "I will collect bones," he went there. While searching for bones under the tree, he heard the sound of a child crying above. Looking up, he saw the queen and asked, "Who are you?" When she replied, "I am a human woman," he asked, "How did you get here?" She answered, "I was brought by a Hatthilinga bird," and he said, "In that case, come down."

The queen replied, "Venerable sir, I am afraid of losing my caste (social status)." When he asked, "What is your caste?" and she said, "I am of the royal caste (Khattiya)," he told her, "I too am of the royal caste." She then requested, "If that is so, please recite the Khattiya-māyā (royal lore)," and the ascetic recited the Khattiya-māyā.
106:
"If that is so, come up and bring my young son down," she said. The ascetic made a path to climb up on one side, ascended the tree, and took the child. When she said, "Do not touch me with your hand," he brought the child down without touching the queen. The queen also descended.

Then he took her to the hermitage and, without violating her virtue, looked after her out of compassion. He brought honey free from bees and naturally grown rice, cooked gruel, and gave it to her. While the ascetic was looking after her in this way, the queen later thought: "I do not know the way I came, nor the way to go. I have no intimacy with this ascetic. If he should abandon us and go elsewhere, both of us will die right here. I should do something to break his virtue so that he cannot leave me." Then, by tempting him with improper dress and covering, she caused his virtue to be ruined. From then on, the two lived together in harmony.

## The Episode of Teaching the Hatthikanta Mantra to Prince Udena

One day after that, while the ascetic was observing the conjunction of the stars, he saw the fading of King Parantapa's star and said, "Dear lady, King Parantapa has passed away in Kosambī." She asked, "Venerable sir, why do you say so? Do you have any grudge against him?" He replied, "Dear lady, I have no grudge against him. I say this because I see the fading of his star." Then the queen wept.

Then he asked her, "Why are you weeping?" When she told him that King Parantapa was her husband, he said, "Dear lady, do not grieve, do not lament, do not weep. For a being who is born, death is certain." She replied, "Venerable sir, I know that death is certain." He asked again, "If you know that, why do you weep?" She answered, "Venerable sir, my son is worthy of the kingship that belongs to his lineage. If he were there in Kosambī, he would have raised the white parasol and become king. Now, there has been a great loss; I weep out of sorrow." He said, "Let it be, dear lady. Do not worry. If you desire the kingship for him, I will make a way for him to obtain it." Then he gave the prince the lute named Hatthikanta, which elephants love, and the mantra.

At that time, following the instructions left by the powerful deity, he told the prince: "If you play this lute string and recite this mantra, many thousands of elephants will come and stay at the foot of the banyan tree, surrounding it like a pavilion." Then he instructed the prince: "Before the elephants arrive, climb the tree. When they come, recite this mantra and play this lute string. All the elephants will flee, not even daring to look back. Then you may descend and return." Prince Udena did as the ascetic instructed and returned to report the matter. On the second day, the ascetic told him: "Today, recite this mantra and play the lute string; all the elephants will flee, looking back again and again." The prince did as instructed and returned to report. On the third day, the ascetic told him: "Today, recite this mantra and play this lute string; the leader of the elephants will come, bowing his back." The prince did as instructed and returned to report.

## Prince Udena Obtaining the Kingship in the Kingdom of Kosambī

Then, the ascetic called the prince's mother and said, "Dear lady, give your son the message you wish to send. In this way, he will go and become king." The queen called her son and said, "Dear son, you are the son of King Parantapa of Kosambī. A monster bird carried me away." She then told him the names of the generals and others, and instructed him, "To those who do not believe, show them this red woolen garment that your father the king used to wrap himself in, and this ring he used to wear." Having given him the red garment and the ring, she sent him away.
107:
The prince asked the ascetic, "What should I do now?" The ascetic replied, "Sit on a lower branch of the banyan tree, recite this mantra, and strike this lute string. The leader of the herd will approach you, offering its back. Sit on its back, go to the kingdom, and take the sovereignty." Prince Udena paid homage to his mother and father, and following the instructions, he sat on the back of the elephant that arrived. Leaning close to its ear, he whispered, "Lord Elephant, I am the true son of King Parantapa of Kosambī. Please take me and give me my father's inheritance, the kingdom."

Hearing this, the elephant trumpeted, "Let many thousands of elephants assemble!" and thousands of elephants gathered. Again, it trumpeted, "Let the old elephants depart!" and the old elephants departed. Once more, it trumpeted, "Let the very young elephants return!" and they also returned. Surrounded by thousands of elephants in their herds, Prince Udena reached a border village and announced, "I am the son of King Parantapa of Kosambī. Let those who desire prosperity come with me." From that border village onwards, he gathered the people's support, went and surrounded the city, and sent a message: "Will you give me battle, or will you give me the kingdom?"

The citizens replied, "We will give neither battle nor the kingdom. Our Queen was carried away by a hatthilinga bird while she was heavy with child. We do not know whether she is alive or dead. As long as we do not hear news of her, we will give neither battle nor the kingdom."

Then Prince Udena said, "I am the son of that Queen," and he mentioned the names of the generals and others. To those who still did not believe his words, he showed the red woolen blanket and the signet ring. The citizens of Kosambī recognized the blanket and the ring, and having no further doubt, they opened the gates and consecrated Prince Udena in the kingship. This is the account of Udena's origin.
108:
## The Future Ghosaka the Treasurer Abandoning His Young Son Due to Exhaustion on the Journey

In the kingdom of Allakappa, when there was a great famine and people were unable to make a living, a man named Kotuhalika took his young son named Kāpi and his wife named Kāḷī, and set out for Kosambī, taking provisions for the journey, thinking, "I will live there." (It is also said that he fled upon seeing many people dying of a pestilence known as the 'snake-wind' disease.) As they traveled, their provisions were exhausted, and being overcome by hunger, they were unable to carry the young child.

Then the husband said to his wife, "Sister, if we remain alive, we shall have another child. Let us abandon him and go on." A mother's heart is naturally tender. Therefore, the wife said, "Lord, I cannot abandon my child while he is still alive." When he asked, "Then what shall we do?", she replied, "Let us carry him in turns." When it was the mother's turn, she lifted the child like a garland of flowers, laid him on her breast, and carried him in her arms before handing him to the father. When it was the father's turn to carry the child, he felt a pain even stronger than his hunger. He said again and again, "Sister, if we live, we shall have children. Let us abandon this boy." The woman repeatedly refused and gave no consent.

The child, exhausted by being shifted back and forth in turns, fell asleep in his father's arms. The father, knowing the child was asleep, let the mother go ahead, and then laid the child on a bed of leaves under a bush and went on. When the mother turned back and did not see her son, she asked, "Lord, where is my son?" When he said, "I have laid him to sleep under a bush," she cried out, beating her breast, "Lord, do not destroy me! I cannot live without my son. Bring my son back to me!" Then he turned back and brought the child. However, the son died along the way. Because he abandoned his son in this place, as a result of that deed, he himself was abandoned seven times in future births. One should not despise an evil deed, thinking, "It is only a small thing."

## The Future Ghosaka the Treasurer Becoming a Dog After Death

As they continued their journey, they reached the house of a certain cowherd. On that very day, there was a festival at the cowherd's house concerning a milch cow. A Paccekabuddha regularly took his meals at the cowherd's house. The cowherd, having fed the Paccekabuddha, was celebrating the festival. Since a large amount of milk-rice (pāyāsa) had been prepared, seeing them arrive, he asked, "Where have you come from?" and after hearing the whole story, the noble-hearted man felt compassion for them and gave them milk-rice with plenty of ghee.
109:
Then the wife said, "Dear husband—if you live, I also live. For many long days and nights, you have had an empty stomach; eat and enjoy as much as you desire." She placed the ghee and curds before her husband, while she herself ate only a tiny amount with a little ghee. The husband ate a great deal, and because he had been intensely hungry for seven or eight days, he was unable to cut off his craving for the taste of food. After the herdsman had given them the milk-rice, he began to eat himself. While Kotūhalika sat watching the herdsman eat, he saw a lump of milk-rice being scooped up and given by the herdsman to a female dog lying under a bench. He thought, "How fortunate this dog is; she regularly receives such food." That night, being unable to digest that milk-rice, Kotūhalika died and was reborn in the womb of that female dog.

Then Kotūhalika's wife performed the funeral rites for the remains and, working for hire in that very house, she obtained a measure of rice. Having cooked it, she offered it into the alms-bowl of a Paccekabuddha and made a prayer, saying, "May this share of merit reach Kotūhalika, who was your servant." Then she thought, "It is proper for me to stay right here. The venerable Paccekabuddha regularly comes to this house. Whether there are offerings to give or not, by paying homage daily, performing small and large duties, and gladdening my mind, I shall cultivate much merit." Thinking thus, the woman remained in the herdsman's house, working for hire as was suitable for her. When about six or seven months had passed, that herdsman's dog gave birth to a single male puppy. The herdsman provided the puppy with milk from a cow. Before long, the puppy grew up.

## Performing many meritorious deeds by relying on the Paccekabuddha while in the life of a dog

Then, when the venerable Paccekabuddha took his meal, he would regularly give a lump of rice to the young dog. Relying on that lump of rice, the dog developed affection for the Paccekabuddha. The herdsman also went to serve and attend to the Paccekabuddha twice a day. While going, in places where there were wild animals along the way, he would strike the bushes and the ground with a stick and make the sound "Su, su" three times to scare the wild animals away. The dog also followed along with the herdsman. One day, the herdsman said to the venerable Paccekabuddha, "Venerable Sir, when I do not have the opportunity, I shall send this dog. Please come by that sign."

From that day on, on days when he could not go himself, he sent the dog, saying, "Dear son, go and fetch the Venerable One." At that single word, the dog would run off. At the places where his master used to strike the bushes and the ground, he would bark and howl three times, and knowing by that sound that the wild animals had fled and hidden, he would proceed. The venerable Paccekabuddha, having performed his morning bodily cleansing duties, would be sitting in the leaf-roofed hut. The dog would go to the place where the Paccekabuddha resided, bark and howl three times at the door of the hermitage to make his arrival known, and then lie down in a suitable place. When the venerable Paccekabuddha noted the time and set out, the dog would go ahead, barking and howling. Along the way, the venerable Paccekabuddha, wishing to test the dog, would turn onto another path. Then the dog would stand across the path in front of the Paccekabuddha, barking and howling, and would make the Venerable One return to the straight and correct path. On another day, even when the dog stood across the front to block him after he had turned onto another path, the Paccekabuddha would not turn back but continued on his way, nudging the dog with his foot.
110:
The dog, knowing that the Paccekabuddha would not return, bit the hem of his inner robe and, pulling him, led him back onto the other straight and correct path. Thus, the dog developed a strong affection for the Paccekabuddha. Later, the Paccekabuddha’s robes became worn and tattered.

Then, a cowherd offered robe-cloth to the Paccekabuddha. The Paccekabuddha said to him, "Lay follower, it is difficult to make a robe alone; I will go to a suitable place to have it made." The cowherd replied, "Venerable sir, please make it right here." "It is not possible, lay follower," he said. "In that case, venerable sir, please do not stay away for long." The dog stood listening to their conversation. The Paccekabuddha, saying "Stay here, lay follower," made the cowherd turn back and, rising into the air, departed toward Gandhamādana Mountain. Seeing him departing through the sky, the dog stood howling in great sorrow. When the Paccekabuddha passed out of his sight, the dog’s heart broke, and he died.

(It is said that animals are straightforward and without guile. Humans, however, think one thing in their hearts and say another with their mouths. Referring to this meaning, it was said: "Deep indeed, venerable sir, is this—namely, humans; but open and clear, venerable sir, is this—namely, beasts.")

## Rebirth as Ghosaka Devaputta after Death as a Dog

Thus, because of his straightforward and guileless mind, when he died, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs, enjoying great splendor. The sound of his voice when whispering in someone's ear reached sixteen yojanas, while his natural speaking voice pervaded the entire celestial city of ten thousand yojanas. Therefore, he was named Ghosaka Devaputta. What was the result of this? It was the result of the merit of howling and barking with a heart full of love and devotion for the Paccekabuddha. That Ghosaka Devaputta did not remain long in the celestial realm and passed away.

(When deities pass away from the celestial realm, they do so for four reasons: exhaustion of life-span, exhaustion of merit, exhaustion of food, or through anger.)
111:
This Ghosaka Devaputta, while enjoying the five cords of sensual pleasure, became mindful-less and passed away due to the exhaustion of food.

## Being Discarded on a Trash Heap and Adopted by the Treasurer of Kosambī after Rebirth in the Human Realm

After passing away from the celestial realm, he took conception in the womb of a courtesan in the city of Kosambī. On the day he was born, the courtesan asked her maid, "What is this (a son or a daughter)?" When told, "Mistress, it is a son," she ordered, "Oh maid, place this child in a winnowing basket and discard him on the trash heap where sweepings are thrown." And so, she had the child discarded.

Courtesans nurture and raise daughters, but not sons. Why? Because a daughter continues their lineage.

Crows and dogs surrounded the child. However, due to the result of his barking and howling out of affection for the Paccekabuddha (in his life as a dog), not even a single crow or dog dared to approach him. At that moment, a man going outside the city saw the gathering of crows and dogs and wondered, "What is this?" He went there, saw the child, and felt a fatherly love for him. Thinking, "I have gained a son," he took him home.

At that time, the Treasurer of Kosambī, while going to the royal palace, saw the court chaplain coming from the palace. He asked, "Teacher, have you observed the omens and the conjunction of the stars today?" "Yes, Great Treasurer," he replied. "What will happen for us? What will happen for the country?" "There is nothing else, but the child born today in this city will become the Chief Treasurer." At that time, the Treasurer’s wife was heavily pregnant. Therefore, he quickly sent a man home, saying, "Go, fellow, find out whether she has given birth or not."

Upon hearing that she had not yet given birth, he visited the King and then hurried home. He called a maid named Kāḷī, gave her a thousand pieces of money, and sent her out, saying, "Go, maid, search this city, give a thousand pieces, and bring back the child born today." While searching, she reached the house where the child had been taken. Seeing the child, she asked the mistress of the house, "On which day was this child born?" When told, "He was born today," she said, "Give this child to me." Starting from one kahāpaṇa, she increased the price until she gave a thousand pieces of money. She then took the child and showed him to the Treasurer. The Treasurer thought, "If a daughter is born to me, I will marry her to this child and make him the master of the Treasurer’s position. If a son is born to me, I will kill him." With this thought, he had the child cared for in his own house.

Being discarded for the second time at the gate of the cattle pen.
112:
Then, after a few days had passed, the wife of that Treasurer gave birth to a son. The Treasurer thought, "If this boy is not here, my own son will receive the position of Treasurer; it is proper to kill him right now." He called a maidservant named Kāḷī and said, "Hey, maid! Go, when the cattle are coming out of the pen, place this child crosswise in the middle of the gateway. The cows will trample and kill him. Come back after finding out whether he has been trampled or not."

That maid went, and just as the cowherd opened the gate of the pen, she placed the child crosswise exactly as the Treasurer had instructed. Although the lead bull usually came out after all the other cattle at other times, on that day, he came out before all the cattle and stood over the child, keeping him between his four legs. Hundreds of cows went out, brushing against both sides of the bull. The cowherd thought, "This bull used to come out after all the cattle in the past, but today he came out before all of them and stands motionless in the middle of the gateway. What could be the reason?" He went and saw the child lying under the bull. Feeling a father's love, he thought, "I have gained a son," and took him home.

When the maid Kāḷī returned home and was questioned by the Treasurer, she reported the matter. He said, "Go, give a thousand pieces of money and bring that child back once more." She gave the thousand pieces, brought him back, and gave him to the Treasurer.

## Abandoned for the Third Time on the Cart Track

Then the Treasurer said to the maid named Kāḷī, "Dear Kāḷī, in this city of Kosambī, five hundred carts will set out early in the morning for trade. Take this child and place him on the track where the cartwheels roll. The oxen will trample him, or the wheels will crush him. Come back only after finding out what happens to him."

That maid took the child and placed him on the track of the cartwheels. At that time, the chief caravan leader was in the front cart. When the oxen of that leader reached that spot, they dropped their yokes. Although they were repeatedly put back into the yokes and driven, they would not go forward. While the caravan leader was struggling with the oxen in this way, dawn broke. The caravan leader, wondering, "What are these oxen doing?" looked at the road and saw the child. Thinking, "What a heavy deed I have almost done!" and with a joyful heart thinking, "I have gained a son," he took the child home. When the maid Kāḷī returned home and was questioned by the Treasurer, she reported the matter. He said, "Go, give a thousand pieces of money and bring that child back once more," and she did as she was told.

## Abandoned for the Fourth Time in the Cemetery

Then once again, the Treasurer said to the maid, "Now, take this child to the cemetery where corpses are thrown and place him in a thicket. There, he will die either by being bitten by animals such as dogs or by being struck by non-human beings (amanussa). Come back only after knowing whether he is dead or alive."

That maid took the child, placed him in the cemetery, and stood at a suitable place to watch. Neither a dog, nor a crow, nor a non-human being was able to approach that child.
113:
It might be asked: "Does this child not have a mother, a father, or any protector such as an elder brother? Who then protects him?" It was the mere act of barking and howling performed with affection toward a Paccekabuddha during his life as a dog that protected that child.

At that time, a goatherd was leading many thousands of goats to their grazing ground and passed by the side of the cemetery. One she-goat, while eating leaves, entered the thicket and, seeing the child, knelt down and gave her milk to him. Even though the goatherd made the sound "Heh! Heh!", she did not come out. Thinking, "I will drive her out by hitting her with a stick," he entered the thicket and saw the she-goat kneeling and suckling the child. He felt a father's love for the child and, thinking "I have gained a son," he took the child and departed. When the maid Kāḷī returned home and was questioned by the Treasurer, she reported the matter. He said, "Go, give a thousand pieces of money and bring him back once more," and she did exactly as she was told.

## Abandoned for the Fifth Time at the Precipice

After that, he said to the maid, "Dear Kāḷī, take this child, climb to the top of the cliff from which robbers are thrown, and hurl him down the precipice. When he strikes the mountain slope, he will be broken into pieces and fall to the ground. Come back only after knowing whether he is dead or alive."

The maid took the child to the top of that mountain and, standing at the summit, threw him down. Supported by that mountain slope, a great bamboo thicket grew following the contour of the mountain. Above that bamboo thicket, a dense ziñjuka creeper grew, covering it completely. When the child fell, he landed on that thicket as if falling onto a woolen carpet. On that very day, it was the turn of the chief reed-mat maker (naḷakāra) to provide bamboo bark. That chief reed-mat maker went with his son and began to cut that bamboo thicket. When the bamboo thicket shook because of the cutting, the child made a sound (cried). The chief reed-mat maker thought, "This sound is like the cry of a child," and when he climbed up one side and saw the child, he was joyful at heart, thinking "I have gained a son," and took him away. The maid Kāḷī also went to the Treasurer and, when questioned by him, reported the matter. He said, "Go, give a thousand pieces of money and bring him back once more," and she did exactly as she was told.

As the Treasurer continued to do various things to him, the child grew up and was named "Ghosaka." He appeared to the Treasurer like a thorn in his eye; the Treasurer could not even look at him directly. Then, while plotting a way to kill him, he went to his friend, a potter, and asked, "When will you fire your kiln?" When the potter replied, "Tomorrow," the Treasurer said, "Then take this thousand pieces..."
114:
## Sent for the Sixth Time to be Killed by Being Thrown into the Fire

While the Treasurer was making such efforts to bring about his death, the boy grew up. He became known by the name Ghosaka. To the Treasurer, the boy was like a thorn in his eye. He could not even look at him directly. On another occasion, while plotting a way to kill the boy, he went to his friend, the Potter, and asked, "When will you be preparing, plastering, and firing the pottery kiln?" When the Potter replied, "Tomorrow," the Treasurer said, "If so, take these thousand pieces of money and perform a task for me."

"Lord Treasurer, what task should I perform?" the Potter asked. The Treasurer replied, "I have a wicked and low-born (avajāta) son. I will send him to you. When he arrives, seize him, take him into a room, cut him into pieces with a sharp cleaver, put him in a large jar, and burn him in the pottery kiln. These thousand pieces are like a deposit to seal our agreement. I will reward you further as deserved later." The Potter agreed, saying, "Very well."

On the following day, the Treasurer called young Ghosaka and said, "Dear son, yesterday I gave an order to the Potter for a certain task. Come, go to that Potter and tell him, 'Finish the task my father ordered yesterday without fail.'" Ghosaka agreed and set off. While Ghosaka was on his way to the Potter's house, the Treasurer's own biological son was playing marbles with his friends. Seeing Ghosaka, he called out, "Brother, where are you going?" When Ghosaka replied, "I am going to the Potter with a message from father," the son said, "I will go there instead. These boys have won many stakes from me. Please play and win back the lost stakes for me."

When Ghosaka said, "I am very afraid of father," the son pleaded, "Do not be afraid, brother. I will carry the message. You are very skilled; until I return, win back the stakes I have lost."

Ghosaka was indeed very skilled at playing marbles. Therefore, the Treasurer's own son repeatedly pleaded with him. Ghosaka then said, "If so, go and tell the Potter: 'Yesterday my father gave an order for a certain task. Finish that task now.'" and sent him off. The Treasurer's own son went to the Potter and delivered the entire message. Then, the Potter killed the boy according to the Treasurer's instructions and threw him into the kiln.

## The Treasurer's Grief Over the Death of His Own Son

Ghosaka played for the rest of the day and returned home in the evening. When the Treasurer saw Ghosaka, he asked, "Dear son, what happened? Did you not go to the Potter?" Ghosaka then explained the reason why he did not go and how his younger brother had gone instead. Upon hearing this, the Treasurer cried out in great distress, "Oh, how wretched I am!" Feeling as if his blood were boiling throughout his body, he raised his arms and wailed, "O Potter, do not destroy me! Do not destroy me!" and ran to the Potter.

When the Potter saw the Treasurer coming in such a state, he said, "Lord Treasurer, do not make a sound. The task you ordered is finished." The Treasurer was overwhelmed by great sorrow, as if crushed by a huge mountain, and experienced immeasurable mental distress. Just as one who harms an innocent person suffers immense misery, so did he. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke these verses:

## Sent for the Seventh Time to be Killed with a Written Letter

Even so, the Treasurer still could not look Ghosaka directly in the eye. While thinking, "By what means can I kill Ghosaka?", he saw a way: "I will send him to the superintendent of a village I own and have him killed." He wrote a letter to the superintendent saying, "This boy is my extremely wicked and foolish son. Kill this boy and throw him into a cesspool. If you do this, I will know how to reward you." He then told Ghosaka, "Dear Ghosaka, there is a superintendent in a village of a hundred that I own. Take this letter and give it to that manager." He then tied the letter to the hem of Ghosaka's garment.
115:
## The Ten Penalties for Harming the Innocent

He who inflicts punishment on those who do not deserve it,
And offends those who are harmless,
Soon comes to one of ten states:

Harsh pain, loss, bodily injury,
Serious illness, or loss of mind;

Trouble from the king, or a heavy accusation,
Loss of relatives, or destruction of wealth;

Or else, fire burns his houses;
After the breakup of the body, the fool is reborn in hell.

Monks, that person who offends with punishment—such as physical punishment—those who are without punishment and are harmless, quickly reaches one of ten states of suffering.

He may reach harsh pain such as a headache; loss of wealth acquired with difficulty; destruction of the body such as the loss of hands or feet; or a heavy illness such as paralysis or being crippled; or madness and distraction of the mind.

He may reach trouble from the king, such as loss of property or demotion from rank; or a heavy and cruel false accusation; or the exhaustion and ruin of relatives who are his support; or the breaking and destruction of his possessions.

Furthermore, fire—either natural fire, lightning, or a fire that starts spontaneously—burns his houses. That person of little wisdom, having suffered one of these ten penalties, is reborn in hell after the breakup of the body.

That Ghosaka was illiterate. Although the Great Treasurer had been unable to kill Ghosaka since his childhood, he still desired to have him killed. How could he have him taught the art of letters? Therefore, Ghosaka, having the very letter that would cause his own death tied to the hem of his garment, said as he was leaving the house, "Father, I have no provisions for the journey." The Treasurer replied, "Dear son, there is no need for provisions. On the way, in such-and-such a village, there is a treasurer who is my friend. Have your breakfast at his house and then proceed."

Accepting this, saying "Very well," Ghosaka paid respects to his father and departed. Upon reaching that village, he inquired about the treasurer's house and went there. The treasurer's wife saw the youth Ghosaka and asked, "Where have you come from?" He replied that he had come from the city. When asked, "Whose son are you?" he said, "Mother, I am the son of the treasurer who is your friend." When she asked, "Are you the youth named Ghosaka?" he replied, "Yes, mother." As soon as she saw him, a motherly love for the youth Ghosaka arose in her.

That treasurer also had a daughter, about fifteen or sixteen years of age, who was very beautiful and pleasing to look at. To guard her, they had given her a single maidservant and made her reside in a magnificent chamber on the top floor of a seven-storied mansion.

At the moment Ghosaka arrived, the treasurer's daughter sent that maid to the market. Then the treasurer's wife saw her and asked, "Where are you going?" When the maid replied, "Mistress, I am going to the market at the command of your daughter," the wife said, "Come here first. Leave aside the task your mistress sent you for. Prepare a seat for my son, wash his feet, apply oil, and prepare a bed for him. Afterward, you shall do the task your mistress sent you for." The maid did exactly as the treasurer's wife had said.
116:
Through previous association, or through present benefit,
Thus is love born, like a lotus in the water.

Just as a lotus, such as a white or red lotus, or any other kind of lotus, when it is born in the water, it arises due to two causes: the water and the silt; in the same way, when that love is born, it arises due to these two causes: either because of having lived together with great affection and joy in a past life, or because of performing many beneficial acts for one another in the present life. Thus, it arises due to these two causes.

## How a Merchant’s Daughter Saved Him from Death

Then, the merchant’s daughter rebuked the maidservant who had returned after a long time, asking why she was late. When she was thus rebuked, the maidservant said to the merchant’s daughter, "My lady, do not be angry with me. Because the merchant’s son Ghosaka arrived, I had to perform such and such services for him, and only then could I go to the market and return." Upon hearing the name "Ghosaka, the merchant’s son," love for him immediately arose in the merchant’s daughter, piercing through her skin and reaching her very marrow.

(The reason is that in her life as the wife of the youth Kotuhalika, she was named Kāḷī and had offered a measure of boiled rice to a Paccekabuddha. By the power of that merit, after passing away from that life, she was reborn in this merchant’s family.)

Therefore, that love which had existed in a previous life overwhelmed and took hold of the merchant’s daughter. Thus, the Blessed One said:

Through previous association, or through present benefit,
Thus is love born, like a lotus in the water.

Then the merchant’s daughter asked the maid, "Mother, where is that merchant’s son Ghosaka now?" When the maid replied, "My lady, he is lying on the bed asleep," she asked, "Is there anything in his hand?" The maid said, "There is a letter tied to the hem of his garment." Thinking, "What kind of letter could this be?" the merchant’s daughter went down while he was sleeping and while her parents were occupied with other things and not watching. She untied and took the letter, entered her private chamber, closed the door, and opened the window. Being skilled in literacy, she read the letter and thought, "Oh, how foolish! He walks around with his own death warrant tied to the hem of his garment. If I had not seen it, his life would be no more." Having thought this, she tore up that letter and wrote another letter in the merchant’s name:

"This youth is my son named Ghosaka. Having brought gifts from my hundred villages, celebrate his marriage with the daughter of this regional merchant. Build a two-story house in the middle of the village where he resides, and provide well-arranged protection with surrounding walls and male guards. Send a message to me saying, 'I have done such and such.' When this is done, I shall know what is appropriate to be done for the uncle."

After writing this, she folded the letter and tied it back to the hem of Ghosaka’s garment.

## The Merchant’s Affliction upon Hearing of Ghosaka’s Marriage to the Regional Merchant’s Daughter

After sleeping for the rest of the day, Ghosaka woke up, ate some food, and departed. Arriving at that village early the next morning, he met the village headman while the latter was performing his duties in the village. Upon seeing the merchant’s son Ghosaka, the headman asked, "Dear boy, what is the matter?"
117:
When he said, "My father has sent this inscribed letter to you," the overseer replied, "My lad, what is this letter? Bring it here." Taking the letter and reading it, he was filled with joy and said, "Look, friends! See how much my master, the great treasurer, loves me. He has sent word to me to arrange a marriage for his eldest son. Quickly, bring wood and other materials." He spoke to the householders and had a house built in the center of the village in the manner previously described. He then had gifts (paṇṇākāra) collected from a hundred villages, brought the daughter of a provincial treasurer, and performed the marriage ceremony. Afterwards, he sent a message to the treasurer saying, "I have performed such and such a task." Upon hearing this message, the treasurer thought, "What I order to be done does not happen; what I do not order to be done, that alone happens." Great distress (domanassa) arose within him. That distress, combined with the grief regarding his son, became one and caused a burning sensation in his heart, leading to severe diarrhea.

## The Great Wisdom of the Provincial Treasurer's Daughter
The treasurer's daughter had given an order: "If anyone comes from the treasurer, do not speak to the treasurer's son first without telling me." Meanwhile, the treasurer thought, "Now I will act so that this wicked and ruined son does not become the heir to my wealth." He said to an overseer, "Uncle, I wish to see my son. Send a personal attendant (pādamūlika) to call him." The overseer replied, "Very well," and after giving him a letter, dispatched a man. The treasurer's daughter, hearing that the messenger had arrived at the gate, had him called and asked, "My lad, what is the matter?" The messenger said, "Lady, the treasurer is ill and has sent for his son to see him." She asked, "My lad, is the father who is ill still strong, or is he weak?" He replied, "Lady, he is still strong and can still take food." Without letting the treasurer's son, Ghosaka, know, she provided the messenger with a place to sleep and provisions, saying, "Go only when I send you; stay here for now." The treasurer again asked the overseer, "Uncle, how is it? Have you not yet sent for my son?" "Lord, I have sent him, but the man who went has not yet returned." "If that is so, send another man." The overseer sent another. The treasurer's daughter treated the second messenger in the same way, providing him with a place and provisions and detaining him. Then, the treasurer's illness became very severe. One bowl would go in as another came out. (This means as one vessel of waste was taken out, another had to be brought in.) Again, the treasurer asked the overseer, "Uncle, how is it? Have you not yet sent for my son?" "Lord, I have sent him, but the man who went has not yet returned." "If that is so, send another man." Thus, the overseer sent a third messenger.
118:
She asked the third messenger about the situation. He said, "Lady, the treasurer is gravely ill. He has stopped taking food and is near death (maccuparāyana). One bowl goes out as another comes in." The treasurer's daughter thought, "Now is the time to go." She told the treasurer's son, "It is said your father is ill." When he asked, "What are you saying, dear?" she replied, "Lord, your father, the great treasurer, is unwell and suffering." When asked, "What should be done now?" she said, "Let us take the gifts (paṇṇākāra) that have come from the hundred villages under your charge and go to see him." Ghosaka, the treasurer's son, agreed, saying, "Very well." He had the gifts brought, loaded them onto carts, and set out. Later, the treasurer's daughter said to him, "Lord, your father is weak. If we travel carrying such a large amount of gifts, it will cause delay. Let these gifts be sent back." She had all those gifts sent to her own parents' house and then told Ghosaka, "Lord, you stand at the side of your father's feet; I shall stand at the side of his head." Upon entering the house, she commanded her men, "Keep guard at both the front and the back of the house." After entering, Ghosaka stood at his father's feet, while the daughter sat at the head.

## The Treasurer Passes Away After Bequeathing Inheritance to Ghosaka
At that moment, the treasurer was lying on his back. The overseer, massaging the treasurer's feet, said, "Lord Treasurer, your son has arrived." When asked, "Where is Ghosaka?" he replied, "Your son Ghosaka is standing at your feet." Then, seeing Ghosaka, the treasurer called the accountant and asked, "How much wealth is in my house?" The accountant replied, "Lord, there are forty crores in gold and silver alone. Of the buildings and goods for daily use, and of the forests, villages, fields, bipeds, quadrupeds, vehicles, and carts, there is this much." When this was said, the treasurer intended to say, "I do not give all this wealth to my son Ghosaka," but instead said, "I give it." Hearing these words, the treasurer's daughter thought, "If this treasurer speaks again, he might say something else." Pretending to be overwhelmed by grief, she disheveled her hair and, weeping and wailing, said, "Father Treasurer, why do you speak such words? We even have to hear such words from you! We are truly unfortunate and devoid of merit!" Saying this, she struck her head against the treasurer's chest, and in such a way that he was unable to speak again, she rubbed her head against his chest and made a great show of weeping.
119:
The treasurer passed away at that very moment.

## Conferring the Position of Treasurer upon Ghosaka

When the treasurer died, they informed King Utena. The King had the treasurer’s funeral rites properly performed and asked, "Does this treasurer have a son or a daughter?" They replied, "Your Majesty, he has a son named Ghosaka. He passed away only after handing over all his property to that son." Later, the King sent for the treasurer’s son. On that day, it rained, and water collected here and there in the palace courtyard. As the treasurer’s son was coming to see the King, the King opened a window and watched him approaching. Seeing him leaping over the water in the palace courtyard, and then standing there after paying homage, the King asked, "Dear boy, are you the one named Ghosaka?" When he replied, "Yes, Your Majesty," the King comforted him, saying, "Do not grieve thinking, 'My father has died.' I shall grant you the position of treasurer, which is your paternal inheritance." Then he dismissed him, saying, "Go, dear boy."

The King remained standing, watching Ghosaka as he departed. While Ghosaka had leaped over the water when coming, he stepped into it and walked slowly when going back. Then the King called him back from that very spot and asked, "Dear boy, when you were coming to me, you came leaping over the water. Why is it that now, when going back, you step into it and walk slowly?" Ghosaka replied, "Your Majesty, at that moment I was a mere boy, and it was a time for play. But now, Your Majesty has promised to grant me a high office. Therefore, it is proper for me to conduct myself with composure and dignity, rather than acting as I did before." Hearing those words, the King reflected, "This man is possessed of steadfast wisdom. I shall grant him the office of treasurer right now." He then granted him the wealth enjoyed by his father, the treasurer, and conferred upon him the office of treasurer along with a hundredfold of everything.

## The Treasurer Ghosaka Performing Meritorious Deeds

The treasurer Ghosaka, mounted on a chariot, made a clockwise procession around the city. Every place he looked upon seemed to tremble. The treasurer’s daughter, sitting and consulting with the servant woman named Kāḷī, said, "Mother Kāḷī, your son Ghosaka has obtained this much prosperity because of me." When asked, "Dear daughter, why do you say so?" she replied, "Mother, this man came to our house with a letter ordering his own death tied to the hem of his garment. When he arrived, I tore up that letter and wrote another letter for the purpose of having him married to me, and I have looked after him for all this time." Kāḷī said, "Dear daughter, you have seen only this much. The treasurer had been trying to kill this boy since he was young and tender, but he was unable to do so. A great deal of wealth has been wasted solely because of this boy."

"Mother, the deed done by the treasurer was indeed very grave," she said, and they continued their conversation. When she saw the treasurer Ghosaka entering the house after circling the city, she smiled, thinking, "This much prosperity has arisen because of me." Then the treasurer Ghosaka asked the treasurer’s daughter, "Why are you smiling?" She replied, "For a certain reason..."
120:
When she said, "I smiled because of [you]," and he asked, "Please tell me the reason," the treasurer's daughter remained silent. Ghosaka the treasurer drew his sword and threatened her, saying, "If you do not tell me, I will cut you in two."

The treasurer's daughter said, "My lord, I smiled thinking that you have obtained this much prosperity only because of me." Ghosaka the treasurer asked, "Indeed, my father handed over his own property to me. In this handing over, what part did you play?" It is said that for all this time, Ghosaka knew nothing of the matter. Therefore, he did not believe the words of the treasurer's daughter.

Then the treasurer's daughter told him everything: "Your father sent you with a death-warrant. I protected you by doing such and such things." Still not believing her, saying, "You are speaking what is not true," he thought, "I will ask my mother Kāḷī." He then asked, "Mother, is it true that my father the treasurer did such a thing?"

"Yes, dear son. From the time you were young, he desired to kill you and made efforts to do so, but he was unable to kill you. Because of you, much wealth has been exhausted. In seven places, you have escaped death. Now, having come from your fief-village, you have attained the position of treasurer along with all the hundreds of rewards."

When Ghosaka the treasurer heard this, he thought, "Heavy indeed is this evil deed! It is not proper for me, who has escaped such a death, to live a life of negligence for the sake of prolonging my life-faculty. I shall become one who is diligent." Thinking thus, he gave away a thousand pieces of money every day and established alms-giving for travelers, the destitute, and so forth. A householder named Mitta became the one who managed the affairs of Ghosaka the treasurer's alms-giving. This is the account of Ghosaka the treasurer.

## How the Girl Who Was to Become Queen Sāmāvatī Came to the City of Kosambī

At that time, in the city of Bhaddavatī, there was a treasurer named Bhaddavatiya who was an unseen friend of Ghosaka the treasurer. Having heard from merchants coming from the city of Bhaddavatī about the prosperity and age of Treasurer Bhaddavatiya, Ghosaka the treasurer desired to form a friendship with him and sent gifts. Treasurer Bhaddavatiya also, having heard from merchants coming from the city of Kosambī about the prosperity and age of Ghosaka the treasurer, desired to form a friendship with him and sent gifts. In this way, the two treasurers lived as friends without having ever seen each other. Later, a plague (wind-illness like snake venom) broke out in the house of Treasurer Bhaddavatiya.

When that illness struck, first the flies died. Then, in succession, insects, mice, chickens, pigs, cattle, female slaves, and male slaves died. Finally, the human members of the household died. Among them, those who broke through the walls and fled survived.
121:
Then the merchant Bhaddavatī, his wife, and his daughter fled in the manner described, and longing for the support of the merchant Ghosaka, they set out on the road to Kosambī. The three of them, having exhausted their provisions on the way, their bodies worn out by the wind and heat as well as by hunger and thirst, arrived at Kosambī with great difficulty. They stopped at a place where water was easily available, bathed, and entered a rest-house at the city gate. After entering the rest-house, the great merchant said to his wife: "Dear sister, if we go in this appearance, even the mother who gave birth to us would not be pleased. My friend, the merchant Ghosaka, is said to give daily alms by spending a thousand coins for travelers, the destitute, and so on. Let us send our daughter to that alms-hall to bring food. After nourishing our bodies in this very rest-house for a day or two, we shall go to see my friend Ghosaka." The merchant's wife agreed, saying, "Very well, lord," and they remained in that rest-house.

## The Young Girl who would become Queen Sāmāvatī Begging for Rice

Again, on the following day at dawn, when the time for alms-giving was announced and the destitute, travelers, and others were going for food, the parents sent their daughter, saying, "Dear daughter, go and bring food for us." Though she was the daughter of a family of great wealth, because of the loss of their fortune, she cast aside her shame and, without feeling embarrassed, took a bowl and went for food along with the crowd of destitute people. When asked, "Dear girl, how many portions will you take?" she replied, "Three portions." Then they gave three portions to the merchant's daughter. When she had brought the rice, the three of them sat down to eat together.

Then the mother and daughter said to the merchant, "Lord, misfortune can indeed befall even great families. Please eat without looking at us or worrying about us; do not think of any anxieties." Thus, they entreated him in various ways and fed him. After eating, the merchant was unable to digest the food and passed away at dawn. The mother and daughter lamented and wept in various ways. On the next day, the young girl went for food while weeping. When asked, "Dear girl, how many portions will you take?" she said, "Two portions." Having brought it, she entreated her mother and fed her. The mother, being entreated by her daughter, ate the food, but she too passed away on that very day, unable to digest it.

## Mitta the Householder Adopts the Young Girl who would become Queen Sāmāvatī

The young girl, being left alone, wept and lamented repeatedly. Due to the various misfortunes that had occurred, she was suffering from extreme hunger and distress. On the following day, while weeping and lamenting along with the beggars, she went for food. When asked, "Dear girl, how many portions will you take?" she replied, "One portion." Mitta the householder, who had noticed the girl taking rice for all three days, said to her, "Hey, you low-born girl! Get away! Have you only today realized the capacity of your belly?" The young lady, endowed with a sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa), felt as if she had been pierced in the chest with a spear or as if salt water had been poured onto a wound. Receiving such harsh and painful words, she asked, "Lord, what do you mean?"

"On the first day, you took three portions; yesterday, you took two portions..."
122:
"Today you have taken a portion for one person; do you only now know the capacity of your own stomach?" When he said this, she replied, "Master, do not think that I took it only for my own sake." "If so, why did you take it thus?" he asked again. "Master, on the first day we were three; yesterday we were two; today I am left alone," she said sorrowfully. The householder asked, "For what reason?" and having heard the whole account from the beginning as told by the girl, he was unable to restrain his tears. Overcome with great sorrow, he said, "Dear daughter, if it be so, do not worry. You are the daughter of the Treasurer Bhaddavatiya; from this day forth, you shall be my very own daughter." He kissed her on the head, took her home, and placed her in the position of his eldest daughter.

## The Reason for the Name Sāmāvatī and Her Being Placed in the Position of Daughter by the Treasurer Ghosaka

The girl, hearing the loud and great noise at the alms-hall, asked, "Father, why do you not give alms after making these people quiet?" "Dear daughter, it is not possible to do so," he replied. "Father, it is possible," she said. When he asked, "How is it possible, dear daughter?", she replied, "Father, fence in the alms-hall and provide two doors of a size sufficient for only one person to enter at a time. Say, 'Enter by one door and exit by the other.' If this is done, they will receive alms quietly."

Hearing this, the householder said, "Dear daughter, this is a good means," and had it done exactly as she said. Previously, her name was Sāmā, given by her parents in her childhood. Because she caused an enclosure (vatī) to be built, her name was combined with the term for enclosure to become Sāmāvatī.

From the time she made those arrangements, the tumultuous noise at the alms-hall ceased. Previously, when the Treasurer Ghosaka heard that noise, he would be pleased, thinking, "That is the sound at my alms-hall." Not hearing the sound for two or three days, he asked the householder Mitta, who had come to wait upon him, "Is the alms-giving to the poor, travelers, and others still going on?" "Yes, lord," he replied. "Then why has the sound not been heard for two or three days?" he asked again. "Lord, I have employed a means so that they receive alms quietly," he explained. "Why did you not do so before?" "Lord, because of my ignorance." "How do you know it now?" "Lord, it was told to me by my daughter."

"I did not know you had a daughter," the Treasurer remarked. Mitta then related the whole story of the Treasurer Bhaddavatiya, starting from the outbreak of the plague, and informed him of how he had placed Sāmāvatī in the position of his eldest daughter. Then the Treasurer Ghosaka said to the householder, "If this is so, why did you not tell me? The daughter of my friend is indeed my own daughter." He had Sāmāvatī summoned and asked, "Dear daughter, are you the daughter of the Treasurer?" "Yes, father," she replied. "If so, do not worry; you are my own daughter." He kissed Sāmāvatī on the head, gave her five hundred women as attendants, and placed her in the position of his eldest daughter.

## King Udena Placing Sāmāvatī in the Position of Chief Queen

Then one day, a festival was proclaimed in the city of Kosambī. When the festival took place, women who had never before gone out went to the riverbank on foot with their attendants to bathe. Therefore, on that day, the maiden Sāmāvatī also went to bathe, passing through the palace square surrounded by five hundred women. King Udena, standing at the lion-window, saw Sāmāvatī and immediately asked, "Whose dancing girls are these?" "Great King, they are not anyone's dancing girls," they replied. "If that is not so, whose daughters are they?" he asked again. "Great King, this is the maiden named Sāmāvatī, the daughter of the Great Treasurer Ghosaka."

King Udena, having fallen in love at first sight, sent a message saying, "Let him send his daughter to me." The Treasurer Ghosaka replied, "Great King, I do not dare to send her." King Udena sent again, saying, "Do not do this; you must send her." [Ghosaka replied,] "Great King, we of the treasurer class, regarding our daughters, even if they are struck or..."
123:
"Because we are afraid of the danger of our daughters being beaten and harassed, we do not dare to send her," they reported. The King became angry, had the treasurer's house sealed with the royal seal, and had the treasurer and his wife seized by their hands and expelled from the house.

When Sāmāvatī returned from bathing and found no opportunity to enter the house, she asked, "Father, what is the reason for this happening?" "Dear daughter, the King sent a message because of you. When we replied that we did not dare to send you, he had the house sealed and expelled us," he explained. "Father, the action you have taken is very grave. When a King sends a message, one should not say 'I will not send her.' Instead, one should say, 'If you take my daughter along with her attendants, I will send her,'" she said. "Very well, daughter, if it pleases you, I shall do so," he replied, and sent a message to the King as his daughter had suggested.

King Udena agreed, saying "Very well," and having taken Sāmāvatī along with her attendants, he consecrated her and appointed her to the position of Chief Queen (Aggamahesī). The remaining women became the attendants of Queen Sāmāvatī. This is the story of Queen Sāmāvatī.

## King Caṇḍapajjota Captures King Udena Using a Wooden Elephant

King Udena had another queen named Vāsuladattā, who was the daughter of King Caṇḍapajjota. In the city of Ujjeni, there was a king named Caṇḍapajjota. One day, while returning from the park, he looked at his own prosperity and asked, "Is there any other king who possesses such prosperity?" When he was told, "What is this prosperity? In the city of Kosambī, King Udena's prosperity is truly immense," the King said, "In that case, we shall capture him." "It is not possible to capture him," they replied. "We shall capture him by some means or other," he insisted. "It is not possible, O King," they said again. "For what reason?" he asked. "That King knows the art called Hatthikanta. By reciting the mantra and playing the Hatthikanta lute, he can make elephants flee or capture them. He is well-provided with elephant vehicles; there is no king equal to King Udena," they reported.

When he asked, "Shall I remain unable to capture this King Udena?", they replied, "O King, if you truly desire to capture him, this King Udena is indeed firm in his position. Nevertheless, have a wooden elephant made and send it near that King's territory. When King Udena hears news of an elephant or horse vehicle, he travels even to distant places. It may be possible to capture King Udena when he arrives there." King Caṇḍapajjota, thinking "This plan seems excellent and appropriate," had a mechanical elephant made of wood, wrapped and covered it with pieces of cloth, and had it painted exquisitely. He then had it released on the shore of a lake near King Udena's territory. Inside the belly of the elephant, sixty men could walk back and forth. They collected elephant dung and scattered it here and there.

Then a forest hunter saw the elephant and, thinking it was worthy of his King, went and reported to the King: "O King, I have seen a noble elephant, white all over like the peak of a silver mountain, which is worthy only of Your Majesty."
124:
King Udena, taking that same hunter as a guide, set out on his elephant with his attendants. Knowing of King Udena's departure, spies went and reported to King Caṇḍapajjota. King Caṇḍapajjota set out, leaving the center empty, and stationed his army on both sides. King Udena, unaware of King Caṇḍapajjota's arrival, pursued the elephant. The men inside the wooden elephant made it flee with great speed. Although the King recited the mantra and played the lute, the wooden elephant continued to flee as if it did not hear the sound of the lute strings. King Udena, unable to catch up with the noble elephant, mounted a horse and continued the pursuit. As he pursued with great speed, his army fell behind and was left far away. King Udena was left all alone. Then, the men of King Caṇḍapajjota, who had been stationed on both sides, captured him and delivered him to their King. At that time, King Udena's army, knowing that he had fallen into the hands of the enemy, established a stockade outside the city and remained there.

## King Udena Teaches the Mantra to Princess Vāsuladattā

King Caṇḍapajjota, having captured King Udena alive, threw him into a thieves' prison, closed the door, and drank the wine of victory for three days. On the third day, King Udena asked the guards, "Friends, where is your King?" The guards replied, "He is drinking the wine of victory, saying 'I have captured my enemy.'" "What kind of behavior is this? Your King's behavior is like that of a woman. Having captured a rival king, is it not proper to either release him or kill him? He keeps us in misery within the prison while he drinks the wine of victory," Udena said. The guards went and reported this to King Caṇḍapajjota.

King Caṇḍapajjota came and asked, "Is it true that you said such words?" When Udena admitted, "It is true, O King," the King said, "Very well, I shall release you. It is said you possess such a mantra; will you give that mantra to me?" "Very well, I shall give it. Learn it at a suitable time for instruction. But how is it? Will you pay me respect?" Udena asked. "Why should I pay you respect? I will not," the King replied. "If you will not pay respect, I cannot give it to you either," Udena said. "If you do not give it, I will inflict royal punishment upon you," the King threatened. Then Udena replied, "O King, if you wish to punish me, then do so. You have power over my body, but you do not have power over my mind."
125:
King Caṇḍapajjota, having heard King Udena’s brave and defiant roar, thought, “By what means can I obtain this mantra?” He then considered, “It is not possible to let another person know this mantra. I shall have my daughter learn it from him, and then I shall learn it from her.” Subsequently, he asked King Udena, “If one were to bow and learn, would you give it to another?” Udena replied, “Indeed, Great King, I will give it to one who bows to me.” The King then said, “In that case, there is a hunchback woman in our palace. While she sits bowing within a curtain, you shall stand outside the curtain and teach the mantra.” Udena consented, saying, “Very well, Great King; whether she be a hunchback or a cripple, I will give it to one who bows.”

Thereafter, King Caṇḍapajjota went to his daughter Vāsuladattā and said, “Dear daughter, there is a man afflicted with white leprosy (saṅkhakuṭṭhī) who knows a priceless mantra. It is not possible to let another person know this mantra. You, dear daughter, shall sit inside a curtain, and after bowing, learn the mantra. That leper will stand outside the curtain and teach you. Then, I shall learn the mantra from you.” In this manner, King Caṇḍapajjota spoke, representing his daughter as a hunchback and King Udena as a white-leper, for fear that they might become intimate with one another. Thus, King Udena, standing outside the curtain, taught the mantra to Princess Vāsuladattā, who sat bowing within the curtain.

## The Quarrel between Teacher and Pupil during the Mantra Lesson and the Five Vehicles of King Caṇḍapajjota

Then one day, although she was made to recite the words of the mantra repeatedly, she was unable to pronounce a certain word clearly. King Udena then rebuked her, saying, “Hey, you hunchback! Your mouth has such thick lips and cheeks. Speak it like this!” Princess Vāsuladattā became angry and retorted, “Hey, you foul and wretched white-leper! What are you saying? Why should a princess like me be called a hunchback?” At that, King Udena lifted the edge of the curtain and asked, “Who are you?” She replied, “I am the King’s daughter, named Vāsuladattā.” Udena said, “When your father spoke to me, he said you were a hunchback.” She replied, “When he spoke to me, he represented you as a man afflicted with white leprosy.” Having said this, the two realized, “The King must have said this for fear of us becoming intimate,” and they indeed became intimate within the curtain.

From that day forward, there was no more learning of the mantra or the art. The King constantly asked his daughter, “Dear daughter, are you learning the art?” She replied, “Yes, father, I am learning.” Then one day, King Udena said to Princess Vāsuladattā, “Dear one, the luxury and happiness provided by a husband is something that neither parents, nor brothers, nor sisters are able to provide. If you were to save my life, I would give you five hundred attendants and grant you the position of Chief Queen.” Princess Vāsuladattā replied, “If my lord is able to stand by those words, I shall save your life.” When he said, “Dear one, I am able,” she consented, saying, “Very well, my lord.” Then Princess Vāsuladattā went to her father, bowed, and stood in a suitable place. King Caṇḍapajjota asked her, “Dear daughter, is the art finished?” She replied, “Father, the art is not yet entirely completed.” When he asked, “Dear daughter, if it is not yet finished, what do you require?” she replied, “Great Father, it would be proper for us to have access to one particular gate and one vehicle.” When asked, “Dear daughter, for what purpose do you need a gate and a vehicle?” she explained, “Great Father, at night, according to the positions of the stars, there is a task to be done for the ritual of the mantra, which involves going to fetch a certain medicinal root. Therefore, it would be proper for us to have access to one gate and one vehicle whenever we go out, whether at the right time or the wrong time.” The King agreed, saying, “Very well.” They then took possession of a gate of their choice. King Caṇḍapajjota possessed five vehicles:

1. A female elephant named Bhaddavatī, which could travel fifty yojanas in a single day.
2. A slave named Kāka, who could travel sixty yojanas in a single day.
3. A horse named Celakaṭṭhi...
