4. The horse named Muñcakesī; these two horses could travel for one hundred leagues.

5. The elephant named Nāḷāgiri could travel for one hundred and twenty leagues.

## The Past Merit of King Caṇḍapajjota for Obtaining the Five Vehicles

Before the appearance of the Buddha, King Caṇḍapajjota was a servant to a certain powerful man. One day, while the powerful man was returning from bathing outside the city, a Paccekabuddha entered the city for alms. Because Māra had deluded all the city dwellers, the Paccekabuddha did not receive even a single spoonful of rice and was leaving with his bowl as clean as it had been washed. When the Paccekabuddha reached the city gate, Māra approached him in a disguised form and asked, "Venerable sir, did you receive anything?"

When the Paccekabuddha replied, "Why? Did you make it so that I would not receive anything?", Māra said, "If that is so, please turn back and enter again. This time I will not do it."

The Paccekabuddha replied, "I will not turn back again." The reason for not turning back was that if the Paccekabuddha were to turn back, Māra would possess the bodies of all the city dwellers and make them clap their hands and mock him in jest. Therefore, he did not turn back and continued on his way. Māra then vanished on the spot.

At that time, the servant saw the Paccekabuddha coming with his bowl as clean as it had been washed. He paid respect with reverence and asked, "Venerable sir, did you receive any alms?" The Paccekabuddha replied, "Layman, I have finished my alms round and am coming out." The layman thought, "The venerable one did not answer what I asked but said something else. He must not have received any alms." Then, looking at the Paccekabuddha's bowl and seeing it empty, he did not have the courage to take the bowl because he did not know for certain whether the rice was cooked at his home. Therefore, he said, "Venerable sir, please wait and endure for a moment," and quickly returned home. He asked, "Is the rice cooked for us?" and when they said, "It is cooked," he spoke to a fellow servant who was nearby, "Friend, there is no one more light-footed and swift than you."
127:
"Go very quickly to the Paccekabuddha and say, 'Venerable sir, please give me your bowl,' and after taking the bowl, come back quickly." Following that single command, the servant ran, took the bowl, and brought it back. The master then filled the bowl with his own meal and said, "Take this alms-bowl quickly and offer it properly to the venerable one. I shall give you a share of the merit from this offering."

That servant man also went quickly, offered the bowl to the Paccekabuddha, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, and made the following aspiration:

## The Aspiration of the Future King Caṇḍapajjota

"Venerable lord, master of Paccekabodhi-knowledge, I have made a great effort to come and go very quickly, thinking that it is almost noon. By the power of this merit of traveling swiftly, may I possess vehicles capable of traveling distances of fifty, sixty, one hundred, and one hundred and twenty leagues. While going and coming, my body has suffered from the heat of the sun; by the power of the merit of enduring that intense heat, in every life I am born, may my glory and power be like the heat of the fierce sun. My master has shared with me the portion of merit from offering this alms-food; by the consequence of that merit of rejoicing in another's merit, may I be a partaker of the Dhamma that you have known and seen."

The Paccekabuddha said, "Layman, may your aspiration be fulfilled," and recited these verses of appreciation:

"Icchitaṃ patthitaṃ tuyhaṃ, khippameva samijjhatu.
Sabbē pūrentu saṅkappā, cando pannaraso yathā.
Icchitaṃ patthitaṃ tuyhaṃ, khippameva samijjhatu.
Sabbē pūrentu saṅkappā, maṇi jotiraso yathā."

Whatever you have wished for and aspired to, may it be fulfilled quickly. May all your good intentions be fulfilled, just as the full moon shines on the fifteenth day. Whatever you have wished for and aspired to, may it be fulfilled quickly. May all your good intentions be fulfilled, just as the wish-fulfilling gem from the peak of Mount Vipulla fulfills all desires.

He performed the appreciation with these two verses. These two verses alone are known as the verses of appreciation of the Paccekabuddhas. In those verses, "Jotirasa" refers to the precious gem that can grant all desires. This was the past deed of King Caṇḍapajjota.

That servant man has now become King Caṇḍapajjota. As a result of that meritorious deed, these five vehicles have appeared.

## King Utena Abducts Princess Vāsuladattā on the Female Elephant and Appoints Her as Chief Queen

After King Utena and Princess Vāsuladattā had secured the gate they desired, one day King Caṇḍapajjota went out to enjoy the park. King Utena thought, "Today is the right time to escape." He filled large leather bags with gold and silver, placed them on the back of the female elephant named Bhaddavatī, took Princess Vāsuladattā with him, and fled. When the palace guards saw King Utena fleeing, they went and informed the King. King Caṇḍapajjota said,

He dispatched the host of soldiers, saying, "Pursue them quickly!" When King Udena realized that the soldiers were pursuing them, he untied a bag of kahāpaṇas and scattered them. The pursuers picked up the coins and then resumed the chase. King Udena then untied a bag full of gold and scattered it. While those soldiers were busy picking them up out of greed for gold, he escaped and reached his own military encampment located outside the city. Upon seeing King Udena returning, his army surrounded him and escorted him into the city of Kosambī. As soon as King Udena reached the palace within the city, he consecrated Princess Vāsuladattā and established her in the position of Chief Queen. This is the story of Queen Vāsuladattā.

## The First Meeting of the Future Queen Māgaṇḍiyā's Father with the Buddha

Furthermore, a maiden named Māgaṇḍiyā, the daughter of a Brahmin, also attained the position of Chief Queen from King Udena. That Queen Māgaṇḍiyā was the daughter of the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya in the Kuru kingdom. Her mother was also named Māgaṇḍiyā. Her paternal uncle was also named Māgaṇḍiya. This maiden Māgaṇḍiyā was exceedingly beautiful, like a celestial nymph. Her father, the Brahmin, not having found a suitable husband for her, used to drive away even those from great and famous families who asked for her hand, rebuking them, "You are not worthy of my daughter."

Then one day, at dawn, the Blessed One surveyed the world and saw that the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya and his wife possessed the sufficing condition for attaining the Fruit of Non-returning. Taking his bowl and robes, he went to the place outside the Brahmin's village where the Brahmin tended the sacrificial fire.

The Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya, seeing the Blessed One's physical form which had reached the pinnacle of beauty, thought, "In this world, there is no other man like this man. This man is worthy of my daughter. I shall give my daughter to him so that she may serve him." He said, "O monk, I have a daughter. For all this time, I have not seen a man worthy of her. You are worthy of her, and she is worthy only of you. It is fitting for you to have her as an attendant, and it is fitting for her to have a good husband to rely upon. Therefore, I shall give her to you. Please wait right here until I return."

## Fetching the Daughter and Wife, and the Blessed One's Footprint

The Blessed One said nothing to the Brahmin and remained silent. The Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya went home in great haste and said, "O lady, O lady! I have found a man worthy of our daughter. Dress her quickly!" Having had her dressed, he took his wife and daughter and set out to the presence of the Blessed One. The whole city was in an uproar. Why was it in an uproar? Because people were saying, "This Brahmin, who for so long has not given his daughter to anyone, saying there was no one worthy of her, now says he has found someone worthy of her today."
129:
For one who is lustful, the footprint is arched;
For one who is hateful, it is heavily pressed at the heel.

“What kind of nature might that man have? Let us go and see that man,” saying thus, a great multitude of people went out together with the Brahmin. When the Brahmin arrived bringing his daughter, the Blessed One did not remain in the place the Brahmin had designated; instead, He displayed His sacred footprint (padacetiya) there and, having departed, stood in another place.

Indeed, the sacred footprints of the Buddhas appear only in the place where they have been intentionally set; they do not appear elsewhere. Only those for whose benefit the footprint was intended can see it. To prevent others from seeing it, even if elephants and other animals should trample upon it, or if a great rainstorm should pour down, or if the Veramba winds should blow, nothing is able to obliterate or destroy that sacred footprint. Then, when the Brahmin woman asked the Brahmin, “Where is that man you spoke of?”, the Brahmin looked here and there, saying, “I told him to wait in this place; where could he have gone?” Seeing the sacred footprint, he said, “This is that man’s footprint.”

## The Footprint and the Brahmin Woman’s Vedic Knowledge

Because the Brahmin woman was proficient and well-versed in the three Vedas, which enable the recognition of signs, she reflected upon the Vedic texts concerning signs with her wisdom. After examining the characteristics of the footprint, she said, “Brahmin, this is not the footprint of one who indulges in the fivefold sensual pleasures,” and she recited this verse:

For one who is deluded, the footprint is dragging;
For one who has drawn back the veil (of passion), the footprint is like this.

“Brahmin, O Great Brahmin. *Rattassa*, for one who is habitually attached by lust, *padaṃ*, the footprint, *bhave*, is *ukkuṭikaṃ*, arched and hollow in the middle. *Duṭṭhassa*, for one who is habitually malicious through anger, *padaṃ*, the footprint, *hoti*, is *sahasānupīḷitaṃ*, pressed down quickly and deep at the heel. *Mūḷhassa*, for one who is habitually foolish and deluded, *padaṃ*, the footprint, *hoti*, is *avakaḍḍhitaṃ*, dragging and showing a trail of indolence. *Idaṃ*, this footprint, *īdisaṃ*, which is like a golden foot-impression, falling evenly and perfectly displaying the one hundred and eight marks, *padaṃ*, is the noble footprint, difficult to encounter, *vivaṭṭacchadassa*, of the Great Being who has opened and broken the roof of craving and crossed over from the three realms.”

Then the Brahmin said to the Brahmin woman: “O lady, you are like one who sees a crocodile in a water pot, or a thief in the middle of the house; you are prone to seeing things irrelevantly in the science of signs. Just keep quiet.” When he said this, she replied again, “O Brahmin, say what you wish to say to me, but this footprint is not that of one who indulges in the fivefold sensual pleasures.”

## The Brahmin Couple Attaining the Stage of Non-Returner

Thereafter, while searching here and there, he saw the Blessed One and said, “This is the very man I spoke of.” The Brahmin went to Him and said, “O Monk, I give my daughter to you so that you may support and care for her.” The Blessed One, without saying whether He desired or did not desire the daughter, said, “O Brahmin, I shall tell you one thing.” When the Brahmin gave permission, saying, “Speak, O Monk,” the Blessed One related how Māra had followed and harassed Him from the time of His Great Renunciation until He sat at the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree. He also told of how the daughters of Māra came to Him while He was staying at the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree to appease the grief of Māra, who was suffering intensely thinking, ‘This person has now escaped my domain.’ He described the temptations they employed, such as appearing in the form of young maidens, and said, “Even then, I had no desire.”
130:
Having seen Taṇhā, Arati, and Rāga,
No desire arose even for sexual intercourse.
What is this body, filled with urine and excrement?
I would not wish to touch it even with my foot.

*Taṇhaṃ*, the daughter of Māra named Taṇhā; *aratiṃ ca*, the daughter of Māra named Arati; *rāgaṃ ca*, the daughter of Māra named Rāgā; *disvāna*, even after seeing them; *me*, for me; *chando api*, even the slightest sensual desire; *na ahosi*, did not arise; *methunasmiṃ*, for the act of sexual intercourse which is the property of those with mutual lust. *Kiṃ*, how could there be desire; *idaṃ*, for this Māgandiyā; *mutta-karīsa-puṇṇam eva*, who is merely filled with urine and excrement? *Na icche*, I do not wish; *samphusituṃ*, to touch; *naṃ*, that daughter of yours, Māgandiyā; *pādāpi*, even with my feet.

Thus He preached this verse. At the conclusion of the verse, both the Brahmin Māgandiya and the Brahmin woman Māgandiyā were established in the Fruit of Non-Returning (anāgāmiphala).

## Māgandiyā’s Grudge Against the Buddha and Her Becoming King Udena’s Queen

As for the maiden Māgandiyā, she thought: “If this monk truly has no need for me, he should simply say he has no need. But now, he describes me as being filled with urine and excrement and says he does not wish to touch me even with his feet. So be it! By virtue of my birth, family, locality, wealth, and the perfection of my youth, when I obtain a suitable husband who can be my refuge, I shall do to the Monk Gotama whatever is fit to be done.” Thus she harbored a grudge against the Blessed One.

Her parents took their daughter Māgandiyā and entrusted her to the care of Cūḷamāgandiya (the maiden’s paternal uncle). They then went forth as monastics and attained the Fruit of Arahantship. The uncle, Cūḷamāgandiya, reflected: “My niece is not suitable or worthy of an inferior person; she is worthy only of a sovereign king.” Having so reflected, he took the maiden Māgandiyā to the city of Kosambī, adorned her with all kinds of ornaments, and presented her to King Udena, saying, “This jewel of a woman is worthy only of Your Majesty.” As soon as King Udena saw the maiden Māgandiyā, a powerful love arose in him. He performed the consecration ceremony, gave her five hundred palace women as attendants, and placed her in the position of Chief Queen (aggamahesī).

## The Three Treasurers of Kosambī and the Five Hundred Hermits of the Himalayas

Thus, King Udena had three Chief Queens, surrounded by fifteen hundred dancing women. At that time, there were three great treasurers in Kosambī: Ghosaka the Treasurer, Kukkuṭa the Treasurer, and Pāvārika the Treasurer. When the time for the four-month rainy season retreat drew near, these treasurers saw five hundred ascetics who had come from the Himalayas wandering for alms in the city. Being filled with faith, they invited them to sit, served them food, and obtained their promise to stay near them for the four months. They then had the ascetics promise to return for the next rainy season before sending them off. From then on, the ascetics lived in the Himalayas for eight months and spent four months with the treasurers.
131:
They had them stay for the four months of the rainy season and, after obtaining a promise to return for the next rainy season, they let them go. From then on, the ascetics lived in the Himalayas for eight months and stayed with those three wealthy merchants for the four months of the rainy season. Later, while coming from the Himalayas, the ascetics saw a large banyan tree in a forest and sat down at its base.

Among those five hundred ascetics, the eldest one reflected: "The deity who protects and maintains this banyan tree will not be one of minor status; he must be a powerful deity. It would be good indeed if this deity were to give drinking water to this group of sages." That deity gave the drinking water. The ascetic then thought of bathing water, and he gave that too. After that, he thought of food, and he gave that as well. Then, this thought occurred to the ascetic: "This deity gives everything just as we think of it. It would be good if we could see that deity." The deity then split the trunk of the banyan tree in two and revealed himself.

Then the ascetics asked the deity: "Lord deity, your prosperity is vast and magnificent. By performing what kind of meritorious deed did you obtain such great prosperity?" "Venerable sirs, please do not ask," he replied, declining to answer. When they urged him, saying, "Deity, please do tell us," he did not dare to speak because he felt very ashamed of the smallness of the meritorious deed he had performed. When he was pressed repeatedly until he could no longer remain silent, he said, "In that case, venerable sirs, please listen," and he began to tell his story.

## Becoming a Tree Deity as the Fruit of a Half-Day Uposatha

That deva-son had been a poor man. While seeking work as a hired laborer, he obtained a job for wages with the Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika and lived depending on him. Later, on one occasion, when an Uposatha day arrived, Anāthapiṇḍika returned from the monastery and asked, "Has anyone told that laborer that today is the Uposatha day?" When they replied, "Lord Merchant, we have not told him," he said, "Then cook dinner for him." At that time, they cooked about a measure of rice for him.

That laborer, having performed various tasks in the forest all day, returned in the evening. When the rice was served to him, although he said, "I am very hungry," he did not eat immediately. He thought: "On other days in this house, there is a great clamor, with people saying, 'Give rice! Give soup! Give curry!' Today, all of them are silent and have gone to bed. They have served food only for me alone. What could be the reason?" Thinking thus, he asked, "Have the others besides me finished eating, or have they not eaten yet?"

When they said, "Dear man, they have not eaten," he asked again, "Sir, why have they not eaten?" They replied: "In this house, they do not eat dinner on Uposatha days. Everyone observes the Uposatha precepts. At the very least, even the nursing infants have their mouths washed, and the Great Merchant has the four sweet foods placed in their mouths, making sure that everyone is an Uposatha observer. When the scented oil lamps are lit, all the children, young and old, stay in their beds and recite the thirty-two parts of the body, such as hair of the head, hair of the body, and so on."
132:
They were reciting and chanting; they did not remember to inform you of the Uposatha day. Therefore, rice was cooked only for you to eat. Please eat that rice.” When this was said, the hired laborer replied, “If it is possible to observe the Uposatha even now in the afternoon, I also wish to be one who observes the Uposatha.” When they said, “The merchant will know about this,” he replied, “If that is so, please ask the great merchant for me.” So they went and asked the great merchant. The great merchant said, “If one refrains from eating now, washes the mouth, and undertakes the factors of the Uposatha, one will obtain the merit of a half-day Uposatha.” Upon hearing the merchant's words, the laborer did exactly as the merchant had said.

Having performed various duties, large and small, throughout the day, the winds in the body of that hired laborer, who was oppressed by intense hunger, became disturbed. That laborer tied a rope around his belly, pulled it by the end of the rope, and rolled about in distress. The great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, hearing of this, had torches lit and brought catumadhura (four-fold sweet medicine). He went to the laborer and asked, “Dear man, what is the matter?” “Master, my winds are severely disturbed,” he replied. “If that is so, dear man, get up and consume this catumadhura medicine.” The laborer asked, “Master, are you also consuming it?”

“Dear man, we have no illness or discomfort. Only you should eat it,” the merchant said. The laborer replied, “Master, although I was unable to observe the full day's Uposatha, let not my undertaking of the half-day Uposatha be deficient,” and he did not wish to eat. Although he was urged repeatedly, “Dear man, do not do this,” he refused. At dawn, he passed away like a withered flower and was reborn as a deity in this banyan tree. Therefore, after recounting this matter, the tree deity said, “The great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika is a devoted follower of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. Depending on that great merchant, I performed the half-day Uposatha, and by the result of that merit, I have obtained this prosperity.”

## The Five Hundred Ascetics Becoming Arahants

As soon as the five hundred ascetics heard the word “Buddha,” they rose from their places, raised their joined hands in reverence to the deity, and asked, “Did you say ‘Buddha’? Did you say ‘Buddha’?” The deity confirmed three times, “I say ‘Buddha’, I say ‘Buddha’.” Then, uttering the exclamation, “Ghosopi kho eso dullabho lokasmiṃ” (Even the sound of this word ‘Buddha’ is rare in the world), they joyfully said, “O Deity, you have made us hear the sound ‘Buddha’, which has not been heard for many hundreds of thousands of aeons.” Then the resident disciples said to their teacher, “If that is so, let us go to the presence of the Teacher.” The teacher said, “Dear disciples, the three merchants have been very helpful to us. Tomorrow, after receiving alms at their houses and informing them of this matter, we shall go. Please wait, dear disciples.” They agreed to wait.

On the following morning, the merchants prepared rice gruel and food, arranged seats, and knowing, “Today is the day our noble ascetics arrive,” they went out to welcome them. They escorted the ascetics to their home, seated them, and offered alms.
133:
They offered alms-food. When those ascetics had finished their meal, they said, "Great merchants, we shall depart." The merchants asked, "Venerable sirs, did you not give your word to stay with us for the four months of the rainy season? Where will you go now?" The ascetics replied, "Great merchants, it is said that a Buddha has appeared in the world, the Dhamma has appeared, and the Saṅgha has appeared. Therefore, we shall go to the presence of the Teacher." The merchants then asked, "Venerable sirs, is it so? Is it proper only for you to go to the presence of that Teacher?"

"Lay followers, there is no restriction for others as well," they replied. Hearing this, the merchants said, "Venerable sirs, if that is so, please wait for a while. We too shall make preparations for the journey and follow you." The ascetics said, "If you make preparations, there will be a delay for us. We shall go ahead; you may follow later." Having said this, those ascetics went ahead to the presence of the Blessed One. As soon as they saw the Buddha, they praised him greatly, paid respectful homage, and sat in a suitable place. Then the Teacher preached the Dhamma to them, giving a graduated discourse. At the end of the teaching, all the ascetics attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). They requested for ordination, and immediately after the words "Etha Bhikkhavo" (Come, monks) were uttered, they became 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monks, bearing miraculously created bowls and robes.

## The Buddha Residing in the City of Kosambī
Those three great merchants also took five hundred carts each, filled with all kinds of offerings such as clothing, butter, honey, and molasses. They arrived in the city of Sāvatthī in due course, paid respectful homage to the Blessed One, and listened to the Dhamma. At the end of the discourse, they were established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). They stayed in the presence of the Teacher for about fifteen days, giving alms, and then requested the Buddha to visit the city of Kosambī. The Teacher, wishing to give his consent, said, "Great merchants, the Tathāgatas delight in secluded places." They replied, "Venerable sir, we understand. It is appropriate for us to come [to invite you] by sending a message." Having said this, they returned to Kosambī. The merchant Ghosaka built the Ghositārāma monastery, the merchant Kukkuṭa built the Kukkuṭārāma monastery, and the merchant Pāvārika built the Pāvārikārāma monastery. Thus, having built three great monasteries, they sent a message to the Buddha to come.

Hearing their message, the Teacher went to Kosambī. The merchants went out to meet him, conducted him to the monasteries, and attended to him in turns. The Teacher stayed in one monastery each day. He would go for alms at the door of the house of whichever merchant's monastery he had stayed in.

## Khujjuttarā Attaining Stream-entry
At that time, a florist named Sumana was an attendant to those three great merchants. That florist Sumana [to the] great merchants...
134:
He said to them thus: "I have served you, great merchants, for a long time, day and night. I also wish to offer a meal to the Blessed One. Please grant me the Blessed One for just one day." They granted permission, saying, "If that is so, friend Sumana, you may provide the meal tomorrow." He accepted, saying, "Very well, masters," and after inviting the Buddha, he prepared the offerings.

At that time, King Utena gave Queen Sāmāvatī eight kahāpaṇas daily for the cost of flowers. A servant of Queen Sāmāvatī named Khujjuttarā would go to Sumana the florist to buy flowers regularly. On that day, when Khujjuttarā arrived, Sumana said, "I have invited the Buddha. Today, I will first honor the Buddha with the choicest flowers. Please wait for a while. After assisting in the meal service and listening to the Dhamma, you may take the remaining flowers and go." Khujjuttarā agreed, saying, "Very well." After serving the community of monks headed by the Buddha, Sumana took the bowl for the purpose of the thanksgiving (anumodanā). The Buddha began to preach the sermon of thanksgiving. While listening to the Buddha’s discourse, Khujjuttarā was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). On other days, she would take four kahāpaṇas for herself and buy flowers with only four kahāpaṇas. However, on that day she attained Stream-entry, she bought flowers with all eight kahāpaṇas.

Then Queen Sāmāvatī asked Khujjuttarā, "How is it, mother? Did the King give us double the flower money today?" She replied, "No, my lady." "Then why are there so many flowers?" she asked again. "On other days, I would keep four kahāpaṇas for myself and bring flowers worth only four kahāpaṇas," she said. "Why did you not take it today?" she was asked. "Because I have attained the extraordinary Dhamma after listening to the discourse of the Perfectly Enlightened One," she replied.

## Khujjuttarā Attaining the Foremost Position as a Bearer of the Tipitaka

Then, instead of threatening or scolding her, saying, "Hey, you wicked servant! Give me back the money you have stolen for so long," the Queen pleaded, "Mother, please let us also drink the Deathless Dhamma that you have drunk." When Khujjuttarā said, "If so, let me bathe first," the Queen had her bathed with sixteen pots of scented water and gave her two sets of smooth, fine cloth. Khujjuttarā dressed in one and draped the other over her shoulder. She had a seat prepared and a fan brought. Sitting on the noble seat and holding the ornate fan, she addressed the five hundred court ladies and preached the Dhamma exactly as it had been taught by the Buddha. After hearing Khujjuttarā’s discourse, all five hundred court ladies were also established in the Fruit of Stream-entry.

All those five hundred court ladies paid homage to Khujjuttarā with great respect and said, "Mother, from today onwards, do not perform menial servant duties. Remaining in the position of a mother and a teacher to us, please go to the Buddha, listen to the Dhamma as taught by Him, and preach it to us." Khujjuttarā did as she was told and subsequently became a bearer of the Tipitaka (tipiṭakadhara). Later, the Buddha appointed her to the foremost position, saying: "Monks, the foremost among my laywomen disciples who are very learned and are preachers of the Dhamma is Khujjuttarā."
135:
The meaning is: Monks, among my female lay disciples who are very learned and who are speakers of the Dhamma, this Khujjuttarā is the foremost.

Queen Sāmāvatī and the five hundred palace women also entreated Khujjuttarā, saying, "Mother, we also wish to see the Blessed One. Please show the Blessed One to us. Let us worship the Blessed One with perfumes, flowers, and so on." When she replied, "Ladies, the royal family is a heavy responsibility; it is not possible to take you outside," they pleaded earnestly, "Mother, do not ruin us; just show the Blessed One to us." She then said, "If that is so, to the extent that you can see through the walls of your living chambers, make holes of that size. While bringing perfumes and flowers, stay in those places and look at the Blessed One as he goes to the doors of the houses of the three treasurers. Stretch out your hands, pay homage, and make offerings." Those five hundred palace women did as Khujjuttarā had said, and they watched, paid homage, and made offerings to the Blessed One both when he was going and when he was returning.

## Striving for the Destruction of Sāmāvatī and Her Followers

Then one day, Queen Māgaṇḍiyā, while walking to and fro after coming out from her palace terrace, arrived at the living quarters of the palace women led by Sāmāvatī. Seeing the holes in the chambers, she asked, "What are these holes?" The palace women, not knowing Māgaṇḍiyā’s state of harboring a grudge against the Blessed One, said, "The Blessed One has come to this city. We stay in this place to look at, pay homage to, and make offerings to the Blessed One." Hearing this, she thought, "So, the ascetic Gotama has come to this city? Now I shall know what ought to be done to that ascetic Gotama. These five hundred women are also his attendants. I shall also know what ought to be done to these women." She then went to the King and reported, "Great King, Sāmāvatī and the five hundred palace women have external aspirations. In just a few days, they will take your life." 

King Utena, thinking, "These women would not do such a thing," did not believe her at all. Even though she reported it repeatedly, he still did not believe her. Then, when he did not believe her even after being told three times, she said, "Great King, if you do not believe my words, go to the living quarters of those five hundred women led by Sāmāvatī and investigate." When King Utena went and saw the holes in the chambers, he asked, "What are these holes?" When he was told the reason, he did not get angry with those five hundred women. Without saying a single word, he simply had the holes closed and had high-level windows made in all the chambers. It is said that high-level windows originated at that time.

## Teaching the Dhamma to Venerable Ānanda Regarding the Abuse

Queen Māgaṇḍiyā, being unable to do anything to those five hundred palace women led by Sāmāvatī, thought, "I will do what ought to be done only to the ascetic Gotama." She gave bribes to the townspeople and commanded, "When the ascetic Gotama enters the city and wanders about, have him abused and reviled by slaves, laborers, and men, and drive him away." The people of wrong view, who had no faith in the Three Jewels, followed the Blessed One who had entered the city, calling him a thief, a fool, a deluded person, a camel, an ox, a donkey, a hell-dweller, an animal, and saying, "There is no happy destination for you."
136:
I shall endure abuse as an elephant in battle endures the arrow shot from a bow; for many people are indeed ill-behaved.

They lead the trained to an assembly; the king mounts the trained. Among humans, the trained one is best, who endures abusive words.

Trained mules are excellent, as are noble Sindh horses and great tusker elephants; but more excellent than those is the one who has trained oneself.

Nāgo: Like a battle-elephant entering the fray. Saṅgāme: In the battlefield. Cāpato: From a bow. Patitaṃ: Released and falling upon oneself. Saraṃ: Various large and small arrows. Titikkhati iva: Just as it endures. Evaṃ: In the same way. Ahaṃ: I, the Buddha. Ativākyaṃ: Abusive words spoken excessively. Titikkhissaṃ: Shall endure. Hi: Indeed, it should be endured. Jano: The people of the world. Bahu dussīlo: Are mostly ill-behaved, speaking as they please and lacking in virtue.

Samitiṃ: To the midst of an assembly or gathering. Gacchantā: Those who go. Dantā: Lead a trained ox or a trained horse when harnessed to a carriage. Rājāpi: Even a sovereign king. Dantā: Mounts only a trained elephant-vehicle or horse-vehicle. Yo: Whosoever. Ativākyaṃ: Can endure abusive, offensive, and reckless words. So: Such a person who has the nature of endurance. Danto: Is truly a trained person. Manussesu: Among humans (or, more than other humans). Seṭṭho: Is one who is praised as being exceptionally noble.

Assatarā ca: Mules born from a female donkey are excellent. Ājāniyā ca: Noble horses that quickly understand what is right and wrong are excellent. Sindhavā ca: Sindh horses are excellent. Kuñjarā: And those called Kuñjara. Mahānāgā ca: Great tusker elephants are excellent only after being well-disciplined and trained. Attadanto: A person who is well-disciplined and trained through the Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). Tato: Is more excellent than all those aforementioned.

They reviled and muttered with these ten forms of abuse, saying, "You deserve only the miserable destination of an evil state," and so on. Hearing such abuse and reviling, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha: "Venerable Sir, these citizens of Kosambī are abusing and reviling us; let us depart from this city to another."

When the Buddha asked, "Dear Ānanda, where do you wish to go?", he replied, "Venerable Sir, we wish to go to another city." The Buddha asked again, "Dear Ānanda, if people in that other city to which we move also abuse us, where shall we go then?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, we shall go to yet another city from there." The Buddha asked again, "Dear Ānanda, if people in that place also abuse us, where shall we go then?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, we shall move to another city from there as well."

"Dear Ānanda, it is not proper or suitable to do so. Where a conflict (adhikaraṇa) arises, it is only proper and good to move elsewhere after that conflict has been settled right there. Dear Ānanda, who are those who are abusing us?" When asked thus, he replied, "Venerable Sir, everyone, starting from the slaves and workers, is abusing us."

"Dear Ānanda, I am like a great tusker elephant that has entered the battlefield. Just as it is the burden of a great elephant entered into battle to endure arrows shot from the four directions, so too, it is my burden to endure the words spoken by many immoral people," the Buddha said. Then, intending to deliver a Dhamma discourse concerning Himself, He spoke these three verses from the Nāga Vagga.

This Dhamma discourse was of great benefit to the many people who had gathered. Having thus delivered the Dhamma teaching, He said, "Dear Ānanda, do not worry. These people will be able to abuse us for only seven days; on the eighth day, they will become silent. For a conflict that has arisen for the Buddhas does not last beyond seven days."

## Attempting the Destruction of Sāmāvatī and Others through the Chicken Ruse

When Queen Māgaṇḍiyā was unable to make the Buddha flee by having Him abused, she pondered, "What shall I do now?" and thought, "These five hundred women, with Sāmāvatī at their head, are the supporters of that ascetic Gotama. I will bring destruction upon these women as well." One day, while attending to King Utena at the place where he drank liquor, she sent a message to her uncle, Cūḷamāgaṇḍiya: "Please bring eight dead chickens and eight live chickens to me. Upon arrival, stay at the top of the staircase and announce your arrival. Then, even if I say 'Come in,' do not enter, but first send the eight live chickens, and later send the eight dead chickens." She also gave a bribe to a young attendant, saying, "Follow my instructions."
137:
The uncle, the brahmin Cūḷamāgaṇḍiya, came and informed the King. Although the King said, "Enter," Cūḷamāgaṇḍiya replied, "I do not wish to enter the King's drinking area." Queen Māgaṇḍiyā sent a young attendant, saying, "Dear boy, go to my uncle." The attendant went and brought the eight live chickens given by the uncle, reporting, "Great King, the chaplain has sent a gift." King Udena remarked, "A fine side dish has come to us; who shall cook it?" Māgaṇḍiyā suggested, "Great King, the five hundred women led by Sāmāvatī are living idly; send it to them, and they will cook and bring it."

The King ordered, "Go, give it to the women led by Sāmāvatī, and tell them to kill and cook it themselves, not letting it pass into another's hands." The attendant agreed, saying, "Very well, Great King," and went and spoke as the King had commanded. However, the women led by Sāmāvatī refused, saying, "We do not take the lives of others." The attendant returned and reported this to the King. Māgaṇḍiyā said, "Great King, have you not seen for yourself? Now you shall know whether they will kill or not. Great King, command them, 'Cook and send it for the ascetic Gotama.'" The King did as Māgaṇḍiyā suggested and sent the order. The attendant took the chickens, but acting as if he were going to them, he gave the live chickens back to the chaplain and brought dead chickens to the women, saying, "Cook these chickens and offer them to the Teacher." The women welcomed him, saying, "Sir, bring them; this is indeed our duty," and they took them.

When the attendant returned to the King, the King asked, "Well, boy?" He reported, "As soon as I said it was for the ascetic Gotama, they came out to meet me and took them." Māgaṇḍiyā said, "See, Great King? These women do not act for a benefactor like you."
138:
"They have aspirations elsewhere, but you did not believe me," she submitted. King Udena, though he heard these words, remained patient and stayed silent. Queen Māgaṇḍiyā thought, "What else can I do?"

## The Plot to Destroy Sāmāvatī and Her Attendants with a Snake

At that time, King Udena spent seven days at a time, in rotation, at the palaces of his three queens: Sāmāvatī, Vāsuladattā, and Māgaṇḍiyā.

Knowing that the King would go to Sāmāvatī’s palace the next day or the day after, Queen Māgaṇḍiyā sent a message to her uncle: "Please clean the fangs of a snake with medicine to remove its venom and send it to me." Her uncle did as requested and sent it. King Udena always took his Hatthikanta lute wherever he went. There was a hole in the soundbox of that lute. Queen Māgaṇḍiyā put the snake through that hole and plugged it with a bunch of flowers. The snake remained inside the lute for two or three days. On the day the King was to go, Māgaṇḍiyā asked, "Great King, to which queen's palace will you go today?" When he replied, "To Sāmāvatī’s," she said, "Great King, today I have seen an unpleasant dream. It is not proper to go there, Sire." But he replied, "I will certainly go." Even after she had forbidden him three times, she said, "If I cannot stop you, then I will go with you, Sire." Although the King tried to turn her back, she did not turn back, saying, "Great King, I do not know what might happen," and she went along with the King.

King Udena, having adorned himself with the clothes, ornaments, flowers, and perfumes provided by the women led by Sāmāvatī, and having enjoyed a fine meal, placed the lute at the head of the bed and lay down. Queen Māgaṇḍiyā, pretending to walk back and forth, removed the bunch of flowers from the hole in the lute. The snake, having been without food for two or three days, emerged through that hole, hissing and spreading its hood, and lay down at the back of the bed.

Seeing the snake, Queen Māgaṇḍiyā cried out loudly, "Disgusting, disgusting! Sire, a snake!" and while reviling both the King and the women, she said, "This extremely foolish King is luckless and does not listen to my words. These women are also luckless and ill-disciplined. What is it that they do not receive from the King? Do you think you will live happily only when this King is dead? Do you live in misery while he is alive? Sire, I warned you that I saw a bad dream today and that it was not proper to go to Sāmāvatī’s palace, yet you did not listen to my words." When King Udena saw the snake, he was terrified by the fear of death and thought, "So these women would do such a thing! Oh, how wicked they are! Even though I was told repeatedly of their wickedness, I did not believe Māgaṇḍiyā's words. First, they sat making holes in their rooms. Then, they sent back the chickens I had sent. And today, they have released a snake in my bed." He became as if ablaze with a great fire of rage.

## The Power of Sāmāvatī’s Loving-kindness

Queen Sāmāvatī gave this advice to the five hundred women: "Mothers, we have no other refuge. Cultivate a mind of loving-kindness equally toward the King, Queen Māgaṇḍiyā, and yourselves. Do not bear anger toward anyone." King Udena took up his bow made of goat-horn, which required the strength of a thousand men to string, and fitting an arrow dipped in poison...
139:
“I am confused, I am bewildered; all directions are lost to me. Sāmāvatī, protect me! Be my refuge.”

Sāmāvatī, the famous Queen named Sāmāvatī. I am greatly deluded and confused. I am bewildered in every way. All my directions, both internal and external, are lost. Sāmāvatī, the famous Queen named Sāmāvatī, please save and protect me. May you, Queen Sāmāvatī, be my refuge and reliance.

“I am even more bewildered; all directions are lost to me. Sāmāvatī, protect me! Be my refuge.”

Sāmāvatī, the famous Queen named Sāmāvatī. This wretched king, as I am called, is greatly bewildered in every way. All my directions, both internal and external, are lost. Sāmāvatī, the famous Queen named Sāmāvatī, please save and protect me. May you, Queen Sāmāvatī, be my refuge and reliance.

Having placed Queen Sāmāvatī in front and arranging all five hundred women in order, the King shot an arrow at Queen Sāmāvatī’s breast. By the power of Queen Sāmāvatī’s loving-kindness (mettā), that discharged arrow turned back and, facing the path it had come, stood as if it were about to pierce the King’s own heart.

The King reflected: “The arrow I shoot can pierce even stone; there is no place in the open sky that can stop it. Yet, this arrow has turned back and is aimed directly at my heart.” With a trembling heart, he thought: “This arrow is not a sentient being; it is a lifeless thing, yet it knows the virtues of Sāmāvatī. I, though a human being, did not know Sāmāvatī’s special virtues.” Having reflected thus, King Udena cast away his bow, raised his hands in reverence, and sat crouching at Sāmāvatī’s feet, reciting this verse [the first verse mentioned above].

When Queen Sāmāvatī heard the King’s words, she did not say, “Very well, O King, take refuge in me.” Instead, she said, “Great King, the Exalted Buddha whom I have gone to for refuge—go to that same Buddha for refuge yourself.”

Sāmāvatī, the disciple of the Fully Enlightened One, spoke these words:
“Do not go to me for refuge; go to the one I have gone to for refuge.
This is the Buddha, O Great King; this is the Buddha, the unsurpassed.
Go to that Buddha for refuge, and may you be my refuge.”

“O Great King, do not take refuge in me. I have taken refuge in the Buddha. This Buddha, whom your consort and sister [I] worship and revere, has fully realized the Four Noble Truths. This Buddha is unsurpassed. O Great King, go to that Buddha for refuge. And may you, Great King, be the refuge (protector) for me, who was wronged.” Thus she spoke.

When she spoke thus, King Udena said, “Now I am even more afraid,” and repeated the verse [the second verse mentioned above].

Then, as Queen Sāmāvatī rejected his request again in the same manner as before, the King said, “If that is so, I take refuge in you, and I take refuge in the Buddha, the Teacher. I also grant you a boon.” She replied, “Great King, let the boon granted by the Great King be accepted.”

## King Udena Grants a Boon to Sāmāvatī and Her Companions

King Udena approached the Buddha, took refuge in him, and invited him. After offering a great alms-giving to the community of monks headed by the Buddha for seven days, he called Queen Sāmāvatī and said, “Dear sister, arise and take the boon I have granted you.” She replied, “Great King, I have no need for gold, silver, or such things. Please grant me only this boon: arrange it so that the Buddha, together with five hundred monks, regularly comes to this palace so that we may hear the sublime Dhamma.” King Udena respectfully paid homage to the Buddha and requested, “Exalted Buddha, please come to this palace regularly with five hundred monks. The palace women, headed by Sāmāvatī, wish to hear the sublime Dhamma.”

Then the Buddha said, “Great King, it is not proper for Buddhas to go to a single place constantly. Many people will be longing for the Buddha’s arrival.” When he said this, the King requested, “Exalted Buddha, if that is so, please appoint and send one monk.” The Buddha appointed and sent the Elder Ānanda. The Elder Ānanda, taking five hundred monks, went regularly to the royal palace. The five hundred palace women, headed by Sāmāvatī, regularly offered alms-food to the Elder Ānanda and listened to the sublime Dhamma.
140:
On one occasion, those five hundred women, headed by Sāmāvatī, heard the Dhamma from the Venerable Ānanda and, being inspired with faith, made an offering of five hundred upper robes. Each upper robe was worth five hundred kahāpaṇas. The King, not seeing a single upper robe on any of those five hundred women of the harem, asked, "Where are your upper robes?" They replied, "We have offered them to our master, the Venerable Ānanda." He asked, "Did that Venerable Ānanda accept all those upper robes?" and they replied, "Yes, Great King, he accepted them all."

## The Venerable Ānanda Receiving Many Robes

King Udena approached the Venerable Ānanda, paid homage, and asked whether those five hundred women of the palace had offered the upper robes. Having heard that the women had indeed offered them and the Venerable Ānanda had accepted them, he asked, "Venerable sir, are there not too many clothes? What will you do with so many clothes?"

"Great King, I will take the clothes sufficient for our use and give the remaining clothes to monks whose robes are worn out," the Elder replied. When he said this, the King asked again, "What will those monks do with their own worn-out robes?" "Great King, they will give them to monks whose robes are even more worn out," he replied. "Venerable sir, what will those monks do with their very worn-out robes?" the King asked. "Great King, they will make them into bedspreads," he replied. "What will they do with the old bedspreads that were already there?" the King asked. "They will make them into floor covers," he replied. "What will they do with the old floor covers that were already there?" the King asked. "Great King, they will make them into foot-wipers," he replied. "What will they do with the old foot-wipers that were already there?" the King asked. "Great King, they will shred the old foot-wipers into small pieces, mix them with soft clay, and use them to plaster the walls," he replied. Hearing this, the King remarked, "Venerable sir, even with such a large quantity, the gifts offered to the noble ones do not go to waste."

When the Elder replied, "Indeed, Great King," King Udena was greatly pleased and had another five hundred clothes brought and placed at the Elder's feet as an offering. 

It is said that the Venerable Ānanda had previously received clothes worth five hundred each, placed at his feet in portions of a thousand, a hundred thousand times. Having placed them at his feet in portions of a thousand...
141:
...he had received clothes worth a thousand each, a thousand times. Having placed them at his feet in portions of a thousand, he had received clothes worth a hundred thousand each, a hundred times. There was no counting the clothes received in quantities of one, two, three, four, five, ten, and so on. It is said that after the Tathāgata had attained Parinibbāna, the Elder traveled throughout the whole of Jambudīpa and gave his own bowls and robes to the monks residing in all the monasteries.

## Māgaṇḍiyā Burning Sāmāvatī and Others to Death

Queen Māgaṇḍiyā thought, "Whatever I do, it does not turn out as intended but happens otherwise. What should I do now?" Then she thought, "There is this way." While King Udena had gone for recreation in the park, she sent a message to her uncle, the brahmin Cūḷamāgaṇḍiya: "Uncle, go to Sāmāvatī’s palace, have the cloth-storehouses and oil-storehouses opened, soak the cloths in the oil jars, wrap them around the pillars, gather all those five hundred women headed by Sāmāvatī together, close the doors securely, lock them from the outside with a mechanical bolt, set the palace on fire with torches, and then come down and leave."

That brahmin uncle went up to the palace, opened the granaries of cloth and oil, and began wrapping the pillars with cloths soaked in the oil jars. Then the five hundred women headed by Sāmāvatī approached him and asked, "Uncle, what is this work you are doing?" He said, "Daughters, the King has ordered these pillars to be wrapped with oil-soaked cloths to make them firm. In a king's palace, it is hard to know what is well-joined or poorly-joined. Daughters, come near me." When those five hundred women came, he put them into a chamber, closed the doors securely, locked them from the outside with a mechanical bolt, and having set the fire from the very beginning, he went down.

Queen Sāmāvatī gave this advice to those five hundred women: "Sisters, for us wandering in the beginningless Saṃsāra, the limit of these bodies being burned by fire in this very way is not easy to determine even by the Buddha's Omniscience. Be diligent with mindfulness." While the palace was burning, even though those five hundred women reached painful feelings, by attending to the meditation subject they had undertaken, some attained the fruit of Once-returning and some the fruit of Non-returning.

## The Death of Sāmāvatī and the Buddha’s Solemn Utterance

Then, many monks, having returned from their alms round after the meal, approached the place where the Blessed One was staying. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those monks addressed the Blessed One thus: "Venerable sir, while King Udena had gone to the park...
142:
The world is bound by delusion, appearing as if it were substantial.
The fool is bound by acquisitions, surrounded by darkness.
It appears as if eternal, but for one who sees, there is nothing.

"The world, the multitude of people, being associated with delusion, appears as if it were of a fit and proper nature. The fool, being bound by the bond of defilements (upadhi) and surrounded by the darkness of ignorance (avijjā), appears as if he were eternal. For one who has seen and known with wisdom, there is no longer any anxiety or concern known as defilement."

"Venerable Sir, the five hundred women, with Sāmāvatī at their head, have passed away as the inner palace burned. What is the destination of these female lay followers? What is their future state?" Thus they asked.

"Monks, among these five hundred female lay followers, there are Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna), Once-returners (Sakadāgāmī), and Non-returners (Anāgāmī). Monks, all of these female lay followers did not pass away without the benefit of attaining the Paths and Fruits," the Buddha declared. Then the Blessed One, having understood the matter, uttered this inspired utterance (Udāna) at that time.

After delivering this inspired utterance, He taught the Dhamma, saying: "Monks, these beings, wandering through the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa), do not always act with diligence to perform only meritorious deeds; being heedless, they also perform demeritorious evil deeds. Therefore, beings wandering through the round of rebirth inevitably experience both happiness and suffering."

## Māgandiyā Receives the Death Penalty (Reward) Along with Her Relatives

King Udena, hearing that Queen Sāmāvatī’s palace was burning, came with great speed but was unable to arrive before it was consumed by fire. Having arrived and extinguished the fire, he sat surrounded by his ministers, overwhelmed with intense sorrow. Reflecting on the virtues of Queen Sāmāvatī, he pondered, "Whose work could this be?" Realizing it must have been done by Māgandiyā, he thought, "If she is questioned by threats and rebukes, she will not speak. I will question her through a clever stratagem."

He then said to the ministers, "O ministers, previously I lived in constant anxiety and suspicion, even when I exerted myself. Sāmāvatī was always seeking an opportunity to destroy me. But now, my mind will be at peace, and I shall be able to live in comfort."

When the ministers asked, "Great King, who has done this?", he replied, "It must have been done by someone out of love for me."

Queen Māgandiyā, standing nearby, heard these words and said, "Great King, no one else would be able to do this. I have done it; I ordered my uncle to carry it out."

(The King then said,) "Apart from you, Māgandiyā, there is no other being who loves me. I am pleased with you. I shall grant you a noble boon; summon all your relatives."

Queen Māgandiyā sent a message to her relatives, saying, "The King is very pleased with me and grants me a noble boon. Come quickly!" The King ordered great honors to be given to everyone as they arrived. Seeing this, even those who were not her relatives gave bribes and came, saying, "We are relatives of Queen Māgandiyā."

King Udena had all of them seized and ordered pits to be dug waist-deep in the palace courtyard. He had all of them sit in the pits, filled them with soil, spread straw over them, and set them on fire. When their skin was burnt, he had them plowed with iron plows, tearing them into pieces and shreds. From Māgandiyā's body as well—
143:
Māgaṇḍiyā’s flesh was sliced from the thickest parts of her body with a sharp knife, placed in an oil pan on a trivet, and fried like cakes, and she herself was made to eat it.

## The Past of Sāmāvatī and Her Followers
In the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a conversation: "Friends, it is truly unsuitable and improper for such a faithful and devoted laywoman to meet such a death." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you sitting together now?" When they replied, "For such a discussion," he said, "Bhikkhus, for Sāmāvatī and the five hundred women, this death is unsuitable for this present existence. However, they have received a death that is entirely suitable for the kamma they committed in the past." When requested by the monks, "Venerable Sir, what was the kamma they committed in the past? Please tell us," he brought forth the past:

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, eight Paccekabuddhas used to eat regularly at the royal palace. Five hundred palace women attended to them. Among them, seven Paccekabuddhas went to the Himavanta. One Paccekabuddha sat entering meditative absorption (jhāna-samāpatti) in a thicket of grass on the riverbank. Then one day, while the Paccekabuddhas were away, the King went to play in the water with those five hundred women. There, after playing in the water for part of the day, the women came out and, being oppressed by the cold, wished to warm themselves by a fire. They wandered here and there, saying, "Look for a place where we can make a fire." Seeing that thicket of grass where the Paccekabuddha was in meditative absorption and thinking it was just a heap of grass, they surrounded it and set it on fire. When the grass burned and fell away, they saw the Paccekabuddha and thought, "We are ruined! Our King's Paccekabuddha is burning. If the King finds out, he will destroy us. Let us make him burn thoroughly." (Having consulted together,) all those women brought wood from here and there...
144:
...and made a pile of wood over the Paccekabuddha, and it became a great heap of wood. Then, they set the great pile of wood on fire, thinking, "Now he will be completely consumed," and they left.

At first, those women were not bound by kamma because they had no intention. But now, at this later time, they were bound by kamma because they had intention. As for the Paccekabuddha, even if wood were piled up by a thousand carts and set on fire while he was in meditative absorption, it would not be able to produce even a wisp of smoke or heat, let alone catch fire. Therefore, that Paccekabuddha arose on the seventh day and went away at his ease. Because of having committed that evil kamma, those women were cooked in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years. By the remaining result of that unwholesome kamma, for a hundred existences, they were burned to death in this very manner whenever their houses caught fire. This was the past evil kamma of the five hundred women led by Sāmāvatī.

## The Past Kamma of Khujjuttarā
When this was said, the monks asked the Teacher: "Venerable Sir, by what kamma did Khujjuttarā become a hunchback? By what kamma is she of great wisdom? By what kamma did she attain the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala)? By what kamma did she become a servant to others?"

"Bhikkhus, during the time when that same King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, among those eight Paccekabuddhas, one Paccekabuddha was slightly hunchbacked. Then, a certain serving woman, wrapping herself in a woolen blanket and holding a small golden bowl, mimicked him, saying, 'Our great Paccekabuddha wanders like this and like that...'

## Those Who Live Though Dead, and Those Who Are Dead Though Living

(21) Appamādo amatapadaṃ, pamādo maccuno padaṃ.
Appamattā na mīyanti, ye pamattā yathā matā.
(22) Evaṃ visesato ñatvā, appamādamhi paṇဍitā.
Appamāde pamodanti, ariyānaṃ gocare ratā.
(23) Te jhāyino sātatikā, niccaṃ daḷhaparakkamā.
Phusanti dhီrā nibbānaṃ, yogakkhemaṃ anuttaraṃ.

Appamāda, which is non-forgetfulness and heedfulness in performing wholesome deeds, is the cause for attaining Nibbāna, the state free from death. Pamāda, which is the lack of mindfulness and being heedful, is the cause of death. Those who are heedful and mindful are not said to die. Those who are heedless are like those who are already dead.

The wise, who possess the wisdom to see cause and effect and are established in heedfulness, knowing this distinction clearly and specifically, rejoice in heedfulness. These wise ones delight with a joyful heart in the domain of the Noble Ones (Ariyas) such as the Buddha, which consists of the nine supramundane states and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, including the foundations of mindfulness.

Those wise ones, possessing the two types of jhāna—namely, ārammaṇūpanijjhāna (meditation on an object) such as the eight attainments, and lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna (meditation on characteristics) such as insight, path, and fruition—who constantly exert physical and mental effort and are always firm in their endeavor, reach Nibbāna, the supreme security from bondage, than which there is no higher state.

"He goes like this," she said, mocking the gait of that great Paccekabuddha by walking in a hunched manner. As a result of that mocking karma, she became a hunchback. The reason for her great wisdom was that, in a past life, she invited Paccekabuddhas to the palace on the first day, had their alms-bowls taken, and had them filled with hot milk rice. Because the bowls filled with very hot milk rice were so hot, the Paccekabuddhas had to keep shifting them from hand to hand. When the woman who had mocked the Paccekabuddha saw this, she offered eight of her own ivory bracelets, saying, "Venerable sirs, please place the bowls on these bracelets and hold them." The Paccekabuddhas did as she suggested. When they looked at the laywoman, she said, "Venerable sirs, I have no need for these bracelets; I have offered them only to you. Please take them and go." Those Paccekabuddhas took them and went to the Nandamūla cave.

Due to the merit of offering those bracelets as bowl-stands, Khujjuttarā became a person of great wisdom in the present life, capable of mastering the Tipiṭaka. Due to the merit of serving the Paccekabuddhas, she attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). This was the karma she performed during the interval between the dispensations of two Buddhas.

## The Past Karma of Khujjuttarā Becoming a Servant

The reason for her becoming a servant who must serve others is that during the time of Kassapa Buddha, a daughter of a treasurer in Bārāṇasī was decorating herself with a mirror in the evening. At that time, an Arahant nun who was a close friend of the treasurer's daughter came to see her. This is true.
146:
Even though the nuns were Arahants who had exhausted their taints, they still wished to see the families who served them in the evening. At that moment, there was no servant present with the treasurer's daughter. The treasurer's daughter said, "Venerable lady, I pay my respects. Please pick up that jewelry box for me." The elder nun reflected: "If I do not pick up this jewelry box for this treasurer's daughter, she will bear a grudge against me and be reborn in hell. If I do pick it up, she will be reborn as a servant to others. Indeed, being a servant to others is better than suffering the intense and burning misery of hell." Reflecting thus, the Arahant nun, out of compassion for the treasurer's daughter, picked up the jewelry box and gave it to her. The Buddha taught that as a result of that unwholesome deed, she became a servant who must serve others.

## The Distinction Between Sāmāvatī and Māgaṇဍiyā

Again, one day, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, five hundred women led by Sāmāvatī were consumed by fire in the palace. The relatives of Māgaṇဍiyā were broken and destroyed with iron plows after straw fires were lit over them. Māgaṇဍiyā herself was cooked in boiling oil. In this event of death and destruction, who are those who are truly alive, and who are those who are dead?"
147:
The Blessed One came and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you sitting together here now as I have arrived?” When they replied, “We are sitting together for such and such a discussion,” he said:

“Monks, those who are heedless in wholesome deeds, even if they live for a hundred years, are as if dead. Those who are not heedless, even if they have passed away, are truly alive. Therefore, although Māgaṇḍiyā is still living, she is as if dead. Sāmāvatī and the five hundred women, though they have passed away, are truly alive. Monks, those who are not heedless in wholesome deeds are called deathless.” Having said this, he spoke these verses:

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth. The teaching became beneficial to the multitude.

The story of Queen Sāmāvatī ends.

## 2. The Story of the Treasurer’s Son Kumbhaghosaka

(Kumbhaghosaka-seṭṭhi-vatthu)

The Teacher, while staying at Veluvana Monastery, spoke this legal discourse beginning with “Uṭṭhānavato,” concerning the treasurer’s son Kumbhaghosaka.

## The Voice of Kumbhaghosaka and King Bimbisāra’s Insight

In the city of Rājagaha, a plague broke out in the house of the Rājagaha treasurer. When that plague occurred, animals starting from flies up to cattle died first. After that, the slaves and laborers died, and finally, the masters of the house. Therefore, that plague eventually seized the treasurer and his wife. When they were afflicted by the disease, they looked at their son standing nearby and, with eyes full of tears, said to him: “Dear son, when this plague occurs, only those who break through the wall and flee survive. You, without looking back at us, flee and if you survive, return later. In such and such a place, we have buried forty crores of wealth. Dig up that wealth and make your living.” Thus they instructed their young son.
148:
When the treasurer’s son heard the words of his parents, he wept with a sorrowful face, paid homage to them, and out of fear of death, broke through the wall and fled. He went to a dense mountain forest and lived there for twelve years before returning to the place where his parents had lived. When he returned, no one recognized him because he had left as a youth and returned with long hair and a beard.

The young man, following the signs given by his parents, went to the place where the treasure was hidden. Finding the wealth intact, he thought: “No one recognizes me. If I dig up the wealth and use it, they might seize and harass me, saying, ‘A poor man has dug up a treasure.’ It would be better if I lived by working for others.” Then, wearing a piece of coarse cloth, he went to the street of laborers, asking, “Is there anyone who wishes to hire a laborer?” Seeing him, the laborers said, “If you do one task for us, we will give you food and wages.” When he asked, “What task is it?” they replied, “The task of waking and urging people. If you are able, get up early in the morning and go around announcing: ‘Fathers, get up! Prepare the carts! Yoke the oxen! It is time for the elephants and horses to go for grass. Mothers, you too get up! Cook the gruel! Cook the rice!’” The young man agreed, saying, “Very well.” Then they gave him a house to live in. He performed that task every day.

Then one day, King Bimbisāra heard the voice of the young man. Now, the King was one who understood all sounds. Therefore, he said, “This is the voice of a man of great wealth.” Then a female attendant in the palace who was near the King thought, “The King would not say something without reason. I should find out about this person.” She sent a man, saying, “Go, dear, and find out about him.” The man went quickly, saw the young man, and returned, reporting, “This is just a poor, lonely man working for hire among the laborers.” Hearing the man’s words, the King remained silent. On the second and third days, hearing the voice again, he said the same thing. The female attendant thought as before and sent the man repeatedly. When he still said, “This is a poor, lonely man,” she thought: “Even though the King hears that this is a poor, lonely man, he does not believe it. He repeatedly says this is the voice of a man of great wealth. There must be a reason for the King’s words.”
149:
[The King] thought, "It is proper to know the truth about this man."

## The Stratagem to Catch Kumbhaghosaka as a Son-in-law

Then, a female palace servant said to the King, "Your Majesty, if I receive a thousand pieces of money, I will take my daughter and bring that wealth into the royal treasury." The King had the thousand pieces given to her.

Taking the money, she made her daughter wear a soiled garment and, leaving the palace with her, went to the street of laborers as if they were wayfarers. Entering a certain house, she said, "Mother, we are wayfarers; let us rest here for a day or two before we proceed."

"Dear daughter, there are many people in this house. We cannot accommodate you. Kumbhaghosaka's house over there is empty; go there," the mistress of the house replied. She then went to Kumbhaghosaka's house and requested, "Sir, we are wayfarers; let us stay in this house for a day or two." Although she was repeatedly refused by him, she did not wish to leave, saying, "Sir, let us stay for just this one day, and we will leave early in the morning."

She stayed there, and the next morning, when Kumbhaghosaka was about to go to the forest, she said, "Sir, leave your rations and go; I will cook food for you."

"Mother, there is no need; I will cook and eat myself," Kumbhaghosaka replied. However, because she pleaded repeatedly and spoke persuasively, he gave her what was needed. She then obtained pots and clean rice from the market and cooked very pure rice in the royal manner, along with two or three kinds of delicious curries and side dishes. When the young man Kumbhaghosaka returned from the forest, she served him the prepared meal. Then, knowing that his mind had become softened after eating the excellent food, she said, "Sir, we are exhausted; let us stay here for another day or two." The young man Kumbhaghosaka consented, saying, "Very well."

After that, she cooked and served him delicious meals in the evening and again the next morning. Knowing that his heart was softened, she said, "Sir, let us stay here for a few more days." While living there, she used a sharp knife to cut the cords of his couch in various places beneath the frame. As soon as the young man Kumbhaghosaka came and sat down, the couch sagged and gave way. He asked, "Why has this couch broken and sagged like this?"

"Sir, I cannot stop the young children; they gather and play right here on this couch," she replied.

"Mother, this trouble has come upon me because of you. Formerly, whenever I went anywhere, I would go after closing the door," he said. She replied, "Dear son, what can I do? I am unable to stop them."

In this manner, she continued to cut the cords for two or three days. Even though the young man Kumbhaghosaka complained and grumbled, she spoke as before. Finally, she left only one or two cords and cut all the rest. That day, as soon as the young man Kumbhaghosaka sat down, the entire webbing fell to the ground. His head was brought down level with his knees. He stood up and said, "What shall I do? Where shall I go now? You have acted as if you do not even own a bed!"

"Dear son, what can I do? I cannot stop the neighboring children. Dear son, let it be; do not worry. Where should you go at such an unseasonable hour?" Saying this, she called her daughter and said, "Dear daughter, prepare a place for your brother to sleep."
150:
The maiden, lying on one side, said, “My lord, come here.” The mother also said to the young Kumbhaghosaka, “Dear son, go and sleep with your sister.” Young Kumbhaghosaka slept on the same couch with that maiden and, having become intimate with her that very day, the maiden [arose and] wept. Then the mother asked the maiden, “Dear daughter, why are you weeping?” She replied, “Mother, such a thing has happened.” The mother said, “Dear daughter, let it be; what can be done now? It is proper for you to have a husband to rely upon, and it is proper for this young man to have a wife to serve him.” Thus, she made Kumbhaghosaka her son-in-law. They lived together in harmony.

## How Kumbhaghosaka Reached King Bimbisāra
After two or three days had passed, that woman [the palace maid] sent a message to the King: “Great King, let a festival be proclaimed in the street of the laborers. Let it be announced that whoever does not celebrate the festival in their house shall be punished with such-and-such a fine.” King Bimbisāra did as she requested. Then the mother-in-law said to Kumbhaghosaka, “Dear son, by the King’s command, a festival must be held in the street of the laborers. What shall we do?” He replied, “Mother, I cannot even make a living by working for hire; how shall I do this?” She said, “Dear son, those who live as householders must sometimes even take on debt. One cannot ignore the King’s command. As for debt, one may be released from it by some means or another. Dear son, go and bring one or two kahāpaṇas from someone.” Grumbling and complaining, the young Kumbhaghosaka went and brought only one kahāpaṇa from the place where his forty crores of wealth were hidden.

The woman sent the kahāpaṇa given by Kumbhaghosaka to the King, and having celebrated the festival with her own money, she sent another message after two or three days in the same manner. Again, the King ordered the festival to be held, decreeing such-and-such a fine for those who did not. Again, the mother-in-law, the palace maid, spoke to Kumbhaghosaka as before, and being pressured, he went to the place where the treasure was kept and brought three kahāpaṇas. The palace maid sent those kahāpaṇas to the King, and after two or three days, she sent another message as before, saying, “Now, please send your men to summon this young man Kumbhaghosaka.” The King sent his men. The King’s men went there and, searching for him, asked, “Who is the one named Kumbhaghosaka?” and upon seeing him...
151:
...seeing the young Kumbhaghosaka, they said, “Come, sir, the King summons you.” Being afraid and saying, “The King does not know me,” and so forth, he did not wish to go.

Then, they forcibly seized him by his hands and other parts and dragged him away. When the mother-in-law saw those king’s men, she threatened and scolded them, saying, “You ill-mannered men! It is not proper for you to seize my son-in-law by his hands and so on.” She then said, “Come, dear son, do not be afraid. After seeing the King, I will have him cut off the hands of those who seized yours.” Taking her daughter and going ahead to the palace, she changed her appearance, adorned herself with all kinds of ornaments, and stood in a suitable place. The King’s men also dragged and brought the young Kumbhaghosaka.

## Kumbhaghosaka Receiving the Position of Treasurer
Then the King said to the young Kumbhaghosaka, who stood there after paying homage, “Are you the one named Kumbhaghosaka?” When he admitted, “Yes, Your Majesty,” the King asked, “Why do you hide your great wealth and not enjoy it?” He replied, “Your Majesty, where would a servant like me, who lives by working for hire, have great wealth?” King Bimbisāra said, “Do not do this. Why do you deceive us?” He replied again, “Your Majesty, I am not deceiving you; I have no wealth.” Then the King showed him those kahāpaṇas and asked, “Whose kahāpaṇas are these?” Recognizing them, Kumbhaghosaka thought, “Oh, I have been foolish! How did these kahāpaṇas reach the King’s hand?” Looking here and there, he saw the mother and daughter, the palace women, adorned with various ornaments and standing near the door of the inner chamber. He realized, “This is a serious matter; these women must have been employed by the King.”

Then the King asked him, “O man, speak! Why do you act like this?” He replied, “Your Majesty, I have no refuge.” The King said, “Is it not fitting for someone like me to be your refuge?” He replied, “Your Majesty, if you would indeed be my refuge, it would be very good.” The King said, “I shall be your refuge. How much wealth do you have?” He replied, “Forty crores, Your Majesty.”
152:
## The Teaching
(24) For one who is energetic, mindful, pure in deed, considerate, self-controlled, living righteously, and heedful, fame and glory increase day by day.

Uṭṭhānavato: for one who possesses energetic effort. Satīmato: for one who is endowed with mindfulness. Sucikammassa: for one who is endowed with blameless and pure actions such as bodily deeds. Nisammakārino: for one who acts with careful consideration and reflection. Saññatassa: for one who is restrained in body, speech, and mind. Dhammajīvino: for one who makes a living righteously. Appamattassa: for one who is heedful. Yaso: wealth, status, reputation, and fame. Abhivaḍḍhati: increases day by day.

When he reported, "Great King, there are about forty crores," the King asked, "What is appropriate for you to receive?" He replied, "Great King, it is appropriate for me to receive carts."

King Bimbisāra had a great many carts harnessed and sent them to bring all that wealth. He had it piled in the palace courtyard and, having assembled the people of Rājagaha, asked, "Is there anyone in this city of Rājagaha who possesses this much wealth?" When they replied, "No, Great King," he asked, "What should be done for this man?" They replied, "Great King, he should be honored." So, with great honor, he appointed the young Kumbhaghosaka to the position of Treasurer (Setthi) and gave his daughter to him in marriage. Then, together with Kumbhaghosaka, he went to the Buddha, paid respectful homage, and said: "Venerable Sir, please look at this man. There is no one as steady and wise as he. Although he is the owner of forty crores of wealth, he did not show any sign of vanity or pride. He lived like a destitute person, wearing rags and earning his living as a hired laborer on the roads. I came to know this through a certain stratagem. After finding out, I summoned him, made him acknowledge his wealth, brought the wealth here, and appointed him as a Treasurer. I also gave my daughter to him, Venerable Sir. I have never seen such a steady and wise person before."

Hearing this, the Buddha said: "Great King, the life of one who lives in this way is called a righteous and proper life. Acts such as stealing others' property cause suffering and destruction in this present world and in the world to come. Therefore, there is no such thing as happiness from such acts. This is true. When a man's wealth is lost, earning a living by farming or hired labor is indeed a righteous and proper life. For one who is endowed with energy and mindfulness, whose deeds of body and speech are pure, who acts with consideration and wisdom, who is restrained in body, speech, and mind, who lives a righteous life, and who remains established in unremitting mindfulness, his power and wealth increase day by day." Then he spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of this verse, the Treasurer Kumbhaghosaka was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Many others also reached the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth. Thus, the Dhamma teaching became beneficial to the multitude.

The Story of the Treasurer's Son Kumbhaghosaka ends.
153:
## 3. The Story of Elder Cūḷapanthaka
(Cūḷapanthakattheravatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Uṭṭhānenappamādena" concerning Elder Cūḷapanthaka.

## The Birth of Mahāpanthaka and Cūḷapanthaka after the Treasurer's Daughter Ran Away with a Slave
In the city of Rājagaha, the daughter of a wealthy merchant named Dhana Setthi reached marriageable age. Her parents kept her on the top floor of a seven-storied palace and guarded her closely. Due to the intoxication of youth, she became infatuated with men and committed misconduct with her own slave. Fearing that "others might come to know of this deed," and being afraid that "if my parents find out about this fault, they will tear me to pieces," she said, "We cannot stay in this place. Let us go to another region."

Taking their portable wealth, the couple left through the main gate and went to an unknown place where others would not recognize them. While living in a certain place, she conceived a child as a result of their cohabitation. When the pregnancy matured, she consulted her husband, saying, "My pregnancy has reached maturity. Giving birth in a place devoid of relatives and kinsmen will bring suffering to both of us. Let us go back to my family home."

The husband, fearing that "if I go there, I will lose my life," delayed the days, saying, "We will go today, we will go tomorrow." The treasurer's daughter thought, "This fool does not dare to go because of his great fault. Parents always desire the welfare of their children. Whether he goes or not, I will go." While the husband was away from the house, she packed the household items, informed the neighbors that she was going to her parents' house, and set out on the road.
