When the man returned home and did not see her, he asked the neighbors and heard that she had gone back to her parents' house. He followed her quickly and caught up with her on the way. Right there on the road, she gave birth. The husband asked, "Dear sister, what is this?" She replied, "Dear husband, a son has been born to me. What shall we do now?" He said, "The purpose for which we were going to your parents' house has been fulfilled right here on the road. What will we do by going there? Let us turn back." Both being of one mind, they turned back. Because the boy was born on the road (pantha), they named him Panthaka. Not long after, she conceived another child. (Everything should be expanded in the same manner as before.) Because this child was also born on the road, the first-born son was named Mahāpanthaka and the second-born son was named Cūḷapanthaka.
154:
## Sending the Panthaka Brothers to their Grandparents

The couple took the two children and returned to their own place of residence. While they were living there, the boy Mahāpanthaka heard other children calling people 'younger uncle, elder uncle, grandfather, and grandmother.' Hearing this, he approached his mother and asked, 'Mother, other children call people grandfather, grandmother, elder uncle, and younger uncle. Do we not have any relatives to call by such names?' She replied, 'Dear son, it is true that you have no relatives here. However, in the city of Rājagaha, there is a merchant named Dhana-seṭṭhī who is your grandfather. We have many relatives there.' He asked again, 'Mother, why then do we not go to Rājagaha?' The merchant's daughter did not tell her son the reason for her departure, but as the children asked repeatedly, she said to her husband, 'These children are wearing me out. Will our parents really eat our flesh if they see us? Come, let us show the children their grandfather’s family.' He replied, 'I will not be able to face them, but I will take you there.' She said, 'Very well, by some means or another, it is proper that the children should see their grandfather’s family.'

The two of them took the children and in due course arrived at Rājagaha. They entered a rest house at the city gate, and the children's mother sent word to her parents of her arrival. Upon hearing the news of their daughter and son-in-law’s arrival, the parents thought, 'In the round of rebirth (saṃsāra), there is no one who has not been a son or a daughter. However, these two have committed a great offense against us. They are not fit to stand before our eyes. Let them take this much wealth and go to live happily elsewhere. But let them send the children here.' They gave wealth and sent a messenger.

The couple took the wealth sent by the parents and handed the children over to the messengers who had come. Thus, the children were sent away.

## The Panthaka Brothers Entering the Dispensation

The children grew up in their grandparents' house. Among them, Cūḷapanthaka was still very young, while Mahāpanthaka went with his grandfather, the merchant, to listen to the Dhamma from the Buddha (Dasabala). As he went regularly to the presence of the Teacher, Mahāpanthaka’s mind inclined toward ordination as a novice (sāmaṇera). He said to his grandfather, 'If you would grant me permission, I would like to ordain as a novice.' The grandfather replied, 'What are you saying, dear son? Compared to the whole world, your ordination is more auspicious to me. If you are able, then ordain.' He then took Mahāpanthaka to the presence of the Buddha. When the Buddha asked, 'How is it, merchant? Have you obtained the boy?', he replied, 'Yes, Bhante. This boy is my grandson, and he wishes to ordain in the presence of the Blessed One.'
155:
The Teacher commanded a monk who practiced the dhutaṅga of alms-gathering, saying, 'Ordain this boy.' The Elder taught him the meditation on the five parts of the body (tacapañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna)—which is the contemplation and development of the five parts: hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, and skin—and then ordained him. Mahāpanthaka learned much of the Buddha’s word, the Tipiṭaka, and upon reaching the age of twenty, he received higher ordination (upasampadā). Through wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra), he practiced meditation and attained Arahantship. While spending his time in the bliss of jhāna and the bliss of fruition (phalasukha), he thought, 'Is it possible to give this bliss to Cūḷapanthaka?' He then went to his grandfather, the merchant, and said, 'Great merchant, if you would grant permission, I would like to ordain Cūḷapanthaka.' The merchant replied, 'Please ordain him, Bhante.'

It is said that the merchant was very devoted to the Dispensation. Furthermore, when asked, 'Which daughter of yours are these the sons of?', he felt ashamed to say they were from the daughter who had run away. For this reason, he easily gave permission for the boys to be ordained.

Elder Mahāpanthaka ordained Cūḷapanthaka and established him in the precepts. However, Cūḷapanthaka was of dull wisdom and could not memorize the following verse even after four months of study:

'Just as a fragrant red lotus (kokanada),
blooming in the morning with its scent undiminished,
behold the radiant Aṅgīrasa (the Buddha),
shining like the sun in the sky.'

(Note: Kokanada refers to a red lotus. Padma refers to the lotus flower. Aṅgīrasa refers to the Buddha, from whose body rays of light emanate.)

## The Past Kamma of Venerable Cūḷapanthaka’s Dullness

In the time of Kassapa Buddha, Cūḷapanthaka had been ordained and was a person of quick and sharp wisdom. At that time, he mocked a certain dull-witted monk while that monk was trying to learn a text. That dull-witted monk, feeling ashamed because of the mockery, did not learn the text nor did he dare to recite it. Due to that unwholesome kamma of mocking another, Cūḷapanthaka became a person of dull wisdom immediately after his ordination in this life. Every word he tried to learn would vanish as he attempted to learn the subsequent words. While he was striving to learn just this one verse beginning with 'Padmaṃ,' four months passed.

Then Mahāpanthaka said to him, 'Brother Cūḷapanthaka, you are unfit for this Dispensation of the Buddha. You cannot even learn a single verse in four months. How will you ever bring the duties of a monk to their consummation? Leave this monastery!' and he expelled him.
156:
Cūḷapanthaka, because of his great devotion to the Buddha's Dispensation, did not desire the state of a layman. At that time, Mahāpanthaka was the monk in charge of assigning meals. Jīvaka, who was raised by Prince Abhaya, took many flowers and perfumes and went to his mango grove. After honoring the Blessed One and listening to the Dhamma, he rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and approached Elder Mahāpanthaka, asking, "Venerable Sir, how many monks are there with the Blessed One?" "There are five hundred monks," the Elder replied. "Venerable Sir, tomorrow please accept a meal at our house, bringing the five hundred monks with the Buddha at their head." Elder Mahāpanthaka said, "Lay devotee, the monk named Cūḷapanthaka is of dull wisdom and has no nature of growth or progress. Excluding that Cūḷapanthaka, I accept the invitation for the rest of the monks." Hearing those words, Cūḷapanthaka thought, "While accepting the invitation for so many monks, this Elder Mahāpanthaka accepts it by excluding me. Undoubtedly, my elder brother must be disappointed in me. What use is this Dispensation of the Buddha to me now? I shall live as a layman, making a living while performing meritorious deeds such as giving." The next morning, he set out early to disrobe.

The Blessed One, surveying the world at dawn, saw this matter. He went out beforehand and stood walking to and fro at the gateway on the path where Cūḷapanthaka would go. As Cūḷapanthaka was going, he saw the Blessed One, approached Him, paid homage, and stood there. Then the Blessed One asked him, "Dear Cūḷapanthaka, where are you going at this early hour?" "Venerable Sir, my elder brother Mahāpanthaka has turned me out of the monastery, so I am going to disrobe," he replied.

## Cūḷapanthaka Thera and the Rajoharaṇa Meditation
"Cūḷapanthaka, your going forth (ordination) was in my presence. When you were turned out by your brother, why did you not come to me? Come, what use is the life of a layman to you? You shall stay with me," the Buddha said. He stroked Cūḷapanthaka's head with His hand, the palm of which was marked with the wheel-signs, and led him away. Seating him at the entrance of the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī), He instructed, "Cūḷapanthaka, face the east and stay right here, rubbing this piece of cloth and saying, 'Rajoharaṇaṃ, rajoharaṇaṃ' (Taking away the dust, taking away the dust)." He gave him a clean piece of cloth created by His psychic power. When the time for the meal was announced, the Buddha, surrounded by the community of monks, went to Jīvaka's house and sat on the prepared seat. Cūḷapanthaka also sat there, looking at the sun and rubbing that piece of cloth, saying, "Rajoharaṇaṃ, rajoharaṇaṃ." As he rubbed it, that piece of cloth became soiled. Then he thought, "This piece of cloth was extremely clean, but because of this body, it has lost its original nature and become so soiled. Indeed, formations (saṅkhāra) are impermanent." Thus, he developed insight by contemplating rise and fall.
157:
...Indeed, formations (saṅkhāra) in the three realms of existence are impermanent," he meditated, developing insight by contemplating rise and fall.

## Cūḷapanthaka Thera Becoming an Arahant
The Blessed One, knowing that Cūḷapanthaka's mind had ascended to the level of insight, said, "Cūḷapanthaka, do not perceive only the piece of cloth as being soiled with dust and dirt. Within you, there are also the dusts of lust and so forth. Remove those dusts of lust and the like." Then He sent forth a radiance, appearing as if He were sitting right in front of him, and spoke these verses:

Lust is called dust, but fine dust is not so called.
'Dust' is a name for lust.
Having abandoned this dust, the monks
Dwell in the Dispensation of the One free from dust.

Hatred is called dust, but fine dust is not so called.
'Dust' is a name for hatred.
Having abandoned this dust, the monks
Dwell in the Dispensation of the One free from dust.

Delusion is called dust, but fine dust is not so called.
'Dust' is a name for delusion.
Having abandoned this dust, the monks
Dwell in the Dispensation of the One free from dust.

Rajo: 'Dust' means rāga, the lust that craves and delights in the five cords of sensual pleasure. Reṇu pana: As for fine dust. Na ca vuccati: It is not yet called so. Rajoti etaṃ: This name 'dust'. Rāgassa: Is for lust, which craves and delights in the five cords of sensual pleasure. Adhivacanaṃ: It is a name. Vigatarajassa: Of the Buddha who is free from the dust of lust. Sāsane: In the Dispensation. Bhikkhavo: Monks, those who habitually contemplate the danger of saṃsāra. Ye: Those monks who. Atthi-santi: Exist. Te: Those monks. Etaṃ rajaṃ: This dust of lust. Vippajahitvāna: Having abandoned. Viharanti: They dwell.

Rajo: 'Dust' means dosa, the anger that is repeatedly formed and does not cease. Reṇu pana: As for fine dust. Na ca vuccati: It is not yet called so. Rajoti etaṃ: This name 'dust'. Dosassa: Is for hatred, which is destructive. Adhivacanaṃ: It is a name. Vigatarajassa: Of the Buddha who is free from the dust of hatred. Sāsane: In the Dispensation. Bhikkhavo: Monks, those who habitually contemplate the danger of saṃsāra. Ye: Those monks who. Atthi-santi: Exist. Te: Those monks. Etaṃ rajaṃ: This dust of hatred. Vippajahitvāna: Having abandoned. Viharanti: They dwell.

Rajo: 'Dust' means moha, the delusion of ignorance. Reṇu pana: As for fine dust. Na ca vuccati: It is not yet called so. Rajoti etaṃ: This name 'dust'. Mohassa: Is for delusion, which is ignorance. Adhivacanaṃ: It is a name. Vigatarajassa: Of the Buddha who is free from the dust of delusion. Sāsane: In the Dispensation. Bhikkhavo: Monks, those who habitually contemplate the danger of saṃsāra. Ye: Those monks who. Atthi-santi: Exist. Te: Those monks. Etaṃ rajaṃ: This dust of delusion. Vippajahitvāna: Having abandoned. Viharanti: They dwell.

At the end of these verses, Cūḷapanthaka attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Along with the analytical insights, the three Pitakas became clear to him.

## Cūḷapanthaka Thera's Display of Psychic Power
In a past life, he was a great king. While circumambulating the city clockwise, he wiped his perspiring forehead with a clean cloth. The cloth became soiled. That king then realized the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā), thinking, "Because of this body, such a clean cloth has lost its natural purity and become soiled. Formations are indeed impermanent." Because of that reason, the Rajoharaṇa meditation became the supporting condition for the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka. Jīvaka, raised by Prince Abhaya, was about to offer the water of donation to the Blessed One when the Blessed One covered the bowl with His hand and said, "Jīvaka, are there not monks still in the monastery?" Then Elder Mahāpanthaka said, "Venerable Sir, there are no more monks in the monastery." The Blessed One said again, "Lay devotee Jīvaka, there is one." Jīvaka then sent a man, saying, "In that case, my good man, go and find out for yourself whether there are monks in the monastery or not."
158:
At that moment, the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka thought, “My elder brother said there are no monks in the monastery; I will show him that there are monks in the monastery,” and he filled the entire mango grove with monks. Some monks were sewing robes; some monks were dyeing robes; some monks were engaged in recitation. In this way, he created a thousand monks, each performing different tasks. The man who had been sent saw many monks in the monastery, returned, and informed the physician Jīvaka, “Master, the entire mango grove is full of monks.” The Elder also, at that very place:

Sahassakkhattuṃ attānaṃ, nimminitvāna panthako.
Nisīdambavane ramme, yāva kālappavedanā.

Panthako: the Elder Cūḷapanthaka. Attānaṃ: himself. Sahassakkhattuṃ: to become a thousand monks. Nimminitvāna: having created. Yāva kālappavedanā: until the time for the meal was announced. Ramme: in the delightful and pleasant. Ambavane: in the mango grove. Nisīdi: he sat.

Then the Blessed One said to the man who had been sent, “Go to the monastery and say, ‘The Teacher calls the monk named Cūḷapanthaka.’” When that man went and spoke as the Buddha had commanded, a thousand mouths rose up, saying, “I am Cūḷapanthaka, I am Cūḷapanthaka.” The man went back and reported, “Venerable Sir, all the monks are indeed named Cūḷapanthaka.” The Buddha said, “If that is so, go and take the hand of the monk who first says ‘I am Cūḷapanthaka’; the rest will disappear.” He did as commanded. At that moment, the thousand monks disappeared. The Elder Cūḷapanthaka went along with that man. At the conclusion of the meal, the Blessed One addressed Jīvaka, “Jīvaka, take Cūḷapanthaka’s bowl; he will perform the anumodanā (blessing) for you.” Jīvaka did as the Buddha commanded. Cūḷapanthaka, uttering a brave sound like the roar of a lion king, gave a discourse, shaking the three Piṭakas like a young lion.

## The Blessed One’s Arrival at the Assembly Concerning the Elder Cūḷapanthaka
The Blessed One rose from his seat and, surrounded by the community of monks, went to the monastery. When the monks had performed their duties, he stood at the entrance of the Gandhakuṭī, gave the Sugata’s advice to the community of monks, taught them meditation subjects, and dismissed them. Then he entered the Gandhakuṭī, which was fragrant with the scent of excellent perfumes and flowers, and lay down on his right side in the noble lion’s posture.

Afterwards, in the evening, the monks gathered from here and there, sitting as if surrounded by a red woolen curtain, and began to speak of the virtues of the Blessed One: “Friends, Mahāpanthaka, not knowing Cūḷapanthaka’s disposition, could not make him learn a single verse in four months and expelled him from the monastery, saying, ‘This person is of dull wisdom.’ But the Blessed One, by virtue of being the unsurpassed King of Dhamma, granted him Arahatship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) within the interval of a single meal. The three Piṭakas also came to his lips along with the analytical insights. Indeed, the power of the Buddhas is great and marvelous!”
159:
Then, the Blessed One, knowing the course of the conversation in the Dhamma Hall, thought, "It is now time for me to go to the Dhamma Hall." Rising from his noble couch, he adjusted his well-dyed double under-robe, fastened his waistband which was as beautiful as a flash of lightning, and donned his great Sugata robe, which resembled a red woolen blanket. Emerging from the fragrant Gandhakuṭi, with the grace of a noble elephant in rut and the majesty of a lion, he proceeded to the Dhamma Hall with the infinite charm of a Buddha. He ascended the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the center of the decorated pavilion and sat there, emitting the six-colored Buddha-rays, appearing like the young sun atop Mount Yugandhara, as if stirring the depths of the ocean.

As soon as the Fully Enlightened One arrived, the assembly of monks ceased their conversation and became silent. The Teacher, looking at the assembly with a heart of tender loving-kindness, thought, "This assembly is exceedingly beautiful. Not even a single monk is fidgeting with hands or feet, nor is there the sound of coughing or sneezing. All these monks are deeply respectful out of reverence for the Buddha, awed by the Buddha-majesty. If I were to sit without speaking for an entire aeon, they would not be the first to initiate a conversation. I alone must know the duty of initiating a conversation; I shall be the first to speak." Then, addressing the monks with a sweet, Brahma-like voice, he asked, "Bhikkhus, what was the subject of your conversation as you sat here?" and "What was the discussion that was interrupted before I arrived?" When they replied, "It was such and such a topic," he said, "Bhikkhus, Cūḷapanthaka is not slow-witted only now; he was slow-witted in the past as well. It is not only now that I have become his refuge; I was his refuge in the past too. In the past, I made him the master of worldly wealth; now, I have made him the master of supramundane wealth." Having said this, at the request of the monks who wished to hear the matter in detail, he brought forth the past:

## The Story of the Past of Elder Cūḷapanthaka

Bhikkhus, in the past, a young man living in the city of Bārāṇasī went to Takkasilā to learn the arts. He became a resident pupil of a world-renowned teacher and, among five hundred young men, was a very helpful student to the teacher, performing all duties such as massaging the feet. However, due to his slow-wittedness, he was unable to learn any art. Even though the world-renowned teacher strove, thinking, "This student is very helpful to me; I will teach him to be proficient," he was unable to make him learn anything. After staying for a long time, the young man, unable to learn even a single verse and becoming discouraged, asked the teacher for permission to return home.

The world-renowned teacher thought, "This student has been very helpful to me. I constantly wish for him to become wise, but despite my wishing, I am unable to make him succeed in learning."
160:
"I must certainly repay this student's service. I will compose a mantra for him and give it to him." Thinking thus, the world-renowned teacher took the young man to the forest and composed this mantra: "Ghaṭṭesi ghaṭṭesi, kiṃ kāraṇā ghaṭṭesi? Ahampi taṃ jānāmi" (You are rubbing, you are rubbing; for what reason are you rubbing? I know it, too). He made him learn it, having him recite it many hundreds of times. He asked, "Is it clear in your mind?" When the student replied, "Yes, it is clear," the teacher thought, "An art that is mastered through effort by one who is slow-witted will not escape or be lost." He gave him travel provisions and sent him away, saying, "Go, you shall live by depending on this mantra. To ensure it does not escape or be forgotten, recite it constantly." When the young man reached Bārāṇasī, his mother, thinking, "My son has returned after learning the arts," honored him greatly.

## The King of Bārāṇasī Learns the Mantra for a Thousand

At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī, while reflecting, "Is there any fault in my bodily actions and so on?" saw no unseemly action of his own. He thought, "One's own faults are not apparent to oneself, but they are apparent to others. I will investigate the citizens." He went out at night in disguise, thinking, "The conversation of people sitting after their evening meal is of various kinds. If I rule unrighteously, they will say, 'We are destroyed by this wicked and unrighteous king through punishments and taxes.' If I rule righteously, they will speak of my virtues, saying, 'May our king be long-lived,' and so on." He wandered about, following the walls of various houses. At that moment, tunnel-thieves were digging a tunnel between two houses to enter both through a single tunnel. The King saw the thieves and stood in the shadow of a house. When the thieves had dug the tunnel, entered the house, and were looking at the goods, the young man woke up and, wishing to recite the mantra, said:

"Ghaṭṭesi ghaṭṭesi, kiṃ kāraṇā ghaṭṭesi? Ahampi taṃ jānāmi."

(The meaning is: You are rubbing. You are offending. For what reason are you offending? I, too, know that reason.)

Hearing the sound of the mantra being recited, the thieves thought, "The young man has discovered our actions; now he will beat and destroy us." Fearing this, they abandoned even the clothes they were wearing and fled in terror in whatever direction they were facing. The King, seeing the thieves fleeing and hearing the sound of the young man's recitation, marked the house where the young man lived and, after investigating the citizens, entered the palace. When dawn broke the next morning, the King called a man and said, "Friend, go to such and such a street, to the house where a tunnel was dug. There is a young man there who has returned from Takkasilā after learning the arts. Bring him here."
161:
On the journey, in a certain house where a tunnel was ruined, there was a young man who had returned after learning his arts in the city of Takkasilā. The King commanded, "Go and fetch that young man." The royal messenger went quickly and said, "The King summons you," and brought the youth. Then the King asked, "Dear boy, are you the youth who has returned after learning arts in Takkasilā?" When he replied, "Yes, Great King," the King said, "Give that art to me as well." The youth replied, "Very well, Great King, please learn it while sitting on a seat of equal height." The King did as requested, and after learning the mantra, he honored the youth with a thousand pieces of money, saying, "This is your teacher's fee."

## The Teacher of the Ghaṭṭesi Mantra Becomes General

At that time, the General asked the King's barber, "When will you shave the King's beard?" The barber replied, "Tomorrow or the day after." The General then gave the barber a thousand pieces of money and said, "I have a task for you." When asked, "What task shall I perform with this thousand?" the General replied, "While pretending to shave the King's beard, sharpen your razor very keenly and cut his throat. When I become King, you shall be the General."

The barber agreed, saying, "Very well." On the day he was to shave the King, he moistened the beard with scented water, sharpened the razor, and holding the King by the hairline at the forehead, he thought, "This razor is still a bit dull; I should cut the throat with a single stroke." He then stood aside and sharpened the razor again. At that moment, the King, remembering his mantra and wishing to recite it, uttered the verse of the mantra: "Ghaṭṭesi ghaṭṭesi, kiṃ kāraṇā ghaṭṭesi, ahampi taṃ jānāmi" (You are rubbing, you are rubbing; for what reason are you rubbing? I too know it).

Upon hearing the recitation of the mantra, sweat poured from the barber's forehead. Terrified, thinking, "The King knows my intention," he threw the razor on the ground and prostrated himself at the King's feet. Since Kings are naturally shrewd, he rebuked the barber, saying, "Hey, you wicked barber! Did you think that a King like me would not know?"

The barber then pleaded, "Great King, grant me my life." The King replied, "Let it be so, do not fear. Speak the truth." The barber confessed, "Great King, the General gave me a thousand pieces of money and told me, 'Pretend to groom the King's beard and cut his throat; when I become King, I will give you the position of General.'"

The King thought, "I have gained my life because of my teacher." He summoned the General and said, "O General, what reward have you not received from me? Now, I cannot bear to look at you. Leave my kingdom and capital immediately." Having banished the General from the country, he summoned the teacher and said, "Teacher, it is only because of you that I have kept my life." He then paid great honor to the youth and appointed him to the position of General. "Cūḷapanthaka was that youth at that time, and I was the world-renowned teacher (Disāpāmokkha)."

The Teacher (the Buddha), having brought forth this past story, said, "Monks, in the past too, Cūḷapanthaka was indeed slow of wisdom. At that time also, I was his refuge and established him in worldly wealth."
162:
"With even a little capital, a wise and discerning man establishes himself, just as one blows a small spark into a great fire."

'Aṇuṃ' means a very small amount, almost negligible. 'Agghiṃ' means fire. 'Sandhamaṃ' means blowing upon it. Just as one creates a great mass of fire by blowing on a small spark, so too a 'vicakkhaṇo' (discerning) and 'medhāvī' (wise) person, even with 'appakena pābhatena' (a small amount of capital), 'samuṭṭhāpeti attānaṃ' (establishes himself), increasing his wealth and property to become a great merchant.

## Preaching the Cūḷaseṭṭhi Jātaka

Furthermore, one day, when the conversation arose, "Oh, the Teacher has become the refuge and support of Cūḷapanthaka! How wonderful!", the Buddha preached the past story in the Cūḷaseṭṭhi Jātaka (of the Ekaka Nipāta).

After preaching this verse, He said, "Monks, it is not only now that I have been the refuge of this Cūḷapanthaka; I was his refuge in the past as well. In the past, I made this Cūḷapanthaka the master of worldly wealth; now, I have made him the master of supramundane wealth. At that time, the young pupil was Cūḷapanthaka, and the wise, clever, and skilled astrologer, the Merchant Cūḷaseṭṭhi, was I myself." Thus He identified the Jātaka.

Again, one day in the Dhamma Hall, the monks raised a discussion: "Friends, although Cūḷapanthaka was unable to learn a four-line verse in four months, he did not give up his effort and was established in Arahantship. Now he has become a master of the supramundane Dhamma-wealth." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered now?" When they replied, "For such a discussion," He said, "Monks, in my Dispensation, a monk who puts forth effort indeed becomes a master of the supramundane Dhamma," and He spoke this verse:

## The Teaching

(25) By effort, diligence, restraint, and self-control, let the wise man make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.

'Uṭṭhānena' means through energetic effort. 'Appamādena' means through diligence, characterized by non-separation from mindfulness. 'Saṃyamena' means through restraint, known as the fourfold purifying virtue (catupārisuddhisīla). 'Damena' means through the taming of the sense faculties. Through these four causal factors, a 'medhāvī' (wise person) endowed with wisdom born of the essence of Dhamma, should make ('kayirātha')—that is, is able to make—for himself an 'island' (dīpa), which is the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala) as a foundation for himself in this extremely deep ocean of Saṃsāra where a foothold is very difficult to find. What kind of island? 'Yaṃ ogho nābhikirati'—one which the fourfold flood of defilements (kilesa-ogha) cannot overwhelm or destroy. Indeed, Arahantship cannot be overwhelmed by the floods.
163:
## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the verses, many people became Stream-enterers and so forth. Thus, the teaching was beneficial to the assembled audience.

The Story of Elder Cūḷapanthaka ends.

## The Teaching
(26) Pamādaṃ anuyuñjanti, bālā dummedhino janā.
Appamādañca medhāvī, dhanaṃ seṭṭhaṃva rakkhati.

(27) Mā pamādaṃ anuyuñjetha, mā kāmaratisanthavaṃ.
Appamatto hi jhāyanto, pappoti vipulaṃ sukhaṃ.

Bālā: the foolish and deluded. Dummedhino: those without wisdom. Janā: people. Pamādaṃ: negligence in wholesome deeds. Anuyuñjanti: they indulge in. Medhāvī: the wise person. Seṭṭhaṃ: noble. Dhanaṃ va: like the seven kinds of treasures. Appamādañca: only heedfulness. Rakkhati: guards.

Pamādaṃ: negligence in wholesome deeds. Mā anuyuñjetha: do not indulge in. Kāmaratisanthavaṃ: the intimacy of craving, which is delight in sensual objects and defilements. Or, the intimacy of craving. Mā anuyuñjetha: do not strive to let it arise. Hi: indeed, that word is fitting. Appamatto: one who is heedful in wholesome deeds. Jhāyanto: one who is accustomed to contemplating and observing the two types of objects and characteristics. Vipulaṃ: abundant. Sukhaṃ: the happiness of Nibbāna. Pappoti: attains.

## 4. The Story of the Proclamation of the Fools' Festival
(Bālanakkhattasaṃghuṭṭhavatthu)

The Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Pamādamanuyuñjanti," while staying at the Jetavana monastery, concerning the Fools' Festival.

## The Buddha Not Entering the City During the Seven Days of the Fools' Festival
On one occasion, a festival called the Fools' Festival (Bālanakkhatta) was proclaimed in Sāvatthī. During that festival, people who were extremely foolish and deluded smeared their bodies with ashes and cow dung, and for seven days, they wandered about shouting vulgar, coarse, and wicked words. There was no one they felt ashamed of, even when seeing relatives, friends, or monks. Standing at every door, they shouted improper and unsuitable words. People, unable to listen to the improper words of those foolish people, had to send money—such as a quarter-kahāpaṇa, a half-kahāpaṇa, or a full kahāpaṇa—according to their means. Those fools took whatever they received at the doors of the townspeople and moved on.

At that time, about five crores of noble disciples (ariyasāvakas) lived in Sāvatthī. They sent a message to the Teacher: "Venerable Sir, for seven days, please do not enter the city with the Saṅgha of monks, but stay only in the monastery." For those seven days, they prepared and sent rice gruel, alms-food, and so on to the Saṅgha of monks at the monastery. They themselves did not leave their houses. When the festival ended, on the eighth day, they invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, had them enter the city for alms, and gave a great offering. Sitting in a suitable place, they said: "Venerable Sir, those seven days passed for us with great suffering."
164:
"Our ears felt as if they were about to break from hearing the improper words of those wicked fools. No one felt shame toward anyone else. Therefore, we did not allow the Exalted One to enter the city, and we ourselves did not dare to leave our houses." Hearing the words of those lay devotees, the Teacher said: "The behavior of foolish and unwise people is indeed like this. But the wise guard heedfulness (appamāda) like a noble treasure and reach the fulfillment of the great Bliss of the Deathless Nibbāna." He then spoke these verses:

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the verses, many people became Stream-enterers and so forth. The Dhamma teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.

The Story of the Proclamation of the Fools' Festival ends.

## 5. The Story of Elder Mahākassapa
(Mahākassapattheravatthu)

The Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Pamādaṃ appamādena," while staying at the Jetavana monastery, concerning Elder Mahākassapa.

## Elder Mahākassapa Contemplating the Passing Away and Rebirth of Beings
One day, while Elder Mahākassapa was staying at the Pipphali Cave, he went for alms in Rājagaha. After the meal, having returned from the alms-round, he developed the light kasina (āloka-kasiṇa). He then sat observing with his divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) beings who were negligent and those who were heedful, and those who were passing away and being reborn in water, on earth, in forests, on mountains, and so forth.
165:
## The Teaching

(28) When the wise man drives away heedlessness by means of heedfulness,
Having climbed the palace of wisdom, sorrowless, he beholds the sorrowing folk.
As one standing on a mountain peak looks down upon those standing on the ground,
So does the steadfast one behold the fools.

Paṇḍito: the wise man. Yadā: at which time. Appamādena: through heedfulness, which is non-forgetfulness and constant mindfulness. Pamādaṃ: heedlessness. Nudati: dispels or removes. Tadā: at that time. So: such a wise man. Paññā-pāsādaṃ: to the palace of wisdom. Āruyha: having climbed. Asoko: being free from the thorn of sorrow. Sokinīṃ: those who possess the thorn of sorrow. Pajaṃ: the multitude of beings. Avekkhati: beholds.

How is this so? Pabbataṭṭho: a person standing on a mountain peak. Bhūmaṭṭhe: those staying on the ground. Avekkhati iva: just as he beholds them. Tathā: in the same way. So dhīro: that wise person, an Arahant. Bāle: the foolish worldlings who are constantly being born and dying. Avekkhati: beholds them.

While the Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana monastery, he reflected with his divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), which is like a celestial eye, "In what manner is my son Kassapa dwelling today?" Upon such reflection, he knew, "He is dwelling while observing the passing away and rebirth of beings." Knowing this, he thought, "The passing away and rebirth of beings is not to be delimited even by a Buddha's knowledge; it is impossible to determine the limit of beings who pass away after taking conception in a mother's womb without the parents' knowledge. To know those beings is not your range, Kassapa; your range is only slight. To know and see all beings who are passing away and being reborn is the range of the Buddhas alone." Having said this, he emitted a radiance, appearing as if he were sitting in front of Kassapa, and spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the verse, many people realized the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and other fruits.

The story of Mahākassapa Thera ends.
166:
## 6. The Story of Two Monks who were Friends, one Heedless and one Heedful
(Pamattāpamatta-dve-sahāyaka-vatthu)

The Teacher spoke this religious discourse beginning with "Appamatto pamattesu" while staying at the Jetavana monastery, concerning two monks who were friends.

## The Difference Between the Heedless and the Heedful

Those two monks, having taken meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) from the Teacher, entered a forest monastery. (A forest monastery is defined as a place located five hundred 'ta' away from the nearest village, where one 'ta' equals four cubits). Among those two monks, one monk would fetch firewood early, prepare a fire-pan, and sit warming himself by the fire throughout the first watch of the night, chatting with the young novices. The other monk, being heedful and striving in monastic practice (samaṇa-dhamma), advised the monk who was warming himself heedlessly, "Friend, do not do this. For the heedless, the four woeful states are like their own home. Those known as Buddhas cannot be pleased through deceit."

That lazy monk did not listen to the advice of the heedful monk. The heedful monk, thinking, "This monk is not amenable to advice," did not speak to him further and continued to strive in monastic practice without negligence.

The lazy monk, after warming himself in the first watch, would enter his room just as the meditating monk finished his walking meditation and entered his own room. The lazy monk would then say, "You lazy monk, you entered the forest just to lie down and sleep. How is this? Having taken meditation subjects from the Buddha, is it not proper to rise up with effort and strive in monastic practice?" After saying this, he would enter his own dwelling, lie down, and sleep.

The energetic monk, however, would practice walking meditation in the first watch, rest in the middle watch, and rise early in the last watch to strive in monastic practice. As he dwelt thus heedfully, he soon attained Arahatship along with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). The lazy monk spent his time only in heedlessness.
167:
## The Teaching

(29) Heedful among the heedless, wide awake among those asleep, the wise man advances like a swift horse leaving a weak one behind.

Appamatto: one who is heedful and not negligent due to having attained abundance of mindfulness, a Khīṇāsava (one whose taints are destroyed). Pamattesu: among beings who remain in the abandonment of mindfulness. Suttesu: among those who sleep soundly in all postures due to the absence of wakeful mindfulness. Bahujāgaro: one who remains in the wakefulness of great abundance of mindfulness. Sīghasso: like a noble Sindh horse of great speed that flies through the sky. Abalassaṃ: like a weak, slow horse with blunt hooves and exhausted strength. Hitvā: leaving it behind in the thickets. Yāti iva: just as it reaches the city. Sumedhaso: the wise one endowed with excellent wisdom. Taṃ: that negligent, weak, and foolish person. Hitvā: leaving them behind in the round of rebirth (saṃsāra). Yāti: goes forth, breaking through the cycle to reach Nibbāna.

Those two monks, having completed the rains retreat, went to the Buddha, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. After exchanging pleasantries, the Buddha asked, "Dear monks, did you practice the monastic Dhamma diligently? Has your monastic task reached its conclusion?" The monk who had been negligent first replied, "Venerable Sir, how could there be diligence for this monk? From the time he left Your presence, he spent his time lying down and sleeping." Then the Buddha asked the other, "Dear monk, how did you live?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, I spent my time carrying firewood, preparing the brazier, and sitting by the fire throughout the first watch of the night without sleeping."

Then the Buddha said to the monk who warmed himself by the fire, "You spent your time being greatly negligent in meditation, yet you claim to be diligent. You treat the heedless as heedful and the heedful as heedless." To clarify the fault of negligence and the benefit of diligence, the Buddha said, "In the presence of my son (the other monk), you are like a lean, weak horse devoid of speed. This monk, in your presence, is like a good, strong horse of great speed," and He spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the verse, many attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The story of the two friends, the negligent monk and the diligent monk, ends.

## 7. The Story of Magha the Youth
(Maghavatthu)

While residing at the Gabled Hall (Kūṭāgārasālā) near Vesālī, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, starting with "Appamādena maghavā," concerning Sakka, the King of Devas.

## Teaching the Story of Sakka to Mahāli the Licchavī Prince

A Licchavī prince named Mahāli lived in Vesālī. Having heard the Blessed One's teaching of the Sakkapañha Sutta, he thought, "The Fully Enlightened One spoke of Sakka's great prosperity. Did He speak having seen it, or without seeing it? Does He know Sakka or not? I will ask Him." Then Mahāli the Licchavī approached the Blessed One, paid respectful homage, and sat in a suitable place. Sitting there, Mahāli the Licchavī said this to the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, has the Blessed One seen Sakka, the King of Devas?" When he asked this, the Buddha replied, "Mahāli, I have seen Sakka, the King of Devas." "Venerable Sir, that Sakka you saw must be a counterfeit, for Sakka, the King of Devas, is difficult to see." "Mahāli, I know Sakka, and I also know the qualities that make one Sakka, by the undertaking of which Sakka attained the status of Sakka."
168:
"I know those qualities, by the undertaking of which Sakka attained the status of Sakka. I know that too."

"Prince Mahāli, Sakka, the King of Devas, in a former birth when he was a human, was a youth named Magha; therefore, he is called Maghavā. Prince Mahāli, Sakka, the King of Devas, in the past when he was a human, gave gifts first; therefore, he is called Purindada. Prince Mahāli, Sakka, the King of Devas, in the past when he was a human, gave gifts respectfully; therefore, he is called Sakka. Prince Mahāli, Sakka, the King of Devas, in the past when he was a human, gave a rest house; therefore, he is called Vāsava. Prince Mahāli, Sakka, the King of Devas, can think of a thousand matters in a moment; therefore, he is called Sahassanetta. Prince Mahāli, Sakka, the King of Devas, has an Asura maiden named Sujātā as his chief consort; therefore, he is called Sujampati. Prince Mahāli, Sakka, the King of Devas, exercises sovereignty and lordship over the Tāvatiṃsa devas; therefore, he is called Devānaminda. Prince Mahāli, Sakka, the King of Devas, when he was a human in a former birth, undertook seven vows (vatapada) completely; by the undertaking of these seven vows, he attained the status of Sakka."

## The Seven Vows to Become Sakka

What are those seven vows?

1. As long as I live, may I be one who supports my parents.
2. As long as I live, may I be one who respects the elders in the family, such as senior relatives (aunts, uncles, grandparents, etc.).
3. As long as I live, may I be one who speaks gentle and polite words.
4. As long as I live, may I not speak divisive words that cause discord between two parties, like a saw cutting through.
5. As long as I live, may I live at home with a heart free from the stain of stinginess.
6. May I be one who is liberal in giving, with open hands, delighting in relinquishment, being approachable for requests, and delighting in sharing gifts with travelers, the lonely, and the helpless; may I delight in sharing even from the food set before me.
7. As long as I live, may I be one who is truthful and upright in speech. May I be without anger; if anger should arise, may I reflect and dispel it quickly.

"Prince Mahāli, in this way, Sakka, the King of Devas, when he was a human in a former birth, undertook these seven vows completely. By the undertaking of these seven vows, he attained the status of Sakka," the Buddha taught.

"Prince named Mahāli, these seven vows are the deeds performed by Sakka when he was the youth Magha." When the Buddha said this, Prince Mahāli, wishing to hear the conduct of the youth Magha in detail, asked, "Venerable Sir, how did the youth Magha practice?" The Buddha said, "If that is so, listen," and He brought forth the story of the past.
169:
Supporting mother and father, respecting the elders in the family,
Speaking gentle and friendly words, abandoning slander.
Engaged in subduing stinginess, truthful, and a man who conquers anger—
Him, indeed, the Tāvatiṃsa gods call a 'Superior Man' (Sappurisa).

*Mātāpettibharaṃ*: one who supports and cares for mother and father. *Kule*: in the family. *Jeṭṭhāpacāyinaṃ*: one who is habituated to paying respect to the elders, such as grandfathers and grandmothers. *Saṇhaṃ sakhilasambhāsaṃ*: one who is habituated to speaking soft, smooth, and pleasant words. *Pesuṇeyyappahāyinaṃ*: one who is habituated to abandoning and cutting off backbiting or slanderous speech. *Maccheravinaye*: in the removal of stinginess. *Yuttaṃ*: engaged. *Saccaṃ*: one who is habituated to speaking the truth. *Kodhābhibhuṃ*: one who suppresses and destroys anger. *Jantūṃ*: a being. *Taṃ naraṃ*: that person who is endowed with such practices. *Ve*: indeed. *Devā Tāvatiṃsā*: the Tāvatiṃsa gods. *Sappuriso iti*: as a 'Superior Man'. *Āhu*: they call.

## The Future Sakka, Magha the Youth, Repairing the Road

In the past, in the village of Macala in the kingdom of Magadha, a youth named Magha went to the place where the villagers performed their work. He cleared the dust with his feet at the spot where he stood, making it pleasant and delightful, and remained there. Another person pushed Magha aside with his arm, removed him from that spot, and stood there himself. Magha, without getting angry at him, made another spot pleasant and delightful and stood there. Another person came and pushed him from that spot as well, removing him with his arm and standing there himself. Magha, without getting angry at that person either, made another spot pleasant and delightful and stood there. In this manner, every man who came out of his house pushed Magha with his arm and removed him from the spot where he stood. 

Magha thought, 'All these people have become happy because of me; this meritorious deed of mine, which gives happiness, must be a source of merit.' On the following day, he took a hoe and cleared a space about the size of a threshing floor to make it pleasant and delightful. All the people went and stood there just as before.

Then, Magha provided fire for them during the cold season and water during the summer. Later, he thought, 'A pleasant and delightful place is indeed loved by all; there is no one who does not love it. From this day forward, it is proper for me to go about leveling the road.' He went out early in the morning, leveled the road, and went about cutting and removing tree branches that needed to be cleared. Then, another person saw him and asked, 'Friend, what are you doing?' He replied, 'Friend, I am preparing the path that leads to the celestial realm.' The other said, 'If that is so, let me also be your companion.' Magha said, 'Friend, be my companion; a road indeed increases the joy of many people and brings much happiness.' From that time on...
170:
...there were two men. Seeing those two men, and having asked and heard in the same manner, another person also became their companion. In this way, one by one, they became thirty-three men. All of them, with hoes, crowbars, and so on in their hands, went about leveling the road, reaching places as far as one or two leagues (yojanas).

When the village headman saw those thirty-three men, he thought, 'These people are engaged in an improper task. If all of them were to bring fish, meat, and so on from the forest, or if they were to brew and drink liquor, or perform other such tasks, I too would receive something.' After thinking thus, he summoned them and asked, 'What work are you doing as you go about?' They replied, 'Lord Headman, we are making the path to the celestial realm.' He said, 'For those living in the household life, it is not proper to act in this way. It is proper to bring fish, meat, and so on from the forest, to brew and drink liquor, and to perform various other tasks.' Those men rejected the headman's words. Even though the headman spoke in this way repeatedly, they continued to reject him.

## The Village Headman Seeking Fault, Resulting in the Punishment of Being Trampled by an Elephant, and Eventually Receiving the Elephant

The headman became angry and thought, 'I will destroy these people.' He went to the King and reported, 'Great King, I see thieves wandering about in a group.' When the King said, 'Go, arrest those men and bring them here,' the headman arrested all of them as the King had said and presented them to the King. The King, without investigating or reflecting, gave the royal command, 'Have them trampled to death by an elephant.'

Magha gave advice to the others, saying, 'Friends, apart from the mind of loving-kindness (mettā), we have no other refuge. Do not be angry with anyone; maintain a mind of loving-kindness equally toward the King, the village headman, the elephant that will trample us, and yourselves.' They did as Magha had told them. Then, due to the power of the loving-kindness of those thirty-three men, the elephant did not dare to even approach them. When the King heard about this, he thought, 'Seeing many people, the elephant must not dare to approach to trample them. Go, cover those men with mats and have them trampled.' When they were sent again to be trampled while covered with mats, the elephant only moved further away.
171:
The King, hearing of the matter, thought, "There must be a special reason for this," and had the men summoned. He questioned them, "Lads, what is it that you do not have, while depending on me?" When they asked, "Great King, what is the meaning of your question?", he replied, "Are you not roaming about in groups committing robbery in the region?" They asked, "Great King, who told you this?" and he replied, "Your village headman reported it."

Then the thirty-three men said, "Great King, we are not thieves. We are clearing the path to the celestial realm and performing such and such meritorious deeds. The village headman urged us to engage in unwholesome acts, and when we did not follow his words, he became angry and, wishing to destroy us, deceived you, Great King, with this report."

"Lads, even this elephant, though an animal, knows your virtues. I, however, being a human, was unable to recognize your goodness. Forgive me for my fault." Having spoken these words of apology, the King gave the village headman, along with his wife and children, to those thirty-three men to serve as their slaves. He also gave them the elephant for their riding and granted them the village to enjoy as they pleased. Those men thought, "We have seen the results of our meritorious deeds even in this present life," and with hearts filled with exceeding faith, they took turns riding the elephant and consulted with one another.

## Reluctance to Give Women a Share in the Merit of Building the Rest-house

"Now we should perform even greater merit. What shall we do?" they asked. They decided, "Let us build a rest-house for the many people at the four-way crossroads." They summoned a carpenter and had the rest-house built. Because they had little desire or affection for women, they did not give the women a share in the merit of the rest-house. In the house of the youth Magha, there were four women: Sunandā, Sucittā, Sudhammā, and Sujātā. Among those four, the woman named Sudhammā consulted with the head carpenter and gave him a bribe, saying, "Brother, please make me the chief person in this rest-house."

The carpenter agreed, saying, "Very well." He first dried the wood for the pinnacle (kaṇṇika), then planed and carved it, completing the pinnacle beforehand. He carved the inscription, "This rest-house is named Sudhammā," wrapped it in cloth, and set it aside.

When the rest-house was nearly finished and the day to install the pinnacle arrived, the carpenter said, "O masters, we have forgotten one thing that needs to be done." They asked, "Friend builder, what is it?" He replied, "The pinnacle." They said, "If that is so, let us go and get one." He replied, "It cannot be made now from freshly cut wood. It is necessary to obtain a pinnacle that has been cut, planed, and carved beforehand." They asked, "What can be done now?" He said, "If there is a pinnacle for sale that has been completed and kept in someone's house, that pinnacle should be sought and purchased at a fair price."
172:
When they searched, they found one in Sudhammā's house, but even though they offered a thousand pieces of money, they could not obtain it for a price. She said, "If you give me a share of the merit for the rest-house, I will donate it." They replied, "We cannot give a share to women."

## Sudhammā Obtains a Share of Merit Through Her Intelligence

Then the carpenter said to them, "Masters, what are you saying? Except for the Brahma world, there is no place devoid of women. Take the pinnacle. Only then will our work be completed." They said, "Very well," took the pinnacle, and finished the rest-house. They divided it into three sections: one section for the nobles, one for the poor, and one for the sick. The thirty-three men laid out thirty-three planks for sitting and gave a signal to the elephant: "When a traveler arrives and sits on a plank laid out by someone, take that guest to the house of the owner of that plank. All services such as massaging the feet and back, providing drinking water, food, and a place to sleep shall be the responsibility of the owner of that plank."

The elephant would take every arriving guest to the house of the owner of the plank. That owner would then perform the necessary duties for the guest on that day. The youth Magha planted a Koviḷāra tree not far from the rest-house and laid a stone slab at its base. People entering the rest-house would look up at the pinnacle, read the inscription, and say, "This rest-house is named Sudhammā." The names of the thirty-three men were not prominent.

## The Meritorious Deeds of Sunandā and Sucittā and the Attitude of Sujātā

The woman named Sunandā thought, "These men, while building the rest-house, did not allow us to share in the merit. But Sudhammā, through her cleverness, has gained a share. I, too, should do something." Thinking, "What should I do?" the idea occurred to her: "It is proper for those who come to the rest-house to have water for drinking and bathing. I will have a pond dug." So she had a pond dug.

The woman named Sucittā thought, "Sudhammā gave the pinnacle, and Sunandā had a pond dug. I, too, should do something. What shall I do?" Then the idea occurred to her: "When people who come to the rest-house leave after drinking and bathing, it is fitting for them to go wearing flowers. I will have a flower garden planted." So Sucittā had a delightful flower garden planted. In that garden, there was hardly any kind of flowering or fruit-bearing tree that was missing; it had all varieties.

Sujātā, however, thought, "I am Magha's cousin and also his devoted wife. The merit performed by Magha is my merit as well."
173:
Thinking, "Whatever merit I perform is just the merit of Magha the youth," she did not perform any wholesome deeds but spent her time merely adorning herself.

## Magha the Youth and Others Being Reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa Heaven and Attaining the Sovereignty of Sakka

Magha the youth lived fulfilling the seven vows: 1. Supporting his parents, 2. Respecting the elders of the family, 3. Speaking the truth, 4. Not speaking harsh words, 5. Not slandering, 6. Not being stingy, and 7. Not giving way to anger. Having attained the state of a "good man" (sappurisa) who is thus praised with the words "Mātāpattibharaṃ... etc.," at the end of his life, he was reborn as Sakka, the King of Devas, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. His thirty-three friends were also reborn in that same Tāvatiṃsa heaven. The carpenter was reborn as the celestial son Vissakamma. At that time, the Asuras lived in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Seeing that "new celestial sons have been born," they prepared a celestial drink. Sakka gave a sign to his followers so that not a single one of them would drink it. The Asuras drank and became intoxicated and heedless. Sakka, thinking, "What is the use of a kingdom shared with these people?" gave a sign to his followers, had the Asuras seized by their feet, and cast them into the great ocean.

Those Asuras fell head-first into the ocean. Then, by the power of their merit, the Asura realm appeared at the base of Mount Sineru, and the Cittapāṭali tree appeared. When the Asuras were defeated in the war between the Devas and Asuras, the celestial city of Tāvatiṃsa, ten thousand yojanas in extent, appeared. The distance between the eastern and western gates of that city was ten thousand yojanas, and likewise between the southern and northern gates. That city was endowed with a thousand gates and adorned with parks and lotus ponds. In the center of the city, as a result of the merit of building the hall, the Vejayanta palace arose, seven hundred yojanas high, adorned with banners three hundred yojanas high. There were gem-encrusted banners on golden poles, golden banners on gem-encrusted poles, pearl banners on coral poles, coral banners on pearl poles, and banners made of the seven kinds of jewels on poles made of the seven kinds of jewels. The banner standing in the middle was three hundred yojanas high. Thus, as a result of the merit of building the hall together with the banners, the Vejayanta palace, one thousand yojanas high and made of the seven kinds of jewels, appeared.

Due to the merit of planting the Koviḷāra tree, the Pāricchattaka tree appeared, with a circumference of three hundred yojanas. Due to the merit of laying a stone slab at the foot of the tree, the Paṇḍukambala stone seat appeared near the Pāricchattaka tree, sixty yojanas long, fifty yojanas wide, and fifteen yojanas thick, with a bright red color like the Jayasumana flower or a red woolen blanket. When Sakka sits on it, half his body sinks in, and when he stands up, it becomes full as before.

## About the Elephant Erāvaṇa

The elephant was reborn as a celestial son named Erāvaṇa. In the celestial realm, there are no animals. Therefore, when he goes out for garden sports, he leaves his celestial form and becomes the elephant named Erāvaṇa, one hundred and fifty yojanas in size. For the purpose of carrying the thirty-three individuals, he created thirty-three heads, each measuring three gāvutas or half a yojana.
174:
In the center of all the heads, he created a head named Sudassana, thirty yojanas in size, for Sakka to sit upon. Above that head, there was a jeweled pavilion twelve yojanas in size. Within that pavilion, banners made of the seven kinds of jewels, one yojana high, arose at intervals. At the edges, networks of golden bells were suspended. When stirred by a gentle breeze, the sound of those golden bells issued forth like celestial songs mixed with the sound of the five-fold musical instruments. In the center of the pavilion, a gem-encrusted throne one yojana in size was prepared for Sakka's enjoyment. Sakka sat upon that gem-encrusted throne. The thirty-three celestial sons sat on jeweled thrones on their respective heads. On each of the thirty-three heads, he created seven tusks. Each of those seven tusks was fifty yojanas in length. On each tusk, there were seven lotus ponds; in each pond, seven clusters of lotuses; in each cluster, seven lotus flowers; in each flower, seven petals; and on each petal, seven celestial maidens danced. Thus, all around, in the area of fifty yojanas on the elephant's tusks alone, there were dance performances. In this way, Sakka, the King of Devas, traveled about enjoying great glory and prosperity.

## The Rebirth of the Meritorious Women in the Celestial Realm

## How the Woman Who Adorned Herself Became a Heron

The woman named Sudhammā, upon her death, was reborn in that same Tāvatiṃsa heaven. For her, the celestial assembly hall named Sudhammā, nine hundred yojanas in size, appeared. There is no other place more delightful than that assembly hall. Eight days every month, the hearing of the Dhamma takes place in that very Sudhammā hall. Even to this day, when people see a delightful place, they say, "It is like the Sudhammā celestial assembly hall."

The woman named Nandā also passed away from the human world and was reborn in that same Tāvatiṃsa heaven. For her, the lotus pond named Nandā, five hundred yojanas wide, appeared.

The woman named Cittā also died and was reborn in that same Tāvatiṃsa heaven. For her, the garden named Cittalatā, five hundred yojanas in size, appeared. In that garden, they lead and delight the celestial sons who have experienced unpleasant omens (pubbanimitta).

As for the woman named Sujātā, after she passed away, she was reborn as a small female heron in a mountain cleft. When Sakka looked for his former attendants, thinking, "Sudhammā, Nandā, and Cittā have been reborn here in this Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Where has Sujātā been reborn?" he saw her reborn as a small female heron in a mountain cleft. He thought, "The foolish woman, because she did not perform any merit, has now been reborn in the animal kingdom as a heron."
175:
"It has come to this; it is now proper to encourage this female heron to perform meritorious deeds and lead her to this Tāvatiṃsa heaven." Having thought thus, Sakka discarded his own form and, in the guise of an inconspicuous poor man, went to the small female heron and asked, "What are you doing, wandering and foraging in this mountain river?" When she asked, "Who are you, lord?", he replied, "I am the youth Magha, who was your husband while living in Macala village." When she asked again, "My lord, where have you been reborn?", he replied, "I have been reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Do you know the place where your companions, the women, have been reborn?" When she said, "Lord, I do not know," he asked, "Those women have also been reborn near me. Do you wish to see those companions?"

## Taking the Heron Sujātā to the Celestial Realm to Show Her
When she said, "Lord, how shall I be able to go to that Tāvatiṃsa heaven?", Sakka said, "I shall take you," and having the small heron perch on the palm of his hand, he took her to the celestial realm. Having released her on the bank of the pond named Nandā, he asked the three celestial queens, "Do you wish to see your companion Sujātā?" When they asked in return, "Great Lord, where is Sujātā?", he told them, "She is on the bank of the Nandā pond." Those three celestial queens also went out and mocked her, saying, "The form of Lady Sujātā is indeed wonderful! Oh, how marvelous is the fruit of adorning one's body beautifully! Now, look at the little beak of that Lady Sujātā; look at her feet; look at her little shanks. The state of Lady Sujātā's entirely white body is indeed beautiful!" and after making fun of her, they departed.

Again, Sakka went to the heron and asked, "Did you see your companions?" When she said, "I have seen them; they went away after mocking and making fun of me. Please send me back only to that ravine which is my home," he took her back to that ravine. Having released her in the water, he asked, "Have you not seen the prosperity and happiness of those who were your companions?" When she said, "Great Sakka, I have seen it," he said, "You too should perform meritorious deeds, the cause for being reborn in that place." When she asked, "Great Sakka, what should I do?", he asked, "Will you observe the advice and exhortation given by me?" When she accepted the responsibility, saying, "I will observe it," he gave her the Five Precepts and, after exhorting her, "Observe them diligently," he departed.

## How the Heron Sujātā Became a Potter's Daughter Due to the Five Precepts and Sakka's Assistance
From that time on, that small female heron sought and ate only fish that had died naturally. After two or three days had passed, Sakka went to test the heron and, creating the form of a dead fish as if it had died on a sandbank, lay there. When the heron saw it, she picked it up with the perception that it was a dead fish. Just as she was about to swallow, the fish moved its tail. The heron released it into the water, thinking, "It is a living fish." Then, after some time had passed, he lay on his back again in front of the heron. The heron picked it up again with the perception that it was a dead fish, and while she was swallowing, he moved the tip of his tail. Seeing that movement, the heron released it again, thinking, "It is a live fish." In this way, having tested her three times and knowing, "She observes the precepts well," Sakka made himself known and said, "I have come to test your virtue. You observe the precepts well, without breaking or spotting them. If you observe them in this way, you will before long be reborn near me. Do not be negligent," and after giving her firm instructions, he departed.

From that time on, there were times when that heron found fish that had died naturally, and there were times when she did not. When she did not find any, after two or three days had passed...
176:
Having passed away when her flesh and blood dried up, by the power and majesty of those five precepts, she was reborn in the city of Bārāṇasī as the daughter of a potter. When the potter's daughter reached the age of fifteen or sixteen, Sakka, the King of Devas, reflected, 'Where has the crane who was Sujātā been reborn?' Seeing her, he thought, 'Now it is time for me to go to the place of that potter's daughter.' He filled a cart with the seven kinds of jewels appearing in the form and size of melons and, driving it, entered the city of Bārāṇasī. He went along the main street crying out, 'O mothers and fathers, buy my melons! Buy my melons!' When people came bringing mung beans, black grams, and so forth, he said, 'I do not sell them for a price.' When asked, 'On what condition will you give them?' he replied, 'I will give them to a woman who observes the precepts (sīla).'

'Lord, what is this thing called sīla? Is it black, or is it blue or some other color?' they asked. He replied, 'You do not even know what sīla is like; how then could you observe it? I will give them only to one who observes the precepts.'

'Lord, this potter's daughter goes about saying, "I observe the precepts." Give them to this maiden.' She also said, 'If that is so, lord, give them to me.' When he asked, 'What kind of person are you?' she replied, 'I am one who possesses the precepts that are never abandoned.' He said, 'It is for your sake alone that I have brought these things.' He drove the cart to her house and, making it so that others could not take them, he gave her the divine wealth in the form of melons. Revealing his identity, he advised her, 'All this is the wealth given for your livelihood. Keep the five precepts unbroken, without holes, untarnished, and unspotted,' and then he departed.

## The Asura Daughter's Garland Ceremony and Sakka's Boldness

That potter's daughter, having passed away from that existence, was reborn in the realm of the Asuras as the daughter of the Asura King, in the house of Sakka's enemy. Because she had carefully guarded her virtue in her lives as a small crane and as a potter's daughter, she was exceedingly beautiful, with a golden complexion and a physical splendor unsurpassed by others. Vepacitti, the King of the Asuras, told every Asura who came, 'You are not worthy of my daughter.' He did not give her to anyone, saying, 'My daughter shall choose a husband worthy of her by herself.' He assembled the host of Asura ministers and others, and gave a garland into his daughter's hand, saying, 'Choose a husband who is worthy of you, whomever you like.'

At that moment, Sakka looked for Sujātā's place of rebirth and, learning of the situation, thought, 'Now it is time for me to go and fetch Sujātā.' He disguised himself as an old Asura and went to stand at the edge of the assembly. As Sujātā looked here and there, through the power of love that had been nurtured by living together in previous lives, her heart was overwhelmed as if by a swift river current. Thinking, 'This is my beloved husband,' she placed the garland over the head of that old Asura. The Asuras were disgruntled and felt shamed, saying, 'Our King could not find anyone worthy of his daughter for all this time, and only now has he found one! Oh, how could this man, older than her grandfather, be worthy of our King's young daughter?' and they departed.
177:
## Sakka Carrying Away Sujātā

The old man took the hand of the Asura King's daughter, Sujātā, and shouting joyfully, 'I am Sakka, the ruler of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven!' he soared into the sky. The Asuras, feeling resentful that 'the old Sakka has deceived us,' pursued him. Mātali the charioteer, his helper and companion, had brought the Vejayanta chariot and was waiting midway. Sakka placed the celestial maiden Sujātā on the Vejayanta chariot and headed toward the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. As they reached the Silk-cotton forest (Simbalivana), young Garuḍas, terrified by the sound of the chariot, began to cry out. Hearing their cries, Sakka asked Mātali, 'Who are these that are crying?' 'Lord Sakka, they are young Garuḍas,' he replied. 'Why are they crying?' 'Hearing the sound of the chariot, they cry out for fear of death.'

'Let not this multitude of beings be crushed and destroyed by the speed of the chariot for my sake alone. Turn the chariot back!' Sakka commanded. Mātali gave the signal with the goad to the thousand Sindhu horses and turned the chariot back. Seeing the chariot turning back, the Asuras thought, 'The old Sakka has been fleeing since leaving the Asura city, but now he turns his chariot back. Surely he must have obtained reinforcements and companions.' Not daring to pursue further, they retreated and entered the Asura city by the same way they came, and never dared to raise their heads again.

## Sujātā Becoming the Celestial Queen

Sakka brought the Asura maiden Sujātā to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and appointed her as the chief over twenty-five million celestial nymphs. Sujātā then asked a boon of Sakka: 'Great King, in this Tāvatiṃsa heaven, I have no parents, no brothers, and no sisters. Wherever you go, I wish for you to take me with you.' Sakka consented, saying, 'Very well,' and gave her his promise.

From that time on, whenever the Trumpet-flower trees (Cittapāṭalī) bloom, the Asuras say, 'It is the time when the celestial Coral trees (Pāricchattaka) bloom in our former realm,' and they ascend to the heavens to wage war. Sakka stationed Nāgas as guards beneath the ocean. After them, Garuḍas; after them, Kumbhaṇḍas; after them, Yakkhas; and after them, the Four Great Kings. Above all, to prevent calamities, he placed statues of Indra holding the thunderbolt (vajira) near the gates of the Tāvatiṃsa city. Even if the Asuras came after defeating the Nāgas and others, upon seeing the statues of Indra from afar, they would flee, thinking, 'Sakka has come out!'

'Mahāli the Licchavi prince, in this way, the youth named Magha practiced the path of heedfulness (appamāda). Because he was thus heedful in performing meritorious deeds, he attained such sovereignty as Sakka and ruled over the two celestial realms. This quality of heedfulness is praised by the Buddhas and other virtuous ones.'
178:
“By relying on heedfulness, one can attain all mundane and supramundane special qualities,” the Buddha said, and then he spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(30) By heedfulness, Maghavā attained the leadership of the gods. 
They praise heedfulness; heedlessness is always blamed.

Maghavā: The youth named Magha, who is now well-known as Maghavā. 
By heedfulness: Because of his non-negligence in performing meritorious deeds. 
Leadership of the gods: He reached the state of being the highest and greatest among the gods of the Cātumahārājika and Tāvatiṃsa realms. 
They praise heedfulness: Wise ones, such as the Buddha, praise and extol the virtue of heedfulness. 
Heedlessness is always blamed: Negligence in performing meritorious deeds is always censured and rebuked by the Noble Ones.

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the verse, the Licchavī prince Mahāli was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Many in the assembled audience also became Stream-enters and attained other fruits.

The story of Magha the youth ends.

## 8. The Story of an Unknown Monk
(Aññatarabhikkhu-vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha spoke this legal teaching, beginning with “Appamādarato bhikkhu,” concerning a certain unknown monk.

## Contemplating the Forest Fire as the Knowledge of the Path
That monk, having received meditation instructions from the Buddha until the attainment of Arahantship, entered the forest. Although he strove and exerted effort repeatedly, he was not yet able to reach Arahantship. Thinking, “I will have the meditation instructions explained to me more specifically,” he left the forest. While returning to the Buddha, he saw a great forest fire breaking out along the way. He quickly climbed to the top of a bare mountain peak where no grass or trees grew and, while sitting there, watched the fire burning the forest and took the flame as his object of meditation. 

(His way of taking the object was:) “Just as this fire goes along burning up large and small fuel without remainder, so too shall the fire of the Knowledge of the Noble Path (Ariyamagga-ñāṇa) go along burning up various large and small fetters (saṃyojana).”

The Blessed One, while staying in the Gandhakuṭi, knew the progression of the monk’s mind and said, “Dear monk, such reflection is indeed true. Just like the large and small fuel of wood and timber, there are small and large fetters arising within the bodies of these beings.”
179:
“One should burn those fetters with the fire of the Knowledge of the Noble Path so that they are incapable of arising again.” Having said this, the Buddha emitted a ray of light and, appearing as if he were sitting right in front of the monk, spoke this verse of light:

## The Teaching
(31) A monk who delights in heedfulness and sees danger in heedlessness 
moves along like fire, burning up fetters, both small and large.

Delighting in heedfulness: Having great delight in the practice of heedfulness; meaning one spends their time in heedfulness. 
Sees danger in heedlessness: One who habitually sees danger in negligence, such as rebirth in hell, or sees heedlessness as a danger because it is the root of such rebirths. 
Monk: The practitioner. 
Like fire burning fuel: Just as this forest fire goes along burning large and small fuel. 
Small and large: Both minor and major. 
Fetters: The ten kinds of fetters capable of sinking beings into the round of rebirth, which is the bond that ties one to the suffering of Saṃsāra. 
Moves along burning: He goes along burning those fetters completely without remainder by means of the fire of knowledge attained through heedfulness, making them incapable of arising again.

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the verse, that monk, while sitting in his original position, burned away all fetters and attained Arahantship together with the four Analytical Insights (Paṭisambhidā). He then came through the air to where the Buddha was, praised and marveled at the Blessed One, whose body had the color of pure Jambonada gold, paid homage, and then departed.

The story of the unknown monk ends.

## 9. The Story of Elder Nigāmavāsī Tissa
(Nigāmavāsītissatthera-vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha spoke this legal teaching, beginning with “Appamādarato,” concerning the Elder Nigāmavāsī Tissa (Tissa who lived in a market town).

## The Buddha Praising the Contented Monk
A certain young man of good family, born and raised in a market town not far from Sāvatthī, went forth in the Buddha’s Dispensation. After receiving full ordination, he became well-known for his special qualities: “The monk named Nigāmavāsī Tissa has few wishes (appiccha), is easily contented (santuṭṭha), delights in seclusion (pavivitta), and possesses exerted energy (āraddhavīriya).” That Elder Nigāmavāsī Tissa habitually wandered for alms only in the village of his relatives. Even when Anāthapiṇḍika and others were giving great alms, or when King Pasenadi of Kosala was giving the Incomparable Almsgiving—
180:
Even when King Pasenadi of Kosala performed the Incomparable Alms-giving, he did not come to Sāvatthī. Other monks reported to the Buddha, saying, "This Elder Nigamavāsī Tissa lives in close association with his relatives, exerting great effort to remain with them. Even when Anāthapiṇḍika and others perform great alms-givings, and even when King Pasenadi of Kosala performs the Incomparable Alms-giving, he does not come." The Buddha summoned the Elder Nigamavāsī Tissa and asked, "Monk, is it true that you do this?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, I do not have close association with relatives. I obtain just enough food to survive, whether coarse or fine, by depending on these people who are my relatives. Thinking, 'When I have obtained enough food for sustenance, what is the use of seeking food again?', I do not go elsewhere. But I have no close association with relatives, Venerable Sir." The Buddha, knowing the monk's natural disposition, said, "Sādhu, Sādhu, monk," and gave him praise. He then said, "Monk, it is not surprising that you, having found a teacher like me, have few wishes. Indeed, this fewness of wishes is my own lineage and tradition." At the request of the monks, he related a story of the past:

## The Story of the Contented Parrot King

In the past, in a fig grove on the banks of the Ganges in the Himālaya forest, many thousands of parrots lived. Among them, a certain parrot king, even when the fruits of his dwelling tree were exhausted, would eat whatever remained—shoots, leaves, or bark—and drink water from the Ganges. Being extremely contented and having few wishes, he did not go elsewhere. Due to the power of his virtue of contentment and fewness of wishes, Sakka's abode trembled. Sakka, reflecting on the cause, saw him and, to test him, made that tree dry up by his divine power. The fig tree became a mere stump, broken and full of holes, and when the wind blew, it made a sound as if it were being struck. Dust came out from its holes. The parrot king ate that dust, drank water from the Ganges, and did not go elsewhere; ignoring the wind and the heat, he sat only on the top of the fig tree stump. Sakka, knowing his extreme fewness of wishes, thought, "I will make him speak of the virtue of friendship, grant him a boon, make the fig tree bear immortal fruit, and then return." He transformed himself into a swan king, and with Sujātā, the daughter of the Asura king, preceding him, he went to the fig grove. Perching on a branch of a nearby tree, wishing to converse with the parrot king, he spoke this verse:

Santi rukkhā haripattā, dumānekaphalā bahū.
Kasmā nu sukkhe koḷāpe, suvassa nirato mano.
181:
## The Teaching

(32) Appamādarato bhikkhu, pamāde bhayadassī vā.
Abhabbo parihānāya, nibbānasseva santike.

Appamādarato: delighting greatly in heedfulness. Pamāde: in negligence. Bhayadassī vā: habitually seeing danger. Bhikkhu: the monk.
Parihānāya: from falling away from tranquillity, insight, the Path, and the Fruit. Abhabbo: is incapable. Aññadatthu: indeed. Nibbānasseva: with Nibbāna alone. Santike: is close.

Suvarāja: O Parrot King. Haripattā: having green leaves. Rukkhā: trees. Anekaphalā: having many fruits. Bahū: many. Dumā: trees. Santi: there are. Kasmā nu: why indeed. Koḷāpe: in the mere stump. Sukkhe: in the dry fig tree. Suvassa: of the parrot. Mano: the mind. Nirato: delights.

The Buddha related this Dhamma teaching and said, "At that time, Sakka was Ānanda, and the parrot king was I myself." He continued, "Monks, this fewness of wishes is my own lineage and tradition. It is not surprising that my son Nigamavāsī Tissa, having found a teacher like me, has few wishes. A monk should indeed have few wishes like the monk Nigamavāsī Tissa. Such a monk is incapable of falling away from the states of tranquillity and insight, or from the Path and Fruit; indeed, he is close to Nibbāna." Then he spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
