At the end of the verse, the Elder Nigamavāsī Tissa attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights. Many others also became Stream-enterers and so forth. The Dhamma teaching became beneficial to the great multitude.

The story of the Elder Nigamavāsī Tissa ends.
The Chapter on Heedfulness ends.
182:
## The Teaching
(33) The mind is wavering and unsteady, difficult to guard and difficult to restrain. The wise person makes it straight, just as a fletcher straightens an arrow.
(34) Like a fish taken from its watery home and thrown onto dry land, this mind quivers all over to escape the realm of Mara.

*Phandanaṃ*: wavering or trembling among the five objects of sensual pleasure. *Capalaṃ*: fickle or unsteady, not staying on a single object, like a village child who cannot stay still in one posture. *Cittaṃ*: the mind or consciousness; it is called 'citta' because of its variety in terms of planes, bases, objects, and activities. *Dūrakkhaṃ*: difficult to guard, like a crop-eating ox in a narrow place, because it is difficult to keep it fixed only on a suitable object. *Dunnivārayaṃ*: difficult to restrain, because it is hard to prevent it from going toward disagreeable objects. *Cittaṃ*: the mind. *Medhāvī*: the wise person. *Ujuṃ*: straight. *Karoti*: makes. *Yathā*: For example, how? *Usukāro*: A fletcher. *Tejanaṃ*: an arrow. *Ujuṃ karoti iva*: just as he makes it straight.

*Okamokato*: from its home in the water. *Ubbhato*: being taken out. *Thale*: on dry land. *Khitto*: thrown. *Vārijo*: a fish that frequents the water. *Paripphandati iva*: just as it quivers and leaps about. *Tathā*: similarly. *Idaṃ cittaṃ*: this mind, which greatly delights in its dwelling place of the five sensual pleasures. Or, the mind (tato: from those sensual pleasures; uddharitvā: having been pulled out). *Māradheyyaṃ*: the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa), which is the realm of the Mara of defilements. *Pahātave*: in order to abandon it. *Kammaṭṭhāne*: in meditation. *Khittaṃ*: when it is placed. *Paripphandati*: it quivers and trembles repeatedly.

## 3. Citta Vagga (The Mind)
## 1. The Story of Venerable Meghiya
(Meghiyattheravatthu)
While residing on Cālikā Mountain, the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Phandanaṃ capalaṃ cittaṃ" concerning Venerable Meghiya.

## Teaching the Thoughtful Meghiya Not to Follow the Mind's Desires
(To clarify the story of Venerable Meghiya, the entire Meghiya Sutta should be expanded.)
Because he was constantly oppressed by three kinds of unwholesome thoughts and was unable to practice meditation in that mango grove, Venerable Meghiya returned. The Buddha called him and said, "Meghiya, what you have done is a very heavy matter."
183:
"Meghiya, I was alone. While another attendant monk had not yet arrived or appeared, you abandoned Me, who was pleading with you to wait just until another monk arrived, and you went off alone. A monk should not be one who follows the whims of the mind in this way. This mind is swift in its movements. It is only proper to bring the mind under one's own control." Having said this, He uttered these two verses.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the verses, Venerable Meghiya was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Many others in the assembly also became Stream-enterers and attained other fruits.

The story of Venerable Meghiya ends.

## 2. The Story of a Certain Monk
(Aññatarabhikkhuvatthu)
While residing at Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Dunniggahassa lahuno" concerning a certain monk.
184:
## The Laywoman Mātikamātā and the Sixty Monks
In the kingdom of King Kosala, at the foot of a mountain, there was a densely populated and prosperous village called Mātikā. One day, about sixty monks, having requested meditation subjects from the Teacher that would lead to Arahatship, went to that village and entered for alms. The owner of that village was named Mātikā. His mother, seeing the monks, invited them to sit in her house and served them with various delicious gruels and foods. She asked, "Venerable sirs, where do you wish to go?"

When they replied, "Great lay devotee, we will go to various places where we can stay comfortably," the mother of the village headman realized, "The noble ones must be looking for a place for the rainy season retreat (Vassa)." She prostrated at their feet and said, "Noble sirs, if you will stay here for these three months of the rainy season, I will take the three refuges and the five precepts and observe the Uposatha duties."

The noble monks accepted, thinking, "Depending on this lay devotee, we shall be able to strive to escape the round of rebirth without worrying about alms food." The laywoman prepared and offered a monastery as a dwelling place for them.

While staying there, they assembled one day and exhorted one another: "Friends, it is not proper for us to live heedlessly. For us, the eight great hells are like our own homes with their doors wide open. We have come here after taking meditation subjects from the living Buddha. It is not possible to please the Buddhas even by following them step by step if one is deceitful; they can only be pleased by honest intention. Be heedless-free! Two monks should not stand or sit in the same place. We shall meet together only at two times: in the evening to attend to the Elder, and in the morning to go for alms. At other times, two of us shall not be together. However, if a monk becomes unwell, he should come to the center of the monastery and strike the bell. Upon hearing the signal of the bell, we will come and provide medicine for that sick monk." Having made this agreement, they lived accordingly.

## Mātikamātā Attains the Stage of Non-Returner with Analytical Insights and Supernormal Powers through the Thirty-Two Parts Meditation
While those sixty monks were living according to their covenant, one day that laywoman (Mātikamātā) took ghee, oil, molasses, and other offerings, and accompanied by male and female servants and workers, went to the monastery in the evening. Seeing not a single monk in the center of the monastery, she asked the men, "Where have the noble ones gone?"

When they replied, "Madam, the noble ones must be sitting in their respective night-quarters and day-quarters," she asked, "What must I do to see them?"
185:
At that time, those who knew the agreement of the Saṅgha said, "Lady, when the bell is struck, the noble ones will assemble." Thus, the great lay devotee had the bell struck. Hearing the sound of the bell, the monks, thinking that some monk might be unwell, left their respective places and assembled in the middle of the monastery. No two monks came by the same path; seeing them coming one by one from different places, the laywoman thought, "My sons must have had a quarrel with one another." After paying homage to the Saṅgha, she asked, "Venerable sirs, have you been quarreling?"

When they replied, "Great lay devotee, we do not quarrel," she asked again, "Venerable sirs, if there was no such quarrel among you, why is it that you did not come together as you do when coming to our house, but instead came one by one from different places?" They replied, "Great lay devotee, we were staying in individual places practicing the monastic duties (samaṇadhamma)." She then asked, "Venerable sirs, what is this called monastic duty?" They replied, "Great lay devotee, we recite the meditation on the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra) and we dwell repeatedly contemplating the rise and fall (khayavaya) within this physical body."

She asked further, "Venerable sirs, is the recitation of this thirty-two parts of the body and the contemplation of the rise and fall within this physical body proper only for you, or is it also proper for us?" They replied, "Great lay devotee, this Dhamma is not forbidden to anyone."

"If that is so, venerable sirs, please give me the meditation on the thirty-two parts of the body as well; please teach and instruct me how to contemplate the rise and fall within this physical body," she requested. They said, "In that case, great lay devotee, learn it," and they had her learn everything.

From then on, as she practiced the recitation of the thirty-two parts of the body and contemplated the rise and fall within herself, she attained the three paths and the three fruits (the stage of a Non-returner) even before those monks. Along with the attainment of the paths, the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) and the mundane supernormal powers (lokiya abhiññā) also came to her.

## How all became Arahants through the grace of Mātikamātā and went to report to the Buddha

That great lay devotee, who was established as a Non-returner, emerged from the bliss of the paths and fruits and looked with her divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). While investigating, "When will my sons attain the higher Dhamma?" she saw that all these sixty monks still had lust, hatred, and delusion, and they possessed neither jhāna nor insight (vipassanā). She further investigated, "Is there the potential (upanissaya) for the fruit of Arahantship in my sons?" Seeing that it existed, she investigated, "Is there suitable lodging (senāsana-sappāya)?" Seeing that suitable lodging existed, she investigated, "Do they have suitable persons (puggala-sappāya)?" Seeing that they had suitable persons, she investigated, "Do they have suitable food (āhāra-sappāya)?" She then saw that they did not have suitable food. From that time on, she prepared various kinds of gruel,
186:
She had various kinds of hard food and many delicious soft foods prepared in abundance. Having invited the monks to sit in her house, she poured the water of dedication and offered them, saying: "Venerable sirs, please take and consume whatever gruel, hard food, or soft food you like according to your preference."

The monks also took and consumed the gruel and other foods as they pleased. Obtaining suitable food and nourishment, the minds of those monks became concentrated. Developing insight with concentrated minds, they attained Arahantship along with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) before long. They then thought: "Oh, this great lay devotee has been our support! If we had not obtained suitable food, we would not have achieved the penetration of the paths and fruits. Now that the rains retreat is over, let us perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony and go to the Teacher."

Those sixty monks, wishing to see the Teacher, took leave of the great lay devotee. The lay devotee replied, "Very well, venerable sirs." She followed them for a distance and returned after speaking many pleasant words: "Venerable sirs, please look upon us with compassion again (visit us again)."

Those monks reached Sāvatthī, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat in a suitable place. When asked, "Monks, are you well? Are you keeping fit? Did you not suffer for lack of almsfood?" they replied, "Venerable Sir, we are well and keeping fit. We did not suffer at all for lack of almsfood. A lay devotee named Mātikamātā, knowing the thoughts and inclinations of our minds, would prepare and offer whatever food we thought of, thinking, 'It would be good if she prepared such food for us.' Thus, she prepared and offered food exactly as we thought." In this way, they spoke of her virtues.

## The Story of a Certain Monk and Mātikamātā

Then, a certain monk, hearing the talk of her virtues and wishing to go there, took a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) from the Teacher. He asked the Teacher, "Venerable Sir, I wish to go to that Mātika village." Leaving Jetavana monastery, he eventually reached the village. On the day he entered the monastery, he thought: "They say this lay devotee knows every thought. I am exhausted from the journey and cannot clean the monastery. It would be good if she sent someone who can clean the monastery."

The lay devotee, sitting in her house and reflecting, knew this matter and sent a man, saying, "Go, clean the monastery and return." The monk, wishing to drink water, thought: "It would be good if she sent some sugar-drink for me." The lay devotee sent that sugar-drink as well. The next morning, he thought: "May she send soft, smooth porridge along with side dishes early in the morning." The lay devotee did so. After drinking the porridge, he thought: "It would be good if she sent such hard food." The lay devotee sent that kind of hard food too. The monk thought: "This lay devotee has sent everything I have thought of. I wish to see her. It would be good if she came to me herself, bringing various delicious foods."

The lay devotee thought: "My son wishes to see me. He desires my coming." Taking the food, she went to the monastery and offered it to the monk.
187:
## The Teaching

(35) Duniggahassa lahuno, yatthakāmanipātino.
Cittassa damatho sādhu, cittaṃ dantaṃ sukhāvahaṃ.

*Duniggahassa*: extremely difficult to restrain. *Lahuno*: swift in arising and ceasing. *Yatthakāmanipātino*: falling upon whatever object it desires. *Cittassa*: of the mind. *Damatho*: training to be disciplined is good. *Sādhu*: is good. *Dantaṃ*: being disciplined through training. *Cittaṃ*: the mind. *Sukhāvahaṃ*: brings the three kinds of happiness: Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna.

Then, when that monk had finished his meal, he asked, "Great lay devotee, are you the one named Mātikamātā?" She replied, "Dear son, I am indeed the one named Mātikamātā." He asked again, "Great lay devotee, do you know the thoughts of others?" She replied, "Dear son, why do you ask me?" He said, "Everything I thought of, you have done. That is why I ask you." She replied, "Dear son, there are many monks who know the thoughts of others." He said, "Great lay devotee, I am not asking about others; I am asking only you." Even when asked so directly, the lay devotee did not say, "I know the thoughts of others," but instead said, "Dear son, those who know the thoughts of others act in this way."

The monk thought, "This is a heavy matter indeed. Worldlings (puthujjanas) think both suitable and unsuitable thoughts. If I should happen to think something improper, she would catch me like a thief caught with stolen goods, pulling him by his topknot, and bring me to ruin. It is better for me to flee from this monastery." He then said, "Great lay devotee, I shall go." She asked, "Venerable sir, where will you go?" He replied, "I shall go to the presence of the Teacher, great lay devotee." She pleaded, "Venerable sir, please stay in this monastery for a while longer."

He replied, "Great lay devotee, I cannot stay; I must go." Leaving the monastery, he went to the presence of the Blessed One.

Then the Teacher asked the monk, "Monk, why do you not stay there?" He replied, "Exalted Buddha, I do not dare to stay. I am unable to stay there." "Why is that, dear son?" the Buddha asked. He replied, "Exalted Buddha, that great lay devotee knows everything I think. Worldlings think both suitable and unsuitable thoughts. I thought, 'If I should accidentally think of something improper, she would bring me to ruin, like a thief caught with stolen goods being pulled by his topknot.' That is why I have returned to the presence of the Blessed One." Then the Blessed One said, "Monk, it is proper for you to stay in that very monastery." He replied, "Exalted Buddha, I cannot. I do not dare to stay there." "Monk, if that is so, can you guard just one thing?" the Buddha asked. He asked, "Exalted Buddha, what is that one thing?" The Buddha replied, "Guard only your mind. The mind is difficult to guard. Restrain your own mind; do not think of anything else. The mind is difficult to restrain." Having said this, he spoke this verse:
188:
## The Benefits of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, many among the assembled multitude became Sotāpannas and attained other fruits. The Dhamma teaching became beneficial to the great mass of people.

## A Certain Monk Attaining Arahantship and Perceiving Faults of the Lay Devotee in Past Lives
The Buddha, having given this advice to that monk, sent him away, saying, "Monk, go; without thinking of any other thing, dwell in that very monastery." The monk, having received the instruction from the Buddha, went to that monastery. He did not dare to think of any external object. The great lay devotee, looking with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), saw the elder and thought, "Now my son has returned, having found a teacher who can give him advice." Discerning this with her own knowledge, she prepared and offered suitable food and other requisites to the monk. Having partaken of the suitable food, within just two or three days, he attained the fruit of Arahantship. While spending his time in the bliss of the Path and Fruit, he thought, "How wonderful! The great lay devotee has indeed been my support. Depending on this lay devotee, I have attained liberation from the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa)." Then he investigated, "First, she has been a support in this present life. In the past, while my continuum of aggregates wandered through saṃsāra, has this lay devotee been a support in my other lives or not?" As he investigated, he recollected ninety-nine past lives. In those ninety-nine lives, she had been his wife and attendant, but because her heart was attached to others, she had deprived him of life when he was her husband. Seeing such a collection of faults in the lay devotee, the elder thought, "How amazing! This great lay devotee has performed such grave deeds."

## The Certain Monk Seeing Past Gratitude towards Mātika's Mother and Entering Nibbāna
The great lay devotee, while sitting in her house, investigated, "How is it? Has my son's task of monkhood reached its end or not?" Knowing that the monk had attained the fruit of Arahantship, she investigated further, "My son, having attained Arahantship, thought, 'How wonderful! This lay devotee has been a great support to me.' Did I also serve as a support in the past or not?" While she was reflecting, the monk was recollecting ninety-nine past lives. [She thought,] "In those ninety-nine lives, I was together with others and deprived this elder of his life."
189:
This elder, seeing such a lack of virtue in me, thought, 'The laywoman has indeed performed a wonderful and heavy deed.' Reflecting, 'While wandering in this Saṃsāra, has there ever been any benefit I have done for my son?', she looked back beyond those ninety-nine births to the hundredth birth and saw: 'In that hundredth birth, I was the wife and attendant of this monk. When he was about to lose his life, I gave the gift of my own life. Indeed, I have performed a great benefit for my son before.' While sitting in her house, she said, 'Venerable Sir, please contemplate further and more specifically.'

The elder, hearing her voice with the divine ear (dibba-sota), contemplated specifically and recollected back to the hundredth birth. Seeing that the laywoman had given her life for him in that birth, he thought, 'Indeed, this great laywoman has performed a great benefit for me in a past life.' Filled with joy, while still at the laywoman's house, he explained the questions regarding the four Paths and Fruits (Magga and Phala) and then attained Parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu).

The Story of a Certain Monk (II) ends.

## 3. The Story of a Certain Dissatisfied Monk
(Aññataraukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu Vatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Sududdasaṃ,' concerning a certain monk who was dissatisfied with the Dispensation.

## The Account of the Merchant's Son who Practiced Meritorious Deeds Step by Step to Escape Suffering

While the Buddha was residing in Sāvatthī, a merchant's son approached his teacher, an elder who used to visit his house, and said, 'Venerable Sir, I wish to be free from suffering. Please teach me a way to be free from suffering.' The elder replied, 'Lay follower, very well. If you wish to be free from suffering, give alms by lottery (salāka-bhatta), give food on the fortnightly days (pakkhika-bhatta), give rains-residence robes (vassa-vāsika), and offer requisites such as robes. Divide your wealth into three parts: use one part for business and work, one part to support your wife and children, and offer one part to the Buddha's Dispensation.' The merchant's son agreed, saying, 'Very well, Venerable Sir,' and performed everything in the order mentioned.

After doing so, he asked the elder again, 'Venerable Sir, what other meritorious deed should I perform beyond this?' The elder said, 'Lay follower, take the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.' Having taken them, he asked again what was beyond that. 'Then take the Ten Precepts,' the elder said. He agreed, saying, 'Very well, Venerable Sir,' and undertook them.
190:
## The Teaching

(36) Sududdasaṃ sunipuṇaṃ, yatthakāmanipātinaṃ.
Cittaṃ rakkhetha medhāvī, cittaṃ guttaṃ sukhāvahaṃ.

Bhikkhu, O monk. Sududdasaṃ, very difficult to see. Sunipuṇaṃ, very subtle. Yatthakāmanipātinaṃ, tending to fall upon whatever object it desires without distinction. Cittaṃ, the mind. Medhāvī, the wise person. Rakkhetha, should guard. Guttaṃ, well-guarded. Cittaṃ, the mind. Sukhāvahaṃ, can bring the three types of happiness: human, divine, and Nibbāna.

Because he had performed meritorious deeds in succession, this merchant's son became well-known by the name Anupubba-seṭṭhiputta (The Merchant's Son of Gradual Progress).

When he asked again, 'Venerable Sir, is there anything else to be done beyond this?' the elder replied, 'If so, become a monk.' Thus, he left the lay life and ordained. For that monk, one monk who was a master of Abhidhamma became his teacher (ācariya), and another monk who was a master of Vinaya became his preceptor (upajjhāya). After he received higher ordination, whenever the Abhidhamma teacher came to him, he would teach him Abhidhamma, saying, 'In the Buddha's Dispensation, this is proper to do, and this is not proper.' His preceptor also, whenever he came to him, would teach him Vinaya, saying, 'In the Buddha's Dispensation, this is proper to do, and this is not proper; this is allowable, and this is not allowable.'

## How the Merchant's Son Monk Became Dissatisfied and How the Practice was Condensed to the Simplest Form

The merchant's son monk thought, 'The duties of a monk are indeed very heavy. I ordained because I wanted to be free from suffering, but in this Dispensation, I do not even see a place to stretch my hand. It might be possible to be free from suffering even while living at home. It is proper for me to return to lay life.' From that time on, because of his dissatisfaction with the Dispensation, he did not practice the recitation of the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattimsākāra), nor did he study the Pali texts. He became thin and gaunt, with veins standing out on his body. Overcome by laziness, he lived with a body covered in scabies and ringworm.

Then, young novices asked him, 'Venerable Sir, what has happened to you? You remain just as you are, whether standing or sitting. You are thin and gaunt, overcome by jaundice, with veins standing out and a body covered in scabies and ringworm. What have you done?'

'Friends, I am very dissatisfied and weary of the Dispensation,' he replied. When they asked why, he told them the reason. The novices informed his teacher and preceptor. The teacher and preceptor then took him to the Buddha. The Buddha asked, 'Monks, why have you come?' 'Venerable Sir, this monk is dissatisfied with Your Dispensation.' 'Is it true, monk?' 'Yes, Venerable Sir.' 'For what reason?' 'Venerable Sir, I ordained only because I wanted to be free from suffering. My teacher teaches me Abhidhamma, and my preceptor teaches me Vinaya. I thought, "In this Dispensation, I do not even have a place to stretch my hand. It is possible to be free from suffering as a layman. I will become a layman." I have made this decision, Venerable Sir.'

'Monk, if you can guard just one thing, there is no need to guard the rest.' 'What is it, Venerable Sir?' 'Can you guard only your mind?' 'I can, Venerable Sir.' 'Then guard only your own mind; it is possible to be free from suffering.' Having given this advice, the Buddha spoke this verse:
191:
“Dear monk, if you can guard just one thing, there is no need to guard the rest.” When the Buddha said this, the monk asked, “Venerable Sir, what is that one thing?” “Can you, monk, guard your mind alone?” the Buddha asked. When the monk replied, “I can, Venerable Sir,” the Buddha gave this instruction and spoke this verse: “If so, guard your mind alone to be free from suffering.”

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, that son of a wealthy man who had become a monk attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Besides him, many others also became Stream-enterers and attained other fruits. The teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.

The story of the obscure dissatisfied monk ends.

## 4. The Story of the Elder Saṅgharakkhita’s Nephew
(Saṅgharakkhita-bhāgineyya-thera-vatthu)

The Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with “Dūraṅgamaṃ ekacaraṃ,” while residing at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, concerning a monk named Saṅgharakkhita.

## The Young Monk Saṅgharakkhita Offering a Robe to His Uncle and Preceptor
In Sāvatthī, a certain young man of good family, after hearing the Buddha’s teaching, left the household life and ordained. Having received full ordination, he became known as Elder Saṅgharakkhita and attained Arahantship within just a few days. The Elder’s younger sister gave birth to a son and named him after the Elder. Because he was the nephew, he was named Bhāgineyya Saṅgharakkhita. When he came of age, he ordained under the Elder himself. After receiving full ordination, he spent the rains retreat (vassa) at a small village monastery. While staying there, he received two pieces of cloth for the rains-retreat robes—one seven cubits long and the other eight cubits long. He thought, “The eight-cubit one shall be for my preceptor (upajjhāya),” and “The seven-cubit one shall be for me.” After the rains retreat, thinking, “I will go and see my preceptor,” he arrived while going for alms along the way. He entered the monastery before the Elder had returned, swept the Elder’s daytime resting place, set out water for washing the feet, prepared the seat, and sat down watching the path for the Elder’s arrival.

When he saw the Elder coming, he went out to meet him, took his bowl and robes, and said, “Venerable Sir, please sit and rest.” After the Elder sat down, the young monk took a palm-leaf fan and fanned him. He offered drinking water, washed the Elder’s feet, brought the eight-cubit cloth, placed it at the Elder’s feet, and said, “Venerable Sir, please use this robe-cloth,” while continuing to fan him. Then the Elder said to the young monk, “Friend Saṅgharakkhita, my robes are complete; you use it yourself.” “Venerable Sir, from the moment I received this cloth, I have designated it for you. Please use it.”
192:
"Please use it, venerable sir," he requested again.

Even though he requested thus, the Elder said again, "Friend Saṅgharakkhita, my robes are complete; you yourself should use it." "Venerable sir, please do not do this; if you use it, it will be of great benefit to me," he requested again. Although the nephew monk requested repeatedly, the Elder simply did not desire it.

## While Planning to Disrobe, Hitting the Preceptor's Head with a Fan

Thus, while that young monk Saṅgharakkhita was standing and fanning, he thought: "In lay life, I am the great Elder's nephew; as a monk, I am his resident pupil (saddhivihārika). Despite this, my preceptor does not wish to use [the robe] with me. If this great Elder does not use it with me, what is the use of my being a monk? I will return to lay life." Then, this thought occurred to the young monk: "The life of a householder is difficult to maintain. If I become a layman, how shall I make a living?" Then he thought, "I will sell this eight-cubit cloth and buy a she-goat. She-goats breed quickly. I will sell each offspring as they are born and build up capital. Once I have capital, I will take a wife. That wife will give birth to a son. Then, I will name the son 'Saṅgharakkhita' after my uncle the Elder. I will place him in a small carriage and, taking my son and wife, I will go to pay respects to my uncle the Elder. While on the way, I will say to my wife, 'Give me my son, I will carry him.' She will say, 'What is the use of you carrying the son? Come and just drive this carriage.' She will take the son, but being unable to hold him properly, she will drop him on the cart track. Then, the wheel will run over the son's body. Then, I will say to the woman, 'You did not give me my son, nor could you carry him properly; you have ruined me!' and I will strike her on the back with a goad-stick." While he was thinking this and fanning, he repeatedly struck the Elder's head with the palmyra-leaf fan.

## The Elder Finding Out, the Monk Fleeing in Shame, and the Buddha's Admonishment

The Elder thought, "This Saṅgharakkhita is striking my head. What is the reason?" Upon investigating, he knew everything the young monk was thinking and asked, "Friend Saṅgharakkhita, you are unable to strike your wife, but what fault is there in me, an old man, that you strike me here?" The nephew monk thought, "How wonderful! I am ruined. My preceptor knows everything I thought. There is no benefit in my being a monk," and throwing down the palmyra fan, he attempted to flee. Then, young monks and novices followed and caught the young monk Saṅgharakkhita and brought him to the Buddha. The Buddha, seeing those monks, asked, "Monks, why have you come? Have you caught a monk?" "Yes, Blessed One," they replied, and explained, "We have caught and brought this young monk who was fleeing because he was dissatisfied with the Dispensation."

Then the Buddha asked, "Dear monk, is it true that you are dissatisfied with this Dispensation?" "Blessed One..."
193:
## The Teaching
(37) Far-wandering, wandering alone, bodiless, lying in a cave.
Those who restrain the mind will be freed from the bonds of Māra.

*Dūraṅgamaṃ*: reaching even to objects located in distant places. *Ekacaraṃ*: arising one after another. *Asarīraṃ*: having no physical form. *Guhāsayaṃ*: dwelling in the cave, meaning it arises depending on the cave of the four great elements, the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*). *Cittaṃ*: the mind. *Ye*: those men, women, laypeople, or monastics who... *Saṃyamessanti*: will well and truly restrain. *Te*: they... *Mārabandhanā*: from the bonds of the defilements (*kilesa-māra*), the suffering of the round of rebirth in the three realms (*tebhūmaka-vaṭṭa*). *Mokkhanti*: will be liberated.

"It is true, Venerable Sir," he replied. "Dear monk, for what purpose did you commit such a serious act? Are you not the son of a Buddha who is possessed of great energy? Having gone forth in the Dispensation of a Buddha like me, you were unable to make yourself known as a Stream-enterer (*Sotāpanna*), a Once-returner (*Sakadāgāmī*), a Non-returner (*Anāgāmī*), or an Arahant. Why did you commit such a serious act?" the Buddha asked again. "Venerable Sir, I am dissatisfied," he replied. When asked, "Why are you dissatisfied?", the young monk related the entire sequence of events, from the day he received the rains-retreat robes until the moment he struck his preceptor with the palmyra-leaf fan, and said, "For this reason, Bhante, I was fleeing." Then the Teacher said to the young monk, "Come, monk, do not think of various things. This mind has the nature of receiving objects that are even far away. One should strive to be liberated from the bonds of lust, hatred, and delusion," and he spoke this verse.
194:
## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, the nephew, the young monk Saṅgharakkhita, attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (*Sotāpatti-phala*). Many others also became Stream-enterers and so forth. The Dhamma teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
The story of the nephew of Elder Saṅgharakkhita ends.

## 5. The Story of Elder Cittahattha
(Cittahattatthera Vatthu)
"To one of unsteady mind..." (*Anavaṭṭhitacittassa*). The Teacher, while residing in Sāvatthī, spoke this Dhamma teaching concerning Elder Cittahattha.

## The Account of the One who Ordained and Disrobed Six Times
A certain young man of good family living in Sāvatthī, while searching for a lost ox, entered the forest. Having found the ox at midday, he let it go into the herd. Thinking, "I will surely obtain at least some food from the venerable ones," and being oppressed by hunger, he entered the monastery, went to the monks, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. At that time, there was rice remaining in the monks' refuse-bowls after they had eaten. Seeing that the man was oppressed by hunger, the monks said, "Take rice from this bowl and eat."

In the time of the Buddha, rice with many soups and curries would arise. That man took just enough rice from the bowl, ate, drank water, washed his hands, and after paying homage to the monks, asked, "Venerable sirs, did you go to an invitation today?"
"Lay follower, there was no invitation. Even when there is none, the monks always receive food in this manner," they said. The man thought, "Even though we work diligently and strive hard at our jobs day and night, we do not get rice with such good curries as these venerable ones. These monks surely eat like this constantly. What is the use of being a layman to me? I will become a monk." He approached the monks and requested ordination. Then the monks said, "Very well, lay follower," and gave him ordination. After becoming a monk, he performed all the major and minor duties. Because he ate the offerings and gifts made to the Buddhas, after two or three days had passed, his body became plump.
195:
Then he thought, "What is the use of living by wandering for alms in the neighborhood? I will return to lay life." Having thought thus, he disrobed and returned home to work. After a few days of performing various tasks at home, his once stout body became thin and withered again. Then he thought, "What is the use of this suffering? I will become a monk again." He went back and ordained once more. After a few days, he again became dissatisfied and disrobed. However, while he was a monk, he was very helpful to the other monks. After a few days, he again became dissatisfied and thought, "What is the use of being a layman? I will ordain again." He went, paid homage to the monks, and requested ordination. Because of his helpfulness, the monks ordained him once more. In this manner, he ordained and disrobed six times. Because he wandered about according to the whims of his mind, the monks named him Elder Cittahattha (Citta-hattha Thera).

## The Story of the Man who attained Stream-entry because his Wife Slept Repulsively
While this man was frequently going back and forth between the life of a monk and a layman, his wife became pregnant. On the seventh occasion when he was about to ordain, he returned home from the forest bringing farming tools such as a plow. After putting the tools away, he entered the bedroom to take his robes. At that moment, his wife was lying down asleep. Her clothes were disheveled and falling off. Saliva was trickling from her mouth, and she was snoring loudly. Her mouth was wide open, and she was grinding her teeth. To him, she appeared like a bloated corpse. He perceived the idea that "This body is impermanent and suffering." Thinking, "I have ordained for so long, yet because of this woman, I have been unable to remain in the monkhood," he took the edge of his robe, tied it around his waist, and left the house.

His mother-in-law, who lived in the adjacent house, saw him leaving in such a manner and thought, "He must be dissatisfied with lay life again. He has just returned from the forest, tied his saffron robe around his waist, and is heading straight for the monastery. What could be the reason?" She entered the house and saw her daughter sleeping. Realizing, "He saw her and left in disgust," she struck her daughter and said, "Get up, you wretched woman! Your husband saw you sleeping and left in disgust. From this day on, he is no longer yours." The daughter replied, "Go away, mother! Where could he go? He will return in a few days." As the man walked along, reciting "Impermanent, suffering," he attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). He went to the monastery, paid homage to the monks, and requested ordination again. The monks said, "We cannot ordain you. Where is your monkhood?"
196:
"Your head is like a whetstone for sharpening knives. Therefore, we cannot ordain you." He pleaded, "Venerable Sirs, please ordain me just this one last time out of compassion." Because of his past helpfulness, the monks ordained him. Within a few days, that monk attained Arahantship along with the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).

Then the monks said to him, "Friend Cittahattha, you should know the time for your return home. This time, your stay as a monk is quite long." He replied, "Venerable Sirs, I used to go when I had the desire for worldly association. Now, that association has been severed. I have become one who no longer goes back." The monks went to the Buddha and reported, "Venerable Sir, when we spoke to this monk, he said such things. He claims to have attained the Fruit of Arahantship. He is speaking what is not true." The Buddha said, "Monks, what he says is true. When my son's mind was unsteady and he did not yet know the True Dhamma, he went back and forth between home and the monastery. Now, my son has abandoned both merit and evil." Then he uttered these verses:

## The Teaching
(38) For one whose mind is unsteady,
Who does not know the True Dhamma,
Whose confidence wavers,
Wisdom does not reach fulfillment.

(39) For one whose mind is free from lust,
Whose heart is not affected by hatred,
Who has abandoned both merit and evil,
For such a wakeful one, there is no fear.

'Anavaṭṭhitacittassa' means one who does not have a steady mind. 'Saddhammaṃ' means the True Dhamma. 'Avijānato' means not knowing. 'Pariplavapasādassa' means having a wavering faith that floats like a raft because it is weak. For such a person, wisdom, both mundane and supramundane, does not reach fulfillment.

'Anavassutacittassa' means a mind not moistened by lust. 'Ananvāhatacetaso' means a mind not struck by anger. 'Puññapāpapahīnassa' means one who has abandoned both merit and evil. 'Jāgarato' means one endowed with the five qualities of wakefulness, such as faith. For such an Arahant (khīṇāsava), there is no danger from the defilements.

## Benefit of the Teaching
The teaching was beneficial to the multitude of people.
197:
## Showing the Faults of Defilements in Relation to Elder Cittahattha

Then one day, in the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a conversation: "Friends, how heavy indeed are the defilements! A clansman endowed with the supporting conditions for the fruit of Arahantship such as this was tossed about by defilements, becoming a layman seven times and ordaining seven times."

The Teacher, hearing the monks' conversation, went to the Dhamma Hall with a gait suitable for that moment. Sitting on the Buddha's seat, he asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?"

When they replied, "For such a discussion," he said, "Monks, defilements are indeed this heavy. If these defilements had a physical form and could be piled up in one place, the universe (Cakkavāḷa) would be too small and the Brahma realm (Brahmaloka) too low. Therefore, there would be no space for the defilements to stay; they are that heavy. They toss about even one like me, a man of noble breed (purisājāneya) endowed with wisdom. What then to say of others?"

Having said this, he added, "I myself, depending on a half-measure of grain and a blunt hoe, became an ascetic and returned to lay life six times."

When asked, "When was that, Venerable Sir? When was that, Sugata?", he asked, "Do you wish to hear, monks?" When they replied, "We wish to hear, Bhante," he said, "Then listen," and brought forth the past.

## The Story of Kudāla-paṇḍita Becoming an Ascetic and Returning to Lay Life Six Times

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Vārāṇasī, a man named Kudāla-paṇḍita went forth into an external ascetic order. Having lived in the Himavanta for eight months, when the ground became wet during the rainy season, he thought, "In my house, there is a half-measure of grain and a blunt hoe.
198:
That victory is not well-won, which victory is turned back into defeat.
That victory is indeed well-won, which victory is not turned back into defeat.

Great King! That victory which is won in a base manner, or which wins over external enemies, is not called a well-won victory. That victory which is won in a noble manner, or which wins over internal enemies, is indeed called a well-won victory.

"Let not this variety of grain perish," he thought. Leaving the monkhood, he cleared a spot with a spade, tilled it, sowed the seeds, and fenced it. When the grain ripened, he harvested it, kept about a measure (nāḷi) of seed, and consumed the rest. That Kuddāla-paṇḍita thought, "What is the use of living in a house now? I will go forth and become a monk again for eight months." Thus he went forth and became a monk. In this manner, depending on a measure of grain and a blunt spade, he became a layman six times and a monk six times. On the seventh occasion, he thought, "Six times I have become a layman and then a monk because of this blunt spade. I shall throw it away somewhere." He went to the bank of the Ganges and thought, "If I see where it falls, I might go down and take it back. I will throw it in such a way that I do not see where it falls." He wrapped the measure of seeds in a piece of cloth, tied the cloth to the blade of the spade, held the spade by the end of the handle, and stood on the bank of the Ganges. Closing his eyes, he swung it three times over his head and threw it into the Ganges. Turning back, he did not see where it fell and shouted three times, "I have won! I have won!"

## Seven Kings Following Suit and Becoming Ascetics
At that moment, the King of Bārāṇasī, having pacified the border regions, was returning. While he was staying in a leaf-hut on the bank of the Ganges and descending to the river to bathe, he heard that sound. To kings, the sound "I have won" is unpleasant. The King went to Kuddāla-paṇḍita and asked, "I have now subdued my enemies and come saying 'I have won.' But you, ascetic, are crying out 'I have won, I have won.' What kind of victory is this?" Kuddāla-paṇḍita the ascetic replied, "Great King, you have conquered external thieves. The enemy conquered by you may later prove unconquered. But I have conquered the internal thief of greed. That thief of greed will not conquer me again. Only the victory over that internal enemy is called a well-won victory." Saying this, he recited this verse.

At that very moment, while looking at the River Ganges, he developed the water kasina (āpo-kasiṇa) and, having attained special meditative absorptions (jhāna), he sat cross-legged in the air. The King, having heard the Dhamma discourse of the Great Being, paid homage, requested to be ordained, and went forth as a monk along with his host of troops. At that time, the assembly was about a league (yojana) in size.
199:
A neighboring king ruling a country near Bārāṇasī heard that the King of Bārāṇasī had gone forth as a monk. Thinking he would take over that king's country, he arrived and saw that such a prosperous, wealthy, and extensive kingdom was empty and silent. He reflected, "Even such a great kingdom as this has been abandoned to become a hermit. He would not have gone forth if it were an inferior place. It is fitting for me also to go forth." After this reflection, he went to the place where the Bodhisatta was staying, approached that Great Being, requested ordination, and went forth along with his retinue. In this same manner, seven kings abandoned their wealth and pleasures, took their many followers, and went forth. The Great Being, having lived the holy life, was reborn in the Brahma world.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching to a close, said, "Monks, at that time I was Kuddāla-paṇḍita. These defilements are indeed heavy burdens in this way."

The Story of Elder Cittahattha ends.

## 6. Story of the Five Hundred Monks
(Pañcasatabhikkhu Vatthu)

The Teacher, while staying at Sāvatthī, told this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Kumbhūpamaṃ," concerning monks who had undertaken the practice of insight.

## The Forest Deities Showing Terrifying Objects to the Five Hundred Monks

It is said that in Sāvatthī, five hundred monks took meditation subjects from the Teacher leading to Arahantship. Thinking, "We shall perform the duties of a recluse," they traveled about a hundred yojanas and reached a large village where many people lived. When the people saw the monks, they invited them to sit on prepared seats, served them with excellent gruel and food, and asked, "Venerable sirs, where are you going?" When told, "We are going to a place that is comfortable," they pleaded, "Venerable sirs, please stay here for these three months of the rains retreat. We will also establish ourselves in the Three Refuges and observe the Five Precepts in your presence." Knowing their acceptance, the people said, "Venerable sirs, there is a large forest grove not far from the village; please stay there," and sent them off. The monks entered that forest grove.

The deities who protected and ruled that forest grove thought, "Virtuous noble ones have arrived at this forest. While these noble ones stay here, it is not proper for us to take our wives and children and live up in the trees." They descended from the trees and sat on the ground, thinking, "The noble ones will stay here for just one night and will surely leave tomorrow." On the following day, the monks went into the village for alms and returned to that same forest grove.
200:
The deities thought, "This community of monks must have been invited by someone for tomorrow's meal; that is why they have returned. Although they did not leave today, I think they will leave tomorrow." In this way, the deities remained on the ground for about half a month. Then they thought, "I think these noble ones will stay here for the entire three months of the rains retreat. Indeed, while these monks stay here, it is not proper for us to climb up and sit in the trees. For three months, taking our wives and children and sitting or standing on the ground is painful. We should do something to make these monks flee."

They began to show severed heads and headless trunks at various places where the monks stayed by night or day and at the ends of the walking paths, and they began to make non-human sounds. From that time on, the monks began to suffer from ailments such as sneezing and coughing. They asked one another, "Friend, what is hurting you?" One said, "I am suffering from sneezing and coughing." Another said, "Friend, today at the end of the walking path, I saw a severed head. I saw a headless trunk at the place where I stay at night. I heard a non-human sound at the place where I stay during the day. This place is one that should be avoided. We are uncomfortable in this monastery; let us go to the Teacher." They departed and, in due course, reached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat at one side.

## Subduing with the Weapon of Loving-kindness Given by the Buddha

Then the Teacher said to those five hundred monks, "Monks, are you unable to stay in that place?" "Yes, Bhante. While we were staying in that place, such terrifying objects appeared to us, and such discomfort occurred. Therefore, thinking 'This place is one that should be avoided,' we abandoned it and have come to the presence of the Blessed One." When they said this, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is fitting for you to go back to that very place. It is fitting to stay there." "Bhante, we do not dare to go and stay there," they replied. "Monks, you went without taking a weapon. Now, go taking a weapon." "What kind of weapon, Bhante?" The Teacher said, "I will give you a weapon. Go taking the weapon given by me."

"What should be done by one who is skilled in good, who has attained the state of peace:
He should be capable, upright, and truly straight, easy to speak to, gentle, and not arrogant."

He taught the entire Metta Sutta and instructed them, "Monks, you should recite this starting from the forest grove outside the monastery and then enter the inner monastery." They paid homage to the Teacher, departed, and in due course reached that place. They performed a group recitation outside the monastery and entered the forest grove while reciting. The deities throughout the entire forest grove, having regained hearts of loving-kindness, came out to meet them.
201:
"Venerable Sir, what are the weapons?" they asked. The Blessed One said, "I shall give you weapons, dear sons. Take the weapons I give you and go."

After preaching the entire Metta Sutta discourse beginning in this way, he dismissed them, saying, "Monks, recite this Metta Sutta from the moment you enter the forest outside the monastery until you enter your dwelling." Having paid homage to the Buddha, those monks departed and, following their route, reached that place. They performed group recitation outside the monastery and entered the forest while still reciting. All the deities dwelling in the forest, having gained a mind of loving-kindness, came out to meet the monks. They requested to take their bowls and robes and to massage their hands and feet, and they provided protection for those five hundred monks in various places. Those deities remained as still as heated oil. Nowhere was the sound of non-human beings heard. The minds of those monks became one-pointed.

Sitting in their night-quarters and day-quarters, the monks directed their minds toward insight. Establishing the vision of rise and fall within themselves, they developed insight, reflecting: "This body is like a potter's vessel because of its breakable nature and its lack of permanence." The Fully Enlightened One, while seated in the Gandhakuṭī, knowing that they had begun their insight meditation, addressed those monks: "Monks, it is just so; this body is indeed like a potter's vessel because of its breakable nature and its lack of permanence."
202:
"...because of its lack of essence, it is just like a potter's vessel." Having said this, the Buddha sent forth his radiance. Even though he remained a hundred leagues away, he appeared as if sitting right before them. Emitting the six-colored rays and manifesting his form clearly, he spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(40) Knowing this body to be like a potter's vessel,
Establishing this mind like a fortified city,
One should fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom,
And protect what is won, remaining unattached.

Monks, know this physical body, which is a collection of hair and so forth, to be like a potter's vessel. Make this insight-mind of yours like a well-secured city. With the weapon of wisdom—which is the wisdom of insight and the wisdom of the Noble Path—one should strike and discard Māra, the defilements. One should also protect with a pure mind the tender insight that has been attained through victory, by making use of suitable dwellings, suitable climate, suitable food, suitable persons, and hearing the Dhamma, and by entering into meditative attainments from time to time. Emerging from those and contemplating formations with a pure mind, one should protect it. One should be unattached, meaning one should not have clinging or attachment to the meditative attainment, not making it a permanent dwelling.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, the five hundred monks, while remaining in their seats, attained Arahantship together with the four analytical knowledges. Praising and honoring the golden-hued body of the Tathāgata, they returned.

The Story of the Five Hundred Monks ends.

## 7. The Story of Elder Pūtigattatissa
(Pūtigattatissa-thera-vatthu)
The Teacher, while residing in Sāvatthī, spoke this legal discourse beginning with "Aciraṃ vatayaṃ kāyo" concerning Elder Pūtigattatissa.

A certain young man of good family living in Sāvatthī, having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, dedicated himself to the Sasana and ordained. Upon receiving higher ordination, he became known as Elder Tissa. This Elder Tissa used to practice meditation while walking. As time passed, a disease arose in his body. Small pustules the size of mustard seeds appeared. Gradually, they grew to the size of mung beans, then chickpeas, then jujube stones, then myrobalan fruits, and then wood-apple fruits, and then they burst. His whole body became covered with sores. He became known as Elder Pūtigattatissa. Later, the bones of Elder Pūtigattatissa broke, and he reached a state where no one could look after or attend to him.
203:
## The Discourse

(41) Before long, alas, this body will lie upon the earth,
Cast aside, devoid of consciousness, like a useless log.

Tissa, the monk Pūtigattatissa. *Ayaṃ kāyo*: this body, a fathom in length and a span in width, an assembly of the thirty-two parts beginning with the hair of the head. *Chuddho*: being cast aside. *Apetaviññāṇo*: being devoid of consciousness. *Niratthaṃ*: having no benefit or use. *Kaliṅgaraṃ*: like a useless log. *Aciraṃ*: before long. *Pathaviṃ adhisessati vata*: will indeed lie upon the surface of the earth.

The robes he wore were stained with pus and blood, resembling a cake called *jālapūva* (which is like a net). His fellow residents, the *saddhivihārika* disciples and others, being unable to care for and clean him, abandoned him. That Elder Pūtigattatissa lay there, having no protector.

It is the custom of the Buddhas not to neglect surveying the world twice a day. When surveying the world in the early morning, they direct their knowledge from the edge of the world-sphere toward the Fragrant Chamber (*Gandhakuṭī*). When surveying in the evening, they direct their knowledge from the Fragrant Chamber outward. At that time, the Elder Pūtigattatissa appeared within the net of the Blessed One's knowledge. The Teacher, seeing the supporting condition (*upanissaya*) for that monk to attain Arahantship, reflected: "This monk has been abandoned by his *saddhivihārika* disciples and others. Now, apart from me, he has no other refuge." He then departed from the Fragrant Chamber and, as if wandering through the monastery, went to the fire-hall. He washed a pot, placed it on the stove, and waited in the fire-hall until the water was hot. Knowing the water was hot, he went and took hold of the edge of the bed where the Elder Pūtigattatissa was lying.

At that moment, the monks said, "Venerable Sir, please move aside; we will take hold of it," and taking the bed, they carried it to the fire-hall. Then the Teacher had a water trough brought and poured hot water into it. He had those monks remove Pūtigattatissa's outer robe, had it scrubbed in hot water, and set it to dry in the sun. Then, standing near Pūtigattatissa, he moistened his body with hot water, rubbed it, and bathed him. At the conclusion of the bath, the outer robe that had been drying in the sun was dry. He then had him wear that robe and had the inner robe he was wearing scrubbed in hot water and set to dry in the sun.

As soon as the water on the monk's body had dried, the inner robe that was drying also became dry. Wearing one robe and wrapped in the other, the monk, with a light body and a concentrated mind, lay on the bed. The Teacher stood at the head of the monk Pūtigattatissa and said, "Dear monk, when this body of yours is devoid of consciousness, it will be without any use and will lie on the earth like a log." (A log refers to a hollow, decayed, heartless, or knotty piece of wood that is useless for construction, whether straight or crooked, and is thus discarded.) Having said this, he spoke this verse:
204:
## The Benefit of the Discourse

At the conclusion of the discourse, the Elder Pūtigattatissa attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*). Many others also became Stream-enterers and so forth. The Elder, having attained Arahantship, passed away into *parinibbāna*. The Teacher had the funeral rites performed for the Elder Pūtigattatissa's body and, taking the relics, had a stupa (*cetiya*) built.

## The Teaching on the Bad and Good Deeds Done as a Bird Hunter

Then the monks asked the Blessed One, "Exalted Buddha, where has the Elder Pūtigattatissa been reborn?" When they asked this, he replied, "Monks, he has attained *parinibbāna*." They asked again, "Venerable Sir, why did the body of such a monk, who was endowed with the supporting condition for Arahantship, become putrid? Why did his bones break? And what was the meritorious deed that served as the supporting condition for his attainment of Arahantship?" The Teacher replied, "Monks, all of this occurred to him solely because of the karma he himself had performed." When they asked, "Venerable Sir, what was the karma he performed?" he said, "In that case, monks, listen." He then brought forth the past:

In the time of the Kassapa Buddha, this man was a bird hunter. He killed many birds and served a person of authority. He sold the birds that remained after serving that person. Thinking that the birds remaining from the sale would rot if killed and kept, he broke the leg bones and wing bones of the birds so they could not fly away, and piled them up. He would then sell those birds the following morning. When he obtained a great many birds, he would also have them cooked for his own benefit.
205:
At that time, one day, while the bird hunter was cooking food of excellent flavor, an Arahant came for alms and stood at the door of the bird hunter's house. Seeing the Elder, the bird hunter felt a sense of devotion and thought, “I have killed and eaten many birds. This noble one has now come and is standing at my door, and there is delicious food in the house. I shall offer alms-food to this noble one.” Having thus resolved, he took the Elder's bowl, filled it, and offered the delicious alms-food. Then, bowing with the five-point prostration, he made a wish: “Venerable Sir, by the power of this merit, may I reach the summit of the Dhamma that you have seen and known.” The Elder gave his blessing, saying, “May it be as you have wished.”

(Relating this story of the past, the Buddha said:) “Monks, by the power of the deed performed at that time, all this has happened to Tissa. Due to the consequence of the evil deed of breaking the bones of birds, Tissa’s body became rotten and his bones broke. Due to the consequence of the meritorious deed of offering delicious alms-food to an Arahant, he has attained Arahantship.”

The Story of Elder Pūtigattatissa ends.

## 8. The Story of Nanda the Cowherd
(Nandagopālaka Vatthu)

The Teacher taught this Dhamma discourse, beginning with “Diso disaṃ,” while staying in the Kosala country, concerning the cowherd named Nanda.

## Nanda the Cowherd Being Killed on His Return After Escorting the Buddha
In Sāvatthī, a cowherd named Nanda, who belonged to the wealthy merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, looked after the herds of cattle. He was wealthy, possessing great riches and many belongings.

From time to time, that cowherd Nanda would take the five products of the cow and go to the presence of the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika. There, he would see the Teacher and listen to the Dhamma. Nanda the cowherd invited the Teacher to come to his own place of residence. The Teacher, waiting for the maturity of Nanda's wisdom, did not go immediately. 

When He knew that Nanda's wisdom had reached maturity, one day, while wandering on tour accompanied by a large community of monks, the Teacher left the main road and sat at the foot of a certain tree near the cowherd’s residence. Nanda the cowherd approached the Teacher, paid homage, and after exchanging pleasantries, invited the Teacher. For seven days, he offered an excellent donation of the five products of the cow to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. On the seventh day, the Teacher gave a discourse of appreciation (anumodanā) and taught the progressive discourse, including the talk on giving (dānakathā) and so forth. At the end of the discourse, Nanda the cowherd was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Taking the Teacher's bowl, he followed the Teacher for a long distance. When the Teacher said, “Lay follower, stay back,” he paid homage and turned back.

At that time, a certain hunter shot and killed Nanda the cowherd. The monks who were following behind saw Nanda the cowherd lying dead, went to the Teacher, and reported: “Venerable Sir, because the Buddha came to this place, Nanda the cowherd gave a great offering, and while returning from escorting You, he has met his death.”
206:
## The Teaching
(42) Diso disaṃ yaṃ taṃ kayirā, verī vā pana verinaṃ.
Micchāpaṇihitaṃ cittaṃ, pāpiyo naṃ tato kare.

Whatever harm a thief may do to a thief, or an enemy to an enemy, a wrongly directed mind can do one even greater harm.

(The monks said:) “Venerable Sir, if the Buddha had not come, the death of Nanda the cowherd would likely not have occurred.” The Teacher said, “Monks, whether I came or not, even if he went to the four cardinal directions or the four intermediate directions, there is no such thing as a means to escape death for Nanda the cowherd. Whatever destruction and ruin thieves or enemies cannot do, only the wrongly directed and wrongly established mind within these beings does.” Having said this, He spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the discourse, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth. The teaching became beneficial to the great multitude.

Because the monks did not ask about the unwholesome karma performed by the lay follower Nanda the cowherd in a previous life, the Teacher did not explain it.

The Story of Nanda the Cowherd ends.
207:
## 9. The Story of the Treasurer’s Son Soreyya
(Soreyyattheravatthu)

"Not a mother, nor a father could do..." The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, gave this Dhamma teaching concerning the treasurer’s son Soreyya.

This story began in the city of Soreyya and concluded in the city of Sāvatthī.

## Soreyya Becoming a Woman for Offending Venerable Mahākaccāyana

While the Buddha was residing happily in Sāvatthī, in the city of Soreyya, the treasurer’s son Soreyya, together with a friend, was riding in a comfortable carriage, accompanied by a large retinue, leaving the city to go bathing (water-playing). At that moment, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, wishing to enter the city of Soreyya for alms, was putting on his double-layered outer robe outside the city. The Venerable Mahākaccāyana possessed a beautiful, golden-hued complexion. Upon seeing the Elder, the treasurer’s son Soreyya thought: "Oh, if only this Elder were my wife! Or if only the complexion of my wife’s body were like the complexion of this Elder’s body!" As soon as he had this thought, his male gender disappeared and female gender appeared. Feeling greatly ashamed, he descended from the carriage and fled. His companions and retinue, not recognizing him—or rather, not knowing the cause—said, "What is the reason for this flight?" That woman then took the road to Takkasilā. The friends of the treasurer’s son, who had become a woman, ran here and there searching for him but did not see him. All of them, after bathing, returned home. When asked, "Where is the treasurer’s son?", they replied that they thought he must have returned after bathing. His parents searched for him in various places, and not finding him, they wept and lamented, and thinking he must be dead, they offered matakabhatta (a meal offered for the benefit of the deceased).

That woman, seeing a caravan leader going to Takkasilā, followed closely behind the carts. Then, the people, seeing her, said, "Why do you follow behind our carts? Whose daughter is this maiden? We do not know her." She replied, "Sirs, do not speak so; just drive your carts, I shall go on foot." As she walked, her feet became blistered, so she gave her ring and requested a seat in one of the carts. The people thought: "In the city of Takkasilā, our treasurer’s son has no wife; let us tell him, and we shall receive a great reward." Then the caravan traders went to the treasurer’s son’s house and said, "Master, we have brought a jewel of a woman for you." Hearing this, the treasurer’s son had her summoned, and seeing that she was of a suitable age and possessed an exceedingly beautiful and charming appearance, he felt great affection for her and took her into his house to live as his wife.
208:
There is no man who has not been a woman, and no woman who has not been a man. Men who commit adultery with the wives of others, after they pass away, are cooked in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years. When they are released from hell and return to the human state, they undergo the state of being a woman for countless hundreds of births. Even the Venerable Ānanda, an Ariya disciple who had fulfilled the perfections for a hundred thousand aeons, while wandering in saṃsāra, was once born into a family of goldsmiths and committed adultery. After being cooked in hell, by the remaining result of that karma, he had to be a woman serving at the feet of men for fourteen births, and for seven births, he underwent castration. As for women, if they perform meritorious deeds such as giving alms, lose their desire for being a woman, and firmly resolve, "May this merit lead to the attainment of a male body," they can attain a male body after death. Also, by serving their husbands respectfully like a household deity and through the power of good conduct, they can certainly attain a male body.

## Meeting an Old Friend after Having Two Children with the Treasurer’s Son in Takkasilā

This treasurer’s son Soreyya, because he had harbored improper thoughts toward the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, attained the state of a woman in this very life. While living together with the treasurer’s son in Takkasilā, a child was conceived in the womb of that treasurer’s wife. After ten months, she gave birth to a son, and when that child could walk, she had another son. Thus, there were two sons born from her womb, and two sons who were born while he was a man in the city of Soreyya; thus, there were four sons in total. At that time, the treasurer’s son who was a friend of that treasurer’s wife came from the city of Soreyya to Takkasilā with five hundred carts and entered the city in a comfortable carriage.

Then, the treasurer’s wife, while opening the window on the upper floor of the palace and looking down at the street, saw the treasurer’s son and recognized him well. She sent a maidservant to summon him, had him seated on the upper floor, and paid him great honor and respect. Then, the treasurer’s son who had just arrived from Soreyya said to the treasurer’s wife of Takkasilā, "Lady, we have not seen you before this; for what reason do you pay us such great honor and respect? Do you know us?" She replied, "Yes, Master, I know you," and then asked, "Are you not residents of the city of Soreyya?" He replied, "Yes, Lady, we are." Then the treasurer’s wife asked about the health of the parents, the wife, and the two sons in the city of Soreyya. The treasurer’s son from Soreyya replied, "Yes, Lady, they are in good health," and then asked, "Lady, do you know these people?"
209:
“Sir, it is true that you know them. Do they not have a son? I am that son,” she said. 

“Lady, do not say such a thing. One day, while we were going out together in a carriage to bathe, we lost track of where he went. Although we searched here and there, we could not find him. So we informed his parents. His parents wept and wailed, and performed the funeral rites for one who has passed away,” he replied. 

“Master, that treasurer's son who went bathing with you in the carriage is indeed me,” she said again. 

“Lady, enough! What are you saying? My friend was a man as beautiful as a celestial youth,” he denied. 

“Master, let it be so, but I am indeed that young treasurer's son.” When she spoke thus, the treasurer asked, “How did you come to be a woman like this?”

“Master, on that day you went to play in the water, did you see the Venerable Mahākaccāyana Thera?” she asked. 

“Yes, I saw him,” he said. 

“Looking at the Venerable Mahākaccāyana Thera, I thought: ‘Oh, would that this Thera were my wife! Or would that the complexion of my wife's body were like the complexion of this Thera's body!’ At the very moment of that thought, my male gender disappeared and female gender appeared. Then, feeling greatly ashamed and unable to say a single word to anyone, I fled and arrived here in Takkasilā, Master,” she explained in detail. 

“Oh, what you have done is indeed a very grave matter! Why did you not tell me? Have you asked the Venerable Mahākaccāyana Thera for forgiveness?” he inquired.

## Becoming a Man Again by Asking Forgiveness from Venerable Mahākaccāyana

When he inquired thus, she replied, “Master, I have not yet asked for forgiveness.” 

“Do you know where the Venerable Mahākaccāyana Thera resides?” he asked again. 

“I understand that he resides depending on this city of Takkasilā. Master, if he should come to our house while wandering for alms, I myself will offer alms-food to my noble master,” she said. 

“If that is so, quickly prepare the offerings. We shall ask the Venerable Mahākaccāyana Thera for forgiveness,” he said. He then went to the place where the Thera was staying, paid respects, sat in a suitable place, and said, “Venerable Sir, please accept alms at my house tomorrow.” 

“Young treasurer, are you not a stranger?” the Thera asked. 

“Venerable Sir, please do not ask about our being strangers. Just please accept my alms tomorrow,” he requested. The Thera consented. At the house, great offerings were prepared for the Thera.

The next morning, the Thera went to the door of that house. Then, having invited him to sit and served him with excellent alms-food, the treasurer's son brought the woman, made her prostrate at the Thera's feet, and said, “Venerable Sir, please forgive my companion.” 

“What is the reason for this forgiveness?” the Thera asked. 

“Venerable Sir, this lady was formerly my dear friend. Having looked at you, he had such a thought. At the moment of that thought, his male gender disappeared and female gender appeared. Venerable Sir, please forgive him,” he pleaded. 

The Thera said, “If that is so, rise. I forgive you.” As soon as the Thera said, “I forgive you,” the female gender disappeared and the male gender reappeared. 

As soon as the male gender appeared, the treasurer's son of Takkasilā said, “Friend, these two children were carried in your womb and born because of me; they are the children of both of us. Let us live together right here in Takkasilā. Do not be weary or dejected.”
210:
## The Teaching
(43) Na taṃ mātā pitā kayirā, aññe vā pi ca ñātakā.
Sammāpaṇihitaṃ cittaṃ, seyyaso naṃ tato kare.

Taṃ karaṇaṃ: the accomplishment of that happiness. Mātā: the mother, the benefactor. Na kayirā: cannot do. Pitā: the father, the benefactor. Na kayirā: cannot do. Aññe ñātakā vā pi ca: other relatives besides the mother and father. Na kareyyuṃ: cannot do. Sammāpaṇihitaṃ: well-established in the ten courses of wholesome action (kusalakamma-patha). Cittaṃ: a good mind. Tato: than the parents and relatives' ability to provide happiness. Naṃ: that person. Seyyaso: to become increasingly noble. Kare-karoti: can do.

"Friend, in this single existence, I was first a man, then became a woman, and have now become a man again. I have reached such a state of transformation. First, two sons were born depending on me, and now, when I was a woman, two sons were born from my womb. Because I have undergone such transformation in a single lifetime, I no longer wish to think of living in a house. I shall ordain in the presence of my master. These two children are your responsibility; do not be negligent in caring for them." Having spoken these words of loving-kindness, he repeatedly kissed and stroked the heads of the young sons, let them lie on his chest, handed them over to the father, left the house, and requested ordination from the Elder.

## Soreyya the Youth Becoming an Arahant
Venerable Mahākaccāyana ordained the treasurer's son Soreyya, taught him meditation, and while traveling, eventually reached the city of Sāvatthī. The new monk became known as Venerable Soreyya. The people living in the countryside, knowing his story, were stirred and created a great stir, approaching the Elder to ask, "Venerable Sir, is it true that such a thing happened?" When he replied, "Yes, lay devotees, it is true," they asked, "Venerable Sir, such a thing can indeed happen. It is said two sons were born from your womb, and two sons were fathered by you. Among those four sons, for which ones do you have stronger affection?" He replied, "Lay devotees, my affection is stronger for the sons who were carried in and born from my womb." People who came again and again asked the same question repeatedly.

As Venerable Soreyya had to repeatedly say that his affection was stronger for the sons born from his womb, he felt embarrassed and began to sit alone and stand alone. Having thus resorted to solitude, he meditated on the rise and fall (khayavaya) of this physical body, and attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). After he became an Arahant, whenever people came and asked, "Venerable Sir, is it true that such a thing happened?" he would answer, "Yes, lay devotees." When they asked again, "For which sons is your affection stronger?" he replied, "I have no affection for any sons." The monks reported to the Buddha, "This Venerable Soreyya is speaking untruth. In previous days, he said his affection was stronger for the sons born from his womb, but now he says he has no affection for any sons. He is declaring something else (Arahantship), Venerable Sir."

The Buddha said, "Bhikkhus, my son Soreyya is not declaring something else. From the time my son saw the Path (Magga) with a well-directed mind, no affection has arisen for any sons.
211:
This fulfillment of the bliss of the Path and Fruit cannot be provided by the mother or the father. Only the mind well-established within these beings can provide the fulfillment of that bliss." Having said this, he spoke this verse:

## Notable Meaning of the Teaching
Parents who give wealth to their children can provide enough wealth for them to live comfortably in a single life without having to work. Even the wealthy parents of Visākhā, who were immensely rich, could only provide enough for her to live comfortably in a single life. There are no parents who can provide their children with the glory of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) over the four islands, let alone the bliss of heaven, the bliss of the first jhana, or the supramundane bliss of the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna. There is no need even to mention it. A well-directed, noble mind, however, can provide all those forms of bliss. Therefore, it is said that it can make one increasingly noble.

## Benefits of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth. The teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.

The story of Soreyya, the treasurer's son, ends.
The commentary on the Citta Vagga ends.
The third chapter (Vagga) is finished.
212:
## The Teaching
(44) Who shall overcome this earth, and this world of Yama together with the world of devas? Who shall discern the well-taught path of Dhamma, as a skilled florist discerns a flower?
(45) The learner (sekha) shall overcome this earth, and this world of Yama together with the world of devas. The learner shall discern the well-taught path of Dhamma, as a skilled florist discerns a flower.

Monks, who shall investigate and discern with his own wisdom this internal earth, which is this individual existence (attabhāva)? Who shall investigate and discern with his own wisdom the four planes of misery (apāya) and this human world together with the worlds of devas and Brahmas? Just as a skilled florist selects and discerns flowers, in the same way, who shall investigate and discern with his own wisdom the collection of Dhamma known as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma), which are well-taught?

Monks, the seven types of learners (sekha) shall investigate and discern with their own wisdom this internal earth, which is this individual existence. The seven types of learners shall investigate and discern with their own wisdom the four planes of misery and this human world together with the worlds of devas and Brahmas. Just as a skilled florist selects and discerns flowers, in the same way, the seven types of learners shall investigate and discern with their own wisdom the collection of Dhamma known as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, which are well-taught.

## 4. Pupphavagga
## 1. The Story of Five Hundred Monks Occupied with Talk about the Earth
(Pathavikathāpasutapañcasatabhikkhu-vatthu)
While staying at Sāvatthī, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Who shall overcome this earth?" concerning five hundred monks who were occupied with talk about the earth.

It is said that those five hundred monks, after wandering through the countryside with the Blessed One, returned to the Jetavana monastery. In the evening, while sitting together in the assembly hall, they talked about the earth in the various places they had visited, saying: "On the way from such-and-such a village to such-and-such a village, the ground is level, or uneven, or very muddy, or very gravelly, or the soil is black, or the soil is red," and so forth.
213:
At that time, the All-Enlightened One arrived and asked, "Monks, for what talk are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "Venerable Sir, we are gathered here talking about the earth in the places we have traveled," the Teacher said, "Monks, this is called the external earth. You should perform the preliminary work of meditation on the internal earth," and he spoke these two verses.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, all five hundred monks attained Arahatship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the assembled audience.

The Story of Five Hundred Monks Occupied with Talk about the Earth ends.

## 2. The Story of the Elder who Meditated on a Mirage
(Marīcikammaṭṭhānikatthera-vatthu)
While staying at Sāvatthī, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Like a bubble" concerning a certain monk who used to meditate on the concept of a mirage.

## This Body Like a Mirage
That monk, having taken a meditation subject from the Teacher, entered the forest thinking, "I will practice the Dhamma of a recluse." Although he strove and exerted effort, he was unable to reach Arahatship. Thinking, "I will ask the Teacher to explain the meditation subject more specifically," he was returning to the Teacher's presence. On the way, he saw a mirage. (A mirage is a phenomenon that appears like water or vapor due to the intense heat of the summer season or the weakness of the eyes.)
214:
## This Body is Like Foam
