(46) Knowing this body to be like foam, and understanding it to be of the nature of a mirage, one should go beyond the sight of the King of Death, having broken the flower-tipped arrows of Māra.

**This body**: this physical frame which is a collection of hair, body hair, nails, teeth, and so forth. **Like foam**: knowing it to be like a globule of foam in the sense of being fragile, weak, and of a temporary nature. **Nature of a mirage**: the nature of being like a mirage which appears as a substance but is actually empty. **Understanding well**: one who knows this clearly. **Of Māra**: belonging to the King Māra. **Flower-tipped arrows**: the three planes of existence (tebhūmaka-vaṭṭa) which are like a delightful garden filled with various kinds of blossoms. **Having broken**: having destroyed them with the sword of the Knowledge of the Path of Arahantship. **Beyond the sight of the King of Death**: one should reach the peaceful city of Nibbāna, where the King of Death cannot see.

"This mirage, which usually occurs in the summer, appears as a physical form to those standing far away, but disappears to those who approach it; even so, this physical body (attabhāva) has the nature of a mirage because of its characteristic of arising and perishing." While he was developing the meditation on the mirage-like nature of the body, he became exhausted from his journey and bathed in the Aciravatī River. While sitting in the shade of a tree on a bank where the water flowed with great force, he saw large clumps of foam forming and breaking due to the impact of the water's surge. He then took it as an object of meditation, thinking, "This physical body also has such a nature because it arises and breaks away."

The Blessed One, while staying in the Gandhakuṭī, saw that monk and said, "Monk, it is just so; this physical body is indeed of such a nature. It has the nature of arising and perishing just like a globule of foam or a mirage." He then uttered this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the verse, that elder attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). He then approached the Buddha, praising and worshipping the Blessed One's golden-hued body.

The story of the elder who meditated on the mirage is finished.

## 3. The Story of Viḍūḍabha

(The Story of Viḍūḍabha)

The Blessed One, while staying at Sāvatthī, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Pupphāni heva pacinantaṃ" concerning Viḍūḍabha, who died along with his retinue, being overwhelmed and drowned by a great flood.

## The Account of King Pasenadi of Kosala, General Bandhula, and Mahāli the Licchavi

In the city of Sāvatthī, the son of King Mahākosala was named Prince Pasenadi. In the city of Vesālī, the son of the Licchavi King was the Licchavi Prince
215:
named Mahāli. In the city of Kusinārā, the son of the Malla King was named Bandhula. These three princes went to Takkasilā to study under a world-renowned teacher (Disāpāmokkha). They met at a rest house outside the city and, after asking each other about their reasons for coming, their lineages, and their names, they became friends. They approached the teacher together and studied their arts. Before long, having mastered their respective arts, they took leave of the teacher and departed together, returning to their own countries.

Among them, Prince Pasenadi demonstrated his skills to his father. The father, being pleased, consecrated him as king. 

Prince Mahāli demonstrated his skills to the Licchavi princes with great effort. During the demonstration, his eyes burst and he became blind. The Licchavi kings thought, "Alas! Our teacher has become blind. Therefore, we will not abandon him; we will look after him." They gave him a city gate that yielded a revenue of one hundred thousand. Relying on that, he lived there teaching the arts to five hundred Licchavi princes.

Prince Bandhula, however, had sixty bundles of sixty bamboos each brought to him. He had an iron rod inserted into the middle of each bundle and had the sixty bundles set upright. When the Malla princes told him, "Cut through these bamboo bundles," he leaped eighty cubits into the air and cut through them with his sword. At the last bundle, he heard a 'kiri' sound from the iron rod. When he asked, "What is this?" and learned that iron rods had been placed in all the bundles, he threw away his sword and wept, saying, "Among all these relatives and dear friends of mine, not even one person loved me enough to tell me this. If I had known, I would have cut them without making the sound of the iron rod."

He then said to his parents, "I wish to kill all these people and take the kingship." His parents forbade him in various ways, saying, "Dear son, this hereditary kingship cannot be obtained by such means." He then thought, "In that case, I will go to my friend," and he went to Sāvatthī.

King Pasenadi of Kosala, hearing of his friend Bandhula's arrival, went out to meet him and brought him into the city with great honor, appointing him to the position of Commander-in-Chief (General). Prince Bandhula then sent for his parents and made his home there in Sāvatthī.
216:
## King Kosala and the Venerable Ānanda

Then one day, King Pasenadi of Kosala, while standing on his palace terrace and looking down at the main street, saw several thousand monks going daily to the houses of the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, the laywoman Visākhā, and the laywoman Suppavāsā for their meals. Seeing them, he asked, "Where are the venerable ones going?" When told, "Great King, two thousand monks go daily to the house of the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika for the regular meals, lottery meals, meals for the sick, and so on; five hundred go to the house of Cūḷa-Anāthapiṇḍika; and similarly to the houses of Visākhā and Suppavāsā," the King, wishing to serve the community of monks himself, went to the monastery. He invited the Teacher along with a thousand monks and gave a great alms-offering with his own hands for seven days. On the seventh day, having paid homage to the Teacher, he requested, "Venerable Sir, please accept my alms-food regularly along with five hundred monks."

"Great King, Buddhas do not accept regular alms-food in a single place; many people look forward to the coming of the Buddhas," the Teacher replied. The King then said, "In that case, please send one monk regularly." The Teacher assigned the responsibility to the Elder Ānanda.

When the community of monks arrived, the King would take the bowl and say, "Let these people perform the service," without making specific arrangements or distinctions. After serving them himself for seven days, on the eighth day, he became distracted and negligent. In a royal palace, unless specifically ordered and urged, people do not prepare seats and invite monks to sit and serve them. Therefore, thinking, "We cannot stay here," many monks left. On the second day, the King was again negligent, and many monks left. On the third day, he was negligent again. At that time, leaving only the Elder Ānanda behind, the rest of the monks departed.
217:
Those who possess merit are considerate of circumstances and protect the faith of the lay supporters. All the disciples who have attained special distinctions—beginning with these eight individuals: the two chief male disciples, the Elders Sāriputta and Moggallāna; the two chief female disciples, Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā; among the male lay followers, the householder Citta and Hatthaka of Āḷavī; and among the female lay followers, Nandamātā of Veḷukaṇṭaka and Khujjuttarā—are of great merit and have fulfilled their aspirations because they have partially fulfilled the ten perfections.

The Elder Ānanda, too, having fulfilled the perfections for a hundred thousand aeons and being endowed with fulfilled aspirations, was of great merit; being one who acts with consideration of circumstances, he remained, protecting the faith of the lay supporter.

## Houses of Lay Devotees Monks Should Not Visit

When King Kosala arrived at the time the monks usually departed and saw the food and snacks remaining exactly as they had been placed, he asked, "What is this? Did the venerable ones not come?" Hearing the reply, "Great King, only the Elder Ānanda came alone," he thought, "They have certainly cut off my alms-offering to this extent," and becoming angry with the monks, he went to the Teacher. He said, "Venerable Sir, I prepared alms-food for five hundred monks, but it is said that only the Elder Ānanda came alone. The prepared food remains exactly as it was. The five hundred monks did not even consider taking their meal in my palace. What could be the reason, Bhante?"

The Teacher, without mentioning the fault of the monks, said, "Great King, my disciples do not have intimacy and trust with you; that is likely why they did not come." Wishing to clarify the reasons for not visiting or visiting families, he called the monks and taught this sutta:

"Monks, it is not fitting to visit a family endowed with nine qualities, or if one has visited, it is not fitting to sit down. What are the nine? 
1. They do not rise to greet one with pleasure. 
2. They do not pay homage with pleasure. 
3. They do not offer a seat with pleasure. 
4. They hide what they have. 
5. Though they have much, they give little. 
6. Though they have fine things, they give what is coarse. 
7. They give disrespectfully, not respectfully. 
8. They do not sit near to listen to the Dhamma. 
9. They do not listen attentively to what is spoken. 
Monks, it is not fitting to visit a family endowed with these nine qualities, or if one has visited, it is not fitting to sit down."

## Houses of Lay Devotees Monks Should Visit

"Monks, it is fitting to visit a family endowed with nine qualities, or if one has visited, it is fitting to sit down. What are the nine? 
1. They rise to greet one with pleasure. 
2. They pay homage with pleasure. 
3. They offer a seat with pleasure. 
4. They do not hide what they have. 
5. Having much, they give much. 
6. Having fine things, they give fine things. 
7. They give respectfully, not disrespectfully. 
8. They sit near respectfully. 
Monks, it is fitting to visit a family endowed with these nine qualities, or if one has visited, it is fitting to sit down."
218:
"Great King, in this way, my disciples will not come because they do not find familiarity with you," the Buddha said. He continued, "Even the wise of old, though they were respectfully attended to in a place where they lacked familiarity, would go only to a place where they felt familiar when they were afflicted with a life-threatening illness." When the King asked, "Venerable Sir, when did they go?" the Buddha recounted the past.

## Ascetics who were bored despite living in the Royal Palace

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, a king named Kesava renounced his kingdom and became an ascetic. Hearing that King Kesava had become an ascetic, five hundred of his men followed suit and became ascetics. He became known as the ascetic Kesava. His barber, who used to dress his hair and beard, also became an ascetic and became his close resident disciple named Kappaka. The ascetic Kesava stayed in the Himavanta for eight months with his followers. During the rainy season, they went to Bārāṇasī for salt and vinegar and entered the city for alms. When the King of Bārāṇasī saw the ascetic Kesava, he was filled with faith. He made them promise to stay in his capital for the four months of the rainy season, settled them in his park, and visited the ascetic every morning and evening to pay his respects. After staying for two or three days, the other ascetics became dissatisfied and bored because they were disturbed by the noise of elephants and other sounds, and they asked for permission to leave.

"Dear sons, where do you wish to go?" he asked. "Teacher, we wish to go to the Himavanta," they replied. "Dear sons, the King took a promise from us on the very day we arrived to stay in this park for the four months of the rainy season. How can we go?" he said. "Teacher, you gave the promise without consulting us. We are unable to stay here. We will stay in a place not far from this park where we can hear news of you," they said. After paying homage to their teacher, they departed. Only the teacher remained, along with his resident disciple named Kappaka. When the King came to pay his respects, he asked, "Where are the noble ones?" "Great King, they all said they were dissatisfied and bored, and have gone to the Himavanta," he replied.

The ascetic Kappaka also soon became bored. Although the teacher repeatedly tried to stop him, he said, "I cannot stay," and departed. However, instead of going to the other ascetics, he stayed in a nearby place, listening for news of his teacher. Later, the teacher, longing for his resident disciples, developed a stomach ailment. Although the King had him treated by skilled physicians, the illness did not subside. Then the ascetic Kesava asked, "Great King, do you wish for my recovery?" "Venerable Sir, if I were able, I would make you well this very moment," the King replied. "Great King, if you wish for my recovery, send me to my resident disciples," he said. The King agreed, saying, "Very well, Venerable Sir." He had the ascetic Kesava placed on a litter and sent four ministers, led by the minister Nārada, with the instruction: "Find out news of my noble teacher and send word back to me." When the resident disciple Kappaka heard the news of his teacher's arrival, he went out to meet him. When asked, "Where are the others?" he replied, "They are living in such-and-such a place." When those ascetics heard of their teacher's arrival, they gathered at that very spot, gave the teacher warm water, and offered various fruits. At that very moment, his illness subsided and he became well.
219:
Within just two or three days, the ascetic Kesava regained a complexion like the color of gold. At that time, the minister Nārada questioned the ascetic Kesava. (The ascetic Kesava replied with these verses:)

## Trust Brings Intimacy, Intimacy Brings Joy

Having abandoned the King of Men, who can fulfill all desires, why, O Blessed Kesava, do you delight in the hermitage of Kappa?

Nārada, there are beautiful, pleasant, and delightful trees in Kappa’s hermitage. The well-spoken, kind, and sweet words of Kappa delight me.

Having eaten fine rice seasoned with pure meat, how can the saltless sāmāka and nīvāra grains satisfy you?

Nārada, whether it be delicious or not, whether it be little or much, wherever one eats with trust, that is where it is truly good. Trust is the supreme flavor.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the King was Moggallāna, the minister Nārada was Sāriputta, the disciple named Kappa was Ānanda, and the ascetic Kesava was I myself." Having thus identified the Jātaka, he said, "Great King, in this way, wise men of the past, when they reached a life-threatening illness, went to a place where they felt love and trust. My disciples, it seems, do not find such trust in your presence."

## King Kosala Receives a Slave Girl while Requesting a Sakyan

King Pasenadi of Kosala also thought, "I should act in a way that creates trust and intimacy with the Saṅgha of monks." While considering how to do this, he thought, "It would be proper to have a princess who is a kinswoman of the Blessed One in my palace. If this were so, the young monks and novices would come to me regularly with trust, thinking, 'The King is a kinsman of the Blessed One.'" He then sent a message to the Sakyans saying, "Give me one of your daughters," and commanded his messengers, "Ask whose daughter she is, and return only after finding out for certain."

The messengers went and requested a maiden from the Sakyans. The Sakyans assembled and consulted each other: "The King is from another region. If we do not give her, he will destroy us. However, he is not of equal birth to our clan. What should be done?" Then Mahānāma said, "I have a daughter named Vāsabhakhattiyā, born from the womb of my slave woman, who has reached the pinnacle of beauty. Let us give her." They agreed and told the messengers, "Very well, we shall give a royal maiden to King Pasenadi." When asked, "Whose daughter is she?", they replied, "She is the daughter of the Sakyan Mahānāma, the son of the Blessed One’s paternal uncle, and her name is Vāsabhakhattiyā."

The messengers went and reported this to the King. The King said, "If that is so, it is very good. Bring her quickly. Kings are full of deceit. They might even send the daughter of a slave. Our King [will accept] only a princess who eats together from the same meal-tray as her father..."
220:
“I desire her,” they reported. Mahānāma the Sakyan consented, saying, “Very well, friends.” He had Princess Vāsabhakhattiyā adorned, and when it was time for his meal, he had her called and made it appear as if he were eating together with her, then handed Vāsabhakhattiyā over to the messengers.

The messengers took the princess and, upon reaching Sāvatthī, reported the matter to the King. The King, with a delighted heart, made Princess Vāsabhakhattiyā the head of five hundred concubines and consecrated her in the position of Chief Queen. Before long, Queen Vāsabhakhattiyā gave birth to a son who had a complexion like gold.

## How the Name Viḍūḍabha Originated

On the day the young prince was to be named, King Kosala sent a messenger to the prince's grandfather, King Mahānāma, asking, “The Sakyan princess Vāsabhakhattiyā has given birth to a son; what name would you like to give the child?” The minister who carried the message was somewhat hard of hearing. He went and reported to the grandfather, King Mahānāma. Upon hearing this, King Mahānāma said, “Even before Vāsabhakhattiyā gave birth to a son, she surpassed all people. Now she will be extremely dear to the King; she will be Vallabhā (Beloved).” The hard-of-hearing minister misheard the word “Vallabhā” and, noting it as “Viḍūḍabha,” approached King Kosala and reported, “Great King, you should name the prince Viḍūḍabha.” King Kosala thought, “This must be an ancient family name of ours,” and gave him the name Viḍūḍabha.

## Viḍūḍabha’s Journey to Kapilavatthu

While Viḍūḍabha was still young, the King, thinking “I will do what is pleasing to the Teacher,” gave him the position of general. As Prince Viḍūḍabha grew up with princely care, at the age of seven, he saw other princes receiving gifts like toy elephants and horses from their maternal grandparents' homes and asked his mother, “Mother, other princes receive gifts and presents from their maternal grandparents' homes. No one sends anything to me. Why is that? Are you an orphan without mother or father?” When Prince Viḍūḍabha asked this repeatedly, Queen Vāsabhakhattiyā deceived him, saying, “My dear son, your relatives are the Sakyan kings. Your grandparents live far away. That is why they cannot send anything.” Later, at the age of sixteen, he said, “Mother, I wish to see your maternal relatives.” Although she forbade him, saying, “My son, it is not suitable; what will you do by going to Kapilavatthu?”, he pleaded again and again. Then, Viḍūḍabha’s mother consented, saying, “If so, then go.” Prince Viḍūḍabha took leave of the Great King and set out with a large retinue.

Princess Vāsabhakhattiyā sent a letter ahead, saying, “I am living happily here in Sāvatthī;”
221:
“...Let the noble Sakyan kings not show any difference to Prince Viḍūḍabha.” The Sakyans, knowing of Viḍūḍabha's arrival, thought, “We cannot pay homage to him,” and sent all the princes younger than Viḍūḍabha to the countryside. When Viḍūḍabha arrived at Kapilavatthu, they assembled in the Santhāgāra (the Santhāgāra is the royal hall where all the affairs of the citizens are decided).

Prince Viḍūḍabha went to the Santhāgāra and stood there.

## Washing the Bench where Viḍūḍabha Sat with Milk

Then they introduced him, saying, “Dear son, this is your grandmother; this is your uncle,” and made him pay homage to them. Viḍūḍabha went around paying homage to everyone, but seeing not a single person paying homage to him, he asked, “How is this? Are there no people who should pay homage to me?” The Sakyans replied, “Dear son, your younger brothers, the princes who are younger than you, have gone to the countryside,” and they showed great hospitality to Viḍūḍabha. Viḍūḍabha stayed for two or three days and then departed with his large retinue.

At that time, a slave woman washed the wooden bench where Viḍūḍabha had sat in the Santhāgāra with milk-water, cursing and reviling, “This is the bench where the son of the slave Vāsabhakhattiyā sat.” A certain soldier, having forgotten his weapon, returned to retrieve it and heard the insults directed at Prince Viḍūḍabha. Upon inquiring about the reason, he learned that “Vāsabhakhattiyā was born from the womb of a slave woman, fathered by the Sakyan named Mahānāma,” and he told the army. A great commotion arose: “Queen Vāsabhakhattiyā is said to be the daughter of a slave!” Hearing this, Prince Viḍūḍabha made a resolution: “Let these Sakyans wash my seat with milk-water for now. When I am established in kingship, I shall take the blood from the throats of all these Sakyans and wash the bench where I sat.”

## The Father’s Lineage is Primary

When Prince Viḍūḍabha reached Sāvatthī, the ministers reported the whole matter to the King. King Pasenadi of Kosala became angry with the Sakyans, thinking, “They gave me the daughter of a slave.” He withdrew the protection and retinue he had given to Princess Vāsabhakhattiyā and his son Viḍūḍabha, and ordered that they be given only what is due to male and female slaves. Two or three days later, the Teacher went to the palace of King Kosala and sat on the prepared seat. The King came, paid homage, and reported, “Venerable Sir, your relatives gave the daughter of a slave to me. Therefore, I have withdrawn the protection and retinue from the Queen and her son, and have kept them by giving only what is due to male and female slaves.” The Teacher said, “Great King, the Sakyans have done what is improper. When giving, they should have given one of equal birth. However, Great King, I shall tell you one thing...”
222:
“Queen Vāsabhakhattiya is the daughter of King Mahānāma and received the consecration in your palace as a true Khattiya. Prince Viṭaṭūbha was also born depending on you, a true Khattiya. What does the mother's lineage matter? The father's lineage alone is the standard,” the Buddha declared. He then related the Kaṭṭhahāri Jātaka as a story of the past: “In the past, wise men gave the position of Chief Queen to a poor wood-gathering woman. The prince born from her womb attained kingship in Bārāṇasī, which was twelve leagues wide, and became known as King Kaṭṭhavāhana.”

King Pasenadi of Kosala, having heard this Dhamma discourse, was pleased, thinking, “Indeed, only the father's lineage is the standard.” He restored the usual protection and retinue to Queen Vāsabhakhattiya and her son Viṭaṭūbha. He also appointed Prince Viṭaṭūbha to the position of commander-in-chief.

## Mallikā's Pregnancy Craving and Bandhula's Bravery

Commander Bandhula had a wife named Mallikā, who was the daughter of a Malla king in Kusinārā. For a long time, Mallikā did not bear any children. Then, Commander Bandhula sent her away, saying, “Go back to your own family home.” Mallikā thought, “I will go only after seeing the Teacher.” She entered Jetavana, and while she stood after paying homage to the Blessed One, she was asked, “Where are you going?” She replied, “Venerable Sir, my husband Bandhula is sending me back to my family home.” When asked, “For what reason?” she replied, “It is said that I am barren and childless.”

(It is said that even if a conception occurs, it may fail due to the affliction of wind, or due to worms, or due to the result of unwholesome kamma. There is no such thing as a truly barren woman.)

When the Buddha said, “If that is the case, there is no need to go. Return home,” Mallikā, with a joyful heart, paid homage to the Buddha and went home. When asked, “Why have you returned?” she said, “I have returned because the Blessed One stopped me.” Commander Bandhula accepted this, thinking, “The All-Enlightened Buddha, who is far-sighted, must have seen a reason.” Before long, Mallikā conceived, and a pregnancy craving arose in her. She informed him, “A craving has arisen in me.” When asked, “What kind of craving?” she replied, “My lord, I wish to descend into, bathe in, and drink the water from the ceremonial coronation tank of the confederate princes in the city of Vesālī.”

Bandhula said, “Very well.” He took his bow, which required the strength of a thousand men to string, placed Mallikā in the chariot, and departed from Sāvatthī. Driving the chariot, he entered Vesālī through the gate assigned to Mahāli the Licchavī. Mahāli the Licchavī was residing near that gate. Upon hearing the sound of the chariot striking the threshold, he said, “This is the sound of Bandhula's chariot. Today, danger will arise for the Licchavīs.”

The guards inside and outside the pond were very strong. An iron net was spread over the top, leaving no space even for birds to enter. However, Commander Bandhula descended from the chariot, drove away the guards by striking them with his sword, cut the iron net, and entered the pond. He let his wife bathe and drink, bathed himself, and then placed Mallikā back in the chariot. He left the city and returned by the same path he had come.
223:
## The Destruction of the Licchavī Princes by Bandhula's Arrow

The guards informed the Licchavī princes. Enraged, the Licchavīs mounted five hundred chariots and set out, saying, "We will capture General Bandhula and Mallikā." When this was told to Mahāli the Licchavī, he said, "Do not go; that Bandhula will kill you all." The Licchavī princes replied, "We will certainly go." Mahāli then advised, "If you must go, turn back when you see the place where the hub of his chariot wheel has entered the earth. If you do not turn back from there, you will hear a sound like thunder ahead; turn back from that place. If you still do not turn back, you will see holes in the fronts of your chariots; turn back from there. Do not proceed further."

Disregarding Mahāli's words, the five hundred Licchavī princes pursued General Bandhula. Seeing them, Mallikā said, "My lord, the chariots are visible." He replied, "Tell me when only a single chariot front is visible." When all the chariots were aligned so that they appeared as one, Mallikā said, "My lord, only a single chariot front is visible."

General Bandhula then said, "In that case, take these reins," and giving the reins to Mallikā, he stood in the chariot and drew his bow. The chariot wheel sank into the earth up to the hub. Even seeing this, the Licchavīs did not turn back. General Bandhula went a little further and twanged the bowstring; it sounded like a thunderclap. Still, the Licchavīs did not turn back but continued their pursuit. Standing in his chariot, Bandhula shot a single arrow. That arrow pierced the fronts of the five hundred chariots, passed through the bodies of the five hundred princes at the place where their waistbands were fastened, and entered the earth.

Unaware that they had been pierced, the Licchavīs continued to pursue him, shouting, "Stop, Bandhula! Stop, Bandhula!" Bandhula stopped his chariot and said, "You are all dead men; I do not fight with the dead." They replied, "Dead men are not like us." He then said, "In that case, loosen the waistband of the very last prince." They did so. As soon as the waistband was loosened, that prince fell dead. Then Bandhula said to all of them, "You are all in the same condition. Go back to your homes, settle your affairs, give your final instructions to your wives and children, and then remove your armor." Following his instructions, they all reached the end of their lives.

## The Death of Bandhula and His Sons

General Bandhula brought Mallikā to Sāvatthī. Mallikā gave birth to twin sons sixteen times. All thirty-two sons were brave, possessed great strength, and attained mastery in all arts. Each son had a retinue of a thousand men. When they went to the royal palace with their father, the palace courtyard was filled with them.
224:
Then one day, people who had lost their cases through deceit in the hall of judgment saw General Bandula approaching. Wailing loudly, they informed General Bandula that the judicial ministers had decided the cases by taking bribes and acting dishonestly. General Bandula went to the court, investigated the case, and restored the property to its rightful owner. The great multitude shouted "Sādhu" in approval. King Pasenadi Kosala asked, "What is this sound?" and upon hearing the reason, he was pleased. He removed all those corrupt ministers from their posts and entrusted the hall of judgment to Bandula alone. From then on, General Bandula judged cases rightly and fairly. Because General Bandula alone was deciding the cases, the former judicial ministers, no longer receiving any bribes and having little gain, slandered him to the King, saying, "General Bandula aspires to the kingship."

The King, believing the words of those former ministers, was unable to restrain and calm his mind. He thought, "If General Bandula is killed right here, I will be blamed." So, he had his spies instigate a disturbance in the borderlands. He then summoned General Bandula and sent him off, saying, "It is reported that the borderlands are in revolt. Go with your sons and capture the thieves." He also dispatched other capable great warriors with them, ordering, "Behead General Bandula along with his thirty-two sons right there and bring back their heads." As soon as General Bandula reached the borderlands, the spies who were posing as thieves fled upon hearing that the General was coming. General Bandula settled the area, making it peaceful for the inhabitants, and turned back. Then, at a place not far from the city, the warriors sent by the King beheaded General Bandula along with his sons.

On that very day, Mallikā had invited the two Chief Disciples along with five hundred monks. Early in the morning, a letter was brought and given to her, saying, "Your husband, General Bandula, has been beheaded along with your sons." Mallikā, knowing the news, did not say a single word to anyone. Placing the letter in her lap, she continued to serve the Sangha. Then, while Mallikā's attendants were serving the monks and carrying a jar of ghee, they broke the jar in front of the Elders. The Captain of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) said, "That which is of a nature to break has broken; one should not worry about it."

Mallikā took the letter from her lap and said, "Venerable Sir, they have sent me this letter saying that the head of my father-like husband, General Bandula, has been cut off along with those of my thirty-two sons. Even hearing this news, I do not worry; why then should I worry about a broken jar of ghee?" The Captain of the Dhamma, the Venerable Sāriputta, recited the verses beginning with "Unmarked and unknown is the life of mortals here" (Sutta Nipāta 579), and after preaching the Dhamma, he rose from his seat and went to the monastery. Mallikā then summoned her thirty-two daughters-in-law and advised them, "Your husbands were innocent, but they have received the fruit of their own past kamma..."
225:
...do not grieve, do not lament, and do not harbor ill-will toward the King."

## The Helpless Passing of King Pasenadi Kosala
The King's spies, hearing Mallikā's words, went and reported their innocence to the King. The King, overcome with remorse, went to Mallikā's house, asked for forgiveness from her and her daughters-in-law, and granted her a boon. Mallikā said, "Let the boon granted to me be reserved." After the King left, she offered food on behalf of the deceased, bathed, and then approached the King. Bowing, she said, "Great King, you have granted me a boon. I have no need for any other boon. Please allow me and my thirty-two daughters-in-law to return to our parental homes." The King consented.

Mallikā sent the thirty-two daughters-in-law to their respective parental homes, and she herself went to her parental home in the city of Kusinārā.

King Pasenadi Kosala then appointed Dīgha Kārāyana, the nephew of General Bandula, to the position of General. However, Dīgha Kārāyana went about seeking an opportunity to harm the King, thinking, "My uncle was killed by this King." The King, from the time he had the innocent Bandula killed, was filled with remorse and could find no peace of mind, nor could he enjoy the pleasures of kingship. At that time, the Teacher was residing near a Sakyan market town named Medāḷupa. King Pasenadi Kosala went there, established a camp not far from the monastery, and thinking, "I will pay homage to the Teacher with a small retinue," went to the monastery. He handed over the five royal regalia to General Dīgha Kārāyana and entered the Perfumed Chamber alone.

(The entire account should be understood as presented in the Dhammacetiya Sutta.)

While King Pasenadi Kosala was inside the Perfumed Chamber, General Dīgha Kārāyana took those five royal regalia, consecrated Prince Viṭaṭūbha as king, and leaving only one horse and one servant woman for the King, he turned back and went to Sāvatthī.

King Pasenadi Kosala, after engaging in pleasant conversation with the Teacher and paying homage to Him, came out and did not see his army. He questioned the remaining servant woman and, upon hearing the news, thought, "I will take my nephew, King Ajātasattu, and capture Viṭaṭūbha." He set out for the city of Rājagaha. Arriving at the city at an improper time when the gates were already closed, he lay down in a rest house. Exhausted by the wind and sun, he passed away right there in that rest house during the night. When the night turned to dawn, [people cried out], "O King of Kosala, you have become helpless..."
226:
"O Great King, the Great King has become helpless." Hearing the voice of that woman lamenting thus, they reported it to King Ajātasattu. King Ajātasattu then performed the funeral rites for his uncle with great honor and ceremony.

## The Shade of Kinsmen is Cooler than the Shade of Trees

When Viṭaṭūbha attained kingship, he remembered that grudge and, thinking, "I will kill all the Sakyans," set out with a vast army. On that day, at dawn, the Teacher, surveying the world, saw the impending destruction of his kinsmen. Thinking, "It is proper to provide protection to my kinsmen," he went for alms in the morning. After returning from the alms-round, he took the lion's posture in the Gandhakuṭi. In the evening, he traveled through the air and sat at the foot of a tree with sparse and hot shade near the city of Kapilavatthu. Nearby, within Viṭaṭūbha's territory, there was a large banyan tree with thick, cool shade. Seeing the Teacher, Viṭaṭūbha approached, paid homage, and said, "Venerable Sir, for what reason do you sit at the foot of this tree with sparse shade in such scorching heat? Venerable Sir, please sit at the foot of that banyan tree which has cool shade." When the Teacher replied, "Let it be, O Great King; the shade of kinsmen is indeed cool," Viṭaṭūbha thought, "The Teacher must have come to protect his kinsmen." He paid homage to the Teacher and returned to Sāvatthī. The Teacher also rose into the air and returned to Jetavana.

## The Result of Evil Kamma

Remembering the fault of the Sakyans, Viṭaṭūbha set out a second time, but seeing the Teacher in the same place, he returned again. He set out a third time, saw the Teacher there, and returned once more. However, when he set out for the fourth time, the Teacher looked into the past kamma of the Sakyans and, knowing that their evil deed of casting poison into the river on a certain day could not be averted, he did not go on that fourth occasion. Viṭaṭūbha set out with a massive army, intending to slaughter the Sakyans.

The kinsmen of the Buddha, however, were not killers of other beings; even at the cost of their own lives, they would not take the lives of others. Those Sakyans thought, "We are well-trained, skilled in archery, and great bowmen. However, it is not proper for us to take the lives of others. We will show our skill and make them flee." Having made this resolution, they put on their armor and set out to engage in battle.

The arrows shot by the Sakyans passed through the gaps between Viṭaṭūbha's soldiers, through the gaps in their shields and ear-holes. Seeing this, Viṭaṭūbha said, "Friends, do not the Sakyans say, 'We are not killers of beings'? Yet they are destroying my men." At that moment, a man said to Viṭaṭūbha, "O King, what are you saying? Please look back." The Sakyans...
227:
...are killing my men," he said again. When the man replied, "Not even one of your soldiers has died," Viṭaṭūbha said, "Friends, if that is so, I urge you to count them." Upon counting, not a single man was found missing or dead. Viṭaṭūbha then retreated from that spot and said, "Friends, kill all those who say, 'We are Sakyans.' But spare the lives of those standing near my grandfather, Mahānāma the Sakyan."

The Sakyans, seeing no other way to save themselves, some stood holding blades of grass in their mouths, and others stood holding reeds. When asked, "Are you Sakyans or not?" those Sakyans would not tell a lie even at the cost of their lives. Therefore, those standing with grass in their mouths said, "Not a Sakyan (Sāka), but grass (Tiṇa)." Those standing with reeds said, "Not a Sakyan, but a reed (Naḷa)." Only those Sakyans who stood near King Mahānāma were spared. Among them, those who stood holding grass became known as the "Tiṇa-Sakyans," and those who stood holding reeds became known as the "Naḷa-Sakyans." Viṭaṭūbha, without even sparing the nursing infants, had them slaughtered, causing a river of blood to flow, and he washed his footstool with the blood from the throats of those Sakyans. In this manner, the Sakyan lineage was brought to destruction by Viṭaṭūbha.

## King Mahānāma Staying in the Naga Realm for Twelve Years

Viṭaṭūbha, having taken his grandfather, King Mahānāma the Sakyan, with him, was returning when, at breakfast time, he sat down at a certain place to eat. When the food trays were brought, he invited his grandfather, saying, "Let us eat together." Those of the warrior caste (Khattiya), even if they must sacrifice their lives, do not eat with the sons of slave women. Therefore, King Mahānāma, looking at a lake, said, "My grandson, my body is soiled; I will bathe." Viṭaṭūbha replied, "Grandfather, very well, please bathe." King Mahānāma thought, "If I do not eat with this Viṭaṭūbha, he will kill me. It is better for me to die by my own choice." He untied his hair, made a knot at the end, inserted his big toes into his hair, and submerged himself in the water.

Due to the power of King Mahānāma's virtue, the Naga realm became hot. When the Naga King investigated the cause and discovered it, he went to King Mahānāma, placed him on his hood, and brought him to the Naga realm. King Mahānāma resided in that Naga realm for twelve years.
228:
King Viṭaṭūbha remained there, waiting and expecting, thinking, "My grandfather the King will come at any moment." When King Mahānāma had been gone for a very long time, Viṭaṭūbha had the pond searched. Even after searching among the clothes and belongings of others by the light of torches, he did not see him. Thinking that the King must have left, he departed.

## The Evil Fate of Viṭaṭūbha and His Men
Viṭaṭūbha reached the Aciravatī River during the night and stayed in a temporary encampment. Some of the soldiers slept on the sandbanks within the river, while others slept on the dry ground outside the river. Among those sleeping inside the river, there were those who were free from the evil unwholesome kamma they had committed in the past. Among those sleeping outside the river, there were those who were not free from the evil unwholesome kamma they had committed in the past. In the places where they slept, ants arose and bit them. They got up, saying, "There are ants in my sleeping place! There are ants in my sleeping place!" Those who were free from past unwholesome kamma went up and slept on the dry ground. Those who were not free from past unwholesome kamma went down and slept on the sandbanks. At that moment, a great cloud arose and a heavy rain fell violently upstream. A torrent of water came down the river and swept King Viṭaṭūbha along with all his retinue and followers into the ocean. There, they all became food for fish and turtles.

## The Past Evil Kamma of the Sakyans
The multitude of people started a conversation: "The death of the Sakyan princes was unjust. It is truly improper that the Sakyans should be killed by being hacked to pieces in such a manner." When the Buddha heard this conversation, he said, "Monks, although such a death is indeed improper for the Sakyan princes in this present existence, they have received a death that is entirely fitting due to the power of the evil kamma they committed in a past life." When asked, "Exalted Buddha, what evil deed did those Sakyan princes commit in a past life?", he replied, "Those Sakyans, acting together as one, once threw poison into a river."
229:
Again, one day, many monks started a conversation in the Dhamma Hall: "While Viṭaṭūbha was returning after killing so many Sakyan princes, even before his own desire was fulfilled, he became food for fish and turtles in the great ocean along with all his forces." The Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit here together?" When they replied, "It is such and such a subject, Bhante," he said, "Monks, before the desires of these beings are fulfilled, King Death, like a great flood that overwhelms and drowns a sleeping village, cuts off the life faculty and causes them to sink into the four oceans of the states of misery (apāya)." He then spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(47) Pupphāni heva pacinantaṃ, byāsattamanasaṃ naraṃ.
Suttaṃ gāmaṃ mahogho va, maccu ādāya gacchati.

Just as a great flood carries away a sleeping village, so does Death carry away the man who is gathering the flowers of sensual pleasures, whose mind is intensely attached to them.

"Flowers" refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure. "Gathering" means even while choosing them. "Whose mind is intensely attached" means one whose mind is deeply clinging through various ways and means. "The man" refers to a being. "A great flood" means a massive torrent of water. "Sleeping" refers to the people of a village who are asleep. "Carries away" means just as it takes them away. "Death" means the King of Death. "Carries away" means he takes them and goes.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth. The Dhamma teaching became beneficial to the multitude.
The Story of Viṭaṭūbha ends.

## 4. The Story of the Maiden Patipūjikā
(Patipūjikākumārī Vatthu)
The Buddha, while residing in Sāvatthī, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Pupphāni heva" concerning a maiden named Patipūjikā.
In the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, a deva named Mālabhārī entered a garden surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs. Five hundred nymphs climbed the trees, plucked flowers, and threw them down. Five hundred nymphs gathered the fallen flowers and decorated the deva. Among those nymphs, one nymph passed away while still on a branch; her body vanished and ceased like the flame of a lamp.
That nymph took conception in a noble family in Sāvatthī. When she was born, she possessed the knowledge of recollecting past lives (Jātissara-ñāṇa). Constantly remembering that she had been the consort of the deva Mālabhārī, when she reached maturity, she made offerings of incense, flowers, and so on, and made a prayer: "May I be reborn in the presence of my lord, the deva Mālabhārī."
230:
## How She Came to be Named Patipūjikā
When that young woman reached the age of sixteen, she went to her husband's house. Even so, she continued to give alms-food by tickets (salāka-bhatta), food given on the fortnights (pakkhika-bhatta), robes for the rainy season (vassāvāsika), and so on. She would make a wish, saying, "May this merit of mine be a support for my rebirth in the presence of my lord and husband." Then the monks, seeing that this young woman was diligent and energetic, and that whenever she performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms, she always wished for her husband, gave her the name "Patipūjikā" (One who honors her husband).

## Fulfillment of the Prayer
This young woman, Patipūjikā, would constantly clean the refectory, set out drinking water and water for use, and prepare the seats. Other people who wished to give alms-food by tickets and so forth would bring their offerings to her and say, "Dear daughter, please present these offerings to the Saṅgha of monks on our behalf." In this way, as she came and went, Patipūjikā gained fifty-six wholesome states of mind with every single step. She conceived a child in her womb, and after ten months, she gave birth to a son. When that child was able to walk, she gave birth to another son. In this manner, she had four sons. One day, after giving alms, making offerings, listening to the Dhamma, and observing the precepts, she passed away at the end of the day due to a sudden illness and was reborn in the presence of her former lord, the celestial son Mālabhārī.

## Explaining Her Life on Earth
The other goddesses, her companions, were still decorating the celestial son Mālabhārī during all that time. When Mālabhārī saw the goddess Patipūjikā, he asked, "You have not been seen since early this morning. Where did you go?" She replied, "I passed away, my lord." "What are you saying?" he asked. "It is true, my lord, I passed away," she said. "Where were you reborn?" he asked. "In a family home in Sāvatthī," she explained.

"How long did you stay in that life?" he asked again. "My lord, after ten months I was born from my mother's womb. When I was sixteen, I went to my husband's house and gave birth to four sons. While performing meritorious deeds such as giving alms and wishing for you, I have returned and been reborn in your presence once again, my lord."

## Spiritual Urgency Regarding Human Life
"What is the lifespan of humans?" he asked. "They live for only about a hundred years," she replied. "Is it only that much?" he asked. "Yes, my lord, it is only about a hundred years," she confirmed. "Do humans who are born with such a short lifespan spend their time in sleep and heedlessness, or do they perform meritorious deeds such as giving alms?" he asked. "What are you saying, my lord? Humans are constantly heedless, as if they were born with an incalculable lifespan and as if they were ageless and immortal," she said.
231:
## The Teaching
(48) Just as a man gathering flowers,
Whose mind is deeply attached to them,
Is overcome by Death (the Ender)
While still unsated in his sensual pleasures.

"Flowers": The five strands of sensual pleasure. "Gathering": Even while in the process of selecting. "Deeply attached mind": A mind that is intensely clinging in various ways. "Unsated in sensual pleasures": Being unsatisfied in seeking, obtaining, enjoying, and accumulating both the objects of sensuality and the defilements of sensuality. "The Ender (Death)": Death brings such a being under its power.

When this was said, a great sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arose in the celestial son Mālabhārī: "It is said that humans who are born with a lifespan of only a hundred years lie down and fall into a deep sleep in heedlessness. When will they ever be released from suffering?"

(A hundred years of human life is equivalent to one day and one night for the gods of Tāvatiṃsa.)

## The Past and Present of Patipūjikā
On the following day, when the monks entered the village and saw that the refectory had not been cleaned, the seats had not been prepared, and the drinking and utility water had not been set out, they asked, "Where is the lay follower Patipūjikā?" The people replied, "Venerable sirs, where could you see the lay follower Patipūjikā? Yesterday, after you had finished your meal and departed, she passed away in the evening." Hearing this, the worldling monks, remembering her kindness and service, were unable to restrain their tears. For the Arahants, spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega) arose.

After finishing their meal, those monks went to the monastery, paid homage to the Buddha, and asked: "Magnificent Blessed One, the lay follower named Patipūjikā performed various meritorious deeds with great diligence and always wished for her husband. She has now passed away. Where has she been reborn, Lord?" The Buddha replied, "Bhikkhus, she was reborn in the presence of her own lord and husband." "Lord, she is not in the presence of her husband," they said. "Bhikkhus, she did not wish for a husband in this human world. In the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, there is a celestial son named Mālabhārī who is her lord and husband. She passed away from her state of decorating Mālabhārī with flowers and has been reborn once again in his presence." "Is it really so, Lord?" they asked. "Yes, bhikkhus, it is so," the Buddha replied.
232:
“Venerable Sir, the life of beings is indeed very short. Even in the morning, they were still offering alms-food to your disciples, yet by the evening, they have passed away due to a disease that arose,” when he addressed the Buddha thus, the Buddha said, “Dear monks, it is true that the life of beings is short. Therefore, while these beings are not yet satisfied or contented with the objects of sensual pleasure (vatthu-kāma) and the defilements of sensual pleasure (kilesa-kāma), Death, having brought them under his power, carries them away while they are weeping and lamenting,” and he spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala) and so forth. The Dhamma teaching became beneficial to the great multitude.

The Story of the Maiden Patipūjikā ends.

## 5. The Story of the Miserly Treasurer Kosiya
(Macchariya-kosiya-seṭṭhi-vatthu)
While residing at Sāvatthī, the Teacher (the Buddha) spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Yathāpi bhamaro pupphaṃ' concerning the miserly treasurer Kosiya. His story originated in Rājagaha.

## The Miserliness of the Great Treasurer
Not far from the city of Rājagaha, there was a market town named Sakkāra. In that town lived a treasurer named Macchariya Kosiya, who possessed a fortune of eighty crores. That treasurer would not give even a drop of oil on the tip of a blade of grass to others, nor would he use or enjoy it himself. Thus, such a great amount of wealth existed for that treasurer. He did not allow it to be of any benefit to his children, wife, or others, nor to ascetics and brahmins. It remained unusable, like a large lake guarded by an ogre (rakkhasa). One day, at dawn, the Teacher arose from the attainment of Great Compassion and, while surveying the world for those worthy of being awakened to the Four Noble Truths, he saw the potential (upanissaya) for the treasurer Macchariya Kosiya and his wife, who lived forty-five leagues away, to attain the fruit of Stream-entry.

On the day before the Buddha saw this, the treasurer had gone to the royal palace to attend upon the King. While returning after serving the King, he saw a man from the countryside who was very hungry, eating a pan-baked cake (kapallaka-pūva) made of barley. Seeing this, a craving for that cake arose in him. Upon reaching his home, he thought, “If I say that I want to eat a pan-baked cake, many people will want to eat with me. If many people eat, much of my sesame, rice, ghee, molasses, and so forth will be exhausted. I will not tell anyone.” Thinking thus, he endured the craving and went about his business. As time passed, he became pale like a withered leaf and his body became such that his veins stood out. Then, unable to endure the craving, he entered his inner chamber and lay down on his bed. Even so, because he was afraid of losing his wealth, he remained silent without saying a single word to anyone.

Then, the treasurer's wife approached him, massaged his back, and asked, “Lord Treasurer, what discomfort has befallen you?” When he replied, “I have no discomfort whatsoever,” she asked again, “Is the King angry with you, Lord Treasurer?”
233:
When he said, “The King is not angry with me either,” she asked again, “If that is so, what is it? Have your children or your servants and workers done something unpleasant to you?” When he replied, “There is no such reason of that nature,” she asked once more, “Do you have a craving for some object, Lord?” Even though she asked thus, he remained silent and lay there without saying a word because he was afraid of losing his wealth. Then his wife said, “Speak, Lord, do you have a craving for some object?” The treasurer, as if struggling to swallow his words, said, “I have a craving.” “What craving is it, Lord?” she asked. He told her that he wished to eat a pan-baked cake.

“If that is the case, why did you not tell me? Are you a poor man? I will now fry enough pan-baked cakes for all the inhabitants of the entire market town,” she said. Then he said, “What benefit is there for you from those inhabitants of the market town? They will do their own work and eat.”

“If that is so, I will fry enough pan-baked cakes for the people living in just one street,” she said. He replied, “I know how very wealthy you are.” “I will fry enough for all the people living in the vicinity of this house,” she said. He replied, “I know how great your desires are.” “If that is so, I will fry just enough for your children and wife,” she said. He replied, “What benefit is there from those children and wife?” “Should I fry just enough for you, Lord Treasurer, and me?” she asked. He replied, “What would you do with it?” When she said, “If that is so, I will fry just enough for you alone, Lord Treasurer,” he said, “If it is fried in a place where many people can see, many people will desire it. Setting aside the good rice, take the broken rice, the brazier, and the pan; take also a little milk, ghee, honey, and molasses, and go up to the top floor of the seven-storied mansion and fry them. There, I will sit and eat alone.” She agreed, saying “Very well,” and having had the necessary items taken, she ascended the mansion. She dismissed the maidservants and had the treasurer summoned. He closed the doors starting from the first one, putting the bolts on all the doors, and having ascended to the seventh floor, he closed the door there too and sat down. His wife lit the fire in the brazier, placed the pan on it, and began to fry the cakes.
234:
## The Psychic Power of Moggallāna

The millionaire’s wife consented, saying, “Very well,” and took what was needed. She went up to the upper floor of the mansion and sent for the millionaire. The millionaire closed all the doors, starting from the main entrance, securing them with bolts and bars. He went up to the seventh floor and stayed there, closing the door of that floor as well. The millionaire’s wife then lit the fire in the hearth, placed the frying pan on it, and began her efforts to fry the cakes.

At that time, early in the morning, the Blessed One called the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and said, “Dear Moggallāna, in the market town of Sakkāra, not far from Rājagaha, the stingy millionaire Macchariya-seṭṭhi is having cakes fried in a pan on the seventh floor of his mansion, fearing that others might see him eating them. Go there, tame the millionaire, and make him free from his stinginess. Then, have the couple bring the cakes, along with milk, ghee, honey, and molasses, and bring them to Jetavana Monastery by your psychic power. Today, I shall remain at Jetavana Monastery with five hundred monks and will take the meal only with those cakes.”

Venerable Mahāmoggallāna replied, “Very well, Bhante,” and accepting the Buddha’s command, he immediately went to that market town by his psychic power. He stood in the air outside the lattice window of that seven-storied mansion, well-robed and properly covered, appearing like a jeweled statue. As soon as he saw the Elder Moggallāna, the millionaire’s heart trembled.

The millionaire thought, “I came to this place precisely because I was afraid of being seen by such people. Yet this monk has come through the air and is standing at the window.” He became agitated. Unable to see any way to get rid of him, he sputtered with anger like salt crystals crackling in a fire, and said, “Monk, even if you stand in the air, what will you get? Even if you walk to and fro, showing your footsteps in the trackless air, you will get nothing.” Venerable Mahāmoggallāna then walked to and fro in that very spot. The millionaire said, “Even if you walk to and fro, what will you get? Even if you sit cross-legged in the air, you will certainly get nothing.” Venerable Mahāmoggallāna then sat cross-legged in the air.

Then he said to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, “Even if you sit cross-legged in the air, what will you get? Even if you come and stand on the sill of the lattice window, you will get nothing at all.” Venerable Moggallāna stood on the windowsill. Then he said to Venerable Moggallāna again, “Even if you stand on the windowsill, what will you get? Even if you emit smoke, you will certainly get nothing.” Venerable Moggallāna then emitted smoke. The entire mansion became filled with a single mass of smoke. It was as if the millionaire’s eyes were being pricked with needles. Fearing that the house might catch fire, he did not say, “Even if you emit flames, you will get nothing.” Instead, he thought, “This monk is very persistent; he will not leave without getting something. Therefore, I will have one cake given to him.” He said to his wife, “Lady, fry one small cake, give it to the monk, and send him away.” The wife put only a small amount of dough into the frying pan, but it became a large cake, filling the entire pan and swelling up.

When the millionaire saw that pan, he said, “You must have taken a lot of dough.” He himself took a tiny bit of dough with the tip of a ladle and put it in. That cake became even larger than the previous one.
235:
In this way, whenever she tried to fry a cake smaller than the previous one, each cake became larger and larger. The Great Treasurer, becoming weary, said to his wife, "Dear wife, give one cake to this monk." When the Treasurer's wife took one cake from the basket, all the cakes stuck together as one. She said to the Treasurer, "My lord, all the cakes are stuck together. I am unable to separate them one by one."

Then the Treasurer said, "I will do it," but he too was unable to do so. Even when both of them held the edges and pulled, they could not separate the cakes. While the Treasurer was struggling with the cakes, sweat poured from his body. His desire to eat them vanished. Then he said to his wife, "Dear wife, I no longer wish to eat these cakes. Give them to this monk along with the basket." So the wife took the basket, approached the Elder Moggallāna, and offered it.

The Elder Moggallāna preached the Dhamma to both of them. He spoke of the virtues of the Triple Gem. He showed the fruits of giving alms, such as "There is [benefit in] giving, there is [benefit in] sacrifice," making it as clear as the full moon in the sky.

## The Treasurer and His Wife Attain Stream-Entry

Upon hearing the Dhamma, the Treasurer, with a clear and faithful mind, said, "Venerable Sir, please come and sit upon this couch and partake of the food." The Elder replied, "Great Treasurer, the Fully Enlightened One is sitting in the monastery with five hundred monks, wishing to eat cakes. If you desire, I shall take you there. Have your wife take the cakes, milk, and so on, and we shall go to the presence of the Teacher." The Treasurer asked, "Venerable Sir, where is the Teacher residing now?" "Great Treasurer, He is residing at Jetavana Monastery, forty-five yojanas from this town." "Venerable Sir, how can we travel such a long distance without passing the noon hour?"

"Great Treasurer, if you desire, I shall take you there by my own psychic power. The top of the stairway in your mansion will remain in its place, but the foot of the stairway will be at the entrance gate of Jetavana Monastery. I shall take you to Jetavana in the time it takes to descend from the upper floor to the lower floor of your mansion." The Treasurer agreed, saying, "Very well, Venerable Sir." The Elder Moggallāna, keeping the top of the stairway there, resolved, "Let the foot of the stairway be at the gate of Jetavana Monastery." It happened exactly as he resolved. Thus, the Elder brought the Treasurer and his wife to Jetavana even faster than the time it takes to descend from the upper floor to the lower floor of a mansion.

The couple approached the Teacher and announced that it was time for the meal. The Teacher entered the refectory and sat upon the prepared noble Buddha-seat along with the assembly of monks. The Great Treasurer offered the water of donation to the assembly of monks headed by the Buddha.
236:
The Treasurer's wife also placed a cake in the Tathāgata's bowl. The Teacher took just enough cakes for his sustenance. The five hundred monks also took just enough for their sustenance. Even as the Treasurer continued to give milk, ghee, honey, sugar, and so on, they did not run out. The Teacher finished his meal along with the five hundred monks. The Great Treasurer and his wife also ate as much as they desired. Yet, there was no end to the cakes. Even after giving to the monks in the entire monastery and to those who eat leftovers, the cakes were not exhausted. They reported to the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, the cakes are not running out." "In that case, discard them at the entrance gate of Jetavana Monastery," He said. So they discarded the cakes in a hollow place near the gatehouse.

(Even to this day, that place is well-known as Kapallapūvapabbhāra, the Slope of the Pan-cakes.)

The Treasurer and his wife approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and stood in a suitable place. The Blessed One performed the Anumodanā (thanksgiving). At the end of the Anumodanā, both of them were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). They paid homage to the Teacher, ascended the stairway at the gatehouse of Jetavana, and found themselves back in their own mansion. From that day on, the Treasurer spent eighty crores of wealth solely on the Buddha's Dispensation.

Again, the next day in the evening, the monks assembled in the Dhamma Hall and sat praising the Elder's virtues: "Friends, behold the power of the Elder Mahā Moggallāna! Without harming faith and without harming wealth, he tamed the stingy treasurer in a mere moment, making him free from stinginess. He made him take the cakes, brought him to Jetavana, placed him before the Teacher, and established him in the Fruit of Stream-entry. Oh, how great is the power of the Elder!" The Teacher, hearing their conversation with his divine ear, came and asked, "Monks, what subject are you discussing as you sit here?" When they told him, He said, "Monks, a monk who trains families should approach them like a bee taking pollen from a flower without harming its color or fragrance, and make them know the virtues of the Buddha. My son Moggallāna is just like that." Praising the Elder, He spoke this verse:

## The Teaching

(49) Just as a bee takes nectar and flies away without harming the flower, its color, or its fragrance, so should a sage move about in the village.

"Bee" refers to any kind of honey-maker. "Flower" means that while moving in a flower garden, it wanders without harming or destroying the flower, its color, or its fragrance. "Flies away" means that after wandering in this way and drinking as much nectar as it needs, it goes to another place to make more honey...
237:
Both are lame, both have crooked hands, both are cross-eyed. Both have boils; I do not see Illīsa.

Both are lame. Both have crooked hands. Both have uneven eyes. Boils have broken out on both of them. I do not see the treasurer Illīsa.

The Buddha, having heard the conversation of the monks with his divine ear, approached and asked, "Monks, what subject are you discussing as you sit here now?" When they replied, "We are gathered to discuss this matter, Bhante," the Buddha said, "Monks, a monk who admonishes a donor should approach like a bee that collects pollen from a flower without harming its faith, without affecting its wealth, without causing the noble donor distress or exhaustion, and without oppression, making the virtues of the Buddha known. My son Moggallāna is of such a nature." Thus, he praised the Elder and spoke this verse.

(Note: Although the word is lengthened to "Munī" due to metrical rules, it should be understood as the short "Muni" when translating the meaning.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

## Summary of the Illīsa Jātaka
The All-Enlightened Buddha, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and wishing to further clarify the virtues of the Elder Moggallāna, said, "Monks, not only now has Moggallāna subdued the stingy treasurer; in the past also, he subdued him and made him understand the connection between action and its result." To reveal this matter, he brought forth the past and spoke this Illīsa Jātaka (the full version of this Illīsa Jātaka is found in the Varuṇa Vagga of the Ekanipāta in the Five Hundred and Fifty Jātakas) with this verse.

The story of the stingy Kosiya Treasurer ends.

## 6. The Story of the Naked Ascetic Named Pāveyyaka
(Pāveyyakājīvaka Vatthu)
While staying in Sāvatthī, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Na paresaṃ vilomāni," concerning an Ājīvaka named Pāveyyaka.
238:
## The Ascetic's Envy Toward the Buddha
In Sāvatthī, a certain female householder supported an Ājīvaka named Pāveyya, treating him as if he were her own son. People living in the houses adjacent to hers, having heard the Teacher's Dhamma teaching, would return and praise the Buddha's virtues in various ways, saying, "Oh, how wonderful is the Dhamma teaching of the Buddhas!" Hearing these words regarding the virtues of the Buddha, the householder wished to go to the monastery to hear the Dhamma and said, "Venerable, I shall go to the presence of the Buddha after informing the Ājīvaka."

The ascetic forbade her, saying, "Do not go." Even though she pleaded with him repeatedly, he continued to forbid her. The householder thought, "This ascetic does not give me permission to go to the monastery to hear the Dhamma. I will invite the Teacher and hear the Dhamma right here in this house." In the evening, she called her young son and sent him, saying, "Go, dear, and invite the Teacher for tomorrow's meritorious deed."

As the boy went, he first visited the dwelling of his teacher, the ascetic, paid respects, and sat down. Then the ascetic asked him, "Where are you going?" When the boy replied, "I am going to invite the Teacher at my mother's word," the ascetic forbade him, saying, "Do not go to the presence of that Great Samana Gotama." The boy said, "Venerable, it is not proper to forbid me; I am very afraid of my mother. I must go." The ascetic then said, "We both shall eat the offerings prepared for this Great Samana Gotama; do not go." The boy replied again, "Venerable, such a prohibition is not suitable. My mother will scold me."

"If that is the case, then go. But after you have invited him for the meal, do not tell him, 'Our house is in such a place, or on such a street, or that he must travel by such a path.' Act as if you are standing in the presence of that Great Samana Gotama, but then run away as if you are taking another path." The householder's son followed the ascetic's advice, went to the Buddha, invited him, and did everything exactly as his teacher had instructed. When he returned to the ascetic and was asked, "What did you do?", he replied, "Venerable, I have done everything as told." The ascetic said, "You have done well. We both shall eat the offerings made to that Great Samana Gotama." When morning dawned the next day, the ascetic went to the house early and was seated in a back room.

The neighbors smeared the house with fresh cow dung, scattered flowers including parched rice as the fifth type, and prepared a seat worthy of the Noble One for the Buddha to occupy. This is true: people who are not well-acquainted with Buddhas do not know how to prepare a seat. Furthermore, there is no such thing as a need to give directions to Buddhas. From the very day he attained Enlightenment under the Bodhi tree, shaking the ten-thousandfold world system, all paths became clear to the Buddhas: "This path leads to hell; this to the animal womb; this to the realm of hungry ghosts; this to the human world; this to the deva world; and this path leads to the deathless Great Nibbāna." There is no need to speak of mere paths to villages and towns. Therefore, the Teacher, taking his bowl and robes early in the morning, arrived at the doorway of the great female lay disciple's house.
239:
## Ignore the Faults of Others

(50) Not the insults of others, nor what others have done or left undone; one should only observe one's own deeds, done and undone.

*Paresaṃ*: of others. *Vilomāni*: harsh, piercing, and selfish words; these should not be taken to heart. *Paresaṃ katākataṃ*: what others have done or not done, whether good or bad; this should not be scrutinized. *Attanova*: only of oneself. *Katāni ca*: deeds that have been done, whether good or bad. *Akatāni ca*: deeds that have not been done, whether good or bad. *Avekkheyya*: one should reflect upon.

## The Naked Ascetic Flees Due to the Sound of 'Sadhu'

That laywoman also went out of her house and, having paid homage to the Buddha with the fivefold prostration (two knees, two palms, and the forehead), invited Him inside. Having seated Him on a prepared noble seat, she offered water of donation and served Him with excellent hard and soft food. Wishing to have the Buddha perform the *anumodanā* (talk of appreciation) after His meal, the laywoman took His bowl. The Buddha began to preach the *Dhamma* of appreciation with a sweet voice endowed with the eight qualities: "pleasant, intelligible, clear, audible, fluid, deep, resonant, and not going beyond the assembly."

The laywoman listened to the *Dhamma*, uttering the cry of appreciation, "Sādhu, Sādhu!" The naked ascetic, who was sitting in the back room of the house, heard the sound of the laywoman giving the cry of appreciation while listening to the *Dhamma* and could not restrain himself. Thinking, "This woman is no longer mine," he came out of the room and fled, reviling both the laywoman and the Buddha in various ways, saying, "You wretched woman, you are ruined! You are making such offerings to this Great Monk Gotama!"

## Mind Your Own Business

The laywoman was ashamed by the insults of the naked ascetic and was unable to direct her knowledge according to the teaching, as her mind had become agitated and distracted. Then the Buddha asked her, "Laywoman, what is it? Are you unable to keep your mind following the teaching?" She replied, "Venerable Sir, because of the words of that naked ascetic, my mind has become agitated and distracted."

The Buddha then said, "Laywoman, one should not pay attention to such insulting words of such a person; rather, it is proper only to reflect upon and observe one's own deeds, what has been done and what has been left undone," and He spoke this verse:
240:
## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the conclusion of the teaching, that laywoman was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The Dhamma teaching also became beneficial to the great multitude.

The story of the Ājīvaka of Pāveyyaka ends.

## 7. The Story of Chattapāṇi the Lay Disciple

(Chattapāṇi Upāsaka Vatthu)

While residing in Sāvatthī, the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Yathāpi ruciraṃ pupphaṃ" concerning the lay disciple Chattapāṇi.

## The Fading of the King's Glory in the Presence of the Buddha

In Sāvatthī, there was a lay disciple named Chattapāṇi who was an Anāgāmī (Non-returner) and a bearer of the Tipitaka. Early in the morning, having undertaken the Uposatha vows, he went to attend upon the Teacher.

(For the noble disciples who have attained the stage of Anāgāmī, there is no such thing as undertaking the Uposatha by way of formal observance; by the power of the Path of Non-returning itself, the practice of celibacy (brahmacariya) and the practice of eating one meal a day (ekabhattika) come to them naturally.)

That lay disciple Chattapāṇi, likewise observing the Uposatha, approached the Teacher, paid respectful homage, and sat down listening to the Dhamma discourse. At that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala came to attend upon the Teacher. Seeing the King approaching, Chattapāṇi thought, "Should I stand up or should I remain seated?" Then he reflected, "I am sitting in the presence of the Supreme King (the Buddha). It is not proper for me to stand up upon seeing a regional king (padesarāja) who rules only a portion of the land. Indeed, the King may be angry with me for not standing, but even if he is angry, I will not stand. For one who stands up upon seeing a king shows respect to the king, not to the Teacher. Therefore, I will not stand." Thus, he remained seated.

(Wise men, even when they see someone not standing while seated in the presence of those who are highly revered, do not become angry.)
241:
When King Kosala saw the lay follower Chattapāṇi, who did not rise from his seat, he felt angry but paid homage to the Buddha and sat in a suitable place. The Buddha, knowing the King's anger, praised the lay follower's virtues: "Great King, this lay follower Chattapāṇi is a wise man. He has realized the Dhamma. He is a bearer of the Tipitaka. He is very skilled in discerning what is beneficial and what is not." Upon hearing these praises of Chattapāṇi's virtues, the King's heart became softened.

## The King's Pride and the Lay Follower's Respect

Then one day, while King Pasenadi of Kosala was staying in the upper palace, he saw the lay follower Chattapāṇi walking through the palace courtyard after his morning meal, carrying a parasol and wearing sandals. He had him called. Chattapāṇi removed his parasol and sandals, approached the King, paid homage, and stood in a suitable place. The King asked, "O lay follower, why did you remove your parasol and sandals?" He replied, "I heard that the King was calling, so I removed them and came." The King said, "Perhaps only now do you recognize our kingship." He replied, "Great King, we always recognize your kingship." The King then asked, "If so, why did you not rise from your seat when you saw me while sitting in the presence of the Teacher the other day?"

"Great King, while I was sitting in the presence of the Supreme King (Aggarāja), the Buddha, if I had risen upon seeing a regional king (padesarāja), it would have shown disrespect to the Teacher. Therefore, I did not rise." The King said, "O great lay follower, let that matter rest. You are wise and skilled in knowing what is beneficial and what is not in this life and the next. You are a bearer of the Tipitaka. Please teach the Dhamma in our palace."

He replied, "I cannot, Great King." "Why not?" the King asked. "Great King, the royal palace is a place of many faults. The duties and affairs associated with it are heavy and difficult." The King said, "Do not say so. Do not feel anxious thinking, 'I did not rise when I saw the King the other day.'" He replied, "Great King, the movements of laypeople involve many faults. Please invite a monk to teach the Dhamma."

## About the Queens Who Studied

The King said, "O lay follower, very well. You may go." After dismissing Chattapāṇi, he went to the Buddha and requested, "Venerable Sir, Queen Mallikā and Queen Vāsabhakhattiyā wish to learn the Dhamma. May the Buddha, along with five hundred monks, regularly come to my palace to teach them the Dhamma." The Buddha replied, "Great King, it is not the way of the Buddhas to go regularly to a single place."
242:
## The Teaching

(51) Just as a beautiful flower,
Brightly colored but without scent,
So is the well-spoken word fruitless
For one who does not practice it.

(52) Just as a beautiful flower,
Brightly colored and fragrant,
So is the well-spoken word fruitful
For one who practices it.

'Ruciraṃ' means beautiful. 'Vaṇṇavantaṃ' means endowed with color and shape. 'Agandhakaṃ' means without scent, like flowers such as the coral tree (kathit) or hibiscus (khaung-yan). Just as such a flower is fruitless, so is the well-spoken word of the Buddha—the Tipitaka—fruitless for one who does not respectfully learn, listen, and practice it.

'Ruciraṃ' means beautiful. 'Vaṇṇavantaṃ' means endowed with color and shape. 'Sagandhakaṃ' means having a good scent, like the blue lotus, jasmine, or other fragrant flowers. Just as such a flower is fruitful, so is the well-spoken word of the Buddha—the Tipitaka—greatly fruitful for one who respectfully learns, listens, and practices it.

When the Buddha said, "There is no such thing [as a Buddha going regularly to one place]," the King requested again, "In that case, Venerable Sir, please grant another monk." The Buddha then assigned the task to the Elder Ānanda.

The Elder Ānanda went regularly and taught the Dhamma to the queens. Among them, Queen Mallikā learned carefully and recited the teachings. Vāsabhakhattiyā, however, did not learn carefully nor did she recite them. Then one day, the Buddha asked the Elder Ānanda, "Ānanda, are the female lay followers learning the Dhamma?" "Yes, Venerable Sir," he replied. "Do they learn carefully?" the Buddha asked. "Venerable Sir, Queen Mallikā learns carefully, recites carefully, and is able to repeat the learned texts. But your relative's daughter, Queen Vāsabhakhattiyā, does not learn carefully, does not recite, and is unable to repeat the learned texts."

Hearing the Elder Ānanda's words, the Buddha said, "Ānanda, the Dhamma taught by me is fruitless for one who does not listen carefully, does not recite, and does not teach, like a flower that has color but no scent. But for one who listens carefully and practices, it brings great fruit and benefit," and he spoke these two verses.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth. The teaching was beneficial to the multitude.

The Story of the Lay Follower Chattapāṇi ends.

## 8. The Story of Visākhā

(Visākhā-vatthu)

"Just as from a heap of flowers..." The Teacher told this Dhamma teaching while staying at the Pubbārāma monastery near Sāvatthī, concerning the female lay follower Visākhā.
243:
## Visākhā’s Parents

That laywoman Visākhā was conceived in the womb of the treasurer’s wife named Sumana Devi, the chief consort of Treasurer Dhanañjaya, who was the son of the great Treasurer Meṇḍaka in the city of Bhaddiya, in the kingdom of Anga.
