When Visākhā was seven years old, the Teacher, seeing the perfection of the spiritual requisites (upanissaya) of the Brahmin Sela and others, as well as those beings worthy of realizing the Four Noble Truths, set out on a journey accompanied by a large assembly of monks and arrived at the city of Bhaddiya. At that time, the great Treasurer Meṇḍaka was the head of the five persons of great merit in that city and held the position of treasurer. The five persons of great merit were: the great Treasurer Meṇḍaka; his chief wife named Candapadumā; his eldest son named Dhanañjaya; Dhanañjaya’s wife named Sumana Devi; and Meṇḍaka’s servant named Puṇṇa.

## The Five Treasurers

It was not only the great Treasurer Meṇḍaka; in King Bimbisāra’s realm, there were five treasurers of immeasurable wealth: Jotika, Jaṭila, Meṇḍaka, Puṇṇaka, and Kākavaliya. Among these five, the great Treasurer Meṇḍaka, learning that the Buddha had arrived at his city of Bhaddiya, summoned his granddaughter, the young girl Visākhā, daughter of Treasurer Dhanañjaya, and said: “Dear granddaughter, it will be a blessing for you and a blessing for us. Accompanied by your five hundred girl companions, mount five hundred chariots, and surrounded by five hundred maidservants, go and welcome the Buddha, the Ten-Powered One.” The young girl Visākhā consented, saying, “Very well,” and did as the treasurer had said. Because she was wise in knowing what was appropriate and what was not, she traveled by chariot as far as the ground was suitable for a vehicle, then dismounted and approached the Teacher on foot. Having paid homage, she sat in a suitable place.

(Regarding the phrase 'the Ten-Powered One, possessing physical and intellectual strength': Physical strength refers to the strength of ten men being equal to one Kāḷāvaka elephant; the strength of ten Kāḷāvaka elephants equals one Gaṅgeyya elephant; ten Gaṅgeyya equal one Paṇḍara; ten Paṇḍara equal one Tamba; ten Tamba equal one Piṅgala; ten Piṅgala equal one Gandha; ten Gandha equal one Maṅgala; ten Maṅgala equal one Hema; ten Hema equal one Uposatha; and ten Uposatha equal one Chaddanta elephant. The strength of ten Chaddanta elephants is equal to the physical strength of the Buddha. Thus, the Buddha’s strength is equal to ten Chaddanta, one hundred Uposatha, one thousand Hema, ten thousand Maṅgala, one hundred thousand Gandha, one million Piṅgala, ten million Tamba, one hundred million Paṇḍara, one billion Gaṅgeyya, ten billion Kāḷāvaka, and one hundred billion human beings. The ten intellectual powers are the ten powers of knowledge, such as the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible [ṭhānāṭhāna-kosalla-ñāṇa].)

## Visākhā’s Attainment of Stream-entry

Then, by the power of the merit she had cultivated in previous lives, the Teacher preached the Dhamma to Visākhā. At the end of the discourse, Visākhā, along with her five hundred girl companions, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The great Treasurer Meṇḍaka also approached the Teacher, and after hearing the Dhamma, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. He invited the Buddha for the following day’s meal. On the next morning, in his own residence, he served the assembly of monks headed by the Buddha with choice food, both hard and soft. In this manner, he provided a great donation for fifteen days. The Teacher stayed in the city of Bhaddiya as long as he pleased and then departed.

## Requesting a Treasurer

At that time, King Bimbisāra and King Pasenadi of Kosala were brothers-in-law, each being the husband of the other’s sister. One day, King Kosala thought: “In King Bimbisāra’s realm, there live five treasurers of great merit and immeasurable wealth. In my realm, there is not even one such person. What if I go to King Bimbisāra and request a treasurer of great merit?” King Kosala went to Rājagaha, and after being received with royal hospitality by King Bimbisāra, he was asked, “For what reason have you come?” He replied, “In your realm, there live five treasurers of great merit and immeasurable wealth. I have come to take one of those five treasurers with me. Please give me one of those five treasurers.” Bimbisāra said, “They are great families of high standing; I cannot move them.” Kosala replied, “If I do not get one, I shall not return to my capital.”
244:
## Sending Dhanañjaya the Merchant to Sāvatthī

At that time, King Bimbisāra consulted with his ministers, saying, "To move great families of noble birth, such as Jotika and others, is like moving the great earth itself. There is a merchant named Dhanañjaya, the son of the great merchant Meṇḍaka. Only after consulting with that merchant Dhanañjaya shall I give you an answer, O King."

He summoned Dhanañjaya and said, "Dear Dhanañjaya, King Kosala says he will return to his country taking a wealthy merchant with him. You must go along with King Kosala."

When he said this, Dhanañjaya replied, "Great King, if your Majesty sends me, I shall go."

"Dear son, if that is so, make all necessary arrangements and follow him," the King said and sent him off. Dhanañjaya did all that was required of him. King Bimbisāra also paid him great honor and sent King Pasenadi of Kosala on his way, saying, "Please take this merchant with you."

King Pasenadi took the merchant and, traveling towards Sāvatthī, reached a pleasant place after one night's journey and took up residence there.

## Founding of the New City of Sāketa

Then Dhanañjaya asked King Kosala, "O Great King, in whose territory is this place located?"

"Merchant, it is within my territory," the King replied.

"How far is Sāvatthī from here?" he asked again.

"It is seven yojanas away," the King said.

"Great King, the interior of the city is very crowded, and our retinue of attendants and servants is very large. If it pleases your Majesty, we would like to reside right here," he requested.

King Kosala agreed, saying, "Very well," and established a city at that spot, gave it to Dhanañjaya, and then departed. Because he himself had taken up residence in that place, the city came to be known as Sāketa.

## A Family Without a Son Perishes

In Sāvatthī, a youth named Puṇṇavaddhana, the son of the merchant Migāra, had reached the age of maturity. Then his parents said to that youth Puṇṇavaddhana, "Dear son, look for a girl in a place of your liking."

"Mother and father, I have no need for a wife of such a nature," he replied. His parents insisted, "Dear son, do not do this. A family without a son cannot endure for long; it perishes. Therefore, dear son, just search for a young girl whom you like."

When he was repeatedly urged, Puṇṇavaddhana the merchant's son agreed, saying, "If that is so, if I find a girl endowed with the five beauties, I shall follow your words."

## The Five Beauties

"Dear son, what are these five beauties?" they asked. He replied, "The beauty of hair, the beauty of flesh, the beauty of bones, the beauty of skin, and the beauty of youth—these are the five."

Indeed:
1. The hair of a woman of great merit is like a peacock's tail; when loosened and let down, it touches the hem of her robe and then curls upwards at the ends. This is called the beauty of hair.
2. The lips that cover the teeth are red like the bimba fruit, even, and well-fitted. This is called the beauty of flesh.
245:
3. The teeth are white, even, and without gaps, shining like a row of set diamonds or a row of well-cut conch shells. This is called the beauty of bones.
4. The skin of a dark-complexioned woman is naturally smooth and clear without the use of powders and such, resembling a garland of blue lotuses. The skin of a fair-complexioned woman resembles a garland of kanikāra flowers. This is called the beauty of skin.
5. Even after giving birth ten times, she remains as if she had given birth only once, her youth unfaded. This is called the beauty of youth.

## Searching for the Bride

Then Puṇṇavaddhana's parents invited and fed one hundred and eight Brahmins and asked, "Are there indeed women endowed with the five beauties?"

The Brahmins replied, "Yes, there are."

"If so, let eight Brahmins go to search for such a girl," they said. They gave them much wealth and said, "When you return, we shall reward you. Go and search for a girl endowed with these five beauties. When you find her, give her this ornament." They gave them a golden necklace worth one hundred thousand and sent them off.

Those Brahmins traveled to great cities and searched, but not seeing any girl endowed with the five beauties, they were returning. On the day of the Vivaṭa-nakkhatta festival, they arrived at the city of Sāketa and thought, "Today our task will be accomplished."

In that city of Sāketa, there was an annual festival called Vivaṭa-nakkhatta. At that time, even families who usually did not go out would leave their homes with their retinues and walk to the riverbank with their bodies uncovered. On that day, the sons of Khattiya Mahāsālas and others would stand along various roads, thinking, "If we see a pleasant girl of the same caste as ourselves, we shall throw a flower garland at her or place a garland on her."

(The meaning of Khattiya Mahāsāla etc.: A king who has buried one hundred crores of coins in the earth and spends twenty baskets of coins daily is called a Khattiya Mahāsāla. A Brahmin who has buried eighty crores and spends ten baskets daily is a Brāhmaṇa Mahāsāla. A householder who has buried forty crores and spends five baskets daily is a Gahapati Mahāsāla. According to the Abhidhāna: A king who buries one hundred or one thousand crores, and daily one cartload of provisions goes out while two cartloads come in the evening, is a Khattiya Mahāsāla. A Brahmin who buries eighty crores, and daily one kumbha of provisions goes out while one cartload comes in the evening, is a Brāhmaṇa Mahāsāla. A householder who buries forty crores, and daily five ambaṇas of provisions go out while ten ambaṇas come in the evening, is a Gahapati Mahāsāla. Sutta Mahāvagga.)
246:
Those Brahmins also entered a rest-house by the riverbank and remained standing there. At that moment, Visākhā, who was fifteen or sixteen years of age, adorned with all kinds of ornaments and surrounded by five hundred maidens, came to the river to bathe and arrived at the place where the Brahmins were. Then, as it began to rain, the five hundred maidens ran quickly and entered the rest-house. When the Brahmins looked at them, they did not see a single one among those five hundred maidens who possessed the five signs of beauty.

## The Brahmins Meet Visākhā

Afterward, Visākhā entered the rest-house walking at her natural pace, and thus her garments and ornaments became wet.

The Brahmins, seeing the four beauties of Visākhā and wishing to see her teeth, said to one another, "Our daughter is of a lazy nature. The husband of this maiden will likely not even get a sip of sour rice-gruel."

Then Visākhā asked those Brahmins, "Great Brahmins, of whom are you speaking?" They replied, "Dear daughter, we are speaking of you."

Visākhā’s voice was sweet and pleasant to the ear, resonating like the sound of a struck bronze vessel. She then asked the Brahmins again in a sweet voice, "For what reason do you say this?"

"Your attendant women entered the rest-house quickly without letting their clothes and ornaments get wet. As for you, you did not even come with such speed, but arrived letting your clothes and ornaments get wet. Dear daughter, that is why we speak thus," they explained.

## Four Who Should Not Go Quickly

Then Visākhā said, "Fathers, do not say such words. I possess much greater strength than these women. However, I did not come quickly because I observed a certain reason."

When asked, "Dear daughter, what is that reason?", Visākhā replied, "Fathers, there are four types of people who do not look graceful when they go quickly. Furthermore, there is another reason."

When asked again, "Dear daughter, who are the four types of people who do not look graceful when running quickly?", she said, "Fathers:

1. A consecrated King, even when adorned with all ornaments, does not look graceful if he runs in the palace courtyard with his loins girt. People would say, 'Why is this King running like a commoner?' and he would surely receive blame. He is graceful only when walking slowly.

2. The King’s auspicious state elephant, even when adorned, does not look graceful if it goes quickly. It is graceful only when moving with the majestic gait of an elephant.

3. A venerable monk does not look graceful if he goes quickly. People would merely criticize him, saying, 'Why is this monk running like a layman?' He is graceful only when moving with a calm and composed gait.

4. A woman does not look graceful if she goes quickly. Others would surely criticize her, saying, 'Why is this woman running like a man?'

These four types of people, fathers, do not look graceful when they go quickly."

When asked, "Dear daughter, you said there is another reason; what is that reason?", she replied, "Fathers, mothers and fathers nurture their daughter to be beautiful and graceful in all her limbs. We are like merchandise for sale; they nurture us for the purpose of sending us to another family's house. If, while going quickly, I were to tread on the hem of my garment or slip on the ground and fall, and break a hand or a foot, it would be a burden to my family. As for my ornaments and clothes, even if they are wet by the rain, they will dry. Seeing this reason, fathers, I remained without going quickly."
247:
## Visākhā Accepts the Marriage Garland

When Visākhā spoke, the Brahmins saw the perfection of her even and beautiful teeth and said to one another, "We have never before seen such perfection of teeth in a maiden of this kind." They gave her a cry of applause and said, "Dear daughter, this garland is truly worthy and suitable for you alone," and they placed the golden garland upon her. Then Visākhā asked the Brahmins, "Fathers, from which country and city have you come?" When they replied, "Dear daughter, we have come from the city of Sāvatthī," she asked again, "Fathers, what is the name of the treasurer's family?" They said, "Dear daughter, it is the treasurer named Migāra." When she asked, "What is the name of the young lord, the treasurer's son?", they replied, "Dear daughter, his name is Young Lord Puṇṇavaddhana."

Visākhā, thinking, "This is a family of equal status to ours," accepted and wore the golden garland, and sent word to her father, "Please send a carriage for us."

(The reason for requesting a carriage was that although Visākhā had come on foot, from the moment she was adorned with the golden garland, she could no longer go on foot. Daughters of wealthy families must travel by carriage and the like. Other maidens may ride in ordinary vehicles. They may go shielding themselves with a sunshade or a palm leaf. If even a sunshade or palm leaf is not available, they must go by lifting the hem of their garment and throwing it over their shoulder.)

For Visākhā’s sake, her father, the great treasurer, sent five hundred carriages. Visākhā, along with her five hundred attendants, mounted the carriages and departed. The Brahmins also followed along with them. When they arrived at the house, the great treasurer asked those Brahmins, "From where have you come?" They replied, "Great Treasurer, we have come from the city of Sāvatthī." He asked, "What is the name of your treasurer?" They said, "His name is Treasurer Migāra." He asked, "What is the name of the treasurer's son?" They said, "His name is Young Lord Puṇṇavaddhana." He then asked, "How much wealth does he have?" When they replied, "Great Treasurer, he has forty crores (400 million)," he thought, "That forty crores of wealth, when compared to our wealth, is but a mere fraction. However, since the time I have found someone to protect my daughter, what other reason is there to consider?" and he gave his consent. Dhanañjaya the Treasurer offered hospitality to those Brahmins, let them stay for one or two days, and then sent them back.

## Reporting News of the Maiden

Those Brahmins returned to Sāvatthī and reported, "We have obtained a maiden for you." When asked, "Whose daughter is she?", they replied, "She is the daughter of the great treasurer Dhanañjaya." Treasurer Migāra thought, "I have obtained a maiden from a great and noble family. Therefore, it is proper to bring the maiden quickly." He then informed King Pasenadi of Kosala of his intention to go to the city of Sāketa.
248:
King Pasenadi of Kosala also thought, "This merchant family possesses great and noble wealth. Having requested him from King Bimbisāra, I have settled him in this city of Sāketa. It is proper that I should honor and support this merchant." Thus, he said, "I too shall go."

Migāra the merchant agreed, saying, "Very well, Your Majesty," and sent a messenger to Dhanañjaya the merchant, saying, "When I come, the Sovereign of Sāvatthī, the Great King, will also arrive. The King's army and retinue are very numerous. Will you be able to provide all the necessary hospitality and satisfy such a large multitude of people, or not?" Dhanañjaya the merchant sent back word, saying, "Even if ten kings were to come, let them come."

Migāra the merchant left only enough people to guard his house in that great city and set out with the rest of his retinue. When he arrived and halted at a distance of half a yojana, he sent word, "We have arrived." Dhanañjaya the merchant sent many gifts and consulted with his daughter, saying:

"Dear daughter, your father-in-law, Migāra the merchant, is arriving along with King Pasenadi of Kosala. Which house should be cleaned and prepared for the merchant? Which house for the King? And which houses for the viceroy and others?" He consulted her in this manner. The merchant's daughter was very wise, possessing an insight as sharp as a diamond (vajira). She had made aspirations for a hundred thousand aeons and was endowed with the fulfillment of past meritorious prayers. Therefore, she arranged everything, saying, "Prepare such-and-such a house for my father-in-law, and such-and-such houses for the King." She summoned the servants and workers and instructed them, "Perform all the duties that should be done for the King for this many people, and for the viceroy and others for that many. You yourselves shall also look after and feed the elephants, horses, and so on, so that the elephant-keepers, horse-keepers, and others may also come and enjoy the wedding festivities."

## The Shortage of Firewood at the Wedding

On that very day, Visākhā's father summoned five hundred goldsmiths and ordered, "Make the ornament called the Mahālatā-pasādhana for my daughter to wear." He gave them a thousand nikkhas of ruddy gold (one nikkha = one thousand yway seeds), along with silver, rubies, pearls, coral, diamonds, and other gems suitable for that gold. King Pasenadi of Kosala stayed for a few days and then sent a message to Dhanañjaya the merchant, saying, "Merchant, it is not possible for us to be supported by you for a long time. Now, let the time for the young lady's departure be known."

The merchant also sent a message to the King, saying, "Now the rainy season has arrived. It is not possible to travel during the four months of the rains. Whatever is needed for Your Majesty's army is my responsibility. Your Majesty may depart only when I send word." From that day on, the entire city of Sāketa was like a constant festival. Flowers, perfumes, clothing, and other necessities were prepared for everyone, starting with the King. Then those people thought, "The merchant is showing honor and hospitality to us alone."
249:
In this way, although three months had passed, the Mahālatā ornament was not yet finished. The supervisors in charge of the various tasks came and reported to the Great Merchant, "There is nothing else lacking, but there is not enough firewood to cook rice for the multitude of people." The Great Merchant replied, "Friends, go and dismantle the old, decayed elephant stables and old houses in this city and use them for cooking." Even after doing this, only half a month passed. Then they reported again, "There is no more firewood." He said, "At this time, it is not possible to obtain firewood. Open the storehouses of cloth, twist the coarse cloths into wicks, soak them in jars of oil, and cook the rice." They did as the merchant said for half a month. Thus, four months passed, and the preparation of the Mahālatā ornament reached completion.

## The Design and Value of the Mahālatā Ornament
In that Mahālatā ornament, diamonds weighing four nāḷis were set. Eleven nāḷis of pearls, twenty-two nāḷis of corals, and thirty-three nāḷis of rubies were also used. It was completed, adorned with these aforementioned gems and the other seven kinds of jewels. This ornament was not woven with thread; silver was used exclusively to perform the function of thread. When placed on the head, this Mahālatā ornament reached down to the tops of the feet. Gold buttons were made by joining rings at various places, and the sockets were made of silver. There was one ring at the center of the top of the head, two at the back of the ears, one at the throat, two at the knees, two at the elbows, two at the thighs, and two at the sides of the waist. A peacock figure was fashioned on that Mahālatā ornament.

On the right wing of the peacock, there were five hundred feathers made of red gold, and five hundred on the left wing. The beak was made of coral. The eyes were made of rubies. The neck and tail feathers were likewise made of rubies. The shafts of the thousand feathers were made of silver, as were the legs. That peacock figure, standing on the top of Visākhā's head, appeared to onlookers like a dancing peacock on a mountain peak. The sound of the thousand silver feather-shafts was as pleasant as divine music or the sound of a five-piece orchestra. Only those who came close could realize that the peacock on Visākhā's Mahālatā ornament was not a real, living peacock. The ornament was worth ninety million, and one hundred thousand was paid as the craftsman's fee.

## Past Meritorious Deeds
As for the question of what past merit resulted in Visākhā obtaining this Mahālatā ornament: during the time of Kassapa Buddha, she donated robe-cloth to twenty thousand monks, and she also provided thread, needles, and dye from her own property. Due to the result of that gift of robes, she obtained this Mahālatā ornament.

## Items Given as Dowry
Thus, after the Great Merchant had spent four months preparing the grand arrangements for his daughter, he gave her a dowry of wealth and possessions: five hundred carts filled with coins, five hundred filled with gold vessels, five hundred with silver vessels, five hundred with copper vessels, five hundred carts filled with fine woolen and silk cloths, five hundred filled with ghee, five hundred filled with oil, five hundred filled with hill-paddy rice, and five hundred carts filled with implements such as plowshares. The Great Merchant Dhanañjaya thought, 'Wherever my daughter goes, let her not have to send word to another's house saying, "I have need of such and such a thing."' Therefore, he provided all necessary equipment. He also gave five hundred carriages, placing in each carriage three beautiful maidservants adorned with all ornaments. He instructed the fifteen hundred attendant women, 'Travel with her, bathing her, feeding her, and adorning her.'
250:
Then the great merchant thought again, "I shall give cattle to my dear daughter." He called his men and commanded: "Friends, go and open the gate of the small cattle-pen. Stand at intervals of three gāvutas (one gāvuta is over three miles) taking three large drums. Stand on both sides of an area one usabha wide (one usabha is 140 cubits or over 200 feet). Do not allow the cattle to go beyond that. When they are thus positioned, sound the drums." Those men did as the merchant said. When the cattle left the pen and reached one gāvuta, they gave the drum signal. Again, when they reached half a yojana, they gave the signal. Again, when they reached three gāvutas, they gave the signal and blocked their passage in width. Thus, in an area three gāvutas long and one usabha wide, the cattle stood rubbing against one another.

The great merchant then said, "These many cattle are enough for my daughter; close the gate," and had the gate of the pen closed. Even when the gate was closed, by the power of Visākhā's merit, strong bulls and cows kept leaping out. Even as the men were trying to stop them, sixty thousand strong bulls and sixty thousand cows came out. An equal number of strong bull-calves followed those cows, leaping out after them. By the result of what merit did these cattle follow even though they were being stopped? They followed by the power of the merit of giving gifts with great devotion to recipients who were saying, "Enough, enough," and trying to stop the giving. In the time of Kassapa Buddha, Visākhā was the youngest of the seven daughters of King Kikī, named Saṅghadāsī. While she was giving the five products of the cow (pañcagorasa) to twenty thousand monks, even when the elders, young monks, and novices covered their bowls with their hands and said, "Enough, enough," she would say, "This is sweet; this is pleasant," and continue to give. By the result of that merit, the cattle now came out even though they were being stopped.

When the merchant gave such a large amount of wealth, his wife said, "You have provided everything for my daughter, but you have not provided male and female servants to perform her duties. What is the reason for this?" He replied, "It is to know those who have affection for my daughter and those who do not. I will not take those who are to come with her by the neck and send them. When she is about to depart in her carriage, I will say, 'Let those who wish to go with her, go; let those who do not wish to go, not go.'"

Then, thinking, "Tomorrow my daughter will depart," he sat in his chamber, had his daughter sit near him, and gave her advice, saying, "Dear daughter, for a woman living in her husband's house, it is proper to observe such and such conduct."

The merchant Migāra, sitting in the adjacent chamber, also listened to the advice given by the merchant Dhanañjaya. The merchant Dhanañjaya advised his daughter thus:

## Ten Rules to be Followed by Daughters-in-law

"Dear daughter, for a daughter-in-law living in her father-in-law's house:
1. The indoor fire should not be carried outside.
2. The outdoor fire should not be brought inside.
3. Give only to those who give."
251:
4. Do not give to those who do not give.
5. Give to both those who give and those who do not give.
6. One should sit happily.
7. One should eat happily.
8. One should sleep happily.
9. One should tend the fire.
10. One should honor the household deities.

Having given these ten pieces of advice, on the following morning, he gathered all the military forces. In the midst of the king's army, he appointed eight householders as guarantors, saying, "If any fault arises in my daughter at the place she goes, you must investigate and clear it." He then had his daughter adorned with the Mahālatā ornament worth nine crores. After giving fifty-four crores of wealth for bath powder and soap, he had her ascend the carriage. In the fourteen revenue-villages under his rule near the city of Sāketa, which were as large as the city of Anurādha, he had a drum sounded, announcing: "Let those who wish to go with my daughter, go!" As soon as the villagers heard the sound of the drum, they thought, "When our mistress is leaving, what is the use of us staying here?" and they departed from the fourteen villages, leaving only a few people behind. The merchant Dhanañjaya also paid respects to King Kosala and the merchant Migāra, followed them for a short distance, and then sent his daughter Visākhā off with them.

## Visākhā's Fulfillment of Social Etiquette

The merchant Migāra, traveling in a small carriage behind everyone else, saw the great multitude and asked, "Who are these people?" When told, "They are the male and female servants who perform the duties for your daughter-in-law," he said, "Who can feed so many people? Beat them and drive them away! If they do not flee, punish them from here!" Visākhā said that she herself would provide food for the multitude. Even though she said this, the merchant Migāra said, "Dear daughter, we have no need for these people. Who can feed them?" and he drove them away by throwing clods of earth and striking them with sticks. Taking the remaining people, he said, "These many are enough for us," and proceeded.

When Visākhā reached the gate of the city of Sāvatthī, she thought, "Should I enter sitting in a covered carriage, or should I enter standing in a chariot?" Then it occurred to her, "If I enter in a covered carriage, the excellence of the Mahālatā ornament will not be visible." Therefore, letting all the citizens see her, she entered Sāvatthī standing in an open chariot. When the citizens of Sāvatthī saw Visākhā's prosperity, they praised her, saying, "This maiden named Visākhā is of such a nature; such magnificent prosperity is truly suitable for this maiden Visākhā." Thus, Visākhā entered the house of the merchant Migāra with great and magnificent splendor. On the day of her arrival, all the people living in the city..."
252:
They thought, “Our Dhanañjaya Seṭṭhī’s daughter, Visākhā, has previously made many offerings to those who arrived at her city. We, too, should make offerings in return.” Accordingly, they sent gifts according to their ability and strength.

Visākhā also distributed the gifts sent by the townspeople to various families within that very city, exchanging the gifts as they arrived and giving them to everyone. Thus, Visākhā sent the gifts while speaking pleasant words appropriate to each person’s age, saying, “Give this to my mother; give this to my father; give this to my brothers; give this to my sisters.” She treated all the inhabitants of Sāvatthī as if they were her own close relatives. Then, at midnight on the night she arrived at the treasurer’s house, a noble mare gave birth to a foal. Visākhā had her maidservants light torches and went to the place where the mare was giving birth. She had the mare bathed with warm water and anointed with oil, and only then returned to her own quarters.

## Visākhā and the Naked Ascetics

The treasurer Migāra, while celebrating his son’s marriage, did not pay attention to the Tathāgata who was staying at the nearby Jetavana Monastery. Instead, prompted by a long-standing affection for the naked ascetics (Acelakas), he thought, “I will also make offerings to my noble lords.” One day, he had milk-rice cooked without water in hundreds of new vessels, invited five hundred naked ascetics (Acelakas = a type of heretic who believes one can only become an Arahant by living without clothes), brought them into his house, and sent a message to Visākhā, saying, “Let my daughter-in-law come and pay homage to the great Arahants.”

When Visākhā, who was a Sotāpanna and a noble disciple, heard the words “great Arahants,” she was filled with joy and went to the place where they were eating. Upon seeing those naked ascetics, she thought, “Such people who are devoid of shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa) cannot be called Arahants. Why did my father-in-law have me summoned?” Feeling disgusted, she said, “How loathsome! How loathsome!” and “Tush! Tush!” and returned to her own quarters, criticizing the treasurer.

## Urging to Expel Visākhā

When all the naked ascetics saw Visākhā, they simultaneously criticized the treasurer, saying, “Lay follower, could you not find another daughter of a good family? Why did you bring this extremely ill-omened woman, a disciple of the ascetic Gotama, into this house? Quickly expel this ill-omened woman from this house!” The treasurer thought, “I cannot expel my daughter-in-law Visākhā just because of the words of these noble lords; she is the daughter of a great family with immense wealth.” He pleaded with them, saying, “Venerable sirs, young people may act either knowingly or unknowingly. Please remain silent.” After dismissing the Acelakas, the treasurer sat in a place suitable for noble persons and began eating milk-rice cooked without water from a golden bowl. At that time, an Elder who was wandering for alms entered the treasurer’s house.
253:
While Visākhā was fanning her father-in-law, the merchant Migāra, she saw the Elder who had come for alms. Thinking, "It is not appropriate for me to speak to my father-in-law," she moved aside so that the merchant could see the Elder.

## One Who Eats Only the Old

That merchant Migāra, due to his foolishness and delusion, even though he saw the Elder, pretended not to see him and continued eating with his head bowed down. Visākhā, realizing that "My father-in-law, despite seeing the noble Elder, pays no attention," said, "Please pass on, Bhante. My father-in-law is eating only the old."

Although the merchant Migāra had remained patient when the naked ascetics (Acelakas) spoke to him, the moment she said, "He is eating only the old," he removed his hand from the food and said, "Take this milk-rice away from here! Drive this woman out of this house! Seize her! Even this daughter-in-law Visākhā makes me out to be an eater of filth at such an auspicious time!"

## Whether Visākhā is at Fault or Not

At that time, all the servants in the house were Visākhā's own servants; who would dare to seize Visākhā by the hands or feet? There was not even anyone who dared to speak out. Hearing her father-in-law's words, Visākhā said: "Father, we cannot leave just because of such words. I was not brought here by you like a slave girl fetching water from a landing place.

Daughters of parents who are still living do not leave just because of this. For this very reason, when my father was coming here, he summoned eight householders and said, 'If any fault arises in my daughter, please investigate and clear it,' and he placed me in the hands of those eight householders. Please summon those householders and have them investigate whether I am at fault or not."

## Visākhā Explains

The merchant, thinking, "She speaks well," summoned the eight householders and said, "This young woman, while I was sitting and eating undiluted milk-rice from a golden bowl at an auspicious time, said that I was 'an eater of filth.' Charge her with this fault and drive her out of this house."

When the eight householders asked, "Is it true, dear daughter?", Visākhā replied, "Fathers, I did not say it in that way. When an Elder wandering for alms stood at the door, my father-in-law, while eating sweet and excellent undiluted milk-rice, paid no attention to the Elder who had come for alms. Therefore, I thought, 'My father-in-law is not performing any merit in this existence; he is only enjoying the fruits of merit performed in the past,' and so I said, 'Please pass on, Bhante. My father-in-law is eating the old.' What fault is there in me for saying this?"

When Visākhā said this, the eight householders said, "Noble Merchant, there is no fault in this. Our daughter has spoken only what is appropriate and good."
254:
"Why are you angry?" they asked.

Then the merchant Migāra said, "O householders, if this is not yet a fault, let it be. But one day, at midnight, this Visākhā went to the back of the house surrounded by male and female servants."

The householders then questioned her, "Dear daughter Visākhā, is it as the merchant Migāra says?"

"Fathers, I did not go for any other reason. I reflected that in this house, a thoroughbred mare was in labor, and it would not be right to sit by without even taking notice. So, I had torches lit and had hot water and other necessities brought, and went with the male and female servants to care for the mare during her delivery."

She then asked, "What fault is there in me for providing such care?"

"Noble Merchant, our daughter has performed a task in your house that even servants would find difficult to do. What fault do you see in her going to the back of the house at midnight to provide such care?" they asked.

"O householders, if this too is not a fault, let it be. However, when Visākhā's father, the merchant Dhanañjaya, was about to come to this house, he gave her ten secret admonitions. I do not know the meaning of those ten admonitions. Let her tell me their meaning. This Visākhā's father said, 'The indoor fire should not be carried outside.' Can we live without giving fire to our neighbors on both sides?"

## Meaning of the 10 Admonitions for the Daughter-in-law

When they questioned her, "Dear daughter, is it as he says?", she replied, "Father householders, my father did not speak referring to ordinary fire. He meant, 'If you see any faults in your mother-in-law, father-in-law, or your benefactor husband, do not stand in other houses outside and speak of them.' This is the meaning. Indeed, there is no fire like the fire of speaking of the faults of one's parents-in-law or beloved husband."

"O householders, let this secret admonition be as explained. But Visākhā's father also said, 'The outdoor fire should not be brought inside.' If the fire in our house goes out, how can we manage without bringing in fire from outside?" he asked.

"Dear daughter, is it as he says?" they questioned again. "Father householders, my father did not speak referring to ordinary fire. He meant, 'If women or men living in neighboring houses speak of the faults of your mother-in-law, father-in-law, or beloved husband, do not bring those words back and repeat them, saying, "So-and-so said such-and-such about your faults."' Indeed, there is no fire like that fire," she explained. In this way, Visākhā was found blameless in this matter as well. Just as in these cases, she was blameless in all the rest.

(The following is the meaning of the remaining eight admonitions:)

Regarding what her father said, "Give only to those who give," it was said meaning, "Give borrowed items only to those who return them."

Regarding "Do not give to those who do not give," it was said meaning, "Do not give borrowed items to those who do not return them."
255:
Visākhā’s father, the great banker, explained the saying 'Give only to those who give' as meaning: 'One should give only to those who, having borrowed household items, return them.' The saying 'Do not give to those who do not give' was said with the meaning: 'One should not give to those who, having borrowed household items, do not return them.' The saying 'Give to both those who give and those who do not give' was said with the meaning: 'When poor relatives and friends arrive, whether they are able to repay or not, it is proper only to give to them.' The saying 'Sit happily' was said with the meaning: 'It is not proper to remain sitting in a place where one should stand up upon seeing one’s mother-in-law, father-in-law, or benefactor husband.'

The saying 'Eat happily' was said with the meaning: 'One should not eat before one’s mother-in-law, father-in-law, and benefactor husband; rather, after serving the parents-in-law and the benefactor husband, and knowing whether everyone has received enough or not, it is proper to eat oneself last.' The saying 'Sleep happily' was said with the meaning: 'One should not go to bed and sleep before one’s mother-in-law, father-in-law, and benefactor husband; rather, after performing the major and minor duties such as massaging their feet and hands which ought to be done for them, it is proper to go to bed and sleep afterwards.' The saying 'Tend the fire' was said with the meaning: 'It is proper to look upon one’s mother-in-law, father-in-law, and benefactor husband as if they were a great mass of fire or a king cobra, with respect and fear.' The saying 'Honor the indoor deity' was said with the meaning: 'One should look upon one’s mother-in-law, father-in-law, and...'
256:
...benefactor husband, honoring and respecting them as if they were deities.'

This is the meaning of the words of advice. Thus, when the banker Migāra heard the meaning of these ten admonitions, finding no words to say in reply, he sat with his head bowed down.

## The Banker Apologizes to Visākhā
Then the eight householders asked the banker Migāra, 'Sir Banker, is there any other fault in our daughter?' When he replied, 'Sirs, there is none,' they criticized him, saying, 'Then why did you groundlessly drive this faultless young woman out of the house?' While the banker Migāra was being criticized, Visākhā said, 'Fathers, although it would indeed have been proper for me to leave at first at my father-in-law’s word, even though I should have left then, my father, the banker Dhanañjaya, placed me in the hands of you eight householders when I came to this house for the purpose of investigating and clearing any faults, great or small, against me. You, fathers, have now known my innocence; it is now proper for me to leave.' She then ordered the male and female servants, 'Prepare the vehicles, carriages, and so on.' Then the banker Migāra, taking the eight householders with him, said to Visākhā, 'Dear daughter, I spoke only out of ignorance; please forgive me.'

## Visākhā Offers Alms to the Buddha
'Father, I forgive you as much as you should be forgiven. However, I am a woman who has seen the Four Noble Truths and has unwavering faith in the Buddha’s Dispensation; we do not wish to live apart from the Saṅgha of monks. If I am allowed to support the Saṅgha of monks according to my wish, then I shall stay.' He gave permission, saying, 'Dear daughter, support your recluses as you wish.' Visākhā then had the Blessed One invited, and on the following morning, she invited Him to enter the house for a meal. The naked ascetics (Acelakas), hearing that the Blessed One was going to the house of the banker Migāra, went and sat surrounding the back of the house. When Visākhā had offered the noble water of donation and prepared all the offerings and honors, she sent word, 'Let my father-in-law, the banker Migāra, come and serve the Buddha, the All-Knowing Lord of the Three Worlds, who possesses the Ten Powers.'

## The Naked Ascetics Forbid Hearing the Buddha’s Dhamma
Then the Ājီvaka naked ascetics stopped the banker Migāra, who wished to go, saying, 'Householder, do not go to the presence of the recluse Gotama.' The banker Migāra sent back word, 'Let my daughter-in-law serve him herself.' After Visākhā had served the community of monks headed by the Buddha and the meal was finished, she again sent word, 'Let my father-in-law, the banker Migāra, come and listen to the Dhamma discourse.' Then, thinking, 'It is very improper not to go now,' the banker Migāra, wishing to hear the Dhamma, started to go, but the Ājīvaka naked ascetics said to him, 'In that case, if you listen to the Dhamma in the presence of the recluse Gotama, listen while sitting outside the curtain.'
257:
Today I understand where a gift bears great fruit;
Truly, for my welfare, has this auspicious daughter-in-law come to my home.

“Venerable Sir, the Blessed One who shines more brightly than the sun and the moon. In this noble Sāsana, giving brings great and extensive noble fruits. I, your disciple, have come to know that Sāsana, where giving is so beneficial, this very day. Indeed, for my benefit, this excellent daughter-in-law has arrived at my home.”

Before the great merchant Migāra arrived, they had already set up a curtain. The great merchant Migāra stayed outside the curtain. The Blessed One said, “Whether you, Migāra, stay outside the curtain, or behind a wall, or behind a stone mountain, or even in another world-system, I, the Buddha, am able to make my voice heard by that person.” Then, as if grasping and shaking the trunk of a great Jambu tree, or as if sending down a great rain of the Deathless (Amata), He began to preach the Dhamma in progressive order.

## The Merchant's Devotion to the Buddha

When the Blessed One finished His discourse, the great merchant Migāra, while still remaining outside the curtain, established himself in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala), which is adorned in a thousand ways. Filled with unwavering and firm faith, and being free from the great doubt regarding the Triple Gem, he lifted the corner of the curtain and came out. He then took the breast of his daughter-in-law Visākhā [metaphorically, as a child to a mother] and said, “From this day forth, you are my mother,” thus placing Visākhā in the position of a mother. From that time on, Visākhā became known as “Migāramātā” (Migāra's Mother). Later, when she had a son, she named him “Migāra.” The great merchant Migāra, after releasing his daughter-in-law's breast, went and prostrated with his head at the two feet of the Blessed One. Stroking and massaging the feet with his hands and kissing them with his mouth, he announced his name clearly three times, saying, “Venerable Sir, I am Migāra. Venerable Sir, I am Migāra.” He then addressed the Buddha, “Venerable Sir, for so long a time, I did not know that giving to this noble Sāsana yields such great fruit. But now, I have come to know it through my daughter-in-law. I am now free from all the sufferings of the four woeful states (apāya).” He further said, “My daughter-in-law Visākhā, who has come to this house, has come for my great benefit, for my prosperity, and for my great happiness,” and he recited this verse.

## The Merchant's Wife Attains Sotāpatti

Visākhā invited the Teacher again for the following day. On that next day, Visākhā's mother-in-law, the merchant's wife, also attained the Fruit of Stream-entry. From that time on, that house became a house with an open door for the Sāsana. Then, the merchant Migāra thought, “My daughter-in-law has been of great service to me. I shall show her a sign of my appreciation. This Mahālatā ornament of my daughter-in-law is very heavy and cannot be worn at all times. I shall have a light ornament made for her, suitable for wearing in all postures, day and night.” Having so thought, he had an ornament called Ghanamatthaka made, which was worth a hundred thousand, solid and smooth...
258:
Visākhā had twenty children,
And four hundred grandchildren.
Her great-grandchildren were eight thousand;
She was well-known throughout Jambudīpa.

Visākhā had twenty children. Her grandchildren were four hundred. Her great-grandchildren were eight thousand. Thus, she was very famous throughout the island of Jambudīpa.

Having had the ornament made, and when that ornament was finished, she invited the community of monks headed by the Buddha and respectfully offered them food. She then had herself bathed with sixteen pots of scented water. She was then dressed in the presence of the Blessed One and made to pay homage to the Buddha. The Blessed One, with a joyful heart, gave a talk of appreciation and then returned to the monastery.

## Visākhā's Children, Grandchildren, and Great-grandchildren

From that time on, Visākhā performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms. Having received eight boons from the Buddha, she became as famous as the moon in the sky and reached a state of great prosperity with many children. Visākhā gave birth to ten sons and ten daughters. Each of those children in turn gave birth to ten sons and ten daughters. Among those grandchildren, each gave birth to ten sons and ten daughters. Thus, the number of descendants in the line of Visākhā's children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren was eight thousand four hundred and twenty. Therefore, the ancient teachers spoke this verse.

## Visākhā's Beauty

Visākhā's life span was one hundred and twenty years, yet there was not even a single grey hair on her head. She always appeared as if she were sixteen years old. When people saw Visākhā going to the monastery surrounded by her children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren, they would ask, "Which of these is Visākhā?" Those who saw her while she was walking would think, "Let her walk a little longer; our lady looks so beautiful while walking." Those who saw her while she was standing, sitting, or reclining would think, "Let her recline a little longer; our lady looks so beautiful while reclining." Thus, it could not be said of Visākhā that she was unattractive in any of the four postures (iriyāpatha)—walking, standing, sitting, or reclining. That Visākhā also possessed the strength of five noble elephants.

## Testing Visākhā's Strength with an Elephant

King Pasenadi of Kosala, having heard that Visākhā possessed the strength of five noble elephants, wished to test her strength. When she was returning from the monastery after listening to the Dhamma, he ordered a noble elephant to be released. The elephant raised its trunk and charged toward Visākhā. Among her five hundred female attendants, some fled, while others surrounded her to protect her. When Visākhā asked, "What is the reason for this?" they replied, "Lady, the King has released an elephant to test your strength." Seeing the elephant, Visākhā thought, "What is the use of fleeing? How shall I catch this elephant?" Then she considered, "If I grasp it firmly, the elephant will suffer and be exhausted." So, she pressed its trunk with just two fingers and pushed it back. The noble elephant could not maintain its balance and fell down into a squatting position in the palace courtyard. The great multitude of people gave a tumultuous cheer. Visākhā then returned home safely with her attendants.

## Leaving the Mahālatā Ornament Behind

At that time in the city of Sāvatthī, Visākhā had many children.
259:
She had many grandchildren and many great-grandchildren. Her children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren were free from disease and pain; they were regarded as highly auspicious. Among all those children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren, not a single one had ever passed away prematurely. The citizens of Sāvatthī would first invite and offer food to Visākhā at auspicious festivals. On one such festival day, while the multitude of people, adorned in their finery, were going to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma, Visākhā, having eaten at the place of invitation, also went to the monastery with the crowd, wearing the Mahālatā ornament. She then removed the ornament, wrapped it in her outer robe to make a bundle, and handed it to her maidservant, saying, "Here, girl, take this bundle."

Visākhā thought, "While going to the monastery, it is inappropriate to enter wearing such a costly ornament that is worn on the head and extends down to the heels." Thus, she removed the ornament, made a bundle of it, and handed it to her maidservant, who, due to her own past merit, possessed the strength of five elephants. Only that maid was capable of carrying that ornament. Therefore, she told her, "Dear, take this Mahālatā ornament for now; I will wear it only when returning from the presence of the Teacher." Having handed it over, she put on the Ghanamaṭṭhaka ornament, approached the Teacher, and listened to the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the sermon, she paid homage to the Buddha, rose, and departed. Her maidservant, however, forgot the ornament due to a lapse in mindfulness. It was the custom of Venerable Ānanda to collect and store any item left behind by the assembly after they had listened to the Dhamma and departed. Thus, seeing the Mahālatā ornament that day, Venerable Ānanda informed the Teacher, "Venerable Sir, Visākhā has gone, forgetting her Mahālatā ornament." The Teacher said, "Ānanda, put it in a suitable place." The Elder then lifted it up and hung it by the side of the staircase.

## Suppiyā’s Intense Devotion

Visākhā, along with the laywoman named Suppiyā, wandered through the monastery to learn what was needed for visiting monks, traveling monks, sick monks, and others. Seeing these laywomen in the monastery, the young monks and novices, who were in need of ghee, honey, oil, and so on, approached them as usual, carrying their bowls and vessels. On that day, they did the same.

(On another occasion, seeing a sick monk, the laywoman Suppiyā asked, "Venerable Sir, what do you need?" When he replied, "I need meat broth," she said, "Very well, Venerable Sir, I will send it." On the second day, failing to find allowable meat, she fulfilled the requirement for meat broth by using flesh from her own thigh. Later, due to her devotion to the Teacher, her body became whole again as before.

The ten types of unallowable meat are: human flesh, elephant meat, horse meat, dog meat, snake meat, lion meat, tiger meat, leopard meat, bear meat, and hyena meat. Furthermore, even if it is allowable meat, it is unallowable if it is seen, heard, or suspected that the animal was killed specifically to feed the monks.)

## Arrangement to Sell the Mahālatā Ornament

Visākhā, after looking after the sick monks, young monks, and novices, exited through another gate and, standing in the monastery precincts, said, "Dear, bring the Mahālatā ornament; I shall wear it." At that moment, the maid remembered that she had come away having forgotten it and said, "Mistress, I have forgotten it." Visākhā said, "If that is so, go and fetch it. However, if my master, the Venerable Ānanda, has picked it up and placed it in such-and-such a place, do not bring it back. I have already renounced and donated that ornament to the Elder."
260:
(The reason for giving such instructions was that Visākhā already knew, "The Elder Ānanda is accustomed to putting away belongings left behind by people of good families." Therefore, she gave these instructions.)

As soon as the Elder Ānanda saw the servant girl, he asked, "Why have you come?" When she replied, "Venerable Sir, I have come back because my mistress forgot her ornament," he said, "I have placed it by the side of a certain staircase; go and take it." The servant girl said, "Venerable Sir, my mistress has made it a rule not to take back any property that has been touched by the hands of the Noble Ones." She returned empty-handed. When Visākhā asked, "Mother, what is the matter?" she reported the situation. "Mother, I will no longer wear an object that has been touched by my master Ānanda. I have renounced it. However, it would be troublesome for the Elder to look after it. I will sell it and offer the proceeds as a suitable (kappiya) gift. Go and bring that ornament back." She sent her back. The servant girl went and brought the Mahālatā ornament.

Visākhā, without wearing the ornament brought by the servant, summoned goldsmiths and had it valued. When the goldsmiths said, "It is worth nine crores, and the workmanship costs one hundred thousand," she said, "In that case, place the ornament on a carriage and sell it." No one was able to pay such a price to buy it.

(The reason they could not buy it was that women worthy of wearing such an ornament are rare. Indeed, in this whole world, only three women obtained the Mahālatā ornament: the great lay devotee Visākhā, Mallikā the wife of the Malla General Bandhula, and the daughter of the treasurer of Bārāṇasī.)

Therefore, Visākhā herself paid the price of the ornament. She loaded nine crores and one hundred thousand onto a cart, took it to the monastery, paid homage to the Blessed One, and said: "Venerable Sir, my master, the Elder Ānanda, has touched my Mahālatā ornament with his hand. From the moment the Elder touched it, I can no longer wear it. I intended to sell it and offer the proceeds as a suitable gift, but seeing no one else capable of buying it, I have paid the price myself and brought the money. Among the four requisites, which one should I offer, Venerable Sir?"

## Building a Monastery for the Sangha

"Visākhā, it is appropriate for you to build a dwelling place for the community of monks at the eastern gate of the city," the Buddha said. Visākhā, with a joyful heart, replied, "Venerable Sir, it is very appropriate and good," and she bought the land for nine crores. She then began to build the monastery with another nine crores.

Then one day, at dawn, while the Blessed One was surveying the world, He saw the spiritual potential (upanissaya) of a treasurer's son named Bhaddiya, who had passed away from the deva realm and was reborn into a treasurer's family in the city of Bhaddiya. After finishing His meal at the house of Anāthapiṇḍika, He set out toward the northern gate.

(Normally, after the Blessed One had accepted a meal at Visākhā's house, He would depart through the southern gate and reside at the Jetavana Monastery. After accepting a meal at Anāthapiṇḍika's house, He would depart through the eastern gate and reside at the Pubbārāma Monastery. When people saw the Buddha heading toward the northern gate, they knew He was setting out on a journey.)
261:
On that day, Visākhā heard that the Blessed One was heading towards the North Gate. She quickly followed him, paid her respects, and asked, "Venerable Sir, do you intend to set out on a journey?" "Yes, Visākhā," the Buddha replied. She then said, "Venerable Sir, I am building a monastery for you, having sacrificed so much wealth. Please turn back, Venerable Sir." The Buddha replied, "Visākhā, this is a journey that does not involve turning back." Thinking, "The Blessed One must surely have seen someone endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya)," she requested, "Venerable Sir, if that is the case, please leave behind one monk who understands what needs to be done and what does not, and then proceed." The Buddha said, "Visākhā, take the bowl of whichever monk you prefer."

## Management by Elder Moggallāna

Although Visākhā held Elder Ānanda in great affection, she thought, "Elder Mahāmoggallāna possesses great psychic power. Depending on him, my work will be completed quickly." Thus, she took Elder Mahāmoggallāna’s bowl. The Elder looked up at the Blessed One, and the Blessed One said, "Moggallāna, take your retinue of five hundred monks and stay behind." The Elder did as commanded. Through his psychic power, people who went fifty or sixty leagues for timber and stone were able to fetch large logs and stones and return on the very same day. Those loading the timber and stones onto carts felt no fatigue, nor did any axles break. Before long, they constructed a two-story mansion. This mansion was adorned with a thousand rooms—five hundred on the lower floor and five hundred on the upper floor. She had the mansion built on a cleared plot of land measuring eight karīsas. Thinking, "A lone mansion does not look beautiful," she surrounded it with five hundred meditation halls, five hundred small mansions, and five hundred long halls.

After wandering for nine months, the Blessed One returned to Sāvatthī. The construction of Visākhā’s mansion was also completed in nine months. For the pinnacle of the mansion, she had a lotus-shaped finial made of solid, beaten red gold, large enough to hold sixty water pots. Hearing that the Blessed One had arrived at the Jetavana Monastery, she went to welcome him and invited him to her own monastery, saying, "Venerable Sir, please take the community of monks and reside here for these four months of the rainy season."
262:
## Visākhā’s Verses of Uplift

Kadāhaṃ pāsādaṃ rammaṃ, sudhāmattikalepanaṃ.
Vihāradānaṃ dassāmi, saṅkappo mayha pūrito.
Kadāhaṃ mañcapīṭhañca, bhisibimbohanāni ca.
Senāsanabhaṇḍaṃ dassāmi, saṅkappo mayha pūrito.
Kadāhaṃ salākabhattaṃ, suciṃ maṃsūpasecanaṃ.
Bhojanadānaṃ dassāmi, saṅkappo mayha pūrito.
Kadāhaṃ kāsikaṃ vatthaṃ, khomakappāsikāni ca.
Cīvaradānaṃ dassāmi, saṅkappo mayha pūrito.
Kadāhaṃ sappinavanītaṃ, madhutelañca phāṇitaṃ.
Bhesajjadānaṃ dassāmi, saṅkappo mayha pūrito.

When (kadā) shall I (ahaṃ) give the gift of a monastery (vihāradānaṃ) in the form of a mansion (pāsādaṃ) that is delightful (rammaṃ) and plastered with white and red clay (sudhāmattikalepanaṃ)? Thus (iti), my (mayhaṃ) desired thought (saṅkappo) has today (ajja) been fulfilled (pūrito).

When (kadā) shall I (ahaṃ) give the gift of monastery furniture (senāsanabhaṇḍaṃ) consisting of beds and chairs (mañcapīṭhañca), as well as mattresses and pillows (bhisibimbohanāni ca)? Thus (iti), my (mayhaṃ) desired thought (saṅkappo) has been fulfilled (pūrito).

When (kadā) shall I (ahaṃ) give the gift of food (bhojanadānaṃ) such as ticket-food (salākabhattaṃ) that is pure (suciṃ) and served with meat and fish (maṃsūpasecanaṃ)? Thus (iti), my (mayhaṃ) desired thought (saṅkappo) has been fulfilled (pūrito).

When (kadā) shall I (ahaṃ) give the gift of robes (cīvaradānaṃ) consisting of cloth from the Kāsī kingdom (kāsikavatthañca), linen, and cotton (khomakappāsikāni ca)? Thus (iti), my (mayhaṃ) desired thought (saṅkappo) has been fulfilled (pūrito).

When (kadā) shall I (ahaṃ) give the gift of medicine (bhesajjadānaṃ) consisting of ghee and fresh butter (sappinavanītañca), honey and oil (madhutelañca), and molasses (phāṇitaṃ)? Thus (iti), my (mayhaṃ) desired thought (saṅkappo) has been fulfilled (pūrito).

"I wish to perform the ceremony of dedicating the mansion and the celebration of the monastery, Venerable Sir," she made the pledge. The Blessed One accepted in silence. From that time on, Visākhā gave alms and made donations to the Saṅgha of monks led by the Buddha only at the monastery.

## A Friend Participates in the Merit

At that time, a female friend of Visākhā brought a piece of cloth worth a hundred thousand and said, "Friend Visākhā, I wish to spread this cloth as a rug in your mansion-monastery; please tell me a place to spread it." Visākhā replied, "Very well, friend. If I were to tell you 'there is no place to spread it,' you might think I do not wish to give you the opportunity. Therefore, look through the two floors of the mansion and the thousand rooms yourself and find a place to spread it."

That friend took the cloth worth a hundred thousand and wandered here and there, but seeing no cloth in the monastery that was of lesser value than the one she brought, she became dejected, thinking, "I shall not receive a share of merit in this mansion-monastery," and stood in a certain spot weeping. Then, Venerable Ānanda saw the woman weeping and asked, "Why are you weeping?" The weeping woman explained the matter to him. Venerable Ānanda said, "Do not worry, I will tell you a place to spread it," and instructed her, "Make this hundred-thousand-worth cloth into a foot-wipe and spread it at the foot of the stairs where feet are washed. The monks will wash their feet and first wipe them on this cloth before entering the monastery. In this way, it will be of great benefit to you, great lay devotee."

## Joyful Utterance After Completing the Various Donations

For four months, Visākhā gave alms to the Saṅgha of monks led by the Buddha within the monastery. On the final day, she offered cloth for robes to the Saṅgha. The robe-cloth received by even the most junior monk was worth a thousand. She filled the bowls of all the monks and offered medicinal requisites. In terms of the wealth sacrificed for these donations, nine crores were spent.

Thus, nine crores were spent on purchasing the land for the monastery, nine crores on the construction of the monastery, and nine crores on the celebration of the monastery—a total of twenty-seven crores of wealth was sacrificed and donated by Visākhā to the Buddha's Dispensation. Being a woman and living in the house of a non-believer, such a great sacrifice as this was never before seen in any other woman except Visākhā. On the day the monastery celebration was completed, in the evening, surrounded by her children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren, she circumambulated the mansion-monastery, thinking, "Whatever wish I previously desired, every one of those wishes has reached its peak of fulfillment," and she uttered these five verses of uplift in a sweet voice.
263:
When the monks heard the sound of Visākhā reciting these verses, they reported it to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, in all this time, we have never heard the lay devotee Visākhā singing. Today, surrounded by her children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren, she goes around the monastery building singing. Has her bile been disturbed? Or has she perhaps gone mad?"

The Blessed One replied, "Monks, my daughter Visākhā is not singing. Rather, her aspiration has been fulfilled. With a joyful heart, thinking, 'My prayed-for wish has reached its ultimate completion,' she goes about uttering an inspired utterance (udāna)." When He said this, the monks asked again, "Venerable Sir, when did she make that prayer?" The Teacher asked, "Monks, do you wish to hear?" and when they replied, "We wish to hear, Venerable Sir," He brought forth the past:

## Visākhā’s Past Deeds and Aspiration
Monks, counting back from this aeon, one hundred thousand aeons ago, a Buddha named Padumuttara appeared in the world. The lifespan of that Buddha Padumuttara was one hundred thousand years. He was surrounded by one hundred thousand Arahants. His royal city was named Haṃsavatī. His father was King Sunanda, and His mother was Queen Sujātā. A certain noble female lay attendant of that Buddha Padumuttara, having requested eight boons and established herself in the position of a mother, served the Teacher with the four requisites day and night. She attended upon Him without fail, both morning and evening.

A certain friend of that lay attendant used to go to the monastery regularly with her. When that friend saw the intimacy with which the attendant spoke with the Teacher and her favored status, she thought, "What merit must one perform to become so favored by the Buddhas?" and she asked the Teacher: "Venerable Sir, what is this woman to You?"
264:
## The Teaching
(53) Just as from a heap of flowers,
Many kinds of garlands can be made;
Even so, by a mortal being,
Many wholesome deeds should be done.

From a heap of flowers: from a collection of various kinds of flowers. Many: numerous. Garlands: various types of floral arrangements. Just as one would make: as one would create. Even so: in the same manner. By one born: by a being who has been born. A mortal: a being who is subject to death. Many: a great deal of. Wholesome deeds: meritorious acts such as giving (dāna). Should be done: ought to be performed.

When she asked, "Venerable Sir, what is this woman to You?", the Teacher replied, "She is the chief among my female lay attendants." She asked again, "Venerable Sir, by performing what merit did she become the chief among lay attendants?" "By making an aspiration for one hundred thousand aeons," He replied. "Venerable Sir, is it possible to obtain this by making an aspiration now?" she asked. "Yes, it is possible," He said. "If that is so, Venerable Sir, please accept my alms for seven days together with one hundred thousand monks," she requested. The Buddha Padumuttara consented.

That friend gave a great gift for seven days, and on the final day, after offering cloth for robes, she paid homage to the Teacher and, prostrating at His feet, made this aspiration: "Venerable Sir, I do not desire any heavenly or royal power as the fruit of this gift. Instead, having received eight boons in the presence of a Buddha like You, and standing in the position of a mother, I wish to be the chief among those who are able to serve with the four requisites—specifically, by offering rain-robes to the Saṅgha for life, offering food to visiting monks, food to departing monks, food to sick monks, food to those attending the sick, medicine to the sick, a constant supply of gruel, and bathing cloths to the community of bhikkhunīs."

The Buddha Padumuttara, reflecting on the future to see if this laywoman's aspiration would be fulfilled, looked ahead one hundred thousand aeons and saw that it would be. He then gave this prophecy: "At the end of one hundred thousand aeons, a Buddha named Gotama will appear in the world. At that time, you will be a lay devotee named Visākhā. Having received eight boons in the presence of that Buddha Gotama and standing in the position of a mother, you will be the chief among the female lay attendants who serve with the four requisites."

## Becoming Saṅghadāsī, Daughter of King Kikī
That laywoman, who was the future Visākhā, performed meritorious deeds throughout her life. When she passed away from that existence, she was reborn in the celestial realm. After wandering through the rounds of rebirth among gods and humans, during the time of Buddha Kassapa, she became the youngest of the seven daughters of King Kikī of Kāsi, named Saṅghadāsī. She did not go to a husband's house but remained unmarried. Together with her elder sisters, she performed meritorious deeds such as giving for a long time. At the feet of Buddha Kassapa, she also made the aspiration: "In the future, standing in the position of a mother to a Buddha like You, may I be the chief among the female lay attendants who serve with the four requisites."
265:
That laywoman, the future Visākhā, wandering through the realms of devas and humans from that time on, was born in this existence as the noble daughter of the treasurer Dhanañjaya, the son of the great treasurer Meṇḍaka. She performed many meritorious deeds in my Dispensation. "Monks, for this reason, my daughter Visākhā is not singing; rather, seeing the fulfillment and perfection of her cherished aspirations, she is uttering an exclamation of joy (udāna)." Having said this, the Blessed One, wishing to teach this Dhamma, said: "Monks, just as a skilled garland-maker, making a large heap of various flowers, would create many kinds of garlands, even so, Visākhā's mind is inclined towards performing various kinds of meritorious deeds." He then spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti) and so forth. The Dhamma teaching became beneficial to the great multitude.

The Story of Visākhā ends.

## 9. The Story of the Question of the Elder Ānanda
(Ānandattherapañha Vatthu)
While residing in Sāvatthī, the Buddha spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Na pupphagandho paṭivātameti," in response to a question asked by the Elder Ānanda.

## Scents that Waft with and against the Wind
One evening, while the Venerable Ānanda was in solitary seclusion, he reflected: "The Blessed One has spoken of three excellent scents: the scent of roots, the scent of heartwood, and the scent of flowers. The fragrance of these scents only goes with the wind; it does not go against the wind. Could there be a kind of scent whose fragrance wafts both with the wind and against the wind?" Then, this thought occurred to the Venerable Ānanda: "What is the use of me deciding this by myself? I will ask the Buddha himself." Venerable Ānanda approached the Buddha and asked: "Venerable Sir, is there any kind of scent whose fragrance goes both with the wind and against the wind?"
266:
Then, the Blessed One, wishing to answer the question of the Venerable Ānanda, replied: "Ānanda, there is indeed a kind of scent whose fragrance wafts with the wind, wafts against the wind, and wafts both with and against the wind." When asked, "Venerable Sir, what is that kind of scent whose fragrance wafts with the wind, against the wind, and both with and against the wind?", the Buddha replied:

"Ānanda, in this world, in whatever village or town, there is a woman or a man who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha; who abstains from taking life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from intoxicating drinks and drugs which cause heedlessness; who is virtuous and of good character; who dwells at home with a heart free from the stain of stinginess, devoted to charity, open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, one to be asked for help, and delighting in sharing and alms-giving.

Recluses and Brahmins in the ten directions speak praise of the virtues of such a woman or man, saying: 'In such a village or town, a woman or a man has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha... and delights in sharing and alms-giving.'

Even the devas speak praise of them, saying: 'In such a village or town, a woman or a man has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha... and delights in sharing and alms-giving.' This, Ānanda, is the kind of scent whose fragrance wafts with the wind, against the wind, and both with and against the wind—namely, the practice of the Refuges, Virtue, and Generosity of such a virtuous person."
267:
Having said this, the Buddha spoke these verses:

## The Scent of Virtue is Supreme
(54) The scent of flowers does not go against the wind, nor does the scent of sandalwood, tagara, or jasmine. But the scent of the virtuous goes against the wind; a good person pervades all directions.

(55) Sandalwood, tagara, lotus, or jasmine—among these kinds of scents, the scent of virtue is supreme.

"Pupphagandho": the scent of flowers cannot go against the wind. Neither the scent of sandalwood (candana), nor the scent of tagara, nor the scent of jasmine (mallikā) can go against the wind. Only the scent of the reputation of the virtuous, which is the scent of virtue, can go against the wind. A good person (sappurisa), through the extraordinary scent of their virtue, pervades and overwhelms all directions with their reputation.

Whether it be the scent of sandalwood, tagara, lotus, or jasmine (vassikī), the scent of virtue of the virtuous is supreme, incomparable, and peerless among these kinds of scents.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth. The Dhamma teaching became beneficial to the great multitude.

The Story of the Question of the Elder Ānanda ends.
268:
## 10. The Story of the Alms-giving to Elder Mahākassapa
(Mahākassapattherapiṇḍapātadinnavatthu)

While residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma discourse, beginning with "Appamatto ayaṃ gandho," in reference to the alms-giving to Elder Mahākassapa.

## Rejecting the Alms Offered by Goddesses

One day, after seven days had passed, Elder Mahākassapa emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) and set out with the intention, "I will wander for alms in the city of Rājagaha, going from house to house in regular order."

At that time, five hundred goddesses with feet as red as those of pigeons, who were attendants of Sakka, the King of Devas, became eager to offer alms to the Elder. They prepared five hundred portions of alms-food and, standing on the road, pleaded, "Venerable Sir, please accept this alms-food; please show us favor."

The Elder replied, "Go away, all of you. I shall show favor only to the poor and the destitute." When they pleaded again, saying, "Venerable Sir, do not destroy us; please show us favor," the Elder, knowing who they were, rejected them again. As they still did not wish to leave and continued to entreat him, he said, "You do not know your own measure. Go away!" and snapped his fingers at them.

## Sakka Disguising Himself as an Old Man

When the goddesses heard the sound of the Elder snapping his fingers, they were unable to remain in his presence. They fled and returned to the celestial realm of Tāvatiṃsa. When Sakka asked, "Where have you been?" they replied, "O King, we went to offer alms to Elder Mahākassapa who had just emerged from the attainment of cessation."

When he asked, "Did you get to give it?" they replied, "He did not wish to accept it." When he asked, "What did he say?" they replied, "O King, he said, 'I shall show favor only to the poor and the destitute.'" When he asked, "In what form did you go?" they replied, "In this very form, O King."

Sakka said, "How could beings like you ever be able to give alms to the Elder?" Desiring to give alms himself, he disguised himself as a very old, frail weaver with broken teeth, grey hair, and a bent body. He transformed his queen, the goddess Sujātā, into a similarly aged old woman. He then created a weaver's street and sat there stretching out the loom threads.

(The attainment of cessation, nirodha-samāpatti, is the attainment where, after entering all the meditative absorptions (jhānas), the four mental aggregates of consciousness and mental factors, as well as the mind-produced materiality, do not arise for seven days, and all suffering ceases. Only Non-returners and Arahants who have attained all the jhānas can enter this attainment.)

## Elder Mahākassapa Going for Alms

Elder Mahākassapa, with the thought, "I shall show favor to the poor and destitute," walked toward the city. Seeing that street just outside the city, he looked and saw the two old people. At that moment, Sakka was stretching the threads, and Sujātā was winding the shuttle. The Elder reflected, "These two old people are still performing the tasks of livelihood even in their old age and frailty. I think there are no people more destitute than these in this city. I will show favor to this poor old couple by accepting even a ladleful of rice or a bit of boiled vegetables offered by them." Having reflected thus, Elder Mahākassapa walked toward the house of the poor old couple.
269:
He stood at the door of the house. The two, pretending not to see him, continued their work for a short while.

Then Sakka said, "An Elder is standing at the door of the house; go and see, my dear." Sujātā replied, "You go and see, master." Sakka, disguised as the old man, came out of the house, paid homage to the Elder with the fivefold prostration, and rising up while groaning and supporting his knees with both hands, he stepped back a little and said, "Which Elder might this be?" He then placed his hand on his forehead, looked up, and said, "Oh, what a blessing! Our master, Elder Mahākassapa, has come to my hut's door after a long time. Is there anything in the house to give?"

Sujātā, pretending to search hurriedly, replied, "Master, there is still something." Sakka then said, "Venerable Sir, without considering whether it is coarse or refined, please show favor to us, your poor and aged disciples," and he took the bowl.

Elder Mahākassapa thought, "Whether what these poor people give is boiled vegetables or a handful of bran-cake, I will show them favor," and he gave the bowl. Sakka entered the house, took rice from a pot, filled the bowl, and placed it in the Elder's hands. That alms-food was filled with many kinds of curries and sauces, and its fragrance pervaded the entire city of Rājagaha.

Then the Elder reflected, "This old man appears to have little merit (is very poor), but the alms-food is of great merit, suitable for those of high status. It is like the food of Sakka. Who could this be?"

## The Difference Between Merit Inside and Outside the Dispensation

Upon reflecting thus, he realized the old man was Sakka and said, "Sakka, you have performed a heavy deed by robbing the poor of the fortune they should have received. By giving alms to me today, some poor person could have attained the position of a general or a great treasurer." Sakka replied, "Venerable Sir, there is no one more destitute than I." The Elder asked, "Sakka, why are you poor when you enjoy the glory of kingship in the celestial realm?"

Sakka replied, "Venerable Sir, it is like this: I performed good deeds when no Buddha had appeared. Now that a Buddha has appeared, three other devas—Cūḷaratha, Mahāratha, and Anekavaṇṇa—who performed good deeds during the Buddha's time, were reborn near me and are more powerful than I. When I go out with my attendants to celebrate a festival and see them, I have to flee and enter my house.
