The radiance from their bodies overwhelms my body, but the radiance from my body does not overwhelm theirs. Venerable Sir, who is more destitute than I?"
270:
“Venerable Sir, it is true that I enjoy such celestial bliss. However, although this is true, I performed meritorious deeds during the time outside of a Buddha's dispensation. When the Buddha appeared, these three devas of equal status—Cūḷaratha, Mahāratha, and Anekavaṇṇa—who had performed meritorious deeds, were reborn in my vicinity. They possess far greater power and radiance than I do. When these devas, accompanied by their attendants and retinues, descend to the streets to enjoy the constellation festival, I have to flee and hide inside my celestial mansion. The radiance and power emanating from their bodies overwhelm and suppress my own. The radiance and power from my body cannot overwhelm theirs. Venerable Sir, where could there be anyone more wretched than I?” he pleaded.

“Sakka, King of Devas, even if it is so, from this day and this time forth, do not give alms to me by such deception,” the Elder replied. Sakka then asked, “Venerable Sir, if I give alms to you by deception, will I gain merit or will I not?” When the Elder replied, “Sakka, you will indeed gain merit,” Sakka said, “Venerable Sir, if that is the case, performing meritorious deeds is my responsibility.”
271:
After Sakka, the King of Devas, had spoken these words, he paid homage to the Venerable Mahākassapa. Then, taking Queen Sujātā with him, he circumambulated the Elder clockwise, ascended into the sky, and while in the firmament, he uttered this inspired utterance:

“Oh, the gift, the supreme gift, is well-established in Kassapa!”

“Dānaṃ—my gift; paramadānaṃ—is indeed a supreme gift. Kassapa—in the great Elder Mahākassapa, the foremost in ascetic practices, who has just emerged from the attainment of cessation; suppatiṭṭhitaṃ—it is well-established. Aho—Oh, what a wonderful gift it is, worthy of applause!” Thus he proclaimed his inspired utterance.

## The Buddha's Inspired Utterance

At that time, the Blessed One, while staying at the monastery, heard the sound of Sakka’s inspired utterance. He called the monks and said, “Monks, look at Sakka, the King of Devas, who is traveling through the sky while uttering words of joy.” When the monks asked, “Exalted Buddha, what has that Sakka done?” the Buddha replied, “That Sakka gave alms to my son Kassapa by deception. Having given that alms, he goes along uttering an inspired expression of joy with a delighted heart.” When they asked again, “Exalted Buddha, how did Sakka know that it was proper to give alms to the Elder?” the Buddha replied, “Monks, devas and humans alike love a monk who is devoted to alms-gathering, such as my son Kassapa.” After saying these words, the Blessed One himself uttered an inspired verse.
272:
## The Scent of Virtue is Nobler than the Scent of Flowers

(56) This scent of tagara and sandalwood is slight;
The scent of the virtuous is supreme, wafting even among the devas.

Tagara-candanānaṃ—of the tagara shrub and red sandalwood; yvāyaṃ gandho—whatever scent there is; atthi—exists; ayaṃ gandho—this scent; appamatto—is of small measure. Sīlavataṃ—of those possessed of virtue; yo ca gandho—whatever scent of virtue; atthi—exists; so gandho—that scent of virtue; uttamo—being extraordinary and supreme; devesu—among the devas; vāti—wafts.

To the monk who is devoted to alms-gathering,
Who is self-reliant and supports no others,
Who is equanimous, peaceful, and always mindful,
Even the devas hold him dear.

Tādino—to one endowed with the quality of 'tādi', being unshakable by the eight worldly conditions; upasantassa—to one whose defilements are stilled; sadā satimato—to one who is always mindful; attabharassa—to one who is self-reliant; anaññaposino—to one who is not supported by others; piṇḍapātikassa—to the monk who goes for alms; bhikkhuno—to such a monk; devāpi—even the devas; pihayanti—hold him dear.

After uttering this inspired speech, the Buddha said, “Monks, Sakka, the King of Devas, came and gave alms because of the scent of my son Kassapa’s virtue,” and he spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth. The teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.

The story of the alms-giving to the Venerable Mahākassapa ends.

## 11. The Story of the Final Passing of Elder Godhika
(Godhikattheraparinibbānavatthu)

While staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery near the city of Rājagaha, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with “Tesaṃ sampannasīlānaṃ,” concerning the final passing (parinibbāna) of Elder Godhika.

## The Final Passing of Elder Godhika

That Venerable Godhika was staying at the black rock slab called Kāḷasilā on the slopes of Mount Isigili—so named because people used to say “This mountain swallows the seers” when they saw five hundred Paccekabuddhas, sons of Queen Madu, enter a cave in the great mountain to reside there. While staying there, being diligent, ardent, and resolute, with a mind directed toward Nibbāna, he attained the liberation of mind through temporary concentration (jhāna) free from the hindrances. However, due to a certain chronic illness, he fell away from that attained jhāna. That Venerable Godhika entered jhāna a second time, a third time, and up to six times, but each time he fell away from it.
273:
Great Hero, Great Wisdom, shining with psychic power and glory.
O Seer, who has transcended all enmity and fear, I pay homage to your feet.
Your disciple, Great Hero, overcome by death,
Desires and intends for death; restrain him, O Radiant One.
How, O Blessed One, can your disciple, who delights in the Teaching,
A trainee (sekha) who has not yet reached the goal, die while famous among the people?

Great Hero, the Buddha who possesses great effort. Great Wisdom, the Buddha who possesses great wisdom. Shining with psychic power and glory. The Buddha who has transcended all enmity and fear. O Seer (Cakkhumā), the Buddha who is endowed with the five eyes: the Buddha-eye (knowledge of the faculties of others and their tendencies), the Dhamma-eye (knowledge of the lower paths and fruits), the All-seeing eye (omniscience), the Divine-eye (clairvoyance), and the Knowledge-eye (knowledge of past lives, etc.). I pay homage to your feet.

Great Hero, the Buddha who possesses great effort. Your disciple, the Elder Godhika, being oppressed by death, desires death. He exerts effort and intends for it. O Radiant One, the Buddha who bears the radiant rays of power, restrain your disciple who desires and strives for death.

O Blessed One, renowned among the people. Your disciple, who delights in the Teaching, is still a trainee (sekha)—one of the seven types of noble persons (the four who have attained the paths and the three lower fruits) who are still practicing the three trainings of virtue, concentration, and wisdom—and has not yet reached the fruit of Arahantship. For what reason should he die?

On the seventh occasion, after attaining jhāna, he thought: “I have fallen away from jhāna six times. For one who has fallen away from jhāna, the destination (gati) is not certain. I will take the weapon now and kill myself.” Taking a razor, he lay on his bed to cut his throat. Mara, knowing the Elder Godhika's intention, thought: “This monk wants to take the weapon. Those who take the weapon are truly indifferent to life. Such people, without attachment to life, develop insight and can even reach Arahantship.” Mara considered, “If I forbid this monk, he will not listen to my words. I will have the Teacher, the Buddha, forbid him.” Disguised, he approached the Teacher and spoke thus: [Verses above].

At that moment, while Mara was addressing the Buddha, the Elder took the weapon. The Buddha, knowing “This is Mara,” spoke this verse:

Thus the wise act; they do not long for life.
Having uprooted craving with its root, Godhika has attained Parinibbāna.

Thus, the wise act. They do not desire or long for a long life. The Elder Godhika, having completely uprooted craving along with its root, has attained Parinibbāna.

## Mara's Search
After saying this, the Buddha, together with many monks, went to the bed where the Elder lay after taking the weapon. At that moment, the Evil Mara, thinking “Where has the rebirth-consciousness of this Godhika been established?”, became like a mass of smoke or a mass of darkness and wandered through all directions, following and searching for the Elder's rebirth-consciousness. The Buddha showed that state of smoke and darkness to the monks and said, “Monks, this mass of smoke and darkness is the Evil Mara. He is following and searching for the consciousness of the clansman Godhika, thinking ‘Where is the consciousness of the clansman Godhika established?’” When asked, “Venerable Sir, where is the consciousness of the clansman Godhika established?”, the Buddha replied, “Monks, with unestablished consciousness, the clansman Godhika has attained Parinibbāna.” Mara, unable to see the place where the Elder's consciousness was established, transformed himself into the form of a young boy, took a Beluva lute of the color of a pale ripe wood-apple, approached the Teacher, and asked with this verse:
274:
Above, below, and across, in the four directions and the intermediate directions,
I have searched but do not find him. Where has that Godhika gone?

Venerable Sir, above, below, and across in the four directions and the four intermediate directions, I have followed and searched. I do not find, see, or know him. Where has that Elder Godhika gone?

The wise one, possessed of steadfastness, a meditator always delighting in jhāna,
Exerting himself day and night, without longing for life.
Having conquered the army of Death, not returning to a new existence,
Having uprooted craving with its root, Godhika has attained Parinibbāna.

That monk Godhika was always wise. He was possessed of steadfastness (concentration). He was a meditator who delighted in jhāna. He exerted himself day and night. He had no longing for life. That monk Godhika, having conquered the army of Death and not returning to a new existence, has completely uprooted craving with its root and attained Parinibbāna.

## The Teaching
(57) Mara does not find the path of those who are perfect in virtue,
Who live in heedfulness, and who are liberated through right knowledge.

Of those who are perfect in virtue, who live in heedfulness (not being without mindfulness), and who are liberated by the five kinds of liberation after knowing through the right cause and method—of such great Arahants like the Elder Godhika who have attained Nibbāna—Mara, even if he searches with all his power, does not find, know, or see the path they have gone.

Then the Buddha spoke thus to the young Mara.
When the Buddha had spoken thus:

## From him, overcome by sorrow, the lute slipped from his arm.
Then that unhappy spirit (yakkha) disappeared right there.

From that Mara, who was oppressed by sorrow, the Beluva lute slipped from his arm. Then that Mara, with a miserable and unhappy mind, disappeared right there.

The Buddha also said, “Evil Mara, what benefit is there for you in knowing the place of rebirth of the clansman Godhika? Even a hundred or a thousand like you could not see or find the place where the clansman Godhika has attained Parinibbāna.” Then he spoke this verse: [Verse 57].

## Benefits of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth. The teaching became beneficial to the great multitude.
The story of Elder Godhika's Parinibbāna ends.
275:
## 12. The Story of the Householder Garahadinna
(Garahadinnavatthu)

While the Teacher was residing at Jetavana Monastery, he spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Yathā saṅkāraṭṭhasmiṃ" concerning the householder Garahadinna, a follower of the Niganthas.

(Nigantha: without bonds. A type of wrong view holder who, despite having wrong practices like knots, claims "My view is without bonds, the smoothest and truest.")

## Sirigutta Invites the Niganthas

In the city of Sāvatthī, there were two friends, the householder Sirigutta and the householder Garahadinna. Among these two, Sirigutta was a disciple of the Buddha, while Garahadinna was a follower of the Niganthas. The Niganthas, who were his teachers, used to say to Garahadinna: "Why do you not advise your friend Sirigutta, saying, 'Why do you approach the ascetic Gotama? What will you gain from him?' If you advise him in such a way that he approaches us and gives us offerings, would that not be proper?" Thus they spoke to him constantly.

Garahadinna, upon hearing the words of those Niganthas, frequently went to Sirigutta and, whether standing or sitting, spoke to him thus: "Friend Sirigutta, what benefit is there for you in the ascetic Gotama? What will you gain by approaching him? Why is it not proper for you to rely on my masters and give them alms?" Thus he spoke repeatedly.

Sirigutta heard Garahadinna's words but remained silent for many days. One day, he said: "Friend Garahadinna, you constantly come to me and say, 'Friend Sirigutta, what will you gain by approaching the ascetic Gotama? Rely on my masters and give them alms.' Tell me first, what do your masters know?"

When he asked this, Garahadinna replied: "Oh, sir, it is wonderful! Do not speak like that. There is nothing unknown to my masters. They know all of the past, future, and present. They know all actions of body, speech, and mind. They know whether a matter will happen or will not happen; they know everything that is possible and impossible."

When Sirigutta asked again, "Do you dare to say this?", Garahadinna confirmed, "Indeed, I do." Sirigutta then said: "If it is as you say, you have done a very burdensome thing by not telling me this for so long. Only today have I learned of the power of the masters' knowledge. Go, friend Garahadinna, and invite the masters on my behalf."

Garahadinna went to the Niganthas, paid homage to them, and said: "My friend Sirigutta invites you for tomorrow's meritorious deed." When they asked, "Did Sirigutta himself tell you?", he replied, "Yes, masters, he told me himself." The Niganthas were delighted and joyful, saying: "Our task is accomplished. From the time Sirigutta gains faith in us, what prosperity will we not have?"
276:
## The Arrangements at the House of Sirigutta the Householder
Sirigutta the householder's house was very large. In that large house, Sirigutta had a long pit dug between two buildings and filled it with filth and mud. At the two outer edges of the pit, he had stakes driven in and ropes tied to them. He had the front legs of the couches placed on the front edge of the pit, while the back legs were rested on the ropes. Thinking, "When they sit down, they will fall headlong," he had rugs spread over the seats in such a way that the pit was not visible. He had very large pots placed outside at the back of the house, their mouths covered and tied with banana leaves and pieces of white cloth. These pots were empty, but he had their rims smeared with gruel, rice grains, ghee, oil, honey, molasses, and cake crumbs. Early in the morning, Garahadinna the householder went quickly to Sirigutta's house and asked, "Has the hospitality for the venerable ones been prepared?" When told, "Yes, friend, it is prepared," he asked again, "Where is this prepared hospitality?" Sirigutta pointed it out, saying, "In these many pots, gruel; in these, rice; in these, ghee, molasses, cakes, and so on have been filled. The seats have also been arranged." Garahadinna said, "Very well," and departed.

When Garahadinna had gone, five hundred Nigaṇṭhas arrived. Sirigutta came out of the house, paid homage to the Nigaṇṭhas with the fivefold prostration, and standing before them with joined palms, he thought: "You supposedly know everything, including the past and so on. So your supporter told me. If you truly know everything as said, do not enter my house. For those who enter my house, there is neither gruel nor rice and such. If you enter without knowing, I will have you fall into the filth pit and have you beaten." Having thought this, he gave a signal to his men: "When you know that the Nigaṇṭhas are about to sit, stand behind them and remove the cloth rugs spread over the seats. Do not let those rugs be smeared with filth and impurity."

## Torturing the Nigaṇṭhas by Dropping Them into the Filth Pit
Then he said to the Nigaṇṭhas, "Venerable ones, please enter here." The Nigaṇṭhas entered and prepared to sit on the arranged seats. Then the men said to them, "Venerable ones, please wait a moment; do not sit yet." When asked, "For what reason?" they replied, "It is proper for the venerable ones who enter our house to sit only after knowing the established custom." When asked, "Laymen, what custom should we know before sitting?" they replied, "All of you should stand by your respective seats and sit down all at once."

The Nigaṇṭhas agreed, saying, "Very well," and thought, "We should do exactly as these people say." Then all the Nigaṇṭhas stood in order by their respective seats. Then the men said to them, "Venerable ones, please sit down quickly and all at once." Knowing they were sitting, the men pulled away the rugs from the seats. As the Nigaṇṭhas sat down all at once, the legs of the couches placed upon the ropes slipped, and the Nigaṇṭhas fell headlong into the pit. When they had fallen into the pit, Sirigutta closed the door, and as each Nigaṇṭha tried to climb out, he had them beaten with sticks, clubs, and rods, saying, "Why did you not know the past, the future, and the present?" Then, thinking, "This much will be enough for these Nigaṇṭhas," he had the door opened. The Nigaṇṭhas tried to flee. However, on the path where they would go, he had the ground, which was smoothed with plaster, made slippery. Because they could not stay upright on that slippery ground, the Nigaṇṭhas kept falling, and he had them beaten again and again, saying, "This much oppression and torture is suitable for you," and then let them go. The Nigaṇṭhas cried out, "You, layman, have ruined us! You, layman, have ruined us!" and went to the door of their supporter, Garahadinna the householder.

## Garahadinna Filing a Complaint
Garahadinna the householder, seeing such ruin, became furious and said, "Sirigutta the householder has ruined us!"
277:
“My masters, who are like fertile fields of merit where seeds of merit are sown, and who are capable of granting worldly prosperity as desired to those in the world including devas who extend their hands in worship and reverence—you have caused them to be struck and beaten, leading them to ruin!” Thus, burning with rage, he went to the royal palace and had the householder Sirigutta fined a thousand kahāpaṇas. Then the King sent a message to the householder Sirigutta. Sirigutta went and paid homage to the King, saying, “Your Majesty, please take the fine only after investigating; do not take it without investigation.” “I shall take it only after investigating,” the King replied. “Very well, Your Majesty,” he said. “In that case, present your case,” the King commanded. “Your Majesty, this householder Garahadinna, who is my friend and a disciple of the Niganthas, frequently approached me and said this while standing or sitting:

‘Friend Sirigutta, what benefit is there for you with the ascetic Gotama? What will you gain by attending upon the ascetic Gotama?’ Starting with these words, Sirigutta reported the entire incident and said, “Your Majesty, if it is proper to take a fine in this matter, please take it.” The King looked at the householder Garahadinna and asked, “Is it true that you said this?” “It is true, Your Majesty,” he admitted. Then the King said to Garahadinna, “While you yourself follow teachers who do not know even this much, for what reason did you tell the disciple of the Tathāgata that they know everything? Let the fine you imposed fall upon you alone.” Thus, he made the fine fall upon Garahadinna himself. The Nigantha teachers of Garahadinna were also beaten and driven away.

## Effort to Seek Revenge After Losing the Case

The householder Garahadinna was angry with the householder Sirigutta and did not speak to him for about half a month. Then he reflected, “It is not proper for me to live like this; it is right for me to also cause ruin to the teachers of this Sirigutta.” Having planned this, he approached the householder Sirigutta and called out, “Friend Sirigutta!” When Sirigutta responded, “What is it, friend Garahadinna?”, he said, “Friend Sirigutta, among relatives and close friends who are intimate, quarrels and disputes may occur. You remain without saying a single word. Why do you do this?” “Friend Garahadinna, because you remained without speaking to me, I also remained without speaking,” Sirigutta replied. “Friend Sirigutta, what is done is done. Let us not break our friendship because of what has happened,” he said persuasively. From then on, the two householders stood and sat together in the same place.

Then one day, the householder Sirigutta said to the householder Garahadinna, “What benefit is there for you with the Niganthas? What will you gain by attending upon those Niganthas? Why is it not proper for you to attend upon my teacher, the Blessed One, and to give alms to the noble ones?” Since the householder Garahadinna was living in anticipation of just such a statement, it was like having an itch scratched with a fingernail. He then asked Sirigutta, “What does your teacher know?” “Friend Garahadinna, in this way...”
278:
"Do not say so; as for my Teacher, there is nothing that is unknown to him. He knows everything in its entirety, including the past and so forth. He discerns the minds of beings through sixteen modes." When Sirigutta said this, Garahadinna replied, "I did not know of such a thing. Why have you remained silent without telling me for so long? Friend Sirigutta, if that is so, go now. Invite your Teacher, the Buddha, for tomorrow's meritorious deed. I shall offer him a meal. Tell him to accept my alms together with five hundred bhikkhus."

Sirigutta the householder approached the Buddha, paid his respects, and said, "Venerable Sir, my friend Garahadinna the householder has asked me to invite the Exalted One to accept his alms tomorrow together with five hundred bhikkhus. However, on a previous day, I did such-and-such a thing to his teachers, the Nigaṇṭhas. I do not know if he intends to retaliate for what I did, nor do I know if he truly wishes to offer alms to the Exalted One with a pure heart. Please reflect upon this, and if it is appropriate, please accept. If it is not appropriate, please do not accept."

## How the Buddha Saw
The Buddha reflected, "What does this Garahadinna wish to do to us?" and saw that he had a large pit dug between two houses, filled it with eighty cartloads of khadira wood, set it on fire, and intended to humiliate them by making them fall into the charcoal pit. Then he reflected again, "By going to the house of the householder Garahadinna, will there be benefit or not?" He then saw the following benefits: "I shall stretch out my foot over the charcoal pit. The mat covering the pit will vanish. Breaking through the charcoal pit, a great paduma lotus the size of a cartwheel will arise. Then, I shall step upon the pericarp of the paduma lotus and proceed to sit on the prepared seat. The five hundred bhikkhus will likewise go and sit. A great multitude of people will assemble. In that assembly, I shall perform the anumodanā with two verses. At the end of the anumodanā, eighty-four thousand beings will attain the realization of the Dhamma. The householders Sirigutta and Garahadinna will become Sotāpannas and will distribute their wealth within the Sāsana. Depending on this clansman, it is proper for me to go." Having seen this, he accepted the invitation for alms.

## How Garahadinna Prepared the Charcoal Pit
Sirigutta went and informed Garahadinna of the Buddha's acceptance, saying, "Make the offerings and preparations for the Buddha, the Chief of the World." Garahadinna thought, "Now I shall know what is comparable to what was done to Sirigutta's teacher, and I shall do it." He had a large pit dug between the two houses, smeared it with cow dung, filled it with eighty cartloads of khadira wood, set the wood on fire to create a mass of glowing acacia coals, and let it smolder for three watches of the night. He then placed planks over the pit, covered them with mats, smeared them with cow dung, and on one side, he laid out a path using weak sticks. He did this with the intention that when they stepped on them, the sticks would break, causing them to stumble and fall into the charcoal pit. At the back of the house, he placed pots in the same manner Sirigutta had done. He also had the seats arranged in the same way. Early in the morning, Sirigutta went to Garahadinna's house and asked, "Friend, are the offerings prepared?" "Friend, yes, they are prepared," he replied. "Where are the offerings?" Sirigutta asked. "Come, let us see," he said, and showed everything in the same manner Sirigutta had shown him. Sirigutta said, "Friend, it is well." A great multitude of people also assembled.
279:
(Regarding the assembly: When an unbeliever invites [the Buddha], a great assembly occurs. The heretics (micchādiṭṭhi) gathered to witness the downfall of the ascetic Gotama. The right-believers (sammādiṭṭhi) gathered thinking, 'Today our Teacher, the Buddha, will preach the sublime Dhamma; we shall witness the majesty and grace of the Buddha.')

## The Blooming of Lotuses in the Charcoal Pit

On the following morning, the Blessed One, accompanied by five hundred monks, went to the house of the householder Garahadinna. Garahadinna came out, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, and stood with joined palms, thinking: 'Venerable One, my attendant told me that you know everything, including the past, and that you can discern the minds of beings through sixteen modes. If you truly know, do not enter my house. For those who enter, there is neither gruel nor rice; I shall cast you all into the charcoal pit and humiliate you.' Having thought thus, he took the Buddha's bowl and said, 'Venerable One, please come this way.' He then added, 'Venerable One, it is proper for those coming to our house to know the protocol.' The Buddha asked, 'Friend, what protocol should be followed?' He replied, 'It is proper for each to enter one by one, and only after the first has sat down should the next one follow.'

(This was Garahadinna's plan: if he saw the one in front fall into the charcoal pit, the rest would not come. He intended to make them fall one by one and thus humiliate them.)

The Blessed One consented, saying 'Very well,' and proceeded alone. When Garahadinna reached the vicinity of the charcoal pit, he stepped back and said to the Blessed One, 'Venerable One, please step forward.' Then, the Blessed One extended his foot over the charcoal pit. The mat disappeared. Breaking through the charcoal pit, lotus flowers the size of chariot wheels sprang up. The Blessed One, treading upon the pericarp of a lotus, proceeded and sat upon the prepared seat. The monks likewise followed and took their seats. A burning sensation arose in Garahadinna's body.
280:
## Empty Jars Filled with Alms-food

Garahadinna went quickly to the householder Sirigutta and pleaded, 'Noble Sirigutta, please be my refuge.' When asked the reason for this plea, he said, 'Friend, there is neither gruel nor rice in my house to offer to the five hundred monks. What shall I do?' Sirigutta asked, 'What have you done?' He replied, 'I had a large pit between the two houses filled with acacia charcoal, intending to make them fall in and humiliate them. But despite my plan, great lotus flowers have broken through the charcoal pit and appeared. All the monks have trodden upon the pericarps of those lotuses and are now seated on the prepared seats. O Noble Sirigutta, what shall I do now?' Sirigutta asked, 'Did you not just show me jars, saying "This many jars of gruel, this many jars of rice"?' He replied, 'Sir, I spoke falsely; the jars are empty.' Sirigutta said, 'Even so, go and look into those jars for the gruel and other food.'

At that very moment, because Garahadinna had called them 'gruel jars,' they became full of gruel. Because he had mentioned 'rice and other food,' they became full of rice and food. Upon seeing this abundance, Garahadinna's entire body was filled with rapture and joy, and his mind became clear and confident. He respectfully served the community of monks headed by the Buddha. When the meal was over, wishing the Buddha to give the blessing (anumodanā), he took the bowl. The Blessed One, while delivering the discourse of appreciation, said: 'Because these beings lack the eye of wisdom, they do not know the virtues of my disciples or the Buddha's Dispensation. Those devoid of the eye of wisdom are called blind; only those possessed of wisdom are called those with sight.' He then uttered these verses:

## The Teaching

(58) As upon a heap of rubbish
Thrown on the highway,
A lotus might grow there,
Pure-scented and delightful.

(59) Even so, among those who are like rubbish,
Among the blind worldlings,
The disciple of the Fully Enlightened One
Outshines them with wisdom.

Mahāpathe: on the great highway. Ujjhitasmiṃ: thrown away. Tattha saṅkāraṭṭhānasmiṃ: in such a heap of rubbish, foul and muddy. Sucigandhaṃ: having a pure, sweet, and fragrant scent. Manoramaṃ: delightful to the heart. Padumaṃ: a lotus flower. Jāyetha yathā: just as it would grow.

Evaṃ tathā: even so. Saṅkārabhūtesu: among those who have become like a heap of rubbish. Andhabhūte - andhabhūtesu: among those who have become like the blind due to the lack of the eye of wisdom. Puthujjane - puthujjanesu: among worldlings. Jāto: born. Sammāsambuddhasāvako: the disciple of the Fully Enlightened One. Paññāya: by his own wisdom. Atirocati: shines brilliantly.
281:
I would rather fall into hell, with feet up and head down;
I will not do what is unnoble. Come, please accept this alms-food.

Venerable Sir, Noble Paccekabuddha. I, who have prepared this alms-bowl to offer, even if I should truly fall into the hell known as the Great Pit of Acacia Embers, eighty cubits deep, with my feet up and my head down, I will not perform the deeds of the ignoble, such as not giving alms or not keeping the precepts. May you, Lord, freely accept and partake of my alms-food.

## Two Wealthy Men Become Stream-Enterers
At the end of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings attained the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. Both the wealthy man Garahadinna and the wealthy man Sirigutta attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). These two wealthy men, Garahadinna and Sirigutta, donated and distributed all their wealth within the Buddha's Dispensation.

## Briefly Preaching the Khadirangāra Jātaka
The Buddha then rose from his seat and went to the monastery. In the evening, the monks in the Dhamma Hall raised a discussion: "Oh, how wonderful are the virtues of the Buddhas! Indeed, lotuses arose by breaking through such a mass of acacia embers."

The Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such a discussion," he said, "Monks, it is not very wonderful that lotuses have now arisen from a mass of embers for me who has become a Buddha. Even when I was a Bodhisatta, before my wisdom was fully matured, lotuses once arose for me."

Being requested, "Venerable Sir, when was that? Please tell us," he brought forth the past and preached this verse:

"I would rather fall into hell, with feet up and head down;
I will not do what is unnoble. Come, please accept this alms-food."

In this way, he preached the Khadirangāra Jātaka in detail.

The story of the wealthy man Garahadinna ends.
The Pupphavagga (Chapter on Flowers) ends.
282:
## 5. Bālavagga
## 1. The Story of King Pasenadi of Kosala and an Unknown Man (Aññatarapurisa-vatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, preached this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Dīghā jāgarato rattī," concerning King Pasenadi of Kosala and a certain unknown man.

## Giving a Position to the Husband to Take the Wife
It is said that King Pasenadi of Kosala, the ruler of Sāvatthī, on a certain festival day, mounted an all-white elephant named Puṇḍarīka, which was fully adorned, and made a clockwise procession around the city with great royal majesty. While the crowd was being cleared, even though they were being struck with clods and sticks and made to run, the multitude of people still turned their necks to look.

(This looking back is the result and benefit of the respectful giving (sakkaccadāna) performed well by kings.)

The wife of a certain poor, unknown man, standing on the upper floor of a seven-story palace, opened a shutter of a window, looked at the King, and then moved away. To King Pasenadi of Kosala, it appeared as if the full moon had entered between clouds. The King, having a heart bound by lust for that woman, became as if he were about to fall from the elephant's back. He quickly finished the clockwise procession of the city, entered the inner palace, and said to a trusted minister, "When we reached such a place, did you see the palace I looked at?" "Yes, Your Majesty, I saw it," he replied.

"Did you see a woman in that palace?" the King asked again. When the minister replied, "Your Majesty, I saw her," the King commanded, "Friend minister, go and find out whether that woman has a husband or not." The minister went, and having learned that she had a husband, returned and reported to the King that she was a married woman. Then the King said, "If that is so, go and summon that woman's husband." The minister went and said, "O man, come; the King summons you."

That man thought, "Danger will surely arise for me because of my wife." Being unable to defy the King's command, he went, paid homage to the King, and stood there. Then the King said, "O man, from today onwards, you must serve me." "Your Majesty, I have no such desire. I will do my own work and pay taxes to Your Majesty. Let me live only at my home," he pleaded. "I have no need for your taxes. From today onwards, perform service for me," the King said, and had a shield and a weapon given to that man.

(The King's intention was this: "I will charge that man with some fault, kill him, and then take his wife." This was the King's plan.)

Then that man, being terrified of the danger of death, served the King with great heedfulness.

## Ordering to Fetch Lotuses and Red Earth
Then the King, not seeing any fault in that man, and being greatly tormented by the bond of sensual desire, thought, "I will charge this man with a fault and exercise royal power." He [ordered] that man...
283:
The King summoned him and said, "My good man, go to a certain place on the river one yojana from this capital. Bring back kumuda lotuses and aruṇavatī clay by the time of my evening bath. If you do not arrive at that time, I will execute you." A royal servant is lowlier than the four types of slaves. Slaves bought with money can say, "My head aches, my back aches," and get to stay. A royal servant has no such right; he must do as commanded. Therefore, that servant thought, "I must certainly go. Kumuda lotuses and aruṇavatī clay are found only in the nāga realm. Where will I find them?" Fearing death, he hurried home and asked, "Dear sister, is my rice ready?" She replied, "Lord, it is still on the stove." Unable to wait for the pot to be taken off, he had some sour gruel brought in a ladle, packed the moist, steaming rice along with whatever curry was available into a basket, and ran the distance of one yojana. As he went, the rice became fully cooked.

## The Benefit of Sharing Merit
Not wanting to make the food "leftovers," he set aside a small portion of the first-served rice. While eating, he saw a traveler and said, "Sir, I have a small portion of rice here that is not leftovers. Please take and eat it." The traveler took and ate it. After the servant finished eating, he threw a handful of rice into the water and washed his mouth. Then, in a loud voice, he proclaimed:

"May the nāgas, garuḍas, and devas who dwell in and protect this part of the river hear my words! The King, wishing to execute me, commanded me to bring kumuda lotuses and aruṇavatī clay. I have given food to a human traveler; that gift has a thousand-fold benefit. I have also given food to the fish in the water; that gift has a hundred-fold benefit. I share the portion of this merit with you. Please bring and give me kumuda lotuses and fine aruṇavatī clay!" He shouted this three times.
284:
The nāga king dwelling in that part of the river heard the voice. Taking the form of an old man, he went to the servant and asked, "What are you shouting about?" When the man repeated his words, the nāga king said, "Give me that share of merit." The man replied, "I share it." When asked again, "Give it to me," he replied, "I share it, lord." After having the merit shared two or three times, the nāga king brought and gave him the kumuda lotuses and the fine aruṇavatī clay.

## Going to the Monastery Because the City Gates Were Closed
King Pasenadi of Kosala thought, "Humans are full of deceit. If that man should obtain them by some means, my purpose will not be fulfilled." Having thought thus, he had the city gates closed early and had the signet and keys brought to him. The servant arrived exactly at the King's bath time. Finding no entry, he called the gatekeeper and said, "Open the gate!" The gatekeeper replied, "I cannot open it. The King closed it early, applied the seal, and took the keys to the palace." The man said, "I am a royal messenger; open the gate!" But still unable to enter, he thought, "Now I have no life left. What shall I do?" He placed a lump of the clay on the upper lintel of the gate, stuck the lotuses into the clay, and in a loud voice cried out, "O citizens! Know that I went on the King's command. The King wishes to destroy me without cause!" After shouting this three times, he thought, "Where shall I go?" and decided, "Monks are kind-hearted. I will go to the monastery and sleep there."

(These beings, in times of happiness, do not even know of the existence of monks, but when overwhelmed by suffering, they wish to go to the monastery.)

Therefore, that servant, thinking "I have no other refuge," went to the monastery and slept in a comfortable place. At that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala, unable to sleep that night as he brooded over that woman, was consumed by the fever of sensual desire. Oppressed by this fever, he thought, "As soon as it is dawn, I will have that man killed and take that woman."

## Hearing the Sounds "Du-Sa-Na-So"
At that very moment, four men who had arisen in the Lohakumbhī hell, which is sixty yojanas in size, were being boiled like rice in a pot...
285:
Tossed about like grains of rice boiling in a pot, they reach the bottom after thirty thousand years, and after another thirty thousand years, they reach the rim of the hell-cauldron once more. Those four denizens of hell, lifting their heads and looking at one another, wished to recite a verse each. However, being unable to do so, they could only utter a single syllable each before sinking back into the Lohakumbhī hell.

King Pasenadi of Kosala, unable to sleep, heard those sounds just after the midnight hour. Filled with fear and trembling, he thought, "What could this be? Is there a danger to my life? Or is it a danger to my Chief Queen? Or will my kingdom itself be destroyed?" Thus, he spent the entire night unable to close his eyes. At dawn, King Pasenadi summoned his Brahmin chaplain and said, "Teacher, just after the midnight hour, I heard a great and terrifying sound. I do not know whether danger will befall the kingdom, the Queen, or myself. Therefore, I have summoned you."

"Great King, what kind of sounds did you hear?" the Brahmin asked. The King replied, "Teacher, I heard the sounds: 'Du', 'Sa', 'Na', 'So'. Investigate the consequences of these four sounds."

## The Brahmin's Scheme regarding Du-Sa-Na-So

At that moment, to the Brahmin chaplain, nothing was clear, as if he had entered a place of total darkness. However, fearing that his gains and honors would diminish if he said "I do not know," he said, "Great King, it is a grave matter."

"What is it, Teacher?" the King asked. "A danger to your life is apparent," the Brahmin replied. The King became doubly afraid and asked, "Teacher, is there any way to avert this?" The Brahmin answered, "Great King, there is a way. Do not be afraid. I am well-versed in the three Vedas."

"What must be obtained?" the King asked. The Brahmin replied, "Great King, by performing the 'Sabba-sata' sacrifice (a sacrifice of all kinds in hundreds), you shall preserve your life."

When asked again what was needed, the Brahmin ordered the gathering of one hundred of each kind of living being: one hundred elephants, one hundred horses, one hundred bulls, one hundred milch cows, one hundred goats, one hundred donkeys, one hundred thoroughbred horses, one hundred rams, one hundred fowls, one hundred pigs, one hundred boys, and one hundred girls. Thus, he had one hundred of each species taken.

(The Brahmin thought: "If I only order the gathering of edible animals, people will say I am just taking food for myself." Therefore, he also ordered the gathering of elephants, horses, and humans.)

The King, thinking "My life alone is my greatest gain," commanded, "Seize all these beings quickly!" The men commissioned for the task seized even more than was ordered.

The great multitude of people, lamenting for the sake of their own sons, daughters, and relatives, made a great outcry. It was as if the great earth itself were resounding with the sound.
286:
## A King with Little Wisdom

Then Queen Mallikā, having heard that sound, went to the King and asked, "Great King, your faculties are not as they usually are; you appear weary and exhausted. What is the reason for this?" The King replied, "Queen Mallikā, do you not know that a swift, poisonous snake is moving near my ear?" She asked again, "Great King, what is the meaning of this?" He said, "During the night, such a sound was heard. When I consulted the Brahmin Chaplain, he said, 'An obstacle to your life is apparent. Therefore, only by performing the great sacrifice known as the Sacrifice of All Hundreds (Sabba-sata) will you regain your life.' Thinking that my life alone is my greatest gain, I have ordered these creatures to be seized."

Queen Mallikā then said, "Great King, you are indeed a great fool. Although you are a great eater, consuming a 'doṇa' measure of rice with many varieties of curries and sauces, and although you rule over two great kingdoms, your wisdom is very little."

## Seek the Buddha's Judgment

When he asked, "Queen, why do you say such a thing?", she replied, "Where have you ever seen the gaining of one's life through the death of another? Why do you take the words of a foolish Brahmin and cast suffering upon the multitude? The Teacher, the Supreme Person of the world including the devas, whose knowledge regarding the past and so forth is unobstructed, resides in the nearby Jetavana Monastery. Go and ask that Teacher and follow only His advice."

Being thus addressed, the King, terrified by the fear of death and unable to say anything, went to the monastery with Queen Mallikā in swift vehicles, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat at a respectful distance. Then the Teacher first addressed him, saying, "Well now, Great King, from where have you come at this time of day?" King Pasenadi of Kosala sat in silence.

## No Danger to the King

Then Queen Mallikā informed the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, it is said that the King heard an evil sound just after the middle watch of the night. Then he informed the Brahmin Chaplain. Hearing this, the Chaplain said, 'There will be an obstacle to your life. To prevent that danger, you will regain your life only if you seize animals of all kinds, a hundred of each, and perform a great sacrifice with the blood from their throats.' The King has ordered the animals to be seized. Therefore, I have brought the King here to the feet of the Blessed One."

When the Buddha asked, "Great King, is it true as the Queen says?", the King admitted, "It is true, Venerable Sir." When asked again, "King, what kind of sound did you hear?", the King related it to the Blessed One exactly as he had heard it. As soon as the Tathāgata heard the King's account, a light appeared. Then He said to the King, "Do not be afraid, Great King. There is no danger to you. Beings who have committed evil deeds, unable to endure their own suffering, uttered such sounds to reveal their pain."

When the King asked, "Venerable Sir, what is the evil deed they committed?", the Blessed One, wishing to explain their deed, said, "If that is so, Great King, listen," and brought forth a story of the past.
287:
## The Detailed Verses of Du-Sa-Na-So

We lived a wicked life; we did not give [alms] while we were able.
Though wealth existed, we did not make a refuge for ourselves.

*Yesaṃ*: for us. (Alternatively) *Yesaṃ no*: we who. *Bhogesu*: while wealth. *Vijjamānesu*: was clearly present. *Na dadamhase*: did not give or offer alms. *Attano*: for ourselves. *Dīpaṃ*: a refuge like an island, namely the merit of wholesome deeds. *Na akamha*: did not make. *Tesaṃ no*: for those of us. *Du-jīvitaṃ*: a wicked life. *Ajīvimha*: we have lived.

Sixty thousand years have fully passed in every way.
For us who are being cooked in hell, when will there be an end?

*Niraye*: in this Lohakumbhī hell, in the molten metal. *Paccamānānaṃ*: for us who are being cooked. *Sabbaso*: in every way. *Saṭṭhivassasahassāni*: sixty thousand years. *Paripuṇṇāni*: are complete. *Kadā*: at what time. *Anto*: the end. *Bhavissati*: will there be?

## The Past Story of Du-Sa-Na-So

In the past, in the city of Bārāṇasī, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, the Buddha named Kassapa appeared in the world. While he was traveling on a journey with twenty thousand Arahants, he arrived at the city of Bārāṇasī. The citizens of Bārāṇasī, in groups of two, three, or many, gathered together and offered *āgantuka-dāna* (alms for visiting monks). At that time, there were four sons of wealthy merchants in Bārāṇasī, each possessing a fortune of four hundred million, who were close friends. They consulted one another, saying, "There is much gold, silver, and wealth in our houses. What shall we do with this wealth?"

While they were consulting, not even one among the four merchant sons said, "While a Buddha of such nature is traveling on a journey, let us give alms, observe the precepts, and perform acts of worship." Instead, one merchant son first said, "Let us live drinking strong liquor and eating delicious meat; this will be the fruit of our lives." Another merchant son said, "Let us live eating fragrant *sāli* rice, which has been aged for three years, along with various choice flavors every day." Another merchant son said, "Let us live eating various kinds of fried and cooked cakes and snacks." But another merchant son said, "Friends, we shall do nothing else. There are no women who do not desire wealth when it is offered. Therefore, let us use our wealth to entice them and commit the act of adultery (*parādārika-kamma*)." All of them agreed, saying, "Excellent, excellent," and settled on his words.

From that time on, those merchant sons sent wealth to beautiful women and committed adultery for twenty thousand years. When they died, they were reborn in the Avīci Great Hell. After being cooked in that hell for the interval between two Buddhas, they died from Avīci and, due to the remaining power of that evil karma, were reborn in the Lohakumbhī (Iron Cauldron) Hell, which was sixty yojanas in size. It took thirty thousand years to reach the bottom, and another thirty thousand years to reach the rim of the Lohakumbhī Hell. When they reached the surface, each desired to recite a full verse, but being unable to do so, they could only utter a single syllable each before sinking back and submerging into the cauldron again. 

When the Buddha asked, "Great King, speak; what was the first sound you heard?", the King replied, "Venerable Sir, I heard the sound 'Du'." The Teacher, wishing to show the full verse that the hell-being had uttered incompletely, said as follows:

[The Teacher then explained the meaning of this verse to the King.] Then he asked, "Great King, what did you hear as the second sound, the third sound, and the fourth sound?" When the King replied, "Such and such sounds, Bhante," the Teacher completed the remainder of the verses:

There is no end; where could an end be? No end is in sight.
For, dear friends, much evil was then committed by both you and me.

*Amhākaṃ*: for us. *Anto*: an end or limit. *Natthi*: there was not. *Anto*: the end of hell. *Kuto*: where would it be? *Anto*: the limit of suffering in hell. *Na paṭidissati*: is not seen. *Hi*: indeed. *Mārisā*: O those like me (friends). *Tadā*: at that time while being human in Bārāṇasī. *Mama ca*: by me as well. *Tuyhañca*: and by you. *Pāpaṃ*: evil. *Pakataṃ*: was committed in abundance.
288:
## The Long Saṃsāra for the Fool

(60) Dīghā jāgarato ratti, dīghaṃ santassa yojanaṃ.
Dīgho bālāna saṃsāro, saddhammaṃ avijānataṃ.

To the one who is awake and cannot sleep, the night, though only three watches long, seems long. To the one who is weary from travel, a league (yojana), though only four gāvutas, seems long. To the fools who do not know the True Dhamma, Saṃsāra, the cycle of wandering, is indeed very long.

Sohan nūna ito gantvā, yoniṃ laddhāna mānusiṃ.
Vadaññū sīlasampanno, kāhāmi kusalaṃ bahuṃ.

If I, having gone from this boiling water hell, should obtain a human birth, I will be one who understands the words of those who ask for alms, I will be endowed with virtue, and I will certainly perform much merit.

Having thus taught these verses in succession and explained their meaning, the Teacher said, "Thus, O Great King, those four persons, though wishing to recite a single verse each, were unable to do so; having uttered only a single syllable each, they entered the Lohakumbhī hell once again."

## Renouncing the Desire for Another's Wife

Upon hearing that Dhamma teaching, a great sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arose within King Pasenadi of Kosala. He thought, "How heavy indeed is this evil deed of committing adultery with another's wife! Having been cooked in hell for the interval between two Buddhas, and after passing away from that hell, being reborn in the Lohakumbhī hell which is sixty leagues in size, and having been cooked there for sixty thousand years, the time of release from suffering for those hell-beings is still not apparent. I too, because of my affection for another's wife, could not sleep for the entire three watches of the night. From this day forward, I will no longer fix my mind on another's wife." Thinking thus, he said to the Tathāgata, "Venerable Sir, today I have realized the length of the night."

That king's servant, who was sitting near that very place, heard the King's words and thought, "I have found a strong support." He then said to the Teacher, "Venerable Sir, the King has first realized the length of the night; I, however, realized for myself yesterday the length of a journey of one league."

The Teacher, connecting the words of both men, said, "To some, the night is long; to some, a journey of one league is long; but to the foolish and deluded, Saṃsāra is long." Wishing to teach the Dhamma, he uttered this verse.

## The King's Servant Becomes a Sotāpanna

At the conclusion of the teaching, that king's servant attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Many others also attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth. The Dhamma teaching was beneficial to the great multitude. King Pasenadi of Kosala, having paid respectful homage to the Teacher, returned to the palace and released all those beings who had been bound and imprisoned.

## Praising the Virtues of Mallikā

When the men and women who were released from the sacrificial bonds went to their homes after washing their heads with water, they prayed, "May our lady, Queen Mallikā, live long!" and spoke in praise of her virtues, saying, "Because of Queen Mallikā, we have received our lives."

In the evening, the monks also spoke words of praise in the Dhamma hall, saying, "Oh, how wise indeed is Queen Mallikā! Depending on her own wisdom, she has given the gift of life (jīvitadāna) to such a great multitude of beings."
289:
While the Blessed One was staying in the Gandhakuṭī, he overheard the conversation of those monks. He then departed from the Gandhakuṭī, entered the Dhamma hall, and sat upon the prepared seat. He asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?" When they informed him, he said, "Monks, Queen Mallikā did not only give the gift of life to a great multitude of people by relying on her wisdom in this present life; she did so in the past as well." To clarify this matter, the Blessed One related a story of the past.

## The Story of the Past: The Sacrifice to the Deity
In the distant past, a prince, the son of the King of Bārāṇasī, approached a certain banyan tree and addressed the deity residing there: "O Lord Deity, there are one hundred and one kings and one hundred and one queens in this Jambudīpa. If I should attain the kingship upon the passing of my father, I shall perform a sacrificial offering to you with the throat-blood of those one hundred and one kings and queens."

When his father passed away, the prince ascended to the throne. Thinking, "I have attained kingship through the power of the deity; I shall now perform the sacrifice for him," he set out with a large army. He brought one king under his control, then allied with him to bring another and another under his power. In this manner, after bringing all the kings under his control, he led them away along with their chief queens. However, because the chief queen of King Uggasena, the youngest of all the kings, named Dhammadinnā, was heavy with child, he left her behind. He then planned, "I shall kill this entire multitude by making them drink a potion mixed with poison," and ordered the area around the foot of the banyan tree to be cleared.

The deity of the banyan tree thought: "This king, having captured all these kings, believes he did so by relying on me, and now wishes to perform a sacrifice to me with their throat-blood. If he kills these kings, the royal lineages in Jambudīpa will be severed. Furthermore, the foot of this banyan tree, my well-cleansed abode, will become impure and defiled. Will I be able to prevent the deed this king is about to commit?" Upon reflection, the deity realized, "I will not be able to do so." He then approached another deity, explained the situation, and asked, "O Lord Deity, would you be able to prevent this?" That deity also refused, saying he was unable. He then approached yet another deity, and that deity also refused.
290:
They refused again. In this manner, she approached the deities throughout the entire universe, but they also refused.

Then she approached the Four Great Kings and pleaded with them, but they said, "We are not able to avert the danger that will arise when we speak." When they said this, she approached Sakka, the King of Devas, and reported the entire matter to him, saying, "O Sakka, if you remain indifferent, the royal lineages in Jambudīpa will be destroyed. Please be the refuge and reliance of these kings."

Sakka replied, "I too am unable to prevent him directly," but added, "However, I will show you a stratagem." He then instructed her on the stratagem as follows: "Go, while the King is watching, dress in red garments, emerge from your tree, and make a gesture as if you are leaving. Then the King, seeing the banyan tree deity leaving, will plead with you in various ways to turn back. When he pleads, tell him: 'O Great King, you promised to perform a sacrificial offering to me with the throat-blood of one hundred and one kings along with their chief queens, yet you have come leaving behind the queen of King Uggasena. I do not wish to accept the offering of such a liar.'"

(Sakka gave this stratagem to the banyan tree deity with the knowledge that: "When this is said, the King will send an order to fetch Queen Dhammadinnā. That Queen Dhammadinnā will then preach the Dhamma to the King and grant the gift of life (jīvitadāna) to this great multitude of people.")

## The Weeping and Laughing of Queen Dhammadinnā

The banyan tree deity did exactly as Sakka had instructed. The King of Bārāṇasī then sent for Queen Dhammadinnā. When Queen Dhammadinnā arrived, she sat down and paid respectful homage only to her own lord, King Uggasena, who was the youngest of all the kings and was sitting in the very last seat. The King of Bārāṇasī became angry with Queen Dhammadinnā, thinking, "While I, the leader of all kings, am present, she pays homage only to her husband, King Uggasena, who is younger than all the other kings."

Then Queen Dhammadinnā said to the King of Bārāṇasī: "O Great King, what relation do I have with you? This noble King Uggasena is my lord and husband; he is the giver of my sovereignty and prosperity. Without paying homage to this noble King Uggasena, how could I pay homage to you, the King of Bārāṇasī?" At that moment, while the great multitude of people was watching, the banyan tree deity praised her, saying, "O Lady, your words are very true!" and honored Queen Dhammadinnā with a handful of flowers.
291:
Again, the King of Bārāṇasī said, "If you do not pay homage to me, why do you not pay homage to this deity of great power and majesty, who bestows upon me the glory of kingship?" She replied, "O Great King, you captured these kings by standing on your own merit; they were not captured and given to you by the deity." Once again, the deity praised Queen Dhammadinnā, saying, "O Lady, it is very true! O Lady, it is very true!" and honored her as before.

Then Queen Dhammadinnā said to the King, "O Great King, you say that this banyan tree deity captured and gave these many kings to you. Now, look at the upper left side of your deity's tree; it is scorched by fire. If your deity is of such great power and majesty, why could he not extinguish that fire?" Once again, the deity praised Queen Dhammadinnā, saying, "O Lady, it is very true! O Lady, it is very true!" and honored her as before.

While Queen Dhammadinnā was speaking these words, she both wept and laughed. Then the King of Bārāṇasī said to her, "What is this? Have you gone mad?" She replied, "O Great King, why do you speak thus? Women like me do not go mad." When he asked again, "Then for what reason do you both weep and laugh?"

She replied, "O Great King, listen; I will explain in detail. In the past, I was a daughter of a good family. While living in my husband's house, I saw a guest who was a friend of my husband. Wanting to cook a meal for that guest, I gave a coin to a maidservant and told her, 'Go, bring some meat.' When the maid returned and said, 'There is no meat,' I cut off the head of a she-goat that was sleeping at the back of the house and prepared a fine meal.

Because I beheaded that one she-goat, I had to suffer in hell, and as a residual result, I have had my own head cut off as many times as the number of hairs on that goat. O Great King, if you kill this many kings, when will you ever be free from suffering? For this reason, thinking of your future suffering, I felt sorrow and wept." Having said this, Queen Dhammadinnā recited this verse.

After reciting the verse, when asked again, "Why did you laugh?" she replied, "O Great King, I laughed with joy, thinking that I have finally become one who is liberated from that suffering." Once again, the banyan tree deity praised Queen Dhammadinnā, saying, "O Lady, it is very true! O Lady, it is very true!" and honored her with a handful of flowers.
292:
Having cut the throat of a single goat, I was cooked in hell and had my throat cut as many times as the number of hairs on its body. O King, great ruler of the land, if you were to cut the throats of many kings and queens, how could you ever find a way to be free from suffering?

Here he grieves, hereafter he grieves; the evil-doer grieves in both places. He grieves and is afflicted, seeing his own impure deeds. (Dhp. 15)

If beings only knew that birth is suffering, one living being would not kill another; for the killer of living beings grieves. (Jātaka 1.1.18)

## The King of Vārāṇasī's Apology and Forgiveness

The King of Vārāṇasī thought, "Oh, what a heavy deed I have committed! This Queen Dhammadinnā, because of killing just one goat, was cooked in hell and, as a remaining result, had her head cut off as many times as the number of hairs on that goat. If I were to kill so many kings, when would I ever attain peace?" Reflecting thus, he released all the kings. He paid homage to those older than himself, raised his hands in salutation to those who were younger, and after asking for forgiveness from all the kings, he sent them back to their respective kingdoms.

The Buddha, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, said, "Monks, it is not only now that Queen Mallikā, relying on her own wisdom, has given the gift of life to a great multitude; she did so in the past as well." He then connected the birth story (Jātaka):

"At that time, the King of Vārāṇasī was Pasenadi Kosala. Queen Dhammadinnā was Queen Mallikā. The deity of the banyan tree was I, the Buddha."

Having thus connected the birth story, and wishing to preach the Dhamma further, he said, "Monks, the act of taking life is something that is neither suitable nor proper to do. Indeed, those who are killers of living beings must grieve for a long time," and he spoke this verse.

At the end of this Dhamma teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and other stages.

The Story of King Pasenadi Kosala and the Unknown Man is finished.
293:
## 2. The Story of the Pupil of Venerable Mahākassapa
(Mahākassapattherasaddhivihārikavatthu)

The Buddha preached this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Carañce nādhigaccheyya" while staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, concerning a co-resident pupil of Venerable Mahākassapa. The story originated in the city of Rājagaha.

## The Exposure of the Deceitful Pupil

While Venerable Mahākassapa was residing in the Pipphali Cave near the city of Rājagaha, two co-resident pupils were attending to him. Among those two pupils, one performed his duties respectfully and well. The other pupil would pretend that whatever duties the diligent monk had performed were done by himself. When he knew that the face-washing water and tooth-sticks had been prepared, he would say, "Venerable Sir, I have prepared the face-washing water and tooth-sticks; please wash your face." He would say the same when it was time to wash the feet or to bathe.

The other pupil, who was diligent in his duties, thought, "This monk constantly pretends that whatever I have done was done by himself. Let it be; I will do something appropriate for this monk." After finishing his meal, while the other monk was sleeping, he heated the bath water, put it in a jar, and placed it behind the bathhouse. However, he left about a ladleful of water in the heating pot and left it on the stove so that steam would continue to rise.

The other pupil, who was not diligent in his duties, woke up in the evening and, seeing the steam rising, thought, "The water must have been heated and placed in the bathhouse." He went quickly, paid homage to the Elder, and said, "Venerable Sir, the water has been placed in the bathhouse; please bathe." He then entered the bathhouse together with the Elder. Not seeing any water, the Elder asked, "Friend, where is the water?"

The young monk went to the kitchen, and when he lowered a ladle into the pot and realized it was empty, he complained, "Look at the work of this wicked, bad monk! He placed an empty pot on the stove and where has he gone? I told the Elder there was water in the bathhouse because I thought there was." Grumbling thus, he took a water jar and went to the river landing. The diligent young monk then brought the water from behind the bathhouse and placed it inside.

Venerable Mahākassapa reflected, "This young monk said, 'I have heated the water and placed it in the bathhouse; please come, Venerable Sir, and bathe,' but now he is grumbling and going to the river landing with a water jar. What is this?" Upon investigating, he realized, "For all this time, this young monk has been presenting the duties performed by the other as if he had done them himself."
294:
When he investigated, "What is the reason for this?", he realized, "For all this time, this young monk has been making it appear as if he himself performed the major and minor duties that were actually performed by the other young monk." Therefore, when the young monk came to attend to him in the evening, the Elder gave him this admonition: "Friend, a monk should only say he has done what he has actually done; it is not proper to say he has done what he has not done. Just now, you said, 'Venerable Sir, the water has been placed in the bathhouse; please go and bathe,' yet when I entered the bathhouse, you were just carrying the water jar and grumbling as you went. Such behavior is not suitable for one who has gone forth."

The young monk, becoming angry, thought, "Look at the Elder's deed! He speaks to me in this way over a mere drop of water." Consequently, on the following day, he did not enter for alms together with the Elder.

## Burning the Monastery out of Malice

The Elder went to a certain place together with the other monk who was perfect in his duties. When the Elder had gone, the ill-behaved young monk went to the house of the Elder's supporting family. When asked, "Venerable Sir, where is the Elder?", he replied, "The Elder is unwell and is just resting at the monastery." When they asked further, "Venerable Sir, what would be suitable for him?", he said, "Give such and such food." They prepared it well according to the young monk's words and offered it. The young monk ate that food on the way and then returned to the monastery. Meanwhile, the Elder received a large, fine piece of cloth at the place he had gone and gave it to the young monk who had accompanied him. That monk dyed the cloth and made it into an inner and outer robe for himself.

On the following day, when the Elder Mahākassapa went to that supporting family's house, they said, "Venerable Sir, we were told by the young monk that you were unwell, so we prepared and sent food exactly as he described. Are you feeling better after consuming it?" The Elder remained silent. Upon returning to the monastery, when the young monk came and sat down after paying respects, the Elder said to him: "Friend, it is said that you did such a thing yesterday. Doing this is not suitable for monks. It is not proper to eat by making a 'viññatti' (a verbal request to those who are not relatives or have not invited such requests)."

The young monk became angry and harbored a grudge against the Elder, thinking, "The other day, over a mere drop of water, he made me out to be a liar. Today, because I ate a handful of alms-food at his supporter's house, he says it is not proper to eat by making a request. Furthermore, that cloth he received, he gave only to the monk who attends him. Oh, the Elder's deed is very burdensome indeed! I shall let him know what is fit to be done to him!" On the following day, while the Elder entered the village for alms, the young monk stayed behind at the monastery. Taking a staff, he smashed the utensils and vessels, set fire to the Elder's leaf-hut (paṇṇasālā), and whatever did not burn, he smashed with a mallet before fleeing. After he passed away, he was reborn in the Avīci Great Hell.

## Reporting to the Buddha

The multitude of people started a conversation: "It is said that a resident pupil (saddhivihārika) of the Elder Mahākassapa, unable to endure a mere admonition, became angry, set fire to the Elder's leaf-hut, and fled." Later, a certain monk left Rājagaha and, wishing to see the Blessed One, went to Jetavana. After paying respects to the Blessed One and exchanging formal greetings, he was asked by the Blessed One, "Monk, where have you come from?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, I have come from Rājagaha." "Is my son Mahākassapa well and healthy?" the Buddha asked. "Venerable Sir, he is well and healthy. However, one of his resident pupils, becoming angry at a mere word of advice, set fire to the leaf-hut and fled," the monk reported. The Blessed One said, "Monk, it is not only now that he has become angry upon hearing an admonition; he was angry in the past as well. It is not only now that he has destroyed a dwelling; he destroyed one in the past too." Having said this, he brought forth the past story.
295:
## The Past Story of the Monkey and the Singila Bird

"Your head is like a human's, and your hands and feet too, O monkey.
Then for what reason do you have no house?"

O monkey! Your head is like a human's head. Your hands and feet are also like a human's hands and feet. This being so, for what reason do you have no house to live in?

"My head is like a human's, and my hands and feet too, O Singila,
But that wisdom which is said to be supreme among humans, that wisdom I do not possess."

O friend Singila bird! My head is like a human's head. My hands and feet are also like a human's hands and feet. But that wisdom which is said to be supreme among humans, that wisdom I do not have.

"For one of unsteady mind, of fickle mind, a betrayer of friends,
And of ever-inconstant virtue, there is no state of happiness.

O monkey, perform an act of power; transcend the habits of monkeys.
Build a hut, O monkey, as a protection against the cold and wind."

O monkey! For one who has an unsteady and restless mind, a fickle and impulsive mind, who betrays friends, and who is always of inconstant virtue, there is no state of happiness.

O monkey! You should perform an act of ingenuity, which is called the power for the arising of wisdom. Transcend the habits of monkeys that cause impurity. Build a house, a hut, which is the means to ward off the cold-producing wind.

(A hut [kuṭī] is a building not larger than 27 cubits in length and 15 cubits, one span, and six finger-breadths in width. It is not smaller than 4 cubits in length and 4 cubits in width. Other buildings are also called 'kuṭī' by convention or metaphor.)

Long ago, when King Brahmadatta reigned in Bārāṇasī, a Singila bird lived in a nest it had built in the Himalayan region. One day, while it was raining, a monkey arrived at that place, shivering with cold. Seeing the monkey, the Singila bird spoke this verse.

The monkey thought, "I indeed have hands and feet. Even so, I do not have the wisdom to investigate and build a house." Wishing to make this matter clear, he spoke this verse.

Then, wishing to reproach him, saying, "How can living in a house be successful for one such as you?" the Singila bird spoke these two verses.

The monkey thought, "This Singila bird makes me out to be one of unsteady and restless mind, of fickle mind, a betrayer of friends, and of inconstant virtue. Now I will show him my nature as a betrayer of friends," and he tore the nest apart and scattered it. While the monkey was grabbing the nest, the bird escaped from one side and flew away. The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching of the Singila Jataka in the Catukka Nipāta, identified the birth:
296:
## The Teaching

(61) If, while wandering, one does not find a companion
Who is better than or equal to oneself,
One should resolutely pursue a solitary life;
There is no fellowship with a fool.

While wandering and seeking a noble friend (kalyāṇamitta), if one does not find one who is superior to oneself in qualities such as virtue, or one who is equal to oneself in qualities such as virtue, one should resolutely practice living alone. Why is that? Because in dependence on a fool, there is no quality such as virtue that constitutes fellowship.

"He makes me out to be one of fickle and impulsive mind, a betrayer of friends, and of inconstant virtue. Now I will show this Singila bird my nature as a betrayer of friends," saying thus, the monkey tore the nest apart and scattered it. As for the Singila bird, even as the monkey was pulling at the nest, it escaped from one side and flew away. The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching of the Singila Jataka in the Catukka Nipāta, identified the birth:

The monk who destroyed the hut was then the monkey; Elder Kassapa was the Singila bird. Having thus identified the birth, the Teacher said, "Monks, not only now, but in the past too, he became angry at the moment of advice and destroyed the hut. For my son Kassapa, living alone is better than living with such a fool," and he spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the Dhamma teaching, the visiting monk who had come from Rājagaha attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). Many others also attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so on. The Dhamma teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.

The story of the pupil of the Elder Mahākassapa is finished.
297:
## 3. The Story of Ānanda the Treasurer
(Ānandaseṭṭhivatthu)
While residing at Sāvatthī, the Teacher told this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Putta matthi," concerning a treasurer named Ānanda.
(Note: Although it should be referred to as 'Ānanda' with the masculine 'a' ending, in Burmese usage, it is common to say 'Ānandā' with the 'ā' ending. The same applies to Sāriputtā and the Ariyasaṅghā.)

## The Death of Ānanda the Treasurer and His Rebirth as a Miserable Outcast
In the city of Sāvatthī, there was a treasurer named Ānanda who possessed wealth amounting to forty crores, but he was extremely stingy. Every half-month, this treasurer Ānanda would summon his kinsmen and give this advice to his son, Mūlasiri, on three occasions: "Do not think that this wealth of forty crores is much. One should not give away existing wealth; one should instead increase and generate new wealth. For even if one spends only a single kahāpaṇa, wealth gradually diminishes for the one who spends it." Therefore:

"Seeing the depletion of eye-ointment,
The accumulation of termite mounds,
And the gathering of honey,
The wise man should manage his household."

He gave such advice. At a later time, that treasurer died without informing his son Mūlasiri about his five great hidden treasures. Because he died stained with the impurity of stinginess rooted in his attachment to wealth, he took rebirth in the womb of a Caṇḍāla woman in a village of a thousand outcast families near a gate of that same city of Sāvatthī.

King Pasenadi of Kosala, the ruler of Sāvatthī, upon hearing of the treasurer Ānanda's death, summoned the treasurer's son Mūlasiri and appointed him to the position of treasurer. Those thousand Caṇḍāla families, who used to earn their living by working together for hire, from the time of Ānanda's conception, could no longer find work, nor could they get enough to sustain themselves, and later, they could not even get a morsel of food. Therefore, the Caṇḍālas thought, "Now, even though we work, we do not get even a morsel of food. There must be an ill-fated person (kāḷakaṇṇī) among us." They divided themselves into two groups until Ānanda's parents were in a separate group. They continued dividing until they concluded, "The ill-fated one has arisen in this family," and they drove out the mother of the former treasurer Ānanda.

That mother, for as long as the child was in her womb, could only find enough food to survive with great difficulty and eventually gave birth to the son. The hands, feet, eyes, ears, nose, and mouth of that child were not in their proper places. Because he was endowed with such physical deformities, he was an extremely ugly child, like a dust-goblin (paṃsupisācaka).

## Revealing the Hidden Treasures from the Past Life
Even though the child was so extremely ugly, the mother could not bear to abandon him. Affection for a child who has dwelt in one's womb is very strong. That mother, while raising him with great hardship, found that on the days she carried the child with her, she received nothing; but on the days she left him at home and went alone, she received her usual earnings. Later, when the child was old enough to wander and search for food to survive, she placed a bowl in his hand and said:
298:
"Dear son, because of you we have reached great suffering. Now I am unable to support you. In this city of Sāvatthī, there is food prepared for the destitute, travelers, and so on. Go and live by wandering for alms there." Thus, she sent him away and abandoned him. As that boy wandered from house to house, he reached the place where he had lived during his time as the treasurer Ānanda. Having the knowledge of recollecting past lives (jātissara), he entered his former home. No one at the first three gateways took notice of him. But at the fourth gateway, when the young children of the treasurer Mūlasiri saw him, they were terrified and began to cry.

Then, the servants of the treasurer Mūlasiri, shouting, "Get out, you ill-fated wretch!" beat and struck him, dragged him out, and threw him onto a rubbish heap. The Teacher, while wandering for alms with the Elder Ānanda as his attendant monk, arrived at that place. Looking at the Elder, and being questioned by the Elder, the Teacher explained the situation. The Elder then had the treasurer Mūlasiri summoned. A great crowd of people gathered. The Teacher addressed Mūlasiri and asked, "Do you know him?" When Mūlasiri replied, "I do not know him," the Teacher said, "He is your father, the treasurer Ānanda." When Mūlasiri did not believe it, the Teacher had the boy reveal the five great hidden treasures to his son, thereby making him believe. Mūlasiri then went to the Teacher for refuge. While teaching him the Dhamma, the Teacher spoke this verse:

62.
"'Sons I have, wealth I have,'
Thus the fool is vexed.
Even oneself is not one's own,
How then sons? How then wealth?"

The meaning is: "I have sons, I have wealth"—thus the fool is struck, vexed, and distressed by craving for sons and craving for wealth. He is vexed thinking, "My sons have perished," or "They are perishing," or "They will perish." The same applies to wealth. Thus, he is vexed in six ways. He is vexed while striving day and night in various ways on land and sea, thinking, "I will support my sons," and he is also vexed while performing agriculture, trade, and so on, thinking, "I will produce wealth." For one who is thus vexed, even oneself is not one's own. Because of that distress, he is unable to make his suffering self happy. Even in the continuity of his life, his self is not his own. When he lies on his deathbed, burning with the pains of death as if by flames of fire, with his joints and ligaments being severed and his bones breaking, even as he closes his eyes to this world and opens them to the next, he realizes that although he was bathed twice a day, fed three times a day, adorned with perfumes and garlands, and nurtured for his whole life...
299:
