The Buddha summoned the treasurer Mūlasiri and asked, “Do you know this boy?” When Mūlasiri replied, “I do not know him, Venerable Sir,” the Buddha said, “He is your father, the great treasurer Ānanda.” As Mūlasiri remained skeptical, the Buddha told the ghost, “Ānanda, the treasurer—tell your son where the five large pots of gold are hidden.” The ghost revealed the location, thereby convincing Mūlasiri. Mūlasiri then took refuge in the Buddha. Wishing to preach the Dhamma further to Mūlasiri, the Buddha uttered this verse:

## The Teaching
(62) “Sons have I, wealth have I,” so the fool troubles himself.
Verily, even oneself does not belong to oneself;
Whence then sons? Whence then wealth?

(Glossary: *Me*—to me; *puttā*—sons; *atthi*—there are. *Me*—to me; *dhanaṃ*—wealth; *atthi*—there is. *Iti*—thus; *bālo*—the fool; *taṇhāya*—through craving and attachment to sons and wealth; *vihaññati*—is troubled and suffers. *Evampi*—even though he suffers thus; *attā hi*—even oneself; *attano*—for one's own; *tāṇāya*—protection or refuge; *natthi*—does not exist. *Puttā*—sons; *kuto atthi*—how can they exist [as a refuge]? *Dhanaṃ*—wealth; *kuto atthi*—how can it exist [as a refuge]?)

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Four Noble Truths. The discourse was beneficial to the multitude.
The Story of Ānanda the Treasurer ends.

## The Teaching
(63) The fool who knows his foolishness is wise at least to that extent.
But the fool who thinks himself wise is called a fool indeed.

(Glossary: *Yo bālo*—the fool who; *bālyaṃ*—his own foolishness; *maññati*—knows as “I am foolish.” *So bālo*—that fool; *tena*—by reason of knowing that foolishness; *paṇḍitovāpi*—is indeed wise; *vā*—or is like a wise man. *Yo bālo*—the fool who; *bālo ca*—being a fool; *paṇḍitamānī*—thinks “I am wise.” *So bālo*—that fool; *ve*—verily; *bālo ti*—as a fool; *vuccati*—is called.)

## 4. The Story of the Two Cut-purses
(Gaṇṭhibhedakacora Vatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha spoke this verse beginning with “Yo bālo,” concerning two thieves who were cut-purses.

## A Pickpocket Attains Stream-entry
Two companions who were thieves followed a crowd going to the Jetavana Monastery to listen to the Dhamma. One thief listened attentively to the Dhamma, while the other looked around for something to steal. Among them, the one listening to the Dhamma attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (*Sotāpatti-phala*). The other thief managed to steal five *māsakas* tied to the hem of a listener's garment. With those five *māsakas*, he was able to provide a cooked meal in his house.
300:
In the house of the other thief who had listened to the Dhamma, however, no meal was cooked. At that time, the thief who had stolen the money, along with his wife, mocked his companion, saying, “You are so very 'wise' that you cannot even provide enough for a meal in your own home.” The thief who had heard the Buddha's Dhamma thought, “This man, because of his extreme foolishness and delusion, considers himself wise.” To report this matter to the Buddha, he went to the Jetavana Monastery with his relatives and informed Him. The Buddha, wishing to teach the Dhamma to that lay devotee, uttered this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, the relatives of the thief who had listened to the Dhamma, along with many others, attained the Fruit of Stream-entry.
The Story of the Two Cut-purses ends.

## The Teaching
(64) Though all his life a fool associates with a wise man,
He understands the Dhamma no more than a spoon tastes the flavor of the soup.

(Glossary: *Dabbī*—the ladle or spoon; *sūparasaṃ*—the flavor of the soup, which may be spicy, salty, astringent, bitter, etc., in six ways; *na vijānāti yathā*—just as it does not know. *Evaṃ*—likewise; *bālo*—the fool; *yāvajīvampi*—even for his whole life; *paṇḍitaṃ*—a wise person; *ce payirupāsati*—if he associates with and stays near. *So bālo*—that fool; *dhammaṃ*—the noble Dhamma taught by the Buddha; *na vijānāti*—does not know.)

## 5. The Story of Venerable Udāyī
(Udāyitthera Vatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha spoke this verse beginning with “Yāvajīvampi ce bālo,” concerning the Elder Udāyī.

## Sitting on the Pulpit Without Attaining the Dhamma
Whenever the senior elders left the Dhamma hall, Venerable Udāyī would go there and sit on the preacher's seat. One day, some visiting (*āgantuka*) monks saw him and, thinking, “This must be a very learned senior elder,” asked him questions concerning the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth. Since he knew nothing at all, they asked, “What kind of monk is this?” They criticized and blamed him, saying, “Though he lives in the same monastery as the Buddha, he does not even know the aggregates (*khandha*), elements (*dhātu*), or sense bases (*āyatana*).” They then reported the matter to the Blessed One.
The Buddha, wishing to teach those visiting monks, uttered this verse.
301:
## Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the Dhamma teaching, the minds of the visiting monks were liberated from the taints (āsavas).
The story of the Elder Udāyī ends.

## The Teaching
(65) Muhuttamapi ce viññū, paṇḍitaṃ payirupāsati.
Khippaṃ dhammaṃ vijānāti, jivhā sūparasaṃ yathā.

Just as the tongue (jivhā) knows the taste of soup (sūparasaṃ), if a wise person (viññū) who is intelligent and discerning associates (payirupāsati) with a wise man (paṇḍitaṃ) even for a moment (muhuttamapi), he quickly (khippaṃ) understands (vijānāti) the noble Dhamma taught by the Buddha.

## 6. The Story of the Monks from Pāveyyaka
(Tiṃsamattapāveyyakabhikkhuvatthu)
While staying at the Jetavana monastery, the Buddha spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Muhuttamapi ce viññū," concerning approximately thirty monks from the Pāveyyaka region.

## Understanding the Dhamma in a Moment
The Buddha first taught the Dhamma in the Kappāsika grove to these thirty Pāveyyaka men who were searching for a woman. At that time, all thirty of them attained the status of "Ehi Bhikkhu" (Come, Monk) ordination, possessing miraculous bowls and robes. They undertook and practiced the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas). Later, after a long period had passed, they approached the Teacher again, and upon hearing the Anamatagga Sutta teaching, they attained Arahatship right in their seats. The monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall, saying, "How wonderful! These thirty monks have understood the Dhamma so quickly." Hearing this, the Buddha said, "Monks, it is not only now that these thirty monks have understood the Dhamma quickly."
302:
In the past, these thirty friends were drunkards who, upon hearing the Dhamma teaching of the Great Tuṇḍila the pig king in the Tuṇḍila Jātaka, quickly understood the Dhamma and undertook the five precepts. Due to that supporting condition (upanissaya), they have now attained Arahatship while sitting in their seats." Having said this, he delivered the teaching and spoke this verse:

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the Dhamma teaching, many monks attained Arahatship.
The story of the thirty monks from Pāveyyaka ends.

Saddhādhanaṃ sīladhanaṃ, hiri ottappiyaṃ dhanaṃ.
Sutadhanañca cāgo ca, paññā ve sattamaṃ dhanaṃ.
Yassa ete dhanā atthi, itthiyā purisassa vā.
Adaliddoti taṃ āhu, amoghaṃ tassa jīvitaṃ.

Faith (saddhā-dhanaṃ), which is the characteristic of believing in the Triple Gem and the law of kamma and its results; Virtue (sīla-dhanaṃ), consisting of both performance and avoidance; Shame (hiri-dhanaṃ), the characteristic of being ashamed of evil; Fear of wrongdoing (ottappiyaṃ), the characteristic of dreading evil; Learning (suta-dhanaṃ), having great knowledge of the Dhamma of the virtuous; Generosity (cāgo), the wealth of giving and sacrifice; and Wisdom (paññā-dhanaṃ), the seventh wealth, which is the ability to know the true nature of things as they are. Whoever, whether a woman (itthiyā) or a man (purisassa), possesses these wealths (ete dhanā), the wise (paṇḍitā), such as the Buddha, call that person "not poor" (adaliddo), but one of great wealth. The wise say that the life (jīvitaṃ) of such a person endowed with these seven noble wealths is not in vain (amoghaṃ) but is fruitful (saphalaṃ).

## 7. The Story of Suppabuddha the Leper
(Suppabuddhakuṭṭhivatthu)
While staying at the Veḷuvana monastery, the Buddha spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Caranti bālā dummedhā," concerning the leper named Suppabuddha.

## Seven Qualities that Prevent Poverty
The story of Suppabuddha the leper is found in the Udāna. At that time, Suppabuddha the leper, sitting at the edge of the assembly, heard the Buddha's teaching and attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Desiring to report the virtue he had attained to the Teacher, but being unable to enter the midst of the assembly, he went to the monastery when the great crowd had finished paying homage to the Buddha and was returning. At that moment, Sakka, King of the Gods, knowing that "This Suppabuddha the leper wishes to make manifest the virtue he has attained in the Buddha's Dispensation," thought, "I will test him." Sakka went and, standing in the air, said: "Suppabuddha, you are a poor, wretched human, a lonely person who must beg for food. I will give you immeasurable wealth if you say, 'The Buddha is not the Buddha, the Dhamma is not the Dhamma, the Saṅgha is not the Saṅgha; I have no need for the Buddha, I have no need for the Dhamma, I have no need for the Saṅgha.'"

Then Suppabuddha asked Sakka, "Who are you?" Sakka replied, "I am Sakka." Suppabuddha said, "You blind fool, you shameless Sakka! You are not fit to speak with me. You call me a wretched, poor, and lonely person. I am not wretched, not poor, and not lonely. I have attained happiness and am a man of great wealth. These seven noble wealths I have mentioned are clearly present in me. Those who possess these seven wealths are never called poor by the Buddhas or the Noble Ones (Ariyas) such as Paccekabuddhas."
303:
## Suppabuddha’s Past Kamma of Being Gored by a Cow

Sakka, the king of devas, having heard the Dhamma talk of Suppabuddha the leper, left Suppabuddha on the way and approached the Blessed One. He reported all that he had said and Suppabuddha’s replies. Then the Blessed One said to Sakka, “Sakka, even a hundred or a thousand Sakkas like you would not be able to make Suppabuddha the leper say, ‘The Buddha is not the Buddha,’ ‘The Dhamma is not the Dhamma,’ or ‘The Saṅgha is not the Saṅgha.’” Suppabuddha the leper also went to the Blessed One, and after exchanging greetings and reporting the special attainment he had gained, he rose from his seat and departed. Not long after he had left, a cow with a young calf gored Suppabuddha the leper to death.

(That cow was not an ordinary cow; a certain yakkhinī, taking the form of a cow, had killed these four people—King Pukkusāti, Bāhiya Dārucီriya, Tambadāṭhika the executioner, and Suppabuddha the leper—in hundreds of existences. It is said that in the past, these four were sons of wealthy merchants. They took a beautiful courtesan to a park, enjoyed themselves for the day, and in the evening, they consulted each other: “There is no one else here besides us. Let us take the thousand coins and all the ornaments we gave this woman, kill her, and then leave.” The courtesan heard their conversation and thought, “These men are shameless; after enjoying themselves with me, they now want to kill me. I shall know what must be done to them.” While being killed by them, she made a wish: “May I become a yakkhinī and be able to kill them just as they are killing me now.” As a result of that, the yakkhinī killed these four people.)

Many monks reported the death of Suppabuddha the leper to the Blessed One and asked, “What is his destination? For what reason did he become a leper?” The Blessed One explained that he had attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. He also explained that because he had seen the Paccekabuddha named Tagarasikhī, spat at him, and treated him with disrespect, he had suffered in hell for a long time...
304:
## The Teaching
(66) Fools of little wit go about with themselves as their own enemies, committing evil deeds that bear bitter fruit.

"Fools" (bālā) refers to those who are ignorant and deluded, not knowing the benefits of both this world and the next. "Of little wit" (dummedhā) means those lacking wisdom. "With themselves as their own enemies" (amitteneva attanā) means acting as if one's own self were a foe or an adversary. "Evil deeds" (pāpakaṃ kammaṃ) refers to unwholesome actions. "That bear bitter fruit" (kaṭukapphalaṃ) means having results that are painful and difficult to endure, like a pungent or bitter taste.

"After suffering in hell for a long time, through the remaining influence of that kamma, he has come to be afflicted with leprosy in this present life." Having spoken thus, the Buddha connected the sequence of events and, desiring to teach the Dhamma further, uttered this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and other fruits.

The Story of Suppabuddha the Leper ends.

## 8. The Story of the Farmer
(Kassaka Vatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana monastery, the Teacher told this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Na taṃ kammaṃ kataṃ sādhu," concerning a certain farmer.

## A Bag of Money or a Deadly Snake?
That farmer was plowing a field not far from the city of Sāvatthī. Some thieves entered the city through a water drain, tunneled into the house of a wealthy family, stole a great amount of gold and silver, and left by the same water drain. One thief, having deceived his accomplices, hid a bag containing a thousand pieces of money in his waist-cloth. As he went to the field to divide the loot with the others and then departed, he did not notice that the bag of a thousand coins had fallen from his waist-cloth. That day, at dawn, as the Teacher surveyed the world, he saw the farmer enter the net of his knowledge. Considering "What will happen?", he saw this: "This farmer will go to plow early in the morning. The owners of the property, following the tracks of the thieves, will see the bag of a thousand coins that fell from the waist-cloth and will seize the farmer. Other than me, there will be no witness for him. Furthermore, the farmer possesses the supporting condition (upanissaya) for the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga). It is proper that I go to that field."
305:
That farmer also went to plow his field early in the morning. The Blessed One, with the Venerable Ānanda as his attendant monk, went to that field. Seeing the Blessed One, the farmer approached, paid respectful homage to the Blessed One, and resumed his plowing. Without saying anything to the farmer, the Blessed One went to the place where the bag of a thousand coins had fallen. Seeing the bag, he said to the Venerable Ānanda, "See, Ānanda, a poisonous snake." "I see, Blessed One, a snake with fierce poison," he replied.

Hearing these words, the farmer thought, "This is the place where I wander at all times, whether at the right time or the wrong time. It is said there is a poisonous snake here." After the Blessed One had spoken only those words and departed, the farmer thought, "I will catch that snake," and taking his goad-stick, he went there. Seeing the bag of a thousand coins, he thought, "The Blessed One must have spoken in reference to this bag of money," and taking the bag, he turned back. Due to his lack of wisdom and skill, he placed it in a certain spot, covered it with dust, and resumed his plowing.

## Escape from Death because of the Buddha

When the night had turned to dawn, people saw the traces of the crime committed by the thieves in the house. Following the footprints, they reached the field. There, they saw the place where the thieves had divided the goods and also saw the farmer's footprints. The owners of the property followed the farmer's footprints, saw the place where the property was hidden, dug up the dust, and took the bag of money. They threatened and beat him, saying, "You plundered the house and then wander about as if you are plowing the field!" They then took him and presented him to the King. Hearing the account, the King ordered the farmer's execution. The King's men bound his hands behind his back and, whipping him with lashes, led him to the place of execution. While being whipped, the farmer did not lament or say anything else, but went along repeating only these words:

"Passa, Ānanda, āsīviso'ti; passāmi, Bhagavā, ghoraviso'ti."

The meaning is: "See, Ānanda, a poisonous snake"—these are the words of the Buddha. "I see, Blessed One, a snake with fierce poison"—these are the words of the Venerable Ānanda. He repeated only these words.

Then the King's men asked the farmer, "You repeat only the words of the Buddha and the Venerable Ānanda. What is the reason for this?" When he replied, "If I may see the King, I will tell him," they took him to the King and reported the matter. Then the King asked him, "Why do you speak thus?" The farmer replied, "Your Majesty, I am not a thief," and he related the entire sequence of events to the King, starting from the time he went out to plow. Hearing his words, the King thought, "Friends, this man points to the Buddha, the Supreme Being in the world, as his witness. It is not proper to impose guilt or punishment upon him. I shall find out the truth of this matter." He then took the farmer with him in the evening, went to the Blessed One, and asked, "Blessed One, did you and the Venerable Ānanda ever go to the place where this farmer stays?"
306:
## The Teaching

(67) Na taṃ kammaṃ kataṃ sādhu, yaṃ katvā anutappati.
Yassa assumukho rodaṃ, vipākaṃ paṭisevati.

Whatever deed (yaṃ kammaṃ), having done (katvā), one repents (anutappati). That deed done (taṃ kammaṃ kataṃ) is not good (na sādhu). The result of that evil deed (yassa kammassa vipākaṃ), one experiences (paṭisevati) while weeping (rodaṃ) with a tear-stained face (assumukho).

"Great King, it is true that I went there," the Blessed One replied. The King asked again, "What did you see there, Blessed One?" "Great King, I saw a bag containing a thousand coins," he said. "After seeing it, what did you say, Blessed One?" the King asked. "Great King, I spoke these words," the Blessed One replied. The King then said, "Blessed One, if this farmer had not been able to provide a witness like you, he would not have kept his life. Because he spoke the words you uttered, this farmer has regained his life."

Hearing this, the Blessed One said, "Great King, it is so. I spoke only those words and departed. One who is wise should not perform a deed which, having been done, causes one to suffer later." Connecting the sequence of the discourse, he spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, the farmer, who was a lay follower, attained the Fruit of Stream-entry. The monks who had gathered also attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and other stages.

The Story of the Farmer ends.

## 9. The Story of Sumana the Florist
(Sumana-mālākāra-vatthu)

While residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Blessed One spoke this legal discourse beginning with "Taṃ ca kammaṃ kataṃ sādhu" in reference to a florist named Sumana.

## Giving Courageously Without Regard for Life

That florist Sumana, every day in the early morning, used to serve King Bimbisāra, the ruler of Rājagaha, with eight measures of jasmine flowers, for which he received eight coins. One day, just as the florist had taken the flowers and entered the city, the Blessed One, surrounded by a great assembly of monks and emitting the six-colored rays, entered Rājagaha for alms with great Buddha-majesty and Buddha-grace. Sometimes, the Blessed One would cover the six-colored rays with his robe and wander like an ordinary alms-collecting monk, as he did when going thirty leagues to meet Aṅgulimāla. At other times, he would emit the six-colored rays, as he did when entering Kapilavatthu and other places.
307:
On certain occasions, emitting rays of six colors, he would wander and enter cities like Kapilavatthu. On that day too, emitting six-colored rays from his body, he entered the city of Rājagaha with the great majesty and splendor of a Buddha.

When Sumana the florist saw the physical form of the Blessed One, which was like the pinnacle of a jeweled stupa, reaching the height of beauty with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics, he was filled with a devoted heart and thought, "What extraordinary service can I perform for the Teacher?" Seeing nothing else, he thought, "I shall worship the Blessed One with these jasmine flowers." Then he thought again, "These are the flowers for the daily service of the King. If the King does not receive these flowers, he might bind me, kill me, or banish me from the country. What should I do?"

Then this thought occurred to Sumana: "Let the King kill me, bind me, or banish me. Even if he gives me wealth, it would only be enough for a living in this single existence. But worshipping the Teacher will lead to my welfare and happiness for many millions of aeons." Thus, he sacrificed his life for the Tathāgata. Thinking, "As long as my devoted heart does not waver or shrink, I shall perform this worship," he worshipped the Teacher with a heart that was joyful, delighted, and increasingly uplifted.

## The Wonder of the Buddha's Power

How did he worship? First, he threw two handfuls of flowers above the Tathāgata; they remained as a canopy over his head. He threw another two handfuls; they descended and remained as a floral curtain on the right side. He threw another two handfuls; they descended and remained in the same way on the back side. He threw another two handfuls; they descended and remained in the same way on the left side. Thus, the flowers, amounting to eight naḷis or eight handfuls, surrounded the Tathāgata on four sides. In front, there was only a space like a large gateway for him to walk. The stalks of the flowers pointed inward, and the petals faced outward. The Blessed One proceeded as if surrounded by a silver plate. Although the flowers were inanimate, because they relied on the animate Blessed One, they moved along with the Teacher as if they were animate, without breaking or falling, and they went together with the Buddha.
308:
They stood wherever he stood.

From the Teacher's body, many rays issued forth, flashing like a hundred thousand streaks of lightning. From the front, back, right, left, and from above his head, the rays issued continuously. Not even a single ray fled to its respective direction without first circling the Teacher three times to the right; then, becoming as large as the trunk of a young palmyra tree, they raced ahead. The entire city of Rājagaha was in an uproar. Among the eighteen crores of people—nine crores inside the city and nine crores outside—there was not a single man or woman who did not take alms-food and come out of their house. The great multitude went before the Teacher, shouting lion-roars and tossing thousands of garments. To make the florist Sumana's virtue known, the Teacher traveled through the city, which was three gāvutas in extent, along the path where the drums were beaten. Sumana's entire body was filled with the fivefold rapture. Having walked with the Tathāgata for a short while, as if submerged in a sea of vermilion, he entered within the Buddha's rays, praised and paid homage to the Teacher, and returned home carrying only the empty basket.

## The Wife's Anxiety over the Husband's Bold Offering

Then his wife asked him, "Where are the flowers?" "I have worshipped the Teacher," he replied. "What will you do for the King now?" she asked again. "Let the King kill me or banish me from the country. I have sacrificed my life to worship the Teacher. All the flowers, all eight handfuls, were used. Such a worship has taken place. The multitude is following the Teacher, making thousands of shouts of 'Sādhu'. This sound of the great multitude shouting is the marvelous sound from the place where I worshipped with the flowers," he explained.

Then his wife, due to her blind folly, did not feel any devotion or joy in such a miraculous wonder. Instead, she scolded and reviled him, saying, "Kings are fierce by nature. Once angry, they cause much harm, such as cutting off hands and feet. Because of what you have done, harm may come to me too." Taking her children, she went to the royal palace. When summoned and questioned by the King, "What is this?", she said, "My husband worshipped the Teacher with the flowers for your service and came home empty-handed. When I asked, 'Where are the flowers?', he said this. I scolded him, saying, 'Kings are fierce; once angry, they cause much harm... harm may come to me too,' and I have left him and come here. Whether the deed he did is good or bad, it is his alone. Know, O King, that I have abandoned him."

The King, who had attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) at the first sight of the Buddha, was a faithful and devoted noble disciple. He thought, "Oh, how blind and foolish this woman is! She does not feel devotion for such a virtuous deed." Pretending to be angry, he said, "Lady, what are you saying? He used my flowers for worship?" "Yes, O King," she replied. "You did well to abandon him. I shall know what to do with the one who worshipped using my flowers." Having dismissed her, he quickly went to the Teacher, paid homage, and walked along with him. The Teacher, knowing the King's devotion, traveled through the city along the drum-beating route and arrived at the gate of the King's house. The King, taking the bowl, wished to invite the Teacher into the house. However, the Teacher showed his intention to sit in the royal courtyard...
309:
“For a hundred thousand eons, he shall not go to a state of woe.
Abiding among devas and humans, as a result of this deed,
In the future, he will become a Paccekabuddha named Sumana.”

“Ānanda, dear Ānanda. As a result of this merit, for a period of one hundred thousand eons, he will not go to the four woeful states—hell, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the host of asuras. Abiding among the worlds of devas and humans, in the future, he will truly become a Paccekabuddha named Sumana.”

“Because of a single moment of anger, kings might cause great harm by cutting off hands, feet, and so on. Because of this offense you have committed, harm might come to me as well.” Thus lamenting, she took her young children and went to the royal palace. When she approached the King, and the King asked, “What is the reason for your coming?” the woman replied, “Your Majesty, my husband, this florist Sumana, offered the flowers intended for Your Majesty to the Buddha and returned home empty-handed. When I asked where the flowers were, he told me this. I scolded and threatened him, saying that kings are cruel and harsh; for a single moment of anger, they might cause great harm by cutting off hands, feet, and so on. I told him that because of the offense he committed, harm might come to me too. Thus lamenting, I have abandoned that florist Sumana and come to this palace. Whether his deed be good or bad, let it belong to him alone. May Your Majesty know that I have abandoned him completely.”

King Bimbisāra, having attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala) upon his very first meeting with the Buddha, was a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) possessed of great faith and devotion. He reflected, “Oh, how wonderful! This woman is exceedingly foolish and deluded. She is unable to find joy and devotion even in such a sublime quality.” The King, appearing as if he were trembling with rage, asked, “Woman, what are you saying? Did that florist Sumana really make an offering to the Buddha with the flowers intended for me?” She replied, “It is true, Your Majesty.” “By abandoning that florist Sumana now, you have done a good thing. That Sumana made an offering with my royal flowers; I shall see to it that I acknowledge what he has done.” Having said this, he dismissed the woman and quickly went to the Buddha, paid homage, and followed him.

## Sumana the Florist Receives the Gift of Eights
The Buddha, knowing the King’s devotion, traveled through the city along the processional route and went to the gate of the royal palace. The King wished to take the bowl and lead the Buddha into the palace. However, the Buddha showed his desire to stay only in the palace courtyard. Knowing this, the King ordered, “Quickly, build a pavilion!” and had a pavilion constructed at that very moment. The Buddha sat there together with the community of monks.

(Why did the Buddha not enter the royal palace? This thought occurred to the Buddha: “If I were to enter and sit inside the palace, the great multitude of people would not be able to see me, and the merit of Sumana the florist would not become famous. But if I sit in the palace courtyard, the great multitude will be able to see me, and the merit of Sumana the florist will become famous.” Such was his thought. Only Buddhas are able to make the merit of virtuous people famous. When other people speak of the merit of the virtuous, they tend to be stingy and secretive, not wishing it to be known.)

The four canopies of flowers stood in the four directions. The great multitude surrounded the Buddha. King Bimbisāra served the community of monks headed by the Buddha with choice food and hard and soft provisions. After the meal, the Buddha gave a talk of appreciation (anumodanā) and, surrounded by the four canopies of flowers as before, he let out a great lion’s roar and returned to the monastery, surrounded by the great multitude. King Bimbisāra followed the Buddha to see him off, and upon returning, he summoned Sumana the florist and asked, “With what intention did you offer the eight measures of flowers to the Buddha, which you were bringing to present to me?” Sumana the florist replied, “Your Majesty, I offered them after sacrificing my life, saying, ‘Let the King kill me if he wishes, or let him banish me from the kingdom.’” The King said, “You are indeed a great man,” and he brought out from the royal palace eight elephants, eight horses, eight male slaves, eight female slaves, eight great ornaments, and eight thousand coins. He also gave eight maidens adorned with all kinds of ornaments and eight excellent villages from which revenue was well-produced. Thus, he bestowed these gifts known as the “Gift of Eights” (Sabbaṭṭhaka), consisting of eight of each item.

## Prediction of Paccekabuddhahood
The Elder Ānanda reflected, “Since this morning, thousands of lion-like cheers and thousands of tosses of garments...”
310:
## The Teaching

(68) That deed is well done which, having been done, one does not repent; and whose fruit one experiences with a delighted and happy mind.

(Word-for-word meaning: *Yaṃ kammaṃ*—whatever deed; *katvā*—having done; *nānutappati*—one does not later regret. *Yassa kammassa*—of which deed; *vipākaṃ*—the fruit; *patīto*—being pleased with the force of joy; *sumano*—being happy with the force of pleasant feeling; *paṭisevati*—one experiences and enjoys. *Tañca kammaṃ*—only that meritorious deed; *kataṃ*—having been done; *sādhu*—is truly good.)

"Even if there were a thousand tosses [of flowers], what would be the reward and benefit to be experienced by Sumana the florist?" Having reflected thus, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Buddha. Then, the Buddha said to the Venerable Ānanda, "Dear son Ānanda, do not record this as having done only a small amount of merit. This man has performed an offering to Me by sacrificing his life. Because this florist has thus gained clarity of mind in Me, such [a great result] will occur," and He spoke this verse.

When the Buddha returned to the monastery and entered the Gandhakuṭi, those jasmine flowers fell at the entrance of the portal. In the evening, the monks initiated a discussion in the Dhamma hall: "How wonderful indeed is the meritorious deed performed by Sumana the florist! By making an offering of flowers to the living Buddha at the cost of his life, he received the reward known as the 'Gift of Eight' (Sabbaṭṭhaka) at that very moment." The Buddha, emerging from the Gandhakuṭi, proceeded to the Dhamma hall by one of the three modes of walking, and having sat upon the Buddha's seat, He asked:

"Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now as I arrive?" When they replied, "We are gathered for such and such a discussion," He said, "Monks, indeed it is so. A deed is such that, because of its performance, no subsequent regret or remorse occurs; at every moment of recollection, only joy arises. Such a meritorious deed should indeed be performed," and wishing to connect the sequence to preach the Dhamma, He spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma.

The Story of Sumana the Florist ends.

## 10. The Story of Uppalavaṇṇā Therī

(The Story of the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā)

While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Madhuvaṃ maññati," concerning the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā.

## Becoming an Arahant by Taking a Sign from a Lamp Flame

That Uppalavaṇṇā Therī, having made an aspiration for the position of Chief Female Disciple at the feet of Padumuttara Buddha and having performed many meritorious deeds for a hundred thousand aeons, wandered through the worlds of devas and humans. When our Buddha appeared, she passed away from the deva world and took rebirth in a merchant's family in the city of Sāvatthī. Because her complexion and features were as beautiful, clear, and radiant as the interior of a blue lotus, they named the girl Uppalavaṇṇā. Later, when Uppalavaṇṇā reached the age of maturity, kings and wealthy merchants from all over Jambudīpa sent messages to her father, the great merchant, saying, "Give your daughter to us." There was no one who did not send a message.
311:
Then the great merchant reflected, "I cannot satisfy the wishes of everyone. I will employ a strategy." Having reflected thus, he called his daughter and asked, "Dear daughter, would you be able to ordain as a nun?" Because she was a being in her final birth (pacchimabhavika), those words spoken by her father were like oil cooked a hundred times poured upon her head. Therefore, she said to her father, "Father, I will ordain." The merchant performed a great ceremony of honor for his daughter, escorted her to the nunnery, and had her ordained. Not long after her ordination, it became her turn to perform duties such as lighting the lamps in the Uposatha hall. Uppalavaṇṇā Therī lit the lamps, swept the Uposatha hall, and taking the sign (nimitta) from the flame of the lamp she had lit, she stood there looking at it repeatedly. She developed jhāna with the fire-kasiṇa (tejo-kasiṇa) as its object, and using that very jhāna as a basis, she attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) and higher powers (abhiññā).

## Nanda the Youth Commits a Crime and is Swallowed by the Earth

At a later time, after wandering on a journey through the countryside, Uppalavaṇṇā Therī returned and entered the forest known as Andhavana to reside there. At that time, the training rule prohibiting nuns from living in the forest had not yet been promulgated. Then, they built a small hut for the Elder Nun in that forest, prepared a couch, and surrounded it with a curtain. Uppalavaṇṇā Therī entered the city of Sāvatthī for alms and then came out. A youth named Nanda, who was the son of her maternal uncle, had been obsessed with her since his days as a layman. Hearing that Uppalavaṇṇā Therī had arrived, Nanda went to Andhavana even before the Elder Nun's arrival, entered the small hut, and hid under the couch. When the Elder Nun returned, entered the hut, closed the door, and sat down on the couch, her eyes had not yet adjusted from the bright sunlight outside to the darkness within. At that moment, Nanda came out from under the couch, climbed onto it, and despite the Elder Nun's protest, "Fool, do not destroy! Fool, do not destroy!", he overpowered her, committed the act he had desired, and left.

Then, as if unable to bear the weight of the great evil committed by the extremely foolish Nanda, the great earth, which is two hundred and forty thousand yojanas thick, split into two. Nanda fell into the interior of the earth and was reborn in the Great Avīci Hell. The Elder Nun reported the matter to her fellow nuns. The nuns reported the matter to the monks. The monks reported it to the Blessed One. Having heard this, the Buddha called the monks and said, "Monks, any fool among my monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen who commits an evil deed does so with a delighted and joyful heart, like a man eating something with a sweet taste like honey or sugar..." and connecting the sequence, He preached the Dhamma by speaking this verse:
312:
## The Teaching

(69) "As long as the evil deed has not yet ripened, the fool thinks it is like honey. But when the evil deed ripens, the fool comes to grief."

"As long as" refers to the duration of time. "The evil deed has not yet ripened" means it has not yet yielded its result, either in the present life or in the future life. During that time, the fool regards that evil deed as being "like honey," meaning he perceives it as something sweet, pleasant, desirable, and agreeable. "But when" refers to the time when the evil deed "ripens," meaning it yields its result, such as when one undergoes various punishments in the present life or experiences great suffering in the realms of misery like hell in the future life. At that time, that fool "comes to grief," meaning he encounters, experiences, or receives suffering.

"Like water on a lotus leaf, or a mustard seed on the point of an awl, he who does not cling to sensual pleasures, him I call a Brahmin."

Just as water does not cling to or remain on a lotus leaf, and just as a mustard seed does not cling to or remain on the point of an awl, even so, for that person who does not cling to or remain attached to the two kinds of sensual pleasures (kāma), him I, the Buddha, call a Brahmin—one who has put away evil.

Wishing to connect the context and deliver the Dhamma teaching, the Buddha spoke this verse: "A certain fool among the disciples—monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen—performs an unwholesome evil deed without consideration. That fool acts with a mind that is increasingly elated and joyful, like a man eating a sweet and excellent flavor found in honey or syrup."

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the conclusion of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and other stages.

## Arrangement for Nuns to Reside Only in the Village

Later, on another occasion, a large assembly of people and monks in the Dhamma Hall raised this discussion: "I suppose even the Arahants enjoy sensual pleasures and indulge in them. Why would they not indulge? They are not dry tree stumps, nor are they anthills; they are indeed beings with bodies of moist flesh. Therefore, they too must enjoy sensual pleasures and indulge in them."

The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such a discussion, Bhante," the Teacher said, "Monks, Arahants do not enjoy sensual pleasures, nor do they indulge in them. For example, just as a drop of water falling on a Paduma lotus leaf does not cling or remain but rolls off and falls away, and just as a mustard seed on the point of an awl does not cling or remain but rolls off and falls away, even so, in the mind of an Arahant, the two types of sensual pleasure—objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and subjective sensuality (kilesa-kāma)—do not cling or remain."

Having said this, the Teacher, wishing to connect the context and preach the Dhamma, spoke this verse from the Brāhmaṇa Vagga:

"Like water on a lotus leaf, or a mustard seed on the point of an awl, he who does not cling to sensual pleasures, him I call a Brahmin."

The meaning of this will become clear in the Brāhmaṇa Vagga itself. Furthermore, the Teacher sent for King Pasenadi of Kosala and said, "Great King, in this Dispensation, just as noble sons, so too noble daughters renounce their large circle of relatives and great wealth to ordain and live in the forest. While they are living thus, wicked persons consumed by lust harass them through low pride and excessive conceit, and cause obstacles to their holy life. Therefore, it is proper to build a residence for the community of nuns (Bhikkhunī Saṅgha) only within the city."
313:
King Pasenadi of Kosala consented, saying, "Very well, Bhante," and had a residence built for the community of nuns on one side of the city. From that time onwards, the nuns resided only within the towns and villages.

The Story of the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā ends.

## 11. The Story of the Elder Jambuka

(Jambukatthera Vatthu)

While residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Māse māse" (Month after month) concerning the Ājīvaka named Jambuka.

## Insulting an Arahant

In the distant past, during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, a certain householder living in a village built a monastery for a certain Elder and supported that Elder who resided there with the four requisites. That Elder regularly took his meals at the householder's home. At that time, an Arahant monk, while wandering for alms during the day, arrived at the door of that householder's house. As soon as the householder saw the Arahant Elder, he was inspired by the Elder's deportment. He invited him inside, respectfully served him with excellent food, and offered a large cloth, saying, "Bhante, please have this cloth dyed and wear it."

He further requested, "Bhante, your hair has grown long; I will bring a barber to shave your hair," and promised, "I will also have a bed brought for your rest and then return."

The resident monk (kulūpaka), who regularly received offerings at that house, was unable to gladden his heart upon seeing the honor shown to the visiting monk. He thought, "This donor shows such honor to this visiting monk whom he has seen for only a moment, but he does not show such honor to me who regularly eats at his house," and he went back to the monastery brooding.

The visiting Arahant also went along with that resident monk and used the cloth given by the householder after dyeing it. The householder also brought a barber to shave the Elder's hair, had a bed prepared, and said, "Bhante, please rest on this very bed." After inviting both Elders for the next day's meal, he departed. The resident monk was unable to endure the honor shown to the visiting Arahant. Later, when evening came, the resident monk went to the visiting Elder's sleeping place and insulted him in four ways:

1. "Friend guest, it would be better for you to eat excrement than to eat food in this householder's house."
2. "It would be better for you to have your hair plucked out with a palmyra nut than to have it shaved by the barber brought by the householder."
3. "It would be better for you to wander about naked than to wear the robe-cloth given by the householder."
4. "It would be better for you to sleep on the ground than to sleep on the bed brought by the householder."

Thus, he insulted him in these four ways.
314:
## Stinginess Regarding the Supporter

The Arahant Elder, reflecting, "Let not this foolish monk perish on my account," did not accept the invitation. Rising early in the morning, he departed at his ease to wherever he desired. The resident monk, having performed his morning duties at the monastery, thought at the time for alms-round, "The visiting monk is still asleep. Let him be awakened by the sound of the bell." With this intention, he struck the bell with only his fingernail [so it made no sound] and entered the village for alms. The householder, having prepared offerings, was watching the path for the arrival of the two Elders. Seeing only the resident monk, he asked, "Venerable sir, where is the visiting Elder?" Then the resident monk said to the householder, "Lay disciple, do not say anything. Your teacher, the visiting monk, went into his room and fell into a deep sleep after you left yesterday. Although I rose early this morning and made the sounds of sweeping the monastery, pouring water into the drinking and washing pots, and even striking the bell, he did not know it."

The householder reflected, "For my lord, who is endowed with such perfect deportment, there should be no such thing as sleeping until this hour. Surely, seeing me making these offerings to him, this venerable monk must have said something unpleasant to him." Because of his wisdom, the householder respectfully fed the resident monk who had come, washed his bowl thoroughly, filled it with food of various excellent flavors, and said, "Venerable sir, if you should see my lord, please offer this alms-food to that noble one." The other monk, taking the food, thought, "If he eats such alms-food, he will become deeply attached to this very place." Thinking thus, he threw away the alms-food on the way. Upon returning to the Elder's dwelling and looking for him there, he did not see him.

## The Result of Evil Deeds

At that time, because of having committed such an evil deed, even the ascetic practices he had performed for twenty thousand years were unable to protect him from falling into the states of woe. Having passed away at the end of his lifespan, he was reborn in the Avīci Hell. After suffering great misery for the interval between two Buddhas, he was reborn in this Buddha's era in the city of Rājagaha, in a family of a wealthy clan with abundant food and drink. From the time he was able to walk, he did not wish to sleep on a bed, nor did he wish to eat food; he would only eat his own bodily waste. Thinking, "He does this because he is young and does not know better," they continued to nurture him. Even when he grew older, he did not wish to wear clothes; he wandered about naked, slept on the ground, and ate only his own bodily waste.

## The One Who Eats Only Excrement

Then his parents thought, "This youth is not suitable for our family. He is simply a shameless person; he would be suitable for the Ājīvakas." They took him to them and said, "Please ordain this boy." Then they ordained him. While ordaining him, the Ājīvakas placed him in a pit up to his neck, laid planks over his shoulders, and sitting upon those planks, they plucked out his hair using the halves of a palm-nut shell. Then the boy's parents invited those Ājīvakas for a meal the next day and departed. When the next day dawned and the Ājīvakas said, "Friend, come, let us enter the village," that young Ājīvaka replied, "You go ahead; I will remain right here," and did not wish to enter the village.
315:
At that time, although they urged that young Ājīvaka repeatedly, he did not wish to follow them, so they abandoned him and departed. When the young Ājīvaka knew that his fellow Ājīvakas had gone, he opened the plank in the latrine (vacca-kuṭī), went down, and making morsels with both hands, he ate the excrement. The Ājīvakas sent food to him from within the village.

He did not want that food either, and though they spoke to him repeatedly, he said, "I have no need for this food. I have already obtained food." When asked, "Where did you get it?" he replied, "I got it right here." In this manner, on the second, third, and fourth days, although those Ājīvakas spoke much to him, he remained saying, "I shall find food right here," and did not wish to go into the village. The Ājīvakas thought, "This young Ājīvaka does not wish to enter the village day after day, nor does he wish to eat the food we send. He says, 'I have obtained food right here.' What is he doing? Let us investigate and catch him." Having thought thus, as they were entering the village, they left behind one or two men to investigate and catch him. Those Ājīvakas acted as if they were following the others but remained hidden. When the young Ājīvaka knew that the Ājīvakas had gone, he went down into the latrine just as before and ate the excrement.

## Expulsion by the Ājīvakas
The Ājīvakas who were hiding and watching saw his behavior and informed the other Ājīvakas. Hearing this, the Ājīvakas said, "Oh, what a grave matter! If the disciples of the ascetic Gotama should know of this, they would spread an ill report of us, saying, 'The Ājīvakas go about eating excrement.' This man is not fit for us." Having consulted thus, they expelled the young Ājīvaka from their presence. Being expelled by his Ājīvaka teachers, the young Ājīvaka went to a place where the public discarded their excrement, where there was a certain flat rock (piṭṭhipāsāṇa). Near that flat rock, which served as a support like a large trunk, was the place where the public discarded their excrement. Having gone there, he ate excrement at night. When the people came to cleanse their bodies, he would stand with one hand leaning on one edge of the rock, lifting one foot and placing it on his knee, with his mouth open facing the wind. Seeing him, the people approached, paid homage, and asked, "Venerable sir, why do you stand with your mouth open?" "I feed only on wind; I have no other food than wind," he replied. When asked again, "If so, why do you stand with one foot on your knee?" he said, "I have noble practice, I have fierce penance. If I were to tread with both feet, the earth would tremble."
316:
## The Nature of Those Who Cannot Distinguish Good and Bad Practice
"Therefore, I stand with one foot lifted and placed on my knee," he said. "That is true. I spend my time standing both day and night; I do not sit, nor do I lie down." People generally believe mere words. Therefore, praising him, they said, "Oh, how wonderful! There are no others who can perform such penance. We have never seen anyone with such conduct and practice before." Most people living in the kingdoms of Anga and Magadha were deeply moved, and approaching him, they brought great offerings month after month. That young Ājīvaka said, "I feed only on wind, I eat no other food. If I were to eat food other than wind, my penance would be destroyed." Thus, he did not desire any of the food they brought. The people pleaded repeatedly, saying, "Venerable sir, do not destroy us. If a person of such fierce penance as yourself should make use of our offerings, it will be for our long-lasting welfare and happiness." Although he rejected them, saying, "I have no pleasure in other food," being pressed by the entreaties of the multitude, he would take a little ghee or molasses on the tip of a blade of grass, place it on the tip of his tongue, and dismiss them, saying, "Go now; this much is enough for your happiness and welfare." In this way, for fifty-five years, that young Ājīvaka spent his time naked, eating only excrement, plucking out his hair, and sleeping on the ground.

## The Arrival of the Buddha
For the Buddhas, the habit of surveying the world at the break of dawn is never abandoned. Therefore, one day at dawn, as the Blessed One was surveying the world, this Ājīvaka (Jambuka the Ājīvaka) appeared within the net of his knowledge. When the Blessed One reflected, "What will happen?" he saw that Jambuka the Ājīvaka possessed the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for the fruit of Arahantship along with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). He thought, "I shall preach a single verse starting with this Jambuka. At the end of that verse of Dhamma, eighty-four thousand beings will attain the realization of the Dhamma. Depending on this son of a good family, the multitude will reach a state of well-being." Having known this, the next day, after wandering for alms in Rājagaha and returning from his alms round, he addressed the Elder Ānanda, saying, "Ānanda, I shall go to the presence of Jambuka the Ājīvaka." When asked, "Venerable sir, will you go alone?" he replied, "Yes, I shall go alone." Thus, the Blessed One set out for the presence of Jambuka the Ājīvaka in the evening.

## Deities Create a Clean Environment
The deities thought, "The Blessed One is going to the presence of Jambuka the Ājīvaka. That Jambuka lives on a flat rock defiled by loathsome excrement, urine, and tooth-sticks. It is proper to make it rain." By their power, they caused it to rain at that very moment. The flat rock became pure, clean, and free of defilement. After that, they rained down flowers of five colors upon the flat rock.
317:
In the evening, the Blessed One went to the place of Jambuka the Ājīvaka and called out, “Jambuka.” Jambuka thought, “Who is this wicked person that addresses me by the name Jambuka?” and asked, “Who is this?” “Jambuka, it is I, the Buddha,” He replied. “Great Samana, why do you call?” he asked. “Give me a place to stay here for just one night,” the Buddha said. “Great Samana, there is no place to stay here,” he refused. “Jambuka, do not do so. Give me a place for one night,” the Buddha said again. “Ascetics seek out other ascetics, humans seek out humans, and beasts seek out beasts. Tell me, are you an ascetic?” he asked. “Yes, I am an ascetic,” He replied. “If you are an ascetic, where is your gourd? Where is your fire-ladle? Where is your sacrificial thread?” he asked. “I have all of these. But because carrying them separately is burdensome, I carry them within me,” He replied. Jambuka became angry, saying, “So you will go about without holding those things!” Then the Blessed One said to him, “Jambuka, let it be. Do not be angry. Just tell me a place where I may stay.” “Great Samana, there is no place to stay here,” he said.

## The Coming of the Deva Kings, Sakka, and Brahma to the Buddha

Not far from Jambuka’s dwelling, there was a mountain grotto. The Blessed One, having observed that grotto, asked, “Who lives in that grotto?” “Great Samana, no one lives there,” he replied. “If so, give that place to me,” He said. “You know best, Great Samana,” he replied. The Blessed One spread His sitting mat in the grotto and sat down. Then, during the first watch of the night, the Four Great Kings came to attend upon the Blessed One, illuminating the four directions simultaneously with their radiance. Jambuka saw the light and wondered, “What kind of light is this?” In the middle watch, Sakka, the King of Devas, arrived. Jambuka saw his radiance as well and wondered, “What light is this?” In the last watch, Mahābrahmā, who is capable of illuminating one universe with one finger, two with two fingers, and ten universes with ten fingers, arrived, illuminating the entire forest at once.

Jambuka saw the radiance of the Brahma and wondered, “What light is this?” Early in the morning, he went to the Blessed One, exchanged greetings, and standing at a respectful distance, asked the Blessed One, “Great Samana, who were those who came to you, illuminating the four directions?” “They were the Four Great Kings,” He replied. “For what reason did they come?” he asked. “They came to attend upon me,” He replied. “Are you then superior even to the Four Great Kings?” he asked. “Yes, Jambuka, I am the King of Kings, even over the Great Kings.” “Who then came in the middle watch?” he asked. “Jambuka, it was Sakka, the King of Devas,” He replied. “Why did he come?” he asked. “He came to attend upon me,” He replied. “Are you superior even to Sakka, the King of Devas?” he asked. “Yes, Jambuka, I am superior even to Sakka.”
318:
“...is an attendant who serves me when I am ill, a steward (kappiyakāraka) who performs tasks great and small. He is like a novice disciple (sāmaṇera),” the Buddha said.

“Great Ascetic, who was it that came in the last watch of the night, illuminating the entire forest?” Jambuka asked again. “The one whom Brahmins and others in the world invoke, saying ‘Namo Mahābrahmuno’ (Homage to Mahābrahmā) when they sneeze or slip—that was indeed Mahābrahmā,” the Buddha replied. “What? Are you even superior to Mahābrahmā?” he asked. “Yes, Jambuka, it is true. I am indeed the Great Brahmā who excels even the Brahmās,” the Buddha said. Then Jambuka said, “Great Ascetic, you are truly an amazing person. Although I have lived in this place for fifty-five years, not even one of them has ever come to attend on me. For all this time, I have lived only on air and remained standing, yet they have never come to attend on me.”

## Jambuka Becomes an Arahant and is Released from Saṃsāra

Then the Blessed One said to Jambuka, “O Jambuka, you have been deceiving the foolish and deluded masses in the world, and now you wish to deceive me as well. Have you not eaten only excrement for fifty-five years? Did you not sleep only on the ground? Did you not wander naked? Did you not pluck out your hair with a piece of a palmyra nut shell? Despite this, you deceive the ignorant people, saying, ‘I live on air, I stand on one leg, I never sit or lie down.’ You wish to deceive me too.”

After saying this, the Buddha continued, “In your previous lives as well, relying on an extremely evil view, you spent so much time eating excrement, sleeping on the ground, wandering naked, and plucking your hair with a piece of a palmyra nut shell. Even now, you hold onto that same evil view.” When Jambuka asked, “Great Ascetic, what evil have I done in the past?”, the Blessed One then revealed to him the evil deeds he had committed in his previous life. While the Buddha was preaching, Jambuka was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and felt shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa), and he sat down in a crouching position. Then the Blessed One threw him a bathing cloth (udakasāṭika). Jambuka put on the cloth, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat to one side. The Blessed One then preached the Dhamma to him, giving a progressive discourse (anupubbikathā). At the end of the teaching, Jambuka attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). He rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and requested both the initial and higher ordination (pabbajjā and upasampadā). With this, his past evil karma was exhausted.

(This Jambuka had insulted an Arahant Elder with four kinds of insults. For as long as this great earth rose by one league (yojana) and three gāvutas, he suffered in Avīci hell. Due to the remaining result of that suffering in Avīci, he reached such a state of perversion for fifty-five years. By becoming an Arahant, that unwholesome karma of Jambuka came to an end.)

## Becoming an Ehi Bhikkhu Monk

The merit of the practice as a monk (samaṇadhamma) performed by Jambuka for twenty thousand years could not be destroyed or prevented.
319:
## The Discourse

(70) Month after month, with the tip of a blade of kusa grass,
A fool may eat his food.
Yet he is not worth a sixteenth part
Of those who have well-understood the Dhamma.

Bālo: the fool who is ignorant and unwise. Māse māse: every month. Patte: when it arrives. Bhojanaṃ: food. Kusaggena: with the tip of a blade of kusa grass. Bhuñjeyya: he may eat. So bālo: that fool who practices such asceticism. Saṅkhātadhammānaṃ: of the Noble Ones (Ariyas) who have fully comprehended the Dhamma. Soḷasiṃ: the sixteenth part of a sixteenth part, which is the two-hundred-and-fifty-sixth part. Kalaṃ: a fraction. Alternatively: Soḷasiṃ: having divided into two hundred and fifty-six parts. Kalaṃ: even a single part. Na agghati: does not reach, or is not worth.

Therefore, the Blessed One stretched out his right hand and called him with the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' (Come, monk) ordination, saying, "Come, monk, lead the holy life to make an end of suffering." At that very moment, Jambuka's lay appearance vanished, and he appeared like a senior elder of sixty years' standing, endowed with the eight requisites.

## The Miracle Shown by Venerable Jambuka

That day was the day when the residents of both Aṅga and Magadha arrived, bringing offerings for Jambuka. Thus, when the men and women of both regions arrived with their offerings and saw the Blessed One and Venerable Jambuka together, they thought: "How is this? Is our Lord Jambuka great, or is the Samana Gotama great?" They further reasoned: "If the Samana Gotama were great, this Lord Jambuka would go to him. It is only because our Lord Jambuka the Ājīvaka is so great that the Samana Gotama has come to him."

The Blessed One, knowing the thoughts of the multitude, said, "Jambuka, clear the doubts of your supporters." Jambuka replied, "Venerable Sir, I have been waiting for this very moment." After saying this, he entered the fourth jhāna, and upon emerging, he rose into the air to the height of a palm tree and declared, "The Blessed One is my teacher, Venerable Sir; I am his disciple." He then descended and prostrated at the Buddha's feet. He rose again into the air to the height of two palm trees, then three palm trees, and so on up to the height of seven palm trees, before descending to make his discipleship known.

Seeing this, the multitude thought, "How wonderful indeed are the Buddhas! They possess incomparable virtues." The Blessed One, wishing to speak to the multitude, said: "For all this time, this Jambuka lived here, placing the offerings you brought on the tip of his tongue with a blade of kusa grass, claiming to fulfill ascetic practices. Even if he were to practice such asceticism for a hundred years, the wholesome intention of his current fasting—born of his conscience regarding time and food—is not worth even a sixteenth part of a sixteenth part of the merit of those who have understood the Dhamma." Thus, connecting the sequence of the discourse, he spoke this verse:
320:
## The Benefit of the Discourse

At the end of the discourse, eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma.

The Story of Venerable Jambuka ends.

## 12. The Story of the Snake Ghost
### (Ahipetavatthu)

While residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Blessed One spoke this legal discourse beginning with "Na hi pāpaṃ kataṃ kammaṃ," concerning a certain snake ghost (ahipeta).

## The Suffering of the Snake Ghost

One day, Venerable Lakkhaṇa and Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, who were among the thousand former matted-hair ascetics (led by Uruvela Kassapa), were descending from Gijjhakūṭa Hill to wander for alms in the city of Rājagaha. Among them, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw a snake ghost and smiled. Then, Venerable Lakkhaṇa asked the reason for the smile, saying, "Friend Moggallāna, why did you smile?"

Venerable Mahāmoggallāna replied, "Friend Lakkhaṇa, it is not yet the time for this question. Ask me this question in the presence of the Blessed One."

After they had wandered for alms in Rājagaha and went to the presence of the Blessed One and were seated, Venerable Lakkhaṇa asked, "Friend Moggallāna, as you were descending Gijjhakūṭa Hill, you smiled. When I asked the reason, you said, 'Ask me in the presence of the Blessed One.' Now, please tell the reason."

Venerable Mahāmoggallāna spoke thus: "Friend Lakkhaṇa, I smiled because I saw a snake ghost. Its physical form was like this: its head was like a human head, but its body was that of a snake..."
321:
Your tongue is five leagues long, and your head is nine leagues long.
Your body rises up to twenty-five leagues.
Having done what action did you come to such suffering?

O Crow Peta! Your tongue is five leagues long. Your head is nine leagues long. Your body rises up to twenty-five leagues. What evil unwholesome deed did you commit to reach such suffering?

“Venerable Moggallāna, I, the Crow Peta, took as much as I desired of the food brought for the Saṅgha of the Great Sage Kassapa.”

“Venerable Moggallāna, I, the Crow Peta, once took as much as I desired of the food brought for the Saṅgha of the Great Sage Kassapa Buddha.”

Because he saw it, he clearly showed a smile. The physical form of that Snake Peta was as follows: the head of that Snake Peta was shaped like a human head, while the rest of the body resembled a snake. This peta is called the Snake Peta (Ahipeta). In size, it was twenty-five leagues long. Flames arising from the head of that Snake Peta burned all the way to the tip of the tail. Flames arising from the tip of the tail burned all the way to the head. Flames arising from the middle of the head burned both sides. Flames arising from both sides entered into the middle,” he said.

## Becoming a Crow Peta for Eating Before the Saṅgha

Venerable Moggallāna, having ascended to the summit of Gijjhakūṭa hill, saw a Crow Peta undergoing suffering and, wishing to ask about the past evil deed of that Crow Peta, recited this verse.

When asked thus, the Crow Peta, wishing to explain to Venerable Moggallāna, addressed him with this verse and said:

“Venerable Sir—in the time of Kassapa Buddha, many monks entered a village for alms. People, seeing the elders and feeling great affection and devotion, invited them to sit in the alms-hall. They washed their feet, anointed them with oil, offered rice gruel and snacks, and while waiting for the time of the alms-meal, they sat listening to the Dhamma. At the end of the Dhamma talk, they took the elders' alms-bowls, filled them with various delicious foods prepared in their own homes, and brought them back. At that time, I was a crow and was perched on the roof of the alms-hall. Seeing the food being brought, I filled my beak three times from an alms-bowl carried by one person and snatched away three mouthfuls of rice. That food was not yet the property of the Saṅgha, nor had it been formally offered to the Saṅgha, nor was it the leftovers from the monks. In fact, it was food brought from their own homes, fit to be eaten by the people themselves, and was merely being brought with the intention of offering it to the Saṅgha. From that food, I snatched and ate three large mouthfuls. My past evil deed was only this much.”
322:
“I passed away and, as a result of that evil deed, suffered in Avīci hell. Now, due to the remaining unwholesome karma, I have been reborn as a Crow Peta on the summit of Gijjhakūṭa hill and am experiencing this suffering,” he replied. This is the Story of the Crow Peta.

## Becoming a Snake Peta for Burning a Monastery

In this instance, it is said that Venerable Moggallāna clearly showed a smile upon seeing the Snake Peta. Then the Teacher, acting as a witness for Moggallāna, stood up and said, “Monks, Moggallāna speaks the truth. I too saw this Snake Peta on the very day I attained Enlightenment. Although I saw it, I did not speak of it. If there were those who did not believe my words, it would be to their detriment. For this reason, out of compassion for others, I did not speak.”

The story of this Snake Peta was also related by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Upon hearing those words, the monks asked about the past evil deed of that Snake Peta. The Teacher then related it to those monks. In the past, near the city of Bārāṇasī, people built and offered a leaf-roofed hut on a riverbank for a Paccekabuddha. While that Paccekabuddha resided in that hut, he regularly entered the city of Bārāṇasī for alms. The city dwellers, both in the evening and morning, would go to attend upon the Paccekabuddha, carrying scents, flowers, and so on. A certain man living in Bārāṇasī plowed a field near the path used by the people. As the multitude of people went to attend upon the Paccekabuddha in the evening and morning, they walked across and trampled that field. Although the farmer forbade them, saying, ‘Do not trample my field,’ he was unable to stop them. Then this thought occurred to the farmer: ‘If the leaf-roofed hut where the Paccekabuddha resides were not in this place, they would not trample my field.’ Having thought thus, while the Paccekabuddha had entered for alms, the farmer broke the pots and vessels used by him and set the leaf-roofed hut on fire. The Paccekabuddha, seeing his dwelling in flames, departed for a place of comfort.

When the people arrived carrying scents and flowers, they saw the burning leaf-hut and asked, “Where has our venerable master gone?”
323:
## The Teaching
(71) Indeed, an evil deed committed does not curdle like fresh milk.
It follows the fool, burning him, like fire covered by ashes.

*Sajju khīraṃ*: Fresh milk that has just come out warm from the cow's udder. *Na muccati iva*: Just as it does not immediately turn sour. *Kataṃ*: Just committed. *Pāpaṃ kammaṃ*: An unwholesome deed. *Na hi vipaccati*: Truly, it cannot produce its bad result immediately. *Vipaccamānaṃ*: When it does produce its bad result. *Bālaṃ*: The fool who is possessed by bad karma. *Ḍahantaṃ*: Causing him to burn. *Anveti*: It follows him. *Yathā*: How? *Bhasmacchannova*: Like [fire] covered with ashes. *Pāvako*: A glowing ember. Just as it burns the one who steps on it, following him, so it is.

The plowman also went along with the crowd and, standing in their midst, said, "I have set fire to the leaf-roofed monastery where the Venerable Paccekabuddha resided." Then, saying, "Seize this wicked man! Because of this wicked man, we no longer have the opportunity to pay homage to the Venerable Paccekabuddha," they struck and beat him with sticks, clubs, and so on, until he died. That plowman was reborn in the great Avīci hell, and for as long as this great earth rose by one league, he was cooked and suffered in that hell. By the power of the remaining result, he was reborn as a snake-ghost (Ahi-peta) on this Gijjhakūṭa mountain. The Blessed One, having taught this past evil deed of the snake-ghost, wishing to connect the sequence of the teaching, spoke this verse: "Monks, this thing called evil is like milk. Just as milk does not spoil or emit a smell immediately upon being milked, so too an unwholesome deed does not produce its result immediately upon being committed. When it does produce its result, at that time, one must burn and grieve with such suffering."

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people became Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna) and so forth.
The Story of the Snake-Ghost ends.

## 13. The Story of the Ghost with Sixty Thousand Hammers
(Saṭṭhikūṭapeta-vatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at the Veḷuvana monastery, told this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Yāvadeva anatthāya," concerning the ghost with sixty thousand hammers.

## The Ghost Beaten by Sixty Thousand Hammers
In the same manner as before, while the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was descending from Gijjhakūṭa mountain with the Venerable Lakkhaṇa, he smiled at a certain spot. When asked by the Venerable Lakkhaṇa about the reason for his smile, he said, "Ask me in the presence of the Blessed One." After going for alms and approaching the Blessed One, while sitting after paying homage, he was asked again by the Venerable Lakkhaṇa and said, "Friend Lakkhaṇa, I saw a ghost with an individual existence (attabhāva) three leagues in size. On the top of his head, sixty thousand iron hammers, glowing, flaming, and blazing, were falling and rising, breaking his head. Each time his head was broken, it became as before."
324:
"I have never seen such an individual existence before in this life," he said, and then added, "I smiled because I saw that ghost." This is true. In the final story of the Petavatthu Pali, referring to this very Saṭṭhikūṭa ghost, this verse was spoken:

Sixty thousand hammers, complete in every way,
Fall upon your head, breaking your skull.

*Bho peta*: O ghost! *Sabbaso*: In every way. *Paripuṇṇာni*: Complete. *Saṭṭhikūṭasahassāni*: Sixty thousand iron hammers. *Tuyhaṃ*: Your. *Sīse*: On the head. *Nipatanti*: They fall. *Tava*: Your. *Matthakaṃ*: The top of the head. *Bhindanti*: They break.

The Blessed One, hearing the words of the Venerable Moggallāna, said, "Monks, I too saw this being while sitting at the foot of the Bodhi tree. Even though I saw him, I did not speak out of compassion for others, thinking, 'If there are those who do not believe my words, it would be to their disadvantage.' But now, I speak with Moggallāna as a witness." Hearing this, the monks asked about the ghost's past evil deed. The Blessed One told them the story of the past.

## Throwing Goat Dung into the Chaplain's Mouth
In the past, it is said, in the city of Bārāṇasī, there was a certain cripple who had reached perfection in the art of slinging stones (sālittaka-sippa). He sat at the foot of a banyan tree at the city gate and, by slinging stones, he would cut and pierce the leaves of that banyan tree. When the village boys said, "Show us the shape of an elephant," or "Show us the shape of a horse," he would show whatever shapes they desired and receive snacks and food from them. Then one day, the King, while going to the park, reached that place. The boys left the cripple between the roots of the banyan tree and fled. When the King entered the foot of the tree at midday, the sunlight through the many holes [in the leaves] touched the King's body. The King looked up, wondering, "What is this?" and seeing the shapes of elephants and so on in the tree leaves, he asked, "Whose work is this?" Hearing the reply, "It is the work of a cripple," he had him summoned and said, "My chaplain is extremely talkative. Even when I say a little, he speaks a lot and oppresses me. Would you be able to throw a measure of goat dung into that chaplain's mouth?" "I can, Your Majesty. Have the goat dung brought, and you and the chaplain sit inside a curtain; I will know what needs to be done here," he replied.

Then the King did as he said. The cripple made a hole in the curtain with the tip of a pair of scissors and, whenever the chaplain opened his mouth while speaking with the King, he threw in one goat dung at a time. The chaplain swallowed each goat dung as it entered his mouth. When the goat dung was exhausted, the cripple shook the curtain. The King, knowing by that signal that the goat dung was finished, said, "Teacher Chaplain, I, who have been speaking with you, have not been able to get a word out of my mouth..."
325:
Skill is indeed good, no matter what kind it may be.
Behold, by the flicking of a cripple, villages in the four directions were obtained.

“O Great King! A skill is indeed good, regardless of what kind it is. Look, Your Majesty! By flicking goat dung, this cripple has obtained four villages in the four directions of the city.”

“Because of your excessive talkativeness, you could not remain silent even after swallowing a measure of goat dung.” Thus he said. The chaplain fell into a state of dejection and from then on, he did not dare to open his mouth to speak with the king. The king, remembering the cripple's favor, had him summoned and, being pleased, said, “Because of you, I have found happiness.” He granted the cripple the wealth known as Sabbaṭṭhaka (the eightfold gift) and gave him four excellent villages in the four directions of the city. Having understood this matter, the wise minister, who advised the king on matters of welfare and Dhamma, recited this verse.

That wise minister at that time was I, the Buddha.

## Becoming a Peta due to Misuse of Skill

At that time, a man, seeing the fortune obtained by the cripple, thought, “This man, despite being a cripple, has attained great fortune by relying on this skill. It is proper for me to learn this skill as well.” Having thought so, he approached the cripple and requested, “Teacher, please teach me this skill.” When the cripple refused, saying, “Dear man, I cannot teach it,” the man thought, “Even if he refuses, I will please him.” He performed various duties such as massaging the cripple's hands and feet. After a long time, having pleased the cripple, he requested again and again. The cripple, unable to refuse because the man had been so helpful, taught him the skill. When the training was complete, he asked, “Dear man, your skill is now perfected. What will you do now?” The man replied, “Teacher, I will go outside the city and test my skill.” The cripple asked, “How will you test it?” The man said, “I will strike a cow or a person and kill them.”

“Dear man, for killing a cow, the fine is a hundred; for killing a person, the fine is a thousand. Even if you work with your wife and children, you will not be able to pay such a fine. Do not ruin yourself. Look for someone who has no mother or father, upon whom striking would result in no fine.” With this instruction, he sent him away. The man agreed, saying, “Very well,” and taking pebbles in his lap, he wandered around looking for someone without a protector. Seeing a cow, he did not dare to strike it, thinking, “This has an owner.” Seeing a person, he did not dare to strike, thinking, “This person has a mother and father.” At that time, a Paccekabuddha named Sunetta was residing in a leaf-hut near the city. The man saw the Paccekabuddha Sunetta entering the city gate for alms and thought, “This person has no mother or father. If I strike him, there will be no fine. I will test my skill by striking him.” Aiming for the Paccekabuddha's right ear-hole...
326:
He aimed at the right ear-hole of the Paccekabuddha and threw a pebble. It entered through the right ear-hole and came out through the left. Intense painful feelings arose. The Paccekabuddha was unable to continue his almsround; he traveled through the air to his leaf-hut and attained Parinibbāna.

When the people did not see the Paccekabuddha coming for alms, they thought, "Something must be wrong," and went to his dwelling. Seeing that the Paccekabuddha had attained Parinibbāna, they wept and lamented. The man, seeing the crowd of people going there, also went and, recognizing the Paccekabuddha, said, "This Paccekabuddha appeared before me at the city gate while entering for alms; I struck him to test my skill." The people cried out, "This villain has struck and killed our Lord Paccekabuddha! Seize him! Seize him!" They beat him and caused his death right there. That villain was reborn in the Avīci Hell. For as long as it took for this great earth to rise by one league, he was cooked in hell. By the remaining result of his karma, he was reborn as a Saṭṭhikūṭa Peta (a ghost with sixty hammers) on the summit of Gijjhakūṭa mountain.

The Teacher, having related this past karma of the Saṭṭhikūṭa Peta, said, "Monks, when skill or power arises in a fool, it arises only for his ruin. Indeed, when a fool gains skill or power, he only works for his own misfortune." Connecting the sequence of the discourse, he spoke this verse:

## The Teaching

(72) Only for his own ruin is knowledge born to the fool;
It destroys the fool's merit, cleaving his head.

**Knowledge (Ñattaṃ):** This refers to the nature of knowing, or being well-known and famous among people due to skill, wealth, or power. **Only for his own ruin (Yāvadeva anatthāya):** It arises only for his own misfortune. Relying on that, he works for his own ruin. **Destroys (Hanti):** It ruins. **Merit (Sukkaṃsaṃ):** The portion of wholesome merit. When skill or power arises in a fool, it arises only to destroy his portion of merit. **Head (Muddhaṃ):** This is a name for wisdom. **Cleaving (Vipātayaṃ):** Destroying or casting down. While destroying his merit, it also destroys his head, which is wisdom.

## Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the discourse, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and other stages.

The Story of Saṭṭhikūṭa Peta is finished.
327:
## 14. The Story of Citta the Householder (Cittagahapati Vatthu)
