While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Asantaṃ bhāvanamiccheyya," concerning the Elder Sudhamma. The teaching originated in Macchikāsaṇḍa and was concluded in Sāvatthī.

## Citta the Householder Inviting the Guests for a Meal
In the city of Macchikāsaṇḍa, Citta the Householder saw the Elder named Mahānāma, who was one of the group of five (Pañcavaggiya), walking for alms. Being deeply inspired by the Elder’s deportment, he took the bowl, invited him into his house, and offered him a meal. At the conclusion of the meal, upon hearing the Dhamma, he attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and became possessed of unshakable faith. Desiring to make his own garden, named Ambāṭakavana, a residence for the Sangha (Saṅghārāma), he poured water over the Elder’s hands and dedicated the donation. At that moment, with the thought "The Buddha’s Dispensation is established," the great earth shook as far as the water’s edge. Citta the Householder had a great monastery built in the garden, which became like an open door for monks arriving from all directions. In Macchikāsaṇḍa, the Elder Sudhamma was the resident monk (nevāsika) of that monastery.

On another occasion, having heard of Citta the Householder’s virtues, the two Chief Disciples (Aggasāvaka), wishing to show him favor, traveled to Macchikāsaṇḍa. When Citta the Householder heard of their arrival, he went out half a league to welcome them. He escorted the Elders to the monastery he had built and donated, and after performing the duties for visiting monks, he requested the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati), saying, "Venerable Sir, I wish to hear a brief Dhamma discourse."

Then the Elder Sāriputta said to him, "Lay follower, we have come a long distance and are quite weary. Nevertheless, listen to a little of the Dhamma," and he preached the Dhamma to Citta the Householder. While listening to the Elder’s discourse, the householder attained the Fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala). The householder paid homage to the two Chief Disciples with great respect and invited them, saying, "Venerable Sirs, please accept alms at my house tomorrow along with a thousand follower monks." Afterward, he invited the resident Elder Sudhamma, saying, "Venerable Sir, please also come tomorrow together with the Great Elders."

## The Monk Sudhamma Becoming Angry with the Lay Follower
The Elder Sudhamma, becoming angry with the thought, "This householder invites me only afterward," refused the invitation. Even though he was pleaded with repeatedly, he continued to refuse. The lay follower said, "Venerable Sir, I understand [your mind]," and departed. On the following morning, he prepared a great alms-giving at his home.
328:
## The Teaching
(73) He may desire false reputation, precedence among the monks,
Authority in the monasteries, and honor from other families.
(74) "Let both laypeople and monastics think that this was done by me alone.
Let them be under my power in whatever needs to be done, whether great or small."
Such is the thought of a fool; his craving and conceit increase.

A foolish monk desires false reputation, which does not truly exist. He desires precedence among the monks, wanting them to surround and follow him. He desires authority in the monasteries and honor from other families. For such a foolish monk, the thought arises: "Let both laypeople and monastics think that they perform duties such as providing lodgings solely for me." 

In any matter, whether great or small, the thought arises: "Let them follow only my will." For that foolish monk, craving (taṇhā) and conceit (māna) increase.

Sudhamma Thera, early in the morning, thought: "What kind of offerings has the householder prepared for the Chief Disciples? I will go and see tomorrow morning." Taking his bowl and robes early in the morning, he went to the householder's home. Although the householder pleaded, "Venerable Sir, please sit and stay for a while," Sudhamma Thera replied, "I do not wish to sit; I will go on my alms round." After inspecting the various offerings prepared for the Chief Disciples, he wished to insult the householder based on his birth, and said, "Lay follower, the offerings are indeed excellent. However, one thing is missing from this collection of offerings."

When asked, "Venerable Sir, what is that offering?", he replied, "Lay follower, it is sesame cake." Because of this, the householder rebuked him with the analogy of a crow. (The meaning is: just as a hybrid crow-chicken, being neither fully crow nor chicken, makes an indistinct sound, so too does the Venerable Sudhamma, though a son of the Buddha, speak improperly and unclearly by saying "sesame cake.") Being rebuked, Sudhamma Thera became very angry and said, "Lay follower, this monastery is yours; I shall depart for another place." Although he was pleaded with and restrained three times, he did not listen and went to the presence of the Blessed One.

Upon arrival, he reported the words spoken by Citta the Householder and himself. The Blessed One blamed Sudhamma Thera alone, saying, "You have insulted and disparaged a faithful lay follower who has confidence in the Triple Gem with low speech." The Blessed One then had him undergo the Paṭisāraṇīyakamma (an ecclesiastical act for a monk who insults a layperson, requiring him to ask for forgiveness) and sent him away, saying, "Go, ask Citta the Householder for forgiveness."

He went there and said, "Lay follower, this fault is mine alone; please forgive me." But the householder refused, saying, "I do not forgive you." Being dejected and unable to gain forgiveness, he returned to the presence of the Blessed One the next morning.

(The Blessed One knew that the householder would not yet forgive him, but thinking, "This monk is stubborn with pride; let him travel this thirty-league path and return once more," He sent him away without telling him the means to obtain forgiveness.)

When he returned again, his pride humbled, the Blessed One gave him a companion monk to follow him and said, "Go, travel with this monk and make the lay follower forgive you." He then said, "It is not proper for one called a monk to have pride or envy, thinking 'my monastery, my place of residence, my male lay follower, my female lay follower'." He added, "For a monk who acts thus, defilements such as evil desires and conceit increase." To connect the context and preach the Dhamma, He spoke these verses.

(For that monk who possessed four types of evil desires and two types of thoughts, insight, path-knowledge, and fruition-knowledge did not increase. Instead, like the rising tide of the ocean, craving in the six doors and nine types of conceit increased.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
329:
## Sudhamma Thera Attaining Arahantship

Sudhamma Thera, after hearing such instruction and advice, paid homage to the Blessed One with great respect, rose from his seat, performed the circumambulation, and went together with the companion monk. He confessed his offense in the presence of Citta the Householder and asked for his forgiveness. Citta the Householder also replied, "Venerable sir, I forgive the offense you have committed. If I have any fault or offense against you, please forgive me as well, venerable sir," thus apologizing in return. Sudhamma Thera, remaining established in the advice given by the Blessed One, attained Arahantship along with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) within just two or three days.

## Citta the Householder’s Journey to Sāvatthī to Pay Homage to the Buddha

Citta the Householder reflected, "I have attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti) without having seen the Blessed One, my Teacher, in person. I am also established in the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi) without having seen the Blessed One. It is proper for me to go and pay homage to the Blessed One." Having reflected thus, the householder prepared five hundred carts filled with sesame, rice, molasses, clothing, and other supplies. He sent word to the Sangha of monks, saying, "Venerable sirs who wish to see the Blessed One, please come along; there will be no hardship regarding alms-food and other necessities." He also informed the Sangha of nuns, the laymen, and the laywomen.

Five hundred monks, five hundred nuns, five hundred laymen, and five hundred laywomen set out together with Citta the Householder. Citta the Householder provided for the three thousand people, including his own retinue, during the thirty-yojana journey in such a way that there was no lack or deficiency of gruel, rice, and other needs. Knowing of Citta’s departure, the devas built pavilions at every yojana and served the multitude with divine gruel, snacks, rice, and drinks. No one lacked anything. Thus, being well-served by the devas and traveling one yojana per day, they reached Sāvatthī in one month. The five hundred carts remained as full as they were at the start. He traveled while distributing only the gifts and offerings brought by devas and humans.

## The Rain of Flowers during Citta the Householder’s Visit

The Blessed One said to the Elder Ānanda, "Ānanda, this evening when the shadows lengthen, Citta the Householder will arrive surrounded by five hundred laymen to pay homage to me." When asked, "Exalted Buddha, will there be any miracle when Citta the Householder comes to pay homage to the Blessed One?" the Buddha replied, "There will be, Ānanda." When asked, "What will it be, Blessed One?" the Buddha said, "When Citta comes and pays homage to me, a dense rain of five-colored divine flowers will fall, covering an area of eight karīsas to the depth of the knees."

When the people of the city heard this news passed along, they thought, "A householder named Citta, endowed with such merit and glory, is coming to pay homage to the Blessed One today. Such a miracle will occur. We shall get to see this Citta the Householder of great merit." Taking offerings with them, they stood on both sides of the road.
330:
When they reached the vicinity of the monastery, the five hundred monks arrived first. Citta the Householder said, "Mothers, you follow behind us," and leaving the laywomen, he entered the presence of the Blessed One surrounded by five hundred laymen. Those standing or sitting in the presence of the Buddhas do not stand here or there; they remain still on both sides of the Buddha’s path. Citta the Householder entered the great path of the Buddha. Wherever Citta, the noble disciple who had attained the three fruits, looked, that place trembled. The great multitude looked on, saying, "This is Citta the Householder." Citta approached the Blessed One, entered within the six-colored rays of the Buddha, and paid homage by clasping the Buddha’s ankles with his hands. At that very moment, the rain of flowers mentioned by the Buddha fell, and thousands of cheers were raised.

## Offering Alms for a Full Month in the Presence of the Buddha

Citta the Householder stayed in the presence of the Blessed One for a full month. While staying there, he invited the entire Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha to remain in the monastery and offered a great donation. He also provided for those who had accompanied him, letting them stay within the monastery grounds. Not even for a single day did he have to take anything from the supplies in his carts; he offered alms and performed all duties using only the gifts brought by devas and humans. 

Citta the Householder paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Exalted Buddha, I came with the intention of offering alms to the Blessed One, and a month has passed on the journey. Another month has passed while I have been here at this monastery. I have not yet had to take out even a small portion of the goods and gifts I brought. For all this time, I have been giving alms using only the gifts brought by devas and humans. Even if I were to stay here at the Great Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī for a whole year, I would not get the chance to distribute my own collection of offerings. I wish to unload all the goods from the carts and return. Please instruct someone to show me a place for storage." The Blessed One said to the Elder Ānanda, "Ānanda, clear a place and give it to this householder." The Elder Ānanda did as the Blessed One commanded.
331:
(The place permitted for storing Citta the Householder's offerings of sesame, rice, and other items is a suitable and allowable kappiya-kuṭi. A kappiya-kuṭi is a dwelling place for monks where food may be stored overnight. There are four types of such dwellings: 1. Ussāvanantika-kuṭi, 2. Gonisādika-kuṭi, 3. Gahapati-kuṭi, and 4. Sammuti-kuṭi. A dwelling place other than these four types is called an akappiya-kuṭi. If food is stored overnight in an unallowable place, monks should not eat it; to do so is an offense of dukkaṭa for storing food indoors.)

## Receiving Seven Kinds of Jewels on the Return Journey from Visiting the Buddha
The lay follower Citta the Householder set out again on his journey with empty carts, accompanied by the three thousand people who had come with him. Devas and humans came forward and, saying, "Noble householder, you have made the journey with empty carts," filled the carts with the seven kinds of jewels. Citta the Householder returned, looking after and providing for the multitude of people solely with the gifts and offerings that had been sent to him. The Venerable Ānanda, having paid homage to the Blessed One, said: "Venerable Sir, when Citta the Householder came to the presence of the Blessed One, it took him a full month; he has also stayed here for a full month. During all this time, he has given great offerings solely with the gifts brought and presented by devas and humans. Now, having emptied five hundred carts, he will return in just one month. It is said that devas and humans came forward to Citta the Householder and, saying, 'Noble householder, you have made the journey with empty carts,' filled those five hundred carts with the seven kinds of jewels.

That Citta the Householder will return, looking after and providing for the multitude of people solely with the gifts and offerings sent to him." Having said this, he asked: "Venerable Sir, does such gain, honor, and renown arise for Citta the Householder only when he comes to the presence of the Blessed One? Or does such gain, honor, and renown arise even when he goes to other places?"

"Ānanda, whether he comes to my presence or goes elsewhere, such honor and renown arise for that householder."
332:
"This lay follower possesses the quality of faith (saddhā). He possesses the quality of devotion (pasanna). He is fully endowed with the quality of virtue (sīla). To whatever place such a person resorts, there gain, honor, and renown arise for him." Having said this, the Blessed One spoke this verse found in the Pakinnaka Vagga:

Saddho sīlena sampanno, yaso bhogasamappito.
Yaṃ yaṃ padesaṃ bhajati, tattha tattheva pūjito.

Saddho: having the quality of faith. Sīlena sampanno: one who is complete in virtue. Yaso: having a good reputation. Bhogasamappito: being endowed with riches and possessions. Yaṃ yaṃ padesaṃ: to whatever region or place. Bhajati: he approaches or goes to. Tattha tattheva: in that very place. Pūjito: he is honored; hoti: it happens.

## Past Meritorious Deeds and Aspiration in the Life of a Hunter
When the Blessed One had thus spoken, the Venerable Ānanda asked about the past meritorious deeds of Citta the Householder. Then the Blessed One, wishing to explain to the Venerable Ānanda, spoke in this manner: "Ānanda, this Citta the Householder, having made an aspiration at the feet of the Blessed One Padumuttara, wandered through the worlds of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. In the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he was reborn in a family of hunters. When he reached adulthood, one day while it was raining, he took a spear and went into the forest to kill deer. While looking for deer, he saw a monk sitting with his head covered in a natural, unformed mountain cave. Thinking, 'A noble one must be sitting there practicing the Dhamma of a recluse; I will bring him almsfood,' he quickly returned home. He had meat brought the previous day cooked on one hearth and rice cooked on another. Seeing other monks walking for alms, he took their bowls, invited them to sit on prepared seats, and served them almsfood. Having instructed others, 'Please serve the noble ones,' he wrapped the cooked rice in a bundle and set out.

On the way, he plucked various flowers, placed them on the bundle of rice, and went to the place where the Elder was sitting. Saying, 'Venerable Sir, please show me favor,' he took the bowl, filled it with the almsfood, and placed it in the Elder's hands. Having made an offering with those flowers, he made this aspiration: 'Just as this delicious almsfood together with the offering of flowers has delighted my heart, so too, in every place I am born, may thousands of gifts come to me and delight my heart, and may there be a rain of five-colored flowers.' That hunter, having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, was reborn in the world of devas. Wherever he was born, a rain of divine flowers fell to the depth of the knees. In this present life, the rain of flowers on the day he was born and when he arrived here, the bringing of gifts, and the filling of his carts with the seven kinds of jewels are the results of the meritorious deeds he performed when he was a hunter."

The Story of Citta the Householder ends.
333:
## 15. Vanavāsītissasāmaṇeravatthu
(The Story of the Novice Tissa of the Forest)
While the Teacher was residing at the Jetavana Monastery, he spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Aññā hi lābhūpanisā" in reference to the Elder Vanavāsī Tissa. The teaching originated in Rājagaha.

## The Almsgiving of the Brahmin Mahāsena in Times of Poverty
In the city of Rājagaha, there lived a great Brahmin named Mahāsena, who was a friend of Vanganta, the father of the Venerable Sāriputta. One day, while the Venerable Sāriputta was wandering for alms, he went to the door of the Brahmin Mahāsena’s house out of compassion for him. However, that Brahmin had lost his wealth and was living in poverty. Thinking, "My son, the Elder, has come to my door for alms, but I am in a state of poverty. He likely does not know of my destitution, and I have nothing to offer as a gift," he was unable to face the Elder and remained hidden. The Venerable Sāriputta went there again the following day. The Brahmin hid just as before. Although he thought, "If I obtain something to give, I shall offer it," he obtained nothing.

Then one day, at a gathering where Brahmins were reciting, he received a bowl of milk-rice along with a piece of coarse cloth. As soon as he reached home with them, he remembered the Elder, thinking, "It is proper for me to offer this alms-food to the Elder."

At that moment, the Venerable Sāriputta, having entered into a meditative absorption and then emerging from it, saw the Brahmin and thought, "The Brahmin has obtained a gift and is waiting for my arrival; it is proper for me to go there." He then put on his double-robe, took his bowl, and showed himself standing at the door of the Brahmin's house. Upon seeing the Elder, the Brahmin Mahāsena’s heart was filled with faith. He approached the Elder, paid respect, and after exchanging pleasantries, invited him to sit inside the house. Taking the bowl of milk-rice, he began to pour it into the Elder's bowl. The Elder accepted only half and covered the bowl with his hand. 

Then the Brahmin said to the Elder, "Venerable Sir, this milk-rice is only enough for one person. Please show me favor for the sake of the next world, and not for this world. I wish to give it all without remainder." He then poured it all in. The Elder partook of the meal right there. After finishing the meal, the Brahmin also offered the piece of cloth he had received, paid homage, and said, "Venerable Sir, may I also realize the same Dhamma that you have seen." The Elder replied, "Brahmin, may it be as you wish," and after giving a talk of appreciation (anumodanā), he rose from his seat and departed. In due course, while wandering on a journey, he arrived at the Jetavana Monastery.
334:
The great brahmin, having given that gift, was filled with a clear and joyful mind, and being delighted, he developed a profound love and affection for the Venerable Sāriputta Thera.

## The Gratitude of the Brahmin Mahāsena in a New Life

That great brahmin, having passed away with a heart full of love and devotion for the Elder, took rebirth in a family in Sāvatthī that served the Venerable Sāriputta Thera. At that very moment, the mother of the conceived child, realizing that "a child has been conceived in my womb," informed her husband, and the husband provided her with the necessary care for the pregnancy.

While the pregnant woman was being cared for in comfort, avoiding foods that were too hot, too cold, or too sour, a pregnancy craving of this nature arose in her: "How wonderful it would be if I could invite five hundred monks, headed by the Venerable Sāriputta Thera, seat them in my house, and offer them pure milk-rice. Then, wearing saffron-dyed robes myself, holding a golden bowl, and sitting at the end of the seating row, I might consume the leftover milk-rice that remains after so many monks have eaten."

Then, her relatives, thinking, "Our daughter's craving is indeed in accordance with the Dhamma," invited the Venerable Sāriputta Thera as the presiding Elder and offered pure milk-rice to the five hundred monks. The woman, wearing one saffron-dyed cloth and wrapping another around her, holding a golden bowl, sat at the end of the seating row and consumed the leftover milk-rice from the Saṅgha. At that moment, her craving was appeased. Until she gave birth, during the various ceremonies performed at intervals, and also during the ceremony performed when she gave birth to her son after ten months, they offered only pure, sweet milk-rice to the five hundred monks headed by the Venerable Sāriputta Thera.

On the day of the birth ceremony, they bathed the child early in the morning, adorned him, and laid him on a magnificent bed upon a woolen blanket worth a hundred thousand. The child, while lying on that woolen bed, gazed intently at the Venerable Sāriputta Thera and thought, "This Elder is my former teacher. Because of this Elder, I have attained this abundance of wealth. It is proper for me to offer a gift to this Elder." When the child was brought forward to receive the precepts, he wrapped his little finger around that hundred-thousand-worth blanket and took it with him.

Then, those carrying the child, thinking, "The blanket is caught on the child's finger," tried to remove the blanket. The child cried loudly. The parents and relatives forbade them, saying, "Step away, do not make the child cry," and they had to bring him along with the blanket. When the child paid homage to the Elder, he withdrew his finger from the blanket and let the blanket fall at the Elder's feet.

## The Naming of Tissa and Sending Him to the Monastery

The parents and relatives did not say, "The young boy did this because he is a foolish and ignorant child," but instead said, "Venerable Sir, may the gift offered by our young son be a gift that is completely and freely relinquished. Venerable Sir, please grant the precepts to your disciple, who has made an offering with a blanket worth a hundred thousand." When the Elder asked, "What is this child's name?", they replied, "Venerable Sir, this young son shall be named Tissa, the same name as yours."

The child's mother also thought, "I should not thwart my young son's inclination." After performing the naming ceremony for the child in this way, they again performed the ceremony for the child's first solid food, the ear-piercing ceremony, and the ceremony for wearing the lower garment.
335:
At the hair-cutting ceremony as well, they offered only pure honey-milk-rice to the five hundred monks headed by the Venerable Sāriputta. When the boy grew up and reached the age of seven, he said to his mother, "Mother, I wish to ordain as a novice in the presence of the Venerable Sāriputta." "Very well, dear son. Long ago, I made up my mind that I should not go against my son's wishes. Dear son, do ordain." Having thus given her consent, she invited the Elder, offered him alms-food upon his arrival, and said, "Venerable Sir, your servant wishes to ordain. I will bring this boy to the monastery in the evening." After sending the Elder away, she took her son to the monastery in the evening with great honor and respect and handed him over to the Elder. The Venerable Sāriputta, wishing to speak with the boy, said, "Tissa, what is called ordination is difficult. When one desires heat, one gets cold; when one desires cold, one gets heat. Monks live with hardship, but you have been raised in comfort." When he said this, the boy replied, "Venerable Sir, I shall be able to do everything exactly according to the way you instruct me."

## Ordination and Receiving a Special Name

The Elder said, "Very well," and taught him the meditation on the five parts of the body ending in skin (tacapañcaka kammaṭṭhāna) by way of reflecting on the repulsive nature of the body, and then ordained him.

(Indeed, it is appropriate to teach the entire meditation on the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra). However, a teacher who is unable to teach the whole should at least teach the meditation on the five parts ending in skin. This is correct. This meditation is one never abandoned by any of the Buddhas. There is no limit to the number of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who have attained Arahantship by meditating on each of the parts, such as hair and so on. But unskilled teachers, when ordaining others, destroy the supporting condition for Arahantship. Therefore, the Elder, having taught the meditation on the five parts ending in skin, ordained him and established him in the ten precepts.)

The boy's parents, performing the celebration for their son's ordination, stayed at the monastery for seven days and offered only pure honey-milk-rice to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. The monks complained, saying, "We cannot eat pure honey-milk-rice every single day." The novice's parents returned home on the evening of the seventh day. On the eighth day, the young novice Tissa entered the city for alms together with the monks.
336:
The people of Sāvatthī, thinking, "The young novice Tissa will enter for alms today; we will pay him honor," made head-rests out of five hundred cloths, prepared five hundred alms-meals, and stood waiting on the road to offer them. On the following day, they came to the vicinity of the monastery and made offerings. In this way, in just two days, the novice received a thousand robes and a thousand alms-meals, which he had distributed to the community of monks. 

At that time, because the novice had given a thousand alms-meals, the monks gave him the name "Piṇḍapātadāyaka Tissa."

## Going to Receive Blankets and the Envious Man

One day, while the novice was walking around the monastery during the cold season, he saw monks warming themselves at fire-rooms and other places. He asked, "Venerable Sirs, why are you sitting here warming yourselves?" When the monks replied, "Novice, the cold oppresses us," he said, "Venerable Sirs, is it not proper to wrap oneself in a blanket during the cold season? For a blanket is able to ward off the cold." "Friend Tissa, you may obtain a blanket because you have great merit from the past. Where would we, who have little merit, obtain blankets?" When they said this, he announced throughout the entire monastery, "Venerable Sirs, if that is the case, let those who desire blankets come with me." Then, thinking, "We shall go with the young novice Tissa and bring back blankets," about a thousand monks set out, following the seven-year-old novice. The young novice, without even a thought of "Where will I get blankets for so many monks?", led those monks and headed toward the city.

As he walked along the row of houses outside the city, he received five hundred blankets and then entered the city. People brought blankets from here and there. A man, coming by the gate of the market, saw a shopkeeper sitting with five hundred blankets spread out for sale and said, "Hey friend, a young novice is coming with about a thousand monks to collect blankets. Hide your blankets!" When the shopkeeper asked, "Does he take what is given, or what is not given?", the man replied, "He takes only what is given." The shopkeeper then said, "If that is the case, if I wish to give, I will give; if I do not wish to give, I will not. You go on your way," and sent him away.
337:
## Obtaining a Thousand Blankets at the Age of Seven

The shopkeeper thought: "This man came of his own accord and told me to cover and keep your blankets. If the novice (Sāmaṇera) only takes the blankets that are offered, and if I wish to give my own property, I shall give it; if I do not wish to give, I shall remain without giving. However, for one who does not give to a recipient who is clearly visible, it is a cause for shame. Therefore, there is no fault in one who covers and keeps his own property. Among these five hundred blankets, two are worth a hundred thousand each. It is proper to cover only these two blankets." Having thought thus, he joined the fringes of the two blankets together, placed them inside the others, and kept them covered. The novice, along with a thousand monks, arrived at that place. As soon as the shopkeeper saw the novice, fatherly affection (puttasineha) arose in him. His entire body was filled with fatherly love. The shopkeeper thought: "Let the blankets be; seeing this novice, it is fitting even to give my own heart's flesh." Out of great affection, he took out those two blankets worth a hundred thousand each, placed them at the novice's feet, and after paying homage, made a wish: "Venerable sir, may I be a partaker of the Dhamma that you have realized."

The novice also gave a blessing (anumodanā) saying, "May it be so."

The novice also received five hundred blankets within the city. Thus, in a single day, he received a thousand blankets and gave them to the thousand monks. At that time, because he gave a thousand blankets, they named him "Elder Tissa, the Giver of Blankets" (Kambaladāyaka Tissa Thera). Thus, a single blanket given on the day of his naming in this life resulted in his obtaining a thousand blankets by the time he was seven years old. In this way, as a result of a single blanket, the novice received a thousand blankets while still only seven years old.

## Receiving Four Names While Living in the Forest at Age Seven

While the novice Tissa was residing at the Jetavana monastery, his relatives and supporters came to him constantly and engaged in conversation. Therefore, the novice reflected: "While I am staying here at Jetavana, if my relatives and supporters come and speak, I cannot remain without speaking. To engage in long conversations with them makes it impossible to establish my own refuge (attainment). It would be well if I were to learn a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) from the Teacher and enter the forest."

That novice, Tissa, approached the Buddha and, having requested a meditation subject leading up to Arahatship, paid homage to his preceptor (upajjhāya). Taking his bowl and robes, he departed from the monastery, thinking: "If I stay in a nearby place, my relatives will call for me." With this in mind, he traveled a distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas.
338:
Then, passing through a certain village gate, he saw an old man and asked: "Lay devotee (upāsaka), is there a forest monastery in this region for those who wish to dwell there?" When the man replied, "There is, venerable sir," the novice said, "If so, please show me the way." As soon as the old lay devotee saw the novice, fatherly affection arose in him. Then, instead of just pointing the way while standing there, he said, "Come, venerable sir, I will show you," and led him there. As the novice went with the old lay devotee, he saw forest and mountain regions adorned with various flowers and fruits along the way and asked, "Lay devotee, what is the name of this place?" The lay devotee told him the names of those places, and upon reaching the forest monastery, he said, "Venerable sir, this is a pleasant place; please stay right here." He then asked the novice's name and said, "It is proper to come to our village for alms tomorrow." After saying this, he returned to the village and informed the people: "A venerable one named Vanavāsī Tissa has arrived at the monastery. Prepare gruel, food, and other offerings for him."

The novice, who was originally named Tissa, subsequently received three more names: "Piṇḍapātadāyaka Tissa" (Tissa the Alms-giver), "Kambaladāyaka Tissa" (Tissa the Blanket-giver), and "Vanavāsī Tissa" (Tissa the Forest-dweller). Thus, within seven years, he received four names.

## The Forest-Dwelling Novice Tissa Attaining Arahatship

Early the next morning, the novice entered that village for alms. The people offered alms and paid homage with great respect. The novice said: "Sukhitā hotha, dukkhā muccatha—May you be happy, may you be released from suffering." Not even one person was able to return home after offering alms to the novice; they all stood there gazing at him. The novice Tissa took only enough alms for his sustenance. All the villagers prostrated themselves at the novice's feet and requested: "Venerable sir, if you stay here during these three months of the rains retreat (vassa), we will take the three refuges, established in the five precepts, and observe the eight Uposatha precepts eight times a month. Therefore, please give us your word to stay here."

The novice, recognizing their helpfulness, gave them his word and went for alms only in that village regularly. Every time they paid homage, he would only say the two phrases: "Sukhitā hotha, dukkhā muccatha," and then depart. The novice spent the first month and the second month there, and as the third month arrived, he attained Arahatship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā).

## The Arrival of Ven. Sāriputta and Four Thousand Monks

Thereafter, when the novice Tissa, the forest-dweller, had performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony at the end of the rains retreat, his preceptor, the Venerable Sāriputta Thera, approached the Buddha and said: "Exalted Buddha, I wish to go to the novice Tissa." The Buddha granted permission, saying: "Go, Sāriputta."
339:
Ven. Sāriputta, taking his retinue of five hundred monks, said while departing, "Friend Moggallāna, I am going to the presence of Tissa Sāmaṇera." Ven. Mahāmoggallāna replied, "Friend Sāriputta, I shall go as well," and set out together with five hundred monks. In this same manner, all the Great Disciples, including Ven. Mahākassapa, Ven. Anuruddha, Ven. Upāli, and Ven. Puṇṇa, set out together with five hundred monks each. The total retinue of the Great Disciples numbered four thousand monks. Having traveled a distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas, they arrived at the alms-village. The lay supporter who regularly attended to the novice saw all four thousand monks at the village gate, went out to meet them, and paid respectful homage.

Then Ven. Sāriputta asked the layman, "Layman, is there a forest monastery in this area?" "Yes, Bhante, there is," he replied. "Is there a monk residing there, or is it vacant?" he asked again. "There is a monk residing there, Bhante," he replied. "What is the name of the monk residing there?" he asked.

"Bhante, Ven. Vanavāsī Tissa resides there," he replied. "If that is so, please show us the way," the Elder said. When asked, "Bhante, who are you all?" the Elder replied, "Layman, we have come to see the novice." Upon looking and recognizing all the Great Disciples, starting with the General of the Dhamma, Ven. Sāriputta, the layman's body was suffused with continuous joy. He said, "Bhante, please wait for a moment," and quickly entered the village, shouting, "O men and women! Starting with Ven. Sāriputta, the eighty Great Disciples have arrived with their retinues to see the novice. Take couches, stools, bedding, oil lamps, and so on, and come out quickly!" At that very moment, the people took the couches and other items, followed in the footsteps of the Elders, and entered the monastery together with them. The novice, recognizing the community of monks, received the bowls and robes of the senior Elders in order and performed the minor and major duties. While the novice was arranging the places for the Elders to stay and putting away the bowls and robes, it became dark and night fell.

## Requesting a New Dhamma Preacher

Ven. Sāriputta said to the lay supporters, "Lay supporters, you should return; it has become dark for you." They replied, "Bhante, today is the day for hearing the Dhamma. We do not wish to go yet; we will listen to the Dhamma. Before today, we have not had even the chance to hear the Dhamma." The Elder then said, "Friend novice, if that is so, light the lamp and announce the time for hearing the Dhamma." The novice did as the Elder instructed. Then the Elder said to the novice, "Tissa, your lay supporters say they wish to hear the Dhamma. Preach the Dhamma to them." At that, the lay supporters rose up all at once and said, "Bhante, our Lord knows nothing of the Dhamma other than these two phrases: 'May you be happy, may you be free from suffering.' Please grant us a Dhamma preacher who can preach other Dhamma talks to us."
340:
## Detailed Explanation of the Regularly Taught Dhamma

Then, the Elder Sāriputta, who was the novice's preceptor, said, "Friend novice, in what way are they happy? In what way are they freed from suffering? Explain the meaning of these two phrases to us."

The novice replied, "Very well, venerable sir," and accepting the ornate fan, he ascended the Dhamma-seat. Drawing out the meanings and reasons from the five Nikāyas, like a great cloud raining heavily over all four continents, he analyzed the aggregates (khandha), the sense bases (āyatana), the elements (dhātu), and the requisites of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma). Having delivered the Dhamma discourse culminating in the Fruit of Arahantship, he said, "Venerable sir, thus happiness comes to one who has reached the Fruit of Arahantship; only one who has reached the Fruit of Arahantship is freed from suffering. Other beings are not freed from the sufferings such as rebirth and the sufferings of falling into hell."

"Excellent, novice! The Dhamma has been well-spoken. You possess a sharp and ready wit (paṭibhāṇa). Now, recite the intoned recitation (sarabhañña)," the Elder said. Thus, the novice also recited the sarabhañña.

## The Audience Splits into Two Groups

When dawn broke, the novice’s lay supporters split into two groups. Some became angry, saying, "We have never seen such a harsh person before. Indeed, while knowing such a Dhamma discourse, why did he remain for so long without reciting even a single verse of Dhamma to those of us who served him in the place of his mother and father?"

Others were delighted and rejoiced, saying, "How fortunate we are! We served this venerable one even though we did not know whether he possessed special virtues or not. Now, we have been granted the opportunity to hear the Dhamma in his presence."

When the Blessed One surveyed the world in the early morning of that day, He saw the lay supporters of the Elder Vanavāsī Tissa entering the net of His knowledge. Upon seeing them, He reflected, "What will happen?" and considered the matter.

## The Buddha Himself Arrives

"Some of the lay supporters of the novice Vanavāsī Tissa are pleased, while others are angry. Those who are angry with my son, the novice Tissa, will be destined for hell. Therefore, if I go there, all those lay supporters will develop a mind of loving-kindness (mettā) toward the novice and be freed from suffering."

Meanwhile, the villagers invited the community of monks, went to the village, had a pavilion constructed, prepared gruel and food, and sat waiting for the arrival of the Saṅgha after arranging the seats. The monks, having attended to their bodily needs, were about to enter the village for alms at the proper time and asked the novice, "Friend Tissa, will you come with us, or will you follow later?"

"I will come only at my time of departure. You go ahead, venerable sirs," he replied. The monks took their bowls and robes and entered the village. The Blessed One, while still at Jetavana Monastery, donned His robes, took His bowl, and traveling in a single thought-moment (cittakkhaṇa), manifested Himself standing at the head of the monks. A great roar of excitement arose throughout the entire village simultaneously: "The Blessed One has arrived!"
341:
## Requesting the Buddha for the Anumodanā

The people, with joyful and uplifted minds, invited the Saṅgha of monks led by the Buddha to be seated, and offered them rice gruel and hard food. Even before the meal was finished, the novice entered the village. The villagers brought out and respectfully offered alms-food to the novice. Having accepted only enough food for his sustenance, the novice approached the Buddha and offered his bowl. The Teacher, stretching out his hand, took the bowl and said, "Come, Tissa," and then showing it to the Elder Sāriputta, he said, "Look, Sāriputta, at the bowl of your own novice."

The Elder took the bowl from the Teacher's hand, gave it to the novice, and said, "Go, sit in your assigned place and finish your meal." After serving the Saṅgha of monks led by the Buddha, the villagers paid homage to the Teacher and requested him to deliver a discourse of appreciation (Anumodanā).

## Increased Devotion to the Novice through the Buddha's Words

Wishing to perform the Anumodanā, the Teacher spoke these words: "Lay followers, it is indeed a gain for you! Because of your resident novice, you have gained the opportunity to see the eighty great disciples, such as Sāriputta, Moggallāna, Kassapa, and Anuruddha. Even I, the Buddha, have come here solely because of your resident novice. Your opportunity to see the Buddha was also gained only because of this novice. It is a gain for you; it is a great gain for you!"

The people thought, "Oh, how wonderful it is for us! We have gained the opportunity to see our lord, who is capable of pleasing the Buddhas and the entire Saṅgha of monks. We have also gained the opportunity to offer gifts to him." Thus, the people who had previously been angry with the novice became joyful and delighted. Those who were already pleased became even more devoted. At the conclusion of the Anumodanā, many attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth. The Teacher rose from his seat and departed. The people followed the Teacher, paid their respects, and then returned.

## Novice Tissa's Reflection upon Seeing the Ocean

As the Teacher walked gracefully along with the novice, he asked about the places previously pointed out to the novice by the lay supporter, saying, "Novice, what is the name of this place? What is the name of that place?" The novice followed, explaining, "Venerable Sir, this is called by such a name; that is called by such a name."

When the Teacher reached the novice's dwelling place, he climbed to the top of the mountain. From that mountain peak, the great ocean was clearly visible. The Teacher asked the novice, "Tissa, standing on this mountain peak and looking here and there, what do you see?" "Venerable Sir, I see the great ocean," he replied. "When you see the great ocean, what do you think?" the Teacher asked again. "Venerable Sir, I think that the tears I have shed while weeping whenever I encountered suffering must be far more than the water in these four great oceans."
342:
"In the four oceans, the water is but a little;
Far more than that is the water of tears, not a small amount.
From the sorrow of a person touched by suffering—
For what reason, friend, are you negligent?"

"In the four oceans, the water is little. The tears shed by a being due to sorrow when touched by suffering are more than that; they are not few. Friend, for what reason are you negligent?"

"Sadhu, Sadhu, Tissa! It is so. Indeed, the tears shed by a single being when experiencing suffering are far more than the water in the four great oceans." Having said this, the Teacher spoke this verse. 

## Novice Tissa's Reflection at His Dwelling Place

Then the Teacher asked the novice Tissa again, "Tissa, where do you live?" "Venerable Sir, I live in this mountain cleft," he replied. "What do you think while living in that mountain cleft?" the Teacher asked. "Venerable Sir, I think that there is no limit to the number of times my body has been discarded in this very place after I have died," he replied. "Sadhu, Sadhu, Tissa! It is so. Tissa, it is just as you say. There is no place on this great earth where these beings, while lying down, have not died before," the Teacher said, and then he related these verses from the Upasāḷaka Jātaka of the Duka Nipāta:

"Fourteen thousand bodies named Upasāḷaka
Have been burned in this very spot;
There is no place in the world that is not a cemetery.

Where truth, Dhamma, non-violence,
Restraint, and self-control exist—
The Noble Ones frequent this;
This is the deathless in the world."

"In this very spot, fourteen thousand bodies, all bearing the name Upasāḷaka, have been cremated. In this world, there is no place that has not been a cemetery. In whom there is truth (the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths), Dhamma (wholesome states), non-violence (compassion), restraint (virtue), and self-control (mastery over the senses)—the Noble Ones (Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Disciples) frequent such a person. In this world, this collection of four qualities is called 'Deathless' because it leads to the end of death."

## The Parinibbāna of Venerable Ānanda

Those like the Venerable Ānanda, however, attain Parinibbāna in a place where they have not died before. It is said that when Venerable Ānanda was one hundred and twenty years old, while reflecting on his life-force, he realized it was exhausted and announced, "On the seventh day from now, I shall attain Parinibbāna." Hearing this news, among the people living on both banks of the Rohiṇī River, those on the near bank said, "We have been of great service to the Elder; he will attain Parinibbāna in our presence." Those on the far bank also said, "We have been of great service to the Elder; he will attain Parinibbāna in our presence." When Venerable Ānanda heard their words, he thought, "The people living on both banks have been very helpful to me. It cannot be said that these people are not helpful. If I were to attain Parinibbāna on this bank..."
343:
“Those living on the other bank will quarrel with those on this bank in order to take my relics. If I attain Parinibbāna on the other bank, those on this bank will likewise quarrel. Even if a quarrel arises, it will arise only because of me; and even if it is settled, it will be settled only because of me.” Thinking thus, he said, “Those living on this bank have been very helpful to me, and those living on the other bank have also been very helpful to me. There is no one who has not been helpful. Let those who usually live on this bank assemble only on this bank, and let those who usually live on the other bank assemble only on the other bank.”

Then, on the seventh day, sitting cross-legged in the air at a height of seven palm trees in the middle of the river, he preached the Dhamma to the great multitude and made a resolution: “Let my body split in the middle, and let one part fall on this bank and the other part fall on the other bank.” While remaining in that same sitting posture, he entered the fire-element meditation (tejokasina-jhāna), and flames arose. His body split in the middle; one part fell on this bank, and one part fell on the other bank. After they had fallen, the many people assembled on both banks wept and lamented. The sound of their weeping was like the sound of the earth trembling. It was even more heart-rending than the weeping at the time of the Buddha's Parinibbāna. For four months, people went about weeping and lamenting, crying out, “When the Elder Ānanda, who used to carry the Buddha's bowl and robes, was present, it was as if the Buddha himself were still with us. Now our Buddha has attained Parinibbāna.” This is a brief account of the Elder Ānanda's attainment of Parinibbāna.

## The Buddha's Return to Jetavana

Then the Buddha asked the novice again, “Dear Tissa, are you afraid or trembling at the sounds of leopards and other forest animals in this grove?” “Venerable Sir, I am not afraid or trembling. On the contrary, when I hear the sounds of those forest animals, what is called delight in the forest arises in me,” he replied, and then recited sixty verses known as the ‘Description of the Forest’ (Vanavaṇṇanā). Then the Buddha addressed the novice, “Dear Tissa.” “Yes, Venerable Sir?” he replied. “We are going back. Will you come along, or will you turn back and stay?” the Buddha asked. “Venerable Sir, if my preceptor, the Elder, wishes to take me along, I will go; if he has me turn back, I will stay,” he replied. The Buddha departed with the community of monks. The novice, however, had the intention to turn back and stay. The Elder Sāriputta, knowing this intention, said, “Friend Tissa, if you wish to turn back, then do so.” The novice paid homage to the Buddha and the community of monks and remained behind. The Buddha then proceeded to the Jetavana monastery.

## The Words Spoken by the Monks in the Assembly

In the Dhamma Hall, a conversation arose among the community of monks: “Friends, oh, how wonderful! The novice Vanavāsī Tissa has done something truly difficult. From the time of his conception, his relatives offered only pure, sweet milk-rice to five hundred monks during the seven auspicious ceremonies. When he became a novice, they offered only pure, sweet milk-rice to the community of monks headed by the Buddha for seven days within the monastery. On the eighth day after becoming a novice, when he entered the village, in just two days...”
344:
## The Teaching

(75) Aññā hi lābhūpanisā, aññā nibbānagāminī.
Evaṃ etaṃ abhiññāya, bhikkhu buddhassa sāvako.
Sakkāraṃ nābhinandeyya, vivekamanubrūhaye.

Lābhūpanisā: the practice depending on gain is one thing; it is indeed different from the practice leading to Nibbāna. Nibbānagāminī: the practice that leads to Nibbāna is another; it is indeed different from the practice leading to gain. Evaṃ: in this way. Etaṃ: these two practices. Abhiññāya: having understood. Bhikkhu: the monk who is. Sāvako: a disciple. Buddhassa: of the Buddha. Sakkāraṃ: should not delight in or long for special offerings and honors. Vivekamanubrūhaye: should repeatedly cultivate the three types of seclusion (viveka).

He received a thousand alms-meals along with a thousand robes. Again, one day, he received a thousand blankets. Thus, while this novice resided in this place, great gain and honor arose for him. [People said,] "Now, having abandoned such gain and honor, he enters the forest and subsists on mixed food; indeed, the novice Tissa performs a difficult task." This praise became well-known.

Then the Teacher came and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit here now?" When they replied, "With such a subject, Venerable Sir," He said, "Monks, indeed it is so. That which is the practice depending on gain is one thing. When one practices in this way, thinking 'I shall obtain gain,' and undertakes the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) such as forest-dwelling for the sake of gain, the doors to the four woeful states (apāya) stand wide open for that monk. However, the monk who, through the practice leading to Nibbāna, rejects and abandons the gain and honor that have arisen, enters the forest, and strives with diligent effort, attains the fruit of Arahantship." Connecting the sequence of the discourse, He spoke this verse:

## Meaning to be Noted in the Teaching

(The practice for obtaining gain is one thing, and the practice for reaching Nibbāna is quite another. A monk who desires gain might perform a small amount of unwholesome action; he must engage in bodily crookedness and so on. Whenever he performs some form of crookedness, gain arises. For example, if one puts a straight hand into a bowl of milk-rice and lifts it, the hand is merely smeared. But if one curves the hand, puts it in, and lifts it, it comes out holding a lump of milk-rice. In the same way, gain arises only when one performs bodily crookedness and such. This is called the unrighteous means to gain. However, gain that arises due to reasons such as physical perfection (upadhi-sampadā), wearing robes properly, great learning, having a retinue, or living in a forest monastery is called righteous gain. A monk who wishes to fulfill the good practice leading to Nibbāna straightforwardly must abandon bodily crookedness and the like. He should be as if blind though not blind, as if mute though not mute, and as if deaf though not deaf. He should be free from crookedness and free from deceit.

Having thus clearly understood the combination of these two principles—the way to gain and the way to Nibbāna—the good monk who is a disciple of the Buddha should not delight in or crave the four requisites and offerings that are unrighteous.)
345:
(One should not obstruct or destroy the four requisites and offerings that are righteous. One should fulfill the three types of seclusion to increase them: Kāya-viveka, which is the state of being alone; Citta-viveka, which is the eight attainments; and Upadhi-viveka, which is Nibbāna. Among these three, Kāya-viveka dispels the entanglement of living in a crowd. Citta-viveka dispels the entanglement of defilements. Upadhi-viveka dispels the entanglement of formations (saṅkhāra). Kāya-viveka is a supporting condition for Citta-viveka. Citta-viveka is a supporting condition for Upadhi-viveka. This means one must practice to increase these three seclusions.)

## Benefits of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The story of Vanavāsī Tissa Sāmaṇera ends.

The Bāla Vagga (Chapter of the Fool) ends.
346:
## 6. Paṇḍitavagga
## 1. Story of Elder Rādha
(Rādhattheravatthu)
The Teacher told this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Nidhīnaṃva pavattāraṃ," while staying at Jetavana Monastery, concerning Elder Rādha.
## How Venerable Sāriputta Remembered the Old Brahmin's Kindness
When this Elder Rādha was a layman, he was a poor Brahmin in Sāvatthī. Thinking, "I will live in the presence of the monks," he went to the monastery and stayed within the monastery grounds, clearing away green grass and weeds, sweeping the precincts, and providing water for washing the face and so on. The monks supported and looked after the poor old Brahmin Rādha, but they did not wish to ordain him. Because he did not receive ordination, the Brahmin became thin and emaciated. Then one day, when the Teacher surveyed the world at dawn, he saw the old Brahmin. Considering "What will happen?" he knew that "He will quickly attain Arahatship." In the evening, as if wandering through the monastery, he went near the Brahmin and asked, "Brahmin, what are you doing as you wander about?" "Venerable Sir, I am performing major and minor duties for the monks," he replied. "Do you receive support from these monks?" the Buddha asked. "Yes, Venerable Sir, I receive only enough food, but they do not wish to ordain me," he replied. On that account, the Teacher assembled the Sangha of monks, inquired about the matter, and asked, "Bhikkhus, is there any monk who remembers a special favor performed by this old Brahmin?"
Venerable Sāriputta replied, "Venerable Sir, I remember. While I was wandering for alms in the city of Rājagaha, this Brahmin had a single ladle of alms-food, which was intended for himself, offered to me. I remember this special favor performed by this Brahmin, Venerable Sir." Then the Teacher said, "Sāriputta, is it not proper for you to release such a person who has done you a favor from the mass of suffering?" Sāriputta replied, "Very well, Venerable Sir, I will ordain him," and he ordained the old Brahmin. That old Brahmin monk received a seat only at the very end of the dining hall. He also suffered hardship regarding gruel and alms-food. Venerable Sāriputta took him and went on a tour. He constantly instructed and admonished the old Brahmin monk, saying, "This you should do; this you should not do." The old monk was easy to speak to (suvaco) and respectfully followed the instructions. Therefore, practicing according to the instructions, he attained Arahatship in just two or three days. Venerable Sāriputta took the old monk, went to the Teacher, paid homage respectfully, and sat down.
Then the Teacher, greeting Venerable Sāriputta, asked, "Sāriputta, is your resident pupil easy to instruct?"
347:
Depending on Alīnacitta, the prince, the large army, joyful and uplifted, captured the King of Kosala alive—who was dissatisfied with his own country—by means of the state elephant.
In the same way, a monk who is endowed with a good friend (kalyāṇamitta) and possessed of stirred-up energy, developing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) for the sake of attaining Nibbāna, the supreme security from bondage, reaches Arahatship, the end of all fetters, in due course.
## The Teaching
(76) One should follow a wise person who points out faults, who gives reproof and is intelligent, as if he were one who points out hidden treasures. It is better, not worse, for one who follows such a wise person.
"Vajjadassinaṃ" means one who points out faults. "Niggyahawādiṃ" means one who is in the habit of admonishing by way of reproof. "Medhāviṃ" means one who is sharp-witted and intelligent. If one should see such a wise person ("Yaṃ paṇḍitaṃ"), one should associate with such a wise person ("Tādisaṃ taṃ paṇḍitaṃ bhaje") as if he were one who points out jars of treasure buried here and there ("Nidhīnaṃva pavattāraṃ"). For one who associates with such a person ("Tādisaṃ bhajamānassa"), it is especially noble ("Seyyo hoti"). It is not base ("Pāpiyo na hoti").
"Venerable Sir, he is exceedingly easy to instruct. When he is told of any fault, he has never once shown anger or resentment," Sāriputta replied. "Sāriputta, if you could get co-residents of such a nature, how many would you take?" the Buddha asked. "Venerable Sir, I would take many such disciples," he replied. Then one day, a discussion arose in the Dhamma Hall: "Venerable Sāriputta is indeed grateful and thankful. Remembering a favor as small as a ladle of alms-food, he ordained the poor Brahmin. Because the Elder is capable of giving admonition, he has obtained a disciple who is capable of receiving it."
## A Brief Account of the Alīnacitta Jātaka Regarding Gratitude
The Teacher, hearing the monks' conversation, said, "Bhikkhus, not only now, but in the past also, Sāriputta was grateful and thankful." To clarify this matter, he related the Alīnacitta Jātaka of the Dukanipāta in detail. At that time, a great lone elephant, knowing the favor done to him by carpenters who had healed his foot, gave them a young elephant that was completely white. That elephant was Sāriputta in a past life. Having told the Jātaka concerning the Elder, he preached the Alīnacitta Jātaka concerning Elder Rādha—
348:
Concerning Elder Rādha, the Buddha said: "Monks, a monk should be one who is easy to speak to and admonish, like Elder Rādha. One should not get angry when one's faults are pointed out and one is admonished. One who gives such admonition should be regarded as one who points out a hidden treasure of gold." Desiring to preach the Dhamma by connecting the sequence, he spoke this verse:

## Meaning to be Noted in the Teaching

(Just as a poor man, out of compassion, is led to a place of treasure pots filled with gold, silver, and so on, buried here and there, with the words 'Come, I will show you the means to live happily,' and is shown the treasure with an outstretched hand saying 'Take this wealth and live happily,' and thus follows that person with joy; so too, one should joyfully associate with a wise person who points out faults, who reproves, and who is possessed of sharp wisdom. Here, there are two types of people who point out faults. One is a person who seeks faults, thinking, 'I will humiliate and shame this person in the midst of the assembly with this improper fault.' The other is a wise person who, seeing various faults, desires to help the person grow in virtue (sīla) and so on, so that they may become skilled if they are not yet, or to support them if they are, with the nature of lifting them up and rescuing them. Of these two, only the latter is intended here.)

## Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so on. The story of Elder Rādha ends.

## 2. The Story of the Monks Assaji and Punabbasu

(Assaji-Punabbasu-vatthu)

While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with 'Ovadeyya,' concerning the monks named Assaji and Punabbasu. However, the teaching originated in Kīṭāgiri.

## Fools Hate Those Who Admonish

Those monks, Assaji and Punabbasu, were the resident pupils (saddhivihārika) of the Chief Disciples. However, they were shameless (alajjī) and wicked monks. They, along with their followers...
349:
...along with five hundred monks, while living in the Kīṭāgiri region, they themselves planted flower bushes and had others plant them. Engaging in various kinds of improper conduct such as this, they committed the act of corrupting families (kuladūsana). Living their lives on the requisites obtained through such corruption, they made that monastery an unsuitable place for virtuous monks to reside. The Teacher, hearing of this matter, summoned the two Chief Disciples along with their followers to perform the act of banishment (pabbājanīyakamma) upon them, saying: "Go, Sāriputta and Moggallāna. Perform the act of banishment on those who do not follow your words. As for those who do follow, advise and instruct them. Indeed, one who advises and instructs is disliked and disagreeable only to the unwise, but is liked and agreeable to the wise." Connecting the sequence, he spoke this verse while preaching the Dhamma:

## The Teaching

(77) One should advise, one should instruct, and one should restrain from what is unseemly. For such a person is dear to the good, but is disliked by the bad.

*Ovadeyya*: should advise. *Anusāseyya*: should instruct. *Asabbhā ca*: from unwholesome states. *Nivāraye*: should prevent (meaning, should establish in wholesome states). *Hi*: indeed. *So*: that person who advises and instructs. *Satam*: to the virtuous (or, of the virtuous). *Piyo*: is dear, liked, and cherished. *Hoti*: is. *Asatam*: to the wicked who seek only gain and livelihood (or, of the wicked; or, of those who strike with verbal arrows). *Appiyo*: is not dear or cherished. *Hoti*: is.

(If one advises when an occasion arises, it is called *ovāda*; if one advises beforehand to prevent a future occurrence, it is called *anusāsanī*. Alternatively, advising in person is *ovāda*; sending a message or letter to advise is *anusāsanī*. Alternatively, advising once is *ovāda*; advising repeatedly is *anusāsanī*. Alternatively, *ovāda* and *anusāsanī* are the same.)

## Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so on. Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Moggallāna also went to the Kīṭāgiri region and advised and instructed those monks. Among those monks, some accepted the advice and practiced rightly. Some disrobed. Some underwent the act of banishment. The story of the monks Assaji and Punabbasu ends.
350:
## The Teaching

(78) Na bhaje pāpake mitte, na bhaje purisādhame.
Bhajetha mitte kalyāṇe, bhajetha purisuttame.

Pāpake: those who are evil. Mitte: friends. Na bhaje: one should not associate with. Purisādhame: those who are base or coarse. Na bhaje: one should not associate with. Kalyāṇe: those who are good. Mitte: friends. Bhajetha: one should associate with. Purisuttame: those who are noble persons, the best of men. Bhajetha: one should associate with.

## 3. The Story of Elder Channa (Channattheravatthu)

The Buddha spoke this legal teaching starting with "Na bhaje pāpake mitte" while residing at the Jetavana monastery, concerning Elder Channa.

## Associate with Good Friends

That Elder Channa thought, "I went out together with our noble son (the Prince) in the Great Renunciation. At that time, I did not see even one other person. But now, these people wander around saying, 'I am named Sāriputta, I am named Moggallāna, we are the Chief Disciples'." Thus, he insulted the two Chief Disciples. When the Buddha heard about this from the monks, he had Elder Channa summoned and admonished him. Elder Channa remained silent only at the moment the Buddha was admonishing him, but after leaving, he continued to insult the Elders as before. When he had insulted them in this way up to three times, the Buddha summoned and admonished him again, saying, "Dear Channa, the two Chief Disciples are your good friends (kalyāṇamitta); they are noble men. You should associate with and serve such good friends." Desiring to teach the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala) and other stages.

## Elder Channa Becomes an Arahant

Even after hearing that advice, Elder Channa continued to insult and revile the monks as before. The monks reported this to the Buddha again. The Buddha said, "Monks, while I am still alive, you will not be able to discipline Channa. But when I have attained Parinibbāna, you will be able to." Therefore, while reclining on the couch at the time of his Parinibbāna, when Elder Ānanda asked, "Venerable Sir, how should we treat Elder Channa?", the Buddha commanded, "Ānanda, the Brahma-penalty (Brahmadanda) should be imposed on the monk Channa." (The Brahma-penalty means: whether he does good or bad, let him do as he wishes; he is not to be praised, not to be blamed, and nothing is to be said to him. It is the act of the entire Saṅgha ignoring and ostracizing him.) After the Buddha had attained Parinibbāna, when Elder Channa heard about the Brahma-penalty announced by Elder Ānanda, he became deeply distressed and sorrowful, fainting and falling down three times. He repeatedly pleaded, "Venerable sirs, please do not destroy me." He then fulfilled the monastic duties correctly without deviation. Before long, he attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā).
351:
The Story of Elder Channa ends.

## 4. The Story of Elder Mahākappina (Mahākappinattheravatthu)

The Buddha spoke this teaching starting with "Dhammapīti sukhaṃ seti" while residing at the Jetavana monastery, concerning Elder Mahākappina.

## Mahākappina's Past Meritorious Deeds

In the past, the future Elder Mahākappina had made a resolution at the feet of Padumuttara Buddha. While wandering through Saṃsāra, he was reborn as the head weaver in a weaver village not far from the city of Bārāṇasī. At that time, about one thousand Paccekabuddhas lived in the Himalayas for eight months and stayed in the inhabited regions during the four months of the rainy season. On one occasion, those Paccekabuddhas arrived near Bārāṇasī and sent eight Paccekabuddhas to the King to say, "Please request manual labor for the purpose of building a monastery."

At that time, the King was engaged in the plowing festival (vappamaṅgala). When the King heard that the Paccekabuddhas had arrived, he came out at that moment, asked the reason for their arrival, and said, "Venerable sirs, there is no opportunity today. Tomorrow is our plowing festival; I will do it on the third day." Having said this, he entered the inner palace without inviting the Paccekabuddhas for a meal. The Paccekabuddhas departed, thinking, "We shall go elsewhere."

At that moment, the wife of the head weaver was going to Bārāṇasī for some business. Seeing the Paccekabuddhas, she paid respect to them and asked, "Venerable sirs, why have you come at an unusual time?" They told her everything from the beginning. Hearing this, the woman, who was endowed with faith and wisdom, invited them, saying, "Venerable sirs, please accept my alms-food tomorrow." They said, "Sister, we are very many." She asked, "How many are there, sirs?" They replied, "About one thousand."

She then said, "Venerable sirs, one thousand weavers live in this village. Each person will offer alms-food to one monk. Please accept the alms-food. I myself will also have the dwelling places built for you to stay." The Paccekabuddhas accepted. The female lay devotee entered the village and proclaimed, "I have seen and invited about one thousand Paccekabuddhas. Prepare the sitting places for the venerable ones, and cook gruel, rice, and other foods to completion!"
352:
Then, she had a pavilion built in the center of the village and seats prepared. On the following morning, she invited the Paccekabuddhas to be seated and served them with exquisite hard and soft foods. After the meal, she gathered all the women of the village and, together with them, paid respectful homage to the venerable Paccekabuddhas. Having obtained their consent to stay for the three months of the rains retreat, she made a proclamation in the village: "O mothers and fathers, let one man from each family take axes, hatchets, and so forth, enter the forest, bring back building materials, and construct a dwelling place for the venerable ones." Upon hearing her words, each villager built a dwelling, and thus they constructed a thousand leaf-roofed huts, complete with night and day quarters. Each person served the Paccekabuddha residing in their own leaf-roofed hut with great devotion, saying, "I shall serve him respectfully; I shall serve him respectfully." When the rains retreat ended, she exhorted them, "Prepare robe-cloths for the venerable Paccekabuddhas who have completed the retreat in your respective leaf-roofed huts," and she had them donate robes worth a thousand each to every Paccekabuddha. After the retreat, the venerable Paccekabuddhas gave a blessing and departed.

## Building a Monastery during the Time of Kassapa Buddha

The villagers, having performed such meritorious deeds, passed away from this human world and were reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as a group of deities known as the Gaṇa-devaputtas. After enjoying celestial bliss there, they were reborn in the houses of wealthy householders in Bārāṇasī during the time of Kassapa Buddha. The former chief weaver became the son of the chief householder. His former wife also became the daughter of the chief householder. When all those women reached marriageable age, they went to the homes of their respective husbands. Then one day, an announcement was made for a Dhamma talk at the monastery. Hearing that "The Buddha will preach the Dhamma," all those householders went to the monastery with their wives to listen to the Dhamma. At the very moment they entered the middle of the monastery, a rain cloud arose and it began to rain. Those who had regular teachers or relatives among the monks and novices entered their private cells (pariveṇas). 

However, since those thousand householders had no such connections, they were unable to enter any cell and stood in the middle of the monastery. Then the chief householder said to them, "Look at our plight! It is shameful for noble sons to be in such a state." When asked, "Master, what then shall we do?", he replied, "We have come to this plight because we have no place of our own where we are welcome." They then said, "Let us all pool our wealth and build a monastery precinct." Agreeing with "Very well, master," the chief householder gave a thousand pieces of wealth. The others gave five hundred each, and the women gave two hundred and fifty each. 

Those thousand householders pooled their wealth and strove to build a large monastery precinct with a thousand gabled cells for the Buddha to reside in. Because the new project was so vast and extensive, when the funds were insufficient, they donated an additional half of what they had previously given. When the great monastery precinct was completed, they held a dedication ceremony and a celebration. They offered a great almsgiving for seven days to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and prepared robes for twenty thousand venerable monks.
353:
The wife of the chief householder, however, did not act like the others; relying firmly on her own wisdom, she performed an extraordinary and special deed, thinking, "I will worship the Teacher." She took a basket of Anojā flowers (yellow amaranth) along with a cloth worth a thousand [pieces of money] which had the color of the Anojā flower. At the time of the thanksgiving (anumodanā), she worshipped the Teacher with the Anojā flowers, placed the cloth at the Teacher's feet, and made an aspiration: "Venerable Sir, in every place and every existence where I am reborn, may my body have the color of the Anojā flower, and may my name be Anojā." The Teacher also gave his blessing, saying, "May it be as you have wished."

## The Rebirth of King Kappina and Others in this Buddha's Time
All those people lived out their life spans and, after passing away from that existence, were reborn in the celestial realm. In the time when our Buddha Gotama appeared, they passed away from the celestial realm. The chief householder was reborn into a royal family in the city of Kukkuṭavatī and, upon reaching maturity, became King Mahākappina. The remaining householders were reborn into the families of ministers. The wife of the chief householder was reborn into a royal family in the city of Sāgala in the kingdom of Madda. Her body had the color of the Anojā flower, and they named her Anojā. When she reached maturity, she went to the palace of King Mahākappina and became the chief queen, known as Anojā Devī. The other women were also reborn into the families of ministers and, upon reaching maturity, went to the houses of those same ministers' sons with whom they had been associated in their previous lives. All those ministers enjoyed wealth equal to that of the King. Whenever the King, adorned with all ornaments, went about riding an elephant, they did the same. When the King went about by horse or chariot, the ministers did the same. Thus, by the power of the meritorious deeds they had performed together, the King and his ministers enjoyed wealth together.

In particular, the King had five horses named Bala, Balavāhana, Puppha, Pupphavāhana, and Supatta. Among these five horses, the King himself rode the one named Supatta. He gave the other four horses to horsemen to bring news. The King fed those messengers early in the morning and sent them off, saying, "Go and search for a distance of two or three yojanas to find out if the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha has arisen, and bring me the good news that leads to happiness." The four horsemen went out through the four gates and searched for two or three yojanas, but finding no news, they returned.
354:
Then one day, the King, mounted on the horse named Supatta and surrounded by a thousand ministers, was going to the park. Seeing about five hundred merchants who appeared weary entering the city, he thought, "These people are exhausted from a long journey. Surely, I shall hear some good news from them." He had them summoned and asked, "Where have you come from?"

## Reporting the Three Jewels and Rewarding with Three Hundred Thousand

"Your Majesty, there is a great city named Sāvatthī, one hundred and twenty yojanas from this capital. We have come from that city," they replied. When he asked again, "Is there any special news that has arisen in your region?" they answered, "Your Majesty, there is no other special news, but the Fully Enlightened Buddha has appeared." At that very moment, the King’s body was suffused with fivefold joy. Unable to take note of anything else, he let a moment pass and asked again, "Friends, what did you say?" When they replied, "Your Majesty, the Buddha has appeared," the King let the time pass in the same manner a second and third time. On the fourth occasion, he asked, "Friends, what did you say?" and when they replied, "Your Majesty, the Buddha has appeared," he said, "Friends, I give you a hundred thousand [pieces of money]."

Furthermore, he asked again, "Is there any other special news?" They replied, "Your Majesty, there is; the Dhamma has also appeared." Upon hearing these words, the King, in the same manner as before, let the time pass for three times. On the fourth occasion, when they said, "The Dhamma has appeared," the King said, "In this case too, I give you a hundred thousand." He then asked again, "Friends, is there yet another piece of news?"

They replied, "Your Majesty, there is; the Saṅgha Jewel has also appeared." Hearing this, the King again let the time pass for three times. On the fourth occasion, when the word "Saṅgha" was spoken, he said, "In this case too, I give you a hundred thousand."
355: ## Renouncing the Kingdom and Going Forth Then, looking at the thousand ministers, the King asked, "Friends, what will you do?" They replied, "Great King, what will you do?" "Friends, because I have heard the words 'The Buddha has appeared, the Dhamma has appeared, the Saṅgha has appeared,' I do not wish to return or turn back. I intend to go and ordain in the presence of the Blessed One," he said. They replied, "Great King, we too will follow you and ordain." The King had a message inscribed on a golden plate and instructed the merchants: "Queen Anojā will grant you three hundred thousand coins. Also, convey this message to her: 'The King has renounced the royal splendor and sovereignty for you; enjoy the wealth as you wish.' If she asks where your King has gone, tell her, 'He has departed to ordain, dedicating himself to the Buddha.'" The ministers also sent messages to their respective wives through the same messengers. The King dismissed the merchants, mounted his horse, and departed immediately, surrounded by his thousand ministers. ## The Buddha's Journey to Welcome Him That day, at dawn, as the Blessed One surveyed the world, he saw King Mahākappina and his retinue. He reflected: "This King Mahākappina, having heard news of the Triple Gem from the merchants and having rewarded them with three hundred thousand coins, has renounced his kingdom. Surrounded by a thousand ministers, he is coming to ordain, dedicating himself to me. He and his retinue will attain Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). I shall go to meet him." Then, on the following morning, like a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) going to meet a minor village headman, the Blessed One took his bowl and robes and traveled a distance of one hundred and twenty leagues.
