He sat at the foot of a banyan tree on the bank of the Candabhāgā River, emitting the six-colored rays. ## Crossing the Three Rivers on Horseback by Contemplating the Virtues As King Mahākappina was traveling, he reached a river and asked, "What is the name of this river?" "Great King, it is called the Aparacchā," they replied. "Friends, what are its dimensions?" he asked. "Great King, it is one gāvuta deep and two gāvutas wide," they answered. He asked again, "Are there any boats or rafts here?" "There are none, Great King," they replied. Then he thought, "While we look for boats and such, birth brings us to aging, and aging brings us to death. I have set out without hesitation, dedicating myself to the Triple Gem. By the power of the Triple Gem, may this water not act as water for me." Having resolved thus and reflecting on the virtues of the Triple Gem, he meditated on the Recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānussati), reciting 'Itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho...' and so on. Together with his retinue, he galloped onto the surface of the water with a thousand horses. The horses galloped as if on a stone slab; only the tips of their hooves became wet. After crossing the Aparacchā River and proceeding forward, he saw another river and asked, "What is the name of this river?" "Great King, it is called the Nīlavāhanā," they replied. "What are its dimensions?" he asked. "Great King, it is half a league deep and half a league wide," they answered. The rest was the same as before. Upon seeing the Nīlavāhanā River, he meditated on the Recollection of the Dhamma (Dhammānussati), reciting 'Svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo...' and so on, and crossed it while galloping.
356:
Having crossed that Nīlavāhanā River, he saw another river and asked, "What is the name of this river?" "Great King, it is named Candabhāgā," they replied. When he asked, "What is the extent of this river?" they answered, "Great King, it is one yojana in depth and one yojana in width." The rest is just as before. Having seen that Candabhāgā River, he repeatedly meditated on the Recollection of the Saṅgha (Saṅghānussati), starting with "The Community of the Blessed One's disciples has practiced well" (Suppaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho), and crossed over with determination.

## Seeing the Buddha's Radiance
As he proceeded after crossing that river, he beheld the six-colored rays emanating from the Teacher’s body. The branches, forks, and leaves of the banyan tree appeared as if they were made of gold. The King thought, "This radiance is not that of the sun, nor of the moon, nor of any among the gods, Māras, Brahmās, Nāgas, or Garuḍas. Surely, the Great Gautama Buddha must have seen me coming for his sake." At that very moment, King Mahākappina dismounted from his horse and, with a bowed body, followed the direction of the rays and approached the Teacher. Entering into the Buddha’s rays as if plunging into a liquid of red arsenic, he paid homage to the Teacher and sat down to one side together with his thousand ministers.

## Becoming Ehi Bhikkhu Monks
The Teacher delivered a graduated discourse to King Mahākappina. At the conclusion of the teaching, the King, along with his retinue, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Then, they all rose from their seats and requested ordination. The Teacher, considering whether miraculously created bowls and robes would appear for these clansmen, realized: "These clansmen gave a thousand robes to a thousand Paccekabuddhas; in the time of Kassapa Buddha, they also gave twenty thousand robes to twenty thousand monks. It is no wonder that miraculously created bowls and robes should come to them." Extending his right hand, the Teacher said, "Come, monks, lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering," thus calling them with the "Ehi Bhikkhu" formula. In that very instant, they became like elders of sixty years' standing, bearing the eight requisites. They soared into the air, then descended, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down.

## Queen Anojā's Triple Reward
Those merchants went to the royal palace and reported the message sent by the King. When Queen Anojā said, "Let them come," they entered, paid homage, and stood at a respectful distance. Then the Queen asked them, "Friends, for what reason have you come?" "The King has sent us to your presence, saying that you should give us three hundred thousand [kahāpanas]," they replied. When they said this, she replied, "Friends, you ask for a very large amount."
357:
"What business did you perform for the King? For what matter was the King so pleased that he had so much wealth given to you?" she asked. "O Queen, we did not perform any other task. We only reported this news to the King," they replied. "Dear friends, would it be possible to tell that news to me as well?" she asked again. "O Queen, it is possible," they replied. "If so, dear friends, please tell me," she said. When they announced, "O Queen, the Buddha, the Supreme One of the Three Worlds, has appeared in the world," the Queen, upon hearing those words, was suffused with rapture throughout her body just as before. For three times she could not take in anything, but on the fourth time, hearing the word 'Buddha', she asked, "Dear friends, how much did the King honor and reward you for this word 'Buddha'?"

"O Queen, he gave a reward of one hundred thousand," they replied. Then she said, "Dear friends, having heard such news, the King acted unsuitably by rewarding you only one hundred thousand. I shall give you a reward of three hundred thousand as my gift." She asked again, "What other news did you report to the King?" The merchants replied, "We also reported this and that matter," and they told the remaining two pieces of news. The Queen, in the same manner as before, was suffused with rapture throughout her body and could not take in anything for three times. On the fourth time, hearing it likewise, she had three hundred thousand given for each.

In this way, the merchants received a total of one million two hundred thousand. Then the Queen asked the merchants, "Dear friends, where is the King?" "O Queen, he has gone to go forth as a monk, dedicating himself to the Teacher," they replied. "What message did the King leave for me?" she asked. When they reported, "The King left all sovereignty and wealth for you; you may enjoy the prosperity as you please," she asked again, "Dear friends, where are the ministers?" "O Queen, they too have gone, saying, 'We will go forth together with the King,'" they replied.

## The Queen Follows the King

The Queen summoned the wives of the ministers and asked, "Dear sisters, your lords and husbands have gone to go forth together with the King. What will you do?" "O Queen, what message did the ministers send to us?" they asked. She replied, "Those ministers have renounced their wealth to you; they sent word that you may enjoy that prosperity as you please." When they asked again, "O Queen, what will you do?" she said, "Dear sisters, that Great King, upon hearing the news, while standing on the road, honored the Triple Gem with three hundred thousand, and renounced the prosperity of the kingdom like a glob of spit to go forth. I, having heard the good news of the appearance of the Triple Gem, have honored the Triple Gem with nine hundred thousand. This wealth is certainly not a cause of suffering for the King alone; it is a cause of suffering for me as well. Who would kneel down on their knees and pick up with their mouth the glob of spit spat out by the King? I have no need for the enjoyment of wealth. I too will go and go forth, dedicating myself to the Teacher."
358:
"Your Majesty—we too will go forth as monastics together with you," they said. "Sisters—if you are able, it is well," she replied. When they acknowledged, "Your Majesty—we are able," she said, "Sisters—very well. If so, come along," and she called them. She had a thousand chariots harnessed, mounted one, and set out with the thousand wives of the ministers. When they encountered a river on the way, she asked the same questions as the King had, and upon learning all the facts, she said, "Look for the path the King took." When they replied, "Your Majesty—we do not see the hoofprints of the horses," she reflected, "The King must have crossed by making an act of truth, saying, 'I have set out for the sake of the Triple Gem.'" Then she thought, "I too have set out for the sake of the Triple Gem. By the power of the Triple Gem, may this water not be like water to me." Having repeatedly recollected the virtues of the Triple Gem, she drove the thousand chariots forward. The water became like the surface of a stone slab. Only the outer rims of the chariot wheels became wet. In this manner, she crossed the other two rivers as well.

## Queen Anojā and Others Becoming Stream-enterers, Mahākappina and Others Becoming Arahants

Then the Blessed One, knowing that Queen Anojā was approaching, performed a miracle such that the monks sitting in his presence would not be visible. As Queen Anojā proceeded, she saw the six-colored rays emanating from the body of the Blessed One. Reflecting in the same way as before, she approached the Teacher, paid homage respectfully, and sat down at a suitable place. She then asked, "Venerable Sir, I believe King Mahākappina has set out for your sake. Where is he? Please show him to us, Lord." The Teacher said, "Sit down for a while; you shall see the King right here." All the women, led by Queen Anojā, were delighted and sat down, thinking, "We shall see our husbands while sitting right here." The Blessed One gave them a graduated discourse. At the end of the teaching, Queen Anojā, together with her thousand attendants, attained the fruit of Stream-entry. The Elder Mahākappina, while listening to the Dhamma discourse being delivered to the women, attained the fruit of Arahantship together with the four analytical insights, along with his thousand former ministers. At that moment, the Blessed One made the monks, led by the Elder Mahākappina who had attained Arahantship, visible to the women led by Queen Anojā.

(If those thousand women, led by Queen Anojā, had seen their husbands wearing saffron robes and with shaven heads the moment they arrived, their minds might not have become concentrated. Without such concentration, they would not have been able to attain the paths and fruits. Therefore, only when they were established in unshakable faith did the Teacher reveal those monks to them, who had already attained the fruit of Arahantship.)

When the women, led by Queen Anojā, saw the monks led by the Elder Mahākappina, they paid homage with the fivefold prostration and said, "Venerable sirs, your task of the holy life has first reached its completion." Then, having paid homage to the Blessed One with clear and humble devotion, they sat in a suitable place and requested for ordination.
359:
## The Teaching
(79) One who drinks the Dhamma lives happily with a serene mind.
The wise man always rejoices in the Dhamma revealed by the Noble Ones.

'Dhammapīti' refers to one who drinks the essence of the Dhamma. 'Sukhaṃ seti' means they sleep happily, or rather, they live happily in all four postures. 'Paṇḍito' refers to the wise person. 'Ariyappavedite' means the Dhamma taught by the Noble Ones, such as the Buddha. 'Dhamme' refers to the Bodhipakkhiya-dhamma (Factors of Enlightenment). 'Vippasannena' means with a mind that is clear, pure, and free from defilements. 'Cetasa' means with the mind. 'Sadā' means at all times. 'Ramati' means they greatly rejoice.

## Anojā Devī and Others Ordaining and Becoming Arahants
The Blessed One said to those female lay devotees, "You all should go to Sāvatthī and ordain at the nunnery." Those one thousand women traveled through the countryside along the way. During their journey, they received many offerings and honors brought by the people. They traveled the distance of one hundred and twenty leagues on foot, ordained at the nunnery, and attained the fruit of Arahantship. The Blessed One, taking the one thousand monks with Him, traveled through the air to the Jetavana Monastery. At the Jetavana Monastery, the Venerable Mahākappina, while at his night quarters or day quarters, used to wander about uttering the inspired exclamation: "Aho sukhaṃ, aho sukhaṃ! Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!"

The monks reported to the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, the Venerable Mahākappina wanders about uttering the exclamation 'Aho sukhaṃ, aho sukhaṃ!' He seems to be lamenting and reminiscing about the royal bliss and the wealth of his kingdom."

The Blessed One had the Venerable Mahākappina summoned and asked, "My son Kappina, is it true that you are uttering an inspired exclamation out of longing for the pleasures of the senses?" Mahākappina replied, "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One knows whether I am uttering this exclamation out of longing for sensual pleasures or not."

The Blessed One said, "Bhikkhus, my son Kappina does not utter this inspired exclamation out of longing for sensual pleasures or for the royal bliss of a kingdom. Indeed, my son experiences the joy of the Dhamma (Dhammapīti). My son utters this inspired exclamation while reflecting on and taking the great Deathless Nibbāna as his object." Connecting the sequence of the discourse, the Buddha spoke this verse to teach the Dhamma:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti) and so forth.
The Story of the Elder Mahākappina ends.

## 5. The Story of Paṇḍita Sāmaṇera
(The Story of the Novice Paṇḍita)
The Blessed One, while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Udakaṃ hi nayanti," concerning the novice Paṇḍita.

In the past, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Kassapa went to the city of Bārāṇasī accompanied by twenty thousand Arahants. The people, assessing their own means, formed groups of eight or ten and offered alms to the visiting monks (āgantuka-dāna). Then one day, at the conclusion of the meal, the Teacher gave these words of appreciation:

## Giving that results in wealth but no retinue
1. "Lay devotees, in this world, some people think, 'It is proper to give only from one's own property; what is the use of urging others?' Thus, they give alms alone and do not urge others. Such a person, in every life they are reborn, attains the perfection of wealth but does not attain the perfection of a retinue.
360:
## Giving that results in retinue but no wealth
2. Some people urge and encourage others to give, but they themselves do not give. Such a person, in every life they are reborn, attains the perfection of a retinue but does not attain the perfection of wealth.

## Giving that results in neither wealth nor retinue
3. Some people neither give themselves nor urge others to give. Such a person, in every life they are reborn, attains neither the perfection of wealth nor the perfection of a retinue, and lives only by eating the scraps of others.

## Giving that results in both
4. Some people give themselves and also urge and encourage others to give. Such a person, in every life they are reborn, attains both the perfection of wealth and the perfection of a retinue." Thus, the Buddha preached the Dhamma with great joy.

Upon hearing this Dhamma teaching, a wise man standing nearby thought, "I will now act in such a way that I shall obtain both perfections: the perfection of wealth and the perfection of a retinue." That wise man paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Venerable Sir, please accept alms from me tomorrow." The Buddha asked, "How many monks do you require?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, how many monks are in your retinue?" The Buddha answered, "There are twenty thousand monks." He then invited them, saying, "Venerable Sir, please accept my alms tomorrow together with all those monks." The Teacher accepted the invitation.

The man entered the village and announced, "O mothers and fathers, I have invited the community of monks headed by the Buddha for tomorrow. Please give alms to as many monks as you are able to support." As he went around, the people assessed their own means and said, "We will provide for ten monks," "We will provide for twenty," "We will provide for a hundred," or "We will provide for five hundred." He recorded the pledges of all the people on a leaf, starting from the very first.

## Taking responsibility for one monk for Mahāduggata
At that time, in the city of Bārāṇasī, there was a man known as "Mahāduggata" (The Great Poor Man) because of his extreme poverty. The man who was collecting the invitations saw Mahāduggata standing before him and said, "Friend Mahāduggata, I have invited the community of monks headed by the Buddha for a meritorious deed tomorrow. Tomorrow, the citizens will be giving alms. How many monks will you feed?"

Mahāduggata replied, "Friend, what need have I for monks? Monks are for those who have wealth and property. As for me, I do not have even a measure of rice or a single betel nut for making gruel tomorrow. I live by manual labor. What need have I for monks?"
361:
Therefore, the man who was making the announcement, even though he said there was no Mahāduggata [available], did not remain silent but approached Mahāduggata and asked, "Friend Mahāduggata, in this great city of Bārāṇasī, many people enjoy pleasures, eating fine food, wearing delicate clothes, adorned with various ornaments, and sleeping on glorious beds. But you work for hire all day and do not even get enough to fill your belly. Even so, do you know, 'Alas, because I did not perform any merit in the past, I receive nothing now'?"

When he replied, "I know, sir," the man said, "Then why do you not perform merit now? You are young and full of strength. Is it not proper for you to give alms according to your ability, even by working for hire?"

While the wise man was speaking, Mahāduggata was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and said, "Please register one monk on the leaf for me as well. I will work for hire and offer alms-food to one monk." The wise man, the announcer, thought, "What is the use of registering for just one monk? It is likely of no consequence," and thus did not record it in the register.

Mahāduggata went home and told his wife, "Dear, tomorrow the city dwellers will provide a meal for the Saṅgha. The man who encourages others also urged me, saying 'Give alms to one monk.' Therefore, we too shall offer alms-food to one monk tomorrow."

Then his wife, without saying "We are very poor, why did you accept?", said, "Husband, you have done a good thing. We have become poor now because we did not give anything in the past. Both of us will work for hire and offer alms-food to one monk." Having said this, the couple left their house and went to a place where work was available.
362:
## Mahāduggata and His Wife Chopping Wood and Pounding Rice

A great merchant saw Mahāduggata and asked, "Friend Mahāduggata, will you work for hire?" "Yes, my lord merchant," he replied. "What will you do?" he asked again. "I will do whatever you require," he said. "In that case, tomorrow we will feed two or three hundred monks. Come, chop some wood." He brought out a hatchet and an axe and gave them to him. Mahāduggata girded his loins firmly and, with great effort, took up the hatchet and axe to chop the wood. The merchant asked, "Friend Mahāduggata, today you are working with extreme effort. What is the reason?" "My lord merchant, I wish to feed one monk tomorrow; that is the reason," he replied. Hearing this, the merchant, with a clear mind, thought, "Oh, how wonderful! This man is doing a difficult thing. Without remaining silent thinking 'I am a poor man,' he says he will work for hire to feed a monk."

The merchant's wife also saw Mahāduggata's wife and asked, "Mother, what work will you do?" When she replied, "Lady, I will do whatever you require," she let her into the granary and gave her a winnowing basket, a pestle, and so on. Mahāduggata's wife pounded and winnowed the grain with great joy, as if she were dancing. Then the merchant's wife asked, "Mother, you are working with such great joy. What is the reason?" "Lady, by working for hire like this, we also wish to feed one monk," she replied. Hearing this, the merchant's wife was also pleased, thinking, "Oh, how wonderful! This woman is doing a difficult thing."

When Mahāduggata finished chopping the wood, the merchant gave him four measures (nāḷi) of hill-paddy rice, saying, "This is your wage," and then gave another four measures, saying, "This is a gift given out of satisfaction." Mahāduggata went home and told his wife, "I have received hill-paddy rice by working for hire. This will be the alms-food. With the wages you received, buy curds, oil, chillies, and other items." The merchant's wife also gave Mahāduggata's wife a jar of ghee, a vessel of curds, spices, and one measure of clean hill-paddy rice. In this way, the couple received a total of nine measures of rice. They were joyful, saying, "We have obtained the offerings," and rose early.

## The Fisherman Giving Four Rohita Fish for the Alms-meal

The wife said to Mahāduggata, "Husband, go and find some vegetables and bring them back." Since Mahāduggata could not find vegetables in the market, he went to the riverbank. With a very joyful heart, thinking, "Today I shall have the opportunity to give food to the noble ones," he sang while picking vegetables. A fisherman who was standing there after casting a large net thought, "This must be the voice of Mahāduggata," and called him, asking, "You are singing with such a joyful heart."
363:
"What is the reason?" he asked. "Friend, I am picking vegetables," he replied. "What will you do with the vegetables?" he asked again. "I will offer a meal to a monk," he said. "Oh, how wonderful! Which monk will be able to eat your vegetables with ease?" he remarked. "Friend, what can I do? I will just feed him with the vegetables I have obtained," he said. "If that is so, come here," he said. "Friend, what should I do?" he asked. "Take these fish and make bundles worth a quarter, a half, and a full unit," he instructed. Mahāduggata did exactly as the fisherman said. People who had invited monks took those fish bundles for the sake of the monks. While Mahāduggata was still making the fish bundles, the time for the alms-round arrived. Noting the time, Mahāduggata said, "Friend, I must go; this is the time for the monks to arrive." When he asked, "Is there any bundle of fish left?" the other replied, "Friend, there is not even one; all the bundles of fish are gone." Then he said, "If that is the case, I have buried four red carp in the sand for myself. If you truly wish to offer a meal to the Saṅgha, take these carp and go," and he gave those fish to Mahāduggata.

## The Buddha and Sakka Surveying Mahāduggata

On that day, when the Buddha surveyed the world in the early morning, he saw Mahāduggata entering the net of his knowledge. As he reflected, "What will happen?" he considered, "Yesterday, Mahāduggata worked for hire along with his wife to offer a meal to a monk. Which monk will he receive?" He further reflected, "People will take the monks to their respective homes based on the assignments already made. Mahāduggata, apart from me, will not find any other monk." It is the nature of Buddhas to show compassion to the poor and destitute. Therefore, the Buddha, having performed his morning ablutions early, sat in the Gandhakuṭi, reflecting, "I will favor Mahāduggata."

When Mahāduggata entered his house carrying the red carp, the Paṇḍukambala stone throne of Sakka showed signs of heat. Sakka, looking for the reason, "What is the cause?" saw that, "Yesterday, Mahāduggata worked for hire with his wife to offer a meal to a monk. Which monk will he receive?" When he reflected further, he saw that there was no other monk for Mahāduggata, and the Buddha was sitting in the Gandhakuṭi to show favor to Mahāduggata.

"Mahāduggata might offer the Buddha the gruel and rice, as well as the vegetable curry, which he had prepared for his own use. It would be good if I were to go to Mahāduggata's house and perform the task of a cook." Having thought thus, Sakka went near Mahāduggata's house in disguise and asked, "Is there any work to be done for hire for anyone?" When Mahāduggata saw him, he asked, "What kind of work will you do?" "Sir, I am skilled in all crafts. There is no craft unknown to me. I also know how to perfectly prepare gruel, rice, and so on," he replied. "Friend, we are in need of your work, but we do not see any wages that can be given to you," Mahāduggata said.
364:
“However, I see no wage to give you,” he said. When asked again, “What work do you have to be done?” he replied, “I wish to offer alms-food to a monk. For that monk, I desire to prepare rice gruel and a meal.” When [Sakka] said, “If you wish to offer alms to the Saṅgha of monks, I do not want a wage. Is merit not suitable for me?” [Mahādugga] urged him, saying, “Friend, if that is so, it is very good; please cook and prepare it.”

## No Monk for Mahādugga to Feed

Sakka, King of the Devas, entered Mahādugga’s house, had oil, rice, and other supplies brought, and sent Mahādugga away, saying, “Friend Mahādugga, go and invite the monk assigned to you.” The man in charge of organizing the alms-distribution (the steward) sent monks to various houses according to the names recorded in the register. Mahādugga went to the steward and requested, “Please give me a monk.” At that moment, the steward remembered and said, “I have forgotten a monk for you.” Mahādugga, as if struck in the chest with a sharp spear, raised his hands and wept, saying, “O organizer, why do you ruin and oppress me? Because you urged me yesterday, I worked for hire all day with my wife, and early this morning I went searching for vegetables along the riverbank. Please, sir, grant me one monk.” People gathered and asked, “Mahādugga, what is the reason for this weeping?”

Mahādugga told them the reason. Those people asked the steward who organized the alms, “Friend, is it true that you urged this Mahādugga to work for hire and offer alms-food to a monk?” When he replied, “Sirs, it is true that I urged him,” they said, “While you could arrange for so many monks, you could not give even one to this Mahādugga. You have indeed committed a grave wrong.”

## Mahādugga Goes to the Blessed One

The steward, feeling dejected by their words, said to Mahādugga: “Friend Mahādugga, do not ruin me. I have come to great distress because of you alone. People have already invited monks for themselves according to the register. There is no one who would take out a monk who is already seated in their house and give him to you. However, the Blessed One has washed his face (it is said that although there is no impurity to be washed away, he washes his face to enjoy the cool vapor or to maintain the customary practice) and is staying in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) alone. The King, the Viceroy, the Commander-in-Chief, and others are waiting, watching for the Blessed One to emerge from the Fragrant Chamber, intending to take his bowl and depart. Buddhas are always compassionate toward the poor. Go to the monastery and pay homage to the Blessed One, saying, ‘Venerable Sir, I am an extremely poor man. Please show me favor.’ If you have merit, you will surely receive [his favor].” Having said this, he sent him away. Mahādugga went to the monastery.
365:
## Mahādugga Obtaining the Buddha’s Alms-bowl

At that time, because Mahādugga had been seen on another day at the monastery as one who ate leftovers, the King, the Crown Prince, and others said, "Friend Mahādugga, it is not yet time for the meal. Why have you come?" Mahādugga replied, "Masters, I know it is not yet time for the meal; however, I have come to pay homage to the Blessed One." Saying this, he went and placed his head upon the threshold of the Gandhakuṭi, paying homage with the fivefold prostration, and entreated, "Exalted and All-Knowing Buddha, in this great city of Bārāṇasī, there is no one more impoverished and weary than your servant. The Blessed Teachers are the refuge and reliance of your servant; please show favor to your servant." The Buddha Kassapa, the One to be Thought Upon, opened the door of the Gandhakuṭi, brought out his alms-bowl, and placed it in Mahādugga’s hands. Mahādugga felt as though he had attained the glory of a Universal Monarch. The King, the Crown Prince, and others looked at each other’s faces. No one was able to take by force the alms-bowl that the Blessed One himself had given. Even so, they said, "Friend Mahādugga, give the alms-bowl to us; we will give you this much money. You are very poor; just take the wealth. What use is the alms-bowl to you?"

Mahādugga replied, "I will not give it to anyone. I have no need for wealth; I will only offer food to the Blessed One." The remaining people, having asked Mahādugga and not receiving the alms-bowl, turned back. The King, however, thought, "Though Mahādugga was persuaded with wealth, he did not give up the Blessed One’s alms-bowl. Since it is the alms-bowl compassionately given by the Blessed One himself, no one is able to take it by force. How much could this Mahādugga’s offerings possibly be? After Mahādugga has made his offering, I will invite the Blessed One to the palace and offer the food I have well-prepared," and so he followed along with the Blessed One. Sakka, the King of Devas, having fully prepared the gruel, hard food, rice, leaf-curry, and so on, spread out a seat worthy of the Blessed One’s sitting and remained there.

## The King’s Address to the Buddha at Mahādugga’s House

Mahādugga invited the Blessed One, saying, "Exalted Buddha, please enter."

(Mahādugga’s house was low, and it was not possible to enter without stooping. However, Buddhas do not stoop when entering a house. When they enter a house, either the great earth sinks down or the house rises up. This is the fruit of the well-given dāna of the Buddhas. When they depart again, everything returns to its normal state.)

Therefore, the Blessed One entered Mahādugga’s house while standing upright and sat upon the seat prepared by Sakka. While the Blessed One was seated, the King of Bārāဏသီ said, "Friend Mahādugga, though we asked, you did not give us the Buddha’s alms-bowl. We wish to see first: what kind of honor and hospitality have you prepared for the Blessed One?" Then, Sakka revealed the gruel, hard food, and other offerings to the King. The fragrant aroma of the gruel and other foods pervaded and filled the entire city.
366:
Having looked at the rice gruel and other offerings, the King addressed the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, how much will the offerings of Mahādugga be? This Mahādugga, having offered his gifts, came with the intention of inviting the Blessed One to his palace to offer food prepared for himself. I have never seen such food before. If I remain here, Mahādugga might be troubled. I shall depart, Venerable Sir." Having said this, he paid homage to the Blessed One and departed. Sakka, the King of Devas, also respectfully attended to and served the Blessed One with rice gruel and other offerings. After the Blessed One had finished his meal and given the blessing (anumodanā), He rose from His seat and departed. Sakka gave a sign to Mahādugga, and Mahādugga took the bowl and followed the Blessed One.

## The Rain of Jewels and Mahādugga Becoming a Great Treasurer

When Sakka returned to the celestial realm, he stood at the door of Mahādugga’s house and looked up at the sky. At that very moment, a great rain of the seven kinds of jewels fell from the sky, filling all the pots in Mahādugga’s house and then filling the entire house. There was no empty space left in Mahādugga’s house. Mahādugga’s wife, taking her young children by the hand, led them out and stood outside the house. When Mahādugga returned after escorting the Blessed One and saw his children outside, he asked, "What is the reason for this?" She replied, "Husband, our entire house is filled with the seven kinds of jewels, and there is no space to enter."

Mahādugga reflected, "Today, my act of giving has indeed borne fruit," and he went to the King, paid homage, and stood there. When asked, "Why have you come?" Mahādugga reported, "Your Majesty, my house is filled with the seven kinds of jewels. Please take this wealth." The King thought, "Oh, how wonderful! The gift offered to the Buddhas has reached its fulfillment this very day." He then asked Mahādugga, "What do you need to receive [this wealth]?"

"Your Majesty, it would be appropriate to have a thousand carts to transport the wealth," he replied. The King sent a thousand carts to bring the wealth and had it piled up in the palace courtyard. The heap of jewels became as high as a palm tree. The King assembled the citizens and asked, "Is there anyone in this city who possesses such wealth?" When they replied, "No, Your Majesty," he asked again, "What should be done for a person who is so immensely wealthy?" They replied, "Your Majesty, it is appropriate to grant him the position of a Treasurer (Seṭṭhi)."

Therefore, the King showed him great honor and conferred upon him the title of Great Treasurer. Afterwards, the King pointed out the site of a former Treasurer’s house to Mahādugga and commanded, "Clear away the bushes growing here, build a house, and live there." While Mahādugga was clearing and leveling the ground, as the earth was dug, jars of gold touching one another appeared. When he reported this to the King, the King said, "These have appeared due to your own merit; you alone should take them." Mahādugga built the house and for seven days gave a great almsgiving to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. Thereafter, he continued to perform meritorious deeds throughout his life and, at the end of his life, was reborn in the celestial realm.

## Becoming the Youth Paṇḍita in the Time of the Current Buddha

After enjoying celestial bliss for the interval between two Buddhas, Mahādugga passed away from that celestial realm during the time when our Buddha appeared and shone brightly. He took rebirth in the womb of a treasurer’s daughter in a family that served the Venerable Sāriputta Thera in Sāvatthī. When the daughter’s parents realized she was pregnant, they provided her with pregnancy care.

Later, a pregnancy craving (dohaḷa) arose in the young woman: "Oh, how wonderful it would be if I could offer a meal of red-fish curry to five hundred monks, starting with the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta Thera, and then, wearing ochre-dyed robes and sitting at the end of the seats, eat the leftovers of those monks." She informed her parents, and when she did as she had craved, the craving was satisfied. Subsequently, apart from the ceremony to satisfy her craving, during the seven auspicious ceremonies (1. the intermittent ceremony, 2. the birth ceremony, 3. the naming ceremony, 4. the first feeding ceremony, 5. the ear-piercing ceremony, 6. the clothing ceremony, 7. the top-knot ceremony), they fed five hundred monks headed by the Venerable Sāriputta Thera with red-fish curry.
367:
(Everything should be understood in the same manner as related in the story of the youth Tissa; specifically, this is the result of the gift of the flavor of red-carp fish curry given when he was Mahādugga.)

On the day of naming the child, the mother said, "Venerable Sir, please grant the precepts to this boy who is your servant." The Elder asked, "What is this boy's name?" She replied, "Venerable Sir, from the time this boy was conceived in my womb, even those in this house who were dull and foolish have become wise. Therefore, my son's name shall be Paṇḍita." Elder Sāriputta then granted the precepts. From the day the boy was born, the mother had the thought, "I will not hinder my son's inclination (ajjhāsaya)."

## The Ordination of Young Paṇḍita, Formerly Mahādugga

When the boy was seven years old, he asked his mother, "Mother, I wish to ordain as a novice under Elder Sāriputta." She said, "Very well, dear. I have already made the resolution not to hinder your inclination." She then invited Elder Sāriputta for a meal and said, "Venerable Sir, this boy, your servant, wishes to ordain. I will bring him to the monastery in the evening." After the Elder left, she gathered her relatives and said, "We shall perform all the honors due to my son while he is still a layman today." After performing great honors, she took the boy to the monastery and requested the Elder, "Venerable Sir, please ordain this boy," and handed him over.

The Elder explained the difficulties of the ascetic life. When the boy replied, "Venerable Sir, I will follow all your instructions," the Elder said, "In that case, come," moistened his hair with water, taught him the meditation on the five skin-parts (tacapañcaka kammaṭṭhāna), and ordained him. The novice's parents stayed at the monastery for seven days, offering alms of red-carp fish curry to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. On the evening of the seventh day, they returned home. On the eighth day, when Elder Sāriputta entered the village for alms, he took the novice with him. He did not go with the assembly of monks. Why did he not go with them? Because the young novice's manner of wearing the robes and holding the bowl, as well as his deportment (iriyāpatha), was not yet graceful. Furthermore, the Elder had duties to perform at the monastery. Even though he was a senior Elder, when the Saṅgha had entered the village, he would walk around the entire monastery, sweeping where it needed sweeping, filling the drinking and washing water jars that were empty, and tidying away the beds and stools that were improperly placed before entering the village. Another reason was his thought: "Let not the outsiders (titthiyas) enter the empty monastery and find cause to disparage us, saying, 'Look at the sitting places of the disciples of the ascetic Gotama!'" Thus, after looking after the entire monastery, he entered the village. Therefore, on that day too, he had the novice carry his bowl and robes and entered for alms later in the day.
368:
## How the Novice Paṇḍita Reflected Upon Seeing a Watercourse and Other Things

While the young novice Paṇḍita was traveling together with his preceptor, he saw a watercourse along the way and asked, "Venerable Sir, what is the name of this?" The preceptor replied, "Novice, it is called a watercourse (mātika)." He then asked, "What do they do with this watercourse?" "They lead water from here and there to perform their farming work," the preceptor replied. The novice asked again, "Venerable Sir, does water have a mind?" "No, friend novice, water has no mind," he replied. "Venerable Sir, can they lead such mindless water to reach wherever they desire?" the novice asked.

"It is true, friend, they can lead it," the Elder replied. Then the novice reflected: "If they can perform tasks such as farming by leading such mindless water to wherever they desire, why should those with minds not be able to practice the Dhamma of a recluse (samaṇadhamma) by bringing their own minds under their control?"

After that, as the young novice Paṇḍita continued forward, he saw fletchers heating arrow shafts over a fire and making them straight while looking with the corner of their eyes. He asked, "Venerable Sir, who are these people?" "Friend novice, they are called fletchers (usukāra)," the preceptor replied. "What are they doing?" he asked. "They heat arrow shafts over a fire and make them straight," the preceptor replied. "Venerable Sir, does this arrow have a mind?" the novice asked. "Friend novice, the arrow has no mind," the preceptor replied. Then the novice reflected: "If they can take a mindless arrow shaft and make it straight by heating it over a fire, why should those with minds not be able to practice the Dhamma of a recluse by bringing their own minds under their control?"

After that, as the young novice Paṇḍita continued forward, he saw wood being planed for rims, hubs, and so on. He asked, "Venerable Sir, who are these people?" "Friend novice, they are called carpenters (tacchaka)," the preceptor replied. "What are they doing?" he asked. "They take wood and make wheels for carts and such," the preceptor replied. "Venerable Sir, do these pieces of wood have minds?" he asked. "Friend novice, they have no minds," the preceptor replied. Then the novice had this thought: "If they can take mindless pieces of wood and make things like cartwheels, why should those with minds not be able to practice the Dhamma of a recluse by bringing their own minds under their control?"

## How Sakka Protected the Novice Paṇḍita

Having seen these reasons, the novice said, "Venerable Sir, if you would take your bowl and robes, I would like to turn back." The Elder, without letting the thought arise, "This novice who has just been ordained is saying this while following behind me," simply said, "Bring them, novice," and took his own bowl and robes. As the novice paid homage to his preceptor and turned back, he said, "Venerable Sir, when you bring food for me, please bring it only with the flavor of red fish (rohitamaccha)." "How shall we get it, friend?" the preceptor asked. "Venerable Sir, if you do not get it by your own merit, you will get it by my merit," the novice replied.
369:
The Elder, thinking that danger might befall the young novice if he stayed outside the monastery, gave him the key and instructed, "Open the door of my cell, enter, and stay inside." The novice did as instructed, focused his wisdom on his physical body (karajakāya), and meditated on his own being. At that time, due to the novice's spiritual power, the throne of Sakka, King of Gods, showed signs of heat.

Sakka, reflecting on the cause, thought: "Pandita Sāmaṇera, having given the bowl and robes to his preceptor, has returned to perform the duties of a recluse. It is fitting that I also go there." He then summoned the Four Great Kings and commanded, "Drive away the birds living near the monastery grounds and keep guard all around." He told the Moon-god, "Pull back and hold the moon's disk," and the Sun-god, "Pull back and hold the sun's disk." Then, he himself went and stood guard at the place where the door-cord is pulled.

## Pandita Sāmaṇera Attaining the Three Lower Fruits

Even when dry leaves fell in the monastery, they made no sound. As the novice's mind became still and concentrated, he meditated on his physical body during the interval before the meal and attained the three fruits. Meanwhile, the Elder thought, "The young novice is staying at the monastery. In which family's house might I obtain food suitable for him?" and went to the house of a devoted supporter. In that house, the people had obtained Rohita fish that day and were waiting for the Elder's arrival. Seeing him, they said, "Venerable Sir, it is good of you to come here," invited him inside, offered gruel and snacks, and then filled his bowl with food flavored with Rohita fish. When the Elder showed signs of wanting to take food away, the people saw this and said, "Venerable Sir, please eat; you shall also receive food to take back to the monastery." After the Elder finished his meal, they filled his bowl with food flavored with Rohita fish and offered it. The Elder, thinking "The novice must be hungry by now," departed quickly.

The Buddha, having finished his meal early that day and returned to the monastery, reflected: "Pandita Sāmaṇera, having given the bowl and robes to his preceptor, has returned to perform the duties of a recluse. Will he complete the task of monkhood?" Upon investigation, he knew the novice had attained the three fruits. Then, reflecting on whether there was the supporting condition (upanissaya) for Arahatship, he saw that there was. He further considered whether the novice could attain Arahatship before the meal and realized he could. Then the Buddha thought: "Sāriputta is coming quickly with food for the novice. He might hinder the completion of the novice's recluse duties. I shall stand guard at the gatehouse. Then I will ask Sāriputta four questions. While those questions are being answered, the novice will attain Arahatship along with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā)." Having so thought, he went and stood at the gatehouse and asked the arriving Venerable Sāriputta the four questions. The Elder answered each question as it was asked.
370:
## Attaining Arahatship While Answering the Four Questions

The Buddha asked Venerable Sāriputta as follows:

1. "Dear Sāriputta, what have you obtained?" "Venerable Sir, I have obtained food (āhāra)."

2. "Dear Sāriputta, what does food bring?" "Venerable Sir, it brings feeling (vedanā)."

3. "Dear Sāriputta, what does feeling bring?" "Venerable Sir, it brings form (rūpa)."

4. "Dear Sāriputta, what does form bring?" "Venerable Sir, it brings contact (phassa)."

(The meaning is: Food eaten by a hungry person removes hunger and brings pleasant feeling. For one who is happy through the consumption of food, the arising of pleasant feeling leads to the perfection of complexion in the body. Thus, feeling brings form. A happy person, through the power of form produced by food, experiences physical and mental happiness, thinking "Now I am at ease," and whether lying down or sitting, experiences pleasant contact.)

When these four questions had been answered, Pandita Sāmaṇera attained Arahatship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā).

## Criticism Regarding Eating After Noon

The Buddha then said to the Elder, "Dear Sāriputta, go, give the food to your novice." Venerable Sāriputta went and knocked on the door. The novice came out, took the bowl from the Elder's hand, placed it in a suitable spot, and stood fanning Venerable Sāriputta with a palm-leaf fan. Then the Elder said to the novice, "Novice, perform the duty of eating." When the novice asked, "Venerable Sir, have you performed the duty of eating?" the Elder replied, "I have finished my meal; you eat." At that moment, the seven-year-old boy, who had been ordained for only eight days, having attained Arahatship like a newly blossomed lotus or blue lily, sat reflecting on what should be reflected upon (paccavekkhaṇā) and performed the duty of eating. After Pandita Sāmaṇera had washed and put away the bowl, the Moon-god released the moon. The Sun-god released the sun. The Four Great Kings released their guard over the four quarters. The sun then slipped away from its midday position. The monks complained, saying, "The shadows have exceeded their measure; the sun has slipped from the zenith. Yet the novice has only just finished his meal. How can this be?"
371:
The Blessed One, knowing this matter, arrived and asked, "Monks, what are you discussing?" When they replied, "Venerable Sir, we are discussing such and such a matter," he said, "Monks, indeed it is so. When a person of merit strives, exerts, and meditates on the Dhamma of a monk, the Moon-deity restrains the moon-disk, the Sun-deity restrains the sun-disk, the Four Great Kings keep guard in the four directions near the Jetavana monastery, and Sakka, the King of Devas, keeps guard at the door-cord. I myself, though being a Buddha who has realized the Four Noble Truths, could not remain indifferent; I went and took guard for my son at the gate-tower. Just as that novice saw the irrigators leading water through channels, the fletchers straightening arrows, and the carpenters shaping wood, and by taking such objects of thought, the wise tame themselves and attain Arahantship." Having thus connected the sequence, he spoke this verse while preaching the Dhamma:

## The Teaching
(80) Irrigators lead the water,
Fletchers bend the arrow-shaft,
Carpenters shape the wood,
The wise tame themselves.

*Nettikā*, those who lead water, *udakaṃ*, lead the water to wherever they desire. *Usukārā*, fletchers, *tejanaṃ*, make the arrow straight. *Tacchakā*, carpenters, *dāruṃ*, shape the wood, making it straight or curved as they wish. *Paṇḍitā*, the wise, *attānaṃ*, tame themselves to attain the Paths and Fruits.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The Story of the Novice Paṇḍita ends.

## 6. The Story of Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya
(Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiyatthera Vatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Selo yathā," concerning the Elder named Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, so called because of his short stature.
372:
## The Teaching
(81) Just as a solid rock
Is not shaken by the wind,
So the wise are not moved
By blame or praise.

*Ekaghano*, solid and without hollows; *selo*, a mountain made of rock; *vātena na samīrati yathā*, just as it is not moved or shaken by the wind; *evaṃ*, in the same way; *paṇḍitā*, the wise; *nindā-pasaṃsāsu*, because of blame or praise; *na samiñjanti*, are not moved by the power of anger or joy.

## The Nature of Arahants
When worldling novices and young monks saw the Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, they would pull him by the head, ears, or nose, and mockingly say, "What is it, little uncle? Are you not bored with the Buddha's Dispensation? Are you enjoying it?" The Elder did not get angry with those novices and young monks, nor did he harbor even a thought of ill-will. In the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a discussion: "Friends, look! When novices and others see the Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, they harass him in such and such ways. The Elder does not get angry with them, nor does he harbor ill-will." The Teacher came and asked, "Monks, what are you discussing?" When they replied, "Venerable Sir, we are discussing this matter," he said, "Monks, it is true that those who have destroyed the taints (Arahants) do not get angry or harbor ill-will. Indeed, they are like solid rock, immovable and unshakable." Having thus connected the sequence, he spoke this verse while preaching the Dhamma:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The Story of Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya ends.

## 7. The Story of Kāṇā's Mother
(Kāṇamātuvatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Yathāpi rahado," concerning the laywoman Kāṇamātā, the mother of the girl named Kāṇā.
(Kāṇā's mother was a Stream-enterer. While she was frying cakes, an alms-collecting monk arrived, and she offered a bowlful of cakes. This happened four times until the cakes were exhausted, preventing Kāṇā from returning to her husband's house. Consequently, the husband took another wife. Regarding this matter, the Buddha laid down a training rule that a monk should not accept more than three bowlfuls of cakes; to accept more is a Pācittiya offense. The story is found in the Vinaya Piṭaka.)
373:
## The Distress of the Maiden Kāṇā
At that time, the lay devotee Kāṇāmātā, thinking it improper to send her daughter back to her husband’s house empty-handed, began frying cakes for her son-in-law. On four occasions, she gave the cakes to four monks, and because of this incident, the Blessed One prescribed a training rule. When Kāṇā’s husband took another wife, Kāṇā heard the news and, whenever she saw monks, she would revile and abuse them, saying, "These monks have destroyed my marriage." The monks, therefore, did not dare to travel along that path. The Blessed One, becoming aware of this matter, went to that place. Kāṇā’s mother paid homage to the Blessed One, invited Him to a prepared seat, and offered Him rice gruel and hard food. After the Blessed One had finished His morning meal, He asked, "Where is Kāṇā?"

"Venerable Sir, having seen the Blessed One, Kāṇā is distressed and stands weeping," she replied. "For what reason?" the Buddha asked. "Venerable Sir, this Kāṇā reviles, abuses, and scolds the monks. Therefore, upon seeing the Blessed One, she is greatly distressed and stands weeping," she explained.

Thereupon, the Blessed One had Kāṇā summoned and said, "Dear daughter Kāṇā, why are you distressed, hiding, and weeping upon seeing me?" Then Kāṇā’s mother reported her daughter's conduct. The Blessed One then asked the lay devotee, "Kāṇāmātā, how is it? Did my disciples take what you gave, or what you did not give?" "Venerable Sir, they took what was given," she replied. "If my disciples, while wandering for alms, arrived at your door and took the cakes you offered, what fault is there in them?" He asked. "Venerable Sir, there is no fault in the noble ones; the fault lies only with my daughter Kāṇā," she answered. The Blessed One then said to Kāṇā, "Dear daughter Kāṇā, my disciples came to your door while wandering for alms. At that time, your mother gave them cakes. In this giving, what fault is there in my disciples?" "Venerable Sir, there is no fault in the noble ones; the fault is mine alone," she replied, and having paid homage to the Blessed One, she asked for forgiveness.

## Attaining Both Supramundane and Mundane Prosperity
Then the Blessed One preached the Dhamma to Kāṇā in progressive order. The maiden Kāṇā attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). The Blessed One then rose from His seat and, while returning to the monastery, passed through the royal courtyard. When King Kosala saw Him, he asked, "Friends, is that not the Blessed One?" When they replied, "Yes, Your Majesty, it is indeed the Blessed One," the King sent word, "Go and inform Him that I, the King, am coming to pay homage." He then approached the Blessed One, who was standing in the courtyard, paid homage, and asked, "Venerable Sir, where have you been?" "To the house of the lay devotee Kāṇāmātā, Great King," He replied. "For what reason, Venerable Sir?" the King asked. "It is said that the maiden named Kāṇā reviles and abuses the monks; I went there for that reason," He said. "But Venerable Sir, have you made her cease her reviling?" the King inquired.
374:
Where one cat finds [a mouse or meat], a second appears there.
A third and a fourth as well; this, O cats, is your cave.

Where, in which place. One cat, a cat. A mouse or meat. Gets, obtains. There, in that place. And a second, a second cat also. Appears, arises. And a third, a third cat also. Appears. And a fourth, a fourth cat also. Appears. Those cats. This cave, this crystal cave. With their chests. Having struck. The end of life, death. Have reached.

## The Teaching
(82) Just as a deep lake is clear and untroubled,
Even so, having heard the teachings, the wise become serene.

Deep, very deep. A lake, the great ocean. Is clear. Is untroubled, not muddy. Just as it is. Even so, in this same way. The wise, those with wisdom. The teachings, the Dhamma that has been preached. Having heard, having listened to. Become serene, they become especially clear in mind.

"Great King, it is well done," the Buddha said. "I have acted so that there is no more reviling of monks, and I have established her in the wealth of the Supramundane Dhamma."

"Venerable Sir, let it be so. You, Lord, have established Kāṇā in the wealth of the Supramundane Dhamma; I shall establish her in worldly wealth," the King replied. Having paid homage to the Buddha, the King departed.

Then, the King sent a covered carriage to fetch Kāṇā. He adorned her with all kinds of ornaments, placed her in the position of his eldest daughter, and announced, "Let those who are capable of supporting my daughter take her."

Then, a Chief Minister who managed all affairs said, "Great King, I shall support your daughter." He took her to his home, handed over all authority to her, and said, "Perform meritorious deeds as you please."

From that day on, the young woman Kāṇā stationed men at the four gates. Although she searched for monks and nuns to personally attend to, she could not find them. The stream of food and offerings prepared at Kāṇā’s gate flowed like a great flood.

(This means that because so many monks and nuns were arriving and being served, she could not easily find specific ones to personally attend to as she used to.)

The monks started a conversation in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, formerly four elder monks caused the young woman Kāṇā to be remorseful. Even though she was so remorseful, because of the Teacher, she attained the perfection of faith. The Teacher has once again made the door of her house a place worthy of being visited by monks. Now, although she searches for monks or nuns to personally attend to, she cannot find them. Indeed, the qualities of the Buddhas are truly wonderful!"
375:
## Kāṇā’s Past
The Blessed One arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?" When they replied, "We are gathered here to discuss this matter, Venerable Sir," the Buddha said, "Monks, it is not only now that these four elder monks have caused Kāṇā’s distress; they have done so in the past as well. It is not only now that I have made Kāṇā follow my words; I have done so in the past as well." Being requested by the monks who wished to hear the details, the Buddha related this Babbu Jātaka (found in the Ekanipāta, 14th, Asampadāna Vagga) in detail:

"The four elder monks were the four cats. The female mouse was Kāṇā. The stone-cutter (or jeweler) was I, the Buddha." Having thus connected the birth-story, he said, "Monks, in the past as well, Kāṇā was distressed, with a murky and agitated mind, but through my words, her mind became clear, like a very deep lake." Connecting the sequence to preach the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.
The Story of Kāṇāmātā ends.

## 8. Story of the Five Hundred Monks
(Pañcasatabhikkhu-vatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Sabbattha ve sappurisā cajanti," concerning five hundred monks.

## The Reason for the Lack of Restraint of the Leftovers-Eaters
During the first period of his Enlightenment (the first twenty years), the Blessed One went to the city of Verañjā. Invited by the Brahmin Verañja, he entered the three-month rains retreat (vassa) together with five hundred monks. The Brahmin Verañja, being deluded by the influence of Māra, did not even for a single day bring the Teacher to mind or establish mindfulness. The people of Verañjā also faced a famine. The five hundred monks, wandering for alms throughout the inner and outer parts of Verañjā, became exhausted as they received no alms-food. Some horse traders provided them with a measure (pattha) of steamed barley each as a regular alms-offering.
376:
Vālodakaṃ apparasaṃ nihīnaṃ, pitvā mado jāyati gadrabhānaṃ.
Imañca pitvāna rasaṃ paṇītaṃ, mado na sañjāyati sindhavānaṃ.
Appaṃ pitvāna nihīnajacco, so majjati tena janinda puṭṭho.
Dhorayhasīlī ca kule jāto, na majjati aggarasaṃ pitvā.

Having drunk the low-quality drink called vālodaka, which has little flavor, the donkeys become intoxicated. Having drunk this refined and flavorful grape juice, the Sindh horses do not become intoxicated.

O King of men, those of low birth (the donkeys), having drunk even a little of that grape juice, become oppressed by it and get drunk. But the Sindh horse, born of noble lineage and capable of bearing burdens, does not get drunk even after drinking the finest juice.

Seeing those exhausted monks, the Venerable Moggallāna desired to let them consume the essence of the earth, and also wished to send them to Uttarakuru for alms. However, because the Blessed One rejected the request made by Venerable Moggallāna, the monks did not show even a sign of complaint regarding the alms-food for a single day; they lived avoiding wrong desires.

After residing in Verañjā for the three months of the rains retreat, the Teacher took leave of the Brahmin Verañja. The Brahmin Verañja, showing respect and honor, was established in the Refuges. Departing from Verañjā and traveling by stages, the Teacher eventually reached Sāvatthī and resided at the Jetavana Monastery. The residents of Sāvatthī prepared offerings for the visiting monks. At that time, about five hundred leftovers-eaters (vighāsāda) lived within the monastery, depending on the monks. After eating the choice food left over by the monks, they would sleep, wake up, go to the riverbank, shout, jump about, engage in wrestling and boxing, and play boisterously. They wandered about behaving improperly both inside and outside the monastery.

## Summary of the Vālodaka Jātaka
The monks discussed in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, look at these leftovers-eaters. During the time of famine in Verañjā, they did not show any such rowdy behavior. But now, because they eat such choice food, they wander about showing many forms of rowdy behavior. The monks, however, remained peaceful while in Verañjā, and even now, they continue to live in perfect peace."
377:
## The Teaching

(83) Truly, the virtuous renounce all things; the peaceful do not speak out of desire for sensual pleasures. Whether touched by happiness or by pain, the wise show neither elation nor depression.

**Sappurisā**: the virtuous ones. **Sabbattha**: in all things, such as the five aggregates and so forth. **Ve**: truly. **Cajanti**: they renounce or give up craving and attachment. **Santo**: the peaceful ones, such as the Buddha and others. **Kāmakāmā**: being those who seek sensual pleasures, or for the sake of sensual pleasures. **Na lapayanti**: they do not speak or utter [for the sake of gain]. **Paṇḍitā**: the wise. **Sukhena**: by happiness. **Atha vā**: or else. **Dukhena**: by pain. **Phuṭṭhā**: although touched. **Uccāvacaṃ**: high or low states (elation or depression). **Na dassayanti**: they do not show.

The Blessed One, having gone to the Dhamma hall, asked, "Monks, what subject are you discussing as you sit here?" When they replied that they were discussing such and such a matter, He said, "In the past, when these individuals were born in the donkey species, there were five hundred donkeys. When they drank the 'Vālodaka'—the inferior, coarse drink with little flavor, made by mixing with water the dregs of the fresh, moist, flavorful grape juice left over by five hundred noble Sindh horses, and strained through a worn-out hemp cloth—they wandered about braying loudly as if intoxicated by honey."

Having preached this Vālodaka Jātaka in detail in the Dukanipāta of the Five Hundred and Fifty Jātakas, He said, "Monks, in this way, the virtuous avoid the worldly conditions and remain unshaken whether in times of happiness or in times of pain." Connecting the sequence of the discourse, He spoke this verse to teach the Dhamma.

(This means they do not act out of evil desire regarding requisites, saying, "Lay disciple, how is it? Are your wife and children well? Is your wealth increasing?" nor do they cause others to say, "Venerable sir, it is true, we are well. There is no danger; please come to our house for alms," and so forth.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The Story of the Five Hundred Monks ends.

## 9. The Story of Elder Dhammika

(Dhammikatthera Vatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana monastery, spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Na attahētu," concerning Elder Dhammika.
378:
## The Teaching

(84) Not for one's own sake, nor for the sake of another,
Should one desire a son, wealth, or a kingdom.
One should not desire success for oneself through unrighteousness.
Such a person is virtuous, wise, and righteous.

**Paṇḍitō nāma**: one who is called wise. **Attahētu**: for one's own sake. **Pāpaṃ**: evil. **Na karoti**: does not do. **Parassa hētu**: for the sake of another. **Pāpaṃ**: evil. **Na karoti**: does not do. **Pāpakammena**: through evil deeds. **Puttaṃ**: a son. **Na icche**: one should not desire. **Dhanaṃ**: wealth. **Na icche**: one should not desire. **Raṭṭhaṃ**: a kingdom or royal prosperity. **Na icche**: one should not desire. **Adhammena**: through unrighteousness. **Attano**: for oneself. **Samiddhi**: the fulfillment of prosperity and happiness. **Na iccheyya**: one should not desire. **Sa so**: such a person. **Sīlavā**: is virtuous. **Siyā**: would be. **Paññavā**: is wise. **Siyā**: would be. **Dhammiko**: is righteous. **Siyā**: would be.

## Practicing the Dhamma One After Another

In the city of Sāvatthī, a certain lay disciple lived a household life in accordance with the Dhamma. Desiring to ordain, one day while conversing pleasantly with his wife, he said, "Dear sister, I wish to ordain as a monk." She replied, "My lord, please wait until I give birth to the child in my womb." He waited, and when the child was able to walk, he asked his wife for permission again. She said, "My lord, please wait until this child reaches the age of maturity." He thought, "What benefit is there for me in asking or not asking this woman? I shall only work for my own escape from the suffering of Saṃsāra." He then left for the forest and ordained.

That monk Dhammika, having taken a subject of meditation and striven in practice, completed the task of a monk (attained Arahantship). To see his son and wife, he went back to Sāvatthī and preached the Dhamma to his son. The son also left for the forest and ordained. Not long after ordaining, he also attained Arahantship.

The former wife of Elder Dhammika thought, "I lived the household life for the sake of my son and husband. Now both of them have ordained. What is the use of me living in the house now? I shall ordain too." She left and ordained as a nun. Not long after ordaining, she also attained the Fruit of Arahantship. Then one day, in the Dhamma hall, the monks started a conversation: "Friends, the lay disciple Dhammika, because he himself was established in the Dhamma, left and ordained, attaining Arahantship. He also became the refuge for his wife and son."

The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what subject are you discussing as you sit here now?" When they replied, "We are sitting here with such a conversation, Venerable Sir," He said, "Monks, one who is wise should not desire the fulfillment of prosperity for one's own sake or for the sake of another. Only in accordance with the Dhamma should there be an escape from the suffering of Saṃsāra through righteous means." Connecting the sequence, He spoke this verse to teach the Dhamma.
379:
## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala) and so forth.
The Story of the Elder Dhammika ends.

## 10. Dhammassavana-vatthu
(The Story of Hearing the Dhamma)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher (the Buddha) gave this Dhamma teaching, beginning with the verse "Appakā te manussesu," concerning the hearing of the Dhamma.

## Listening to the Dhamma Without Respect
It is said that the people living in a certain street in the city of Sāvatthī, being in harmony, organized a group donation and arranged for a Dhamma talk to be held throughout the three watches of the night. However, although the Dhamma was preached throughout the three watches, they were unable to listen to it. Some, being dependent on delight in sensual pleasures, returned to their homes. Some, being dependent on ill-will, and some, being dependent on pride, also returned home. Some, being overcome by sloth and torpor, sat right there and were unable to listen, nodding and blinking their eyes. The next day, when the monks learned of this incident, they raised the matter in the Dhamma Hall. The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such and such a discussion," the Teacher said, "Monks, these beings for the most part depend on the realms of existence; they remain attached only to those existences. Those who reach the far shore of Nibbāna are indeed few." Connecting the sequence of the discourse, he spoke these verses:

## The Teaching
(85) Few among men are those who reach the far shore (Nibbāna).
But the rest of these people only run along this shore.

(86) But those who practice according to the Dhamma in the well-expounded Dhamma,
those people will cross over the realm of Death (Maccu), which is very difficult to cross.

(In these verses:) "Appakā" means few, not many. "Pāragāmino" means those who reach the far shore of Nibbāna. "Athāyaṃ itarā pajā" means that the remaining mass of beings only run along the shore of the view of self (sakkāya-diṭṭhi); this means they are the majority. "Sammadakkhāte" means well-expounded, well-spoken. "Dhamme" means the Dhamma of the teaching. "Dhammānuvattino" means those who...
380:
## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The Story of Hearing the Dhamma ends.

## The Teaching
(87) Abandoning the dark states, the wise man should cultivate the bright states.
Having gone from the home to the homeless, in that seclusion where it is difficult to find delight,

(88) There he should seek great delight. Having abandoned sensual pleasures and possessing nothing,
the wise man should cleanse himself from the defilements of the mind.

(89) Those whose minds are well-cultivated in the factors of enlightenment,
who, without clinging, delight in the relinquishing of grasping,
they, with taints exhausted and full of radiance, have attained Nibbāna in this world.

"Paṇḍitော" (the wise man). "Kaṇhaṃ dhammaṃ" (dark states, i.e., unwholesome actions). "Vippahāya" (having abandoned). "Sukkaṃ dhammaṃ" (bright states, i.e., wholesome actions). "Bhāvetha" (should cultivate) up to the Path of Arahatship. How should he cultivate? "Okā" (from the home, called craving). "Nikkhamitvā" (having departed). "Anokaṃ" (the homeless, the supreme peace of Nibbāna). "Āgamma" (relying on). "Bhāvetha" (should cultivate). "Yattha viveke" (in which seclusion of Nibbāna). "Dūramaṃ" (it is difficult for beings to delight).

"Paṇḍitော" (the wise man). "Kāme" (sensual objects and sensual defilements). "Hitvā" (having abandoned). "Akiñcano" (being without worries such as lust). "Tatra viveke" (in that seclusion of Nibbāna). "Abhiratiṃ" (great delight). "Iccheyya" (should desire).
"Cittaklesehi" (from the hindrances that defile the mind). "Attānaṃ" (himself). "Pariyodapeyya" (should cleanse).

"Yesaṃ" (those persons). "Sambodhiyaṅgesu" (in the factors of enlightenment which are the causes of awakening). "Sammā" (rightly). "Cittaṃ" (the mind). "Subhāvitaṃ" (has been well-cultivated). "Ye" (those persons). "Anupādāya" (without clinging to anything through the four types of grasping). "Ādānapaṭinissagge" (in Nibbāna, which is the relinquishing of grasping). "Ratā" (delight). "Khīṇāsavā" (those whose taints are exhausted). "Jutimanto" (those who are radiant with the light of the knowledge of the Path of Arahatship). "Te" (those persons). "Loke" (in the world of the aggregates, etc.). "Parinibbutā" (have attained peace through the two Nibbāna elements).

## 11. The Story of the Five Hundred Visiting Monks
(Pañcasata-āgantuka-bhikkhu-vatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching, beginning with the verse "Kaṇhaṃ dhammaṃ vippahāya," concerning five hundred visiting monks.
381:
The meaning of "Okā anokamāgamma" is: "Oka" is called attachment (home), and "Anoka" is called non-attachment (homelessness). Having departed from attachment and relying on Nibbāna, which is known as non-attachment, one should cultivate while aspiring for it. "Tatrābhiratimiccheyya" means that in that seclusion of Nibbāna, known as non-attachment, where it is difficult for these beings to find delight, one should desire delight there. "Hitvā kāme" means having abandoned the sensual objects and sensual defilements, and becoming one who possesses nothing (akiñcano), one should desire delight in seclusion. "Cittaklesehi" means from the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa). "Attānaṃ pariyodapeyya" means one should purify or cleanse oneself. "Sambodhiyaṅgesu" means in the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). "Sammā cittaṃ subhāvitaṃ" means the mind has been thoroughly cultivated and developed through the right method and cause. "Ādānapaṭinissagge": "Ādāna" is called grasping; in the non-grasping known as the relinquishing of that [grasping], those who delight without clinging to anything through the four types of grasping. "Jutimanto" means those possessed of great power, who remain illuminating the phenomena such as the aggregates with the radiance of the knowledge of the Path of Arahatship. "Te loke" means in this world of aggregates and so forth. "Parinibbutā" means they are said to have attained Nibbāna through the two types of Nibbāna: Sa-upādisesa (with fuel remaining) from the time of attaining Arahatship because the cycle of defilements has been exhausted, and Anupādisesa (without fuel remaining) by the cessation of the final consciousness because the cycle of the aggregates has been exhausted. They have reached the state beyond designation (apaṇṇattika), like a lamp that has gone out.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the Dhamma teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The Story of the Five Hundred Visiting Monks ends.
The Commentary on the Chapter of the Wise is finished.
The Sixth Chapter.

## Visiting the Buddha After the Rains Retreat
It is said that five hundred monks who were residing in the Kingdom of Kosala, having stayed for the three months of the rains retreat, when the time of the end of the retreat arrived, went to the Jetavana Monastery saying, "We shall see the Teacher." Having arrived, they paid respectful homage to the Buddha and sat in a suitable place. The Teacher, having noted the temperament of those monks, spoke these verses in order to preach the Dhamma.
382:
The Chapter on Flowers (Pupphavagga) is finished.

## 7. The Chapter on the Arahant (Arahantavagga)

## 1. The Story of Jīvaka’s Question (Jīvakapañhavatthu)

(The Story of Jīvaka’s Question)

The Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with “Gataddhino,” while residing in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove, concerning a question asked by Jīvaka.

(The story of Jīvaka is explained in detail in the Cūḷavagga Khandhaka.)

## Inquiring about the Heat due to the Bandaging of the Wound

On one occasion, Devadatta, having joined forces with King Ajātasattu, climbed Mount Gijjhakūṭa with a malicious intent, thinking, “I will kill the Teacher,” and rolled down a large stone. Two mountain peaks caught that stone. A splinter that broke off and flew from the falling stone struck the Blessed One’s foot and caused blood to flow. Intense and severe painful feelings arose. The monks carried the Teacher to Maddakucchi. From there, the Blessed One, wishing to go to Jīvaka’s Mango Grove, said, “Carry me to that mango grove.” The monks took the Blessed One and went to Jīvaka’s Mango Grove. When Jīvaka heard of the incident, he went to the Teacher’s presence, applied a strong medicine to treat the wound, bandaged it, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, I have treated a person inside the city; I will go to him and return. May this medicine remain just as it is bandaged until I return.” Having gone and performed what was necessary for that man, Jīvaka arrived back at the time the city gates were being closed, but he could not reach them before they were shut.

Then this thought occurred to Jīvaka: “Alas, I have done a heavy deed.”
383:
## The Teaching

(90) For him who has completed the journey, who is free from sorrow,
Who is liberated in every way, who has abandoned all bonds,
No burning is found.

Gataddhino: One who has traveled the long journey of Saṃsāra. Visokassa: One who is free from sorrow. Sabbadhi: In all things such as the aggregates. Vippamuttassa: One who is liberated. Sabbaganthappahīnassa: For one who has abandoned all four bonds (gantha). Paritāho: The mental burning known as defilements. Na vijjati: Does not exist.

“I bandaged the wound on the Blessed One’s foot with strong medicine as if it were the foot of an ordinary, obscure man. This is the time to remove that bandage. If it is not removed, a burning sensation will arise in the Blessed One’s body throughout the night,” Jīvaka thought. At that moment, the Teacher addressed the Elder Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, Jīvaka could not reach the gates before they closed while returning this evening. However, he thought, ‘This is the time to remove the bandage from the wound.’ Remove that bandage.” Thus, the Elder Ānanda removed it. The wound disappeared like bark falling from a tree. Jīvaka arrived quickly at the Teacher’s presence before dawn and asked, “Venerable Sir, how is it? Did a burning sensation arise in your body?” The Teacher, wishing to connect the context and preach the Dhamma, said, “Physician Jīvaka, for the Tathāgata, all burning was extinguished at the foot of the Bodhi tree,” and spoke this verse:

(Since cold and heat are not yet absent from the body of an Arahant, Jīvaka asked referring to physical heat. The Teacher, wishing to preach the Dhamma, answered that it does not exist, referring to mental heat.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The Story of Jīvaka’s Question is finished.

## 2. The Story of Elder Mahākassapa (Mahākassapattheravatthu)

(The Story of Elder Mahākassapa)

The Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with “Uyyuñjanti,” while residing at Veḷuvana Monastery, concerning the Elder Mahākassapa.

## The Monks’ Criticism of Elder Mahākassapa

On one occasion, when the Teacher had completed the rains retreat in the city of Rājagaha, he informed the monks, “Bhikkhus, after half a month has passed, I shall set out on a journey.”

(It is the custom of the Buddhas who wish to travel with the monks to inform them half a month in advance. By informing them thus, the monks would prepare their bowls and dye their robes, etc., and travel comfortably. Thus he informed them.)

While the monks were preparing their bowls and so forth, the Elder Mahākassapa also washed his robes.
384:
The monks criticized: "Why is the Elder washing his robes? In this city of Rājagaha, there are eighteen crores of people living both inside and outside the city. Among them, those who are not relatives of the Elder Mahākassapa are his supporters; those who are not his supporters are his relatives. They honor and respect the Elder with the four requisites. Abandoning such great support, where could this Elder go? Even if he were to go, he would not be able to go further than the Māpamādakandara Gully."

(Whenever the Buddha reached a certain gully, he used to say to the monks who ought to return, "You return from here; do not be negligent." Therefore, that gully is called the Māpamādakandara Gully. This statement was made in reference to that gully.)

The Buddha, while setting out on a journey, thought: "In this city, there are eighteen crores of people living both inside and outside. Monks should attend to the auspicious and inauspicious occasions of the people. It is not proper to leave the monastery empty. Whom should I ask to return?" Then, this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "These people are the relatives and supporters of Kassapa. It is appropriate to ask my son Kassapa to return." He then said to the Elder Mahākassapa: "Dear Kassapa, it is not proper to leave the monastery empty. Monks are needed for the auspicious and inauspicious occasions of the people.
