You return together with your followers." "Very well, Bhante," the Elder replied, and taking his followers, he returned. Then the monks criticized: "Friends, did you see? Did we not just say so? Why is Venerable Mahākassapa washing his robes? It has happened exactly as we said: 'This Venerable Mahākassapa will not follow the Buddha.'"

## The Buddha's Praise of Being Like the Moon

When the Buddha heard the monks' words, he stopped and asked: "Monks, what is it that you are talking about?" "Bhante, we are talking about the Elder Mahākassapa," they replied, and reported the entire matter exactly as they had spoken. Hearing this, the Buddha said: "Monks, you want to say that my son Kassapa is attached to supporters and requisites. My son Kassapa...
385:
...returned because he wanted to follow my words. This Kassapa, even when making his aspiration in a past life, made the aspiration: 'May I be unattached to the four requisites, like the moon, and be able to approach families.' He has no attachment to families or the four requisites. When I taught the moon-like practice and the practice of the noble lineage (Ariyavaṃsa), I taught it starting with my son Kassapa."

The monks asked the Buddha: "Exalted Buddha, when did the Elder make this aspiration?" "Monks, do you wish to hear?" He asked. "Yes, Bhante, we wish to hear," they replied.

The Buddha told them: "Monks, counting back from this aeon, a hundred thousand aeons ago, a Buddha named Padumuttara appeared in the world," and he related the Elder's entire past conduct, starting from the aspiration made at the feet of Buddha Padumuttara. That story is detailed in the Thera-pāḷi (Theragāthā). After detailing the Elder Mahākassapa's past conduct, the Buddha connected the sequence and, wishing to deliver a Dhamma teaching, spoke this verse:

## The Teaching

(91) The mindful strive; they do not delight in an abode.
Like swans leaving a lake, they abandon every home.

*Mindful (satīmanto):* Those who have attained expansive mindfulness, the Arahants, exert effort and strive in the qualities they have realized, such as jhāna and vipassanā, through the five masteries of advertence, attainment, emergence, resolution, and reviewing. *They do not delight in an abode (na nikete ramanti te):* They have no delight in any place of attachment. *Like swans (haṃsāva):* This is the main metaphor of the teaching. The meaning here is: Just as swans in a lake rich in food, after taking their food, fly away at the time of departure without any attachment to that place, not thinking "my water, my lotus, my lily, my seed-pod," but instead fly up and go playing in the sky; even so, Arahants, wherever they may dwell, remain unattached to families and so forth, and at the time of departure, they leave that place without attachment or longing, not thinking "my monastery, my dwelling, my supporters." *Abandon every home (okamokaṃ jahanti):* This means they abandon every level of attachment.

(Just as all birds such as swans, after feeding at a feeding ground, fly away without attachment to the fruits, leaves, water, or lotuses, saying "my fruit, my leaf," etc., so too Arahants depart without attachment to monasteries, male supporters, or female supporters.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The Story of Venerable Mahākassapa ends.
386:
## The Teaching
(92) Those who have no accumulation, who have fully understood food, whose range is the void and the signless liberation—their path is hard to trace, like that of birds in the sky.

Yesaṃ: to those persons. Sannicayo: accumulation. Natthi: there is not.

## 3. The Story of the Elder Belaṭṭhasīsa
(Belaṭṭhasīsattheravatthu)
While staying at the Jetavana monastery, the Buddha spoke this religious teaching beginning with "Yesaṃ sannicayo natthi" with reference to the Elder Belaṭṭhasīsa.

## The Promulgation of the Training Rule due to Drying Rice
That Elder Belaṭṭhasīsa, after going for alms in a village street and finishing his meal, went for alms again in another street. Having taken the dried rice and brought it to the monastery, he stored it, thinking, "The constant seeking of alms is indeed suffering." He spent two or three days in the bliss of meditative absorption (jhāna) and, when he needed food, he would consume that dried rice. The monks found out and criticized him, then reported the matter to the Buddha. On account of this, the Buddha promulgated a training rule for the monks to avoid making accumulations in the future. However, as the Elder had acted out of fewness of wishes (appicchatā) before the training rule was promulgated, the Buddha declared him faultless. Connecting the sequence of the discourse, the Buddha spoke this verse to teach the Dhamma:

(Accumulation of wholesome and unwholesome kamma is called kamma-sannicaya. Accumulation of the four requisites is called paccaya-sannicaya. Among these, for a monk living in a monastery, keeping one lump of molasses, a quarter-measure of ghee, and one nāḷi of rice does not count as accumulation of requisites. Keeping more than that counts as accumulation. The meaning is that both kamma-sannicaya and paccaya-sannicaya do not exist for such persons.)

Ye: those persons. Pariññātabhojanā: who have fully understood food through the three types of full understanding.

(Knowing one of the items like gruel as being gruel is ñāta-pariññā. Specifically understanding food through the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment is tīraṇa-pariññā. The wisdom that abandons greed and desire for the food consumed is pahāna-pariññā. It means they can fully understand food and meals through these three types of full understanding.)

Suññato vimokkho ca: also the void Nibbāna. Animitto vimokkho ca: also the signless Nibbāna. Yesaṃ: of those persons. Gocaro: the object. Hoti: is.

(Nibbāna is called "Suññata-vimokkha" because of the absence of greed, hatred, and delusion, and because of liberation from them. It is called "Animitta-vimokkha" because of the absence of signs like greed, and because of liberation from them. It is called "Appaṇihita-vimokkha" because of the absence of longing like greed, and because of liberation from them. By the word "ca," this liberation is also included; it means they dwell making that three-named Nibbāna the object through the wisdom of Fruition.)

Tesaṃ: of those persons. Gati: the destination. Ākāse: in the sky. Sakuntānaṃ: of birds. Gati iva: like the path. Durannayā: is hard to trace. Or, cannot be known.
387:
(Just as the path of birds flying in the sky cannot be known because their footprints are not seen, similarly, the destination of those who have no two-fold accumulation, who have understood food through the three-fold full understanding, and who have Nibbāna as their object, cannot be known. It cannot be pointed out as going to any of the five groups: the three realms of existence, the four modes of birth, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, or the nine abodes of beings, because their path is not manifest.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people reached the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The story of the Elder Belaṭṭhasīsa ends.

## 4. The Story of the Elder Anuruddha
(Anuruddhattheravatthu)
While staying at the Veḷuvana monastery, the Buddha spoke this religious teaching beginning with "Yassāsavā" with reference to the Elder Anuruddha.

## The Buddha Threading the Needle while Sewing the Robe
One day, the Elder Anuruddha, having worn-out robes, was searching for robe material in places like rubbish heaps. A woman who had been his wife in his third previous existence was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as a goddess named Jālinī. When that goddess saw the Elder searching for cloth for robes, she took three divine cloths, thirteen cubits long and four cubits wide, and thought, "If I give these in this way, the Elder will not accept them." She then placed them in a rubbish heap in front of the Elder Anuruddha as he was searching for cloth, in such a way that only the fringes of the cloths were clearly visible. The Elder, while wandering and searching for cloth along that path, saw the fringes of the cloths. When he took hold of the fringes and pulled them, he saw the divine cloths of the aforementioned size. Thinking, "This material is indeed an excellent and valuable dust-heap (paṃsukūla) robe," he took them and departed.

Later, on the day of sewing the Elder's robe, the Buddha went to the monastery accompanied by five hundred monks and sat down. The eighty Great Elders also sat in that same monastery. To sew the robe, the Elder Mahākassapa sat at the foot (the beginning part) of the robe.
388:
## The Teaching

(93) He whose taints are exhausted, who is not dependent on food, whose range is the liberation that is empty and signless—his path is difficult to follow, like that of birds in the sky.

To whom (yassa): to that person. The taints (āsavā): the four taints. Are exhausted (parikkhīṇā): have been completely ended. And on food (āhāre ca): also regarding nutriment such as alms-food. Not dependent (anissiṭo): having no dependence through craving or views. And the liberation that is empty (suññato vimokkho ca): and the Nibbāna that is empty. And the liberation that is signless (animitto vimokkho ca): and the Nibbāna that is signless. Whose (yassa): of that person. Range (gocaro): is the object. Is (hoti): it is. His (tassa): of that person. Path (padaṃ): the destination, like a footprint. Like the track of birds in the sky (ākāse sakuntānaṃ padaṃ iva): like the footprints of birds in the sky. Difficult to follow (durannayaṃ): cannot be known.

Venerable Sāriputta sat in the middle. Venerable Ānanda sat at the edge of the robe. The community of monks twisted the thread. The Buddha threaded the eye of the needle. Venerable Mahāmoggallāna went about bringing whatever was needed. A goddess entered the village and exhorted the people, saying, "Our lord, Venerable Anuruddha, is making a robe. The Teacher, surrounded by the eighty Great Disciples and five hundred monks, is staying at the monastery. Please take gruel and other offerings and go to the monastery," thus fulfilling the alms-food. Venerable Mahāmoggallāna also brought many large rose-apples before the meal. The five hundred monks were unable to finish eating them all. Sakka, the King of the Gods, leveled the ground at the place where the robe was being made; the ground became as if dyed with the color of lac. A great heap of gruel, rice, and hard and soft food remained after the monks had eaten.

The monks complained, "What is the use of so much gruel and other food for this many monks? Should not the relatives and supporters be told to bring only a certain measured amount? Venerable Anuruddha likely wishes to make known the abundance of his relatives and supporters." Then the Teacher asked them, "Monks, what are you discussing?" When they replied, "Venerable Sir, it is such and such," He asked, "Monks, do you think that Anuruddha had all this brought?" "Yes, Venerable Sir," they replied. "Monks, my son Anuruddha does not speak such words. Indeed, those whose taints are exhausted do not speak words connected to requisites. This alms-food arose through the power of the devas." Having thus connected the sequence, He spoke this verse while teaching the Dhamma:

(Just as it is impossible to know the tracks of birds flying in the sky, saying, 'They stepped here with their feet, they struck here with their breasts, here with their heads, or here with their wings,' so too it is impossible to know the path of a person who is free from taints, independent of food, and who takes the threefold Nibbāna as their object, by saying, 'He has gone by the path of hell, or by the path of the animal realm,' and so on.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, many people reached the Fruit of Stream-entry and other stages.

The story of Venerable Anuruddha ends.
389:
## The Teaching

(94) He whose senses have reached tranquility, like horses well-tamed by a charioteer, who has abandoned pride and is free from taints—even the gods envy such a stable one.

By a charioteer (sārathinā): by a skilled charioteer. Well-tamed (sudantā): well-disciplined. Like horses (assā yatha): like horses. Whose (yassa): of that Arahant. Senses (indriyāni): the faculties such as the eye. Tranquility (samathaṃ): to the state of being calmed and concentrated. Have reached (gatāni): have attained. Who has abandoned pride (pahīnamānassa): who has discarded conceit. Free from taints (anāsavassa): who is free from the four taints. Such a stable one (tādino): who is unshaken by desirable or undesirable objects. Such an Arahant (tassa): to that person. Even the gods (devāpi): even the celestial beings. Envy (pihayanti): love and admire.

## 5. The Story of Venerable Mahākaccāyana

(Mahākaccāyanattheravatthu)

While staying at the Pubbārāma monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Yassindriyāni" concerning Venerable Mahākaccāyana.

## The Love and Admiration of Sakka, King of the Gods

On one occasion, on the full moon day of the Great Pavāraṇā, the Teacher sat beneath the palace of Migāramātā Visākhā, surrounded by the Great Disciples. At that time, Venerable Mahākaccāyana was living in the Avanti regions. That Venerable Mahākaccāyana was accustomed to coming even from a great distance to honor the hearing of the Dhamma. Therefore, when the elder monks sat down, they would leave a seat for Venerable Mahākaccāyana before sitting. Sakka, the King of the Gods, came together with a celestial retinue from two heavens, and after honoring the Teacher with divine perfumes and garlands, he stood and, not seeing Venerable Mahākaccāyana, reflected, "Where is my lord Kaccāyana? He is not seen. It would be truly good if he were to arrive."

At that very moment, the Elder arrived and showed himself already seated in his own seat. When Sakka saw the Elder, he paid homage and firmly held his ankles, saying, "My lord has come well indeed! I was hoping for my lord's arrival," and he massaged the feet with both hands, honored him with perfumes and garlands, and after paying respect, stood at a suitable place. The monks complained, "Sakka shows favoritism in his honor. Without showing such honor to the other Great Disciples, upon seeing Mahākaccāyana, he quickly held his ankles and said, 'My lord has come well indeed! I was hoping for my lord's arrival,' and after massaging the feet with both hands and paying respect, he stands at a suitable place."

When the Teacher heard their talk, He said, "Monks, monks like my son Mahākaccāyana, who have guarded their sense-doors, are dear to both gods and humans alike." Having thus connected the sequence, He spoke this verse while teaching the Dhamma:
390:
The Teacher, having heard the words of those monks, said, "Monks, monks like my son Kaccāyana, who have guarded doors in their sense faculties such as the eye, are indeed loved by both devas and humans." Desiring to preach the Dhamma in connection with this, he uttered this verse:

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The story of the Elder Mahākaccāyana ends.

## 6. Story of the Elder Sāriputta
(Sāriputtattheravatthu)
The Teacher told this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Pathavisamo," while residing at the Jetavana monastery, concerning the Elder Sāriputta.

## The Accusation of Striking against Venerable Sāriputta
On one occasion, the Elder Sāriputta, having completed the rains retreat (vassa) and wishing to set out on a journey, took leave of and paid homage to the Buddha, then departed with his retinue. Many other monks also followed the Elder. The Elder, addressing the well-known monks by their names and clans, sent them back. A certain monk, who was not well-known by name or clan, thought, "Oh, if only he would address me by name and clan and then send me back." The Elder, in the midst of the large community of monks, did not notice that monk. That monk, thinking, "He does not favor me like the other monks," harbored a grudge against the Elder. The corner of the Elder's double robe (saṅghāṭi) also happened to touch that monk's body. Because of that too, he harbored a grudge.

Thinking, "Now the Elder will have passed the precincts of the monastery," he approached the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, the Elder Sāriputta, thinking 'I am one of your Chief Disciples,' struck me as if breaking my ear and departed on his journey without even apologizing." The Teacher had the Elder Sāriputta summoned. At that moment, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna and the Elder Ānanda thought, "The Teacher is not unaware of this monk's grudge; he must wish to have our elder brother roar his lion's roar. Let us assemble the congregation." Taking keys in their hands, they opened the doors of the cells and urged, "Sirs, come forth! Now the Elder Sāriputta will speak fearless words in the presence of the Buddha," thus assembling the large community of monks. The Elder Sāriputta also arrived, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down.
391:
## Venerable Sāriputta's Address with Nine Similes
Then the Teacher questioned the Elder Sāriputta about that matter. The Elder Sāriputta, without saying "I did not strike this monk," but wishing to speak of his own virtues, said, "Venerable Sir, if a monk's mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati) were not well-established, he might strike a fellow practitioner here and depart on a journey without apologizing." Then he said, "Venerable Sir, just as on the great earth (mahāpathavī), people throw clean things and also throw unclean things..." In this manner, he clearly declared his state of mind being like the earth, and also like water, fire, air, a dust-remover (rag), an outcaste boy, and a bull with broken horns. He also declared his weariness with his own body, like a rotting snake carcass, and his carrying of his body without lack of mindfulness, like the youth named "Medakathālikā" who climbs to the top of a bamboo pole. (This matter is taught in the ninth sutta of the Nālanda Vagga, Satipaṭṭhāna Saṃyutta, Mahāvagga Saṃyutta.)

(While the Elder was speaking of his virtues with these nine similes, the great earth shook nine times, extending to the water's edge. When he brought forth the similes of the dust-remover, the outcaste boy, and the Medakathālikā, the worldling monks were unable to restrain their tears. Spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega) arose in the Arahants.)
392:
## The Accusing Monk's Apology
Even as Venerable Sāriputta Thera was recounting his own virtues, a burning sensation arose throughout the body of the accusing monk. At that very moment, the monk prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, confessed his offense of false accusation, and begged for forgiveness. The Blessed One called Venerable Sāriputta and said, "Sāriputta, forgive this monk, who is empty of the paths and fruits, before his head splits into seven pieces; accept his apology."

The Elder squatted, and with palms joined in reverence, said, "Venerable Sir, I forgive that venerable one. And if I myself have any fault, may that venerable one also forgive me."

The monks remarked, "Friends, look at the incomparable virtue of the Elder! He does not harbor even the slightest anger or great resentment toward a monk who accused him with such falsehood; instead, he himself squats with palms joined and asks for forgiveness."

When the Buddha heard this, he asked, "Monks, what are you discussing?" When they replied, "Venerable Sir, we are discussing such and such," the Buddha said, "Monks, it is impossible to provoke slight or great anger in those like Sāriputta. Monks, Sāriputta's mind is like the great earth. It is like a city pillar (Indakhīla). It is like a lake of clear water." Having said this, he connected the discourse and spoke this verse:

## Verse
(95) Like the earth, he is not resentful; like a city pillar, such a one is firm and well-disciplined.
Like a lake free from mud, such a one has no more rounds of rebirth.

[Explanation:] He who is like the earth and like a city pillar does not conflict; that is, he is neither compliant nor resistant. He remains unshaken by the eight worldly conditions. He is of good conduct. Like a lake free from mud, his mind is clear. For such a person, there are no more rounds of rebirth in the happy or unhappy destinations.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the conclusion of the teaching, nine thousand monks attained Arahantship together with the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).

The Story of Venerable Sāriputta Thera ends.

## 7. The Story of the Novice of Venerable Tissa of Kosambī
(Kosambīvāsītissattherasāmaṇeravatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this religious discourse beginning with "Santaṃ tassa manaṃ hoti" concerning the novice of Venerable Tissa.

## The Wise Disciple and the Teacher's Release from Offense
A young man of good family living in the city of Kosambī, having ordained in the Buddha's Dispensation and received higher ordination, became well-known as "Venerable Tissa of Kosambī" (Kosambīvāsī Tissa Thera) because of his residence there.

After the rains retreat in Kosambī, a lay supporter brought three robes, as well as ghee and molasses, and placed them at the Elder's feet to be offered.
393:
The Elder asked the lay supporter, "Lay disciple, what is this?" "Venerable Sir, did I not invite you to spend the rains retreat? Monks who have completed the rains retreat in our monastery receive these gains. Venerable Sir, please accept them." "Let it be, lay disciple, I have no need for these gains." "Venerable Sir, what is the reason?" "Friend, I do not even have a novice to serve as a kappiyakāraka (attendant)."

"Venerable Sir, if there is no kappiyakāraka, my son shall become a novice under the Venerable One." The Elder consented. The lay disciple brought his seven-year-old son to the Elder and offered him, saying, "Please ordain this boy as a novice." Then the Elder moistened the boy's hair, gave him the meditation on the five parts of the body ending in skin (tacapañcaka kammaṭṭhāna), and ordained him. At the very end of the shaving with the razor, that novice attained Arahantship together with the four analytical knowledges.

After ordaining the boy and staying at that monastery for half a month, the Elder, wishing to see the Teacher, had the novice take the requisites and set out. On the way, they entered a certain monastery.

The novice took the bedding and seating for his preceptor and cleaned them. While the novice was cleaning the place, it became late and dark, so he was unable to clean a place for himself. Then the Elder, seeing the novice who had come to attend to him at the proper time, asked, "Novice, have you cleaned a place for yourself?" "Venerable Sir, I did not get the opportunity to clean one." "If that is so, stay in my place. Staying outside in a place for visitors would be painful for you." Saying this, he took the novice into the lodging.

The Elder, however, being a worldling (puthujjana), fell asleep as soon as he lay down. The novice reflected: "Today is the third day I have stayed in the same lodging with my preceptor. If I were to lie down and sleep, the Elder would fall into the offense of sleeping in the same lodging (sahaseyya)." Thinking, "I will pass the night sitting up," he sat in a cross-legged posture near the preceptor's bed and passed the night in that way.

Early in the morning, the Elder woke up and thought, "It is proper to have the novice go outside." He took a fan placed at the side of the bed, struck the novice's mat with the edge of the fan's leaf, and while lifting the fan upward, said, "Novice, go outside." The handle of the fan struck the novice's eye, and at that moment, the eye was destroyed.

(If one sleeps until dawn with a novice in the same lodging for three days, from sunset to dawn on the following night, one must not sleep with the novice; otherwise, an offense is committed. One is allowed to sleep together for only three days. With a woman, however, there is no permission for even a moment during the night.)
394:
## The Teacher's Distress over the Pupil's Eye Injury

The handle of the fan struck the eye. At that very moment, the eye burst and was destroyed. When told, "Go outside," the novice immediately asked, "Venerable Sir, what is it?" and stood up. He did not say, "Venerable Sir, my eye has burst and is destroyed," but covering it with one hand, he went out. Even while performing his minor and major duties, he held his eye with one hand and, taking a handful of broom with the other, swept the latrine and the place for washing the face. Having set out the water for washing the face, he swept the compound. Then, when the novice offered the tooth-stick to his preceptor, he offered it with only one hand.

Then the preceptor said to the novice, "This novice is indeed untrained. It is not proper to offer a tooth-stick to teachers and preceptors with only one hand." "Venerable Sir, I know that it is not proper to do so. However, even though I know this, my other hand is not free," he replied. "Novice, how is that?" he asked again. The novice related the matter from the beginning. As soon as the Elder heard it, his heart was filled with spiritual dread (saṃvega). Saying, "Alas, I have indeed committed a heavy deed," he said, "Good man, novice, forgive me. I did not know this. Be my refuge," and with hands joined in salutation (añjali), he sat in a crouching position at the feet of the seven-year-old novice. Then the novice said to the Elder, "Venerable Sir, I did not speak for the sake of such an apology and salutation. I spoke thus because I wished to protect your mind. In this matter, there is no fault on your part, nor is there any fault on mine. This fault belongs only to the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa). Do not think of it further. I remained silent without reporting it only to protect you from remorse, Venerable Sir." Even though the Elder was being comforted by the novice to put him at ease, he was not comforted. Filled with spiritual dread, he took the novice's requisites and went to the presence of the Teacher (the Buddha).

The Blessed One also sat watching the arrival of that monk, Tissa, a resident of Kosambī. The Elder went and paid homage to the Teacher. After exchanging pleasantries with the Teacher, when asked, "Monk, are you well? Has any excessive discomfort occurred?" the Elder replied, "Blessed One, I am well. I have no excessive discomfort. However, I have never before seen anyone endowed with such extraordinary qualities as this young novice."

"Dear monk, what has this young novice done?" the Buddha asked. The Elder related the whole matter from the beginning to the Blessed One, saying, "Blessed One, when I asked for forgiveness, he said to me, 'In this matter, there is no fault on your part, nor is there any fault on mine. This occurrence is only the fault of the round of rebirths. Do not think of it further,' and he even comforted me to put me at ease."
395:
## The Verse

(96) Calm is his mind, calm is his speech and action.
He is one who has been liberated through right knowledge,
One who is peaceful and poised.

*Sammā*: by right means. *Aññā*: having known. *Vimuttassa*: of one who is liberated from defilements. *Upasantassa*: of one who is calmed by the calming of internal passion and so forth. *Tādino*: of such a nature. *Tassa*: of that Arahant novice. *Manaṃ*: the mind. *Santaṃ*: is peaceful due to the absence of covetousness and so forth. *Hoti*: it is. *Vācā ca*: and the verbal action. *Kammaṃ ca*: and the physical action. *Santaṃ*: is peaceful. *Hoti*: it is.

"He did not show even a slight anger or great anger towards me. Blessed One, I have never before seen a person endowed with such qualities," he reported. Then the Teacher said to that Elder, "Dear monk, those who are Arahants (Khīṇāsava) do not get angry with anyone, nor do they harbor ill will. Having calmed faculties, they possess only a calm mind." Connecting the sequence, he spoke this verse while teaching the Dhamma:

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the conclusion of the teaching, the Elder Tissa, a resident of Kosambī, attained Arahantship together with the four Analytical Knowledges (paṭisambhidā). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the rest of the multitude.

The story of the novice of Elder Tissa, the resident of Kosambī, ends.

## 8. The Story of Elder Sāriputta

(Sāriputtatthera Vatthu)

The Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Assaddho" (The faithless) while residing at Jetavana Monastery, in reference to Elder Sāriputta.

## The Claim that Elder Sāriputta had not Abandoned Wrong View

On one occasion, about thirty forest-dwelling monks came to the presence of the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down. The Teacher, seeing that these monks possessed the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for the Fruit of Arahantship together with the Analytical Knowledges, called Elder Sāriputta and asked a question concerning the five faculties: "Dear Sāriputta, do you believe that the faculty of faith (saddhindriya), when developed and frequently practiced, plunges into the Deathless (amata) and has the Deathless as its end?" Elder Sāriputta replied, "Blessed One, in this matter—that the development of the faculty of faith leads to the Deathless—I do not go by faith in the Blessed One. Blessed One, those who have not known, not seen, not understood, not realized, and not touched that matter with wisdom, they alone would go by faith in others in that matter." Upon hearing that answer, the monks started a conversation: "Elder Sāriputta has not yet abandoned wrong view; even to this day, he does not have faith in the All-Enlightened Buddha." Hearing those words, the Buddha said, "Dear monks, what kind of words are you speaking? I asked Sāriputta, 'Do you believe that there is anyone capable of realizing the Paths and Fruits without developing the five faculties and without practicing tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā)?' And Sāriputta answered, 'I do not believe that there is such a person who realizes thus.' It is not that he does not believe in the result (vipāka) of gifts given or merits performed,"
396:
## The Teaching
(97) The man who is without blind faith, who knows the Unconditioned, who has severed the link (of rebirth), who has destroyed all opportunities (for rebirth), and who has renounced all desires—he is indeed the greatest of men.

“It is not that he does not believe in the virtues and grace of the Buddha and others. This Sāriputta does not go by the faith of others regarding the states of Jhāna, Vipassanā, Path, and Fruit that he himself has realized; therefore, he is beyond reproach.” Having said this and connecting the sequence of the discourse, the Buddha spoke this verse:

## The Meaning of the Riddle
[Literal/Negative Interpretation:]
*Yo naro*, whichever man; *assaddho ca*, is also without faith; *akataññū ca*, and is ungrateful for favors done; *sandhicchedo ca*, and is a house-breaker who pierces walls; or, who steals by breaking in; *hatāvakāso*, who destroys the dwelling places of people in towns and villages; *vantāso*, who seizes with such greed that he would even vomit up and discard cherished possessions. *Sa ve naro*, that man indeed; *uttamaporiso*, is a 'great man' who has had his ignorance removed. (This is the unintended meaning given by those who do not understand the riddle.)

[Intended/Spiritual Interpretation:]
*Yo naro*, whichever man; *assaddho*, is not one who believes in his own attained virtues through the words of others (meaning he believes through personal experience); *akataññū ca*, and knows Nibbāna, which is not made by causes; *sandhicchedo ca*, and cuts the connection of the cycle of Saṃsāra; *hatāvakāso ca*, and destroys the opportunity for rebirth in any plane of existence (meaning there is no future life because the seeds of Kamma are exhausted); *vantāso ca*, and has discarded all craving like vomit. *So naro*, that man; *ve*, indeed; *uttamaporiso*, is a supreme man. (This is the intended meaning.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the verse, those thirty forest-dwelling monks attained Arahantship together with the four Analytical Insights (Paṭisambhidā). The discourse was also beneficial to the rest of the assembly.

The story of the Elder Sāriputta ends.

## 9. The Story of the Elder Revata of the Acacia Forest
(Khadiravaniya Revata Thera Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this legal discourse beginning with "Gāme vā" concerning the Elder Revata who lived in the Acacia (Khadira) forest.

## The Wedding of Seven-Year-Old Revata
The Elder Sāriputta, having renounced eighty-seven crores of wealth to ordain, also caused his three sisters—Cālā, Upacālā, and Sīsupacālā—and his two brothers—Cunda and Upasena—to ordain. Only the youth Revata remained at home. Then, Revata's mother thought: “My son Upatissa has renounced so much wealth to ordain, and then caused his three sisters and two brothers to ordain as well. Only Revata remains at home. If this Revata is also allowed to ordain, all this wealth of ours will be lost, and our lineage will be broken. I will bind Revata with the bond of marriage while he is still young.” The Elder Sāriputta, however, had already instructed the monks beforehand: “Venerable sirs, if Revata comes wishing to ordain, please ordain him as soon as he arrives. My mother and father hold wrong views. What is the use of asking their permission? I myself am his mother and father.”
397:
“If he comes, ordain that Revata immediately upon his arrival. My mother and father are of wrong view. What is the use of asking them? I myself am his mother and father.” Revata's mother, wishing to bind the youth Revata with the bond of household life at the age of seven, requested a young girl from a family of equal status. After fixing the date and dressing the youth in fine ornaments, she took him with a large retinue to the house of the young girl's relatives.

Then, when the relatives of both parties had assembled for the wedding ceremony, they placed the hands of the couple in a water bowl and spoke auspicious words. The relatives, wishing for the prosperity of the young girl, said: “Dear daughter, may you see the truth (Dhamma) seen by your grandmother, and may you live as long as your grandmother, dear.” The youth Revata thought, “What is this truth seen by this grandmother?” and asked, “Who is this grandmother?” Then they said to him, “Dear boy, do you not see this grandmother who is one hundred and twenty years old, with broken teeth, grey hair, wrinkled skin, a body covered in liver spots, and a back as bent as a rafter? This is the girl's grandmother.” He asked again, “What? Will this young girl also become like this?” They replied, “Dear boy, if she lives long, she will.” Revata thought, “A body of such a nature will reach such a state of ruin through old age. My eldest brother Upatissa must have seen this state. It is proper for me to run away and ordain this very day.” Subsequently, the relatives placed Revata together with the young girl in a single carriage and set out.

## The Youth Revata's Escape and Ordination as a Samanera
After traveling a short distance, the youth Revata made an excuse of needing to relieve himself and said, “Please stop the carriage for a moment. I will get down and return shortly.” He got down from the carriage, stayed in a thicket for a short while, and then returned. After going a bit further, he got down again using the same excuse and then got back in. He did this again in the same manner. Then Revata's relatives thought, “Surely, the urges to relieve himself are frequent for this boy,” and because of this, they did not keep a very strict watch over him. Revata went a bit further, got down again with the same excuse, and said, “You all drive on ahead. We will come slowly from behind.” After saying this, he got down and headed toward a thicket. His relatives, thinking “He will follow from behind,” drove the carriage on. Revata escaped from that thicket and reached a place where thirty monks were staying. He paid homage to them and said, “Venerable sirs, please ordain me as a Samanera.”
398:
“Young man, you are adorned with all kinds of ornaments. We do not know whether you are a prince or the son of a minister. How then can we ordain you as a novice?” When they said this, he replied, “Venerable sirs, do you not know me?” “Young man, we do not know you,” they said. “I am the youngest brother of Upatissa, venerable sirs,” he replied. “Who is this person named Upatissa?” they asked. “Oh, that is right. Venerable sirs, you call my elder brother ‘Sāriputta’. That is why you did not know when I said ‘Upatissa’,” he explained. “What? Are you the younger brother of the Elder Sāriputta?” they asked again. “Yes, venerable sirs,” he replied. “In that case, come. Your brother has already given his permission beforehand.” Having said this, the monks had Revata's ornaments removed and placed in a suitable spot. After ordaining him as a novice, they sent word to the Elder Sāriputta.

## The Buddha and Elder Sāriputta Set Out
Upon hearing the news, the Elder Sāriputta said to the Buddha, “Exalted Buddha, word has been sent that the forest-dwelling monks have ordained Revata as a novice. I wish to go, see Revata, and then return, Lord.” The Buddha said, “Wait a while, Sāriputta,” and did not give permission to go. After a few days had passed, the Elder Sāriputta asked the Buddha again. The Buddha said, “Wait a while, Sāriputta, we shall also go,” and still did not grant permission to go.

The novice Revata thought, “If I stay here, my relatives will follow and call me back.” Having learned the subjects of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) from those monks until the attainment of Arahantship, he took his bowl and robes and wandered until he reached a Khadira (Acacia) forest thirty yojanas away. Within that very three-month rains retreat, he attained Arahantship along with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). After the Pavāraṇā ceremony, the Elder Sāriputta again asked the Buddha for permission to go to that Khadira forest. The Buddha said, “Sāriputta, we shall also go,” and set out together with five hundred monks. After traveling some distance, the Elder Ānanda stood at a fork in the road and said to the Buddha, “Venerable Sir, of the paths leading to the novice Revata, this path is a circuitous route of sixty yojanas and is inhabited by humans. This other path is a direct route of thirty yojanas but is occupied by non-humans. By which path shall we go, Lord?” The Buddha asked, “Ānanda, has Sīvali come with us?” “Yes, Lord, Sīvali has come,” he replied. “If Sīvali has come, take the direct path,” the Buddha commanded.
399:
## The Great Merit and Fortune of Elder Sīvali
As the Buddha traveled along that path, the deities thought, “We shall perform offerings and honor to our master, Elder Sīvali.” They created monasteries at intervals of one yojana and, not allowing the monks to travel further than one yojana at a time, they rose early in the morning and brought divine gruel and other offerings, asking, “Where is our master, Elder Sīvali, staying?” The Elder had the offerings brought to him presented to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. In this way, the Buddha, along with his retinue, traveled the thirty-yojana difficult journey while enjoying the fruits of Elder Sīvali's merit. When the Elder Revata learned of the Buddha's arrival, he created a Gandhakuṭi for the Buddha, as well as five hundred peaked houses, five hundred walkways, and five hundred night and day quarters. The Buddha stayed with Revata for about a month. While staying there, he continued to enjoy only the fruits of Elder Sīvali's merit.

## The Two Elderly Monks Face Hardship
At that place, two elderly monks thought to themselves when entering the Khadira forest, “Since this monk is so busy with this much construction work (navakamma), how will he be able to practice the Dhamma of a recluse? The Buddha has come to the presence of such a monk who is preoccupied with construction work only out of consideration for him being Sāriputta's younger brother.” At dawn that day, the Buddha, surveying the world, saw those monks and knew the thoughts in their minds. Therefore, after staying there for about a month, on the day of departure, the Buddha made a psychic resolution (adhiṭṭhāna) such that those elderly monks would forget their oil tube, water vessel, and sandals. Having made this resolution, he departed. When they had gone outside the precincts of the monastery, the Buddha withdrew his psychic power.

Then those two elderly monks said, “I have forgotten such and such an object,” and “I have also forgotten mine.” Both turned back, but because they did not recognize the place, they wandered about being pricked by the thorns of the Khadira trees. Only when they saw their belongings hanging from a Khadira tree did they take them and depart.

## Speaking to Visākhā
The Buddha, leading the Saṅgha of monks, returned in just one month, continuing to enjoy the fruits of Elder Sīvali's merit, and entered the Pubbārāma monastery. Then, those two elderly monks washed their faces early in the morning and went to the house of Visākhā, who was accustomed to offering food to visiting monks, thinking, “We shall drink gruel.” After drinking gruel and eating hard food, they sat down. Then Visākhā asked those two elderly monks, “Venerable sirs, did you also go with the Buddha to the place where Elder Revata resides?”
400:
## The Teaching
(98) Whether in a village or in a forest, in a valley or on the hills, wherever Arahants dwell, that place is delightful.

[Word-by-word gloss: Gāme vā, whether in a village. Yadi vā, or else. Raññေ vā, whether in a forest. Ninne vā, whether in a low-lying valley. Yadi vā, or else. Thale vā, whether on the high ground or hills. Yattha, in whichever place. Arahanto, the Arahants. Viharanti, dwell. Taṃ bhūmi, that place. Rāmaṇeyyakaṃ, is delightful and pleasant.]

When she asked, "Bhante, did you go together to the place where the Venerable Revata dwells?", they replied, "Laywoman, it is true that we went."

When she asked again, "Bhante, is the place where the Venerable Revata dwells delightful?", they said, "Laywoman, how could that place of Revata be delightful? That place is merely a dense and tangled forest of thorny acacia trees; it is like a realm of hungry ghosts (petas)."

Then two other young monks arrived. The laywoman offered them gruel and snacks and asked the same question. The two young monks said, "Laywoman, it is beyond praise. The dwelling of the Venerable Revata is like the Sudhammā celestial hall. It is as if it were created and arranged by psychic power."

Visākhā the laywoman reflected and understood: "The elder monks who came first spoke in one way. These young monks speak in another. The elder monks who came first must have returned when the psychic power was withdrawn after something was forgotten. These young monks must have returned while the place was still created and arranged by psychic power." Knowing this through her own wisdom, she thought, "I will ask the Teacher when he arrives," and she waited. 

A moment later, the Teacher, surrounded by the community of monks, went to Visākhā's house and sat on the prepared seat. After Visākhā had respectfully served the community of monks headed by the Buddha and the meal was over, she paid homage to the Teacher and asked: "Venerable Sir, among the monks who went with you, some say that the Venerable Revata's dwelling is a dense acacia forest. Others say it is delightful. What is the reason for this, Bhante?"

Hearing this, the Teacher said, "Laywoman, whether it be a village or a forest, wherever Arahants dwell, that place is indeed delightful." Connecting the sequence, he spoke this verse while teaching the Dhamma:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

## Inquiry into the Past Kamma of Venerable Sīvali
On another occasion, the monks discussed: "Friends, for what reason did the Venerable Sīvali stay in his mother's womb for seven years, seven months, and seven days? For what reason did he suffer in hell? By what result did he become foremost in receiving gains and fame?" Hearing this discussion, the Teacher asked, "Monks, what are you discussing?" When they replied, "Venerable Sir, we are discussing such and such," he spoke, wishing to relate the past kamma of that venerable one:
401:
## The Merit Competition in the Time of Vipassī Buddha
"Monks, ninety-one aeons ago from this present one, the Buddha named Vipassī appeared in the world. On one occasion, after wandering through the countryside, he returned to his father's royal city. The King, having prepared an 'offering for guests' (āgantuka-dāna) for the community of monks headed by the Buddha, sent a message to the citizens: 'Come and be my companions in this almsgiving.' The citizens did as the King requested and then thought, 'We shall give an offering even more excellent than the one given by the King.' They invited the Teacher and, having prepared the offering for the next day, sent word to the King. The King came, saw their offering, and thought, 'I shall give an offering even more excellent than this,' and invited the Teacher for the following day. The King could not outdo the citizens, nor could the citizens outdo the King.

On the sixth occasion, the citizens thought, 'Now, tomorrow, we shall give an offering such that it cannot be said, "This or that requisite is missing from this offering."' Having prepared the offering for the next day, they looked to see what might be missing and saw only that there was no fresh honey; there was plenty of cooked honey. To obtain fresh honey, they took four thousand kahāpaṇas and sent men to the four city gates.

## The Countryman Who Offered Honey
At that time, a man from a country village, while coming to see the village headman, saw a honeycomb on the way. He drove away the bees, cut the branch, and taking the honeycomb along with the branch, entered the city, thinking, 'I will present this to the village headman.' The man who had gone out for honey saw that countryman and asked, 'O man, is that honeycomb for sale?' When he replied, 'Sir, it is not for sale,' the other said, 'Take this kahāpaṇa and give me the honeycomb.' The man who owned the honey thought, 'This honeycomb is not worth even a quarter (pāda), yet this man offers a kahāpaṇa. He must have many kahāpaṇas; I should increase the price.' Then he said to him, 'I cannot give it.' 'Then take two kahāpaṇas,' the other said. 'I will not give it for two either,' he replied. In this way, he increased the price until the man who wanted to buy the honey brought a bundle of money and said, 'Then take this thousand.'

Then the owner of the honey said to the buyer, 'What is this? Are you mad? Or do you have no place to keep your kahāpaṇas? You say, "Take a thousand and give me the honey," which is not worth even a quarter. What is the meaning of this?' The buyer replied, 'O man, I know. But I have a task to perform with this honey; that is why I speak thus.' The owner asked, 'Sir, what is that task?'"
402:
“We are preparing a great offering for the Blessed One Vipassī, who is accompanied by sixty-eight thousand monks. In that offering, only fresh honey is missing; that is why we are buying it in this way,” they said. He replied, “If you wish to offer it to the Buddha, I will not give it for a price. However, if I may also receive a share of the merit in this offering, then I will give it.” The buyer returned and told this to the citizens. When the citizens realized the greatness of the honey-seller's faith, they agreed, saying, “Excellent, excellent! May you receive an equal share of the merit.” The citizens then invited the community of monks headed by the Buddha to be seated, offered them gruel and snacks, brought a large golden bowl, and had the honeycomb squeezed into it. That same countryman also had a jar of curd which he had brought as a gift. He poured that curd into the bowl, mixed it with the honey, and offered it to the community of monks headed by the Buddha, starting with the Buddha himself. That honey-curd sufficed for all the monks, who took as much as they desired, and there was even a surplus remaining.

(One should not wonder, “How did such a small amount of honey reach so many people so thoroughly?” It reached them solely through the power of the Buddha. The range of a Buddha is not to be pondered. Indeed, it is true. Four things have been declared as ‘unthinkable’ (acinteyya): the range of a Buddha (buddha-visaya), the range of psychic powers (iddhi-visaya), the range of the world (loka-visaya), and the range of the results of kamma (kamma-visaya). One who ponders these unthinkables will only partake of madness.)

## The Dreadful Result of Kamma for Sīvalī and His Mother

Having performed such a meritorious deed, that honey-seller was reborn in the celestial realm at the end of his life. After wandering through saṃsāra for this long a time, he eventually passed away from the celestial realm and was reborn into the royal family of Bārāṇasī. Upon the death of his father, he attained the kingship. That king, thinking “I will capture a certain city,” went and besieged it. He sent a message to the citizens: “Either give me the kingdom or do battle.” The citizens replied, “We will neither give the kingdom nor do battle.” They exited through small side-gates to fetch wood, water, and so on, and carried out all their necessary tasks. The King of Bārāṇasī, guarding the four main gates, blockaded the city for seven years and seven months. Then the king's mother asked the attendants, “What is my son doing?”

When she heard the news, “Great Queen, he is doing such-and-such,” she said, “My son is unwise, ignorant, and foolish. Go! Tell that kingly son to blockade the city by closing even the small side-gates.”

When the King of Bārāṇasī heard his mother's message, he did exactly as she said. The citizens, being unable to go outside, killed their own king on the seventh day and handed over the kingdom to the King of Bārāṇasī. Because of this evil deed, at the end of his life, he was reborn in the Avīci hell. He was cooked in that hell for as long as it took for this earth to grow upwards by one league. Because he had closed the four small gates, when he passed away from that hell, he took conception in the womb of that very same mother. He had to stay in his mother's womb for seven years and seven months, and for seven days, he lay transversely across the birth canal. “Bhikkhus, in this way, Sīvalī was cooked in hell for this long a time due to the evil deed of besieging and taking the city back then. Because he closed the four small gates, when he passed away from that life, he took conception in the womb of that very same mother and remained in the womb for this long a time. However, due to the meritorious deed of having offered fresh honey, he became one who attained the pinnacle of gains and the pinnacle of fame,” the Buddha declared.
403:
He who has transcended both merit and evil, who is free from attachments, sorrowless, stainless, and pure—him I call a Brahmin.

Bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, he who has abandoned both merit and evil, and has transcended the attachment of passion for sense objects; who is without sorrow, without the dust of defilements, and is pure—him I call a Brahmin, one who has put aside evil.

On another day, the monks raised a discussion: "How wonderful is the gain of the novice Revata! How wonderful is his merit! This novice is so meritorious that, though he is but one, he has created five hundred gabled houses and so forth for the sake of five hundred monks." The Teacher came and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit here?" When they replied, "It is this," he said, "Monks, my son has neither merit nor evil; he has abandoned both merit and evil." Then he spoke this verse in the Brāhmaṇa Vagga.

The Story of Elder Revata of the Acacia Forest ends.

## 10. The Story of an Unknown Woman
(Aññatara-itthi-vatthu)

While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher told this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Ramaṇīyāni," concerning an unknown woman.

## The Various Wiles of Women

A monk who observed the practice of alms-gathering, having taken a meditation subject from the Teacher, entered an old garden to practice the Dhamma of a recluse. A certain courtesan, who was known as an ornament of the city, made an appointment with a man, saying, "I will go to such-and-such a place; you should come there." She went, but the man did not come. While looking for his arrival and not seeing him, she became bored and wandered here and there until she entered the garden. Seeing the Elder sitting cross-legged, she looked around and saw no one else. Thinking, "This too is a man; I will delude his mind," she stood before the monk and repeatedly loosened and refastened her garment, let down and tied up her hair, and clapped her hands and laughed. Spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arose in the Elder, pervading his whole body. He reflected, "What is this?"

## The Words of the Buddha's Instruction

The Buddha, considering, "What is happening to the monk who took a meditation subject from me and went to practice as a recluse?" saw the woman and knew her improper behavior and the Elder's state of saṃvega. While remaining in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), he spoke to the monk: "Monk, the place where seekers of sensual pleasure find no delight is exactly the place where those free from passion (rāga) find delight."
404:
## The Teaching

(99) Delightful are the forests where the worldling finds no joy. Those free from passion will find delight there, for they are not seekers of sensual pleasure.

Forests are delightful. In those forests, the common folk do not find delight. Arahants, who are free from passion, will find delight. Why? Because they are not seekers of sensual pleasure.

Having said this and emitting a ray of light, wishing to teach the Dhamma to that monk, he spoke this verse.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, the Elder, while still sitting there, attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). He then traveled through the air, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.

The Story of an Unknown Woman ends.

The Explanation of the Arahanta Vagga is finished.

The Seventh Chapter.
405:
## 8. Sahassa Vagga

## 1. The Story of Tambadāṭhika, the Executioner
(Tambadāṭhika-coraghātaka-vatthu)

While staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Teacher told this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Sahassamapi ce vācā," concerning Tambadāṭhika, the executioner of thieves.

## One who served as an executioner for fifty-five years

It is said that four hundred and ninety-nine thieves made their living by plundering villages and so forth. Then a man with piercing eyes and a red beard, named Tambadāṭhika, went to them and said, "I too will live with you." They showed him to the bandit chief and said, "This man also wishes to live with us." The bandit chief looked at him and thought, "This man is extremely cruel, capable of biting off his mother's breast or drawing the blood from his father's throat to eat." Thus he rejected him, saying, "There is no place for this man to stay with us." Although rejected, Tambadāṭhika returned and served a close disciple of the bandit chief, pleasing him. That disciple took him to the bandit chief and pleaded, "Lord, this man is of good character; he will be of great help to us. Please accept him." The bandit chief then accepted him.

One day, the city dwellers together with the king's men captured those thieves and brought them before the ministers of justice. The ministers ordered their heads to be cut off with an axe. Then, while searching for someone who could kill these thieves, they found no one willing. They said to the bandit chief, "If you kill these thieves, you will receive your life and also rewards. Kill them." But the bandit chief did not wish to kill them because they were his followers who depended on him. In this manner, they asked the four hundred and ninety-nine thieves. All of them refused. Finally, they asked Tambadāṭhika, who had piercing eyes and a red beard. He accepted, saying, "Very well," and by killing all those thieves, he received his life and rewards. In the same way, five hundred more thieves were brought from the south of the city and shown to the ministers. When their execution was ordered, starting from the bandit chief, they asked others but found no one willing. They asked, "On a previous day, a man killed five hundred thieves; where is he?" Being told he was seen in such-and-such a place, they summoned him and ordered, "Kill these; you will receive rewards." He accepted, saying, "Very well," and by killing all of them, he received rewards.
406:
In this way, when five hundred robbers were brought from the southern part of the city and presented to the ministers, the ministers ordered their heads to be cut off. Starting from the chief of the robbers, they were questioned, but when it was seen that no one was willing to kill them, they asked, "On a previous day, a man killed five hundred robbers; where is that man?" Upon being told, "We saw him in such and such a place," they sent for the executioner Tambadāṭhika and ordered him, "Kill these people, and you shall receive a reward." Tambadāṭhika agreed, saying "Very well," and by killing all those people, he received the rewards graciously bestowed upon him. Then, thinking, "This man is a good executioner," and "We shall make this man the permanent executioner," they consulted and gave that position to Tambadāṭhika alone, bestowing rewards upon him. That Tambadāṭhika also killed five hundred robbers brought from the west and five hundred from the north. Having thus killed two thousand robbers brought from the four directions, from that time onwards, he performed the work of an executioner for fifty-five years, killing one, two, or three people brought daily.

## Tambadāṭhika’s Removal from Office

When Tambadāṭhika grew old, he was unable to cut off a head with a single blow; he had to strike two or three times, causing the people to suffer. The citizens thought, "Another executioner will surely arise; this man causes excessive suffering to people. What is the use of him?" and they removed Tambadāṭhika from his position as executioner. Because he had been performing the work of an executioner previously, he had not obtained these four things: to wear new, unwashed clothes; to drink milk porridge prepared with fresh ghee; to wear jasmine flowers; and to be anointed with perfumes. On the day he was removed from office, he said, "Cook milk porridge for me," and having had new clothes, jasmine flowers, and soft perfumes brought, he went to the river, bathed, and returned home wearing the new clothes, adorned with flowers, and with his body anointed with perfumes, and sat down. Then, milk porridge prepared with fresh ghee was placed before Tambadāṭhika, and water for washing hands was brought.
407:
Subhāsitaṃ suṇitvāna, nagare coraghātako.
Anulomakhantiṃ laddhāna, modati tidivaṃ gato.

Bhikkhave, O monks. Nagare, in the city of Rājagaha. Coraghātako, the executioner. Subhāsitaṃ, the well-spoken Dhamma. Suṇitvāna, having heard. Anulomakhantiṃ, conformity-knowledge. Laddhāna, having gained. Tidivaṃ gato, having reached the Tusita heaven. Modati, he rejoices.

At that moment, the Venerable Sāriputta, having emerged from his meditative attainment, reflected, "Where should I go today?" While looking at his alms-round area, he saw the milk porridge in Tambadāṭhika's house. He then considered, "Will that man be able to support and assist me?" and knowing, "If he sees me, he will be able to support and assist me; and having done so, this clansman will obtain great prosperity," he robed himself, took his bowl, and showed himself standing at the door of Tambadāṭhika's house.

Upon seeing the Elder, Tambadāṭhika, with a clear and faithful heart, thought: "For a long time, I have performed the work of an executioner; many people have been killed by me. Now, milk porridge has been prepared in my house. The Elder has also come and stands at my door. Now it is proper for me to give a gift to this venerable one." Thus thinking, he set aside the porridge placed before him, approached the Elder, paid homage, and invited him inside. He poured the milk porridge into the bowl, added fresh ghee, and stood fanning the Elder. At that time, Tambadāṭhika had a strong desire to drink the milk porridge because he had not received it for a long time. The Venerable Sāriputta, knowing Tambadāṭhika's desire, said, "Lay disciple, drink your own porridge." Tambadāṭhika gave the fan into the hand of another person and drank the porridge. The Elder also said to the man who was fanning, "Lay disciple, you go; do not fan me." While that other person was fanning, Tambadāṭhika drank the porridge until his stomach was full, then came and stood fanning the Elder, and took the bowl of the Venerable Sāriputta who had finished his meal.

## Unable to Focus on Dhamma due to Long-time Killing

The Venerable Sāriputta endeavored to give a Dhamma talk of appreciation to Tambadāṭhika. That Tambadāṭhika was unable to focus his mind and follow the Dhamma teaching preached by the Elder. The Elder, noting this behavior, asked, "Lay disciple, why are you unable to focus your mind and follow the teaching?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, for a long time I have performed cruel deeds; many people have been killed by me. As I remember my own evil deeds, I am unable to focus my mind and follow the teaching of the Venerable One." The Elder, thinking, "I will trick him," asked, "Lay disciple, did you do it of your own will, or were you made to do it by others?" When he replied, "Venerable Sir, the King made me do it," the Elder said, "Lay disciple, if that is so, does unwholesome kamma occur to you?" The lay disciple, being of dull intellect, when the Venerable Sāriputta spoke thus, thought, "Indeed, I have no unwholesome kamma," and happily requested, "Venerable Sir, if that is the case, please preach the Dhamma."

## Tambadāṭhika Dies by a Cow's Gore

While the Venerable Sāriputta was preaching the Dhamma of appreciation, Tambadāṭhika, with a concentrated mind, developed conformity-knowledge (anulomika-khanti) which is on this side of the Path of Stream-entry while listening to the Dhamma. (Anulomika-khanti is the insight knowledge that occurs prior to the Path, in accordance with the Path.)
408:
The Elder, having given the blessing (anumodanā), departed. A female ogre in the form of a cow ran toward the lay follower Tambadāṭhika, who was returning after accompanying the Elder for a short distance, and gored him to death. Having passed away, Tambadāṭhika was reborn in the Tusita heaven. In the Dhamma hall, the monks were discussing: "The executioner committed cruel deeds for fifty-five years and only today was he freed from that cruelty. Today he offered alms-food to the Venerable Sāriputta and died this very day. Where might he have been reborn?"

The Blessed One arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?" When they informed Him, He said, "Monks, that Tambadāṭhika has been reborn in the Tusita heaven." They asked again, "Venerable Sir, what are You saying? Having killed so many people for such a long time, has he really been reborn in the Tusita heaven?" The Buddha replied, "Monks, it is true that he was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Tambadāṭhika obtained a good friend. Having heard the Dhamma from Sāriputta and developed conformity knowledge (anulomika-ñāṇa), he was reborn in the Tusita heaven upon passing away from this life and this body."

The monks asked further, "Venerable Sir, the preaching of the blessing (anumodanā) is not very powerful, while the unwholesome kamma committed by Tambadāṭhika was very great. How could he achieve such a special distinction merely by listening to the Dhamma for such a short time?" The Blessed One said, "Monks, do not measure the Dhamma I have taught as being little or much. Even a single word is superior if it is based on benefit." Wishing to connect the sequence and preach the Dhamma, He spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(100) Though there be a thousand words
Composed of meaningless lines,
Better is one word of sense,
Hearing which one is pacified.

"Composed of meaningless lines" refers to words connected with useless descriptions of the sky, mountains, forests, etc., which do not lead to liberation. No matter how many such words there are, they are inferior. "One word of sense" refers to a single meaningful word—such as "This is the body," "This is mindfulness of the body," "He has attained the three knowledges," "The Buddha's teaching is done"—hearing which one is pacified through the subsiding of lust and so forth. Even a single word that accomplishes the goal, is connected with Nibbāna, and explains the aggregates, elements, sense bases, powers, factors of enlightenment, and foundations of mindfulness, is indeed superior.

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The story of Tambadāṭhika the executioner ends.

## 2. The Story of the Elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya
(Bāhiya-dārucīriya-tthera-vatthu)
The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana monastery, told this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Though there be a thousand verses," concerning the Elder Dārucīriya.

## Misconception due to others' words
Once, many people set out to sea in a boat. The boat was wrecked in the middle of the great ocean, and they became food for fish and turtles. One merchant among them grabbed a plank and, through his effort, reached the shore of the port of Suppāraka. That man had no clothes or garments. Seeing nothing else to wear, he wrapped himself in pieces of dry wood and bark, making a garment. Taking a bowl from a shrine, he went to the port of Suppāraka.
409:
When people saw him, they gave him gruel, rice, and so forth, and praised him, saying, "This man is surely an Arahant." When clothes were brought to him, he thought, "If I wear or wrap myself in these, my gains and offerings will decrease." So, he rejected those clothes and continued to wear only the wooden bark garments. Then, as many people called him an Arahant, the thought arose in his mind: "Whatever Arahants or those who have entered the path to Arahantship there are in the world, I am one of them." Then, a deity who was a former relative (Puraṇa-sālohita) of his thought thus. "Puraṇa-sālohita" refers to one who had practiced the Dhamma together with him in the past.

## Seven Monks Climbing the Mountain to Practice Dhamma
In the past, when the dispensation of the Kassapa Buddha was declining, seven monks, seeing the improper behavior of novices and others, were struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Thinking, "As long as the dispensation has not yet disappeared, we shall make a refuge for ourselves," they paid homage to the Golden Cetiya and entered the forest. Seeing a mountain, they said, "Let those who have attachment to life turn back; let those who are free from attachment climb this mountain." They constructed a ladder, and all seven monks climbed the mountain. Then, they pushed the ladder away and practiced the Dhamma. Among those seven monks, the eldest (Saṅghatthera) attained Arahantship after just one night. That Elder, having used a tooth-wood called Nāgalatā at Lake Anotatta and brought alms-food from the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru), said to those monks, "Friends, use this tooth-wood, wash your faces, and partake of this alms-food." They asked, "Venerable Sir, how is this? Did we make a pact that 'the monk who first attains Arahantship shall bring alms-food and the remaining monks shall eat it'?" He replied, "Friends, there was no such pact."

"If that is so, if we too can achieve the special distinction like you, we shall bring it and eat it ourselves," they said, and refused the food. On the second day, the second Elder attained the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala). He also brought alms-food in the same manner and invited the remaining monks. Those monks asked again, "Venerable Sir, how is this? Did we make a pact that 'without eating the alms-food brought by the Great Elder, we shall eat the alms-food brought by the second Elder'?" He replied, "Friends, there was no such pact." "If that is so, if we too, like you, can achieve the special distinction and are able to eat by our own manly effort, then we shall eat," they said, and refused. Among those monks, the one who attained Arahantship passed into Parinibbāna. The one who was a Non-returner was reborn in the Brahma realm. The other five Elders, being unable to achieve the special distinction, became emaciated and passed away on the seventh day. They were reborn in heaven, and when our Buddha appeared, they passed away from that heaven and were reborn in various families.
410:
Among those five, one became King Pukkusāti. One became Kumārakassapa. One became Dārucīriya. One became Dabba, the prince of the Mallas. One became Sabhiya the wandering ascetic. Regarding the monk who was reborn in the Brahma realm among those seven monks, the term 'the Great Brahmā, a former blood relative' refers to him.

(In some texts, it is written as Pukkusāti. Pukkusāti is the common name used. Bāhiya Dārucīriya—one who has external practices and wears wooden clothing; for ease of address, the name Bāhiya Dāruci is used.)

## Assistance from the Great Brahmā, an Old Friend

The Great Brahmā had this thought: "This person named Bāhiya Dāruci, who mistakenly thinks he is an Arahant because of his wooden-stick-and-rope clothing, once climbed a mountain by constructing a ladder of palm trunks with me to practice the Dhamma of a recluse. If he continues to wander holding this view, he will be ruined. I shall cause him to feel a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega)." Then, he approached Bāhiya Dāruci and said:

"Friend Bāhiya, you are not an Arahant, nor have you entered the path to Arahantship. You do not even possess the practice by which you might become an Arahant or enter the path to Arahantship."

When this was said, Bāhiya Dāruci, whose practice was external to Arahantship, looked up at the Great Brahmā standing in the sky and thought: "Alas, I have committed a very grave matter. I thought to myself, 'I am an Arahant,' yet this Brahmā tells me, 'You are not an Arahant, nor have you entered the path to Arahantship.' Is there indeed another person in the world who is an Arahant?" Then he asked the Great Brahmā: "Great Brahmā, is there now in the world an Arahant or one who has entered the path to Arahantship?"

Then the Great Brahmā told Bāhiya Dāruci: "Friend Bāhiya, in the northern regions, there is a city named Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One, who is worthy of offerings and has perfectly realized all truths by himself, is currently residing. Bāhiya, that Blessed One is indeed an Arahant, and he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of attaining Arahantship."

Having heard the words of the Great Brahmā during the night, Bāhiya, with a heart full of spiritual urgency, departed from the port of Suppāraka at that very moment and reached the city of Sāvatthī in just one night's stay across the entire journey. He traveled the entire distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas in only one night. He traveled by the power of the Great Brahmā. Some also say it was by the power of the Buddha.

## Requesting the Buddha to Teach the Dhamma

At that moment, the Blessed One was entering the city of Sāvatthī for alms. Since Bāhiya had already finished his morning meal, [he was free from] physical lethargy...
411:
He asked many monks who were walking to and fro in the open air to dispel their drowsiness, "Where is the Blessed One now, venerable sirs?" The monks replied, "He has entered Sāvatthī for alms." They then asked Bāhiya, "Where have you come from?" "I have come from the port of Suppāraka, venerable sirs," he said. "When did you set out?" they asked. "I set out yesterday evening, venerable sirs," he replied. "You have come from a great distance. First, sit down. After washing your feet and anointing them with oil, rest for a while. You will see the Teacher when he returns," they said. "Venerable sirs, I do not know the danger to the life of the Blessed One or to my own. I have traveled a distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas in a single night without stopping or sitting anywhere. I shall rest only after I have seen the Teacher," he replied.

Having said this, Bāhiya entered Sāvatthī in haste. Upon seeing the Blessed One, the Lord of Glory, walking for alms with incomparable Buddha-splendor, he thought, "After a long time, I have finally seen the Gotama, the Fully Enlightened One." From the spot where he first saw him, he approached with a bowed body and, right there in the middle of the street, prostrated with the five-point prostration. Firmly grasping the Blessed One's ankles, he said, "May the Blessed One, venerable sir, teach me the Dhamma. May the Sugata teach me the Dhamma, so that it may be for my long-term welfare and happiness." Then the Teacher refused him, saying, "It is not the right time, Bāhiya; we have entered among the houses for alms."

Hearing the Teacher's words, Bāhiya replied, "Venerable sir, while wandering in Saṃsāra, there is no such thing as not having obtained edible food before. I do not know the danger to the life of the Blessed One or to my own. Please teach me the Dhamma." The Teacher refused him a second time.

The Teacher thought: "From the moment he saw me, this Bāhiya's entire body has been continuously suffused and overwhelmed with rapture. Because of this powerful surge of rapture, he will not be able to penetrate the Dhamma even if he hears it. Let him first settle into neutral equanimity. Moreover, because he has traveled a distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas in a single night, his physical exhaustion is great. Let that exhaustion also subside."

## Attainment of Arahantship and Being Gored by a Cow

For this reason, having refused him twice, when requested for the third time, the Teacher, standing right in the middle of the street, taught the Dhamma in this manner: "Therefore, Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: In the seen, there will be only the seen," and so forth.

Bāhiya—dear Bāhiya. Yasmā—because. Diṭṭhe—in the seen object. Diṭṭhamattaṃ—only the seen. Bhavissati—will be. Tasmā—therefore. Iha—in this world. Te (taya)—by you. Evaṃ—thus. Sikkhitabbaṃ—it should be trained.

While listening to the Teacher's Dhamma, Bāhiya exhausted all taints and attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights. At that very moment of becoming an Arahant, he requested ordination from the Blessed One. When asked, "Are your bowl and robes complete?" he replied, "They are not complete, venerable sir." Then the Teacher said to Bāhiya, "If so, go and seek a bowl and robes," and then departed. 

It is said that while practicing the Dhamma of a recluse for twenty thousand years, he had thought, "A monk should use what he receives for himself without looking to others." Thus, he had never supported or honored another monk with even a single bowl or a single robe. Therefore, the Teacher, knowing that a bowl and robes created by psychic power would not manifest for Bāhiya Dārucīriya, did not grant him ordination by the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' method. While Bāhiya Dārucīriya was wandering about in search of a bowl and robes, a female yakkha in the form of a cow came and gored him in the left thigh, causing his death.

## Building a Stupa and Bestowing the Title of Foremost in Quick Realization
412:
## The Teaching
(101) Though a verse may consist of a thousand words, if they are joined with useless meanings, it is not superior. That single word of a verse, hearing which one is calmed (of passions and so forth), is superior.

The Teacher, having wandered for alms and finished his meal, came out with many monks and saw the body of Bāhiya lying in a rubbish heap. Upon seeing it, he instructed the monks: "Monks, standing at the door of a certain house, have a small couch brought, carry this body out of the city, cremate it, and build a stupa."

The monks did as the Buddha instructed. Having done so, they returned to the monastery, approached the Buddha, reported what they had done, and asked about Bāhiya Dārucīriya's destination in the next life. Then, the Buddha informed those monks of Bāhiya Dārucīriya's attainment of Parinibbāna and declared:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ khippābhiññānaṃ yadidaṃ bāhiyo dārucīriyo."

"Monks, among my monk disciples who possess quick direct knowledge (khippābhiññā), Bāhiya Dārucīriya is the foremost."

Thus, the Buddha placed Bāhiya Dārucīriya in the position of Etadagga. Then the monks asked the Buddha: "Venerable Sir, you say that Bāhiya has reached Arahantship. At what time did Bāhiya reach Arahantship?" "Monks, he reached it at the time he heard my Dhamma," the Buddha replied. "Venerable Sir, when did you preach the Dhamma to Bāhiya?" "While I was walking for alms, standing in the middle of the street," he replied. "Venerable Sir, the Dhamma preached by you while standing in the middle of the street was very brief. How could Bāhiya achieve such high distinction with only that much?" they asked. Then the Buddha said to those monks: "Monks, why do you say so? Do not measure my Dhamma as 'little' or 'much.' Even a thousand verses, if they are based on what is useless, are not superior. If based on benefit, even a single verse is superior." Desiring to connect the sequence and preach the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The story of the Elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya ends.
413:
## 3. The Story of the Elder Nun Kuṇḍalakesī
(Kuṇḍalakesītherī Vatthu)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha preached this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Yo ca gāthāsataṃ bhāse," concerning Kuṇḍalakesī.

## The Merchant's Daughter and Her Union with the Thief
In the city of Rājagaha, there was a merchant's daughter about sixteen years of age, who was extremely beautiful, lovely, and pleasing to behold. Women of that age are often filled with desire for men and are fickle regarding them. At that time, her parents had her stay in a magnificent chamber on the top floor of a seven-storied mansion. They provided her with only one young maidservant as an attendant.

At that time, a young man of good family who had committed a theft was caught. His hands were bound behind his back, and he was being led to the execution ground, being whipped with rods at every crossroads. When the merchant's daughter heard the sound of the great crowd, she wondered, "What is this sound?" Standing on the balcony of the mansion and looking out, she saw the thief and her heart became bound to him in love. Longing for that thief, she rejected her food and lay down on her small couch.

Then her mother asked her, "Dear daughter, what is the reason for you staying like this without eating?" "If I get that man who was caught as a thief and led away, I shall live.
