If I do not get him, I have no life; I shall die right here," she said. The mother replied, "Dear daughter, do not do this. You will get another husband who is equal to us in birth and wealth." "I have no need for any other man. If I do not get this thief, I will die," she insisted. The mother, unable to make the daughter listen, informed the great merchant father. The merchant father also could not make the daughter listen, and thinking, "What can be done?", he sent a man with a bundle of a thousand pieces of money to the king's officer who was leading the thief away, saying, "Take this thousand and give that thief to me."

The officer agreed, took the money, released the thief, and after killing another person, reported to the King, "Your Majesty, the thief has been executed." The merchant then gave his daughter to that thief. From that time on, thinking, "I shall please my husband," the merchant's daughter adorned herself with all kinds of ornaments and personally prepared gruel and other foods for the thief.

## The Plot to Kill the Merchant's Daughter for Her Belongings
After two or three days had passed, the thief plotted: "When shall I be able to kill this merchant's daughter, take her ornaments, sell them at a tavern, and enjoy the proceeds?" Having plotted thus, the thief thought, "There is one way," and he rejected his food and lay down on his small couch. Then the merchant's daughter approached him and asked, "My lord, what pain do you have?" "Dear sister, I have no pain at all," he said. "Then what is it? Are my mother and father angry with you?" she asked. "Dear sister, they are not angry," he replied. "If that is so, what is the reason for this?" she asked again. "Dear sister, on that day when I was bound and led away, I vowed to make a sacrificial offering to the deity who guards the cliff where thieves are thrown, and thus I regained my life. It is only through the power of that deity that I have obtained you."
414:
"My dear, I have vowed to make a sacrificial offering to the deity," he said. When she asked what it was, he replied, "My dear, on the day I was being led away bound, I promised an offering to the deity dwelling at the Robbers' Cliff and thus gained my life. You too were obtained by me through the power of that very deity. I am thinking, 'I must fulfill my vow to the deity,' my dear."

"My lord, do not worry. I will perform the offering. Tell me, what is required?"

"Sweet milk-rice prepared with little water, and flowers including parched rice as the fifth kind."

"Very well, my lord, I shall prepare it," she said. Having prepared all the sacrificial offerings, the merchant's daughter said, "Come, my lord, let us go."

"In that case, my dear, send back your relatives, take your expensive clothes and ornaments, and adorn yourself. We shall go happily, laughing and playing."

She did as the thief said. Then, when they reached the foot of the mountain, he said to her, "My dear, from here onwards only the two of us will go. Send back the rest of the people along with the carriage, and you yourself carry the vessel of offerings."

She did as the thief said. The thief took her and climbed the mountain where thieves are thrown.

(One side of that mountain is accessible to people. The other side is a sheer precipice. Standing at the top of the mountain, they throw thieves down that side. They fall to the ground, breaking into pieces. Therefore, it is called 'Corapapāta' [Robbers' Cliff].)

## The Merchant's Daughter's Plea

Standing at the top of that mountain, the merchant's daughter said, "My lord, perform your sacrificial offering." The thief remained silent. Again, when she asked, "My lord, why are you silent?" he said to her, "I have no need for the offering; I have brought you here by deception."

"For what reason, my lord?" she asked.

"To kill you, take your ornaments, and flee."

Threatened by the fear of death, she was terrified and said, "My lord, both I and these ornaments belong to you. Why do you speak like this?"

Although she pleaded repeatedly, saying "Do not do this," he replied, "I will certainly kill you."

"If that is so, what benefit is there for you in my death? Take these ornaments and grant me my life. From now on, consider me as dead, or let me live as your slave, performing all your tasks." Saying this, she uttered this verse:

"These golden armlets, all adorned with lapis lazuli—
Take all these ornaments, my lord; may you be blessed.
And declare me to be your slave."

(My lord, may you be blessed. All these golden armlets and ornaments are inlaid with lapis lazuli. Take all these ornaments, and declare me to be your servant and slave.)
415:
Do not lament excessively; quickly tie up the bundle of ornaments.
There is no life for you; I shall take all the goods.

*Bāle*, O foolish woman! *Bāḷhaṃ*, excessively. *Mā paridevesi*, do not lament. *Khippaṃ*, quickly. *Bhaṇḍikaṃ*, the bundle of ornaments. *Bandhāhi*, tie up. *Tuyhaṃ*, for you. *Vā*, (alternative grammatical marker). *Jīvitaṃ*, life. *Na atthi*, there is none. *Sabbaṃ*, all. *Bhaṇḍakaṃ*, the goods. *Gaṇhāmi*, I shall take.

A man is not wise in all circumstances.
A woman, too, is wise, being discerning in various matters.

*Bho*, O friends! *Sabbesu ṭhānesu*, in all circumstances. *Puriso*, a man. *Paṇḍito*, wise. *Na hoti*, is not. *Itthīpi*, a woman too. *Tattha tattha*, in various matters. *Vicakkhaṇā*, being endowed with discerning wisdom. *Paṇḍitā*, wise. *Hoti*, is.

Hearing those words, the thief said, "If I do this, you will go back and tell your parents. I will certainly kill you; do not lament excessively," and he spoke this verse.

## The Deity’s Applause upon the Thief’s Death
The merchant's daughter thought, "Oh, this matter is very heavy indeed. Wisdom is not made for the purpose of cooking and eating; rather, it is made for the purpose of reflection and investigation. I shall see what must be done to this thief." Then she said to the thief, "My lord, when you were captured as a thief and being led away, I told my parents. They sacrificed a thousand pieces of money to have you released and brought you to live in our house. Since then, I have been of great service to you. Today, I wish for you to allow me to see you clearly and pay homage to you."

The thief said, "Dear lady, very well; see me clearly and pay homage," and he stood at the edge of the mountain. Then the merchant's daughter circumambulated him three times to the right and paid homage at the four directions, saying, "My lord, this is my last sight of you. Now, there will be no more seeing me for you, nor seeing you for me." She embraced him from the front and back, and while he was off guard, standing at the edge of the mountain, she stood behind him, grabbed his shoulders with one hand and the hem of his garment at the back with the other, and threw him down the mountain precipice. The thief struck the mountain slope, was broken into pieces, and fell to the ground. The deity residing at the top of the "Corapapāta" (Thieves' Cliff) saw the actions of both and, giving a cry of "Sādhu" to the woman, recited this verse.

(If one gives praise focusing only on the good wisdom and reflection used to escape danger, there is no fault. However, if one gives praise out of delight in the killing of the thief, it falls under the category of "doing it oneself, inciting others, consenting, and praising," all of which are blameworthy.)

## Becoming a Paribbājikā After Killing the Husband
After throwing the thief down the precipice, the merchant's daughter thought, "If I go home, they will ask, 'Where is your husband?' If I am asked and I say, 'I killed him,' they will pierce me with the spears of their mouths, saying, 'You wretched woman, we spent a thousand pieces to bring that man, and now you have killed him!' Even if I say, 'He wanted to kill me for my ornaments,' they will not believe me. There is no use in my returning home." Thinking thus, she discarded her ornaments right there, entered the forest, and wandering along, reached a hermitage of female wandering ascetics (*paribbājikās*). She said, "Ladies, please grant me ordination in your presence." Then they ordained her. As soon as she was ordained, she asked, "Ladies, what is the highest practice in your ordination?" They replied, "Sister, one should either develop *jhāna* by practicing with the ten *kasiṇas* or learn a thousand doctrines. This is the highest benefit in our ordination." She said, "Ladies, I am not yet able to attain *jhāna* first, but I will be able to learn the thousand doctrines."

## Challenging to a Debate with a Rose-apple Branch
416:
Then, having made the merchant's daughter learn a thousand arguments, they said, "You have learned the craft. Now, wander throughout the surface of Jambudīpa and look for those capable of debating with you." Giving a rose-apple branch into the hand of the female ascetic, they sent her off, saying, "Go, sister. If a layman is able to debate with you, become his foot-servant (wife). If a monk is able, ordain in his presence."

She became known by the name "Jambu Paribbājikā." Leaving that grove, she wandered about asking questions of everyone she saw. There was no one capable of debating with her. Upon hearing the words, "Jambu Paribbājikā is coming here," people would flee. When entering a village or market town for alms, she would make a heap of sand at the village gate, plant the rose-apple branch there, and say, "Let him who is capable of debating with me trample and destroy this rose-apple branch," and then enter the village. There was no one capable of approaching that spot. When one rose-apple branch withered, the merchant's daughter would take another. Wandering in this manner, she reached Sāvatthī, placed the branch at the gate, spoke as before, and entered for alms. Many village children stood surrounding the rose-apple branch.

## The Debate with Venerable Sāriputta

Then, the Elder Sāriputta, while wandering for alms and having finished his meal, came out of the city. Seeing the children surrounding the rose-apple branch, he asked, "What is this?" The children explained the matter to the Elder. "Children, if that is so, trample and destroy this branch," he said. "Venerable sir, we are afraid," they replied. "I will answer the questions. Trample and destroy it without fear," he said. Encouraged by the Elder's words, the children trampled and destroyed the rose-apple branch, pulling it up and throwing it away just as the Elder Sāriputta had instructed. The female ascetic returned and scolded the children, saying, "I have no business debating with you. Why did you trample and destroy my branch?" They said, "The Elder Sāriputta made us trample it." She then asked, "Venerable sir, did you cause my branch to be destroyed?" "Yes, sister, I did," he replied. "If that is so, please answer my questions," she said.

## Unable to Answer the Question "What is the One?"

"Very well, I shall answer them," he said. When the shadows lengthened in the afternoon, the female ascetic went to the Elder Sāriputta to ask her questions. The whole of Sāvatthī was in an uproar. "Let us listen to the talk of the two wise ones," the citizens said, following her to the Elder, paying homage, and sitting to one side. The female ascetic said to the Elder, "Venerable sir, I will now ask the questions." "Ask, sister," he replied. 

The female ascetic then asked a thousand arguments. The Elder Sāriputta answered every question she asked. Then the Elder said to the female ascetic, "Is this the extent of your questions? Are there any others?" "Venerable sir, there are only these thousand," she replied. "You have asked many questions,"
417:
"We shall also ask a single question; will you answer our question?" he said. "Venerable sir, if I know it, I will answer; please ask," she replied. Then the Elder asked the question: "Ekaṃ nāma kiṃ? (What is the one?)" The wanderer did not know how this question should be answered and asked, "Venerable sir, what is the name of this question?" "Sister, it is called a Buddha's question," he replied.

(The answer is: Sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā. All beings—meaning the five aggregates—subsist on nutriment, which is the cause of their existence.)

## Becoming a Bhikkhunī and Attaining Arahantship

"Venerable sir, please give that question to me as well," she requested. "If you become like me, I shall give it," he said. "In that case, please ordain me, venerable sir," she replied. Then the Elder Sāriputta informed the bhikkhunīs and had her ordained. When the wanderer named "Jambū" received ordination, she became known as "Kuṇḍalakesī Therī." Within just a few days, she attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā).

The monks then started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Kuṇḍalakesī Therī did not have much experience in hearing the Dhamma, yet she reached the pinnacle of a recluse's duty. It is said she came here after winning a great battle against a thief."

The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?" When they replied, "It is such and such, Bhante," the Teacher said: "Monks, do not measure the Dhamma I have taught as 'little' or 'much.' Even a hundred verses are not noble if they are connected with what is useless; even a single word of Dhamma is noble if it brings about benefit. Victory does not truly belong to one who conquers ordinary external thieves; victory truly belongs only to one who conquers the internal thieves of defilements (kilesa)." Having thus made the connection, he spoke these verses to teach the Dhamma:

## The Teaching

(102) Yo ca gāthāsataṃ bhāse, anatthapadasañhitaṃ.
Ekaṃ dhammupadaṃ seyyo, yaṃ sutvā upasammati.

(103) Yo sahassaṃ sahassena, saṅgāme mānuse jine.
Ekañca jeyyamattānaṃ, sa ve saṅgāmajutttamo.

Even if one should recite a hundred verses composed of useless words, those verses are not noble. That single word of Dhamma is noble which, upon hearing, brings peace from passions such as lust.

A warrior might conquer a million men (a thousand times a thousand) on the battlefield. Such a person is a conqueror among conquerors on the battlefield. However, the practitioner (yogāvacara) who conquers himself—who is but one—is indeed the greatest of all victors on the battlefield, a supreme general.
418:
## Benefits of the Teaching

At the conclusion of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The Story of Kuṇḍalakesī Therī ends.

## Six Things Leading to Ruin (Anattha)

Ussūraseyyaṃ ālasyaṃ, caṇḍikkaṃ dīghasoṇḍiyaṃ.
Ekassaddhānagamanaṃ, paradārūpasevanaṃ.
Etaṃ brāhmaṇa sevassu, anatthaṃ te bhavissati.

Brahmin, sleeping until sunrise, laziness, harshness and irritability, long-term addiction to intoxicants, traveling a long distance alone, and committing adultery with another's wife—these six exist. Brahmin, you should try to indulge in these six things; then ruin (anattha) will surely come to you.

## 4. The Story of the Brahmin who Asked about Ruin

(Anatthapucchaka-brāhmaṇa-vatthu)

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Attā hauve," concerning a Brahmin named Anatthapucchaka.

That Brahmin thought, "I wonder if the All-Knowing Buddha knows only what is beneficial (attha), or if he also knows what is harmful (anattha). I shall ask him about this matter." He approached the Teacher and asked, "Magnificent Buddha, I believe you know only what is beneficial, and do not know what is harmful."

"Brahmin, I know what is beneficial and I also know what is harmful," the Teacher replied. "In that case, please teach me about what is harmful," the Brahmin requested. Then the Teacher spoke this verse to the Brahmin.
419:
## The Teaching
(104) Self-conquest is indeed better than [conquering] these other people. For a man who has tamed himself and always lives restrained in conduct.
(105) Neither a god, nor a gandhabba, nor Māra together with Brahmā, can turn into defeat the victory of such a person.

*Attadantassa*: of one who has tamed himself. *Niccaṃ*: always. *Saññatacarino*: of one whose conduct is restrained in body, speech, and mind. *Tathārūpassa*: of such a nature. *Jantuno*: of a being. *Posassa*: of one who can be called a man. *Jitaṃ*: victory/conquest. *Apajitaṃ*: into defeat. *Devo vā*: even a god. *Neva kayirā*: cannot make. *Gandhabbo vā*: even a gandhabba. *Na kayirā*: cannot make. *Brahmunā saha*: together with Brahmā. *Māro vā*: even Māra. *Na kayirā*: cannot make. *Tasmā*: therefore. *Tassa*: of that great man. *Jitaṃ - jito*: the victory achieved by conquering the defilements. *Attā*: the self. *Have*: indeed. *Seyyo*: is excellent. *Itarā*: other than this, such as winning at dice or in war. *Yā ca ayaṃ pajā*: those other beings who exist. *Tassā pajāya*: of those beings. *Jitaṃ - jito*: the victory achieved in games and such. *Attā*: the self. *Na seyyo*: is not excellent.

Upon hearing these words, the old Brahmin praised the Buddha, saying, "O Great Teacher, the Supreme Leader of all groups—excellent, excellent, Blessed One! You truly know what is beneficial and what is harmful." The Buddha replied, "Brahmin, there is no one like me who knows benefit and harm in this way." Then, discerning the Brahmin's inclination, the Buddha asked, "Brahmin, how do you earn your living?" When he replied, "Great Gotama, I earn my living by playing dice," the Buddha asked again, "How is it for you? Do you win or do you lose?" He replied, "I win sometimes, and I lose sometimes, Bhante." The Buddha then said, "Brahmin, this winning is but a small thing. The victory of one who conquers others is not excellent. Only the victory of one who conquers himself by overcoming defilements is truly excellent. No one can turn the victory of such a self-conquered person into defeat." Connecting the discourse, He spoke these verses:

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The Story of the Brahmin Anatthapucchaka ends.
420:
## The Teaching
(106) Month after month, one might sacrifice a thousand [pieces of money] for a hundred years; yet if one were to honor, even for a moment, a single person who has developed himself, that honor is indeed better than a hundred years of sacrifice.

*Yo*: whichever person. *Sataṃ*: a hundred. *Samaṃ*: years. Or *Sataṃsamaṃ*: for the duration of a hundred years. *Māse māse*: month after month. *Sahassena*: by sacrificing a thousand pieces of wealth. *Yajetha*: should offer and honor ordinary persons. *Yo ca*: and whichever person. *Bhāvitattānaṃ*: an Ariya (Noble One) whose mind is greatly developed and permeated with the qualities of insight (vipassanā). *Ekañca*: even a single such person. *Muhuttamapi*: even for a moment. *Pūjaye*: should honor and offer to. *Tesaṃ*: of those two people. *Pūjanāsu*: among their offerings. *Sāyeva pūjanā*: that very act of honoring an Ariya for even a moment. *Seyyo*: is excellent. *Vassasataṃ*: for a hundred years. *Hutaṃ*: the sacrifice made to ordinary persons. *Yañce seyya*: is not excellent.

## 5. The Story of Venerable Sāriputta's Uncle
(Sāriputtatherassa Mātulabrāhmaṇavatthu)
While residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching starting with "Māse māse," concerning the uncle of the Elder Sāriputta.

## Sacrificing to Ascetics Desiring the Brahma World
The Elder Sāriputta went to his uncle, the Brahmin, and asked, "Brahmin, do you perform any kind of meritorious deed?" "I do, Bhante," he replied. "What kind of merit do you perform?" "Month after month, I give alms by sacrificing a thousand pieces of wealth, Bhante." "To whom do you give?" "To the Nigaṇṭhas (naked ascetics), Bhante." "Desiring what benefit do you give?" "Desiring the Brahma world, Bhante." "Brahmin, is this way of giving the path to reaching the Brahma world?" "Yes, Bhante, it is the path." "Who told you so?"

"My teachers told me, Bhante." "Neither you nor your teachers know the path to the Brahma world. Only the one Buddha knows. Come, Brahmin, I will have the path to the Brahma world explained to you." Saying this, he took the Brahmin to the Buddha and reported, "Exalted Buddha, this Brahmin says such and such. I pray, Blessed One, please teach this Brahmin the path to the Brahma world." The Buddha asked, "Brahmin, is it true as Sāriputta says?" When he replied, "Yes, Great Gotama, it is true," the Buddha said, "Brahmin, rather than the alms you have given for a hundred years in this manner, even a moment's looking upon my disciple, the Saṅgha, with a confident heart, or giving even a single spoonful of alms-food, is far more fruitful." Connecting the discourse, He spoke this verse:
421:
## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, the great brahmin attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). Many others besides the great brahmin also attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The story of Venerable Sāriputta's maternal uncle is finished.

## The Teaching
(107) Though a person should tend the fire in the forest for a hundred years, yet if he were to honor even for a moment one who has developed himself, that honor is indeed better than the sacrifice offered for a hundred years.

Yo ca jantu, and whatever being. Vassasataṃ, for a period of a hundred years. Vane, in the forest. Aggiṃ, the fire. Paricare, should tend. Yo ca, and whatever person. Ekañca, even one. Bhāvitattānaṃ, a noble person (Ariya) whose mind is developed through the excellence of insight (vipassanā). Muhuttamapi, even for a moment. Pūjaye, should honor. Tesu, among those two people. Tassa, of that second person. Sāyeva pūjanā, that very honoring alone. Seyyo, is better. Vassasataṃ, for a hundred years. Hutaṃ, the sacrifice of fire by killing animals. Yañce seyyo, is not better (than that).

## 6. The Story of Venerable Sāriputta’s Nephew
(Sāriputtatt herassa Bhāgineyyavatthu)
While residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Teacher told this Dhamma teaching, "Yo ca vassasataṃ jantu," etc., concerning the brahmin who was the nephew of Venerable Sāriputta.

## Sacrificing to Fire with Animals Desiring the Brahma World
Venerable Sāriputta approached his nephew and asked, "Young brahmin, do you perform any meritorious deeds?" When he replied, "Yes, venerable sir, I do," the Elder asked again, "What merit do you perform?" "Every month, I kill one animal and tend the fire, venerable sir." When asked, "For what purpose do you do this?", he replied, "It is said that this tending of fire is the path to the Brahma world." "Who told you this?" "Venerable sir, my teachers told me."

"Neither you nor your teachers know the path to the Brahma world. Come, let us go to the Teacher." He took his nephew to the Buddha, reported the matter, and said, "Exalted One, please teach the path to the Brahma world to this brahmin." The Teacher asked, "Is it so?" and when the brahmin replied, "Yes, Master Gotama, it is so," the Teacher said, "Brahmin, even if you tend the fire in this way for a hundred years, your fire-tending does not equal even a moment's honor paid to my disciples, the Saṅgha." Connecting the sequence and wishing to teach the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, the brahmin attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). Many others besides the brahmin also attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The story of Venerable Sāriputta's nephew is finished.
422:
## The Teaching
(108) Whatever sacrifice or offering a person seeking merit might make in the world for a whole year, all that does not equal a fourth part of the homage paid to those who are upright; homage to the upright is better.

Loke, in the world. Puññapekkho, desiring merit. Yaṃ kiñci, whatever without exception. Yiṭṭhaṃ vā, a great sacrifice well-given by way of performing auspicious ceremonies and so forth. Hutaṃ vā, a small sacrifice prepared and offered in various ways to noble guests; or a gift given with faith in kamma and its results. Vassasataṃ, for a whole year. Mahājanassapi, even to the common people gathered from the whole universe. Yajetha, if one should offer or honor. Taṃ sabbampi, all those great and small sacrifices and gifts. Ujjugatesu, towards the noble ones (Ariyas) who are upright. Abhivādanā - abhivādanāya, of the meritorious intention of paying homage. Catubhāgaṃ, a fourth part. Na eti, does not reach or is not worth. Tasmā, therefore. Abhivādanameva, only the paying of homage to the noble ones. Seyyo, is better.

## 7. The Story of Venerable Sāriputta’s Friend
(Sāriputtatt herassa Sahāyakabrāhmaṇavatthu)
While residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Teacher told this Dhamma teaching, "Yaṃ kiñci yiṭṭhaṃ va," etc., concerning the brahmin who was the friend of Venerable Sāriputta.

## Performing Great Sacrifices Desiring the Brahma World
Venerable Sāriputta approached his friend and asked, "Brahmin, how is it? Do you perform any meritorious deeds?" When he replied, "Yes, venerable sir, I do," the Elder asked again, "What merit do you perform?" He replied, "I perform sacrifices to the extent of a great sacrifice, venerable sir."

After asking all that was to be asked, he took the brahmin to the Buddha, reported the matter, and said, "Exalted One, please teach the path to the Brahma world to this brahmin." The Teacher asked, "Brahmin, is it so?" and he replied, "Yes, Master Gotama, it is so." "Brahmin, the gift you give to the common people for a whole year by performing great sacrifices does not reach or equal even a fourth part of the meritorious intention that arises in those who pay homage with a devout heart to my disciples, the noble disciples (Ariya-sāvakas)." Connecting the sequence and wishing to teach the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

## Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, the brahmin attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). Many others besides the brahmin also attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The story of Venerable Sāriputta's friend is finished.
423:
## 8. The Story of the Youth Āyuvaḍḍhana
(Āyuvaḍḍhanakumāra-vatthu)
The Teacher told this Dhamma teaching while residing in the forest hut known as Araññakuṭi near the city of Dīghalaṅghika, concerning the youth Dīghāyu.

## The Brahmin Who Worried Excessively
Two brahmins living in the city of Dīghalaṅghika went forth as external ascetics and practiced asceticism (tapacaraṇa) for forty-eight years. Among those two brahmins, one thought, "My lineage will perish; I will return to the lay life." Having sold the merit of his practices to others, he obtained a wife along with a hundred cows and a hundred kahāpaṇas, and established a household. Later, that brahmin's wife gave birth to a son. His companion, the ascetic brahmin, went to another place and eventually returned to the city of Dīghalaṅghika. When the brahmin heard of his friend's return, he took his wife and son to see him. Upon arrival, he placed the son in the mother's hands and paid respects himself first. The mother then placed the son in the father's hands and paid respects herself. The ascetic said, "Dīghāyukā hotha—May you both live long." However, when the young son was made to pay respects, he remained silent.

(It is said that earthworms eat and then spit out soil for fear that the earth will run out. Plovers sleep on their backs with their legs up for fear that the sky will collapse. Cranes do not drink water for fear that the water will run out. Brahmins who practice the Dhamma give up their practice and marry for fear that their lineage will perish. These are the four confused ones who worry excessively. Some also say that elephants tread lightly for fear that the earth will collapse.)

## No Blessing Due to Danger
Then, the brahmin asked the ascetic, "Venerable sir, why did you say 'Dīghāyukā hotha' when we paid respects, but said nothing when this young son paid respects? Is there some danger for this child?" "Lay brahmin, there is danger for this child," he replied. "Venerable sir, how long will he live?" he asked again. "Lay brahmin, he will live for only seven days," was the reply. "Venerable sir, is there a way to prevent it?" he asked. "I do not know the way to prevent it," the ascetic said. "Venerable sir, who might know?" he asked. "The Ascetic Gotama would know; go to him and ask," he said. When suggested to go there, the brahmin said, "I am afraid of the decline of my ascetic practice." "If you have love for your son, do not think about the decline of your practice; just go to the Ascetic Gotama and ask," the friend replied. Then the brahmin went to the Buddha and paid respects himself first. The Buddha said, "Dīghāyuko hohi—May you live long." When the wife paid respects, He gave her the same blessing, but when the young son paid respects, He remained silent.

The brahmin questioned the Buddha in the same manner as before. The Buddha also answered in the same way.
424:
(Although that ascetic brahmin could not penetrate the Omniscient Knowledge, he compared his own mantra knowledge with the Omniscient Knowledge. However, he did not know the means to prevent the danger.)

## Protecting from the Demon's Danger by Chanting Paritta
The brahmin asked the Buddha, "Exalted Buddha, is there a way to prevent the danger?" "It is possible, great brahmin," He replied. "How should it be done, Lord?" he asked. "If you build a pavilion (maṇḍapa) at the entrance of your house, place a platform (pīṭhikā) in the middle of that pavilion, arrange eight or sixteen seats surrounding that platform, and have the monks who are my disciples sit in those seats to chant paritta protection continuously for seven days, then the danger to this child may be averted," He said. "O Great Gotama, I am able to build the pavilion and so on, but where can I get the monks who are your disciples?" he asked. "If you do this much, I will send my disciple monks," He said. "Very well, O Great Gotama," the brahmin agreed joyfully. Having completed all the tasks at the entrance of his house, he went to the Buddha. The Buddha sent the monks. The monks went and sat in those places. They had the child lie on the platform. The monks chanted paritta continuously for seven nights. On the seventh day, the Buddha Himself arrived. When the Buddha arrived, all the deities in the universe assembled. A demon (yakkha) named Avaruddhaka had served King Vessavaṇa for twelve years and had received a boon from him: "On the seventh day from now, you may take this child." Therefore, the demon Avaruddhaka also came and stood there.

When the Buddha arrived at that place, powerful deities assembled. When the powerful deities assembled, the lesser deities retreated further and further, and finding no space, they had to move away as far as twelve leagues (yojanas). The demon Avaruddhaka also had to retreat to that distance of twelve leagues. The Buddha Himself performed the paritta protection throughout the night.

## How He Was Named Āyuvaḍḍhana
When the seven days had passed, the demon Avaruddhaka could not get the child. On the eighth day, just as dawn broke, they brought the child and made him pay respects to the Buddha. The Buddha blessed him, saying, "Dīghāyuko hohi—May you, young man, live long." When asked, "O Great Gotama, how long will this child live?" He replied, "Great brahmin, he will live for one hundred and twenty years." At that time, they named the child "Youth Āyuvaḍḍhana" (The Increaser of Life). When this youth Āyuvaḍḍhana reached maturity, he traveled about surrounded by five hundred lay followers (upāsakas). Then one day, in the Dhamma hall, the monks raised a discussion: "Friends, do you see? The youth Āyuvaḍḍhana was supposed to die on the seventh day."
425:
## The Teaching

(109) Abhivādanasīlissa, niccaṃ vuḍḍhāpacāyino.
Cattāro dhammā vaḍḍhanti, āyu vaṇṇo sukhaṃ balaṃ.

Niccaṃ: always. Abhivādanasīlissa: for one who is in the habit of bowing respectfully. Vuḍḍhāpacāyino: for one who honors those who are senior in age, virtue, or seniority. Puggalassa: for such a person. Āyu ca: the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) also. Vaṇṇo ca: beauty also. Sukhañca: happiness also. Balañca: strength also. Iti: in this way. Cattāro: these four. Dhammā: beneficial qualities. Vaḍḍhanti: increase.

"This person will now be able to live for one hundred and twenty years," and so he traveled about surrounded by five hundred lay followers. People began to say, "How wonderful it is that there is a cause for these beings to live a long life!" The Blessed One arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?" When they replied, "We are gathered to discuss this matter, Bhante," the Buddha said, "Monks, it is not just about living a long life; when these beings honor those possessed of virtue, they can increase in four qualities. They can be free from danger and live out their full lifespan." Desiring to connect the sequence and teach the Dhamma, he spoke this verse.

## Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, the youth Āyuvaḍḍhana, together with five hundred lay followers, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Many others also reached the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

The story of the youth Āyuvaḍḍhana ends.

## 9. The Story of the Novice Saṅkicca

(Saṅkicca Sāmaṇera Vatthu)

The Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana monastery, told this Dhamma teaching starting with "Yo ca vassasataṃ jīve" concerning the novice Saṅkicca.

## Foreseeing the Danger

In Sāvatthī, about thirty sons of good family, having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Buddha, ordained in the Buddha's Dispensation with unwavering minds. When these monks had reached five vassa (years) since their higher ordination, they approached the Teacher. Having heard about the two duties—the duty of study (ganthadhura) and the duty of insight (vipassanādhura)—they felt unable to strive in the duty of study because they had ordained in their old age. Desiring to fulfill the duty of insight, they requested, "Bhante, please teach us the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) leading up to Arahantship." After receiving the teaching, they asked the Buddha for permission, saying, "Exalted Buddha, we wish to go to a certain forest dwelling."

The Buddha asked, "Monks, where will you go?" When they named the place, the Buddha realized, "In that place, a danger will arise for these monks because of a certain scavenger (vighāsāda). However, that danger will be calmed if the novice Saṅkicca goes with them. Then, the goal of their monkhood will reach fulfillment."

## How the Future Novice Came into the Human World

The one known as the novice Saṅkicca was a novice disciple of the Elder Sāriputta. He was only seven years old from birth. The mother of that novice was the daughter of a wealthy family in Sāvatthī. While the future novice Saṅkicca was in her womb, she died suddenly of a certain disease. When her body was being cremated, the entire body burned except for the flesh of the womb. Then, they removed the flesh of the womb from the pyre and poked it with stakes in two or three places. The tip of a stake struck the corner of the child's eye. In this way, after poking the flesh of the womb, they threw it into a heap of embers, covered it with embers, and left. Only the flesh of the womb burned away, but on top of the embers, the child, who had a complexion like gold, appeared as if he were lying inside a lotus.

(For a being in his final birth (pacchimabhavika), even if he were pressed by Mount Meru, there can be no end of life until he reaches Arahantship.)
426:
## How He Came to be Named Saṅkicca

Then, on the following morning, those who came to extinguish the funeral pyre saw the child lying in that manner. Filled with wonder and amazement, they thought, "Why is it that while so much wood has been consumed and the whole body burned, this child is not burned? What will become of him?" They took the child to the village and asked the fortune-tellers. The fortune-tellers said, "If this child lives as a householder, his relatives and kinsmen up to the seventh generation will become poor. If he ordains as a monk, he will travel about surrounded by five hundred monks." Because the corner of his eye was broken by the stake (saṅku) that struck him, they named him "Saṅkicca." Later on, he became well-known by the name Saṅkicca. Then his relatives thought, "Let it be as the fortune-tellers said; when he grows up, we will have him ordained under our master, the Elder Sāriputta," and they raised him.

## The Novice Saṅkicca Attaining Arahantship

When the boy was seven years old, he was told, "Dear boy, while you were in your mother's womb, your mother died. Even when her body was being cremated, you were not burned." Upon hearing these words from his relatives, the boy thought, "I have been freed from such a danger. What is the use of living in a house? I will become a monk." He informed his relatives of his wish. The relatives agreed, saying, "Very well, dear boy," and took him to the Elder Sāriputta, saying, "Bhante, please ordain this boy." The Elder gave him the meditation on the five parts of the body ending in skin (taca-pañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna) and ordained him. At the very end of the shaving of his hair, the novice Saṅkicca reached Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). This is the novice known as Saṅkicca.

## Sending the Novice to the Forest Monastery

The Teacher, knowing that "If the novice Saṅkicca goes along, that danger will be calmed, and then the goal of their monkhood will reach fulfillment," said, "Monks, go after seeing your elder brother, the Elder Sāriputta." The monks replied, "Very well, Bhante," and went to the presence of the Elder.
427:
When they went to the elder and were asked, "What is the reason, friends?" they replied, "Venerable sir, we have taken meditation subjects from the Teacher and wish to enter the forest. The Teacher told us, 'Go after seeing your elder brother.' Therefore, we have come here." The elder thought, "The Teacher must have seen a reason for sending these monks here."

Reflecting on what that reason could be, he understood it and said, "Friends, do you have a novice?" "No, venerable sir," they replied. "Friends, if you have none, take this novice Saṅkicca and go," he said. "Venerable sir, we do not need one. Having a novice would be a burden for us. What use is a novice for those living in the forest?" they replied. "Friends, this novice Saṅkicca will not be a burden to you; rather, you will be a burden to him. Moreover, when the Teacher sent you to me, he did so expecting that I would send the novice with you. Take him and go," he said. Saying "Very well, venerable sir," the thirty-one monks took leave of the elder Sāriputta and departed from the monastery. While traveling, they reached a village of a thousand families, a hundred and twenty leagues away.

When the people saw the monks, their hearts were filled with faith. They served them respectfully and asked, "Venerable sirs, where are you going?" When told, "To a place that is comfortable, lay followers," they prostrated at their feet and requested, "Venerable sirs, if you stay here for the Rains Retreat, we will take the five precepts and observe the Uposatha." The elders consented. Then the people prepared night quarters, day quarters, walking paths, and leaf-roofed huts, and served them with great effort, saying, "Today we shall serve, tomorrow we shall serve."

## The Mutual Agreement

On the day of entering the Rains Retreat, the elders made an agreement: "Friends, we have taken meditation subjects from the living Buddha. It is not proper to please the Buddhas with any practice other than the fulfillment of the practice. For us, the gates of the lower realms are wide open. Therefore, except for the time of going for alms in the early morning and the time of attending to the senior elder in the evening, we shall not be together in one place. If any monk becomes unwell or falls ill, he should strike the bell, and we will go to him and provide medicine. At all other times, whether by night or by day, we shall diligently apply ourselves to our meditation subjects without negligence."

## The Arrival of the Scavenger

While they were living according to this agreement, a poor man who lived by depending on his daughter experienced a famine in that place. Wishing to live by depending on another daughter, he set out on a journey. As the elders were returning to their dwelling after wandering for alms in the village...
428:
...they bathed in a river along the way and sat on a sandbank to eat their meal. At that moment, the poor man arrived at that spot and stood to one side. The elders asked him, "Where are you going?" He explained his situation. The elders, moved by compassion for the poor man, said, "Lay follower, you seem very hungry. Go, bring a leaf, and we will each give you a morsel of rice." When he brought the leaf, they each gave him a morsel of rice mixed with curry and side dishes, just as they were eating themselves.

(It is said that this is the proper conduct: a monk who wishes to give food to someone who arrives while he is eating should not give the first portion, but should give a little or much in the same manner as he himself is eating. Therefore, the monks gave in that way.)

When the man had finished his meal, he paid homage to the elders and asked, "Venerable sirs, were you invited by someone?" "No, lay follower, there was no invitation. People offer such food every day," they replied. He thought, "Even though we work hard all the time, we cannot get such food. What is the use of going elsewhere? I will live right here with these monks." Then he said to them, "I wish to stay with you, venerable sirs, performing duties and services." "Very well, lay follower," they said. He went with them to their dwelling place and served them well, greatly pleasing the monks. After two months, he wished to see his daughter and thought, "If I ask the venerable sirs for permission, they will not let me go. I will go without asking." So, he departed without informing them.

(This was his only gross mistake: departing without informing the monks.)

## The Ingratitude of the Scavenger

On the path he took, there was a forest. In that forest, five hundred robbers were living, having made a vow to a deity: "Whoever enters this forest, we will kill him and make a sacrifice to you with his flesh and blood." It was now the seventh day of their vow. Therefore, on the seventh day, the robber chief climbed a tree to keep watch. Seeing the poor man approaching, he gave a signal to the robbers.
429:
Knowing that the poor man had entered the middle of the forest, the thieves surrounded and captured him, binding him firmly. They produced fire using a fire-drill and a spindle, piled up firewood to make a great bonfire, and sharpened spits. Seeing their actions, the poor man asked, "Masters, neither pigs nor deer are seen in this place; for what reason are you doing this?"

"We will kill you and make a sacrificial offering to the deity with your flesh and blood," they replied. Terrified by the fear of death and unmindful of the monks' kindness, the man, seeking only to save his own life, said: "Masters, I am an eater of leftovers (vighāsāda). I have grown up eating discarded food. One who is an eater of leftovers is a wretched person (kāḷakaṇṇi). But the noble ones who have gone forth from various families are of the warrior-noble (Khattiya) class. Thirty-one monks reside in such-and-such a place. Kill those monks and make your sacrifice; the deity will be exceedingly pleased with you."

Hearing this, the thieves thought, "This man speaks well," and "What is the use of this wretched person? We shall kill the monks of the warrior-noble class and make the sacrifice." They said, "Come, show us where they live." Making that same poor man their guide, they reached the place. Not seeing the monks in the middle of the monastery, they asked him, "Where are the monks?" Having lived there for two months, the man knew their routine and said, "They are sitting in their respective places for day-seclusion and night-seclusion. Strike this bell; they will assemble at the sound of the bell." The leader of the thieves struck the bell.

## The Monks' Consultation Due to the Danger of Thieves

Hearing the sound of the bell, the monks thought, "The bell is struck at an improper time; someone must be unwell." They came and sat on the stone slabs prepared in order in the middle of the monastery. The Senior Elder (Saṅghatthera), looking at the thieves, asked, "Lay followers, who struck this bell?"

The leader of the thieves replied, "Venerable sir, I struck it." "For what reason?" "We have made a vow to a forest deity. To perform the sacrifice, we wish to take one monk and go." Hearing this, the Great Elder said to the monks, "Friends, a matter concerning the younger brothers must be resolved by the elder brother. I will sacrifice my life for you and go with these men. Let there be no danger to all of you. Practice the recluse's Dhamma diligently (appamāda)."

The second elder below the Great Elder also said, "Venerable sir, a matter concerning the elder brother is the responsibility of the younger brother. I will go. May you all be diligent in practicing the recluse's Dhamma." In this manner, saying "I will go, I will go," all thirty monks rose in order.
430:
(Thus, those thirty monks were not sons of the same mother, nor sons of the same father, nor were they Arahants free from passion; yet, for the sake of the others, they sacrificed their lives in turn. Among these monks, there was not even one who was capable of saying, "You go, you go.")

## Novice Saṅkicca Follows the Thieves

Hearing the words of those monks, Novice Saṅkicca said, "Venerable sirs, please remain as you are. I will sacrifice my life for you and go." The thirty monks said, "Friend novice, even if we were all to be killed together, we could not let you go alone." "Venerable sirs, what is the reason?" "Friend novice, you are the novice of the General of the Dhamma, Elder Sāriputta. If we were to let you go, the Elder would reproach us, saying, 'They took my novice and handed him over to the thieves.' We would not be able to bear that reproach. Therefore, we cannot let you go."

"Venerable sirs, when the Blessed One sent you to my preceptor, and when my preceptor sent me along with you, they did so having seen this very reason. Venerable sirs, please remain as you are; I alone will go." Having said this, Novice Saṅkicca paid homage to the thirty monks and said, "Venerable sirs, if I have committed any fault against you, please forgive me," and then he departed.

## The Sword Bending and Curling

At that time, a great sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arose in the monks. Their eyes were filled with tears, and their hearts trembled. The Great Elder said to the thieves, "Lay followers, this novice is still young. Seeing you lighting the fire, sharpening the spits, and spreading the leaves, he might become frightened. Place this young novice in a suitable spot and then carry out those tasks." The thieves took the novice, placed him in a suitable spot, and performed all the tasks. When the tasks were completed, the leader of the thieves drew his sword from its scabbard and approached the novice. The novice sat down and entered into a meditative absorption (jhāna). The leader of the thieves raised the sword with force and brought it down on the novice's shoulder to cut him. The sword bent and curled, its edge striking its own edge. Thinking, "I did not strike well," the leader of the thieves straightened the sword and struck again. The sword swayed and bent like a palm leaf, reaching down to the hilt.

(At that time, even if one were to crush the novice with Mount Sineru, there was no one capable of killing him; what need is there to speak of a sword?)
431:
## The Robber Chief Throws Down His Sword and Inquires
Upon seeing the novice's miracle, the robber chief thought, "In the past, my sword could cut through stone pillars and heartwood as if they were lotus stalks. Now, it has bent at once like a rolled palm leaf. This sword, though inanimate, recognizes the virtues of this novice. I, though animate, did not." Filled with remorse, the robber chief threw the sword on the ground, prostrated at the novice's feet, and said: "Venerable sir, we entered the forest for the sake of wealth. Even a thousand men tremble when they see us from afar; let alone two or three. But for you, venerable sir, there is not even a trace of fear. Your face shines like gold in a furnace or like a fully blossomed Mahāleghā flower. What is the reason?" Wishing to inquire, he spoke this verse:

"You have no trembling, no fear; your complexion brightens even more. Why do you not lament in the face of such great danger?"

[Word-for-word translation of the verse:]
Te: For you, venerable sir. Tāso: trembling. Natthi: there is not. Bhayaṃ: fear. Natthi: there is not. Bhiyyo: even more. Vaṇṇo: complexion. Pasīdati: is bright. Evarūpe: in such. Mahabbhaye: a time of great danger. Kasmā: why. Na paridevesi: do you not lament?

The novice arose from meditation and, wishing to teach the robber chief, said: "Friend, headman—the physical body of an Arahant is like a burden placed upon the head. Whether that body breaks or perishes, he is only glad and does not fear." He then recited these verses:

"There is no mental pain for one who is without longing, O headman. All fears have been transcended by the sage whose fetters are destroyed.
When the lead to existence is destroyed, and the Dhamma is seen as it truly is, there is no fear of death, just as there is no fear when laying down a burden."

[Word-for-word translation of the verses:]
Gāmaṇi: Friend headman. Isi: the Arahant. Sabbaṃ: all. Bhayaṃ: danger. Atikkanto: has transcended. Khīṇasaṃyojano: has destroyed the fetters. Anapekkhaassa: For the Arahant who has no longing for body or life. Cetasikaṃ: mental. Dukkhaṃ: suffering. Natthi: there is not.
Bhavanettiyā: Because of the destruction of craving, which is like a cord leading to the three realms of existence. Khīṇāya: due to its destruction. Bhāravoropanaṃ yatha: like the laying down of a heavy burden. Diṭṭhadhamme: in this very life. Yathā tathā: as it truly is. Nibbhayaṃ: without fear. Maraṇaṃ: death (attaining Parinibbāna). Hoti: occurs.

## The Five Hundred Robbers Consult Each Other
Hearing the novice's words, the chief looked at the five hundred robbers and asked, "What will you do?" When they asked, "And what will you do, master?" he replied, "Friends, having seen such a miracle, I have no use for the life of a householder. I shall ordain in the presence of this noble one." They said, "We shall do the same." He said, "Very well, dear ones." Then all five hundred robbers bowed to the novice and requested ordination.

## The Robbers Ordain
Saṅkicca Sāmaṇera used the robbers' own swords to cut their hair and the fringes of their garments. He dyed the robes with red earth, had them wear them, and established them in the ten precepts. As he led the new monks away, he thought: "If I go without seeing the elder monks, they will not be able to practice the recluse's Dhamma. Since the time the robbers took me away, not even one of those monks has been able to restrain or stabilize their tears."
432:
"Thinking 'Is the novice killed or not?', they will not be able to focus on their meditation subject. Therefore, I will go only after seeing them." Surrounded by the five hundred monks, he went there. The elders, relieved at seeing him, asked, "Good Saṅkicca, have you regained your life?" He replied, "Yes, venerable sirs. These men wanted to kill me but were unable to. Having gained faith in my virtues and heard the Dhamma, they have ordained. I have come to see you before I go. Please practice the recluse's Dhamma diligently. I shall go to the Teacher." He bowed to those monks and, taking the five hundred new monks, went to his preceptor, the Venerable Sāriputta. When asked, "Saṅkicca, have you gained pupils?" he replied, "Yes, venerable sir," and related the events. Venerable Sāriputta said, "Go, Saṅkicca, and see the Teacher." He bowed and went to the Buddha. The Buddha also asked, "Saṅkicca, have you gained pupils?" He replied, "Yes, Blessed One," and related the events. The Buddha asked the monks, "Is it so, monks?" and they replied, "Yes, Blessed One." The Buddha said, "Monks, rather than living a hundred years as an immoral person committing robbery, even a single day of life established in virtue is better." Connecting the discourse, he spoke this verse:

## The Teaching
(110) Though one should live a hundred years, immoral and uncontrolled, yet better is a single day's life of one who is virtuous and meditative.

[Word-for-word translation:]
Yo ca: And whoever. Dussīlo: being immoral. Asamāhito: being uncontrolled. Vassasataṃ: for a hundred years. Jīve: should live. Tato: than that hundred-year life of an immoral person. Sīlavantassa: of one who is virtuous. Jhāyino: of one who constantly meditates on objects like kasinas or characteristics like impermanence. Ekāhaṃ: for a single day. Vā: or. [even for a moment]. Jīvitaṃ: life. Seyyo: is better.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, all five hundred monks who were formerly robbers attained Arahantship along with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). The teaching was also beneficial to the great multitude gathered there.

## The Firm Truth of Adhimutta Sāmaṇera
At another time, when Saṅkicca had been a monk for ten years, he accepted a novice. (There is a rule established because of Venerable Upasena that one should not accept a novice until one has ten years of standing; if one does, it is an offense of wrong-doing.) That novice was Adhimutta Sāmaṇera, the nephew of Venerable Saṅkicca. When Adhimutta reached the age of twenty, the Elder Saṅkicca called him and said, "I will perform your higher ordination (upasampadā)..."
433:
“Go, ask your relatives about the duration of their lives and return,” he was sent away. While Adhimutta Sāmaṇera was going to his parents, he was captured by five hundred robbers on the way for the purpose of a sacrificial offering. Having preached the Dhamma to those robbers, they became possessed of hearts full of faith and released him (saying, “You must not tell anyone of our presence in this place”). Upon being released, he saw his parents coming from the opposite direction. Although they were heading towards the very path where the robbers were, he did not tell them, wishing to protect the truth he had pledged to the robbers. When the parents were harassed by the robbers, he heard the voices of his parents lamenting, “Our son Adhimutta, you too must have joined with the robbers, for you did not tell us!” When the robbers realized that the novice had not told even his parents, they were moved with faith and requested ordination. Adhimutta Sāmaṇera, like Saṅkicca Sāmaṇera, ordained all of those robbers and brought them to his preceptor. The preceptor, Saṅkicca Mahāthera, sent them to the Buddha, where Adhimutta reported the matter. The Teacher asked, “Monks, is it true as said?” and when they replied, “Yes, Bhante,” he connected the sequence as before and, wishing to preach the Dhamma, spoke this verse:

(The meaning is the same as before.)

The Story of Saṅkicca Sāmaṇera ends.

## 10. The Story of Khāṇu-Koṇḍañña Thera
(Khāṇu-Koṇḍaññatthera Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with “Yo ca vassasataṃ,” concerning Khāṇu-Koṇḍañña Thera.

## Steadfastness like a Tree Stump

That Elder, having taken a subject of meditation from the Teacher and living in the forest, attained Arahantship. Thinking, “I will inform the Teacher,” he set out from the forest. Becoming exhausted on the way, he stepped off the path and sat on a flat rock, entering into a meditative absorption. At that time, five hundred robbers, having plundered a village and tied their loot into bundles according to their strength, were carrying them on their heads. Having traveled a long distance and being exhausted, they thought, “We have come a long way; let us rest on this flat rock.”
434:
Leaving the path and approaching the flat rock, even though they saw the Elder, they perceived him as a tree stump (khāṇu). Then one robber placed his bundle of goods on the Elder's head. Another also placed his bundle leaning against him. In this way, all five hundred robbers surrounded the Elder with five hundred bundles of goods. They themselves sat down and fell asleep. At dawn, they woke up and, while taking their respective bundles, saw the Elder. Thinking he was a non-human spirit, they began to flee.

## The Robbers Ordain

Then the Elder said to the robbers, “Lay followers, do not be afraid. I am a monk.” The robbers prostrated at the Elder's feet and asked for forgiveness, saying, “Venerable Sir, please forgive us; we thought you were a tree stump.” After asking for forgiveness, the leader of the robbers said, “I will ordain under the Venerable One.” The remaining robbers, being of one mind, said, “We too will ordain,” and requested ordination from the Elder. The Elder, like Saṅkicca Sāmaṇera, ordained all of them. From then on, he became known as Khāṇu-Koṇḍañña. He went to the Teacher with those monks. When the Teacher asked, “Koṇḍañña, have you obtained disciples (antevāsika)?” he reported the matter. The Teacher asked, “Monks, is it true as reported?” and they replied, “Yes, Bhante. We have never before seen such power in another person; therefore, we have ordained.” The Teacher said, “Monks, rather than living a hundred years established in the actions of those with little wisdom, a single day of life for you who are now endowed with wisdom is better.” Connecting the sequence and wishing to preach the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

## The Teaching

(111) Though one should live a hundred years, unwise and uncontrolled,
Yet better is a single day's life of one who is wise and meditative.

(Yo ca: and whoever. Duppañño: being without wisdom. Asamāhito: being without concentration. Vassasataṃ: for a hundred years. Jīve: should live. Tato: than that hundred-year life of the unwise. Paññavantassa: of one who has wisdom. Jhāyino: of one who constantly contemplates an object such as a kasina or a characteristic such as impermanence. Ekāhaṃ: for even a single day, or even a single moment. Jīvitaṃ: living. Seyyo: is better.)

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, all five hundred monks attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial to the great multitude of people who had gathered.

The Story of Khāṇu-Koṇḍañña Thera ends.

## 11. The Story of Sappadāsa Thera
(Sappadāsatthera Vatthu)

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with “Yo ca vassasataṃ,” concerning the Elder Sappadāsa.
435:
## The Monk Whom the Poisonous Snake Did Not Bite

In Sāvatthī, a certain young man of good family, having heard the Dhamma taught by the Teacher, went forth and received higher ordination. Later, becoming dissatisfied, he thought, "For a young man of good family like me, the state of a householder is not suitable. It is better for me to die while remaining in the monkhood." Thinking thus, he wandered about seeking a means of death. Then one day, early in the morning, after finishing their meal, some monks went to the monastery and saw a snake in the fire-hall. They put it in a pot, covered it, and left the monastery. The dissatisfied monk, having also finished his meal, saw those monks and asked, "Friends, what is this?" When they replied, "Friend, it is a snake," he asked again, "What will you do with this snake?" They replied, "We will release it."

Hearing their words, he thought, "I will let this snake bite me and die." He said, "Please bring it; I will discard it." Taking the pot from their hands, he sat in a certain place and tried to make the snake bite him. The snake did not wish to bite. He lowered his hand into the pot and stirred it here and there. He even opened the mouth of the fierce, poisonous snake and inserted his finger. Yet, the snake did not bite him. He thought, "This is not a venomous snake; it is a house snake," and discarding it, he returned to the monastery. Then the monks asked him, "Friend, did you discard the snake?" He replied, "Friends, that was not a poisonous or fierce snake; it was a house snake." They said, "Friend, it was indeed a poisonous and fierce snake. It hissed loudly with its hood expanded. We caught it with great difficulty. Why do you speak thus?" He replied, "Friends, although I tried to make it bite my finger and even inserted my finger into its mouth, I could not get it to bite." Hearing this, the monks remained silent.

## Attaining Arahantship

Then one day, a barber came to the monastery with two or three razors. He placed one on the ground and shaved the monks' hair with another. That monk took the razor placed on the ground, thinking, "I will slit my throat with this razor and die." He leaned his neck against a tree, placed the blade of the razor against his windpipe, and while standing there, he reflected on his virtue from the time of his higher ordination. He saw his virtue to be stainless, like the disc of the full moon or a well-polished gem. As he contemplated that virtue, pervasive rapture (pharaṇā-pīti) arose, spreading throughout his entire body. Suppressing that rapture and developing insight, he attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Then, taking the razor, he returned to the center of the monastery.

Then the monks asked him, "Friend, where did you go?" He replied, "Friends, I went to slit my windpipe with this razor and die." They asked, "Since that was the case, why did you not die?"
436:
When he said, “Now I am one who is no longer fit to carry a weapon. Although I intended to cut my throat with this razor, I have cut away all defilements with the razor of knowledge,” the monks reported to the Blessed One, “This monk is falsely claiming the fruit of Arahantship.”

## How He Came to be Named Sappadāsa
Hearing their words, the Buddha said, “Monks, those who are Arahants do not take their own lives with their own hands.” “Venerable Sir, you speak of this monk as an Arahant. If he is thus endowed with the supporting condition for Arahantship, why was he so weary and dissatisfied? What was the cause of his supporting condition for Arahantship? And why did that snake not bite him, Venerable Sir?” When they asked this, the Buddha explained the reason concerning the monk and the snake: “Monks, in this monk's third previous existence, that snake was his slave. That snake did not dare to bite the body of its own master.” From that time on, that monk became known by the name Sappadāsa (the monk who has a snake as a slave).

## The Cause in the Past
It is said that in the time of Kassapa Buddha, a certain young man of good family, having heard the Dhamma from the Teacher, was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and went forth. Having received higher ordination, at another time, when dissatisfaction (anabhirati) arose, he told a companion monk. That companion monk repeatedly spoke of the disadvantages of the lay life. Hearing this, the monk who had been dissatisfied in the Dispensation became very delighted in the Dispensation. While he was previously dissatisfied, he sat by the shore of a pond to clean his monastic requisites which had become dirty. His companion monk also sat near him. Then, the monk who was cleaning his requisites said to his companion, “Friend, when I was about to leave the monkhood, I intended to give these requisites to you.”

That companion monk, giving rise to greed, thought, “What benefit is it to me whether he remains a monk or leaves the monkhood? Now I will take these requisites.” From that day on, he spoke of the virtues of the lay life, saying, “Friend, what is the use of our lives now? We wander for alms at the houses of others with bowls in our hands, and we cannot converse with a wife and children,” and so on. Hearing the words of his companion monk, the monk again became weary and dissatisfied. He thought, “When I said ‘I am dissatisfied,’ this monk first spoke of the disadvantages of the lay life, but now he repeatedly speaks of its virtues. What could be the reason?” Realizing, “It is because of greed for these monastic requisites,” he himself turned his mind back. Thus, because he had encouraged another monk to leave the monkhood in the time of Kassapa Buddha, dissatisfaction arose in him now.

## The Good Deed for Becoming an Arahant
That same monk had fulfilled the duties of a monk for twenty thousand years at that time. That practice of Dhamma has now become the supporting condition for the fruit of Arahantship. Having heard this from the Blessed One, the monks asked further, “Exalted Buddha, it is said that this monk attained Arahantship while standing with the blade of a razor against his throat. Can the Path of Arahantship arise in such a short moment, Venerable Sir?”
437:
“Yes, monks, for a monk who has aroused effort, the Path of Arahantship can arise even before his foot reaches the ground as he lifts it to step. For a person who is lazy, even a hundred years of life is not as good as a single moment of life for one who has aroused effort.” Having said this, and connecting the sequence, he spoke this verse to teach the Dhamma:

## The Teaching
(112) Though one should live a hundred years,
Lazy and of little effort,
Better is a single day of life
For one who makes a firm effort.

**Yo ca**, and whoever. **Kusīto**, is lazy. **Hīnavīriyo**, has weak effort. **Hutvā**, being so. **Vassasataṃ**, for a hundred years. **Jīve**, should live. **Tato**, than that hundred-year life of a lazy person. **Vīriyaṃ**, effort. **Daḷhaṃ**, firmly. **Ārabhato**, for one who arouses. **Ekāhaṃ**, even a single day. Or, even a single moment. **Jīvitaṃ**, life. **Seyyo**, is better.

## The Benefit of the Teaching
At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.
The Story of Elder Sappadāsa ends.

## 12. The Story of Elder Nun Paṭācārā
(The Story of Paṭācārā Therī)
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching beginning with “Yo ca vassasataṃ” concerning the elder nun named Paṭācārā.

## The Beginning of the Lives of Paṭācārā and the Slave
That elder nun Paṭācārā was the daughter of a wealthy merchant in Sāvatthī who possessed forty crores of wealth, and she was extremely beautiful. When she reached the age of sixteen, they kept her under guard on the top floor of a seven-storied palace. Despite being kept thus, she committed misconduct with one of her young servants. Later, the girl's mother and father promised her to a young man of equal social status and set a date for the wedding. As that day approached, the merchant's daughter said to the young servant, “They will certainly give me to such-and-such a young man. If I go to my husband's house, even if you come bringing a gift for me, you will not be allowed to enter. If you truly have love for me, take me away right now and flee to some place or other.”
438:
## Disguising and Following the Servant
The young servant replied, "Very well, my lady." She said, "In that case, I will be at such-and-such a place at the city gate early tomorrow morning. You must find a way to get out and meet me there." Having said this, he waited at the appointed place on the second day. The treasurer's daughter also left the house early in the morning, wearing dirty clothes, with her hair disheveled, her body smeared with bran dust, and carrying a water pot on her head as if she were going out with the maidservants, and arrived at that place. The young servant took her and went to a distant place, making his dwelling in a village. After plowing a field in the forest, he would bring back firewood, leaves, and other things. As for her, she brought water in a pot and performed tasks such as pounding rice and cooking with her own hands, thus experiencing the results of her own evil deeds.

## Giving Birth on the Road
Subsequently, she conceived a child in her womb. When her pregnancy was full-term, she pleaded with her husband, "I have no one here to help me. Parents are known to have tender hearts toward their children. Please take me to them; my delivery will take place at their home." That servant-husband refused, saying, "My dear, what are you saying? If your parents see me, they will subject me to various forms of punishment. I cannot go there." Although she pleaded repeatedly, she did not gain permission to go. So, while the man was away in the forest, she informed the neighbors, saying, "If he comes and asks where I have gone when he does not see me, please tell him that I have gone to my family home." Then, she closed the door of the house and departed. When the husband returned and did not see her, he asked the neighbors and, upon hearing the news, followed her, thinking, "I will bring her back." When he found her, he pleaded in various ways, but could not make her return. Then, at a certain place, the winds of labor (kammaja-vātā) began to move within her. She entered a thicket and said, "My dear, the winds of labor have moved within me." She lay down on the ground, tossing and turning, and after much suffering, gave birth to a son. Thinking, "The purpose for which I was going to my family home has been fulfilled," she returned home with her husband and continued to live there.

Later, she conceived again. When she was full-term, she pleaded with her husband as before, but not gaining permission to go, she took her son on her hip and departed in the same manner. When her husband followed and said, "Please stop," she did not wish to return. Then, as they were traveling, a great unseasonable storm arose. The sky became filled with continuous torrents of water, as if ablaze with lightning all around and as if breaking apart with the sound of thunder.
439:
At that moment, the winds of labor moved within her. She called to her husband and said, "My dear, the winds of labor have moved within me. I cannot bear it. Please find a place for me that is sheltered from the rain." 

## The Servant's Death by Snakebite
The servant-husband, searching here and there with an axe in his hand, saw a bush growing on top of an anthill and began to cut it. At that moment, a fierce and deadly venomous snake emerged from the anthill and bit him. Instantly, his body turned blue as if being burned by internal flames, and he fell dead on that very spot. The woman, experiencing great suffering and looking for her husband's arrival, did not see him and gave birth to another son. The two children, unable to endure the force of the wind and rain, cried out with loud wails. She placed both children between her breasts and, pressing herself to the ground with her knees and hands, remained in that position throughout the night. Her entire body became bloodless and pale, like the color of a withered leaf. When the sun rose, she took one son, who was the color of a piece of flesh, on her hip and led the other by the finger, saying, "Come, dear, your father went this way." Following the path her husband had taken, she saw his blue, stiffened corpse lying on the anthill and lamented repeatedly, crying, "Because of me, my husband has died on the road!" and continued her journey.

## The Infant Taken by a Hawk and the Elder Son Swept Away
Because it had rained heavily all night, she saw the Aciravatī River full of water, reaching the depth of knees, waist, and even breasts. Due to her distraught state of mind, she did not dare to enter the water with both children. She left the elder son on the near bank, took the newborn, and crossed to the other side. She laid the infant on a bed of broken branches and, thinking, "I will go back for the other one," she left the infant. Unable to cross easily, she kept turning back to look as she went. When she reached the middle of the river, a hawk saw the infant and, thinking it was a piece of meat, swooped down from the sky. Seeing the hawk swooping for her son, she raised both hands and shouted loudly three times, "Shoo! Shoo!" (Su! Su!). Because of the distance, the hawk did not hear her, picked up the infant, and flew into the sky. The elder son, standing on the near bank, saw his mother in the middle of the river raising both hands and shouting loudly. Thinking, "She is calling me," he quickly entered the water and was swept away by the current.
440:
In this manner, a hawk carried away the merchant's daughter's younger son. The elder son was swept away by the water.

## Death of Parents and Brother in a House Collapse

As that merchant's daughter went along weeping and lamenting, saying, "One of my sons has been carried off by a hawk, one son has been swept away by the water, and my husband has died on the road," she saw a man coming from Sāvatthī and asked, "Dear man, where do you live?"

"Mother, I live in Sāvatthī," he replied.

"Dear man, in Sāvatthī, on such-and-such a street, there is a family of such-and-such a name. Do you know them?" she asked again.

"Mother, I know them. But do not ask about that family. If you know of anyone else, ask about them instead," he said.

"Dear man, I have no business asking about others. I only wish to ask about that merchant's family," she said.

"Mother, you do not allow me to remain silent. Did you see the rain falling all through the night today?" he asked. 

"Dear man, I saw it. Indeed, that rain fell all night long for me alone, and for no one else. I will tell you the reason for that rain falling on me later. First, please tell me what happened at the house of that merchant's family."

"Mother, this night, the rain accompanied by wind struck and collapsed the house upon the merchant, the merchant's wife, and the merchant's son—all three of them. They are being cremated on a single funeral pyre. Mother, the smoke from that cremation of the three together is still visible."

At that moment, the merchant's daughter did not even notice her garment falling off. Reaching a state of madness, she went about naked, weeping and lamenting:

"Both my sons have passed away, and my husband is dead on the road.
My mother, father, and brother are burning on a single pyre."

My: *mayhaṃ*. Both my sons: *ubho puttā*. Have passed away: *kālaṅkatā*. My dear husband: *pati*. On the road: *panthe*. Is dead: *mato*.
My mother: *mātā ca*. My father: *pitā ca*. My brother: *bhātā ca*. On a single funeral pyre: *ekacitakasmim*. Are being cremated: *ḍayhare*.

Thus, she wandered about in a daze, driven mad by her grief. When people saw the mad merchant's daughter, they called out, "Madwoman! Madwoman!" and some took rubbish and dust and threw it on her head, while others struck her with clods of earth.

## Aspiration from the Past

While the All-Knowing Buddha, the Teacher of the Three Worlds, was seated in the midst of the eightfold assembly at the Great Jetavana Monastery preaching the Dhamma, He saw the merchant's daughter approaching—one who had fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for a hundred thousand aeons and was endowed with a noble aspiration.

It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she saw the Teacher Padumuttara take a certain nun who was a master of the Vinaya by the arm and, as if placing her in the Nandana Grove, appoint her to the foremost position (etadagga). Seeing this, she performed a great act of merit and made an aspiration, saying, "May I also receive the foremost position among the nuns who are masters of the Vinaya in the presence of a Buddha like You."

## Arriving in the Presence of the Buddha

Padumuttara Buddha, extending His knowledge of the future and knowing that her aspiration would be fulfilled, gave the prophecy: "In the future, in the dispensation of the Buddha named Gotama, this laywoman will become the foremost disciple among the nuns who are masters of the Vinaya, under the name Patācārā."

When the Blessed One saw the merchant's daughter, who was endowed with such meritorious aspirations, coming from afar, He thought, "Except for Me, there is no one else who can be a refuge for this merchant's daughter."
441:
The Buddha gave the prophecy: "She will be the foremost." Seeing her approaching from afar, she who had made such an aspiration and was endowed with noble resolve, the Teacher thought, "Except for Me, there is no one else capable of being her support," and He caused her to come directly towards the monastery.

As soon as the assembly saw her, they said, "Do not let this madwoman come here to where the Buddha is."

The Blessed One said, "Move aside; do not hinder her." When she had come to a place not far away, He said, "Sister, regain your mindfulness."

At that very moment, through the power of the Buddha, she regained her mindfulness. Then, noticing that her garment had fallen off, she felt shame and dread (hiri-ottappa) and sat down in a crouching position.

## Reporting the Full Account of Events

Then a man threw her an upper garment. She put on that garment, approached the Blessed One, and paid homage with the fivefold prostration at His feet, which were the color of gold, saying, "Venerable Sir, be my support; be my refuge. A hawk has carried off one of my sons. One son was swept away by the water. My husband died on the road. My parents and my brother were crushed by their house and are being cremated on a single funeral pyre."

## Such Events Have Occurred Before in Saṃsāra

Upon hearing the words of the merchant's daughter, the Blessed One said, "Patācārā, do not grieve. You have come into the presence of one who is truly capable of being your protection, your refuge, and your support." He continued, "Just as your son was carried off by a hawk, one son was swept away by water, your husband died on the road, and your parents and brother were crushed by their house, even so, in this Saṃsāra, the tears you have shed while weeping at the death of sons and others are far more than the water in the four great oceans." He then spoke this verse:

"The water in the four oceans is but a little,
Compared to the many tears shed, which are not few,
By a person afflicted by suffering and grief.
Why, O daughter, do you remain negligent?"

Dear daughter Patācārā: *paṭācāre*. In the four oceans: *catūsu samuddesu*. The water: *jalaṃ*. Is but a little: *parittakaṃ*. By a being: *narassa*. Afflicted: *phuṭṭhassa*. By suffering and hardship: *dukkhena*. The tears: *assujalaṃ*. Born of grief: *socanā*. Are more: *bahum*. Than the water of those four oceans: *tato*. They are not few: *anappakaṃ*. Dear daughter Patācārā: *amma*. You: *tuvaṃ*. For what reason: *kiṃkāraṇā*. Are you negligent: *pamajjasi*?

## Preaching the Anamatagga Sutta

Thus, as the Blessed One preached the discourse on the incalculable beginning of Saṃsāra (Anamatagga Sutta), the grief in Patācārā's body became thin. Then, knowing that her grief had diminished, the Blessed One addressed her again, saying, "Patācārā, for one who is going to the next world, children and others cannot be a protection, a shelter, or a refuge. Therefore, even if they exist, such children and others are as if they do not exist. A wise person should purify their virtue and should quickly clear the path leading to Nibbāna." Desiring to preach the Dhamma, He spoke these verses:
442:
