Sons are no protection, nor father, nor kinsmen; for one overcome by the Ender (Death), there is no protection among kin.

Realizing this fact, the wise man, restrained by virtue, should quickly clear the path leading to Nibbāna.

For one overcome by the Ender, sons are not for protection, nor is a father, nor are kinsmen. There is no protection among relatives.

Knowing this reason, knowing this purpose, the wise man, restrained by virtue, should quickly clear the path leading to Nibbāna.

## Attaining the Fruit of Stream-entry

At the end of the teaching, Patācārā, burning away defilements as numerous as the dust on the earth, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Many others also attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

## Becoming a Bhikkhunī and Taking Water as an Object of Meditation

After becoming a Stream-enterer, Patācārā requested the Buddha for ordination. The Buddha sent her to the presence of the bhikkhunīs and had her ordained. Once she attained the higher ordination, she became known as Patācārā because of her prominent conduct. One day, while taking water with a pot and washing her feet, the water she poured flowed a short distance and stopped. On the second pouring, the water flowed further than before. On the third pouring, the water flowed even further than that. In this manner, the bhikkhunī Patācārā took that very water as her object of meditation and, analyzing the three stages of life, reflected: “Just like the water I poured first, these beings die in the first stage of life. Like the water poured the second time which flowed further, they also die in the middle stage of life. Like the water poured the third time which flowed furthest, they die in the last stage of life as well.”

While the Buddha was staying in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), he radiated his light and appeared as if standing before the bhikkhunī Patācārā to preach, saying: “Dear daughter Patācārā, it is just as you have reflected. Rather than living a hundred years without seeing the rise and fall of the five aggregates, the life of one day or even a single moment of one who sees their rise and fall is more noble.” Connecting the sequence, he spoke this verse to teach the Dhamma:

## The Teaching

(113) Though one should live a hundred years, not seeing the rise and fall (of the five aggregates), yet better is the life of a single day for one who sees the rise and fall.

Though one should live for a hundred years without seeing the arising and passing away of the five aggregates, the life of a single day, or even a single moment, of one who sees the arising and passing away of the five aggregates is more noble than that hundred-year life of one who does not know the rise and fall.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the conclusion of the teaching, the bhikkhunī Patācārā attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā).

The story of Patācārā Therī ends.
443:
## 13. The Story of Kisāgotamī Therī

(Kisāgotamī Vatthu)

The Buddha, while staying at the Jetavana Monastery, gave this Dhamma teaching beginning with “Yo ca vassasataṃ,” concerning the Elder Kisāgotamī.

## The Merit of the Maiden who Turned Charcoal into Gold and Silver

In the city of Sāvatthī, in the house of a certain treasurer, forty crores of wealth turned into mere charcoal and remained so. When the great treasurer saw that charcoal, he was overcome with great grief, refused food, and lay down on his bed. A friend of that treasurer came to the house and asked, “Friend, why do you grieve?” Upon hearing the reason, he said, “Friend, do not grieve. I know a way. Do this.” When asked, “Friend, what should I do?”, he replied, “Spread a mat in your shop in the market, make a pile of that charcoal on the mat, and sit there as if selling it. Among the people who come and go, some will say, ‘Other merchants sell cloth, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth. But you sit here selling charcoal.’ To those people, you should say, ‘What else can I do if I do not sell my own property?’ But if someone says to you, ‘Other merchants sell cloth, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth, but you sit here selling gold and silver,’ you should ask that person, ‘Where is the gold and silver?’ If they say, ‘This is the wealth,’ you should say, ‘Then bring that gold and silver,’ and receive it with your hands. When given in this way, it will become gold and silver in your hands.”

“If that person is a maiden, you should bring her to your house for your son, entrust the forty crores of wealth to her, and use only what she gives you. If that person is a youth, you should give him your daughter who has reached marriageable age, entrust the forty crores of wealth to him, and use only what he gives you.” The treasurer, pleased with the idea, said, “That is a good way,” and sat in his shop as if selling a pile of charcoal. Some people said to the great treasurer, “Other merchants sell cloth, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth. Why is it that you sit here selling charcoal?” He replied to them, “What else can I do if I do not sell my own property?” Then, a maiden named Kisāgotamī—so known because of her lean body—who was the daughter of a ruined merchant family, came to the market entrance for some business of her own. Seeing the great treasurer, she said, “Father treasurer, how is this? Other merchants sell cloth, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth, but you, father, sit here selling gold and silver.” When he asked, “Dear daughter, where is the gold and silver?”, she replied, “Is the great lord treasurer not holding that very gold and silver?” He said, “Dear daughter, then bring that gold and silver; give it to me.” Kisāgotamī took a handful and placed it in the treasurer's hands. That wealth became only gold and silver.
444:
## Madness due to the Death of a Son

Then, the wealthy merchant asked Kisāgotamī, "Dear daughter, which is your house?" When she replied, "It is such-and-such a house," he realized that she was without a husband. He then gathered his wealth and brought Kisāgotamī for his son, making her the mistress of forty crores of wealth. All of that wealth consisted only of silver and gold. Later, Kisāgotamī conceived a child. After ten months, she gave birth to a son.

When the young son was old enough to walk, he passed away. Because Kisāgotamī had never seen death before, she prevented those who were taking the dead son to be cremated, saying, "I will first ask for medicine for my son." Carrying the dead body in her arms, she went from house to house, asking, "Do you know of any medicine for my son?" Then people said to her, "Mother, you have gone mad; you are wandering around asking for medicine for a dead son."

## Searching for a Physician to Cure the Dead Son

Kisāgotamī, however, thought, "I will surely find a physician who knows the medicine for my son," and continued to wander. Then, a wise man saw her and thought, "This daughter of mine must have given birth to her first-born son and has never seen death before. It is proper that I should be a refuge for her." He said, "Dear daughter, I do not know the medicine, but I know a good physician who does." When she asked, "Father, who knows it?", he replied, "My daughter, the Omniscient Buddha knows. Go and ask him." Kisāgotamī said, "I will go, father; I will ask, father." She approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and standing in a suitable place, asked, "Venerable Sir, is it true that you know the medicine for my son?" "Yes, I know," he replied. "What is required to obtain it, Lord?" she asked.

"It is proper to obtain a pinch of mustard seeds," he said. "I will get them, Lord," she replied. "But from whose house should they be obtained?" she asked. "They should be obtained from a house where no son, daughter, or anyone has ever died before," he replied. Kisāgotamī said, "Very well, Lord." She paid homage to the Buddha, took the dead son in her arms, entered the village, and standing at the door of the first house, asked, "Are there any mustard seeds in this house?"
445:
Taṃ puttapasusammattaṃ, byāsattamanasaṃ naraṃ.
Suttaṃ gāmaṃ mahoghovā, maccu ādāya gacchati.

Just as a great flood sweeps away a sleeping village, so death seizes and carries away the person who is intoxicated with children and cattle, and whose mind is deeply attached to various things.

## The Teaching

(114) Yo ca vassasataṃ jīve, apassaṃ amataṃ padaṃ.
Ekāhaṃ jīvitaṃ seyyo, passato amataṃ padaṃ.

Though one should live a hundred years without seeing the Deathless State (Nibbāna), yet better is the life of a single day—or even a single moment—of one who sees the Deathless State.

"They are said to be medicine for my son," she said. When they said, "There are," she said, "Then please give them to me." When they brought and gave her the mustard seeds, she asked again, "Mother, has no son or daughter ever died in this house?" They replied, "Dear daughter, what are you saying? The living are but few; the dead are many." She said, "If that is so, take back your mustard seeds; this is not medicine for my son," and she returned them.

## Finding the Dhamma while Searching for Mustard Seeds

In this manner, Kisāgotamī went about asking from the beginning. Without taking mustard seeds from even a single house, she thought in the evening, "This is a very heavy task. I thought only my son was dead, but in the entire village, the dead are far more numerous than the living." As she thought thus, her soft heart, which was filled with love for her son, became firm. She abandoned the dead son in the forest, went to the Blessed One, paid homage, and stood in a suitable place. Then the Blessed One asked her, "Did you obtain the pinch of mustard seeds?" "I did not, Lord. In the whole village, the dead are far more numerous than the living," she replied. Then the Blessed One said to her, "You thought only your son was dead, but this death is the fixed nature of all beings. King Death, like a great flood, drags away all beings before their desires are fulfilled and casts them into the ocean of the four woeful states (apāya)." Desiring to preach the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

## Becoming a Sotāpanna

At the end of the verse, Kisāgotamī was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). Many others also attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

## Ordaining as a Bhikkhunī and Meditating on the Flame

Then Kisāgotamī requested the Buddha for ordination. The Blessed One sent her to the bhikkhunīs and had her ordained. After receiving higher ordination, she became known as Kisāgotamī Therī. One day, when it was her turn to perform duties in the Uposatha hall, she sat lighting a lamp. Seeing the flames of the lamp flickering out and arising, she took it as an object of meditation: "Just like these flames, beings arise and cease; only those who have reached Nibbāna are no longer seen." The Blessed One, while sitting in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī), sent forth his radiance and appeared as if sitting before her, saying, "Dear daughter Gotamī, just as you have reflected, these beings arise and cease like the flames of a lamp; only those who have reached Nibbāna are no longer seen. Better than the life of a hundred years of those who do not see Nibbāna is the life of even a single moment of one who sees Nibbāna." Connecting the sequence of the discourse, he spoke this verse:

114.
"Yo ca vassasataṃ jīve, apassaṃ amataṃ padaṃ,
Ekāhaṃ jīvitaṃ seyyo, passato amataṃ padaṃ."

In that verse, 'amataṃ padaṃ' means the state free from death, which is the Great Immortal Nibbāna. The rest is the same as before.
446:
## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the teaching, Kisāgotamī Therī, while remaining in her seat, was established in Arahantship along with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā).

The story of Kisāgotamī Therī ends.

## 14. The Story of Bahuputtikā Therī

(Bahuputtikattherī Vatthu)

While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching, beginning with "Yo ca vassasataṃ," regarding Bahuputtikā Therī.

## Dividing the Inheritance among the Children

In Sāvatthī, it is said that in a certain family, there were seven sons and seven daughters. When all those children reached adulthood, they established their own households and became prosperous in their own right. Later, their father passed away. Even after her husband's death, the great laywoman (mahā-upāsikā) did not yet divide the family wealth. Then the children said to her, "Mother, since our father is dead, what use is the wealth to you? Are we not able to support you?"

Hearing the words of her children, the mother remained silent, but when they asked her repeatedly, she thought, "My children will look after me; what use is it for me to keep wealth separately?" and she divided all the property among them. After a few days, the wife of the eldest son said, "Oh, our mother-in-law is truly amazing; as if she had given two shares to her eldest son, she comes only to our house." The wives of the other six sons said the same. Even when she went to the houses of her daughters, starting with the eldest, they spoke to the elderly mother in the same manner.

## Becoming a Bhikkhunī

Having been treated with contempt, the great laywoman thought, "What is the use of living with these children? I will live as a nun." After making this decision, she went to the nunnery and requested ordination. The nuns ordained her. Having received higher ordination, she became known as Bahuputtikā Therī. She thought, "I have ordained in my old age; I must be diligent." While performing the major and minor duties for the bhikkhunīs, she thought, "I will practice the ascetic Dhamma (samaṇadhamma) all night."

On the ground floor, she held a pillar with her hand and practiced the ascetic Dhamma while pulling herself around it. Even while walking in meditation, thinking, "In the dark, my head might hit a tree or a bedstead...
447:
...in some place," she held a tree with her hand and practiced the ascetic Dhamma while pulling herself around it. Thinking, "I will follow only the Dhamma taught by the Teacher," she reflected on the Dhamma and practiced while repeatedly recollecting it.

The Teacher, while staying in the Gandhakuṭī, sent forth his radiance as if sitting right in front of her, and speaking with the Therī, said, "Bahuputtikā, rather than living a hundred years without reflecting on and seeing the Dhamma I have taught, living even for a moment seeing the Dhamma I have taught is better." Connecting the sequence of the discourse, he spoke this verse:

## The Teaching

(115) Yo ca vassasataṃ jīve, apassaṃ dhammamuttamaṃ.
Ekāhaṃ jīvitaṃ seyyo, passato dhammamuttamaṃ.

Whoever lives for a hundred years without seeing the noble ninefold supramundane Dhamma; better than the hundred-year life of that person who does not see the supramundane Dhamma is the life of one who sees the noble supramundane Dhamma for even a single day, or even for a single moment.

## The Benefit of the Teaching

At the end of the verse, Bahuputtikā Therī was established in the fruit of Arahantship along with the four analytical insights.

The story of Bahuputtikā Therī ends.

The Sahassa Vagga (Chapter of Thousands) ends.
